# Preface

The first part of the *Brihat Samhita* <note>The "Great Compilation," a 6th-century encyclopedic work by Varahamihira</note>, edited by the venerable Dr. Krishnachandra Dwivedi, was presented by the University last year in the month of Chaitra <note>March/April</note> for the service of astronomers and lovers of Sanskrit literature. In that same series, it is a matter of good fortune that the second part of this book, edited by the eminent scholar Shri Dwivedi, is now being published and offered to Sanskrit scholars. With the publication of this part, the work reaches its completion.

In ancient times, there were various methods of composing texts—such as *Sutra* <note>aphorisms</note>, *Bhashya* <note>commentary</note>, *Vritti* <note>gloss</note>, *Vivriti* <note>exposition</note>, *Varttika* <note>critical notes</note>, *Churnika* <note>prose commentary</note>, *Vyakhyana* <note>explanation</note>, and *Tika* <note>sub-commentary</note>. Among these, the *Samhita* <note>compilation</note> style was also prominent. A *Samhita* means a detailed description of many subjects gathered together in one place. As the etymology of the word *Samhita* states: *Sam* (properly) + *Dha* (from the root meaning to hold or place), resulting in the term 'Samhita' in the feminine form. Because of this, works such as the Rigveda Samhita, Yajurveda Samhita, Samaveda Samhita, Atharvaveda Samhita, Jaya Samhita <note>an early name for the Mahabharata</note>, Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Garga Samhita, and others come to mind. The defining characteristic of *Samhita* texts was that, along with the primary subject, a vast number of secondary subjects were included in one place. In the Vedic Samhitas, one sees diverse materials concerning spirituality, divinity, physical nature, history, geography, and astronomy. Regarding the Mahabharata, this famous saying is well-known:

->'Whatever is found here may be found elsewhere; what is not here is found nowhere else.'<-

The *Charaka Samhita* and *Sushruta Samhita* are strictly sciences of medicine <note>Ayurveda</note>; yet, in them, many subjects such as the individual soul, the Supreme Soul, the living being and God, auspicious and inauspicious actions, merit and sin, worldly and otherworldly happiness and sorrow, and the creation and dissolution of the universe are also woven together.

In this tradition of *Samhita* composition, we present this work, the *Brihat Samhita*, composed by Shri Varahamihira along with the *Vivriti* <note>exposition</note> composed by the illustrious Bhattotpala. Although this is a primary text of the science of astronomy/astrology <note>Jyotisha</note>, like a geographical encyclopedia, a vast variety of spiritual, historical, geographical, mythological, and religious subjects are also observed here. To provide just a small direction:

->Kapila spoke of Primordial Nature <note>Prakriti</note>, while Kanabhuk <note>Kanada</note> spoke of substances as the cause of this universe.<-
->Some called Time the cause, others Nature, and others Action. (1.7)<-

->Here, the cause of creation is viewed through the lens of philosophy.<-

->The immortals said to Brahma: "O Lord, we are not able to fight the demons in battle."<-
->"Therefore, we have come to you, the refuge of those seeking shelter." (42.1)<-
->The Lord Kesava <note>Vishnu</note> in the Ocean of Milk said to the gods: "The banner which He will give to you—"<-
->"Upon seeing that, the demons will not stand before you in battle." (Ibid.)<-

->Here, history and mythology are presented.<-

<note>original: "वृहत्संहिता" - Brihat Samhita</note>

# Page 2

‘Those situated in the western half of the Shona, Narmada, and Bhimarathi rivers.’ (16.9) <note>original: "शोणस्य नर्मदाया भीमरथ्याश्च पश्चिमादर्द्धस्थाः"</note>

In such passages, the content is **geographical**.

> ‘May all the gods who desire worship here arrive.’ (47.20) and so on.
> ‘The priest should offer oblations into the fire at the primary site.’ (47.77) and so on.

Here, the content concerns **religious rites**.

‘The Shakyas, Yavanas <note>Greeks or foreigners from the West</note>, Magadhas, Shabaras, Pragjyotishas, Chinese, and Kambojas.’ (16.1) and so on.

Here, **various nations** are mentioned. Similarly, there is the chapter on the "Praise of Women," where those who revile women are themselves rebuked:

> Oh, the audacity of the wicked who slander faultless women!
> It is like thieves who, while stealing, shout at the victim, "Stop, thief!" (Chapter on the Praise of Women, Verse 15)

Here is the **praise of women**. Likewise, it describes who the religious practitioners were at that time and whom they worshipped:

> One should know the *Bhagavatas* as worshippers of Vishnu, the *Magas* of the Sun, the ash-covered Brahmins of Shiva, those who know the sequence of the circle <note>Mandalas</note> of the Mother Goddesses, and the Brahmins of Brahma. One should know the *Shakyas* <note>Buddhist monks</note> as worshippers of the All-Beneficent, Peaceful-Minded one [Buddha], and the naked ones <note>Digambara monks</note> as worshippers of the Jinas. Whosoever has taken refuge in a particular deity should have their rituals performed by the practitioners of that specific tradition according to their own rules. (59.19)

Similarly, there is the occasional use of **Arabic words** <note>original: "अरबीकशब्दानामपि"</note> other than Sanskrit.

Thus, because of the inclusion of various, wonderful, and extraordinary topics—such as practical astrology, <term>Ayurveda</term> <note>traditional Indian medicine</note>, omens, portents, pacification rites, nourishment, <term>Vrikshayurveda</term> <note>the science of plant life</note>, religious, spiritual, geographical, and historical matters—this *Great Compilation* <note>Brihat Samhita</note> is truly a "Great Compilation." It is a highly useful work, the "anointed crown" of Sanskrit literature. I feel great joy in presenting this book, consisting of the second part up to the concluding chapter, into the lotus-hands of the learned.

It is a characteristic of Sanskrit literature that one science is entirely interconnected with another. **Astrology** <note>Jyotisha</note>, however, is the guide for all sciences. Religious festivals, from the perspective of the Law Books <note>Dharmashastra</note>, require the direction of astrology. Our science of medicine <note>Ayurveda</note> considers the determination of the auspicious moment <note>Muhurta</note> through astrology to be essential above all else in contexts such as beginning treatment, collecting herbs, and preparing medicines or elixirs. Likewise, for distinguished astrologers, there is an indispensable importance in the various principles of philosophy and the deep scholarship of the Law Books. In this *Brihat Samhita*, a clear picture of such diverse knowledge and science can be observed.

It is a matter of great joy that this **University** is richly endowed with a tradition of such scholars. As a symbol of that tradition, the former Heads of the Department of Astrology of this University—

# Auspicious Invocation

I bow to Ganesha, the first among gods to be worshiped, the son of the Mountain-Daughter <note>Parvati</note>, the Lord of Obstacles, the granter of success, the embodiment of auspiciousness, the giver of happiness, and the elephant-faced one; may he eternally spread peace. (1)

I bow to Annapurna, the mother of the world, beloved of Shiva, saluted by all people, the goddess of good fortune, the sole embodiment of compassion, the sovereign of Kashi <note>Varanasi</note>, and the granter of perfection. (2)

I bow to the supreme Lord Vishvanatha, the sole master of the universe, an ocean of mercy, whose form is the entire cosmos, the bearer of the Ganges, the benefactor, who is easily pleased, and who is beyond all qualities or distinctions. (3)

He who is the sustainer of all worlds, the lord of the celestial wanderers <note>the planets</note>, possessing a thousand rays, the life and the eye of the world; he who nourishes all things moving and unmoving with his unerring divine form, worshiped by hosts of wise men and saluted by all people. (4)

I bow to the Sun, the progenitor of creation and the rest, of priceless form, a treasury of light, eternally moving, the most excellent mass of brilliance, worshiped by the gods, the stimulator and the Lord. (5)

I bow to that great knowledge, Bagalamukhi, clad in yellow garments, the most excellent goddess,
->seated upon a golden throne, the Divine Mother adorned with golden ornaments.<-
She who strikes fear into enemies and always grants good fortune and wealth to those who worship her;
->even when merely remembered, she who is auspicious and dressed in yellow spreads complete well-being. (6)<-

# Introduction to the Book

The *Brihat Samhita* is a vast jewel of a book, a great encyclopedia in the science of the astrologer <term>Daivajna-shastra: the science of those who know the divine will through the stars</term>. It is celebrated, complete, honored by the wise, and shines upon the earth as a great wonder.

A jewel in the court of the Great Vikramaditya, Varaha was a great scholar of perfected knowledge. He was well-versed in all branches of the "Eye of the Vedas" <note>Jyotisha or Astrology/Astronomy is traditionally called the eye of the Vedas</note>, a man of great intellect and a renowned author.

The teacher Varahamihira, a crest-jewel among scholars, attained the highest fame by composing various treatises. (9)

Through his rishi-like vision <note>the intuitive sight of a seer</note>, everything was seen; nothing was unknown to the wise and supreme teacher Varaha. (10)

In the first part, the deliberation on the movements of the planets and their fruits was made; in the latter part, the characteristics of architecture <note>Vastu</note> and other subjects are properly established. (11)

This book, known as the *Compendium* <note>original: "Saṃhitā"</note>, is a great work created by a man of genius. It is held in the hearts of the virtuous today, like a garland of jewels. (12)

It is joined with the science of architecture <note>term: Vāstuvidyā; the ancient Indian system of influence of laws of nature on human dwellings</note> and the characteristics of cattle and other animals; it is further adorned with the descriptions of the physical traits of men and others. (13)

The consecration of gems and jewels, the traits of beasts and birds, and the characteristics of lunar days, lunar mansions <note>term: Nakṣatra; the 27 sectors of the ecliptic</note>, and zodiac signs shine forth here. (14)

The wise author has described the omens of birds and crows, as well as the signs related to royal umbrellas, fly-whisks, beds, and seats. (15)

Having properly presented and considered the opinions of previous teachers, this man of genius has demonstrated his own supreme and excellent views. (16)

Indeed, there is nothing in this world useful for the life of men that has not been observed and described by the noble Varāhamihira. (17)

This jewel of a book has been properly refined and published by the great scholar Kṛṣṇacandra, through immense labor. (18)

May this *Varāhī Saṃhitā* <note>The Bṛhat Saṃhitā of Varāhamihira</note> always serve for the delight of astrologers, for their deep knowledge, and for their insight. (19)

The entire work of Varāha is sufficient for mastering the course of astrology; this knowledge of the astrologers stands like a vast ocean. (20)

This wonderful *Compendium* composed by the Teacher Varāha remains radiant and ever-growing, surpassing all others in dignity. (21)

Shri Kṛṣṇacandra, pure in soul, lineage, and learning, is the best among the virtuous in conduct and is honored for his many virtues. (22)

His mother was Rajalā, a woman of great vows and a treasury of merit; his father was the famous Kubera—both are blessed on this earth. This scholar, expert in the science of light <note>term: Jyotiḥśāstra; encompasses astronomy, astrology, and mathematics</note>, enriched by good fame and righteousness, has edited this work of Varāha by the grace of Lord Shiva. (23)

# Introduction

Among the ancient nations of the world, there were only two primary knowers of the <term>Jyotish Shastra</term> <note>The traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</note>: India and Greece. A thousand years before the Christian Era, the banyan tree of astrology in India was so highly developed that people from other nations, pierced by the sharp arrows of sorrow, sought rest under its shade. Many great seers of this country, as well as eminent scholars such as **Aryabhata** and **Lalla**, composed numerous texts on this science. A leading scholar named **Varahamihira**, having obtained divine power through the worship of the Sun, wrote several astrological texts including the *Brihat Jataka*, *Brihat Samhita*, and *Laghu Jataka*. He was born in the village of Kapitthaka in the Ujjain district. Because the *Brihat Jataka* was written in a concise, aphoristic style, many scholars desired to write commentaries on it; however, this need was first fulfilled by King **Kalyanavarman** of the royal capital of Devaraja. He belonged to the Vyaghrapada lineage, the same lineage as Bhishmacharya from the *Mahabharata*. Later, the knowledge of astrology reached the Persians and the people of Chaldea, China, and Egypt through the Indians of the Asian continent.

From 149 AD to 1860 AD, many researchers and astronomers of the Western world wrote numerous books regarding the motion and positions of the planets in the sky with the help of various instruments. A brief description of them is as follows:

1. A few years before the Christian Era, there was an astronomer named **Pythagoras** in Greece. In 149 AD, there was another astronomer named **Hipparchus**. They were highly honored there as the originators of the Greek system of astronomy. They produced a work regarding the motion of the Sun and the Moon.

2. Around 150 AD, there was a Greek king named **Ptolemy**. He was both an astronomer and a mathematician. He wrote a book titled *Tetrabiblos* <note>original: "Taitraviblas"</note>. He established an observatory at **Alexandria** and published a book named *Syntaxis* regarding planetary orbits, time, equinoxes, motion, and eclipses, which is famous by the name *Almagest*. For 1400 years, this book was accepted by the people of Arabia and other Western countries as if it were a divinely ordained text.

3. In the year 733 AD, there was a Hindu astronomer in the royal court of the **Caliph**.

<summary>This introduction traces the origins of astrology and astronomy to ancient India and Greece, highlighting key figures like Varahamihira and Ptolemy while asserting India's early global influence on the science.</summary>
<keywords>Jyotish Shastra, Varahamihira, Aryabhata, Ptolemy, Almagest, history of astronomy, Indian astrology, Greek astronomy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the historical timeline of global astronomical developments, focusing on the transmission of knowledge between Indian, Arabic, and European civilizations, leading into the Renaissance scientific revolution.</meta>

Page 8

4. In the year 800 CE, the Greeks <note>The text uses 'Yavana', which historically referred to Greeks/Ionians but here likely refers to the Islamic Caliphate scholars who translated Indian works</note> translated the famous Indian texts of Arithmetic and Algebra <note>original: "Ankaganita" and "Bijaganita"</note> from the science of astronomy into the Arabic language.

5. In the year 827 CE, the Greeks published an Arabic translation of the book named *Almagest* composed by Ptolemy <note>original: "Talamy"</note>.

6. Around the year 1300 CE, the people of Western Europe, having studied the science of astronomy from the Greeks, translated the Arabic version of the *Almagest* into the Latin language. At that same time, the King of Castile named Alfonso wrote a new treatise on the science of astronomy.

7. Ulugh Beg (whose name means "Honorable" in Sanskrit), the grandson of Tamerlane <note>original: "Taimurlang"</note>, established a magnificent observatory <term>Vedhashala: a place for astronomical observation</term> in Samarkand. Having completed Ptolemy's unfinished "Star Catalog" <note>original: "Nakshatra-sthiti-patrakam"</note> through his own calculations, he published a book named the *New Star Catalog* in the year 1437 CE.

8. To obtain true knowledge of the system of the universe's structure, Western astronomers (such as Ptolemy, Pythagoras, Newton, and others) exerted great effort but did not achieve complete success.

Copernicus, an astronomer from the country of Poland, discovered the true nature of the universe's structure in 1507 CE. After long effort, research, and gaining full experience through the cooperation of mathematics and observation, he published a book on this subject in the year 1543 CE. He saw the printed copy of that book only at the very end of his life. People are able to benefit greatly from that work.

9. In the year 1577 CE, at the request of astronomers, a King of Denmark established an observatory for Tycho Brahe. Regarding the stars, this result was known: that a King would take birth in the northern part of Finland and he would bring about the destruction of Germany. Accordingly, Gustavus Adolphus was born in Finland. He conquered Germany. This event is famous in history.

10. Galileo, an astronomer of Holland <note>The text attributes Galileo to Holland, likely due to the Dutch invention of the telescope which he perfected</note>, received great honor in 1600 CE for using the telescope <term>Durbin-yantra: literally 'far-seeing instrument'</term> for the first time to understand the motion and position of the planets. With the help of this instrument, objects located 250,000 miles away appeared as if they were only 40 miles away.

11. In the year 1619 CE, the learned researcher and astronomer Kepler wrote a book on the subject of "By which path, at what speed, and at what distance do the planets orbit the Sun?" Because of this, people began to make precise calculations of observations using the telescope.

<summary>This page outlines the global evolution of astronomy from 800 CE to the 17th century, detailing the translation of Indian and Greek works into Arabic and Latin, and the revolutionary contributions of Ulugh Beg, Copernicus, Tycho Brahe, Galileo, and Kepler.</summary>
<keywords>History of Astronomy, Almagest, Ulugh Beg, Samarkand Observatory, Copernicus, Tycho Brahe, Galileo, Telescope, Kepler's Laws, Translation Movement</keywords>

12. In the year 1667 AD, the extraordinary scholar and researcher named Newton published a book titled 'Principia' <note>original: *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*</note>. In that book, it was established as a principle that there is a force of atomic attraction <note>gravity</note> toward matter and inert objects, and they exert a mutual attraction on one another. By this principle, the planets always perform their revolution around the Sun.

13. In the year 1830 AD, the invention of the light-writing apparatus <note>photography</note> occurred—that is, the construction of a telescope for the purpose of capturing images of the Sun, Moon, and other celestial bodies.

14. In the year 1860 AD, the construction of the spectrograph telescope <note>literally "color-writing telescope"</note> took place, by which the actual images of the forms and colors of the planets could be captured.

In this manner, through the most difficult labor lasting over a thousand years, Western astronomers and researchers, having thoroughly understood the science of astronomy <term>Jyotish-shastra: the traditional Indian term for both astronomy and astrology, here used for the physical science</term>, revealed the Western system of astronomy through their mathematics.

### The History of the Discovery of the Two Planets 'Herschel' and 'Neptune'

William Herschel was a famous telescope maker, researcher, and astronomer. While living under the patronage of King George III of England, in the context of counting stars on the night of March 23, 1781 <note>The text says 1787, but the historical date of discovery was 1781</note> at 10 o'clock, he saw a large-sized star in the zodiac sign of Gemini. When he looked again with a telescope a thousand times more powerful than the one he had first used, he realized it was a comet. From that time, while engaged in research regarding its position and motion, he realized it was a planet. Because the scholar named William Herschel conducted the research on that star through the generous patronage of King George III, the name of that planet became 'Herschel' <note>Uranus was briefly called *Georgium Sidus* or 'Herschel' before the current name was standardized</note>.

In the myths of the Greek country, the orbit of Saturn <note>Saturn</note> is above the orbit of Jupiter <note>Jupiter</note>. Therefore, they consider the planet Saturn to be the father of Jupiter. This new planet is above the orbit of Saturn; therefore, they consider it the father of Saturn and the grandfather of Jupiter. However, among the gods of the people of the Greek country, the one named Uranus was the oldest of all; therefore, according to the opinion of Western researchers and astronomers, the name of 'Herschel' was announced as 'Uranus'. But because the harmony of the new planet's motion and position did not align with observations, William Herschel's curiosity continued to grow until the year 1789 AD. Finally, he directed a researcher and astronomer of the country of France named Bouvard <note>Alexis Bouvard</note> to show the tables of the Herschel planet alongside the tables of the motion and position of the planets Jupiter and Saturn. By him, the work of constructing tables was begun in the year 1820 AD. In the year 1820 AD, with a difference of twenty (20) minutes of arc; in 1840 AD, with a difference of ninety (90) minutes; and in 1844 AD, with a difference of two (2) minutes, a doubt arose in his mind that upon this planet...

<summary>This page chronicles the impact of Newton's Principia and the evolution of astronomical tools, specifically focusing on the discovery of Uranus by William Herschel and the subsequent mathematical discrepancies in its orbit.</summary>
<keywords>Isaac Newton, Principia, Gravity, Photography, Spectroscopy, William Herschel, King George III, Uranus, Alexis Bouvard, Planetary Tables, History of Astronomy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of modern planetary discoveries and their integration into Indian astronomical thought, following the mention of Uranus (Herschel) on previous pages.</meta>

The influence of the gravitational force of another planet was observed. Therefore, with the consensus of all researchers and astronomers <note>original: "jyotirvidām"</note>, a researcher from Berlin named Dr. Galle <note>The text reads "Bāla," likely a phonetic Sanskritization of Galle</note> performed an observation on September 23, 1846 AD, at the 26th degree of the zodiac sign Aquarius <note>original: "Kumbha-rāśi"</note> and saw a planet at that precise location. Upon seeing this new planet, all the researchers, scholars, and astronomers of the Western world were overjoyed. Afterward, meeting together, they unanimously decided to name that planet **'Neptune.'** Since in Greek mythology the deity of water is famous by the name **'Neptune,'** the name of the newly discovered planet was also unanimously fixed as **'Neptune.'** Thus, the date of discovery for the planet Herschel <note>Uranus</note> was March 23, 1787 AD. Following that, through sixty (60) years of continuous research and effort since the time of the scholar named Herschel, the discovery of the planet **'Neptune'** was achieved on September 23, 1846 AD.

After that, the famous Indian scientist and astronomer named Janardan Balaji Modak designated the names of **'Uranus and Neptune'** as Prajapati and Varuna, respectively. Since the water deity of this country is Varuna and Prajapati is the Great Ancestor of all, and because the qualities and characteristics of these two planets fully correspond with the descriptions in the Puranas <note>Ancient Indian mythological and historical texts</note> of this country, naming them accordingly is entirely appropriate. This is a wonderful and miraculous coincidence. A detailed description of these two can be seen elsewhere.

The biographical details of the teacher Varahamihira and the description of his works should be viewed in the first volume under the heading **'Background.'**

In this manner, the author of the *Brihat Samhita* <note>The Great Compilation by the 6th-century polymath Varahamihira</note> established the exposition of the science of astrology <term>Jyotishashastra: the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</term> in relation to all conditions pertaining to living beings. I believe that such a comprehensive work could only be accomplished by a superhuman individual. By studying the *Brihat Samhita* from beginning to end, one realizes that this book was composed after tireless study, reflection, and practice in all fields of <term>Nakshatravijnana: the science of the stars/constellations</term>, having personally experienced the truth. In this book, just as there is mention of the daily life and political affairs ranging from a small hut to a royal palace, there is likewise mention of the development of everything from villages to the largest cities, and the methods for constructing advanced and grand buildings, roads, and temples. Furthermore, a thorough description of agricultural science, creepers, vessels, and medicinal herbs is provided in this text. It is also true that this book serves as an encyclopedia of <term>Khagolavijnana: astronomy</term>. This creation of Indian intellect influences all astronomers of the world, and everyone accepts the influence of this work with respect and joy.

The Sampurnanand Sanskrit University is publishing the second edition of this important text. Through this, scholars, students, teachers, and ordinary citizens will certainly benefit, and the university will be honored by this work. Therefore, the university family deserves our thanks.

I express my constant gratitude to my colleagues who have fully cooperated in such a distinguished task. The honorable Vice-Chancellor of the University, Dr. Mandan Mishra, performed the inauguration of the first volume of this *Brihat Samhita* at the Rashtrapati Bhavan <note>The official residence of the President of India</note> in the capital. Now, we hope that the inauguration of this second volume will also be performed by some distinguished and glorious scholar.

# Introduction
## [ Of the First Edition ]

> I bow to the Son of the Wind <note>Hanuman</note>, by whom Sugriva, the noble Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, and the monkeys were profoundly aided.

In the first half of the *Brihat Samhita* <note>The "Great Compilation," an encyclopedic work by Varahamihira</note>, the subject is generally astrology and the influence of planets and constellations; however, in the second half, the topics are general matters of astrology that do not depend on mathematical calculations. Among these are *Vastu-vidya* <term>Architecture/Science of Habitation</term> and *Dakargala* <term>Water Divining/The Bolt of Water</term>, which concerns how much digging is required in the earth to obtain water. In this context, Varahamihira has declared that he composed the chapter on water divining after reviewing the works composed by the Sage Sarasvata:

->Having observed the *Dakargala* which was composed by the Sage Sarasvata,<-
->I have composed this in *Arya* meter; I shall also speak of the work of Manu in other meters.<-
->(53, 99)<-

The second half of the verse mentions the water divining work composed by Manu as well. In the current versions of the *Manava-Shastra* <note>The Laws of Manu</note>, this water divining or these specific verses do not exist. However, Bhattotpala <note>A famous 10th-century commentator</note> has extracted verses from the sciences of the Sage Sarasvata and Manu in his commentary, stating: "And so says Sarasvata" (53, 66) and "And so says Manu" (53, 102).

Nowadays, when digging wells and similar structures, people are able to split through rocky ground with the help of machines. In that era, when there was a primary lack of tools for splitting rocky ground, those methods had to be contemplated deeply. When a rock being split does not break, one should burn wood of the *Tinduka* tree along with *Palash* wood <note>Butea monosperma</note> to make the rock fire-red. Then, when sprinkled with water mixed with milk, they reach a state of breaking (53, 112). When an extremely hard rock cannot be broken, this remedy should be applied: water boiled with the ashes of the *Mokshaka* tree <note>Schrebera swietenioides</note> mixed with the ashes of *Shara* reed should be used to sprinkle the rock seven times after it has been heated by fire according to the previously mentioned method—the sprinkling must be done after heating it again and again. Then the breaking of that rock occurs (53, 113). Two other methods in the book are also worth seeing. Even if breaking does not occur after doing this, a method for tempering a chisel is given, by which the breaking of stone may happen through a tool:

->A paste made of the milk of the *Arka* plant <note>Calotropis gigantea</note>, the soot from a ram's horn,<-
->and the dung of pigeons and rats should be applied.<-
->Then, after tempering the chisel in oil and sharpening it,<-
->there will be no failure of the tool against the stones.<-
->(53, 116)<-

---

->CCO. Vashishtha Tripathi Collection. Digitized by eGangotri<-

### He also says another thing—

> When iron is treated with an alkaline solution of plantain <note>original: "kadalyā"; refers to the ash of the banana tree</note> mixed with buttermilk and left to stand for a full day, and is then properly sharpened on a whetstone, it will not break against stone, nor will its edge be blunted by other metals.

->( 53, 110 )<-

Following this, the characteristics of wind and other elements are described. After the chapter named "Characteristics of Cattle," there is an explanation of the "Characteristics of Dogs." In that section, if a dog has three paws with five claws each, while the fourth (the front right) is equipped with six claws; has reddish lips and a reddish tip of the nose; a gait like that of a lion; a bushy tail; a gaze resembling that of a bear; and ears that are long and soft, and if he walks while sniffing the ground—such a dog, in a short time, brings full prosperity <note>original: "Lakshmi"; the goddess of wealth and the concept of fortune</note> to the home of his protector.

> The dog who has three paws with five claws, but the front right paw with six; who has copper-colored lips and nose; who has the gait of a lion <note>original: "mṛgeśvara"; literally 'lord of beasts'</note> and walks sniffing the earth; who has a bushy tail, eyes like a bear, and long, soft ears—he quickly creates abundant wealth in the house of the one who nourishes him.

->( 61, 1 )<-

And if a female dog <term>kukkuri (female dog)</term> possesses the characteristics mentioned below, she protects the entire kingdom:

> She who has five claws on her left [hind] paw and five on her front paw, but six claws on her front left paw; who has eyes like the Mallika flower <note>whitish or pale eyes</note>, a curved tail, and tawny, hanging ears—that well-nourished female dog protects the nation.

->( 61, 2 )<-

A rooster <term>kukkuta (rooster/cock)</term> also, when endowed with the characteristics mentioned below, brings about the increase of the King, the nation, and the horses:

> The rooster who has straight feathers and toes; whose face, claws, and crest are copper-colored; who is white in color and crows with a pleasant sound at the end of the night <note>at dawn</note>—he is the giver of growth to the King, the kingdom, and the cavalry.

->( 62, 1 )<-

# PREFACE
->[ To The First Edition ]<-

In the preparation of the second volume of the <term>Bṛhat-Saṃhitā</term> <note>The "Great Compilation," an encyclopedic 6th-century Sanskrit work on astrology, divination, and natural science by Varāhamihira</note> with <term>Bhaṭṭotpala’s</term> <term>Vivṛti</term> <note>A famous 10th-century commentary or "explanation" (Vivṛti) that clarifies the original verses</note>, I found another manuscript in the <term>Vizianagram Sanskrit Series Library</term>, which supplied the place of the second incomplete “fragment” up to forty-five chapters termed “<term>A</term>” <note>original: "अ" (the first letter of the Sanskrit alphabet, used here as a manuscript label)</note> (see the preface to the first volume of this work). In spite of its imperfections, so very common in all the seven other manuscripts, it was useful in several places in the preparation of the present volume.

Like the first volume, the present one has also been supplied with an appendix containing the names of the books and the names of their authors quoted herein. Further, I have added a table of the most important and interesting passages with numberings of pages and lines, very carefully prepared for the convenience of such readers as cannot afford to give a thorough reading to the whole of it—which it so richly deserves. This table, moreover, contains the names of <term>Teachers</term> <note>original: "Āchāryas"</note> and their works from which quotations are taken by <term>Bhaṭṭotpala</term> in his commentary.

In conclusion, I express my sincere thanks to <term>Scholar Muralīdhara Jhā</term> <note>original: "Paṇḍit Muralīdhara Jhā"</note>, <term>Master of Astrology</term> <note>original: "Jyautiṣachārya"</note>, one of my worthy students, for the valuable help he has rendered in correcting the proof sheets.

SUDHĀKARA DVIVEDI.

*The 1st September, 1897*

# Victory to the Beloved of Sri Janaki <note>original: "Śrī-jānakī-vallabho vijayate"; a devotional salutation to the Hindu deity Rama, the husband of Sita/Janaki</note>
## Introduction
### [ Of the First Edition ]

->We bow our heads to that Rama, by whom the unfaithful one born of the lineage of Pulastya <note>referring to the demon-king Ravana</note> was humbled,<-
->and by whom the devoted Sabari <note>a famous female devotee in the Ramayana known for her simple faith</note> was honored.<-

For the printing of this second half of the *Great Compilation* <term>Brihat Samhita: a 6th-century encyclopedic text by Varahamihira covering astrology, planetary movements, eclipses, and architecture</term> along with its commentary, we obtained another manuscript from the Vizianagaram Sanskrit Series Library. This was used in place of the manuscript designated 'A' (mentioned in the introduction to the first volume), which contained only 45 chapters. Although this new manuscript was, like all others, exceedingly full of errors, it nevertheless provided great assistance in many places. In this second half, just as in the first, I have included an index to identify the various teachers and other texts whose quotations appear, so that they may be recognized through their own words. Although this entire *Samhita* with its commentary is worthy of study and reflection, I have—with great effort—highlighted the particularly useful subjects at the beginning of this volume, providing specific chapter, page, and line numbers for the readers' quick understanding. In that same section, I have listed the names of those teachers and texts whose statements were included by Bhattotpala <note>the 10th-century commentator who is essential for understanding Varahamihira's work</note> in this commentary. In the correction and editing of this book, the assistance of my capable student, Mr. Muralidhara Sharma (surnamed Jha), who obtained the degree of *Jyotishacharya* <term>Master of Astrology/Astronomy</term> at the Government Sanskrit College in Kashi <note>modern-day Varanasi</note>, is highly praiseworthy. Therefore, I acknowledge his help with thanks.

->May this work of the illustrious Utpala, now edited by the wise friend Sudhakara,<-
->be a boat that removes sorrow and serves the purposes of good people.<-

Vikram Samvat 1954 <note>approximately 1897 CE</note> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;}
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Sudhakara Dvivedi**
Wednesday, 5th day of the dark fortnight of Bhadrapada }

### Now, the Science of Architecture is Explained

At the very beginning, the author speaks to demonstrate the traditional authority of the text:

> Now, therefore, this knowledge of architecture, which has descended through the lineage of sages from the Lotus-Born <note>original: "Kamalabhū"; referring to Brahma, the Creator</note>, is being composed by me for the pleasure of learned astrologers. ||1||

"Now, therefore" indicates the transition from previous topics. "From this collection of signs," I now compose this knowledge of architecture for the "pleasure of learned astrologers" <note>original: "vidvat-saṃvatsara"; literally 'learned years,' a term for scholars of the calendar and divination</note>. Or rather, it is done for the sake of causing that pleasure. What kind of knowledge is it? That which has been received through the traditional lineage of sages, such as Garga and others, starting from the presence of Brahma, the Lotus-Born. ||1||

### Now, two verses are spoken to demonstrate the origin of architectural knowledge:

> It is said that there was once some kind of being that obstructed the heaven and the earth with its body. The host of gods suddenly seized it and threw it down, facing the earth. ||2||
> 
> In whatever limb each specific god seized it, that god remained presiding right there. The Creator then fashioned that being, filled with gods, into the "Vastu-Man." ||3||

The word "It is said" <note>original: "kila"</note> indicates a traditional legend. There was "some kind of being"—meaning one whose name was not specified and whose nature was unknown. It was "obstructing the heaven and the earth" <note>original: "rodasī"</note>, meaning it filled the space with its physical form. That being was suddenly seized by the "host of gods" (the group of immortals) and "thrown down facing the earth" (cast down with its face toward the ground).

Furthermore, on whichever limb a particular "god" (celestial being) stood and seized it, that god remained "presiding" or established right there. The Creator, Prajapati, fashioned that being—who is "filled with gods"—into the <term>Vastu-Nara</term> <note>The "Architectural Man," a cosmic figure whose body forms the grid for all buildings</note> or <term>Vastu-Purusha</term> <note>The "Spirit of the Site"</note>. As Brihaspati <note>The preceptor of the gods</note> says:

> Long ago, in the Golden Age <note>Krita Yuga</note>, a great being arose. It began to pervade the entire world with its body.
> 
> Seeing this, the gods, including Indra, were filled with wonder and overcome by fear. Then, burning with anger, they seized that demon.
> 
> He was thrown down with his face toward the ground, and those gods stayed right there upon him. Brahma then designated him as the Vastu-Purusha. ||2-3||

---

1. <note>original: "vidvatsaṃvatsaraprītyā"</note>—This is an alternative reading.

Now, the author will describe five types of houses each for everyone, starting from kings down to the priestly class.

First, he states the measurements for the houses of kings:

> ->The best royal house should be one hundred and eight cubits <note>original: "hastas"; a cubit is a traditional unit of length based on the forearm</note> in width.<-
> ->The other four houses are each reduced by eight cubits respectively, and their length is one and a quarter times their width. ||4||<-

The "best" or primary royal residence should be constructed with a width of one hundred and eight cubits. The other four types of houses should be made smaller by eight cubits each. This means: the first royal house is 108 cubits wide, the second is 100, the third is 92, the fourth is 84, and the fifth is 76 cubits wide. For each of these houses, the length should be the stated width plus one-quarter <note>original: "sapāda"; literally "with a quarter"</note> of that width. For example, the length of the first house would be 135 cubits, the second 125, the third 115, the fourth 105, and the fifth 95. Thus it should be understood. And so says the sage Kaśyapa:

> ->The royal palace should be one hundred and eight cubits in width.<-
> ->This is the primary one; the others should be reduced by eight cubits each.<-
> ->One should determine their length by adding a quarter to the width.<-
> ->Thus, a king may build five distinct types of houses.<-

In this way, the Teacher <note>referring to Varāhamihira, the author</note> has described five houses for each class. Therefore, any measurement less or more than this is not auspicious. ||4||

Now, he states the measurements for the houses of the Commander-in-Chief <term>Senāpati: the head of the military forces</term>:

> ->Sixty-four cubits, reduced by six cubits for each subsequent type, are the widths for the houses of a Commander-in-Chief.<-
> ->Thus there are five houses, and their length is the width plus one-sixth part. ||5||<-

Sixty-four cubits, reduced by six for each, determines the width. Specifically: the first house is 64 cubits, the second 58, the third 52, the fourth 46, and the fifth 40. In this manner, there are five houses. The length is the width "combined with a sixth part." This means for every house, the stated width plus one-sixth of that width becomes the length. Here is the technical rule for calculation: divide the total by the divisor to get the cubits; multiply the remainder by twenty-four to get the finger-breadths <note>original: "aṅgulas"</note>; and multiply that remainder by sixty to get the barley-corn units <note>original: "yavaṅgulas"</note>. This rule applies everywhere. ||5||

### Now he describes the proportions for the houses of Ministers—

> **Sixty, reduced by four each, are the five houses of a Minister.**
> **The length is increased by one-eighth of its own width; half of that is for the Royal Queens. ||6||**

There are five types of houses for a Minister <note>original: *saciva*, meaning a counselor or minister</note>. Their widths start at sixty and are reduced by four each. Specifically: the first house is 60 <term>cubits</term> <note>The "hastas" or cubits mentioned later are the standard unit of measurement, roughly 18 inches</note>, the second is 56, the third is 52, the fourth is 48, and the fifth is 44. For each house, the length is determined by adding one-eighth of that width to itself.

"Half of that is for the Royal Queens": the Queens are the principal wives. For these wives of the King, the houses should be made half the size of the Minister's proportions. This means: whatever width and length were stated for the five houses of the Minister, the houses for the Royal Queens should be made with half of those values. For example: the width of the first house is 30, the second is 28, the third is 26, the fourth is 24, and the fifth is 22. The length for all of them should be increased by one-eighth of their respective widths. ||6||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the houses for the Crown Prince—

> **In the same way, eighty reduced by sixes are for the Crown Prince.**
> **The length is increased by one-third; five houses for his younger brothers are half of those. ||7||**

In this same manner, eighty reduced by six each represents the width of the five houses for the Crown Prince <note>original: *yuvarāja*, the heir apparent</note>. Specifically: the first is 80 cubits in width, the second is 74, the third is 68, the fourth is 62, and the fifth is 56. The width of each house, when increased by its own third part, becomes the length.

"Five houses for his younger brothers": for the younger brothers of that Crown Prince, five houses should be made using half of those widths and lengths. Specifically: the width of the first is 40, the second is 37, the third is 34, the fourth is 31, and the fifth is 28. The length for all of them is increased by one-third. ||7||

### Now he describes the house characteristics for Feudatory Chiefs, Chief Royal Officers, Chamberlains, Courtesans, and Artists—

> **The difference between the King’s and the Minister’s houses is for the Feudatory Chiefs and Chief Royal Officers.**
> **The difference between the King’s and the Crown Prince’s houses is for Chamberlains, Courtesans, and Artists. ||8||**

The difference <note>the mathematical interval</note> between the five houses of the King and the five houses of the Minister should be used for the Feudatory Chiefs <note>original: *sāmanta*, local governors or vassal kings</note> and the Chief Royal Officers. This is stated...

It follows—that for the high-ranking feudal lords <note>original: "samanta-pravara"</note> and royal officers, the width and length should be determined by the difference between the width and length of the King’s and the Minister’s residences. Likewise, the difference between the measurements of the King’s residence and the Crown Prince’s residence should be used for the houses of the chamberlains <note>original: "kanchukina," often attendants of the women's quarters</note>, the chief masters of ceremonies, courtesans, and those skilled in the arts—specifically those proficient in singing, instrumental music, dance, painting, and the art of leaf-cutting <note>an ancient decorative art</note>. ||8||

->Now he describes the five houses for the superintendents, officials, factory managers, and envoys:<-

> For all superintendents and officials, the house should be equal to the Treasury or the Jewel-house.
> The difference between the Crown Prince’s and the Minister’s measurements is for the factory managers and envoys. ||9||

For the superintendents of the stables for horses, elephants, and cows, as well as the heads of the kitchens and other such departments—and for all others appointed to specific administrative duties—the house should be equal to the Treasury <note>original: "kosha-ratna-tulyam"</note>. That is, one should make it according to the measurements of the treasury building or the pleasure-house. The measurements for the treasury and pleasure-houses will be discussed later. Regarding the phrase "the difference between the Crown Prince and the Minister": the difference between the Crown Prince’s measurements and the Minister’s measurements should be applied to the managers of workshops <note>original: "karmanta," referring to industrial or agricultural worksites</note> and to envoys. Some read this as "the difference between the feudal lord and the minister," meaning the measurement derived from the difference between the lord's and the minister's house sizes. However, the elder architects do not favor this reading because the resulting measurements are too small. ||9||

->Now he states the architectural proportions for the Astrologer, the Physician, and the Priest:<-

> Starting from forty, decreasing by four, for five houses.
> The length for the Astrologer, Priest, and Physician is the width plus one-sixth. ||10||

Now for the Astrologer, the Physician, and the Priest. The Astrologer <note>original: "daivajna," one who knows the divine will through stars</note> is the practitioner of the calendar; the Physician <note>original: "bhishaj"</note> is the doctor; the Priest <note>original: "purohita"</note> is the royal chaplain. The widths of their five types of houses start at forty cubits and decrease by four. Specifically: the width of the first house is 40, the second is 36, the third is 32, the fourth is 28, and the fifth is 24. The length should be that same width increased by one-sixth. For each house, the length is its own width plus a sixth part of that width. ||10||

->He now states the height of the building and the length for a single-hall house:<-

> In any building, the width itself is the certain height that brings auspiciousness.
> In houses consisting of a single hall, the length is twice the width. ||11||

The width specified for a house in the science of architecture <note>Vastu</note> is the same measure that determines its height; this proportion is considered auspicious. For example, as it was stated that the primary house of a king should be one hundred and eight cubits <note>term: Hasta (cubit), a traditional unit of measurement from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</note> in width, it should likewise be made one hundred and eight cubits in height. In the case of single-hall houses <note>Ekashala</note>, the length should be twice the width. As the sage Kashyapa says:

->In four-hall houses, the height is equal to the width.<-
->For a single-hall house, the length is twice the width. || 1 ||<-

### Now he describes the house dimensions for the four social classes, beginning with the Brahmins—

->The width for the four classes begins at thirty-two, decreasing by four each time,<-
->down to sixteen; beyond that is for the very lowest classes. || 2 ||<-
->For Brahmins, the length is the width plus one-tenth; for Kshatriyas, plus one-eighth.<-
->For Vaishyas, it is plus one-sixth; for Shudras, it is plus one-fourth. || 3 ||<-

Regarding the "four classes" <note>Chaturvarnya</note>: This refers to the nature of the four social orders—the Brahmin <note>priests/scholars</note>, Kshatriya <note>warriors/rulers</note>, Vaishya <note>merchants/farmers</note>, and Shudra <note>laborers</note>. Among these four, the width for a Brahmin's house starts at thirty-two cubits and decreases by four units at a time. This continues "down to sixteen." This means: the primary house width for a Brahmin is thirty-two cubits, with four other options each reduced by four cubits. For a Kshatriya, the primary width is twenty-eight cubits, with three other options reduced by four cubits each. For a Vaishya, the primary house is twenty-four cubits, with two others reduced by four. For a Shudra, the principal house is twenty cubits, and the other is sixteen. Thus, there are five types of houses for a Brahmin, four for a Kshatriya, three for a Vaishya, and two for a Shudra. Beyond this, smaller and inferior dimensions are for those of very low standing, such as the Chandalas and Shvapakas <note>marginalized groups outside the four-fold system</note>.

For Brahmins, the length should be the stated width plus one-tenth of itself; this applies to all five types of their houses. Similarly, for a Kshatriya, it is increased by one-eighth. For a Vaishya, it is increased by one-sixth of its own measure. For a Shudra, it is "plus a quarter," meaning increased by one-fourth. As stated in the treatise known as the *Kirana Tantra*:

->In the residence of a twice-born <note>Brahmin</note>, the width should be thirty-two cubits.<-
->One should determine its length as the width plus one-tenth.<-
->For the other three, starting with the Kshatriya, the measurements previously mentioned<-
->should be reduced successively by four cubits.<-
->Their lengths should be increased by one-eighth, one-sixth, and one-fourth respectively. || 12.3 ||<-

# 572
## In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 52]

### Now he describes the dimensions for the treasury and pleasure-house, as well as the house dimensions for royal officials—

->The treasury and pleasure-house are determined by the difference between the dimensions of the King’s and the Commander-in-Chief’s houses.<-
->The houses of royal officials are determined by the difference between the dimensions of the Commander-in-Chief’s house and those of the four castes.<-

The treasury and the pleasure-house should be constructed using the measurement that is the difference between the previously mentioned dimensions of the King’s house and the Commander-in-Chief’s house. The treasury <term>Koshabhavana: a storehouse for wealth or a mint</term> and the pleasure-house <term>Ratibhavana: a house for recreation and enjoyment</term> share the same proportions. For royal officials, the dimensions are determined by the difference <note>literally "the gap" or "interval"</note> between the Commander-in-Chief’s house and the houses of the four castes <term>Chaturvarnya: the four social classes of Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra</term>. 

In this context, when a Brahmin serves as a royal official, one should subtract the Brahmin’s residential dimensions from the Commander-in-Chief’s dimensions; the remainder determines the scale for a set of five houses. The same logic applies to the Kshatriyas and others. Specifically, for a Kshatriya royal official, the primary house is determined by the difference between the second Commander-in-Chief house type and the Kshatriya residential scale. This continues sequentially: the third with the second, the fourth with the third, and the fifth with the fourth. Thus, the difference with the third Commander-in-Chief house determines the primary house of a Vaishya, and the fourth determines that of a Shudra.

### Now he describes the architectural dimensions for the Parashavas and others, and the inauspiciousness of houses that are too small or too large—

->For the Parashavas and others, the house should be equal to half the sum of their respective parental dimensions.<-
->A building that is smaller or larger than its prescribed measure is inauspicious for everyone.<-

Next, we consider the <term>Parashavas: children born of a Brahmin father and a Shudra mother</term>. Similarly, the <term>Bhurjakantaka: born of a Vaishya mother</term> <gloss>1</gloss> and the <term>Murdhavasikta: born of a Kshatriya mother</term>. For these individuals, the house should be equal to half the sum of their parental measures. One should take the specific measures of both parents, add them together, and divide by half; that resulting measure is the scale for the house of a Parashava and the others. For example, one takes the measure of a Brahmin and a Shudra, combines them, and halves it. That is the measure for a Parashava’s house. This applies similarly to the sons of Vaishya and Kshatriya mothers. For everyone—from kings down to the Parashavas—a building <term>Vastu</term> that is smaller or larger than its prescribed measure brings no good fortune.

### Now, according to other authorities, he describes the height limits for animal pens, hermitages, and storage houses for grain, weapons, fire, and pleasure—

->For animals and hermits, the dimensions are unlimited; so too for houses of grain, weapons, fire, and pleasure.<-
->The masters of the Shastras do not desire a height exceeding one hundred cubits.<-

For animals (four-legged creatures) and for those in the stages of life <term>Ashramins: specifically ascetics or monks</term>, the dimensions of the house are unmeasured—meaning they may be as large as desired. This also applies to the granary where grain is stored, and the armory where weapons are kept...

...where they are established, as well as for the fire-house <note>original: "vahnigṛhasya" - a room for the sacred domestic fire</note> or sacrificial hall, and the pleasure-house <note>original: "ratigṛhasya" - a private room for enjoyment or rest</note> or sporting chamber. For these, the measurements are unlimited. However, the authors of the scriptures who are experts in the knowledge of architecture <term>Vāstuvidyā: the ancient Indian science of architecture and placement</term> do not desire a height exceeding one hundred cubits <term>Hasta: a unit of measurement, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm</term>. A house should not be constructed higher than one hundred cubits. This serves as an exception to the rule: "In architecture, whatever is the width, that same measurement for the height is certain to bring auspiciousness." <note>This refers to verse 11 of this same chapter</note> And so says the sage Garga:

-> Wise men should construct a four-hall house <note>original: "catuḥśāla" - a building with four wings surrounding a central courtyard</note> one hundred cubits high. <-
-> Half of that height is declared to bring auspiciousness for a single-hall house. ||16|| <-

Now, he describes the measurements of the hall <note>original: "śālā" - the main room or interior space</note> and the veranda <note>original: "alinda" - a gallery or porch outside the room</note> for all buildings, using the example of a General or a King:

-> For Generals and Kings, seventy is added to the width and the sum is divided in two. <-
-> The hall is determined by dividing [one part] by fourteen; the veranda by dividing [the other] by thirty-five. ||17|| <-

In the architecture for a General or a King—or for anyone else excluding the four social classes—one should take the width, add seventy to it, and divide the result into two parts. In one part, by dividing by fourteen, whatever is obtained in cubits and digits <term>Aṅgula: a "finger's breadth," the smallest standard unit of linear measure</term> shall be the measurement for the hall. By the word "hall" <note>śālā</note>, the interior of the house is meant. In the other part, by dividing by thirty-five, whatever is obtained in cubits and the like shall be the measurement for the veranda. By the word "veranda" <note>alinda</note>, one should understand that which is made outside the wall of the hall, serving as a walkway facing the courtyard and covered by a lattice. The previously mentioned maximum area of one hundred and eight cubits and so on refers to the site measurements; this current rule refers to the method of construction. ||17||

Now he describes the measurements of the hall and veranda for the four social classes <note>original: "cāturvarṇya" - the traditional four-fold division of society</note>:

-> Starting from thirty-two cubits, the halls are four, four, three, three, and three cubits, <-
-> increased by seventeen, three, fifteen, thirteen, and four digits respectively. ||18|| <-
-> Three, three, two, two, and [two] are the cubits [for verandas] in decreasing order; their digits <-
-> are twenty minus one <note>19</note>, eight, twenty, eighteen, and three. ||19|| <-

"Starting from thirty-two cubits" means starting from thirty-two for the classes beginning with the Brahmins. For them, the halls should be made four, four, three, three, and three cubits. And of what kind are these cubits? They are increased by seventeen, three, fifteen <note>original: "tithi" - a symbolic word for 15, based on the lunar days</note>, thirteen, and four <note>original: "kṛta" - a symbolic word for 4</note> digits. To illustrate: in the first and primary house of the four classes, the hall should be four cubits and seventeen digits; in the second, four cubits and three digits; in the third, three cubits and fifteen digits; in the fourth, three cubits and thirteen digits; and in the fifth, three cubits and four digits...

Regarding the construction: In this way, the house that is considered "second-tier" for a Brahmin is the "prime" house for a Kshatriya <note>the warrior/ruling class</note>. That which is second-tier for a Kshatriya is prime for a Vaishya <note>the merchant/landowner class</note>, and that which is second-tier for a Vaishya is prime for a Shudra <note>the laboring class</note>. By this method, the standard measurements for the halls are established. ||18||

Regarding the measurements of three, three, two, and two: These cubits <term>Hasta: a unit of measurement roughly equal to 18 inches or the length of a forearm</term> are combined with fingers <term>Angula: a finger's breadth, 1/24th of a cubit</term> starting from twenty-one and decreasing. Even if the measurement for the <term>Alinda: a terrace or veranda</term> is not explicitly stated for the dwellings of the four classes, it can be understood as follows:

In the first house of a Brahmin, the veranda measurement is three cubits plus nineteen fingers. <gloss>The text says "one less than twenty," meaning nineteen.</gloss> In the second, it is three cubits plus eight fingers. In the third, two cubits plus twenty fingers. In the fourth, two cubits plus eighteen fingers. In the fifth, two cubits plus three fingers. Thus, as the number of cubits decreases, these specific finger-measurements should be added according to the house type. 

On this point, some read the text as: "these fingers are applied in reverse order." Others explain it thus: "these fingers represent a reduction or loss to be subtracted from the cubits." However, the elder master-builders <note>Sthapatis</note> do not accept this latter interpretation. Just as the details for the four classes were described for the General of the Army and royal officials, the same should be applied to the halls and verandas here. ||19||

### Now he describes the proportions of the walkway and the names of the buildings characterized by them:

> **The walkway should be made equal to one-third of the hall's measurement, situated outside the main building.**
> **If it is located at the front, that building is named *Soshnisha* (Turbaned). ||20||**
> **If it is at the back, it is named *Sayashraya* (With Refuge). If situated at the sides, it is *Savashtambha* (With Support). If it surrounds the building on all sides, it is *Susthita* (Well-Established). All of these are praised by the experts of the Shastras <note>sacred sciences</note>. ||21||**

Regarding "equal to one-third": The walkway <term>Vithika: a gallery or path</term> should be constructed outside the building area, measuring one-third of the hall's dimensions. <note>1</note> If this walkway is at the front (the eastern part) of the house, the building is called *Soshnisha*.

If it is at the back (the western part) of the site, the building is called *Sayashraya*. If it is located on the two sides (South and North), or perhaps at the front and back together, it is called *Savashtambha*. If it exists on all four sides, the building is called *Susthita*. All of these are praised and commended by those who know the characteristics of architecture <note>Vastu-vidya</note>. So it is said in the treatise named *Kirana*:

> **That which is the third part of the hall, with that one should make the walkway.**
> **If the walkway is at the front, that house is named *Soshnisha*.**

---

<header>Chapter 52] Chapter on the Science of Architecture (Vastu-vidya).</header>

->If the support is at the back, it is called *Sayashraya*; if supported on both sides, it is *Savashtambha*.<-
->If it is supported on all sides, it is called *Susthita* (Well-established). Thus it is said. [Verses 20-21]<-

### Now he describes the measurement of stories for all buildings—

->The height of a house should be one-sixteenth of its width plus four cubits.<-
->For all subsequent stories, the height is reduced by one-twelfth of the previous story's height. [Verse 22]<-

Whatever width has been stated for the building, one-sixteenth of that plus four cubits <term>cubit (hasta): a traditional unit of length, roughly 18 inches</term> becomes the height of the house; this refers to the height of the ground floor. For example, if a king’s palace has a width of 108 cubits, one-sixteenth of that is 6 cubits and 18 digits <term>digit (angula): 1/24th of a cubit</term>; adding four cubits makes it 10 cubits and 18 digits. This is the measurement for the ground floor. The same logic applies elsewhere. The story above that should be made less by one-twelfth. This means one should subtract one-twelfth of the first story's measurement to get the height of the next. Similarly, the story above that should be reduced by one-twelfth of the one below it. In this way, for all stories, the measurement should be progressively reduced by one-twelfth as one goes higher. [Verse 22]

### Now he explains the knowledge of wall measurements and the distinction between those made of baked bricks and wood—

->The wall thickness for all houses is one-sixteenth of the width.<-
->This applies to those made of baked bricks; for those made of wood, there is no fixed rule. [Verse 23]<-

For all houses, from those of kings down to the lowest classes <note>original: "parashavanta," referring to the social hierarchy of the time</note>, one-sixteenth of the width becomes the measurement for the wall thickness. For example, for a king’s house with a width of 108 cubits, one-sixteenth is 6 cubits and 18 digits; this is the wall thickness. Others should be understood similarly. As Garga <note>An ancient sage and authority on astrology and architecture</note> says:

> One should design the house wall as one-sixteenth of the width.
> It should not be made thinner or thicker, as it is not auspicious for the master of the house.

This wall measurement applies to structures made of baked bricks. For other structures made of wood, there is no "option" <note>original: "vikalpa," meaning a fixed rule or alternative here</note>; this specific calculation does not apply. For those, one may build as desired. Not only the wall thickness, but the width, length, and height may be made according to preference. As stated in the treatise called *Kirana*:

> This width is for baked bricks; for wooden ones, it is as desired.
> A house for the twice-born <note>The upper social classes</note> and others should be built bright and facing its proper direction.
> One should design it knowing the measurements in cubits such as nine, thirteen, etc. [Verse 23]

### Now, he describes the knowledge of doorway measurements for all structures belonging to those outside the four-fold caste system, by way of the King and the Commander-in-Chief—

**Seventy plus an eleventh part is the width for the King and the Commander-in-Chief.**
**The height is equal to that in inches; the width of the door is half of that height. ||24||**

In this context, the mention of the King and the Commander-in-Chief is illustrative <note>original: "upalakshana," meaning a specific example used to represent a broader category</note>. The King is the sovereign; the Commander-in-Chief is the general of the army. For the King, the Commander, or anyone else outside the four castes <note>likely referring to those in specialized administrative or military roles not strictly bound by the standard domestic rules</note>, the width or extent of the house should be increased by its own eleventh part and then added to seventy. The resulting sum represents the height of the doorway in inches <note>term: angula; a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to a finger's breadth</note>. 

For example: if the King’s house width is 108 cubits <note>term: hasta; a cubit, roughly 18-24 inches</note>, its eleventh part is approximately 9.8. Adding this to 108 and then adding 70 results in 187.8. This number represents the doorway height in inches. This is how it should be understood for others as well. Regarding "the width is half": the width (breadth) of the doorway should be made exactly half of this calculated height. For instance, the width of the King’s palace door would be 99 inches. The same logic applies to others. ||24||

### Now, he describes the doorway measurements for the four castes—

**For Brahmins and the others, a fifth of the width plus eighteen inches,**
**increased by an eighth part, is the width; the height of the door is three times that. ||25||**

For the castes beginning with Brahmins—namely Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras—one should take a fifth part of the house's width and add eighteen inches to it. Then, increase that sum by its own eighth part. The resulting figure is the width of the doorway in inches. 

For example: if a Brahmin’s house width is 32 cubits, the fifth part is roughly 6 cubits. These are converted to inches. Adding eighteen inches makes 24 <note>this follows a specific conversion logic in the commentary</note>. Adding an eighth part (3 inches) results in 27 inches as the width measurement. The height is then three times this width. ||25||

### Now, he describes the thickness and breadth of the doorframes and thresholds, and the measurements for the top and base of a pillar—

**The thickness in inches should equal the number of cubits in the height.**
**This applies to both side-posts; for the threshold and lintel, it should be one and a half times that. ||26||**
**The breadth of these is the height multiplied by seven and divided by eighty.**
**For a pillar, it is the height multiplied by nine and divided by eighty, reduced by a tenth at the top. ||27||**

Whatever the height of the doorway is in cubits, that same number should be used in inches for the thickness (density) of the two side-posts <note>term: shakha; the vertical side-posts of a door frame</note>. The word "also" implies possibility—that this rule applies even when there are many posts.

<note>The text explains that the threshold and top-piece (udumbara) must be 1.5 times thicker than the side-posts for structural integrity. For pillars, the base is thicker than the top to ensure stability, following a specific ratio of reduction (one-tenth).</note>

<page-num>577</page-num>
<header>Chapter 52] The Chapter on Architecture (Vastu Vidya)</header>

For example, the height of a king’s palace doorway is 188 digits <note>original: "angulas"</note>. Therefore, the height is eight and a half cubits <note>original: "hastas"</note>. This same number of digits constitutes the thickness of the two side-posts. This applies to other cases as well.

*Regarding the phrase "one and a half times that for the two threshold-lintels":* The thickness of those side-posts multiplied by one and a half should be the measure for the two "Udumbara" beams. For instance, in a king's house, if the side-post thickness is 12 digits, then for the others <margin>1. Verse 29 of this same chapter.</margin> it is calculated accordingly. The "Udumbara" refers to the two pieces of wood placed above and below the side-posts, known as the threshold and the lintel. ||26||

*Regarding "from seven times the height":* Whatever the height of the door is, one-eightieth part of seven times that height is the width (breadth) to be made for these side-posts and lintels. For example: the king's door height is 188 digits; one-eightieth of seven times this is 16 and a half digits. This is the width for all of them. This applies elsewhere too.

*Regarding "multiplied by nine":* When the height of a pillar is multiplied by nine, one-eightieth part of that is the measure of the width at the base of the pillar. That same measure, reduced by one-tenth of itself, is the width at the top of the pillar. For example, in a king's palace, the measure of the ground floor is 10 cubits and 18 digits. This is the height of the pillar. One-eightieth of nine times this is 28 <unclear>digits</unclear>. This is the width at the base. That same measure reduced by one-tenth is the width at the top. From this, the circumference is three times that. This is shown merely as an illustration. Otherwise, according to the rule "dividing the pillar into nine parts, the carrying part is one portion," this division should be understood for the middle section, whether it be square or otherwise. ||27||

->Now he states the names of the pillars and their types:<-

**A square pillar is called Ruchaka; one with eight sides is Vajra; one with double that (sixteen sides) is Dvivajra; one with thirty-two sides in the middle is Pralinaka; and the round one is called Vritta.** ||28||

A pillar that is square in its middle section—meaning it possesses four equal edges—is named **Ruchaka**. One which has eight equal edges in the middle is named **Vajra**. One which is double that, having sixteen equal edges, is named **Dvivajra** (double-Vajra). One which is endowed with thirty-two edges in the middle is named **Pralinaka**. And that which is circular or perfectly round in the middle is designated as **Vritta**. These are the five types of pillars. All of them yield auspicious results. It is understood by implication that others are not desired. Why was the "middle" specified here? Because by the rule "dividing the pillar into nine parts," the design of the top and bottom sections will be different. Thus it is said in the treatise <term>Kirana</term>:

> A four-sided pillar is Ruchaka; a pillar joined with eight edges is considered Vajra.
> Dvivajra has sixteen edges, and Pralinaka has double those edges (thirty-two).
> A pillar that is round all around is called Vritta by the best of the twice-born. ||28||

***

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 52]

Now, to demonstrate the construction of the lower and upper parts of the pillar, he says:

->**Divide the pillar into nine parts; one part is the base, another part is the pot.**<-
->**The lotus and the upper lip should likewise be made with one part each. ||29||**<-

Divide the pillar—the total height of the pillar—into nine parts, making nine distinct divisions. There, at the very bottom part, the *base* <note>original: "vahanam"; the load-bearing foot of the column</note> should be made. The base is that part of the pillar by which it is raised and supported on the ground. Above this part, the second part is the *pot* <note>original: "ghata"; a bulbous, jar-shaped molding</note>. The next part after that is the *lotus* <note>original: "padma"</note>; it should be shaped exactly like a lotus flower. In the same manner, the part above the lotus—which is the ninth part—should be made as the *upper lip* <note>original: "uttaroshtha"</note>. The upper lip is where specific decorative figures are carved for beauty. Thus, the lotus is made with one part and the upper lip with one part. Some authorities desire the upper lip in the eighth part and the lotus in the ninth. The meaning is this: when the pillar is divided into nine, in the four sections at the top and bottom, decorative elements like gold-work <insert>or carvings</insert> are made; the remaining five parts should be made as a four-sided shaft <note>the central body of the pillar</note>. And so it is said in the treatise called *Kirana*:

> Having divided the pillar into nine, one should make the base and the pot;
> The lotus and the upper lip should be fashioned, each in its own part. || 29 ||

Now he states the measurements for the main beams, the secondary beams, and the cross-beams:

->**The thickness of the main beams should be equal to the pillar, placed one above the other.**<-
->**For the secondary and cross-beams, the thickness is reduced by one-quarter each. ||30||**<-

They are called *main beams* <note>original: "bharatula"</note> because they "weigh" or support the load. The timber that is placed horizontally atop the pillar is designated as the main beam. Because there are many pillars in palaces and similar structures, the plural "main beams" is used. The other timber placed above the main beam is designated as the *secondary beam* <note>original: "tula"</note> or *cross-beam* <note>original: "upatula"</note>. The thickness or density of the main beams should be equal to the pillar's measurement. For example, if the width of a pillar in a king's house is twenty-eight digits <term>angulas: ancient units of measurement roughly equal to a finger-breadth</term>, the same applies to the main beams. So it is elsewhere. The thickness of the secondary and cross-beams placed above these main beams should be one-quarter less than theirs. For example, in a king's house, it would be twenty-one digits. Elsewhere, it should be reduced by a "foot" <note>one-fourth</note>. Because of the repetition in the text, some increase the number of beam types to four: the main beam, the supporting beam, the secondary beam, and the cross-beam. Their thickness should be reduced by one-quarter progressively from the main beam. These are placed one on top of the other. ||30||

In this architectural practice, there are five types of four-winged houses <note>original: "catuhshala"; a house with four blocks surrounding a central courtyard</note>, named: *Sarvatobhadra* (Good on all sides), *Nandyavarta* (Turning of joy), *Vardhamana* (Prospering), *Svastika*, and *Ruchaka*. Among them, he first states the characteristics of the *Sarvatobhadra*:

->**A building with uninterrupted galleries on all sides is the Sarvatobhadra.**<-
->**It should be built for kings and groups of gods, equipped with four doors. ||31||**<-

# Chapter on the Science of Architecture

<margin>Chapter 52</margin>

When a building has no interruption or obstruction in the movement of the <term>alindas</term> <note>verandas or galleries</note> on all sides and in all directions, that building is known as **Sarvatobhadra** <note>literally "good on all sides"</note>. This design should be constructed for kings and for groups of deities <note>temple complexes</note>. It is characterized by four doors; meaning, doors should be placed in all four cardinal directions. As the sage Garga says:

->Where there is no separation of the verandas on any side,<-
->that building is Sarvatobhadra, equipped with four doors.<-

Now, the characteristics of the **Nandyavarta** <note>a "joyful turning" pattern</note> are described:

->Nandyavarta is formed by verandas starting from the hall-walls and ending in a clockwise direction.<-
->In this design, one should omit the western door and construct the remaining ones.<-

Starting from the <term>shala-kudya</term> <note>the main walls of the halls</note>, and ending in a clockwise fashion with the verandas, the building is named Nandyavarta. It is characterized by those verandas that have gone to the end in a clockwise manner. In all four halls, the verandas reach the end of the hall's clockwise rotation. In this Nandyavarta layout, one should omit or leave out the western door and construct the remaining three doors: East, South, and North. As Garga says:

->With all small verandas moving clockwise from the hall walls,<-
->and without a western door, it is remembered as Nandyavarta.<-

Now, the characteristics of the **Vardhamana** <note>the "prosperous" or "increasing" design</note> are described:

->The veranda at the door reaches the end; the others follow clockwise and are auspicious.<-
->In this Vardhamana design, the southern door should not be constructed.<-

The veranda located at the main door of the primary building is the "door-veranda." That should be made to reach the end; meaning, it is attached to the south and north halls. The second veranda is the southern one, moving clockwise, and it is auspicious or beautiful. The others follow from that, also reaching the end in a clockwise manner. A building characterized by such verandas is Vardhamana. In that Vardhamana, a southern door must not be made. The other three—East, West, and North—should be constructed. As Garga says:

->The door-veranda reaches the end, and the other three move clockwise.<-
->Leaving out the southern door, it is remembered as Vardhamana.<-
