Alternatively, one should perform a test using flowers of colors corresponding to the four classes—white, red, yellow, and black—to see which is most suitable. This means placing flowers of these colors inside a pit <note>original: "shvabhra"</note> overnight. On the following day, the color of the flower that has not withered or dried up indicates that the site is auspicious for the corresponding class. Or, quite simply, whichever piece of land brings peace and joy to a person's mind is considered auspicious for them; in such a case, no further technical examination is required. On this subject, the sage Garga says:

->Whichever land is selected for the construction of a house,<-
->one should dig a pit in the center, measuring one cubit in all directions.<-
->A wise man should then refill that pit with the same earth he dug out.<-
->If the earth overflows, it signifies prosperity; if it falls short, it is condemned.<-
->If it is level, it is considered neutral. Alternatively, there is another method:<-
->After filling the pit, one should walk a hundred steps and then return.<-
->If the pit remains full until one's return, that land is highly praised.<-
->Or, one may place various garlands in that pit in a specific order.<-
->Whichever garland remains fresh the longest, the person of that corresponding class should dwell there.<-
->Alternatively, place four lamp-wicks in an unbaked earthen pot.<-
->The direction in which the lamps burn the longest is the auspicious direction for that person.<-

Now, he describes other characteristics of the land:

->White, red, yellow, and black soils are praised for the Brahmins and the other classes respectively.<-
->So too is land that smells like clarified butter, blood, food, or wine. [94]<-
->Land covered with Kusha grass, reeds, Durva grass, or Kasha grass respectively,<-
->is prosperous for each class, as is soil that tastes sweet, astringent, sour, or pungent. [95]<-

For the <term>Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras</term> <note>The four traditional social classes of ancient India: priests/scholars, warriors/rulers, merchants/farmers, and laborers.</note>, white, red, yellow, and black soil is praised in that specific order. White-colored earth is best for Brahmins. Red or blood-colored earth is for Kshatriyas. Yellow or greenish-yellow earth is for Vaishyas. Black earth is for Shudras. Similarly, soil smelling of clarified butter <note>ghee</note> is for Brahmins; smelling of blood for Kshatriyas; smelling of food for Vaishyas; and smelling of wine for Shudras.

Land joined with *Kusha* <note>sacred grass used in rituals</note> brings auspiciousness to Brahmins. Land thick with *Shara* <note>reeds used for arrows</note> is for Kshatriyas. Land with *Durva* <note>bent grass</note> is for Vaishyas. Land covered in *Kasha* <note>thatch grass</note> is for Shudras. In this order, the land is praised. Furthermore, tastes that are sweet, astringent, sour, and pungent bring growth to the corresponding classes. Sweet for Brahmins, astringent for Kshatriyas, sour for Vaishyas, and pungent for Shudras. As Garga says:

# The Great Compilation with Commentary
## [Chapter 52]

->Land that is sweet, filled with *darbha* grass <note>Desmostachya bipinnata, a sacred grass used in rituals</note>, smelling of clarified butter, and sloping toward the north is auspicious for Brahmins.<-

->Land that is red, smelling of blood, astringent in taste, filled with *sharaveera* <note>likely a type of reed or hardy grass</note>, and sloping toward the east is known to be for the Kshatriyas <note>the warrior and ruling class</note>.<-

->Land that slopes toward the south, is sour in taste, covered in *durva* grass <note>Cynodon dactylon, a common sacred grass</note>, smelling of food grains, and yellow in color is praised for the Vaishyas <note>the merchant and agricultural class</note>.<-

->Land that slopes toward the west, is black, rough, covered in *kasha* grass <note>Saccharum spontaneum</note>, smelling of wine, and pungent in taste is blessed for the Shudras <note>the laboring class</note>. Thus [verses 94-95].<-

Now he describes the ritual for beginning the construction of a house:

->The master of the house, having gone to a land that has been ploughed, where seeds have sprouted, where cows have dwelt, and which has been praised by Brahmins, at a time indicated by the Astrologer;<-
->Having performed worship of the deities with various kinds of food, curd, unbroken grains, fragrant flowers, and incense, and having honored the architects and the Brahmins;<-
->The Brahmin, touching his head; the Kshatriya, his chest; the Vaishya, his thigh; and the Shudra, touching his feet, should draw the line to begin the house. [Verses 96-98]<-

"Ploughed" means turned with a plough. "Where seeds have sprouted" means land where sown rice or grains have grown. "Where cows have dwelt" means a place where cattle have resided. "Praised by Brahmins" means it has been commended by them. The meaning is that cows and Brahmins have stayed there for at least one night. By doing this, the purification of the ground occurs. As it is said:

> By sweeping, by smearing with cow dung, by sprinkling with water, by scraping, and by the residing of cows—the earth is purified by these five methods.

The master of the house, the owner, goes to such land at a time—a moment endowed with all virtues and free from afflictions—indicated by the *Samvatsara* <note>the royal astrologer or astronomer</note>. [96]

"With various kinds of food" refers to many types of eatables like cakes, sweet dumplings, and wafers. Likewise, with curd, "unbroken grains" (barley), fragrant flowers, and incense, he performs the "worship of the deities"—the adoration of the gods and the Lord of the Field <note>Kshetrapala, the guardian deity of the land</note>. Then, having "honored" or fully worshipped the "architects" <term>Sthapatis</term> <note>master builders or traditional architects</note> and the Brahmins. [97]

"The Brahmin, touching his head" etc.: If the master of the house is a Brahmin, he should touch his own head and then draw the customary line with whatever desired object. And so on...

# Chapter on the Science of Architecture (Vastu-Vidya)

A member of the warrior class <note>Kshatriya</note> should touch his chest, a member of the merchant class <note>Vaishya</note> his thighs, and a member of the laboring class <note>Shudra</note> his feet before drawing the initial line at the start of house construction. ||98||

Having established that, the author describes the characteristics of the act:

> One should draw the line with the thumb, the middle finger, or the index finger. Using gold, gems, silver, pearls, curd, fruit, flowers, or unbroken grains <note>Akshata; usually consecrated rice</note> brings good fortune. ||99||

> Drawing with a weapon leads to death by a weapon; with iron, imprisonment; with ashes, fear of fire. Drawing with grass leads to fear of thieves, and a line scratched with wood brings fear of the king <note>legal or governmental trouble</note>. ||100||

> A crooked line, or one drawn with the foot, brings fear of enemies and distress; so too does a misshapen line. Lines made with hide, charcoal, bone, or teeth lead to misfortune for the master of the house. ||101||

> A line drawn toward the left <note>counter-clockwise</note> causes enmity; those drawn toward the right <note>clockwise</note> indicate the coming of wealth. Harsh words, spitting, or sneezing at this time are declared inauspicious. ||102||

If the master of the house <note>Grihapati</note> draws that line, he should use the thumb, the middle finger, or the index finger. <gloss>The index finger is the second after the thumb; the middle is the third; the ring finger is the fourth; and the pinky is the fifth.</gloss> If he draws it using gold, or a gem, or silver, or pearls, or curd, or fruits such as the wood-apple <note>Shriphala</note>, or flowers, or unbroken grains like barley—if he uses any of these, it brings auspiciousness and welfare to the master. ||99||

Regarding "with a weapon": If he draws that line with a weapon, then the death of the house-owner will occur by a weapon. Similarly, iron leads to "bondage" or imprisonment. Ashes lead to "fear of fire" or the danger of conflagration. Grass leads to "fear of thieves" or the danger of robbers. A line scratched with wood causes "fear of the king" or danger from the authorities. ||100||

A line that is "crooked" (unclear) or "drawn with the foot" gives rise to fear of enemies and various distresses. A "misshapen" line—one that is either invisible or not pleasing to the mind and eye—also brings fear of enemies and distress. If the line is made with "hide" (leather), "charcoal," "bone," or "teeth," it results in "misfortune" (lack of well-being) for the master or owner of the house. ||101||

A line drawn "toward the left" (counter-clockwise) from one's own position creates enmity. For a line drawn "toward the right" (clockwise), one should predict "wealth" or prosperity. <gloss>A clockwise line is one moved from the left side toward the right side.</gloss> Furthermore, at the time of the inquiry, "harsh words" (rough or illogical speech), "spitting" (releasing phlegm from the mouth), or "sneezing" (sound from the nose) are "declared" or said to be inauspicious and undesirable. ||102||

Now, wishing to explain <term>Shalyajnana</term> <note>the knowledge of hidden obstacles or foreign objects beneath the ground</note>, the author first gives the rule for that:

> When the house is half-finished or completed, the <term>Sthapati</term> <note>the master architect/builder</note> entering the house should observe the omens: where the <term>Grihapati</term> <note>the master of the house</note> is standing and which part of his body he touches. ||103||

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary
## [Chapter 52]

**If a bird, illuminated by the sun, cries out with a harsh sound at that time, then a bone corresponding to the body part touched [by the owner] should be declared to be in that spot. || 104 ||**

Whether a house is half-finished or fully completed, the architect <note>original: *sthapati*</note> entering therein should observe the omens and signs. He should note where the house-owner <note>original: *grihapati*</note> is standing, on which part of the "Vastu Purusha" <note>the symbolic cosmic man underlying the floor plan</note> he is positioned, and which part of his own body he is touching.

This is further explained regarding the "sun-illuminated" direction. Here, the characteristics of the "blazing" <note>dipta</note> directions are explained as follows: From sunrise until the end of the first watch <note>term: *prahara* — a period of about 3 hours</note> of the day, the Northeast is "burning," the East is "blazing," and the Southeast is "smoking"; the remaining five directions are "calm." After the first watch until the end of the second watch, the East is burning, the Southeast is blazing, and the South is smoking; the rest are calm. After the second watch until the end of the third watch, the Southeast is burning, the South is blazing, and the Southwest is smoking; the rest are calm. After the third watch until sunset, the South is burning, the Southwest is blazing, and the West is smoking; the rest are calm. After sunset until the first watch of the night, the Southwest is burning, the West is blazing, and the Northwest is smoking; the rest are calm. After the first watch of the night until the second watch, the West is burning, the Northwest is blazing, and the North is smoking; the rest are calm. After the second watch until the third watch of the night, the Northwest is burning, the North is blazing, and the Northeast is smoking; the rest are calm. After the third watch of the night until sunrise, the North is burning, the Northeast is blazing, and the East is smoking; the remaining five are calm.

At the time of entering the house, if a bird <note>original: *shakuni*</note> situated in the direction that is "blazing" due to the sun and facing the sun cries out with a harsh or rough sound, then a bone <note>original: *asthi*</note> originating from the same body part that the house-owner touched should be declared to be buried in the ground where the owner is standing. The Master <note>Varahamihira</note> has not explicitly stated the depth here. However, it is implied by the phrase "corresponding to the body part touched." This indicates that the depth of the extraneous substance <note>term: *shalya* — hidden defects or bones under the foundation</note> in the ground is proportional to the size of that body part. As stated in another tradition:

-> Whatever part of his own body the house-owner touches at the time of inquiry, <-
-> one should declare a hidden bone from that body part at a depth of one cubit in the earth. <-
-> || 103-104 || <-

He says something further:

**Or if at the time of the omen, other animals such as elephants, horses, or dogs cry out in response, then a bone from that animal, originating from the corresponding body part, is present there. || 105 ||**

At the time of the omen, if other living beings like elephants, horses, dogs, etc. [make noise]...

# Chapter on the Science of Architecture
## Chapter 52

An elephant, a horse, or dogs—"dogs" refers to the domestic canine, and the term "etcetera" includes camels, goats, sheep, cats, and so on. If these animals cry out or make a sound—specifically, if any of these animals cry out while facing the sun <note>original: "ravi-dipta," meaning the direction illuminated by the sun, often considered an intense or "blazing" omen</note> at the time an omen is sought—then a "thorn" <note>original: "shalya," referring to hidden underground impurities like bones or charcoal that must be removed</note> originating from that specific animal is present in that location. The bone will be found at a spot corresponding to the body part of the householder <note>original: "grha-bhartr"</note> that he happens to be touching at that moment. The depth of the object is to be determined as previously described. ||105||

**The author says further—**
->If a donkey brays while the measuring line is being stretched out, it indicates a bone-thorn.<-
->If a dog or a jackal leaps over the measuring line, a thorn must be pointed out.<- ||106||

If the braying or sound of a donkey (a burro) is heard while the measuring line is being laid out, it tells of or indicates a <term>bone-thorn</term> <note>original: "asthi-shalya," specifically a skeletal remain buried underground</note>. Alternatively, if the line is jumped over or crossed by a dog or a jackal, a bone-thorn originating from that animal should be declared. The location corresponds to the body part touched by the householder, and the depth is as stated before. ||106||

**Now, he describes the knowledge of auspicious omens—**
->When a bird chirps sweetly in a "peaceful" direction, then it should be announced:<-
->There is wealth in that spot, or at the part of the body occupied by the lord of the house.<- ||107||

At that time, if a bird chirps a sweet melody in a "peaceful" direction <note>original: "shanta-dish," a direction not facing the sun or wind, considered calm and favorable</note>, then wealth <note>original: "artha," meaning money or treasure</note> should be predicted at the spot where the bird is perched. Alternatively, it may be predicted at the part of the "Vastu-Man" <note>the symbolic "Site Person" or spirit of the plot</note> corresponding to the limb the householder is touching. The manual science <note>the method of measurement</note> is as previously mentioned regarding the touched limb.

In the initial digging of the earth, the depth of that "thorn" should be declared as equal to the height of the householder standing with his arms raised. And so says **Garga** <note>an ancient legendary sage and astronomer</note>:

> At the time of inquiry, on which limb is the householder standing?
> Which limb does he touch, or what auspicious or inauspicious thing does he say?
> The master builder <note>original: "sthapati"</note> should first observe this, and afterwards investigate the hidden thorn.
> The sounds of conches, kettledrums, clay drums, and war drums;
> The sight of yogurt, unbroken grain, flowers, and fruits;
> A scholar expert in the knowledge of architecture should announce the thorn to the inquirer based on these.
> If a bird situated in a "blazing" direction <note>facing the sun</note> makes a harsh sound,
> One should point out a thorn resembling the touched limb at that location.

> One should dig the earth at the spot where a limb of the <term>Prashna-Purusha</term><note>The "Question Personified," a divinatory figure mapped onto the ground</note> is touched or submerged; there, one should certainly declare the presence of an <term>Shalya</term><note>A "thorn" or foreign object buried in the ground, such as bone or charcoal, believed to cause bad luck</note> beneath.

## Now, he describes other signs of good and bad fortune:

> If the measuring cord breaks, death follows; if the foundation peg is driven in face-down, great disease occurs. If the master of the house or the architects suffer a lapse of memory, death is to be predicted. — Verse 108
> If the water-pot slips from the shoulder, a headache occurs; if it is overturned, there is a calamity for the lineage. If the pot breaks, the workmen die; if it slips from the hand, the master of the house dies. — Verse 109

While the measuring cord is being stretched out, if it happens to break, then the master of the house dies. Likewise, while the foundation peg is being driven in, if it goes in "face-down" (upside down), the master of the house suffers a great illness. Furthermore, when a lapse of memory or confusion occurs for the master of the house or the <term>Sthapatis</term><note>Master builders or architects</note>, then their own death should be predicted. — Commentary on Verse 108

While the <term>Kumbha</term><note>A ceremonial water pot used in rituals</note> is being carried, if it slips or moves from the shoulder, the master of the house will suffer from head pains. If it is overturned (turned upside down), there is an "upstroke" or calamity for his entire family. If the pot breaks, there is the "slaying of the workers"—meaning the death of the laborers. If the pot falls after slipping from the hand, the master of the house dies. — Commentary on Verse 109

## Now, he speaks to demonstrate the laying of the foundation stone:

> <margin>1. Another reading says: "In the North-East."</margin> Having performed worship in the South-East corner, one should first lay the foundation stone. The remaining stones and the pillars should be raised in a clockwise direction. — Verse 110
> Accompanied by umbrellas, garlands, and garments, and treated with incense and ointments, the pillar should be raised; the raising of the doorframe should likewise be done with great effort. — Verse 111

In the South-East corner (the direction of Agni, the fire god), after performing worship and offerings with garlands, scents, incense, clothing, gold, wine, meat, and other gifts, one should first place the foundation stone. The remaining stones are to be laid in a clockwise sequence. This means: having laid the stone in the South-East, one then proceeds to the South...

Then, one should perform the laying of the foundation stones <term>Shilanyasa; the ritual placement of the first stones of a structure</term> in the southwest, then in the west, then in the northwest, then in the north, then in the northeast, and finally in the eastern direction. Some authorities read that one should first perform the worship and lay the stone in the northeast corner. It is observed among master builders <term>sthapati; traditional architects and master craftsmen</term> in the world that after first laying the foundation stone in the northeast—the quarter of the Lord <note>Ishana-kona</note>—the remaining stones are then laid in a clockwise direction. The pillars should also be raised in this same manner; just as the foundation stones were laid, the raising of the pillars must be carried out accordingly.

The text now describes the specific rewards and methods for pillars and doors: A pillar should be raised while adorned with a parasol, garlands, and cloths. Likewise, it should be offered incense and scented pastes. In that very same manner and with great effort, the raising of the doorframe should be performed. This means that just as a pillar is raised while decorated with a parasol, garlands, and cloth, and treated with incense and ointment, the door must be raised similarly. As the sage Garga says:

->At the time of laying the foundation stones, one should prepare the ritual materials:<-
->Gems born of the ocean, gold, and silver;<-
->All types of seeds, perfumes, reeds, and sacred Darbha grass;<-
->White flowers, clarified butter, Ketaki flowers, and yellow pigment <note>Gorochana; a bright yellow pigment used for tilaks, traditionally said to come from a cow</note>;<-
->Meat, wine, and various kinds of fruits.<-
->One should place pots filled with milk-rice in every corner.<-
->Various kinds of foods and diverse drinks should be offered.<-
->Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules at the auspicious moment provided,<-
->And having performed the worship in all corners of the house according to the ordinance,<-
->Then, with the sound of "Auspicious Day!" <note>Punyahaghosha; a ritual proclamation of a day's sanctity</note>, one should carry out the laying of the stones.<-
->Starting from the northeast, one should place them in a clockwise direction.<-
->By this very same ordinance, the lowering <insert>or fixing</insert> of the pillars and doors<-
->Should be performed by one who knows the rules of architectural science <term>Vastu-vidya</term>, with a concentrated mind.<-
->This is the mantra for laying the foundation stones, specified by the ancient sages:<-
->“O Nanda! O daughter of Vashishtha! O you who are beneficial to progeny through the Vasus!<-
->O long-lasting one, O giver of joy, O Nanda! O daughter of Vashishtha! May you delight in this house!<-
->O Bhadra! O descendant of Kashyapa! Bring auspiciousness to this worship.<-
->O fortunate one of good vows, O Goddess! O daughter of Kashyapa! May you delight in this house!<-
->O Jaya! O descendant of Bhrigu! Bring auspiciousness to the people.<-
->O Goddess, creator of prosperity! O daughter of Bhrigu! May you delight in this house!”<-

### Regarding the Characteristics of the Gnomon—

->From trees such as the Nyagrodha <note>Banyan</note>, Bilva, Khadira,<-
->Shami, Vata, Udumbara, Devadaru <note>Himalayan Cedar</note>, or other milky and fruit-bearing trees native to the land, grown in pleasant soil;<-
->the craftsman, having fasted, should take a sharp axe and cut from the middle of these.<-
->Then, in the northern direction of the Lord of the Quarters, under an auspicious astrological sign, he should take the gnomon.<-
->Measuring one cubit <note>approx. 18-24 inches</note>, and four others at half that measure,<-
->he should take them and keep them in the house until the time for the consecration of this gnomon.<-
->The first is called *Nanda* <note>Joyful</note> in the northeast corner; the second is *Subhaga* <note>Fortunate</note> in the southeast;<-
->*Sumangali* <note>Auspicious</note> is placed in the southwest; and *Bhadrakari* <note>Prosperity-bringer</note> goes to the northwest corner.<-
->The selection of these stones—Nanda and the others—marked with the footprints of a bull, horse, or the Pun-naga flower,<-
->unbroken, firm, and possessing good characteristics, has been described.<-
->The Tortoise, the Serpent Shesha, Janardana <note>Vishnu</note>, Lakshmi, and Dhruva <note>the North Star/Fixed point</note> are established in the center of the house.<-
->The lords of the doors, the guardians of the directions, and the elephants of the quarters are to be worshipped with offerings and sacred mantras.<-
->Having worshipped the gnomon with baths, water offerings, garlands, clothes, incense, and ointments,<-
->and having dug at the fixed stone, one should establish the gnomon and the ritual pot.<-
->Filling it completely with parched grain, unbroken rice, grains, the five products of the cow, honey, and clarified butter,<-
->one should perform the ritual according to the rules with the Rig-Veda hymns <note>original: "ऋग्भिस्तथैव"</note>; the fire sacrifice should be performed to the north of the fixed point.<-

### Now, the Purification of the Ascendant <note>Auspicious timing</note>—

->The establishment of a residence is best done when the sun is in Sagittarius, Libra, Taurus, Gemini, Virgo, or Aquarius.<-
->The fourth house is called the house of the residence; if it is a water-sign, they declare it auspicious.<-
->If this is not possible, those who know the transcendental sciences say a combination of Venus and the Moon is acceptable.<-
->The ritual should be done in the sub-division <note>Navamsha</note> of these signs, in an auspicious lunar mansion, avoiding the 12th, 8th, and trine houses of the patron.<-

When Venus and Mercury are situated in the center <note>the 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses</note>, the trines <note>the 5th or 9th houses</note>, the eleventh house of gain, or the second house of wealth, and are not in the twelfth house of loss, the house will be prosperous, sturdy, and filled with people. If Mercury and Jupiter are in the twelfth or third houses, prosperity is likewise predicted.

The same positive result should always be declared when the Sun, Mars, and Saturn are in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses. If these planets are positioned otherwise, one should specifically expect danger from thieves, fire, wounds, disease, and lethargy.

When the Moon is in the third, fourth, sixth, or eleventh house from the Ascendant, the house should be built; it will be filled with women, wealth, grain, and servants. If the Moon is in other positions, the results are contrary, though a house built under an excellent lunar mansion <note>Nakshatra</note> may overcome these defects.

The formal entry into the house for Brahmins and the other castes should be performed as previously described. However, for the entry of cattle, goats, sheep, and vehicles, it may be done without the requirement of "fixed" signs, provided it is done during their own auspicious eighth astrological divisions.

### Now, the Vedic Hymns—

I shall now describe in due order the Vedic hymns <note>Mantras</note> prescribed for the "Fixed" pillar <note>Dhruva</note>, the Spirit of the Site <note>Vāstuna-puruṣa</note>, and the joints of the doors.

"May the sacrifice consisting of the Tortoise-hymn increase during the offering ritual." For the Serpent-King Śeṣa, use "Salutations to the serpents"; for Janārdana <note>Viṣṇu</note>, use "This [step] Viṣṇu [strode]."

For the Fixed pillar, the hymn "May your glories go toward glory" is remembered. For the Sun-god Savitṛ, the wise say the hymn is "Savitṛ, the producer of glories," which is also used for the Gnomon <note>Śaṅku, the central ritual pillar</note>.

### Now, the Deities of the Gnomon—

For Brahma, use "Brahma was first born"; for Aryaman, use "May they go to Aryaman." For Vivasvat, use "Savitṛ, the producer of glories."

For Indra, "Indra is the measurer" should be recited; for Mitra, "Mitra’s ointment" is remembered. For Rudra, the hymn "O Rudra, be gracious to us" is proclaimed.

For Bhūdhara <note>the Earth-holder</note>, use "Stay right here"; for Rambhara, use "The great horse." Thus are the thirteen deities of the Spirit of the Site proclaimed.

Regarding the gods in the four directions for the collection of door-hymns: the hymns for the stars were told previously; now hear the auspicious verses.

For the Nandini door, use "That Rudra who is in the fire"; for Subhagā, use "For the offering"; for Sumangalī, use "The auspicious woman"; for Bhadrikā, use "May we hear with our ears what is auspicious."

I shall now describe the offerings <note>Bali</note> for these: milk-rice, curd, sweetmeats, clarified butter, milk, parched grain, fried grain, unbroken rice, and fruits.

One should perform the fire-oblation <note>Homa</note> to the north of the Fixed pillar. With a concentrated mind, one should sacrifice clarified butter while reciting the "Your glory" and other hymns.

->At the time of entry, the ritual is like the *Sthalipaka* <note>original: "स्थालीपाक" - a simple domestic sacrifice of cooked rice</note>.<-
->The fire-oblation should be performed with the hymns of the *Pancharanga-pravahana* <note>A specific set of Vedic verses used for purification</note>.<-
->The baskets of the gods and the verse "From joint to joint" <note>original: "काण्डात्काण्डप्ररोहणम्" - a Vedic verse (Rigveda 10.97.19) used to invoke growth and vitality</note> should be used.<-
->Then the verse "A youth comes with nectar" <note>original: "युवा सुधामेति" - likely referring to the *Yuva Suvasah* hymn</note> should be recited while circumambulating.<-
->The offerings of water for the feet and the guest-offering <note>original: "पाद्यमर्घ्यादिकं"</note> shown in the *Shantikapa* <note>A ritual manual for propitiatory rites</note>—<-
->All of that should be adopted here as it is traditionally heard.<-
->Thus, for the peace of the temple, and in all initiations and sacrifices,<-
->The entry into the construction should be spoken of according to the independent rules. Thus ends the section. [110-111]<-

Now, regarding the pillars and other parts, if animals settle on them, or if they tremble, fall, or are poorly situated:

<margin>He states the result—</margin>
->**If birds and other creatures settle on them, or if they tremble, fall, or are poorly placed,**<-
->**The result specified for them is the same as that for the Banner of Indra.** [112]<-

"Birds" refers to winged creatures. By the word "others," one should include reptiles, honeybees, and so forth. "Settled" <note>original: "अवलीनैः"</note> means clinging to or attached to the pillars or doors. Likewise, if the pillars and such "tremble" (move) or "fall" (go down), the result is "the same as that for the Banner of Indra" <note>original: "शक्रध्वज" - the ceremonial pole raised during the festival of Indra; its movements were used for divination</note>. Whatever good or bad result was stated for Indra's Banner is specified here for the pillars. As it is said regarding Indra's Banner:

> "If vultures, owls, pigeons, crows, or herons stay on the banner, there is great unrest and danger to the King.
> By a blue jay, they say there is danger to the Crown Prince; a hawk falling on it causes eye disease.
> If the ceremonial umbrella breaks or falls, the King dies; honeybees clinging to it bring thieves.
> A meteor strike kills the Royal Priest, and a lightning strike kills the King's Queen.
> A falling flag causes the destruction of the Queen; the falling of the basket causes drought.
> The breaking of the banner at the middle, top, or base kills the Ministers, the King, and the Citizens respectively.
> If covered in smoke, there is danger from fire; if by darkness, there is mental confusion.
> If broken or fallen due to serpents, the Ministers will cease to be.
> If it withers starting from the North, the Brahmins and other castes suffer in order;
> If the 'Maiden' <note>A specific cross-beam on the banner pole</note> breaks, the death of a harlot is foretold.
> By the snapping of the ropes, children suffer; by the crushing of the 'Mother' <note>Another structural part of the pole</note>, the King's mother suffers.
> Whatever the mimes or children do there, such will be the future, whether evil or auspicious."

Everything stated in that context should be applied here to the Master of the House <note>original: "गृहपति" - the owner or patron of the building</note>. [112]

# Chapter 52: The Chapter on the Science of Architecture

<page-num>611</page-num>
->Now, the specific characteristics of the site are described:<-

> **If the site is elevated in the East or North, there is a loss of wealth and sons; if it has a foul smell, there is the death of sons.**
> **If it is crooked, there is the destruction of kinsmen; and if the directions are confused, there are no pregnancies (or loss of the fetus). ||113||**
>
> **If one desires the expansion of the house, then one should expand it equally on all sides.**
> **If there is a fault in a single area, one should make the expansion either in the East or in the North. ||114||**

In a site <term>Vastu (the architectural plot)</term>, if it is elevated in the East or North, there is a loss of wealth and sons. Similarly, in a site that has a foul smell, the death of sons occurs. If it is crooked—meaning it is not properly aligned according to the divisions of the compass—there is the destruction of kinsmen. In a site where the directions are confused <note>original: "dig-mudhe," referring to a plot where the cardinal points cannot be clearly determined</note>, pregnancies do not occur, or they are lost. ||113||

Similarly, elevation in other directions should also be understood to yield undesirable results. Therefore, if one desires the expansion of the house, for that reason, one should expand it equally and uniformly in all directions. If an expansion must be made in a single area—which usually carries a fault—one should do so in the East or in the North. ||114||

Now, regarding what was said—that if there is a fault in a single area, it should be in the East or North—one might ask for what reason this is done. To explain this, the author describes the "minor faults" associated with specific directions:

> **Expansion in the East causes enmity with friends; in the South, there is fear of death.**
> **In the West, there is the destruction of wealth; in the North, expansion causes mental anguish. ||115||**

If an expansion occurs in the East of the site, there is enmity with friends. If the expansion is in the South, there is a fear of death. From expansion in the West, there is the destruction or loss of wealth. From expansion in the North, there is mental anguish or distress of the mind. Because these are considered "minor faults" <note>compared to the total ruin mentioned in verse 113</note>, it was said that if a single-sided expansion must be made, it should be in the East or North. ||115||

Next, the author describes what should be placed in which direction within a <term>Chatushala (a house with four halls surrounding a central courtyard)</term>:

> **The house of the gods (shrine) should be in the Northeast, and the kitchen should be made in the Southeast.**
> **Household utensils and furniture should be in the Southwest, and wealth and grain in the Northwest. ||116||**

In a four-hall house, the shrine <note>original: "deva-griham," a room for worship</note> should be made in the Northeast. In the Southeast, the kitchen <note>original: "mahanasam," the place for cooking</note> should be located. In the Southwest, the household utensils and furniture...

The placement of household items should be performed accordingly. In the North-West direction <note>Marutya/Vayavya</note>, the storage of wealth, money, and grains should be situated.

Here, the Teacher <note>Varahamihira</note> has spoken of the general divisions; however, in the treatise known as the *Kirana*, a more specific breakdown is recited. As follows:

->The room for prosperity <note>Shrigriha; likely a reception or treasury room</note> is said to be in the East; the kitchen in the South-East.<-
->The bedroom in the South, and the armory in the South-West.<-

->The Elephant <note>Bhadra</note> always in the place of goods; and the Empty <note>Rikta</note> in the house of the gods. Thus it is said.<- || 116 ||

### Now he speaks of the auspicious and inauspicious results of water according to the directions:

->Water situated in the East and other directions leads to: loss of sons, fear of fire, and fear of enemies;<-
->Quarrels with women, wickedness of women, poverty, and the increase of wealth and progeny.<- || 117 ||

If water is situated in the East of the site, there is loss of sons (death of children). Likewise, in the South-East, there is fear of "the crested one" <note>Shikhibhaya; meaning fire</note>. In the South, fear of enemies. In the South-West, quarrels with women (disaffection of women). In the West, wickedness of women (madness or bad character). In the North-West, poverty (lack of wealth). In the North, an increase of wealth. In the North-East, an increase of progeny (sons) occurs. || 117 ||

### Now he says that one should cut other trees for the sake of the house, excluding these specific ones:

->Those that are dwellings for birds, broken, dried up, burnt, or located in temples or cemeteries;<-
->And excluding milky trees, Dhava, Vibhitaka, Nimba, and Arani—one may cut the others.<- || 118 ||

Where birds have their dwelling (home) on a tree; also a tree that is broken; one that is burnt (scorched by fire); one located in a temple (situated in the house of a god); or situated in a cemetery. Likewise, "milky trees" <note>Kshirataru; trees that exude sap, such as the Peepal</note>, the *Dhava* <note>Anogeissus latifolia</note>, the *Vibhitaka* <note>Terminalia bellirica</note>, the *Nimba* <note>Neem</note>, and the *Arani* <note>Premna serratifolia</note>—excluding these trees, one should cut and prepare the remaining others. || 118 ||

# Now he describes the characteristics of tree-cutting and the knowledge of auspicious and inauspicious signs based on how it falls—

> Having performed offerings and worship at night, one should fell the tree during the day in a clockwise direction.
> Falling toward the North or East is auspicious; if it falls otherwise, it should not be accepted. ||119|| <note>The verse number 199 in the source appears to be a typo for 119 based on the subsequent numbering.</note>

One should fell the tree—the timber—during the day, having performed <term>Bali-puja</term> (the ritual offering of food and worship) at night. The cutting should be done in a clockwise manner, starting from the North-East and proceeding through the East, South-East, South, South-West, West, North-West, and ending in the North. If the intended tree falls toward the North or the East, it is considered "blessed" or excellent. If it falls otherwise—meaning in any of the remaining directions—it should not be accepted; it must be rejected. ||119||

# Now he describes the auspicious and inauspicious signs regarding "foreign bodies" (defects) within the tree—

> If the cut surface is natural in appearance, then that wood is auspicious and fit for a house.
> But if a yellow circular mark is seen, one should predict a monitor lizard residing in the middle of the tree. ||120||
> If the mark is the color of madder, there is a frog; if blue, a snake; if reddish, a chameleon.
> If it is the color of mung bean, there is a stone; if brownish, a mouse; and if it looks like a sword (dark), there is water. ||121||

If the cut of the tree is "without alteration"—meaning free from unnatural discolorations—then for that reason, that wood is auspicious and suitable for use in a house. If, upon the cut surface of the tree, a yellow circular mark is seen (deviating from its natural appearance), then one should declare that a <term>Godha</term> (a monitor lizard, a specific type of creature) is situated inside the middle of the tree. ||120||

Similarly, if a mark the color of <term>Manjistha</term> (madder, a reddish-purple dye) is seen, there is a frog. In a blue circle, there is a snake. In the same manner, in a reddish or tawny circle, there is a <term>Sarata</term> (a specific creature, which some identify as a chameleon). In a mark resembling the color of <term>Mudga</term> (mung bean), there is a stone. In a brownish-grey mark, a mouse. In a mark resembling a sword—meaning dark or blackish—water is to be known as being inside the tree. The same signs apply to stones and other materials. ||121||

# Now he states the rules of conduct for the master of the house—

> One who desires prosperity should not sleep above grain, cows, teachers, fire, or the gods; nor should one sleep parallel to the main beam.
> One should not sleep with the head toward the North or West, nor naked, nor with wet feet. ||122||

One desiring <term>Shri</term> (prosperity or the goddess Lakshmi) should not sleep on top of—meaning above the position of—grains (such as rice), cows, teachers (or elders), fire, or the gods. The beams have been mentioned—

->From the Disease-deity to the Ancestors, from the Fire-deity to the Withering-thread, and from Wealth;<-
->From the Chief to the Intense, from the Victorious to the Large Bee, and from the Infinite to the Beautiful-Necked.<-
<note>These names refer to specific points or deities on the Vastu Purusha Mandala (the sacred architectural grid). The verse describes the alignment of structural beams (Vamshas).</note>

One should not sleep by placing a bed across these beams or following their alignment in a way that intersects them.
<margin>One should sleep.</margin>
One should not sleep with the head facing the North or the West. One should not sleep naked or while wearing daytime clothes. Furthermore, one should never sleep with wet feet. Additionally, a householder should sleep in such a way that there are no "elephant-tusks" <term>Nagadanta: wooden wall-pegs or brackets used for hanging items</term> located at the foot of the bed. As Vishwakarma <note>The divine architect of the gods</note> says:

->A bed placed directly under a main beam destroys the family.<-
->A bed placed in line with the house's orientation is fine, but wall-pegs at the foot bring ruin.<-

### **Now he describes the characteristics of entering the house—**

->One should enter a house scattered with many flowers, adorned with arched gateways and jars filled with water;<-
->Where the gods have been honored with incense, perfumes, and offerings, and which resounds with the chanting of Brahmins.<-

One should enter such a house. What kind? One where there is a "scattering of many flowers," meaning a collection of various types of blossoms. Also, "with arched gateways," meaning one should construct ceremonial arches <term>Torana</term> at the front of the house. It should be "adorned with jars filled with water," meaning decorated with water-pots. It should be a place where the "gods are honored" or worshipped with "incense" such as Guggulu, "perfumes" such as Aguru (aloeswood), and "offerings" (sacrificial gifts). It should also be "joined with the sound of Brahmins," meaning the sound of the Vedas being chanted by the twice-born. Here, "honoring the gods" is mentioned generally; however, it refers to the deities residing within the center of the Vastu plot, not the external ones like the Fire-god, the Rain-cloud, or Aryaman. It is also stated in other treatises:

> For the success of the master's work, there are forty-five gods <note>literally "nine times five"</note>;
> Because they reside there entirely, from the head to the limbs of the Vastu-deity.
> Even more specific external gods were mentioned by Hiranyagarbha <note>a name for Brahma, the Creator</note>.
> I shall proclaim the deities of the dwellings in order:
> One should know the Lord of Creatures (Prajapati) at the door, and the Lord of Uma (Shiva) in the doorway area.
> Balarama and Yama are situated in the Southern direction.
> Skanda, Shesha, and Varuna are situated in the Western direction.
> The Adityas, Vasus, and Rudras have taken refuge in the Northern direction.

<meta>Chapter 53]</meta>

Lord Brahma and Mahendra <note>The King of the Gods, Indra</note> are established in the Eastern direction. Glory, Fortitude, and Prosperity reside in the center of the dwelling site. A wise man, having performed the fire sacrifice in the center of the house, should worship the deities in all the intermediate points and the cardinal directions in their proper order. Having performed the worship of the family deities for the householders, one should worship all the goddesses in the cardinal and intermediate directions in sequence.

->And so it is read in another treatise (Tantra):<-

The priest, according to the prescribed rites, should worship all the external and internal deities as they are situated within the site. Thus it is said. ||123||

->In the "Great Ocean of Architecture" composed by the teacher Varahamihira,<-
->Utpala has created this "Boat of Commentary" for seekers to attain their desires.<-

->Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, named "The Science of Architecture,"<-
->in the Commentary on the Samhita composed by the venerable Bhattotpala.||52||<-

## Now, Water Divination is Explained.

->### First, the author speaks to demonstrate the purpose of this study:<-

> I shall now describe "Water Divination," through which the discovery of water is made—a subject that brings religious merit and fame. Just as there are veins <term>shira: channels or vessels</term> within the bodies of men, situated at various depths (some high, some low), so too are they arranged within the earth. ||1||
>
> Water falling from the sky possesses but a single color and a single taste, yet it acquires various tastes and multiple colors due to the specific characteristics of the soil. Therefore, the water should be examined in relation to the earth it occupies. ||2||

"Now," meaning after this section on the Science of Architecture, I, Varahamihira, "describe" or speak of Water Divination <note>original: "Dakargalam"</note>. Of what nature is it? It is "meritorious and famous," meaning it brings about religious merit and bestows renown. Why is it called Water Divination? To this he says: "through which the discovery of water" <note>original: "jalaupalabdhih"</note>—the finding or obtaining of water—is achieved. "Just as," or in the same manner that "veins" (vessels) exist "within the bodies" or limbs of "men" (human beings) "situated at various depths" in a high or low state, "so too" in that same manner, they are "within the earth" (the ground) situated at various depths; some are high (near the surface) and others are low (deep). ||1||

Regarding "with a single color": Water <note>original: "ambhas"</note> falling from "the sky" (the atmosphere) possesses a single color and a single "taste" (flavor). However, "due to the specific characteristics of the soil," because the earth is of many types, it attains "various tastes" (multiple flavors) and "multiple colors." It is to be "examined" as being "equal to the earth" <note>meaning the water takes on the properties of the soil it flows through</note>...

In this manner, the varied colors of the earth should be examined and considered as equal to the color of the ground, according to its various tastes and colors. As the author will state later:

> "Copper-colored earth mixed with gravel produces an astringent taste; reddish-brown earth produces a potash-like <note>alkaline</note> taste. In pale-white earth, saltiness is predicted, while in blue-colored earth, the water is desired for its sweetness." <note>original: "sasharkara tamramahi..." - this refers to verse 104 of this chapter</note> || 2 ||

### Now, the general description of the water veins:

Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirriti, Varuna, Vayu, Soma, and Shiva are the gods to be known, in order, as the lords of the directions starting from the East. || 3 ||

The veins are designated by the names of these directional lords, and the ninth one in the center is named the "Great Vein" <term>Mahashira (the primary central water source)</term>. From these, hundreds of others have branched out, famous by various names. || 4 ||

The vein that rises upward from the netherworld <note>Patala</note> is auspicious, as are those situated in the four cardinal directions. Those originating from the intermediate corners <note>the diagonal directions like Northeast or Southwest</note> are not auspicious. Hereafter, I shall describe the signs of these veins. || 5 ||

Indra and the other gods are, in sequence, the lords or masters of the directions beginning with the East. Specifically: Indra is the lord of the East; Agni <note>Anala</note> of the Southeast; Yama, the lord of the ancestors, of the South; Nirriti, the lord of demons, of the Southwest; Varuna, the lord of waters, of the West; Vayu <note>Pavana</note> of the Northwest; Soma <note>Indu/The Moon</note> of the North; and Shiva <note>Shankara/Rudra</note> of the Northeast. || 3 ||

A vein is identified by the name of the lord of that direction. For example, the vein in the East is called *Aindri* (belonging to Indra), in the Southeast it is *Agneyi*, and in the South it is *Yamya*. The rest should be understood in the same way. Thus, there are eight veins in the eight directions. The ninth, in the middle, is named the *Mahashira*. In the center of all these cardinal and intermediate locations, the ninth, the Great Vein, exists. From these nine, hundreds of other types of veins have branched out and emerged, which are well-known by their specific names and designations. As will be stated:

> "The vein named *Kumuda* flows at a depth of three man-lengths." <note>original: "kumuda nama shira..." - refers to verse 23 of this chapter</note> || 4 ||

The vein that rises upward from the netherworld is auspicious, and those veins situated in the four cardinal directions are also auspicious. Veins arising from the corner directions (intermediate points) are not auspicious. Following this, I shall describe the "vein-signs" <note>shira-nimittani</note> or the indicators of these water veins. || 5 ||

The author explains those signs:

### If a Cane tree is found in a waterless region, then three cubits to the west of it,
### at a depth of one and a half *Purusha*, water flows in a western vein. [6]
### The signs are: at half a *Purusha* depth, a pale frog and yellow earth are found;
### there is also "split-rock" <note>original: "Putabhedaka," a type of layered stone that breaks easily into sheets</note> in that spot, and water lies beneath. [7]

In a waterless region—that is, a place naturally devoid of water, such as a desert—if a Cane tree <note>original: "Vetasa"</note> is seen, then at a distance of three cubits <note>original: "Hasta," the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</note> to the west of that tree, and at a depth of one and a half *Purusha* <note>a unit of measurement based on a man's height</note> when excavated, one should declare that there is water. By the word *Purusha*, one should understand here a man with his arms raised. The standard definition used everywhere is that this measures 120 digits <note>approximately 7.5 feet</note>. In that excavation, a western vein of water flows.

The signs at a depth of half a *Purusha* are as follows: A frog <note>original: "Manduka"</note> that is pale or slightly white in color. Following that, yellow-colored earth. Then, in that pit, there is "split-rock" stone. It is called "split-rock" because it breaks apart in layers <note>original: "putai-bhidyata"</note>. Beneath that is the water. Thus says the sage Sarasvata:

> Seeing a Cane tree in a waterless place, three cubits
> to the west of that tree, water is known to be at a depth of one and a half.
> A *Purusha* here is declared to be twice sixty digits.
> Digging there to half a *Purusha*, a pale-colored frog appears;
> Yellow earth and split-rock stone follow, then water.
> One should point out that a water-vein situated in the west flows there.

He mentions another:

### Three cubits to the north of a Jamun tree, a vein flows eastward at a depth of two *Purusha*.
### The earth smells like iron and is pale; at one *Purusha* depth, there is a frog. [8]

In a waterless region, if a Jamun tree <note>original: "Jambu"</note> is seen, then three cubits to the north of that tree, at a depth of two *Purusha*, an eastern vein flows. Here too there are signs. At one *Purusha* depth, the earth smells like iron. After that, it is pale or slightly white, and then a frog is found. [8]

He mentions another:

### If an anthill is found near a Jamun tree to its east,
### then on the southern side of that anthill, sweet water is found at a depth of two *Purusha*. [9]

# Chapter 53: On Water Divination

->**At the depth of half a "man," there is a fish and a stone resembling a pigeon. The soil there is blue, and there is plenty of water for a long time. ||10||**<-

If an anthill <note>Sanskrit: *valmika*, often associated with underground moisture in ancient Indian hydrology</note> is found near a Jambu tree <note>The Rose Apple tree (*Syzygium cumini*)</note> to its east, then one should measure three cubits <note>Sanskrit: *hasta*, the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</note> to the south of that Jambu tree. Where the master does not specify a particular measurement, the previously mentioned standard should be applied everywhere—this is the tradition. Thus, at a distance of three cubits and a depth of two "men" <note>Sanskrit: *purusha*, a unit of depth roughly equal to the height of a man with his arms raised, approx. 120 digits</note>, there is sweet water.

There are also signs there: at a depth of half a "man," a fish is seen. Then a stone appears that is the color of a pigeon. Furthermore, the soil there is blue in color. There will be abundant water for a very long time. As the sage Sarasvata says:

> If an anthill is seen to the east of a Jambu tree,
> One should declare water to be three cubits to the south of the tree.
> At two "men" depth; at half a "man" there is a fish and a stone like a bird,
> Then the soil is blue; then one should declare the water to be sweet. ||9-10||

**He says another thing:**

->**To the west of an Udumbara tree, at exactly three cubits and a depth of two and a half "men," there is a white snake and a stone like collyrium; below is a vein of good water. ||11||**<-

If an Udumbara tree <note>The Cluster Fig tree (*Ficus racemosa*)</note> is seen in a waterless region, whether it is joined with an anthill or not, then at a distance of three cubits to the west of that Udumbara, at a depth of two and a half "men," there is a vein of excellent water. Here too are the signs: at a depth of half a "man," a white snake is seen. Then a stone appears like collyrium <note>Sanskrit: *anjana*, a black mineral used as eye-liner</note>, meaning it is very black. Below that, a vein of beautiful water flows. ||11||

**He says another thing:**

->**If an anthill is visible to the north of an Arjuna tree, then water is found three cubits to the west of that Arjuna at a depth of three and a half "men." ||12||**<-

->**At half a "man" there is a white lizard; at one "man" the soil is grey, then black, then yellow, then white with sand; then one should point out immeasurable water. ||13||**<-

If an anthill is seen to the north of an Arjuna tree <note>*Terminalia arjuna*</note>, then at a distance of three cubits to the west of this Arjuna, at a depth of three and a half "men," there is water. ||12||

Regarding the white color: Here are the signs. When the earth is dug to the depth of half a <term>Purusha</term> <note>A "Purusha" or "man-length" is a traditional unit of measurement, approximately 6 feet or the height of a man with his arms raised.</note>, a white-colored <term>Godha</term> <note>An iguana or large monitor lizard.</note> is seen. At the depth of one man, the soil is grey (a mix of black and white). Below that, the earth is black. Then, it becomes yellow-colored. Below that, it is white and sandy. Beyond that, one should declare there is an immeasurable and abundant supply of water. !!13!!

He says another thing—

->If a <term>Nirgundi</term> tree is covered by an anthill, then three cubits to the south,<-

->Then comes sand mixed with gravel, and then, in sequence, water appears.<- !!15!!

The <term>Nirgundi</term> <note>Vitex negundo, a large aromatic shrub.</note> is a specific plant, commonly known in forests. "Covered by an anthill" means it is joined with a mound of earth made by termites. In that case, to the south of the Nirgundi tree, at the distance of the "stated cubits"—meaning three cubits—and at a depth of two and a quarter men, there is sweet, tasty water that is inexhaustible. !!14!!

A <term>Rohita</term> <note>A species of reddish fish, often the Rohu.</note> colored fish is found at half a man's depth. Then the soil is reddish-brown. Beyond that, it is somewhat pale or white. Then comes sand mixed with <term>Sarkara</term> <note>Small pebbles or gravel.</note>. Following this sequence, water is found. !!15!!

He says another thing—

->If an anthill is seen to the east of a <term>Badari</term> tree, water lies to the west.<-
->It should be predicted at a depth of three men; at half a man, a white house-lizard is the sign.<- !!16!!

If an anthill (a mound of earth made by termites) is seen on the eastern side of a <term>Badari</term> <note>The Jujube or Ber tree (Ziziphus mauritiana).</note> tree, then on the western side of that tree—at a distance of three cubits as previously mentioned—water should be declared at a depth of three men. At half a man's depth, a white <term>Griha-godhika</term> is seen. A <term>Griha-godhika</term> is a "wall-fish" or common house gecko. As the authority Sarasvata says:

> If an anthill is seen on the eastern side of a Badari tree, water
> should be declared three cubits to the west at a depth of three men.
> At a depth of half a man, a house-lizard is seen,
> white in color; below that, the water is pure. !!16!!

He says another thing—

->At a depth of three and a quarter men; and at one man's depth, a <term>Dundubha</term> snake is the sign.<- !!17!!

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 53]

The word *cet* <note>original: "चेच्छब्दो"</note> is used in the sense of "if." If, in a waterless region, a Jujube tree <term>Badari: Ziziphus mauritiana</term> is seen growing together with a Flame-of-the-Forest tree <term>Palasha: Butea monosperma</term>, or if it is found near an anthill <term>Valmika</term>, then water exists to the west of that Jujube tree at a distance of three cubits <term>Kara/Hasta: a unit of length, roughly 18 inches</term> and at a depth of three and a quarter man-lengths <term>Purusha: the height of a man with arms upraised, approx. 6-7 feet</term>. The sign found there is as follows: at the depth of one man-length, a *Dundubha* <note>a non-venomous lead-colored water snake</note> is seen. As Sarasvata says:

> ->Where a Jujube is joined with a Palasha, to the west,<-
> ->At a distance of three cubits and a depth of three and a quarter man-lengths, there is water.<-
> ->At one man-length, a non-venomous Dundubha snake is the sign;<-
> ->Below is sweet water that flows for a long time.<-

**He says another thing:**

> ->Where a Wood-apple and a Cluster-fig are joined, leave three cubits to the south;<-
> ->At three man-lengths there is water, and at half a man-length, a black frog. // 18 //<-

Where there is a union of the Wood-apple <term>Bilva: Aegle marmelos</term> and the Cluster-fig <term>Udumbara: Ficus racemosa</term>—meaning where these two trees grow together—one should move three cubits to the south <note>original: "yamya", the direction of Yama</note>. At a depth of three and a half man-lengths, water will be found. At a depth of half a man-length, a black frog is seen. // 18 //

**He says another thing:**

> ->If an anthill is seen on a Ficus Oppositifolia, a water-vein is there;<-
> ->At three and a quarter man-lengths, it flows toward the west. // 19 //<-
> ->The soil is pale yellow and the stone is the color of milk;<-
> ->At half a man-length, a mouse resembling a white water-lily appears. // 20 //<-

The *Kakodumbarika* is the *Phalgu* tree <term>Ficus oppositifolia</term>. Where this is seen, if an anthill—a mound of earth made by termites—is seen nearby, then a water-vein <term>Shira</term> exists right at that anthill. At a depth of three and a quarter man-lengths, that vein flows toward the west. // 19 //

Now for the signs: first, the soil is pale yellow <note>original: "apandu-pitika"</note>. Then, a stone the color of "cow-juice" (milk), meaning white, is found. At a depth of half a man-length, a mouse <term>Mushaka</term> as white as a night-blooming lily <term>Kumuda</term> comes into view. // 20 //

**He says another thing:**

> ->When a Kampillaka tree is seen in a waterless region,<-
> ->A vein flows three cubits to the east, first heading south. // 21 //<-

# Chapter 53 — The Chapter on Water Divining

<page-num>631</page-num>

The *Saptaparna* <note>original: "सप्तपर्ण" (Alstonia scholaris), known as the Blackboard tree or Seven-Leaf tree</note> is a specific type of tree. If it is found in conjunction with an anthill <note>original: "वल्मीक" (valmika); often associated with underground moisture in ancient Indian hydrology</note>, then to the north of that *Saptaparna* tree, at a distance of one cubit <note>term: "हस्त" (hasta) - a unit of measurement roughly 18 inches, the length of a forearm</note>, water should be declared to exist at a depth of five men <note>term: "पुरुष" (purusha) - a unit of depth based on a man's height with arms raised, roughly 6-7 feet</note>. The following signs will appear:

At a depth of half a man, there is a green, parrot-colored frog. Also, the earth there is the color of yellow orpiment <note>original: "हरिताल" (haritala) - arsenic trisulfide, a bright yellow mineral</note>. There is a black stone resembling a cloud. Below that, there is a northern vein carrying auspicious, pure water. As the sage Sarasvata says:

> Where a *Saptaparna* tree is joined with a serpent's home <note>original: "भुजङ्गगृह" (bhujanga-griha) - a poetic term for an anthill</note>,
> To the north, at one cubit's distance, five men deep,
> Water is to be declared. At half a man's depth, a green frog appears.
> The earth is like yellow orpiment, the stone like a cloud; then the vein
> Is known to be in the north, providing good, long-lasting, and sweet water. (Verses 29-30)

He says another thing:

> When a frog is seen sitting beneath any tree,
> Water is one cubit away from it, at a depth of four and a half men. (Verse 31)

> At the depth of one man, there is a mongoose; then blue, yellow, and white soil.
> A stone resembling a frog is seen there. (Verse 32)

Beneath any tree whatsoever, if a frog is seen staying at the root, then to the north of that tree, at a distance of one cubit, water is found at a depth of four and a half men.

The signs here are: at one man's depth of digging, a mongoose appears; then blue soil, then yellow. Then white soil, and then a stone shaped like a frog is seen. Below that is the water.

As Sarasvata says:

> Where a frog stays beneath any tree,
> Water is to the north of the tree, one cubit away, at a depth of
> Four and a half men. At one man's depth, a mongoose and blue soil;
> Then yellow and white, then a stone looking like a frog is seen. (Verses 31-32)

He says another thing:

> If a snake's nest is seen situated to the south of a *Karanja* tree <note>original: "करञ्ज" (Millettia pinnata), the Indian Beech tree</note>,
> Three cubits to the south, at a depth of three and a half men, there is a vein. (Verse 33)

**A tortoise appears at half a man's depth, and first the eastern vein breaks through.**

If a snake's residence—a termite mound—is seen situated to the south of a **Karanja** <note>Indian Beech (Millettia pinnata)</note> tree, then at a distance of two cubits <note>term: Hasta; a measurement from elbow to fingertip, approx. 18 inches</note> to the south of that tree, at a depth of three and a half "men" <note>term: Purusha; a unit of depth based on a man with upstanding arms, approx. 6-7 feet</note>, a water vein exists. ||33||

Then another, a second vein to the north, breaks through with sweet, tasty water. # Chapter 53: On Water Divination

He <note>The author, Varahamihira</note> says another thing—

-> If there is a serpent’s abode <note>original: "sarpāvāsa" - a termite mound or snake hole</note> to the west of a **Kadamba tree**, water is found to the south. At a distance of three cubits <note>term: hasta - a measurement from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18 inches</note> and at a depth of five and three-quarters men <note>term: purusha - a unit of depth based on a man's height with arms raised, roughly 6-7 feet</note>, there is water. <-

-> In this spot, a northern vein <note>term: shirā - an underground stream or "vein" of water</note> flows; the water smells of iron and is imperturbable <note>meaning: inexhaustible or very deep</note>. At the depth of one man, a frog the color of gold appears, and the earth is yellow. <-

If a termite mound is seen on the western side of a **Kadamba tree**, then at a distance of three cubits to the south and at a depth of six men minus a fourth part <insert>meaning: five and three-quarters</insert>—

Water flows there. In that place, there is a northern vein <note>original: "kauberī" - associated with Kubera, the lord of the North</note>, and in it flows water that smells like iron and is "imperturbable," meaning it is very abundant. When a hole the depth of one man is dug, a frog resembling gold appears. The earth there is yellow in color.

He says another thing—

-> If a **Palmyra palm** or a **Coconut tree** is surrounded by a termite mound, then six cubits to the west and at a depth of four men, a southern vein flows. <-

If a **Palmyra tree** is joined with a termite mound, or if a **Coconut tree** is surrounded by a termite mound, then at a distance of six cubits to the west of that Palmyra or Coconut tree, and at a depth of four men, a southern vein flows.

He says another thing—

-> If there is a serpent’s shelter to the south of a **Kapittha tree** <note>the Wood-apple tree</note>, water should be declared to the north. Leaving a space of seven cubits and digging to a depth of five men, there is water. <-

-> At the depth of one man, there is a variegated snake; the earth is black, and there is "shale-splitting" stone <note>original: "putabhit" - stone that breaks into layers or flakes</note>. Then there is white earth. A vein exists to the west, and another vein to the north. <-

"To the south" etc.: If there is a termite mound to the south of a **Kapittha tree**, then to the north of that tree, after leaving a distance of seven cubits and digging five men deep, water is to be predicted.

"A variegated snake" etc.: When one man's depth is dug, a variegated snake—black, white, and tawny—appears. Likewise, the earth is black. Then there is "shale-splitting" stone. It is called "shale-splitting" because it breaks apart in layers or flakes. After that, the earth is white. In that spot, there is one vein to the west, and subsequently, there is another vein to the north.

He says another thing—

**If a Jujube tree or a snake-hole is seen to the left of an Ashmantaka tree, water is found three and a half man-lengths deep, six cubits to the north of it.** <note>Verse 43. The Ashmantaka is likely *Bauhinia racemosa*. A "man-length" (purusha) is a technical unit of depth, roughly the height of a man with arms raised, approx. 120 digits.</note> **In the first man-length of digging, a tortoise is found, then grey stone and moist earth. The first vein of water flows south, and the second flows northeast.** <note>Verse 44</note>

If a Jujube tree <term>Badari; Ziziphus mauritiana</term> or a snake-hole <term>Valmika; anthill or serpent's nest</term> is seen to the left—that is, the northern direction—of an Ashmantaka tree, then at a distance of six cubits <term>Kara; a cubit or forearm's length</term> to the north of that Ashmantaka, water exists at a depth of three and a half man-lengths.

Regarding the signs there: when one man-length is excavated, a tortoise is seen. Then grey stone (blackish-white). Then moist earth. At first, there is a southern water-vein. The second is a northeastern (Ishana) vein.

He says another thing—

**If there is an anthill to the left of a Haridra tree, water is found to the east at a distance of three cubits and a depth of five and one-third man-lengths.** <note>Verse 45. Haridra is likely the Yellow Teak or *Adina cordifolia*.</note> **At the first man-length, a blue snake is found; the earth is yellow, and there is a stone like an emerald. Then the earth is black. The first vein is western, and the other is to the south.** <note>Verse 46</note>

If an anthill is seen to the left (north) of a Haridra tree, then to the east of that Haridra tree, at a distance of three cubits, water exists at a depth of five and one-third man-lengths.

Now, when the first man-length is dug, a blue snake is seen, then yellow earth. The stone is like an emerald <term>Marakata; emerald-like green stone</term>. Then the earth is black. First, there is a western (Varuni) vein, and the second is to the south.

He says another thing—

**If signs of marshy plants are seen in a waterless region, such as Virana grass or soft Durva grass, water is found one man-length deep.** <note>Verse 47. Virana is *Fragrant Vetiver*; Durva is *Cynodon dactylon*.</note> **Where Bharangi, Trivrita, Danti, Sukarapadi, Lakshmana, or Navamalika are found, water is two cubits to the south at a depth of three man-lengths.** <note>Verse 48. These are various medicinal herbs and climbers.</note>

<note>The plants mentioned in verse 48 are: Bharangi (Clerodendrum serratum), Trivrita (Turpeth root), Danti (Baliospermum montanum), Sukarapadi (Ipomoea pes-tigridis), Lakshmana (a medicinal plant often identified with Mandrake or similar), and Navamalika (Double Jasmine).</note>

In a waterless region where signs or omens characteristic of marshy lands <note>original: "Anupa"</note> are observed—meaning those specific indicators usually found in places with abundant water—one can find a source. Likewise, where the **Virana** <note>a fragrant grass, *Chrysopogon zizanioides*</note> and **Durva** <note>Bermuda grass, sacred in many rituals</note> are found to be exceptionally soft and delicate, water exists at a depth of one "man" <note>term: "Purusha" (a unit of depth equal to the height of a man with his arms raised, roughly 6-7 feet)</note>. ||47||

The plants **Bhangi**, **Trivrta**, **Danti**, **Sukarpadi**, **Lakshmana**, and **Navamalika** <note>various medicinal shrubs and creepers</note> are all well-known by these names. Wherever these medicinal plants <note>original: "Oshadhi"</note> are found, water is located two cubits <note>term: "Hasta" (the length of a forearm, approx. 18 inches)</note> to the south, at a depth of three "men." ||48||

### He further says—

> **Trees that are glossy, with long hanging branches, or those that are stunted and spreading, indicate water nearby.**
> **Trees that are hollow, have withered leaves, or appear parched are devoid of water.** ||49||

Glossy trees, those with long hanging branches, stunted <note>very short</note> but wide-spreading trees—all these indicate that water is near. Conversely, trees that are hollow <note>lacking a solid core</note>, have withered or discolored leaves, or appear parched and lusterless are "abandoned by water." This means no water will be found there. ||49||

### He further says—

> **The Tilaka, Amrataka, Varunaka, Bhallataka, Bilwa, Tinduka, and Ankola;**
> **The Pindara, Shirisha, Anjana, Parushaka, Vanjula, and Atibala—** ||50||
> **If these are very glossy and surrounded by anthills, then water is found**
> **three cubits to the north, at a depth of four and a half "men."** ||51||

The **Tilaka** <note>a specific flowering tree</note>, **Amrataka** <note>hog plum</note>, **Varunaka**, **Bhallataka** <note>marking nut</note>, **Bilwa** <note>wood apple</note>, **Tinduka**, **Ankola**, **Pindara**, **Shirisha**, **Anjana**, **Parushaka**, **Vanjula**, and **Atibala**—these are all specific types of trees, some of which are quite common. If these are found surrounded by very "glossy" <note>moist or healthy-looking</note> anthills <note>original: "Valmika"</note>, then to the north of these trees, at a distance of three cubits and a depth of four and a half "men," there is water. ||51||

### He further says—

> **Where a patch of grass grows on otherwise barren ground, or where a patch of ground is barren amidst lush grass,**
> **a water-vein is indicated there; or alternatively, wealth may be told to be hidden in that spot.** ||52||

"Where there is no grass," etc. In a place where the earth is generally devoid of grass but a patch of grass-covered land is seen, or conversely, in a place generally covered in grass where a patch of land is found without grass, a water-vein is indicated beneath that spot. This means water will be found there. One may also predict wealth or treasure. In that location, some authorities suggest the depth is four and a half <term>Purushas</term> <note>A 'Purusha' is a unit of measurement based on the height of a man with arms upraised, roughly 120 digits or 6-7 feet.</note>. ||52||

### He says another thing—

> **Where there is an exchange between thorny and thornless trees, water is found three cubits to the west. After digging to a depth of three and one-third Purushas, there may also be wealth. ||53||**

Where a thorny tree, such as a <term>Khadira</term> <note>Acacia catechu</note>, grows in the midst of thornless trees like the <term>Palasa</term> <note>Butea monosperma or 'Flame of the Forest'</note>, or by inversion, where a thornless tree grows in the midst of thorny ones, then at a distance of three <term>Hastas</term> <note>A 'Hasta' or cubit is the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, approx. 18 inches.</note> to the west of that tree, and after digging to a depth of three and one-third Purushas, there is water below, or there may be wealth. ||53||

### He says another thing—

> **Where the earth gives a deep sound when struck by the feet, there is water at that spot at a depth of three and a half Purushas; there lies a northern vein. ||54||**

In a place where the earth, when struck by the feet, produces a deep or sweet resonance, at that very spot, at a depth of three and a half Purushas, there will be a <term>Kauberi</term> <note>Literally 'belonging to Kubera,' the god of the North; signifying a northern water-vein.</note> or northern vein. This means water will be present there. ||54||

### He says another thing—

> **If one branch of a tree is bent down or appears pale, water should be known to exist under that branch at a depth of three Purushas. ||55||**

If a single branch of a tree is drooping or bent low, or if it appears pale and discolored, then directly under that branch, after digging to a depth of three Purushas, water is to be found. ||55||

### He says another thing—

> **When there is a deformity in the fruit or flowers of a tree, a vein exists three cubits to the east at a depth of four Purushas; beneath is stone and yellow earth. ||56||**

When a tree exhibits a deformity or unnatural appearance in its fruits and flowers, then three cubits to the east of that tree, at a depth of four Purushas, there is a water-vein. Furthermore, there is stone beneath, and the soil is yellow. ||56||

### He says another thing—

**If a Yellow-berried Nightshade is seen without thorns and with white flowers,**
**water should be declared beneath it at a depth of three and a half men.** <note>original: "tri-purusha" (three men) and "ardha-purusha" (half a man). A "purusha" is a unit of measure based on the height of a man with arms raised, roughly 120 digits or 6-7 feet.</note> **॥57॥**

If the Yellow-berried Nightshade <note>Sanskrit: *kantakarika* or *nidigdhika*</note> is devoid of thorns and bears white flowers, then beneath that plant, at a depth of three and a half men, water should be predicted. ॥57॥

### He says another thing—

**Where a Date Palm has two heads in a waterless region,**

In whatever waterless region a Date Palm <note>Sanskrit: *kharjuri*</note> with two heads <note>a bifurcated trunk</note> should exist, then to the west of that palm tree—at a distance of two cubits <note>Sanskrit: *hasta*; approximately 3 feet</note>—water should be declared at a depth of three men. > If a Date Palm has two heads in a dry place, water is indicated two cubits to the west at a depth of three men. ॥58॥

**If a Karnikara tree or a Palasha tree has white flowers,**
**water exists two cubits to the right at a depth of two men. ॥59॥**

If a Karnikara tree <note>Pterospermum acerifolium</note> should have white flowers, or if a Palasha tree <note>Butea monosperma, usually known for orange-red flowers</note> should have white flowers, then in that place, two cubits to the right <note>Sanskrit: *savyena*, interpreted here by the commentator as *dakshinena* or right-side</note> of the Karnikara or Palasha, water is found at a depth of two men. ॥59॥

**Where heat or smoke rises from the earth, there is water at a depth of two men;**
**a vein with a great flow of water should be pointed out there. ॥60॥**

On whatever ground heat is seen, or where smoke is seen rising, there at a depth of two men, a water-vein <term>shira: an underground stream or aquifer</term> consisting of a great flow of water should be declared. ॥60॥

### He says another thing—

**In that spot of a field where the crops produced meet with destruction,**
**or appear glossy and extremely pale, a great water-vein lies there at a depth of two men. ॥61॥**
