# In the Commentary on the Great Compilation [Chapter 53]

In whichever specific area or spot of a field the crops produced meet with destruction; or, conversely, in that same spot the crops become exceedingly glossy <note>indicating high moisture</note>, or appear extremely pale or extremely yellow—in that very spot, at a depth of two "men" <term>Purusha: a unit of measurement based on the height of a man with upstanding arms, roughly 6-7 feet</term>, there is a "Great Vein" <note>Mahāśirā: a major underground water current</note>. This means a great volume of water flows there. ||61||

Having thus described the knowledge of water in forest and marshy lands, I shall now speak of the science of underground veins in the desert:

->**I shall hereafter describe how the veins exist in desert regions.**<-
->**The veins situated within the earth run like the necks of camels.**<-

A desert region is a land mass devoid of water. In what manner the veins exist in the desert, I shall explain from this point forward. Just as the necks of camels are curved or crooked, in that same manner, the veins situated beneath the ground travel in a winding fashion; this implies they are located at a very great depth. ||62||

Regarding this, he says:

> **If there is an anthill to the northeast of a Pilu tree, water is found to the west.**
> **A vein traveling northward should be known to exist at a depth of five men.** ||63||
> **The first sign is a frog; the soil is tawny, then it becomes green.**
> **Beneath a man's height there is a stone; water is to be pointed out under that.** ||64||

"To the northeast" etc.: If to the northeast (the direction of the deity Ishana) of a Pilu tree <note>Salvadora persica, commonly known as the toothbrush tree</note> there is an anthill—a mound of earth made by termites—then water exists to the west of that same Pilu tree at a distance of four and a half cubits, at a depth of five "men." There, a "northward-traveling" vein—one that moves toward the northern direction—is to be recognized.

"The sign" etc.: In the first "man" of excavation, a frog is the sign. Then the earth is tawny; after that, it becomes green-white. Below all these signs, at the bottom, there is a stone. Beneath that stone, water is to be declared. And so says Sarasvata <note>An earlier authority on water divining often cited in this text</note>:

->If there is an anthill to the northeast of a Pilu tree, one should predict water<-
->at four straight cubits to the west, at a depth of five men.<-

"Of the Peelu" means if an anthill is seen to the east of a Peelu tree <note>Salvadora persica, often called the toothbrush tree.</note>, then from that same Peelu tree, at a distance of four and a half cubits toward the south, water is to be announced at a depth of seven men. ||65||

He says another thing:

If a snake-home or anthill is seen to the north of a Karira tree <note>Capparis decidua, a leafless thorny shrub.</note>, then at a distance of four and a half cubits to the south of the Karira, sweet and pleasant water is to be known at a depth of ten men. Here, at the first man's depth of digging, a yellow-colored frog is seen. As Sarasvata says:
> If an anthill is seen to the north of a Karira, one should predict water
> at four and a half cubits to the south, at a depth of ten men.
> At the first man's depth, a yellow frog is seen as the sign. ||67||

He says another thing:

"Or if there is a Suvarna-named..." This "or" is used in the sense of "and." If a serpent's home—an ant-hill—is seen to the left, meaning the north, of a Suvarna tree, then at a distance of two cubits to the south, after digging to a depth of fifteen man-lengths, water is found below. ||70||

"Badari..." refers to when a Badari and a Rohita tree are joined or entwined. Even without an ant-hill—whether an ant-hill exists there or not—then to the west of those two trees, at a distance of three cubits, water is found below at a depth of sixteen man-lengths. ||72||

# Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 53]

> **If a snake, shining like black eye-salve <note>original: "añjana-prabhaḥ"</note>, is seen when the earth is dug to the depth of half a man, then sweet water will be found there, flowing for a long time. || 85 ||**

->Here he mentions a specific distinction:<-

> **The signs described for the desert region should not be used to predict water in a jungle <note>In this context, "Jāṅgala" refers to a semi-arid or scrubland region, not a rainforest</note> region. For signs involving the Rose Apple, Reed, and others, the depth in cubits <note>original: "puruṣas", literally "man-lengths"</note> should be doubled in the desert. || 86 ||**

The signs and characteristics mentioned for the desert region should not be used to declare the presence of water in a "Jangala" (moderately dry) region. Regarding the phrase "Rose Apple, Reed, and others": if the signs involving the Rose Apple and Reed—such as <term>“A Reed in a waterless place”</term> <note>See verse 6 of this chapter</note> and <term>“To the north of a Rose Apple tree at a distance of three cubits”</term> <note>See verse 8 of this chapter</note>—are seen in a desert land, then the depth in "man-lengths" <note>A "puruṣa" is a unit of measure roughly equal to the height of a man with his arms raised, approx. 120 digits</note> previously stated must be doubled. || 86 ||

->He states another rule:<-

> **The Rose Apple, Trivṛtā, Maurvī, Śiśumārī, Sārivā, Śivā, Śyāmā,**
> **The creepers Vārāhī, Jyotiṣmatī, and Garuḍavegā; || 87 ||**
> **Sūkarikā, Māṣaparṇī, and Vyāghrapadā—if these are found at the home of a snake (an anthill),**
> **Then water is found three cubits to the north of the anthill, at a depth of three man-lengths. || 88 ||**

<term>Jambu (Rose Apple tree)</term>, <term>Trivṛtā (Indian Jalap)</term>, <term>Maurvī (Bowstring Hemp)</term>, <term>Śiśumārī</term>, <term>Sārivā (Indian Sarsaparilla)</term>, <term>Śivā (Yellow Myrobalan)</term>, <term>Śyāmā (Black Creeper)</term>—these are medicinal herbs and creepers, as are those mentioned next. What are they? <term>Vārāhī</term>, <term>Jyotiṣmatī (Staff Tree)</term>, and <term>Garuḍavegā</term>. || 87 ||
If the herbs <term>Sūkarikā</term>, <term>Māṣaparṇī</term>, and <term>Vyāghrapadā</term> are found growing on an anthill (the snake's home), then one should declare that water exists three cubits <note>original: "hastas" or hands/forearms</note> to the north of that anthill, at a depth of three man-lengths. || 88 ||

->Does this apply everywhere? He says no:<-

> **This applies to moist (Anūpa) lands; in jungle (Jāṅgala) lands, it is at five man-lengths.**
> **By these same signs in a desert (Maru) region, one should say it is at seven man-lengths. || 89 ||**

What has been stated applies to "Anūpa" lands, which are regions with abundant water. An "Anūpa" region is one with plenty of water. In "Jāṅgala" (moderately dry) land, using these same signs, the depth should be stated as five man-lengths. By these same previously mentioned signs and omens, in a desert land, one should say the depth is seven man-lengths. || 89 ||

He states another rule—

**Where the earth is of uniform color and devoid of grass, trees, anthills, and shrubs, water is found at that spot where a visible change occurs in the soil. ||90||**

In whatever place the earth is of a uniform color and is "devoid of grass, trees, anthills, and shrubs"—meaning it lacks grass, trees, anthills, and shrubs (defined here as a cluster of branches sharing a single root)—if there is a "change" or a variation in appearance at a specific spot on that ground, water will be found there at a depth of five <term>Purushas</term> <note>A 'Purusha' is a unit of measurement based on the height of a man with his arms raised, approximately 6 to 7 feet.</note>. Thus says Sarasvata:

->Where the earth is of one color and lacks trees, shrubs, grass,<-
->and anthills, but shows a reversal in appearance at one spot,<-
->water is situated there at a depth of five Purushas. ||90||<-

He states another rule—

**Where the ground is glossy, low-lying, sandy, or resonant, water is found at a depth of four and a half or five Purushas. ||91||**

In whatever region the earth is glossy (oily in texture), low-lying, contains sand, or is "resonant" (producing a sound when struck), water exists in that place at a depth of four and a half or five Purushas. ||91||

He states another rule—

**To the south of glossy trees, there is abundant water at a depth of four Purushas. Even in a dense forest, one should predict water in the same way near any tree that appears deformed. ||92||**

Where there are glossy or sap-rich trees, there is "abundant" (plentiful) water to the south of those trees at a depth of four Purushas. Even in a "dense forest" (a thicket of trees), if one tree among many appears "deformed"—meaning it shows a variation in its natural form or a difference in its flowers and fruits—one should predict water from that tree in the same manner. This means water will be found to the south at four Purushas. ||92||

He states another rule—

**Where the earth sinks underfoot, water is found at three and a half Purushas in both arid and marshy lands. Water is also found where many insects live without an apparent nest. ||93||**

# Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 53]

Where—meaning in whatever location—the earth or ground sinks downward when pressed by the feet, whether in a <term>Jangala</term> <note>arid or desert-like region</note> or an <term>Anupa</term> <note>marshy or well-watered region</note> land, water is found at a depth of one and a half <term>Purushas</term> <note>A 'Purusha' is a unit of measurement based on a man's height with arms raised, roughly 120 digits or 7-9 feet</note>. Furthermore, in a place where many insects or worms are seen without a visible nest or colony, water is present there as well. Because of the word "also," this is also at a depth of one and a half Purushas. **[93]**

->He says another thing:<-

> If the earth is hot everywhere but cold in one spot, or cold everywhere but hot in one spot, water is found at three and a half Purushas. If a rainbow, a "sun-dog" <note>original: "matsya" or fish-shaped optical phenomenon</note>, or an anthill is seen on the ground in either arid or marshy lands, water is four cubits <note>original: "hasta" or forearm-length</note> below. **[94]**

Wherever the earth is generally hot but cold in one specific spot, or conversely, generally cold but hot in one spot, water exists there at a depth of three and a half Purushas. A rainbow—the bow of the gods—which arises from the contact of sunbeams, or a "fish" <note>original: "matsya," likely referring to a parhelion or mock sun</note> which is a <unclear>shining</unclear> reflection, or an anthill: if these are seen on the ground in arid or marshy regions, water is found four cubits beneath that spot. **[94]**

->He says another thing:<-

> If one anthill in a row of anthills is taller than the others, a water-vein lies beneath it. Also, water is present where crops wither or fail to grow. **[95]**

Among a row of anthills, if one stands out as significantly taller, then water—a "vein"—is found four cubits beneath that tall anthill. On ground where crops that have sprouted begin to wither, or where sown seeds fail to grow at all, water is found four cubits below. This applies to both arid and marshy lands. As the sage Sarasvata says:

> If one anthill in a row is taller, water is beneath it. Where crops do not grow or they wither, water is surely to be pointed out at four cubits depth in that very earth. **[95]**

->He says another thing:<-

> Where a Banyan, a Palasha, and a Cluster Fig grow together, water is beneath them. Likewise, where a Banyan and a Sacred Fig are joined, a water-vein flows to the north. **[96]**

<margin>By trees</margin> Where the three trees—the Banyan <note>Nyagrodha</note>, the Palasha, and the Cluster Fig <note>Udumbara</note>—are found growing together in a cluster, water is found three cubits beneath them, and the water-vein there flows toward the north. Similarly, in the case of a Banyan and a Sacred Fig <note>Pippala</note> growing in union, water should be declared to be below in the same manner: at a depth of three cubits with the vein flowing north. As Sarasvata says:

# Chapter on Water Divination

->**Where the Palasha <note>Butea monosperma</note> and Udumbara <note>Cluster fig</note> trees are found growing together with a Nyagrodha <note>Banyan</note>, or where a Vata <note>another variety of Banyan</note> and Pippala <note>Sacred fig</note> are joined, there is water beneath.**<-

### Now he describes the characteristics of wells—

->**If a well is located in the Agneya <note>South-east</note> corner of a village or a city, it constantly causes fear and usually brings about fires that consume humans. (97)**<-
->**In the Nairrita <note>South-west</note> corner, it causes the loss of children; in the Vayavya <note>North-west</note> corner, it causes danger to women. Avoiding these three directions, wells in the remaining directions are auspicious. (98)**<-

If a well is situated in the Agneya corner—that is, the south-eastern direction—of a village or city, then that well constantly, at all times, creates fear in that village or city. Generally, it causes "burning with humans," meaning it creates a danger of fire that burns people and property. (97)

If a well is in the Nairrita corner—the south-western direction—of a village or city, it causes the "wasting" or loss of children. In the Vayavya corner—the north-western direction—it causes fear or danger to women. Leaving aside these three mentioned directions, in the other five—East, South, West, North, and Ishani <note>North-east</note>—wells are bringers of good fortune and auspiciousness. (98)

Having observed the system of water divination taught by the Sage Sarasvata, he now says he will describe the system of Manu:

->**Having observed the Water Divination composed by the Sage Sarasvata, this has been composed in Arya verses; now I shall describe the system of Manu in various meters. (99)**<-

Having seen and examined that which was composed by the Sage Sarasvata, this [previous section] was written in *Arya* <note>a specific Sanskrit poetic meter</note> verses. Now I shall tell of the *Manava* <note>belonging to Manu</note> water divination in other poetic meters. (99)

### He describes it thus:

->**Where trees, shrubs, and creepers are glossy and their leaves are without holes, there is a water-vein. Or where there are Lotus, Kshura, Ushira <note>Vetiver</note>, Kula, Gundra, Kasha, Kusha <note>sacred grasses</note>, Nalika, or Nala reeds. (100)**<-
->**Where there are Date palms, Jambu <note>Java plum</note>, Arjuna, or Vetasa <note>Reed-cane</note> trees, or where trees, shrubs, and creepers are full of milky sap; where there are Chhatra, Ibha, Naga, Shatapatra <note>Lotus</note>, Nipa, Naktamala, and Sinduvara trees. (101)**<-

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 53]

->Where the *Vibhitaka* <note>Terminalia bellirica, a large forest tree</note> or the *Madayantika* <note>Henna or a similar flowering shrub</note> is found,<-
->there is water at a depth of three *purushas* <note>A 'purusha' is a unit of measure based on a man's height with arms raised, roughly 5-6 feet; three purushas equals approx. 15-18 feet</note>.<-

->there too, at the base, water is found at a depth of three *purushas*. || 102 ||<-

Regarding the phrase "Where they are glossy": The word "where" (*yatah*) is used here in the locative sense. In whatever ground the trees, shrubs <note>defined here as a cluster of branches from a single root</note>, and creepers are all glossy or "oily" in appearance, and where their leaves are "without holes" (undamaged by insects or disease)—in that very spot, a water-vein exists at a depth of three *purushas* below. 

Alternatively, if there is the land-lotus, the *kshura* <note>Gokshura or puncture vine</note>, *ushira* <note>fragrant vetiver grass</note>, or *kula*; or if these are found with *gundra* <note>a type of grass or bulrush</note>; or if *kasha*, *kusha*, *nalika*, or *nala* <note>various species of reeds and sacred grasses</note> are present—all these are specific types of grasses.

Where the Date Palm, the Rose Apple (*Jambu*), the *Arjuna* tree, or the Cane (*Vetasa*) are found; or where there are trees containing milky sap; or where shrubs and creepers are full of milky sap. Where the *Chatra* <note>Mushroom or umbrella-shaped plant</note>, the *Ibha* <note>Elephant-ear plant</note>, the *Naga* <note>from which Nagakesara is derived</note>, the hundred-petaled Lotus, the *Nipa* tree, and the *Naktamala* <note>Karanja tree</note> are found together with *Sinduvara* <note>the Five-Leaved Chaste tree</note>.

Where the *Vibhitaka* tree and the *Madayantika* substance are found in a region, there will be water at a depth of three *purushas* beneath the surface. Regarding "a mountain upon another mountain": alternatively, where a second mountain sits atop a mountain, water exists at the base of the upper one at a depth of three *purushas*. 

And so says Manu <note>referring to an ancient authority on the subject, likely the sage Manu mentioned in technical treatises</note>:

> Where shrubs, trees, and creepers are found with unbroken leaves, 
> there water is found below at a depth of three *purushas* when excavated. 
> Lotus, *Kshura*, *Ushira*, *Kula*, *Gundra*, *Kasha*, or *Kusha*; 
> *Nalika*, *Nala*, Date Palm, Rose Apple, Cane, and *Arjuna*; 
> Where trees and creepers are found with milky sap and bearing fruit; 
> *Chatra*, *Ibha*, *Naga*, *Nipa*, the hundred-petaled Lotus, and *Vibhitaka*; 
> *Sinduvara*, *Naktamala*, and the fragrant *Madayantika*; 
> Wherever these are found, water is there at a depth of three *purushas*. 
> Where there is another mountain atop a mountain, water is there; 
> One should point to it at the base of that very spot at a depth of three *purushas*. || 100-102 ||

<summary>This page details botanical indicators such as glossy leaves, milky sap, and specific plant species (like the Rose Apple and Date Palm) that reveal underground water at a depth of roughly 18 feet. It also notes that unique geological features, like stacked mountains, serve as markers for hidden springs.</summary>

# Chapter 53: The Science of Water Divination

He says another thing—

> Where the earth is joined with *Maunjika*, *Kasha*, and *Kusha* grasses,
> And where the soil is blue and gravelly;
> In that place, there is abundant and sweet-tasting water,
> Or where the soil is black or red. || 103 ||

In the land which is joined with *Maunjika*, *Kasha*, and *Kusha* <note>These are specific varieties of sacred and hardy Indian grasses often used in rituals</note> (specific types of grasses), and where the earth is blue-colored and contains gravel (small pebbles), in that land there is abundant (plentiful) and sweet-tasting (pleasant) water. Where the soil is black-colored or red-colored, there too, there should be abundant and sweet water. || 103 ||

Now he describes the qualities of the earth—

> Gravelly, copper-colored earth makes water astringent;
> Tawny earth makes the water alkaline;
> In pale-white earth, saltiness is predicted;
> Sweet water is found in blue-colored earth. || 104 ||

The land which is gravelly and copper-colored makes the water astringent <note>term: Astringent (Kashaya) - a dry, puckering taste like unripe fruit</note> in taste. Tawny-colored earth makes the water alkaline <note>term: Alkaline (Kshara) - salty or soapy in taste</note>. In pale-white earth, the water is said to be salty. In blue-colored earth, the water is sweet. || 104 ||

He says another thing—

> Teak, *Ashvakarna*, *Arjuna*, *Bilva*, *Sarja*,
> *Shriparni*, *Arishta*, *Dhava*, and *Shimshapa* trees;
> If these trees, shrubs, and creepers have holes in their leaves and appear withered,
> They indicate that water is far away. || 105 ||

Teak, *Ashvakarna*, *Arjuna*, *Bilva*, *Sarja*, *Shriparni*, *Arishta*, *Dhava*, and *Shimshapa*—all these are specific types of trees. Where these exist with leaves full of holes, and likewise where trees, shrubs, and creepers have holes in their leaves and are withered (lacking moisture/oiliness), they indicate water is at a distance (not nearby). This means the water is very deep in that place. || 105 ||

He says another thing—

> Earth that has the color of the sun, fire, ashes, camels, or donkeys is declared waterless;
> If there are red sprouts, milky *Karira* plants, and red earth, there is water beneath a stone. || 106 ||

# With Commentary on the Bṛhat Saṃhitā [Chapter 53]

The earth <note>original: "vasudhā bhūḥ"</note> which possesses a color similar to the sun, fire, ashes, a camel, or a donkey is declared to be waterless. Likewise, where Karīra trees <note>Capparis decidua, a leafless thorny shrub</note> are found with red sprouts and contain sap, and if the earth there is also red in color, water will be found beneath a stone in that location. ||106||

He says another thing—

->**A stone that has the luster of lapis lazuli, mung beans, or a dark cloud,**<-
->**or resembles the color of a ripening Udumbara fruit;**<-
->**or which looks like collyrium when broken, or is tawny-brown—**<-
->**that stone should be known to have abundant water very near to it. ||107||**<-

A stone which has a color similar to the lapis lazuli gem <note>original: "vaidūrya"</note>, mung beans, a cloud, or is of a dark black hue; likewise, a stone that resembles the color of a well-ripened Udumbara fruit <note>Ficus racemosa, the cluster fig</note>; and a stone which, upon being broken <note>original: "bhañjane"</note>, looks like collyrium <note>black eye-salve</note>, or a stone that is tawny-brown in color—that stone should be understood as having "abundant water nearby," meaning it possesses a great and accessible supply of water. ||107||

He says another thing—

->**That which resembles a pigeon, honey, or clarified butter,**<-
->**or is equal in color to linen cloth;**<-
->**or that which has the same appearance as the Soma plant—**<-
->**that stone also yields water quickly and inexhaustibly. ||108||**<-

A stone which is similar to a pigeon <note>likely referring to a blue-grey color</note>, or resembles honey or clarified butter <note>ghṛta</note>; and that which has the same appearance and color as the Soma plant <note>the sacred plant used in Vedic sacrifices</note>—that stone also produces water quickly, and that water is inexhaustible and steady. ||108||

He says another thing—

->**One marked with variegated copper-colored spots,**<-
->**resembling pale white, ashes, a camel, or a donkey;**<-
->**or like a large black bee, or the flower of the Aṅguṣṭhaka,**<-
->**or the color of the sun or fire—such a stone is waterless. ||109||**<-

A stone which is joined with copper-colored spots or various colored marks, and is also pale white; or resembles ashes, a camel, or a donkey...

<note>The commentator explains the colors of unfavorable rocks.</note>
A rock that is like a donkey has a color similar to one. "Like a shringa" means it has the color of a large black bee. *Anjisthika* refers to a specific type of shrub; or it means the rock is the color of its flower. This implies a dark red or purple hue. A rock that is the color of the sun or of fire is "waterless" <note>Sanskrit: *vittoya*</note>, meaning it contains no water.

He says something else as well:

->Those rocks which have the appearance of moonlight, crystal, pearls, or gold;<-
->those which have the luster of sapphire, cinnabar, or collyrium;<-
->and those which resemble the rays of the rising sun or yellow orpiment;<-
->these are auspicious. This verse is the word of the Sages.<-

Rocks that have the appearance of moonlight <note>Sanskrit: *chandratapa*</note>, or of crystal <note>a clear quartz</note>, or of pearls <note>from a pearl necklace</note>, or of gold <note>Sanskrit: *hema*</note>—meaning they share those colors. Also, those rocks which have the luster or brilliance of sapphire <note>Sanskrit: *indranila*</note>, or of cinnabar <note>Sanskrit: *hingulaka*, a well-known bright red mineral</note>, or of collyrium <note>Sanskrit: *anjana*, an extremely black eye-salve</note>. And those which resemble the rays of the rising sun—meaning they are the same color as the rays seen at sunrise, which is to say, very red. And those which are like yellow orpiment <note>Sanskrit: *haritala*, a yellow arsenic sulfide</note>. All of these are auspicious. In this context, the following verse is the "word of the Sages" <note>Sanskrit: *munivachah*</note>, meaning it follows the sacred tradition or lineage of the Rishis.

Then he gives the words of the Sages:

->For these rocks are unbreakable and auspicious,<-
->always inhabited by Yakshas and Nagas.<-
->In the kingdoms of the kings where these are found,<-
->there shall never be a drought.<-

All these rocks are "unbreakable" <note>Sanskrit: *abhedya*, meaning they do not crumble easily</note>. Because they are "auspicious" <note>Sanskrit: *shiva*, bringing good fortune</note>, they are always—at all times—frequented and inhabited by *Yakshas* <note>nature spirits</note> and *Nagas* <note>serpent deities associated with water</note>. In the nations or countries of the kings where these rocks exist, there will never be a lack of rain; the meaning is that Indra <note>the god of rain</note> will always pour rain upon them.

Now, he describes the method for breaking these rocks:

->When a rock does not break, then<-
->having kindled a fire with the wood of the Palasha<-
->and Tinduka trees until the rock is fire-colored,<-
->it will break when sprinkled with lime-water.<-

# On the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 53]

When a rock being split does not break or yield, what should be done at that time? It is said—having kindled a continuous fire upon the surface of the rock using the wood of the *Palash* <note>Butea monosperma, often called 'Flame of the Forest'</note> along with the wood of *Tinduka* trees <note>Diospyros embryopteris or Indian Persimmon</note>, and having made the rock the color of fire <note>glowing red-hot</note>, it is then sprinkled with lime-water <note>original: "sudhambu-sikta"; water mixed with lime or milky sap</note>. Once saturated with this water, it undergoes splitting and reaches a state of breakage. ||112||

He mentions another method:

->Water boiled with the ashes of the *Mokshaka* tree,<-
->Which is then poured seven times;<-
->This, combined with the ash-salts of *Shara* reed,<-
->Causes the bursting of a rock previously heated by fire. ||113||<-

The *Mokshaka* is a tree popularly known as *Manivaka* <note>Schrebera swietenioides</note>. Water boiled with the ashes of this *Mokshaka* should be combined with the ash-salts of *Shara* <note>Saccharum munja, a type of tough grass</note>. With this mixture, the rock—which has been heated by fire according to the previously mentioned method—should be doused seven times. One must heat it and then douse it. From this, the bursting or breaking of the rock occurs. ||113||

He describes yet another method for breaking rock:

->Buttermilk, fermented rice-gruel, and liquor,<-
->Combined with horse-gram and jujube fruits;<-
->Left to stand for seven nights, these liquids<-
->Split the heated rock through repeated dousings. ||114||<-

Buttermilk is churned curd. Fermented rice-gruel is *Sauvira* <note>a sour medicinal liquid</note>. Liquor is well-known. These are combined with *Kulattha* <note>Horse-gram, Macrotyloma uniflorum</note>. Into this, *Badara* <note>Jujube</note> fruits are added or thrown in. All these, having been left to stand for seven nights, will split or burst the rock—which has been thoroughly heated according to the earlier rule—through the process of dousing. ||114||

He mentions another:

->Neem leaves and bark, sesame stalks,<-
->Prickly chaff-flower, *Tinduka*, and *Guduchi*;<-
->The ash-salt of these, strained with cow urine,<-
->Breaks the stone when heated and doused six times. ||115||<-

<note>The ingredients listed are: Neem (Azadirachta indica), Sesame (Sesamum indicum), Apamarga (Achyranthes aspera), Tinduka (Indian Persimmon), and Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia, a medicinal vine).</note>

Regarding the Neem mixture: The leaves and the bark should be from the Neem tree itself. The "stalks of sesame" refers to the inner pod-like structures where the sesame seeds reside. This should be combined with *Apamarga* <note>Achyranthes aspera, a medicinal plant</note> and the fruit of the *Tinduka* <note>Diospyros embryopteris, or Indian Persimmon</note>. *Guduchi* is the same as *Amrita* <note>Tinospora cordifolia, known as "the nectar of immortality"</note>. A caustic ash is prepared from these combined ingredients and then strained or filtered with cow urine. When a stone or rock is heated and then sprinkled with this solution six times—following the previously mentioned method—it will break apart. ||15||

Now he describes the "tempering of tools" <term>Shastrapana: the process of hardening or treating metal tools to increase their durability</term>:

->The milk of the *Arka* plant <note>Calotropis gigantea</note> mixed with the soot from burnt ram's horn,<-
->combined with the excrement of pigeons and rats, forms a paste.<-
->After applying this, the tool—having been rubbed with oil—is heated;<-
->once sharpened, it will suffer no damage even against hard stones. ||16||<-

The "tool" <term>Tanka: a chisel or stone-cutting instrument</term> refers to the weapon or implement. This verse was previously explained in the section regarding the characteristics of swords. ||16|| <margin>See verse 25 on page 544 of this book.</margin>

He mentions another method:

->When iron is treated with the caustic ashes of a banana tree mixed with buttermilk<-
->that has stood for a day, and is then properly sharpened,<-
->it will not break against stone,<-
->nor will it become blunt when striking other metals. ||17||<-

This was also explained in the section on the characteristics of swords. ||17|| <margin>See verse 26 on page 544 of this book.</margin>

Now he describes the characteristics of a reservoir <term>Vapi: a stepped well or water tank</term>:

->An embankment running East to West holds water for a long time, while one running North to South does not.<-
->The latter is often breached by waves driven by the force of the winds.<-
->If one must build such a bank, he should shield the water's impact with strong timber,<-
->or reinforce the embankment with stones and well-trodden earth on both sides. ||18||<-

An embankment <term>Pali: the dike or retaining wall of a reservoir</term> that is long from East to West holds water for a very long time. One that is long from North to South does not hold water for long, because it is frequently destroyed by the "breaching" or agitation of waves driven by the wind. If one desires to maintain such a North-South embankment...

The builder, in order to manage the impact of the water, should reinforce it with heartwood. On the embankment, where there is contact with water, one should create a protective covering on the wall using strong heartwood or timber. Furthermore, for every layer of the embankment <note>original: "praticayam"</note>, it should be trampled and compacted by elephants and horses; the "etcetera" here implies camels, buffaloes, and bulls, so that the structure becomes exceptionally firm. ||118||

Intermingled with Bakula trees. One should cause the banks or edges of the embankment to be covered and pervaded by these. ||119||

In one part or location, an outlet gate—an exit for the water—should be made. Of what kind? A water-channel constructed of stones—meaning a path for the water built up with rocks. And this should be "set in a frame" <note>original: "koshashthitam"</note>, meaning established at the base. There, having made a door-panel without any gaps or holes, and having placed a plank over the covering, one should then "fill it with dust"—meaning one should cover it over with soil. ||120||

Anjana is a well-known specific tree; some say it is the Sauviraka. Musta is a type of grass <note>nut-grass</note>. Ushira is well-known <note>vetiver</note>. With what else? Along with the powders of Rajakoshataka <note>Luffa</note> and Amala <note>Indian Gooseberry</note>—

And with the powder of *Amalaka* <note>Indian Gooseberry or Emblic Myrobalan</note>. ->by this treatment it becomes pure, delicious,<-

Whichever water—liquid—is turbid (not clear), pungent (bitter), salty, or tasteless (lacking a pleasant flavor), or if it should be of an unpleasant odor (foul-smelling)? That water, through this combination, becomes pure (clear), delicious (sweet), and sweet-smelling (possessing a fine scent); likewise, it becomes endowed with other qualities—joined with those properties that counteract pungency and saltiness. ||122||

Now he states the lunar mansions <term>Nakshatras: the 27 divisions of the sky through which the moon passes</term>:
->Hasta, Magha, Anuradha, Pushya, Dhanishtha, the three Uttaras, and Rohini;<-
->along with Shatabhishak—this group is praised for the commencement of wells. ||123||<-

Hasta, Magha, Anuradha, Pushya, Dhanishtha, the three Uttaras (namely Uttara-Phalguni, Uttara-Ashadha, and Uttara-Bhadrapada), as well as Rohini and Shatabhishak—this term is used for distinction. This group of stars—this collection of lunar mansions—is desired and praised for the beginning of [digging] wells. ||123||

Now he describes the ritual of consecration:
->Having made an offering to Varuna, one should first place a stake of Banyan or Rattan at the location of the water-vein,<-
->having honored it with flowers, perfumes, and incense. ||124||<-

Having performed an offering—a gift—to Varuna, the Lord of the Waters, and having prepared a stake of Banyan (*Vata*) or a stake of Rattan (*Vetasa*), and having honored it with flowers, perfumes (scented substances), and incense (such as *Guggulu* <note>a fragrant resin</note> and others), one should first—at the very beginning—place it at the location of the vein; he should bury it or establish it firmly in the area of the water-vein. ||124||

# Now, the Chapter on the Science of Plant Life is Explained.

First, the author speaks to demonstrate the purpose of this study:

->**Reservoirs of water are not pleasing if they are devoid of shade on their margins.**<-
->**Therefore, one should establish gardens along the edges of the water. || 1 ||**<-

Because water reservoirs—meaning sources of water such as ponds, wells, and lakes—are not "pleasing" (delightful to the mind) if they are "devoid of shade on their margins" (lacking shade around the perimeter). Therefore, for that reason, one should "establish" (construct or plant) "gardens" specifically along the "water margins" (the edges of the water). A "garden" <term>arama: a place where one takes delight</term> refers here to a plantation of trees. || 1 ||

### Now, he describes the characteristics of the soil:

->**Soft soil is beneficial for all types of trees; one should sow sesame there.**<-
->**When the sesame is in bloom, one should crush it into the earth; this is the first work for the soil. || 2 ||**<-

For all trees, "soft" (sweet and supple) "soil" (earth) is "beneficial" (conducive to welfare or excellent). On such ground, one should first "sow" (plant) "sesame." When those "sesame plants" are "in bloom" (having produced flowers), one should "crush" (trample or grind) them into the ground. This is the "first" (initial) "work" (action) to be performed on the earth. And so says Kashyapa <note>An ancient sage often cited as an authority on agriculture and architecture</note>:

> "Lands that are marshy, with soft soil, and joined with Durva and Virana grasses;
> There, auspicious trees, bearing fragrant fruits and branches, should be planted." || 2 ||

Now, he names the trees that should be planted first:

->**The Arishta, Ashoka, Punnaga, and Shirisha, along with the Priyangu;**<-
->**These auspicious trees should be planted first in gardens or in homes. || 3 ||**<-

The Arishta <note>Soapberry tree</note>, Ashoka, Punnaga <note>Alexandrian laurel</note>, and Shirisha <note>Rain tree</note>—these specific types of trees—what are they like? They are "along with the Priyangu" (accompanied by the Priyangu creeper/tree) and are "auspicious" (praiseworthy). They should be "planted first" in the garden. "Or in homes"—meaning they should be planted first in domestic spaces as well. And so says Kashyapa:

> "The Ashoka, Champaka, Arishta, Punnaga, and Priyangu;
> The Shirisha, Udumbara, and the Parijata are the best.
> These trees are known to be auspicious; one should plant them first,
> In temples, as well as in parks, homes, and groves." || 3 ||

# Chapter 54: The Science of Plant Health (Vrikshayurveda)

Now the author describes the rules for those plants that can be grown from cuttings:

> The Jackfruit, Ashoka, Banana, Rose-apple, Monkey-jack, and Pomegranate;
> The Grapevine, the Palivata <note>likely a species of ebony or a citrus variety</note>, the Citron, and the Atimuktaka <note>a fragrant creeper, often identified as Mountain Jasmine</note>. ||4||
> These trees should be planted as cuttings after being smeared with cow dung;
> They should be planted either by grafting onto a rootstock or onto a trunk. ||5||

The Jackfruit; the Ashoka; the Banana; the Rose-apple; the Monkey-jack; the Pomegranate; the Grapevine (also called *mrdvika*); the Palivata (also called *ucca*); the Citron (also called *matulunga*); and the Atimuktaka.

These trees, starting with the Jackfruit, are "cutting-plantable" (*kandaroруa*). One should take the "cuttings" (branches), smear them with cow dung, and plant them. Furthermore, they are best planted by "root-cutting" (*muloccheda*) or on the "trunk" (*skandha*). <note>This refers to grafting techniques</note>. One may cut the root of another tree and plant a different species upon that severed root; or, one may cut another tree halfway up the trunk, carve out the trunk, and plant a different species there. In that process, one should apply a coating of clay. As Sage Kashyapa says:

> The Grape, Atimuktaka, Rose-apple, Citron, and Pomegranate;
> The Banana, the Bahula <note>Cardamom or a variety of Bakula</note>, and the Ashoka are to be sown as cuttings.
> Any other trees that are in flower or fruit
> Should also be smeared with cow dung and planted for successful growth. ||4-5||

Now, he speaks regarding the rules for the timing of planting trees:

> Those with no branches should be planted in the cool season (*Shishira*); those with branches in the early winter <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "Himagame"</note>;
> And those with well-developed trunks should be planted at the start of the rainy season <gloss>2</gloss>, keeping them in their original orientation. ||6||

Trees that have not yet produced branches or sprouts should be planted in the cool season (*Shishira*), which is the months of Magha and Phalguna <note>mid-January to mid-March</note>. Those that have developed branches should be planted in the early winter (*Hemanta*), the months of Margashirsha and Pausha <note>mid-November to mid-January</note>. Those with "good trunks"—meaning those possessing large branches—should be planted at the arrival of the rains (*Pravrit*), the months of Shravana and Bhadrapada <note>mid-July to mid-September</note>. Some read the text as "those with branches at the arrival of the clouds (*Ghanagame*) and those with trunks in the middle of the rains (*Varshagarbhe*)." "Arrival of clouds" means the start of the rainy season; "middle of the rains" means the peak of the monsoon.

These should be planted "according to their direction" (*yathadiksthan*). This means that the side of the tree that originally faced East in its previous location must be made to face East again when it is replanted elsewhere. The same alignment should be maintained for all the cardinal directions.

As Sage Kashyapa says:

# On the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 54]

> Trees that have not yet developed branches should be planted in the **Dewy Season** <note>Sishira: approximately late January to March</note>.
> Those that have developed branches should be planted according to the rules in the **Winter Season** <note>Hemanta: approximately late November to January</note>.
> Those trees that have well-developed trunks and branches should be planted during the **Rainy Season**. || 6 ||

The author says something further:

> With **ghee**, **vetiver**, **sesame**, **honey**, **vidanga**, **milk**, and **cow dung**:
> After smearing the tree from the root to the trunk with these, one should perform the **transplanting** and **re-planting**. || 7 ||

**Ghee** is clarified butter; **vetiver** <note>original: "ushira"</note> is well-known; **sesame**; **honey** is the product of bees; **vidanga** <note>a medicinal plant, *Embelia ribes*, used here for its anti-fungal/anti-parasitic properties</note>; **milk** is cow's milk; and **cow dung** is the excrement of the cow. With these substances—ghee and the rest—one should smear the trees from the root to the trunk (meaning from the very base up to the tips of the branches) and then perform the **transplanting**. **Transplanting** <note>original: "sankramanam"</note> means moving the tree to another location. The meaning is that one should take it to another place and plant it. As it is said:

> Ghee, milk, as well as honey, vetiver, sesame, and cow dung;
> Smearing with vidanga from the root allows for transplanting and re-planting.
> This means planting during the transfer is auspicious. || 7 ||

Now, he describes the ritual for planting:

> Having become pure, and having performed the **worship** of the tree with baths and ointments,
> One should plant it; once planted in this way, it grows with those very same leaves. || 8 ||

Having become **pure** (composed in mind), one should perform the **worship** (reverence) of the tree through **baths** (washing) and **ointments** (anointing), and then plant it. In this manner, the tree that is planted grows along with the very same leaves it possessed when it was moved, and it does not wither. || 8 ||

Now, he describes the rules for **watering** those that have been planted:

> In the **Hot Season**, water in the evening and morning; in the **Cold Season**, every other day;
> And in the **Rainy Season**, whenever the earth is dry, the planted trees must be watered. || 9 ||

Planted trees should be watered in the **Hot Season** (Summer) both in the evening and the morning. "Evening" refers to the late afternoon, and "morning" refers to the forenoon. In the **Cold Season** (Winter and the Dewy Season), they should be watered **every other day** (literally: placing a day in the middle/interval). In the **Rainy Season** (the monsoon time), they should be watered whenever the ground becomes dry. || 9 ||

Now, he lists the trees that grow in **marshy** <note>anupa: moist or watery soil</note> regions:

> The Rose Apple, the Reed, the Water-Cane, the Kadamba, the Cluster Fig, the Arjuna,
> The Citron, the Grapevine, the Monkey Fruit, and the Pomegranate. || 10 ||

# Chapter 54: The Science of Plant Life (Vrikshayurveda)

**The Vanjula, Naktamala, Tilaka, Panasa,**
**Timira, and Amrataka—these sixteen are known as water-loving species.** ||9||

The Rose Apple <note>Jambu</note>, the Cane <note>Vetasa</note>, the Vanira <note>a variety of cane</note>, the Kadamba, the Cluster Fig <note>Udumbara</note>, the Arjuna, the Citron <note>Bijapuraka or Matulunga</note>, the Grapevine <note>Mridvika or Draksha</note>, and the Monkey Fruit <note>Lakucha</note>, along with the Pomegranate <note>Dadima</note>. ||10||

The Vanjula, the Naktamala <note>Indian Beech</note>, the Tilaka, the Panasa <note>Jackfruit</note>, and in the same manner the Timira and the Amrataka <note>Hog Plum</note>. The word "and" <note>Sanskrit: cha</note> is used here to complete the set. These sixteen types of trees are "marsh-born" <term>Anupaja: plants that thrive in watery or marshy soil</term>; they grow in places with abundant water. ||11||

Now, to explain what the ideal distance should be between planted trees, the author says:

**The best spacing is twenty cubits; sixteen is middling.**
**The distance from one spot to another for trees should be twelve at the minimum.** ||12||

The distance from one spot to another—from one location to the next—should be twenty cubits <note>A 'hasta' or cubit is roughly 18 inches, the length from the elbow to the fingertip</note> all around the tree; this is the best measurement. A distance of sixteen cubits is middling, and a distance of twelve cubits is the lowest or least desirable. This means that where one tree is planted, another should be planted at a distance of twenty, sixteen, or twelve cubits. As the sage Kashyapa says:

->A distance of twenty cubits is remembered as the best for trees.<-
->Sixteen is known as middling, and twelve is remembered as the lowest.<- ||12||

Why is such a distance maintained between them? To answer this, he says:

**Trees grown too close together, touching one another,**
**and with their roots entangled, become cramped and do not yield fruit properly.** ||13||

Those trees that are grown in close proximity, touching one another, and cramped by roots that have become entangled or joined together, are "oppressed." Therefore, they do not yield or give fruit properly. ||13||

Now, he describes the diagnosis of their diseases:

**From cold, wind, and sun, disease arises; its signs are yellowing leaves,**
**lack of growth in shoots, the drying of branches, and the oozing of sap.** ||14||

Disease arises or is produced in them due to excessive cold, wind, or sun. A tree should be known as "diseased" <term>Saroga</term> by these signs: "pale-leafedness" <note>Pandupatrata: chlorosis or yellowing</note>, the lack of growth or prosperity in the new shoots, the "drying of branches" <note>Shakhashosha: loss of moisture/withering</note>, and the "oozing of sap" <note>Rasasruti: bleeding or exudation</note>. ||14||

# On the Treatment of Trees [Chapter 54]

Now, the author describes the medical treatment for these trees:

> First, the treatment for these involves cleansing with a blade. 
> Then, one should smear them with a paste of *Vidanga*, ghee, and mud, 
> and sprinkle them with milk and water. ||15||

Now follows the medical treatment for these trees. First, one must perform a cleansing of the wounds and such with a blade <note>shastra: a surgical instrument or knife</note>. Whatever part is rotten or moist with decay should be removed with the blade. Then, one should take *Vidanga* <term>Vidanga: Embelia ribes, a plant used in Ayurveda as an antimicrobial and anti-parasitic agent</term>, ghee <note>clarified butter</note>, and mud or clay; these should be mixed together and the affected areas should be thoroughly smeared with the paste. After that, one should sprinkle or drench the tree with "milk-water"—water mixed with milk. By doing this, they become free from disease. And so says **Kashyapa:** <note>An ancient sage and authority on agriculture and medicine</note>

<margin>Kashyapa's verses on tree pathology</margin>

> Those trees which are defined by their branches, canopies, and leaves; 
> those which are devoid of leaves and fruit, or are parched, or have pale leaves; 
> those suffering from cold, heat, rain, or wind, or from tangled roots; 
> or those trees that suffer disease due to the scratching of elephants—
> for these to be healed and made new again, 
> one should first cleanse them with blades and then apply an ointment. 
> One should smear them with mud mixed with *Vidanga* and ghee. 
> A sprinkling of milk-water brings about the healing of all trees. ||15||

### Now, the treatment for the failure of fruit is described:

> When fruit fails, a sprinkling of cooled, boiled milk 
> with Horse-gram, Black-gram, Mung beans, Sesame, and Barley 
> leads to an abundance of flowers and fruit. ||16||

When trees suffer from a loss of fruit, one should use Horse-gram, Black-gram, Mung beans, Sesame, and Barley. With these ingredients, milk should be boiled <note>shrita: decocted or boiled</note> and then cooled. This milk should then be used for sprinkling the trees to ensure a great increase in flowers and fruits. ||16||

### Now, a formula for the sake of growth is described:

> Two *Adhakas* of powdered dung from sheep and goats, one *Adhaka* of sesame, 
> one *Prastha* of barley meal, one *Drona* of water, 
> along with one *Tula* of beef; ||17||
> after these have sat for seven nights, the mixture should be used 
> to sprinkle the trees, thickets, and creepers, 
> to ensure flowers and fruit at all times. ||18||

The "sheep" (*avika*) is the well-known species of ram; the "goat" (*aja*) is the common goat. One should take two *Adhakas* <term>Adhaka: an ancient measure of capacity, roughly 3 kilograms or liters</term> of the powdered dung of these two—one *Adhaka* of sheep dung powder and one *Adhaka* of goat dung powder. With the hand, it is mixed—meaning thrown into milk. Having taken it out again, it should be separated using a hand smeared with ghee <note>clarified butter</note> until it becomes a single mass. This process should be performed every day for ten days. Then, it is rubbed many times with cow dung. "Kroda" means a boar; "Mriga" means a deer. "Krauda" refers to that which belongs to a boar, and "Marga" to that which belongs to a deer. It is then fumigated with "Krauda-marga-pishita"—the flesh of boars and deer; one should fumigate it while it is placed inside a vessel.

Then, combined with "Amisha" <note>flesh or meat</note> and with boar fat and marrow, it is planted in "Parikarmita" ground—meaning soil that has been prepared. The preparation is done by first sowing sesame seeds <note>a traditional method of soil enrichment</note>. Then, that seed is well-saturated, sprinkled with water mixed with milk. When this is done, it is born—it grows—already possessed of flowers. **[Verses 19-20]**

### Now he describes the procedure for the Tamarind:

> Even the Tamarind produces a creeper when treated with the powders and meals of rice, black gram, and sesame,
> combined with putrid meat, and constantly sprinkled and fumigated with turmeric. **[Verse 21]**

The word "even" <note>original: "api"</note> is used to indicate possibility. Even the Tamarind produces a "Vallari" <note>a creeper or new sprout</note>; it becomes a fresh sprout, even though it is extremely hard <note>referring to the hardness of the tamarind seed coat</note>. By what means? By the powders and meals of rice, black gram, and sesame—specifically the powder of Vrihi <note>paddy/rice</note>, Shali <note>fine rice</note>, Masha <note>black gram</note>, Til <note>sesame</note>, and Saktu <note>barley meal or flour</note>. Of what kind? Combined with "Puti-mamsa"—moist, decaying meat. Sprinkled with these and constantly—at all times—fumigated with turmeric. This is what is meant: the tamarind seed, having been sprinkled with the combined powders of rice, black gram, sesame, and meal along with putrid meat, should be fumigated with turmeric. It then produces a creeper. From the use of the word "even," what doubt can there be regarding the sprouting of other [softer] seeds? **[Verse 21]**

# Chapter 54: On the Exploration of Water and Agriculture

### On Soil Preparation and Planting

**With powdered substances:** One should fill the pit with powdered black gram, sesame, and barley. After filling the pit with earth, one should layer it with these internal substances. The meaning is this: after filling a layer of about four fingers' depth with earth, one should then fill it with the black gram mixture. Again, fill a similar measure with earth, and again with the black gram mixture. Then, one should strike it <note>meaning to tamp or compress the soil</note> with water mixed with fish flesh. With this water containing fish meat, one should repeatedly pound the pit until it reaches a state of density and hardness. || 25 ||

**Planted:** Then, a tree seed planted there at a depth of four fingers, and sprinkled with fish-water—that is, water mixed with fish and meat—quickly becomes a creeper with beautiful sprouts. What kind of creeper? One that is amazing <note>literally "causing wonder"</note>. It covers the entire supporting pavilion or arbor. || 26 ||

## Now he describes the planting of others:

> A seed soaked a hundred times in the paste of the fruit of the *Ankola* tree <note>Alangium salviifolium, known in traditional medicine</note>, or in the oil of that fruit, or likewise in the fruit of the *Shleshmantaka* tree <note>Cordia myxa or the Glue Berry tree</note> || 27 ||
>
> If planted in soil mixed with hail-stones <note>original: "karaka-unmishra-mridi"; refers to soil cooled or affected by hail</note>, it produces growth in that very instant. That the branch becomes laden with the weight of fruit—what wonder is there in that? || 28 ||

The *Ankola* is a tree; with the paste of the fruit produced from it—the "paste" being the slimy or mucilaginous part of the fruit—the seed of any tree is soaked or "infused" a hundred times. Or, it is infused a hundred times with the oil of that *Ankola* fruit. Alternatively, the same seed may be infused a hundred times with the fruit of the *Shleshmantaka* tree, using either its paste or its oil. || 27 ||

And that seed, when planted in soil mixed with hail, produces birth in that very moment. In the very moment or hour it is sown, it grows. That the branch or vine becomes endowed with a "burden of fruit"—meaning it is bent down by the weight of the fruit—what is the surprise in that? The meaning is that this result will certainly occur. || 28 ||

## Now he describes the planting of the Shleshmantaka:

> A wise man should take the seeds of the *Shleshmantaka*, remove their shells <insert>de-husk them</insert>, and soak them in the slimy water of the *Ankola* fruit in the shade <gloss>1</gloss> seven times in this manner. || 29 ||

**Having rubbed them with buffalo dung and placed them in its dried manure;**
**when sown in a mixture of hail-water and soil, they bear fruit within a day. || 30 ||**

A wise and intelligent person should take the seeds of the Shlesmataka tree <note>Cordia myxa, often called the Indian cherry</note>, remove the husks to strip them of their natural coating, and then soak them in the shade with the slimy, mucilaginous liquid of the Ankola fruit <note>Alangium salvifolium</note>. One should repeat this process seven times. After soaking them in the Ankola liquid, they should be dried in the shade, then soaked and dried again, repeating this until seven cycles are completed. || 29 ||

Then, those seeds should be rubbed and coated with the fresh dung of a buffalo. Having done this, one should deposit and keep those seeds within a heap of dried buffalo manure. They should remain there inside a vessel until such time as soil is prepared by mixing it with "hail-water" <note>original: "karaka-jala"; water from melted hailstones, considered to have unique potency</note>. When sown in a spot prepared with this hail-water and earth, they bear fruit within a single day. This means they produce fruit in just one day. || 30 ||

### Now he describes the lunar mansions for planting trees—

**The Fixed, the Soft, Mula, Vishakha, Jupiter’s star,**
**as well as Shravana, Ashvini, and Hasta;**
**These are the stars declared <gloss>1</gloss> by the divine-sighted for the planting of trees. || 31 ||**

The three "Later" stars <note>Uttara Phalguni, Uttara Ashadha, Uttara Bhadrapada</note> and Rohini are the "Fixed" stars. Anuradha, Chitra, Mrigashira, and Revati are the "Soft" stars. These, along with Mula, Vishakha, Tishya <note>Pushya</note>, Shravana, Ashvini, and Hasta, are the <term>Nakshatras</term> <note>lunar mansions or constellations used in Vedic astrology</note> stated for the work of sowing and planting trees. They were declared by the "divine-sighted"—those sages like Garga and others whose vision can perceive subtle truths. Some read the text as "praised" <note>original: "shastani"</note> instead of "declared." || 31 ||

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 55]

Having established [the site], one should construct a temple—a house for the deity—for the increase of glory and righteousness, meaning for the growth of one's fame and spiritual merit. ||1||

Regarding this very subject, the author speaks in praise:

->**By those desiring to attain the worlds reached through sacrifice and charity,**<-
->**A residence for the gods should be made; for both are seen to be present here.**<-

<term>Ishta</term> <note>original: "इष्टं"</note> refers to sacrifices and similar rituals, while <term>Purta</term> <note>original: "पूर्तं"</note> refers to public works like ponds, wells, and tanks. As it has been said:

->That gift which is given in sacrifices is called *Ishta*; other acts are regarded as *Purta*.<-
->A twice-born man should sacrifice with the *Ishta* rites, animal sacrifices, and the four-month seasonal rites.<-
->He who sacrifices with the Agnishtoma <note>a five-day Vedic fire ritual</note> and other sacrifices is a possessor of *Ishta*.<-
->Step-wells, wells, tanks, and temples for the deities,<-
->And the distribution of food are declared by the teachers to be *Purta*.<-

By those desiring to be—meaning those wishing to reach—those worlds or holy places that are obtained through sacrifice and charity, a residence for the gods (the Suras) should be made; meaning a house for the gods must be constructed. Because in this temple, "both are seen." This means the fruit or reward belonging to both sacrifice and charity is found and obtained here. Thus says the sage Kashyapa:

->Whatever humans perform through sacrifices such as *Ishta* and *Purta*;<-
->The sacrifice known as *Ishta* is proclaimed to be the Agnishtoma and other animal sacrifices.<-
->Step-wells, wells, tanks, and temples for the deities,<-
->Always ensure a stay in heaven; such giving is termed *Purta*.<-
->A residence for the gods should be made, for both [merits] are obtained here. ||2||<-

The author now describes in what kind of places the gods take delight:

->**In places provided with water and gardens, whether man-made or natural,**<-
->**In such places, the deities approach and manifest their presence.**<-

In places joined with water and accompanied by gardens or groves. "Man-made" means constructed by effort, and "natural" means those formed on their own. In these places, the deities approach <term>Sannidhya</term> <note>original: "सान्निध्यं"</note>, meaning they come to be closely present. ||3||

He describes further what these places are like:

->**In lakes where the sun's rays are warded off by the umbrellas of lotus leaves,**<-
->**Where the waters are made pure by the paths of white lilies tossed by the movement of swans.**<-

->Where the cries of swans, ducks, cranes, and ruddy geese resound,<-
->And where water-creatures rest in the shade of the *Nichula* trees along the banks. (5)<-

In such lakes, the various deities always and at all times take delight and play. What kind of lakes? Those where the sun's rays are warded off by the "umbrellas" of lotus leaves; specifically, the *Nalini* <note>a type of lotus plant</note> acts as a parasol, and by this lotus-parasol, the rays of the sun are cast away or neutralized. In these waters, the white lilies (*Kahlara*) are tossed about by the shoulders of the swans, and the clear water forms paths or "alleys" where these flowers are scattered. (4)

Swans, ducks (*Karandava*), cranes (*Krouncha*), and ruddy geese (*Chakravaka*)—all these are specific types of birds. Deities always delight in those lakes where the cries of these birds are heard, and likewise where water-dwelling creatures rest in the shadows of the *Nichula* <note>The *Barringtonia acutangula*, a tree that grows near water</note> trees situated along the edges or boundaries. (5)

He further describes other such places:

->Where the cranes form a tinkling waistband, and the swans provide a sweet voice;<-
->Where the sounding water is the garment, and the *Shaphari* fish form the girdle. (6)<-
->Where the flowering trees on the banks are the ear-ornaments, and the confluences are the rounded hips;<-
->Where the sandy banks are the high breasts, and the swans are the white raiment—in such rivers [the gods delight]. (7)<-

In whatever place such rivers exist, there the deities always take delight. What are these rivers like? The cranes, because of their rhythmic cries, are the "waist-band" or the expansive girdle of the river. The "sweet voice" or charming conversation of the river is the melodious warbling of the *Kalahamsas* <note>Supreme or Royal Swans</note>. The water itself is the garment or cloth. The *Shaphari* <note>Small, glistening silver fish</note> are the girdle-strings. A girdle (*Mekhala*) is tied over the clothing; it is commonly known as a *Nivi* <note>The knot or pleat of a woman's lower garment</note>. As it is said:

> The *Nivi* is the knotting of a woman's garment situated at the hips. (6)

Regarding "Flowering banks": In places where such rivers flow, the deities always delight. The trees in full bloom along the edges are the "ear-ornaments" (*Uttamsa*) <note>Flowers worn behind the ear or a garland for the head</note>. The high, elevated regions of the sandy banks (*Pulina*) are the breasts. The swans, because of their whiteness, are the white robes of the river. In such rivers, the deities find pleasure. (7)

He mentions other types of places where they delight:

->In the outskirts of forests, by rivers, mountains, and waterfalls,<-
->The deities always delight, as well as in cities full of gardens. (8)<-

# The Great Compilation with Commentary
## [Chapter 55]

At the edges of forests—meaning in the vicinity of woodlands. The word "edge" applies to each of the following locations: by rivers (streams), on mountains (hills), and on lands near waterfalls—lands adjacent to rivers and similar places that are joined by waterfalls or falling water. Waterfalls are so called because they "fall" or flow constantly. In these places, the gods always take delight and play at all times. Also in cities—towns that possess gardens, meaning those where parks and groves are found, they always take delight. And so says Kashyapa <note>An ancient sage and authority on architecture and ritual</note>:

> Where there are ponds rich with green and shining water, covered with birds,
> Adorned with forests and groves, with trees always in full bloom;
> Filled with swans and ducks, echoing with the songs of cuckoos,
> Sweet with the humming of six-legged bees, and joined by dancing peacocks;
> There the gods find pleasure, remaining ever-present due to the beauty of the surroundings. || 8 ||

Now, he speaks of the qualities of the soil for performing the consecration:

> The types of soil prescribed for Brahmins and the other classes in the construction of dwellings,
> Those same soils are recommended for them even in the building of temples. || 9 ||

"For Brahmins and the others" refers to the four classes: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras. The soils which were prescribed or described for them in the context of building houses <note>Vastu-karmani: the practice of architecture</note> are as follows:

> "White, red, yellow, and black soils are praised for the Brahmins and the other classes respectively.
> The scent of the earth should be like clarified butter, blood, food, and wine respectively.
> The ground should be covered with Kusha grass, Shar-reeds, Durva grass, and Kasha grass in order.
> According to the class, the soil brings prosperity and tastes sweet, astringent, sour, and pungent."

This is how it should be understood. For the Brahmins and the other classes, those same soils are praised or considered auspicious for the temples of the gods. || 9 ||

Now, he describes the characteristics of the "Vastu Purusha" <note>The "Spirit of the Site," a symbolic diagram used in Hindu architecture</note> and the division of the doors for the house of the deity:

> A temple should always be made with a grid of sixty-four squares.
> And a central door, placed exactly in the middle of the direction, is praised therein. || 10 ||

At all times, a temple—a house of the gods—should be made as a sixty-four-square grid. This was previously shown as "the grid of eight-by-eight squares." In that temple, a central door—one situated in the middle—is praised or desired, provided it stands exactly aligned with the cardinal direction. || 10 ||

### Now he describes the rules for temple construction —

> Whatever the width may be, its height should be double that amount.
> The "waist" <note>the middle part or basement molding of the temple</note> is declared to be equal to one-third of that height. || 1 ||
>
> The inner sanctum <term>garbha: literally "womb," the innermost chamber</term> should be half of the total width; the remaining portions all around are the walls.
> The door should be wide by one-fourth of the sanctum's width, and its height should be twice its width. || 2 ||
>
> The doorpost <term>shakha: the vertical frame of the door</term> should be wide by one-fourth of the door's height; the threshold <gloss>1</gloss> and lintel should be the same.
> The thickness of the doorposts is recorded as being equal to one-fourth of their width. || 3 ||
>
> Doors are praised when they have three, five, seven, or nine decorative vertical frames.
> At the bottom fourth-part of the doorpost, one should place the two door-keepers. || 4 ||
>
> The remaining space should be decorated with auspicious birds, "trees of fortune" <note>Shrivriksha</note>, swastikas, sacred jars, amorous couples, creeping vines, and playful goblins <note>Pramathas, the attendants of Shiva</note>. || 5 ||
>
> The idol, including its pedestal, should be eight parts of the door's measurement.
> Of those, the idol itself is two parts, and the pedestal is the third part. || 6 ||

**"Whatever the width"** means: whatever the width or diameter of that temple <note>original: "devagriha" - house of the god</note> may be, the total elevation or height is double that width. For example, the Meru-style temple has a width of thirty-two cubits <note>original: "hasta" - a measurement from elbow to fingertip, approx. 18 inches</note>. Double that width makes the height sixty-four cubits. The "waist" of the temple is said to be equal to one-third of that height. For example, the height of the Meru temple is sixty-four cubits. One-third of that is twenty-one cubits and eight inches <note>original: "angula" - finger-breadth</note>. The waist is made according to this measurement. The "waist" refers to the point where the temple structure begins above the stairs.

**"Half the width"** means: the inner sanctum is half of the stated width of the temple. For example, the width of the Meru is thirty-two cubits. Half of that is sixteen. The sanctum of the Meru is according to this measure. The other walls are all around in all directions and intermediate points. After leaving one cubit open on all sides for circumambulation <note>original: "bhramana"</note>, the remaining three cubits should be supported by the wall. The door is wide by a measurement of one-fourth of the sanctum. For example, the sanctum of the Meru is sixteen cubits. One-fourth of that is four cubits. This is the width of the door. The height must be made double the width. Thus, the height of the Meru door should be eight cubits.

**"From the height"** means: the doorpost should be made with a width equal to one-fourth of the door's height. For example, the height of the Meru door is eight cubits. Of this—

# Chapter 55: On Temple Architecture

**"One-fourth part is two cubits."** <note>original: "hastas" - a cubit is roughly the length of a forearm, about 18 inches.</note> This refers to the width of the doorpost <term>shakha: the vertical side-posts of a doorway</term>. In the same manner, the threshold and lintel <term>udumbara: the horizontal beams at the top and bottom of the door frame</term> should be constructed. Some texts read this as "the two *udumbaras*" (referring to both the upper and lower beams). **"Equal to a quarter of the width."** The thickness or depth of the doorposts is traditionally stated to be equal to one-fourth of their width. For example, if the width of the doorpost for a Meru-style temple is two cubits (36 inches), then the thickness should be twelve digits <note>original: "angulas" - a finger-width, 24 of which make a cubit</note>, which is one-fourth of that width.

**"With three, five, seven, or nine."** The doorway is considered auspicious and desirable when it is adorned with three, five, seven, or nine decorative vertical frames. If the required width of the doorpost is not filled by three frames, one should use five; if still not filled, then nine. On the bottom fourth of the doorposts, one should place figures of the door-keepers, such as Nandi holding his staff.

**"The remainder."** The remaining three-quarters of the doorpost should be beautified with auspicious birds—such as swans, ducks, ruddy geese, and pheasants—as well as "Trees of Fortune" <note>Shrivriksha</note>, *Svastika* designs (a specific sacred symbol), jars <note>ghatas/kalashas</note> resembling the proportions of the "Architectural Man" <note>Vastu-purusha</note>, amorous couples <note>mithunas</note>, leafy creepers, and the playful attendants of Shiva <note>pramathas</note>.

**"By one-eighth of the door measurement."** The height of the divine image <note>pratima</note> together with its pedestal <note>pindika</note> should be the total height of the door minus one-eighth of that height. Of this total height of the image-assembly, two parts should be the image itself, and the third part should be the pedestal. For example: if the door height of a Meru temple is eight cubits, one-eighth of that is one cubit. Subtracting this, the total height for the image and pedestal is seven cubits. Of these seven cubits, two-thirds (four cubits and sixteen digits) is the height of the image, and one-third (two cubits and eight digits) is the height of the pedestal. This logic should be applied to all temples. As the sage Kashyapa says:

> Temples should be built according to the city's proportions, possessing auspicious marks.
> They should be neither too high nor too low, and perfectly aligned with the cardinal directions.
> One should place the structure in the center of a sixty-four square grid.
> A central door is best and highly praised when aligned with the main directions.
> The height should be twice the width; the "waist" <note>kati: the middle section of the wall</note> should be at the third part.
> The inner sanctum <note>garbha</note> should be half the total width, with walls built around it.
> The door should be one-fourth the width of the sanctum, and its height twice its own width.
> The width of the doorposts is recorded as one-fourth of the door's height.
> The threshold and lintel are always said to follow the measurement of the doorposts.
> The thickness of the doorposts is proclaimed to be one-fourth of their width.

The doorframes should consist of one, three, five, seven, or even nine vertical sections <note>original: "shakha"; these are the decorative vertical bands of a doorframe</note>. These are highly recommended for the entrances, provided they are not obstructed by the door-leaves themselves. At a height of one-fourth of the doorframe, one should place the two door-guardians <note>original: "pratihara"</note>. The remaining space should be decorated with various auspicious motifs: mischievous spirits <note>original: "pramatha"</note>, birds, *jivajiva* birds, leeches, the "Tree of Fortune" <note>original: "shrivriksha"</note>, swastikas, lotuses, and beautiful swans. Between the leaf-patterns, one should depict lovely creepers, the celestial planets, and deities such as Ganesha <note>original: "vainayaka"</note>.

The deity, along with its pedestal <note>original: "pindika"</note>, should be installed in a sanctum that is well-adorned and auspicious. Two parts of the total height should be allocated to the idol, and the third part to the pedestal. The drainage channel <note>original: "sravanadronika"</note> for the ritual fluids is prescribed to be on the left side. This area is also for the disposal of old floral offerings <note>original: "nirmalya"</note>, the presentation of food offerings, and the performance of sacrifices, worship, and cleaning. # On the Characteristics of Temples [Chapter 55]

In that context of temple characteristics, there is the temple named **Meru** <note>Named after the sacred mountain at the center of the universe</note>. It is **hexagonal**, meaning it has six corners or edges. It is **twelve-storied**, meaning it has twelve levels built one above the other. It features **varied niches**, meaning there are various types of interior window-openings or apertures within it. It is **equipped with four doors**, having entrances in all four cardinal directions. It is **thirty-two cubits wide** <term>hastā: a cubit, roughly the length of a forearm</term>; by implication of its width, its height is sixty-four cubits. And so says **Kashyapa** <note>An ancient sage and authority on architecture</note>:

-> "Thirty-two cubits wide, with four doors and six sides," <-
-> "The stories there should be constructed with varied niches," <-
-> "Twelve levels rising one above the other, adorned with circular domes." <-
-> "This temple is known as Meru, as specified by Vishvakarman." <note>The divine architect of the gods</note> ||20|| <-

**Now he describes the characteristics of the Mandara and Kailasa temples:**

-> "The Mandara is thirty cubits wide, has ten stories, and is equipped with a spire." <-
-> "The Kailasa also has a spire; it is twenty-eight cubits wide and has eight stories." ||21|| <-

The term "hexagonal" applies to all these descriptions until the definition of the Nandana temple. The temple known as **Mandara** is thirty cubits in extent, meaning thirty hands wide. By implication of its width, its height is sixty cubits. It is also hexagonal. It is **ten-storied**, possessing ten levels, and is **equipped with a spire**. And so says Kashyapa:
-> "This second temple is thirty cubits wide." <-
Regarding the **Kailasa**: The word "also" implies a similar nature. The Kailasa is also hexagonal. It is **spired**, meaning it possesses peaks. It is **twenty-eight**, meaning twenty-eight cubits wide. By implication of its width, its height is fifty-six cubits. It is **eight-storied**, possessing eight levels. And so says Kashyapa:

-> "The Kailasa is eight-storied and is recorded as twenty-eight cubits." <-
-> "Hexagonal and endowed with a spire, this is the third temple." ||21|| <-

**Now he describes the characteristics of the Vimana and Nandana temples:**

-> "The one called Vimana is twenty-one cubits wide and fitted with latticed windows." <-
-> "The Nandana has six stories, is thirty-two cubits wide, and has sixteen domes." ||22|| <-

The type called **Vimana** is hexagonal. It is **fitted with latticed windows**, meaning it is equipped with window-openings characterized by stone lattices and "starling-eyes" <note>Small decorative perforations</note>. It is **twenty-one cubits wide** <note>original: "tri-sapta" or three-times-seven</note>. By implication of its width, its height is forty-two cubits. It also has eight stories. And so says Kashyapa:

->The *Vimana* type is equipped with latticed windows and is twenty-one cubits wide.<-
->The fourth type of temple is hexagonal and has eight stories.<-

Regarding the *Nandana*: The temple named *Nandana* is hexagonal. It is "six-storied," meaning it is equipped with six levels. It is "thirty-two," meaning thirty-two cubits <note>A cubit or *hasta* is a traditional unit of length, roughly 18 inches.</note> in width. Based on this width, its height is sixty-four cubits. It is equipped with sixteen *andas* <note>literally "eggs"; these are the dome-shaped finials or ribbed stone ornaments atop a temple</note>. The *anda* is placed at the top of the temple. As Kashyapa <note>An ancient sage and authority on architecture</note> says:

->The *Nandana* should be hexagonal and thirty-two cubits wide.<-
->The fifth temple is considered to be six-storied with sixteen finials. Thus it is said. (22)<-

### Now he describes the characteristics of the *Samudra* and *Padma* types:

->The one named *Samudra* is circular; the *Padma* is shaped like a lotus; both are eight cubits wide.<-
->Each has a single spire and only one story. (23)<-

The one named *Samudra* is "circular," meaning perfectly round like a *mudga* bean. The *Padma* is "lotus-shaped," resembling a lotus flower and equipped with eight petals. Both of these temples are "eight cubits wide." Based on this width, their height is sixteen cubits. They "should have a single spire," meaning both are characterized by one spire or finial. Furthermore, both of these temples have only a single story. As Kashyapa says:

->The *Samudra* should be circular, and the *Padma* shaped like a lotus.<-
->They are eight cubits wide, with a single story adorned with a spire. Thus it is said. (23)<-

### Now he describes the characteristics of the *Garuda* and *Nandivardhana* types:

->The *Garuda* is shaped like the divine eagle; the *Nandi* is twenty-four cubits wide.<-
->They should be made with seven stories and adorned with twenty finials. (24)<-

The one named *Garuda* is "shaped like Garuda," meaning it has the form of the mythical bird, complete with wings and a tail. "And the *Nandi*": the word "and" indicates a grouping. The one named *Nandivardhana* is also shaped like the *Garuda* form, but is devoid of the wings and tail. They are "six times four" in width, meaning both the *Garuda* and *Nandivardhana* are twenty-four cubits wide. Their height is forty-eight cubits. Likewise, they are "seven-storied," meaning equipped with seven levels. Both the *Garuda* and *Nandivardhana* are adorned with twenty finials. As Kashyapa says:

->The *Garuda* is shaped like the eagle-king, adorned with wings and a tail.<-
->The *Nandi* is known to have the same shape, but is without the wings and other features.<-

The one named **Kunjara** is "elephant-backed," meaning it has the shape of an elephant's back. It is "sixteen cubits on all sides from the base," meaning its diameter or width is sixteen cubits in all four directions. <insert>Another reading says: "sixteen cubits well-extended from the base."</insert> Thus, its height is thirty-two cubits <note>Following the standard rule that height is twice the width</note>. It is shaped like a standing elephant and has one story. The **Guharaja** is shaped like a cave <note>original: "guhākāraḥ"</note>. It is sixteen cubits wide and its height is thirty-two cubits. These are also single-storied. For both of these, the roof-ridge <gloss>the hollows of the Valabhi</gloss> should have "three gabled windows." This means they are equipped with three *Chandrashalas*. > The Kunjara resembles the back of an elephant and is sixteen cubits wide.
> The Guharaja is shaped like a cave and is known to be sixteen cubits in diameter.
> A well-featured roof-ridge with three gabled windows should be made for them.
> These are proclaimed as the tenth and eleventh types of temples. 25.

> The **Vrisha** has a single story and a single spire, and is twelve cubits wide and circular all around.
