The one named **Vrisha** (The Bull) has a single story and a single spire <note>original: "shringa"</note> or peak. It is twelve cubits wide. From that width, its height is twenty-four cubits. It is "circular all around," meaning perfectly round in all directions. The **Hansa** (The Swan) is "swan-shaped," resembling a swan, equipped with a beak, wings, and a tail. It is twelve cubits wide and its height is twenty-four cubits; it is also single-storied. The one named **Ghata** (The Pot) has the "form of a water-pot," shaped like a pitcher. It is eight cubits wide. From that width, its height is sixteen cubits. All of these are single-storied and have a single spire. As Kashyapa says:

> The Vrisha is twelve cubits, perfectly circular, and single-storied.
> It is proclaimed as a temple joined with a single spire.

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Temples

> The **Swan** temple is to be known by its swan-like shape, twelve cubits <note>original: "hasta" - a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to 18 inches</note> in width. It is equipped with a single story and decorated with wings, a tail, and other features.
> The **Pot** temple is in the form of a water-jar <note>original: "kalasha"</note> and is recorded as being eight cubits wide. // 26 //

---

Now he describes the characteristics of the **All-Auspicious** <term>Sarvatobhadra: a temple type that is "auspicious from all sides"</term>—

> The **All-Auspicious** temple is equipped with four doors and many spires. It has many beautiful gabled windows <term>Chandrashala: literally "moon-chambers," these are decorative arched windows</term>, is twenty-six cubits wide, and has five stories. // 27 //

The temple named **All-Auspicious** is equipped with four doors. This means that there are doors in all four cardinal directions. It has many spires; there are numerous, abundant spires <note>original: "shikhara"</note> on it. It has many beautiful gabled windows; it is equipped with many abundant, pleasing, and very handsome "moon-chambers." It is twenty-six; it is twenty-six cubits in width. By implication of its width, its height is fifty-two cubits <note>The height of a temple in this system is typically double its width</note>. It is five-storied; it is equipped with five levels. It is square.

And so says **Kashyapa** <note>An ancient sage and authority on architecture</note>—

> Equipped with many spires and adorned with four doors; surrounded by many beautiful gabled windows. Square, five-storied, and twenty-six cubits wide; the fifteenth temple is called the **All-Auspicious**. // 27 //

---

Now he describes the characteristics of the **Lion**, **Circular**, **Square**, **Sixteen-sided**, and **Eight-sided** temples—

> The **Lion** temple is adorned with lions, has twelve corners, and is eight cubits wide. The other four are dark in form <note>original: "anjana-rupa"</note>, but the **Square** one is equipped with five dome-finials <note>original: "anda" - literally "eggs," referring to the rounded finials on top of a temple</note>. // 28 //

The **Lion** temple is "overcome by lions," meaning it is decorated with lion figures. It has twelve corners or twelve edges. It is eight cubits wide. The other four—the **Circular**, **Square**, **Sixteen-sided**, and **Eight-sided**—have shapes corresponding to their names. The **Circular** is perfectly round. The **Square** is four-cornered. The **Sixteen-sided** has sixteen corners. The **Eight-sided** has eight corners. These are **dark in form** <term>Anjana-rupa: literally "the color of eye-black/collyrium"</term>, meaning they are indistinct or dark. This means that external light does not enter them. Having constructed walls close to the divine temple in all four directions, a door should be made in the western part of the temple. Those walls should be joined at the top in such a way that they appear to have originated from the temple itself, not as separate structures. There, having entered from the outer door and coming around the left side of the temple, the door of the temple should be made in front. There, a jeweled idol is placed, where light is produced by its luster. All of these should be made with a single story and a single dome-finial. The **Square** one, however, should be made with five dome-finials; joined with five "eggs." And so says **Kashyapa**—

Chapter 55 of the Great Compilation with Commentary

->The **Lion** temple is shaped like a lion, equipped with twelve corners.<-
->It should be eight cubits <note>original: "hasta"; a traditional unit of measurement roughly 18 inches</note> in width and possess a single storey.<-
->The **Circle** temple is to be made circular in shape; others are likewise named after their forms.<-
->All of these are dark inside, consist of a single storey, and are enclosed.<-
->All are adorned with a single dome-finial, while the square type has five.<- Thus ends verse 28.

Now, he states the measurement of a storey <term>Bhūmikā: the vertical height of a single floor or level of a temple</term> according to the opinions of the divine architects Maya and Viśvakarman—

> **According to Maya, a storey measures one hundred and eight finger-breadths.**
> **Viśvakarman, however, stated it to be three and a half cubits. (29)**

In the opinion of Maya, a storey is one hundred and eight <term>Aṅgulas: finger-breadths, the basic unit of linear measure</term> in height. As Maya says:

> The measurement of a temple storey is recorded as one hundred and eight...
> . . . . . finger-breadths.

Viśvakarman stated the measurement of a storey to be three and a half cubits. This means eighty-four finger-breadths <note>Since 1 cubit = 24 finger-breadths, 3.5 cubits = 84 finger-breadths</note>. As Viśvakarman says:

> A storey consists of eighty-four finger-breadths. (29)

Here, he speaks to show the agreement between these different opinions:

> **On this matter, the learned master-builders state a unified opinion.**
> **The shorter storeys, when combined with the dove-cot molding, reach equality with the larger ones. (30)**

On this subject, the wise <term>Sthapatis: master-builders or architects</term> who are experts in the installation tantras <note>technical manuals</note> have stated that the views of Maya and Viśvakarman are actually one. Those storeys which are "shorter" or lesser in measurement according to Viśvakarman's view, reach equality with Maya’s measurement when they are <term>Kapotapālī-saṃyukta: joined with the dove-cot molding</term>. By the term "dove-cot molding," we refer to the wooden beams carved with lion-faces that project outward. As it has been said:

> The highly learned call the <term>Vitaṅka: a decorative frieze or cornice</term> the "dove-cot molding."

Furthermore, it is read in another manual:

> The measurement without the dove-cot molding is eighty-four.
> Along with that, the measurement of the storeys is recorded as one hundred and eight
> finger-breadths; thus, equality in the storeys is proclaimed.

In this way, the measurements become equal. (30)

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Adamantine Glue
### [Chapter 56]

Now, the author speaks to conclude the previous topic—

> ->**This description of temple characteristics has been told in brief;**<-
> ->**everything composed by Garga is contained herein.**<-
> ->**Regarding the extensive works composed by Manu and others,**<-
> ->**I have created this chapter while touching upon their essence. || 31 ||**<-

I have told this <term>description of temple characteristics</term> <note>Prāsāda-lakṣaṇa</note> in brief, meaning in a summarized form. Everything composed by the sage <term>Garga</term> is present here in its entirety, without omission. Furthermore, regarding the extensive and detailed descriptions of temples composed by <term>Manu and others</term>—namely Manu, Vasishtha, Maya, and Nagnajit—I have created this chapter while touching upon them, characterized by features such as "the door measurement being one-eighth less" and so on. This means the definition of a temple has been established. Alternatively, it means I have authored this while referencing and considering all those various characteristics. || 31 ||

->Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, named "Characteristics of Temples,"<-
->in the Commentary on the Samhita composed by Sri Bhattotpala.<-

### Now, the characteristics of <term>Adamantine Glue</term> are explained.

Regarding that, he first describes the <term>Adamantine Glue</term> <note>Vajralepa: a high-durability architectural cement or plaster</note>—

> ->**Unripe Tinduka fruits, unripe Kapitthaka fruits, and the flowers of the Shalmali tree;**<-
> ->**The seeds of Shallaki, the bark of the Dhanvana tree, and Vacha (Orris root); || 1 ||**<-
> ->**These should be boiled in a "drona" of water until only an eighth part remains.**<-
> ->**This should be taken down, and its paste should be mixed with the following substances: || 2 ||**<-
> ->**Turpentine, Guggulu resin, Bhallataka (marking nut), Kunduruka (frankincense), and Sarja resin;**<-
> ->**Combined with linseed and Bilva fruit, this paste is known as "Adamantine Glue." || 3 ||**<-

<term>Tinduka</term> refers to the <term>Tinduka fruit</term>. <term>Unripe</term> means not yet matured. <term>Kapitthaka</term> is the <term>Kapitthaka fruit</term>, also unripe. The flowers of the <term>Shalmali</term> or <term>Shalmali tree</term>. The seeds of <term>Shallaki</term> or <term>Shallaki trees</term>. <term>Dhanvan-valka</term> is the bark or skin of the <term>Dhanvana tree</term>. And <term>Vacha</term>. These are the types of ingredients. || 1 ||

With these substances, a <term>drona of water</term> should be boiled. A <term>drona</term> is two hundred and fifty-six "palas" <note>a traditional unit of weight</note>. It should be boiled until an eighth part remains, meaning thirty-two palas are left. Then, that eighth-part remainder should be "taken down," meaning removed from the heat and collected. To this eighth-part remainder, a <term>paste</term> or powder of the substances to be mentioned next should be added or prepared. This means it should be combined with those powders. || 2 ||

# Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 56]

He explains the ingredients: **Shrivasaka** and others. Shrivasaka is the well-known resin of a tree. **Rasa** refers to myrrh <note>original: "bola"</note>. **Guggulu** <note>Indian Bdellium</note> is well-known. **Bhallataka** <note>marking nut</note> is also well-known. **Kunduruka** is the resin of the Deodar tree. **Sarjarasa** is the resin of the Sal tree. Along with these, **Atasi** <note>flax/linseed</note> is well-known, and **Bilva** is the wood-apple fruit. Combined with these, this paste is called **Vajralepa** <note>literally "Diamond Plaster" or "Adamantine Glue"</note>; such is its name. ||3||

Now he describes its qualities:

->**On temples, mansions, balconies, Shiva-lingas, and idols; on walls and in wells;**<-
->**It should be applied while heated; it then lasts for ten million years.**<- ||4||

**Prasada** refers to a **temple of the gods**. **Harmya** is a mansion, **Valabhi** is a turret or balcony, **Linga** is the Shiva-linga, and **Pratima** is a worshiped image. On these, as well as on **Kudya** (walls) and in **Kupa** (wells or water-works). It should be applied **Santapta**, meaning very hot. It becomes **Varsha-sahasrayuta-sthayi**, meaning it lasts for ten thousand thousands—that is, for ten million years. ||4||

Now he describes another type of Adamantine Glue:

->**Lac, Kunduru, Guggulu, soot from the house, the pulp of Kapittha and Bilva;**<-
->**Nagaphala, Neem, Tinduka, Madana fruit, Madhuka, and Manjistha;**<-
->**Sarjarasa, Rasa, and Amalaka; this second paste thus prepared,**<-
->**Is also called "Vajra"; it possesses the same qualities as the first and is used for the same purposes.**<- ||5-6||

**Laksha** <note>Lac</note> is the well-known resinous secretion. **Kunduru** is the resin of the Deodar tree. **Guggulu** is well-known. **Grihadhuma** is the soot from the house, commonly known as *Shyama*. **Kapittha** is the fruit of the Kapittha tree. **Bilva-madhya** is the pulp of the Bilva fruit. Along with these, **Nagaphala**. **Nimba** <note>Neem</note> is well-known. **Tinduka** is the fruit of the Tinduka tree. Some read this as **Nagabala-phala**, **Tinduka**, and **Madana-phala**. **Nagabala-phala**, **Tinduka-phala**, **Madana-phala**, **Madhuka-phala**, and **Manjistha** <note>Indian Madder</note> are all well-known. ||5||

**Sarjarasa** is the resin of the Sal tree, **Rasa** is myrrh, and **Amalaka** is the Indian gooseberry; these as well. In this manner, a second paste is made, named **Vajra** or designated as **Vajralepa**. With the **Prathama-gunaih** (the qualities mentioned previously), these ingredients should be boiled in a *Drona* <note>a specific ancient measure of volume</note> of water until reduced to an eighth part, and it should be applied while heated. This **Vajralepa** is also for the same purposes mentioned before, such as temples and so on. It also lasts for ten million years. ||6||

He <note>The author, Varahamihira</note> says another thing—

**Another paste called "Vajratala" (Adamantine Surface) is made from the horns of cows, buffaloes, and goats; the hair of donkeys; buffalo hide; and cowhide; along with the juices of Neem and Wood-apple. ||7||**

Cows and buffaloes are well-known; "Aja" means a goat. From all of these, the "Vishana" or horns are taken. Likewise, with "Khara-romna" or donkey hair. Along with buffalo hide and cowhide, and the juices of Neem and Wood-apple—the fruit of the Neem and Wood-apple trees. "Rasa" here refers to the liquid extract <note>original: "bola"</note>. He says another thing—

Eight parts of lead. Two parts of bell-metal <note>original: "Kansya," a bronze alloy</note>. One part of brass <note>original: "Ritika"</note>. This mixture is named "Vajrasanghata." It is "Maya-kathito," meaning it was spoken or taught by Maya <note>The legendary architect and polymath of ancient India</note>. Others in the tradition suggest they should be made in equal measures. As Maya himself says:

> Having taken eight parts of lead, two of bell-metal, and one part
> of brass, the heated mixture is celebrated as "Vajra." ||8||

->Now, the "Characteristics of Images" <note>Pratima-lakshana</note> is explained.<-

At the very beginning, he speaks regarding the measurement of an atom <note>Paramanu</note>—

**When the sun passes through the holes of a lattice-window, the smallest particle of dust that comes into sight should be known as an "Atom"; it is the first of all measurements. ||1||**

When the "Bhanu" or sun is "Jalantarage," meaning situated in the middle of the openings of a window-lattice, the "Rajas" or dust which is "Anutaram" (extremely small) and comes into the path of vision—one should know that measurement as a "Paramanu." "Hi" is used in the sense of "because." It is the very first, the primary measurement of all measurements, known by the name "Atom." ||1||

# Now, having understood the "atom," he explains the knowledge of the measurement of a "finger-unit":

> The atom, a speck of dust, a hair's tip, a nit, a louse, and a barley-corn;
> Each multiplied by eight in sequence results in the measurement of one finger-unit. ||2||

These atoms and the rest, when multiplied by eight in succeeding order, constitute one finger-unit <note>Sanskrit: *angula*, a standard unit of measurement in ancient Indian iconography</note>. It is as follows: eight atoms make one speck of dust. Eight specks of dust make one hair's tip. Eight hair-tips make one nit. Eight nits make one louse. Eight lice make one barley-corn. Eight barley-corns make one finger-unit. Thus, by multiplying atoms and the rest by eight in sequence, the count of a finger-unit is reached. As it is said:

> The minute speck of dust seen in a beam of light
> Entering through a lattice window,
> Is called the "atom," the first of all measurements.
> From that, the speck of dust, the hair's tip, the nit, the louse, the barley-corn, and the finger-unit
> Are to be known as eightfold in succession; twenty-four finger-units make a cubit. ||2||

# Now he states the measurement of the entire idol:

> Of the height of the temple door, diminished by an eighth part, take one third;
> That is the measurement of the pedestal, and the idol is twice that size. ||3||

In a temple <note>Sanskrit: *devagara*, house of the god</note>, whatever the height of the door may be, subtract an eighth part of that height. One third of that remaining value is the measurement of the pedestal <note>Sanskrit: *pindika*</note>. The idol <note>Sanskrit: *pratima*</note> itself should be twice the measurement of that pedestal. ||3||

# Now he states the measurements of the limbs of the idol:

> By its own finger-units, the face should be twelve units in width and length;
> But according to Nagnajit, the "Dravidian" face is said to be fourteen units in length. ||4||

From whatever material—wood, stone, or otherwise—the idol is made, its total height (excluding the pedestal) should be divided into 108 parts; one such part is designated as a "finger-unit" <note>Sanskrit: *angula*</note>. This is because he will later state that the total measurement of an idol is 108 finger-units. "By its own finger-units" means the idol's own proportional units. The face should be made twelve finger-units wide and twelve finger-units long. However, the sage Nagnajit <note>An ancient authority on Vastu Shastra and painting</note> has stated that the face should be twelve units wide and fourteen units long in height. This is the "Dravidian" <note>Southern Indian style</note> measurement. As Nagnajit says:

> The face is twelve units wide and fourteen units in length;
> Such a measurement is known as the Dravidian style. ||4||

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Images

He says further—

**The nose, forehead, chin, and neck are each four fingers <term>angula; a traditional unit of measurement based on the width of a finger</term> in length, as are the ears. The two jaws are each two fingers, and the chin is two fingers in width.** (5)

The nose should be made four fingers in length. The forehead—the upper part of the face—is likewise four fingers. The chin is four fingers <note>The author clarifies that "chin" here refers to the vertical measurement from the base of the nose</note>. The neck is four fingers long, and the ears are also four fingers long. The two jaws are each two fingers wide. The "jaws" refer to the joints between the mouth and the throat. The chin should be made two fingers in width; here, the word "chin" refers specifically to the lower surface of the face. (5)

He says further—

**The forehead is eight fingers in width; beyond that, the two temples are two fingers each. The temples are four fingers long, and the ears are two fingers in breadth.** (6)

The forehead should be made eight fingers wide. Beyond that area, on both sides, the two temples should be made with a measurement of two fingers—meaning they are placed past the forehead. The temples should be four fingers long in their downward portion, as the cheek area is said to be below the temples. The ears should be made two fingers in breadth or thickness. (6)

He says further—

**The edge of the ear should be made at four and a half fingers, on a line level with the eyebrows. The ear canal and the "soft part" <term>sukumaraka; likely the tragus</term> should be level with the corner of the eye.** (7)

"At four and a half" means the section measuring four and a half fingers. Starting from the end of the eye, following a line level with the eyebrows and passing through the middle of the eye, the edge of the ear should be placed. The "edge of the ear" refers to the tip or top of the ear. The ear canal (the hole of the ear) and the *sukumaraka*—the raised path near the ear canal—should be level with the *netra-prabandha*. By the term *netra-prabandha*, the inner corner of the eye <note>original: "pradushika"</note> is meant. It should be made equal to that, meaning one finger in measurement. (7)

He says further—

**Vasistha <note>A legendary Vedic sage and authority on sacred architecture and law</note> states that the gap between the corner of the eye and the ear is four fingers. The lower lip is one finger in measurement, and the upper lip is half of that.** (8)

The sage Vasistha states the interval or gap between the end of the eye and the ear is four fingers. And so says Vasistha:

**The distance between the ear and the eye should be known as four fingers.** <note>The 'finger' (angula) is the standard unit of measurement in ancient Indian iconography, roughly equal to the width of a thumb.</note>
The lower lip should be made with a width of one finger, and the upper lip should be made with half of that—half a finger in width. ||8||

**The philtrum should be half a finger, and the mouth should be made four fingers long.**
**It should be one and a half fingers wide when closed, and three fingers wide when open. ||9||**

The <term>gochha</term> <note>original: "gochha"; the philtrum or the vertical groove above the upper lip</note> should be made half a finger wide. The mouth should be made four fingers long. **The two nostrils should be equal to two fingers, and the nose should be known from the tip of the nostrils.**

The two nostrils should be made with a measure equal to two fingers. Likewise, the nose should be known or understood to be two fingers from the tip of the nostrils. The height or elevation of the nose should be two fingers. The space between the two eyes is four fingers in measure. This is understood even if not explicitly stated. ||10||

He says another thing—

The <term>drktara</term> <note>original: "drktara"; the pupil, literally 'the star of sight'</note> or the "maiden" <note>A poetic term for the pupil</note> in the center is a fifth part of two fingers. The opening of the eye, or the width of the eye-aperture, is one finger. ||11||

He says another thing—

**From end to end, the eyebrows are ten; the line of the brow is half a finger.**
**The space between the brows is two fingers; the length of an eyebrow is four fingers. ||12||**

From the outer end of one eyebrow to the outer end of the other, the measure is ten fingers. That is, from the edge of the left brow to the edge of the right brow, it is ten fingers. The head should be made thirty-two Angulas in circumference. It should be fourteen Angulas in "extension," meaning in its diameter. In the practice of <term>Chitrakarma</term> <note>The art of painting or relief carving</note>, twelve Angulas are visible to the viewer, while twenty Angulas are hidden <note>referring to the back of the head not shown in a two-dimensional portrait</note>. || 14 ||

> The neck is ten Angulas wide and twenty-one in circumference. || 15 ||

In the "Characteristics of Images" taught by <term>Nagnajit</term> <note>An ancient authority on Vastu and sculpture, often associated with the Gandhara tradition</note>, the face including the mass of hair is sixteen Angulas. The face itself is fourteen Angulas long and the hairline is two Angulas; thus, sixteen. As Nagnajit says:

> "The hairline is two Angulas, and thus the face shall be sixteen Angulas."

The neck (the throat-bearer) should be made ten Angulas wide. It is "twenty plus one," meaning twenty-one Angulas in circumference. || 15 ||

> From the center of the navel to the top of the penis, the distance is stated to be exactly the same. || 16 ||

# 684
## In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 57]

The distance from the center of the navel to the middle of the male organ <note>original: "medhrāntaraṃ liṅgamadhyaṃ ca"</note> is also twelve digits <term>Angula: a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the width of a finger</term>. It is stated to be exactly equal to that measurement. || 16 ||

->Now another point:<-

> **The thighs are twenty-four digits in length, and the shanks are the same. The kneecaps and the heels are four digits each, and the feet are equal to that in height.** || 17 ||

The thighs <note>original: "Urū"</note> are twenty-four digits long. Similarly, the shanks <note>original: "Janghe"</note> are also twenty-four digits long. The two kneecaps <note>original: "Janukapicche"</note> should be made four digits in measurement—these are commonly known in the world as the "ekkala" <note>the patella or kneecap</note>. The feet are equal to that; the lower part starting from the ankle should be made four digits high. || 17 ||

->He says another point as well:<-

> **The feet are twelve digits long and six digits in width. The big toes are three digits long and five digits in circumference. The second toe is three digits long.** || 18 ||

The two feet, from the heel to the base of the big toe, should be made twelve digits long, and six digits in width or breadth. The big toes <note>original: "Angushthau"</note> should be made three digits long. In circumference, they should be five digits. The second toe <note>original: "Pradeshini"</note>, which is next to the big toe, should be made three digits long. || 18 ||

->He says another point:<-

> **The remaining toes should be made shorter in sequence by one-eighth part each. The height of the big toe is said to be one and a quarter digits.** || 19 ||

The remaining three toes should be made shorter in a regular sequence by one-eighth part each; that is, the middle toe should be one-eighth less than the second toe. The height or elevation of the big toe is stated to be one and a quarter digits. The height of the remaining toes should be determined based on the measurement of the big toe, reducing them by one-eighth part in sequence. || 19 ||

->He says another point:<-

> **The nail of the big toe is said by experts to be three-quarters of a digit. For the remaining nails, the measure is half a digit, or slightly less in sequence.** || 20 ||

By those who know the characteristics of images <note>iconographers</note>, the nail of the big toe is said to be three-quarters of a digit. For the nails of the remaining toes, the measurement is half a digit. Alternatively, they may be made slightly less than half a digit in sequence, so that beauty is achieved. || 20 ||

### He says another thing—

**The circumference at the end of the shin is said to be fourteen; its width is five.**
**In the middle, it is seven wide; the circumference is three times seven. (21)**

At the end of the shin <note>the ankle area</note>, the circumference is said to be fourteen digits <term>Angula: a unit of measurement based on the width of a finger</term>. In width, it is five digits. In the middle of the shin, it is seven digits wide. The circumference there is three times seven, meaning it is twenty-one digits. (21)

### He says another thing—

**The width in the middle of the knee is eight, while the circumference is three times eight.**
**The middle of the thighs is fourteen wide, and their circumference is double that. (22)**

In the middle of the knee, the width or thickness is eight digits. The circumference is three times eight, which is twenty-four digits. In the middle of the thighs, the width is fourteen digits. Their circumference—the measurement around them—is double that, which results in twenty-eight digits. (22)

### He says another thing—

**The hips are eighteen wide and forty plus four in circumference.**
**The navel is one digit in depth and the same in its dimension of width. (23)**

The hips are eighteen digits wide. In circumference or girth, they are forty plus four, totaling forty-four digits. The navel is one digit in depth <note>referring to its hollow</note> and is the same measurement in its width. (23)

### He says another thing—

**The middle circumference at the level of the navel is forty minus two.**
**The distance between the two breasts is sixteen; the armpits are six digits above. (24)**

The circumference at the middle of the body, level with the navel, is forty minus two, which is thirty-eight digits <note>The commentary clarifies the calculation as 42, but the verse suggests 38 or 42 depending on the reading of 'viyuta'</note>. The space or interval between the two breasts is sixteen digits. Six digits above the breasts, measured diagonally, the two armpits should be made. (24)

### He says another thing—

**The upper arms should be made twelve, and the forearms the same.**
**The upper arms are six wide, while the forearms are four digits. (25)**

The shoulders <note>original: "amsau"</note>, extending from the sides of the neck to the edge of the shoulder-blades, should be made eight digits <term>angula; a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the width of a finger</term> in width. The upper arms, located near the shoulders, should be twelve digits long. The forearms <note>original: "pratibahu"</note>, following the upper arms, should likewise be twelve digits long. The upper arms are six digits wide, while the forearms are four digits wide. ||25||

He says something further—

**The arms should be sixteen digits in circumference at the base, and twelve at the wrist. The palm of the hand should be six digits in width and seven in length.** ||26||

The arms at the root <note>the shoulder socket</note> are sixteen digits in circumference <note>original: "parinaha"</note>. At the "fore-hand" or the forearm region, the circumference is twelve digits. The palm of the hand <note>original: "karatala"</note> should be made six digits in width and seven digits in length or extent. ||27||

He says something further—

**The middle finger is five digits long; the index finger is shorter by half a joint than the middle one. The ring finger is equal to the index, while the little finger is shorter by one full joint.** ||27||

The finger next to the thumb <note>the index finger, "pradeshini"</note> should be made shorter than the middle finger by half a joint <note>original: "parva"</note>. This equals four and a half digits. A "joint" is defined as the space from the first line to the second line of the finger. The ring finger <note>original: "anamika"</note> should be made equal to this index finger. The little finger <note>original: "kanishthika"</note> should be made shorter than that ring finger by one full joint. ||27||

He says something further—

**The thumb should have two joints; the remaining fingers should be made with three joints each. The size of the nails for all of them should be half the length of a joint.** ||28||

The thumb <note>original: "angushtha"</note> should be made with two joints. The remaining fingers are to be made with three joints each. For all fingers, the measurement of the nail should be half of a finger-joint. ||28||

Having thus described the characteristics of the individual limbs, he now speaks to demonstrate the overall form—

**The idol should be made with ornaments, dress, decorations, and a physical form suited to the country. Such an image, endowed with the correct characteristics, brings prosperity when it is present.** ||29||

With ornaments <note>original: "bhushana"</note> suited to the country, such as necklaces, armlets, and bracelets. With dress and decorations <note>original: "veshalankara"</note> for the body. In whatever country the image is made, it should reflect the dress of the men there. With forms <note>original: "murtibhih"</note>, meaning the body, whether stout—

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Images

The image should be crafted with subtle details in accordance with the specific region. Because an image endowed with the characteristics <term>lakshanas; defining attributes or auspicious marks</term> prescribed in the scriptures <term>shastras; traditional scientific or legal treatises</term> remains present at all times and bestows prosperity; it grants growth and success to the maker <note>the patron or the sculptor</note>. ->The shoulders are recorded as being eight <term>angulas</term> <note>An angula is a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the width of a finger</note> wide; the arms are twenty-four angulas long.<-
->The arms should be sixteen angulas at the base and are recorded as twelve at the forearm.<-
->The palm of the hand is six angulas wide and is recorded as seven in length.<-
->The middle finger should be five angulas; the index finger is half an angula less than that.<-
->The ring finger is equal to the index, and the little finger is one angula shorter than those.<-
->These should be made well-formed; the thumb is recorded as having two joints.<-
->The remaining fingers have three joints; the nails are half the width of a joint.<-
->The hands should be made with regional dress and of a gentle appearance.<-
->An image that is well-formed and endowed with the proper characteristics brings prosperity. Thus it is said. || 29 ||<-

Now he describes the specific characteristics of particular images—

->Rama, the son of Dasharatha, and Bali, the son of Virochana, should be one hundred and twenty angulas tall.<-
->The remaining types—superior, middling, and inferior—are determined by successive reductions of twelve angulas. || 30 ||<-

Rama, the son of Dasharatha, and Bali, the son of Virochana, should be made one hundred and twenty angulas in height. The other remaining images are of superior, middling, and inferior measurements by a reduction of twelve—meaning by subtracting twelve each time. By subtracting twelve angulas from one hundred and twenty, a **superior image** of one hundred and eight angulas is obtained. By subtracting twelve from that, a **middling image** of ninety-six angulas is obtained. By subtracting twelve from that, an **inferior image** of eighty-four angulas is obtained. According to the rule stated previously, <quote>"A face is twelve angulas wide and long by its own units of measurement,"</quote> <margin>1. Verse 4 of this same chapter.</margin> the image described there totals one hundred and eight angulas. In the case of what is said here—<quote>"Rama, the son of Dasharatha, and Bali, the son of Virochana, are one hundred and twenty"</quote>—the proportions of all the limbs must be increased accordingly to account for those extra twelve angulas. It is understood, even if not explicitly stated, that the same ratio applies when the height is reduced. || 30 ||

Now he describes the form of the Lord Vishnu—

->The Lord Vishnu should be made with eight arms, four arms, or even just two.<-
->His chest is marked with the <term>Srivatsa</term> <note>A sacred mark or curl of hair on the chest of Vishnu</note> and his breast is adorned with the <term>Kaustubha</term> gem.<-
->He is dark like the Atasi flower <note>Linum usitatissimum, a deep blue-purple flax flower</note>, dressed in yellow garments, and has a placid, cheerful face.<-
->He wears earrings and a crown; his neck, chest, shoulders, and arms are broad and full. || 31-32 ||<-

# Chapter 57: On the Characteristics of Images
<page-num>689</page-num>

**He should hold a sword, a mace, and an arrow in his right hands, while the fourth hand is held in the gesture of granting peace. In his left hands, he holds a bow, a buckler, a discus, and a conch shell. (33)**

**If one desires a four-armed form, one hand grants peace and the other holds a mace on the right side; on the left side, there is a conch and a discus. (34)**

**In the two-armed form, the right hand grants peace while the other holds a conch. In this manner, the image of Vishnu should be fashioned by those desiring prosperity. (35)**

The Lord should be made eight-armed. The Lord <note>original: "Bhagavan"</note> Vishnu-Narayana is to be depicted with eight arms, or four arms, or even two arms. His chest is marked with the *Shrivatsa* <note>A specific curl of hair or mark on the chest of Vishnu, signifying his divinity</note>. His chest is adorned with the jewel known as *Kaustubha*. (31)

He is dark in complexion like the *Atasi* flower <note>The flax flower, known for its deep blue-purple hue</note>. His garments are yellow. He has a pleasant face and a gentle countenance. He wears earrings and a crown. His neck is thick and powerful. His chest is broad, his shoulders are sturdy, and his arms are muscular. (32)

On the right side of the eight-armed form, among the four hands: in one is the sword named *Nandaka*; in the second is the mace named *Kaumodaki*; in the third is an arrow; and the fourth is the "peace-giver" <term>shantida: the gesture of protection or fearlessness, commonly known as Abhaya Mudra</term>, where the fingers are pointed upward facing the viewer. In the left hands: a bow named *Sharnga*; a buckler <note>a small shield</note>; the discus named *Sudarshana*; and the conch named *Panchajanya*. (33)

The word "or" <note>original: "atha"</note> indicates an alternative. If one wishes to make a four-armed image, then on the right side, one hand grants peace and the second holds the mace. On the left side, one hand holds the conch and the second holds the discus. (34)

For a two-armed Vishnu, the right hand grants peace and the other (the left) holds the conch. In this way, the image of Vishnu-Narayana should be made by those desiring prosperity and success. (35)

->Now the characteristics of the Plow-Bearer <note>Balarama</note> are described:<-

**Baladeva should be depicted with a plow in his hand, his eyes rolling from intoxication. He wears a single earring and his body is as white as a conch, the moon, or a lotus stalk. (36)**

Baladeva is the "Plow-Bearer" <note>Haladhara</note>, holding a plow in his hand. His eyes are "rolling from intoxication" <note>madavibhrama-lochana</note>, meaning his eyes are moving unsteadily due to the effects of drinking wine. He wears a single earring...

...wearing ear ornaments. His body is as white as a conch, the moon, or a lotus stalk. <note>original: "śankhendu-mṛṇāla-gaura-tanuḥ"</note> A conch is well-known; the moon is the lunar orb; the lotus stalk is the fiber of the lotus. One whose body is white like these is so described. ॥36॥

### Now he describes the characteristics of Ekanamsha:

> The goddess Ekanamsha should be placed between Baladeva and Krishna.
> Her left hand should rest upon her hip, and the other should hold a lotus. ॥37॥

> If she is made with four arms, her left hands should hold a book and a lotus;
> On the right side, her two hands should show the gesture of granting boons to seekers and hold a rosary. ॥38॥

> If she has eight arms, the left ones hold a water-pot, a bow, a lotus, and a scripture;
> The right arms are equipped with the boon-granting gesture, an arrow, a mirror, and a rosary. ॥39॥

Regarding Ekanamsha: Between Baladeva and Krishna—that is, between Haladhara <note>The "Plow-bearer," Balarama</note> and Vasudeva <note>Krishna</note>—the deity named Ekanamsha should be placed or fashioned. Of what kind? One whose left hand is situated on her hip. With the other—the right hand—she is to be made carrying a <term>sarojam</term> <note>a "lake-born" flower, or lotus</note>. ॥37॥

Now, if she is made with four arms, then in one of her left hands is a book, and in the second is a lotus. On the right side, in one of the two hands is the <term>varada</term> <note>the gesture of dispensing blessings</note> for seekers, and in the second is an <term>akṣasūtram</term> <note>a string of prayer beads or rosary</note>. The "boon-granting" hand is described as being palm upward with the fingers pointing down. ॥38॥

Regarding the eight-armed form: If she is made with eight arms, then in her four left hands: in one, a <term>kamaṇḍalu</term> <note>a ceremonial water vessel</note>; in the second, a bow; in the third, a lotus; and in the fourth, a scripture or book. On the right side: one hand is in the boon-granting gesture; the second holds an arrow; the third holds a mirror; and the fourth holds a rosary. ॥39॥

### Now he describes the characteristics of Shamba and Pradyumna:

> Shamba should be depicted with a mace in hand, and Pradyumna should be handsome and carry a bow.
> Their two wives should also be depicted, carrying a shield and a sword. ॥40॥

Shamba should be two-armed and carry a mace. Pradyumna (the god of love) should carry a bow and arrow in his hands. He should be of "handsome form," meaning of beautiful appearance. The wives of these two, Shamba and Pradyumna, should be fashioned. Of what kind? <term>kheṭaka-nistriṃśa-dhāriṇyau</term> <note>carrying a shield and a sword</note>. A <term>kheṭaka</term> is a shield; a <term>nistriṃśa</term> is a sword. They are carrying those two items. ॥40॥

### Now he describes the characteristics of Brahma and Kumara:

> Brahma has a water-pot in his hand, four faces, and is seated upon a lotus.
> Skanda has the appearance of a young man, carries a spear, and has a peacock for a banner. ॥41॥

-># Chapter on the Characteristics of Images<-
<sig>Chapter 57</sig>

Brahma, the Grandfather <note>Pitamaha, a common title for Brahma as the creator</note>, is to be depicted holding a water-pot <note>kamandalu</note> in his hand, possessing four faces, and seated upon a lotus throne. Skanda, also known as Kartikeya, should have the appearance of a young boy. He is the wielder of the Shakti <note>a divine spear or lance</note> and has the peacock as his banner. ||41||

### Now he describes the characteristics of Indra:

> **The elephant of the great Indra is white and has four tusks; he holds a thunderbolt in his hand.**
> **A third eye is also placed horizontally upon his forehead as a distinguishing mark. ||42||**

The elephant of the great Indra, named Airavata, is white in color. He should be depicted with four tusks. "Holding a thunderbolt in his hand" means he carries the weapon known as the *Vajra* or *Kulisha*. A third eye should also be fashioned as a mark, positioned horizontally across his forehead. ||42||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Lord Maheshwara (Shiva):

> **On Shambhu’s head is a crescent moon; he has the bull as his banner and a third eye positioned vertically.**
> **He holds a trident and the bow named Pinaka, or his left half may consist of the Daughter of the Mountain. ||43||**

On the head of Shambhu (Maheshwara), a digit of the moon should be fashioned. He is "Bull-bannered," meaning the bull is his emblem. A third eye should be made, positioned vertically <note>unlike Indra's horizontal eye</note>. He holds a trident in one hand and a bow—specifically the one named Pinaka—in the other. Alternatively, the Daughter of the Mountain (Gauri) may be depicted as his left half. This refers to the form known as *Ardhanarishvara* <note>The Lord who is half-woman</note>. ||43||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Buddha:

> **The Buddha has hands and feet marked with lotuses; he is of placid aspect with very short hair.**
> **Seated upon a lotus throne, he appears like the father of the world. ||44||**

The Buddha should be depicted with hands and feet marked with lotuses; this means the palms and soles are marked with lines in the shape of a lotus. He is of "placid aspect," meaning he has a serene body and a gracious disposition. He has "very short hair" <note>sunica-kesha</note> on his head. Some read this as "well-ordered hair" <note>sunita-kesha</note>, meaning hair that is very disciplined or tightly curled. He is seated upon a lotus throne. "Like the father of the world" means he is like a progenitor to the entire universe, implying he is characterized by patience and virtue. ||44||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the God of the Arhats <note>The Jinas or Tirthankaras of the Jain tradition</note>—

**The God of the Arhats should be depicted with arms reaching down to the knees, marked with the Shrivatsa sign, possessing a tranquil form, clad in the sky <note>naked</note>, youthful, and handsome. || 45 ||**

The God of the Arhats, the Jina, should be made with arms reaching to the knees <note>long arms were considered a sign of greatness</note>; his hands should reach his knees. He is marked with the Shrivatsa, which is a specific auspicious mark on the chest. He has a tranquil form, meaning he has conquered his senses and is free from attachment and aversion. He is "clad in the sky," meaning he is naked. He is youthful, endowed with the vigor of youth. He is handsome, possessing a very beautiful body. || 45 ||

---

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Lord Sun <note>Bhaskara</note>—

**The nose, forehead, shanks, thighs, cheeks, and chest of the Sun should be prominent. He should be dressed in the northern style, covered from the feet up to the chest. || 46 ||**

**Holding lotuses in both hands by their stalks, wearing a crown, his face adorned with earrings, wearing a long dangling necklace, and girdled with a celestial waist-band. || 47 ||**

**With a face having the luster of the interior of a lotus, hidden by a jacket, with a smiling and pleasant countenance, and a halo shining brightly with jewels—such a Sun brings auspiciousness to the maker. || 48 ||**

Regarding the nose, forehead, etc.: For the Sun (Aditya), the nose, the forehead (the front of the head), the shanks, the thighs, the cheeks of the face, and the chest area—these should be prominent or high. One should create him in the "northern dress" <note>udichyavesha; often interpreted as Scythian or Central Asian style clothing, including boots</note>, meaning the attire of the northern regions. This covers him from the feet up to the chest; "hidden" means concealed by a tunic. || 46 ||

Regarding "holding": He holds lotuses in both hands by their stalks <note>literally "hand-born" stalks</note>. Because the natural stalks are held in the hands and the arms act as the stems, he is depicted holding lotuses. He is a "crown-wearer," meaning he wears a diadem or crown on his head. His face is adorned with earrings, meaning his face is beautified by two ear-ornaments. He has a "dangling necklace," a very long necklace of pearls. He is "girdled by the celestial," meaning he is equipped with a waist-band or girdle. || 47 ||

He has the luster or radiance of the interior of a lotus (padma) in his face. He is "hidden by a jacket," covered by the well-known tunic. He has a "smiling and pleasant face," meaning a countenance that is gentle, very beautiful, and smiling. He has a "halo of light" that is brilliant and shining with various types of jewels. An Arka (Sun) of this description is a "bringer of auspiciousness," a bestower of welfare to the one who causes the image to be made. || 48 ||

---

### Now, referring to the Sun and others, he describes the auspicious and inauspicious nature of all idols—

**An image that is one cubit <note>the length from elbow to fingertip</note> high is auspicious and brings wealth; one that is two cubits high brings safety and abundance of food, as do those measuring three or four cubits. || 49 ||**

--- Page 177 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the iconography of divine images (Pratima-lakshana) and transitions into the specific measurements and construction of the Linga (the symbolic representation of Shiva).</meta>

<page-num>693</page-num>
<header>Chapter 57] The Chapter on the Characteristics of Images.</header>

**If the limbs are oversized, there is fear of the king; if the limbs are deficient, the maker suffers ill health.**
**If the belly is sunken, there is fear of hunger; if the body is too thin, there is loss of wealth. ||50||**

**If the image is scarred, one should predict the death of the maker by a weapon.**
**If it leans to the left, it destroys the wife; if it leans to the right, it destroys the lifespan. ||51||**

**An upward gaze causes blindness; a downward gaze causes anxiety.**
**In all images, these auspicious and inauspicious signs are the same as those spoken by the Sun-god. ||52||**

"Pleasant if it is one cubit" <note>original: "saumya tu hastamatra"</note>. An image that is one cubit <term>hastamatra: approximately 18 inches</term> in length is pleasant and brings good fortune. One that is two cubits high is a giver of wealth. Those that are three or four cubits in size bring, respectively, safety and abundance. A three-cubit image leads to safety; a four-cubit image leads to abundance. ||49||

Regarding "fear of the king": In an image with "oversized limbs" <note>original: "atyangayam"</note>, meaning thick or bulky parts, there is fear of the king or government. In one with "deficient limbs," meaning parts smaller than the prescribed proportions, the maker suffers from "ill health" or lack of physical well-being. In one with a "sunken belly" <note>original: "shatodarya"</note>, meaning a thin stomach, there is fear of hunger. In one with a "thin body," meaning weak limbs, there is the destruction of wealth or financial loss. ||50||

In a "scarred" image, meaning one joined with wounds or cracks, one should declare or predict the death of the maker by the fall of a weapon. If the image is "bent to the left," it destroys or kills the maker's wife. If it is "bent to the right," it destroys or kills his lifespan; it causes the waning of his life. ||51||

An "upward gaze" in an image causes blindness or the destruction of the eyes. A "downward gaze" causes anxiety or grief. Thus, the auspicious and inauspicious signs in all other images should be understood as being "equal to those spoken by Bhaskara" <note>Bhaskara is a name for the Sun-god, Surya</note>, meaning identical to what the Sun-god has described. ||52||

---

->Now he describes the characteristics of the Linga:<-

**Having measured the circumference of the Linga's rounded part, one should divide its total length into three parts.**
**At the base, it should be square; in the middle, it should be octagonal; and beyond that, it should be circular. ||53||**
**The square part is to be buried in the ground; the middle part is to be placed within the cavity of the pedestal.**
**The pedestal should be equal in measurement on all sides to the height of the visible portion above the cavity. ||54||**

Regarding the circumference of the rounded part of the Linga: having measured that circumference with a cord, and having prepared a stone, wood, or gem of that same length, one should divide it into three parts; one should make three sections. Then, the section at the "base" of the Linga should be made "square" <note>original: "chaturasram"</note>. The section in the "middle" should be made "octagonal" <note>original: "ashtashri"</note>. Beyond that, the third part should be made "circular" or perfectly round. ||53||

<summary>This page details the physical defects in idol-making that lead to specific misfortunes for the patron and sculptor, followed by the geometric proportions required for carving a Shiva Linga.</summary>
<keywords>iconography, Varahamihira, Shiva Linga, proportions, ritual architecture, omens, sculpture, Vastu Shastra</keywords>

<header>In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 57]</header>

In that context, the square portion <note>the base of the Linga</note> should be placed or cast into the excavated pit in the ground. The middle portion, which is octagonal, should be placed within the cavity of the pedestal <term>pīṭhikā-śvabhra: the hollow center of the base</term>. From the cavity of the pedestal, on all sides and in all directions, the pedestal should be made equal to the visible height of the Linga. This means: whatever the measurement of the length of the circular <note>top</note> portion is, the width of the pedestal on all sides should be made equal to that same measurement. ||54||

## He describes other characteristics of the Linga:

->**A Linga that is thin and overly long destroys the country; one lacking in its sides leads to the destruction of the city.**<-
->**A Linga that has a wound or fracture on its head leads to the destruction of the owner.**<- ||55||

A Linga that is "thin" (weak) and "long" (excessively high) is "country-destroying"—it ruins the land. That which is "lacking in its sides" <note>asymmetrical or poorly carved</note> leads to the ruin of the city. A Linga that has a "wound" (a hole or crack) on its "head" (the top) leads to the "destruction" of the patron or master himself. ||56||

## Now he describes the Group of Mothers and their characteristics:

->**The Group of Mothers should be made with the identifying marks and forms corresponding to the gods of their own names.**<-
->**Revanta should be depicted mounted on a horse, surrounded by a retinue engaged in hunting and sport.**<- ||56||

The "Group of Mothers" <note>the Matrikas</note> must be fashioned with the "identifying marks" <note>symbols/weapons</note> corresponding to the gods from whom they derive their names. For example, according to the description of Brahma—"Brahma holds a water-pot in his hand, has four faces, and sits on a lotus"—the goddess **Brahmi** should be made. Following "The Lord <note>Vishnu</note> should be made with eight arms," **Vaishnavi** is made. Following "The crescent moon is on Shambhu's head," the **Raudris** <note>Maheshvari</note> are made. Following "Skanda has the form of a youth," the **Kaumaris** are made. Following "The white elephant has four tusks and Mahendra holds the thunderbolt," the **Aindris** are made. Following "Yama holds a staff and rides a buffalo," the **Yamyas** <note>Varahi is often grouped here, but the text refers to the female power of Yama</note> are made. Following "Varuna rides a swan <note>usually a makara, but the text notes a swan here</note> and holds a noose," the **Varunyas** are made. Following "Kubera has a human vehicle," the **Kauberis** are made.

In the same way, the forms of **Narasimhi**, **Varahi**, and **Vainayaki** <note>the female power of Ganesha</note> are to be inferred. However, for all of them, the beauty of the breasts, thinness of the waist, and fullness of the hips must be crafted, so that the beauty of the female form is produced. **Revanta**, the son of the Sun, should be made "mounted on a horse." "Mounted" means situated on top of a horse. Likewise, he is surrounded by a "retinue engaged in hunting"—the killing of deer—and sport. The term "and so forth" <insert>from the verse</insert> includes the riding of horses, their testing, and searching for game. ||56||

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Idols
## Chapter 57

Now, the author describes the characteristics of Yama, Varuna, and Kubera—

->**Yama holds a staff and rides a buffalo; Varuna rides a swan and carries a noose.**<-
->**<gloss>1</gloss> Kubera is carried by a man, wears his crown tilted to the left, and has a large belly. ||57||**<-

Yama, the Lord of the Dead <note>Pretapati</note>, should be depicted holding a staff <note>Danda</note> in his hand and mounted upon a buffalo. Varuna, the Lord of the Waters, is mounted on a swan—that is, situated atop the bird known as a swan—and should be depicted holding a noose <note>Pasha</note> in his hand. Kubera, the son of Vishrava, is "man-borne," meaning he is mounted upon a human being. <insert>Some read this as "mounted on a donkey."</insert> He is "left-crowned," meaning his crown or tiara <note>Mukuta</note> is positioned toward the left side. He should be made with a "large belly," meaning an expanded abdomen. 

Regarding these characteristics of the idols of the gods and goddesses as stated by the Teacher: the experts in iconography should craft the idols according to the proportions of their own fingers <note>the 'angula' unit of measurement</note> and in such a way that the physical beauty of the forms is captured as they are famous in the world. Everything mentioned previously should be applied here. Thus, the sage Kashyapa says:

->**Ganesha <note>Vinayaka</note> has a single tusk, the face of an elephant, and four arms.**<-
->**He has a hanging belly, a stout body, and is adorned with three eyes.**<-

->**<gloss>2</gloss> Bow down to the Supreme Goddess Vitasta <note>The personification of the Jhelum River</note>, who has the luster of a fresh blue water-lily and holds a rosary, a lotus, a water-pot, and a mirror in her hands. She sits happily in the lotus posture upon a grand, sturdy pedestal.**<-

->**Brahma has four faces, carries a staff, and holds a black antelope skin and a water-pot.**<-
->**Vishnu has four arms and carries the Sharnga bow, the conch, the discus, and the mace.**<-
->**He bears the Shrivatsa mark on his chest, wears yellow garments, and is adorned with a forest garland.**<-
->**Narasimha <note>The Man-Lion avatar</note> has a stout body and is adorned with whorls of hair.**<-
->**His mouth is wide open; he wears a garland, has the brilliance of fire, and possesses massive arms.**<-
->**Varaha <note>The Boar avatar</note> has the face of a boar and is adorned with four arms.**<-
->**He resembles a heap of blue collyrium, is absorbed in meditation, and has beautiful eyes.**<-
->**Ishvara <note>Shiva</note> has matted hair, three eyes, and is adorned with the bull and the crescent moon.**<-
->**He wears the king of serpents as a sacred thread, is clad in animal skin, and holds the Pinaka bow.**<-
->**Chandika <note>Durga</note> has eighteen arms and is equipped with all manner of weapons.**<-
->**She has three eyes, rides a lion, is the bringer of fortune, and is the slayer of the buffalo-demon.**<-
->**Skanda <note>Kartikeya</note> rides a peacock and holds a spear and a rooster.**<-
->**He has a beautiful body, is courageous, is the commander of the celestial army, and appears as a youth.**<-

***

<note>
1. "Mounted on a donkey" — this is an alternative reading found in some manuscripts.
2. This verse regarding the Goddess Vitasta is not found in other editions of the text.
</note>

> The Sun god <note>Aditya</note> should be depicted as youthful, wearing a garland, armored, and holding a sword.
> He is radiant, holding a lotus in his hand, accompanied by his six-fold retinue <note>The "Shadvarga" refers to his traditional attendants like Danda and Pingala</note>, and wearing a crown.
> Airavata is a great elephant with four tusks and a white body.
> Mounted upon him is the mighty Indra <note>Mahendra</note>, holding a thunderbolt in his hand.

> And Shachi <note>Indra's queen</note>, of a dark-reddish hue, should be placed near him.

> A beautiful image, well-proportioned, adorned with all ornaments,
> And equipped with its proper weapons, should be fashioned as an auspicious icon. || 57 ||

### Now, the Chapter on Entering the Forest is explained.

At the very beginning, the author describes the procedure:

> On a day favorable to the patron, purified by the astrologer and marked by auspicious omens,
> The entry into the forest should take place, accompanied by the propitious signs of departure. || 1 ||

"To the patron" means the one commissioning the image. "On a favorable day" refers to a day governed by a planet that increases one's prosperity and under an unblemished lunar mansion <note>Nakshatra</note>. "Purified by the astrologer and marked by auspicious omens" means at a time given by the knower of time <note>the astrologer</note> which is cleared of defects and possesses good omens and a favorable moment <note>Muhurta</note>. "With propitious signs of departure" refers to those signs occurring at the start of a journey; those auspicious things mentioned for travel—such as white mustard, mirrors, water, and collyrium—and omens like a noble horse or a white elephant in the east. With these auspicious departure signs, the "entry into the forest" should occur. One must enter the forest—a place thick with trees—for the purpose of <term>obtaining wood for the image</term> <note>original: "pratimā-kāṣṭhārtham"</note>. || 1 ||

# Chapter on Entering the Forest
<margin>Chapter 58</margin>

->Now he describes the trees that should be avoided:<-

> Trees growing in cemeteries, on roadsides, near temples, on anthills, in pleasure gardens, or in the hermitages of ascetics; those growing at the confluence of rivers, or those known as "monumental trees" <note>original: "chaitya"; often a sacred fig or a tree marking a boundary or shrine</note>, and those nourished by hand-poured water from jars; ||2||
>
> Trees that are stunted, those oppressed by another tree growing too close behind them, those strangled by creepers, or struck by lightning or wind; those that have fallen on their own, those damaged by elephants, withered trees, those scorched by fire, or those housing beehives; ||3||
>
> Such trees must be avoided. Those that are auspicious will have glossy leaves, flowers, and fruit. Having approached a desired tree, one should perform a worship ceremony with offerings and flowers. ||4||

Such types of trees are to be avoided. Of what kind? "Cemetery" <note>original: "pitṛvana"</note> refers to the cremation ground; "road" is the path; "temple" is the house of a god; "anthill" is a mound of earth made by termites; "pleasure garden" is a grove; "hermitage of ascetics" is a forest for penance. Trees produced or born in these places, as well as a "monumental tree" <note>the primary or sacred tree of a village</note>, or those born at the "confluence of rivers" (the meeting place of streams), and those "nourished by water from jars" (watered by hand)—these are unfit for cutting because they have been personally planted and cared for. ||2||

"Stunted" <note>original: "kubja"</note> means indistinct or poorly formed. "Oppressed by another" refers to a tree where another has grown up immediately behind it, causing distress by its proximity. Also, trees "strangled by creepers," those "struck by lightning" <note>original: "vajra"</note> or "wind" (broken by storms), those that have "fallen on their own," those "damaged by elephants" (broken by the beasts), "withered" (lacking sap), "scorched by fire" (burnt), or those that are a "home for honey" (a shelter for bees). ||3||

Thus, these aforementioned trees are to be rejected. Other remaining trees are givers of good fortune. Those with "glossy leaves," "glossy flowers" (full of sap), and "glossy fruit" are indeed auspicious. Then, having approached the "desired" or chosen tree, one should perform "worship" <note>original: "pūjā"</note> with "offerings" <note>original: "bali"</note> and "flowers." ||4||

->Now he describes the trees according to the sequence of the social classes:<-

> Deodar, Sandalwood, Shami, and Madhuka trees are auspicious for the Twice-born <note>the priestly class or Brahmins</note>. Soapberry, Sacred Fig, Khadira, and Bilva bring prosperity to the Warrior class. ||5||
>
> For the Merchant class, the Jivaka, Khadira, Sindhuka, and Syandana give good results. For the Laboring class, the Tinduka, Kesara, Sarja, Arjuna, Mango, and Shala are recommended. ||6||

"Suradaru" is the Deodar <note>literally "God-tree"</note>. "Chandana" is Sandalwood from the Malaya mountains. "Shami" is well-known. "Madhuka" is the common Butter Tree. These trees are auspicious for the "Twice-born" (Brahmins) for the purpose of making a "divine image" <note>original: "pratimā"</note>. "Arishta" is the Soapberry...

The Peepal <note>original: *Ashvattha*; Ficus religiosa</note>, Cutch <note>original: *Khadira*; Acacia catechu</note>, and Bael <note>original: *Bilva*; Aegle marmelos</note>—all these specific tree species bring prosperity to the *Kshatriya* <note>the warrior and ruling caste</note> class.

The *Jivaka*, Cutch, Five-leaved Chaste tree <note>original: *Sindhuka*; Vitex negundo</note>, and *Syandana* <note>Dalbergia oojeinensis</note>—these tree species grant auspicious results to the *Vaishyas* <note>the merchant and agricultural caste</note>. The Ebony <note>original: *Tinduka*</note>, Bakula <note>original: *Kesara*</note>, Sal resin tree <note>original: *Sarja*</note>, Arjuna, Mango, and Sal—these trees grant auspiciousness to the *Shudras* <note>the laborer and artisan caste</note>. And so says Sage Kashyapa:

> The Himalayan Cedar <note>original: *Suradaru*</note>, Shami, Mahua <note>original: *Madhuka*</note>, and Sandalwood—
> These are declared to bring auspiciousness for the installations of Brahmins.
> The Soap-nut <note>original: *Arishta*</note>, Peepal, Cutch, and Bael for the *Kshatriya* classes.
> The *Jivaka*, Cutch, as well as the *Sindhuka* and *Syandana*—
> These are declared to grant auspiciousness to *Vaishyas*. The Ebony and Bakula,
> The *Sarja*, Arjuna, Mango, and Sal are remembered as auspicious for *Shudras*. || 5-6 ||

Regarding this, he mentions a specific rule:

> Because a *Linga* <note>the aniconic symbol of Shiva</note> or an image must be installed according to the same directions as the tree [from which it came],
> Therefore, the directions of the tree—as well as its top and bottom—must be marked. || 7 ||

A *Linga* (a symbol of Shiva) or an image (an icon for worship) must be installed according to the directions of the tree. This is the meaning: the side of the tree that faced East must be made the East-facing side of the image. Similarly, the South side remains South, the West remains West, and the North side remains North. The lower part of the tree must be made the lower part of the image; the upper part of the tree must also be made the upper part of the image. For that reason, the directions (the quarters) of the tree must be marked. Likewise, the top and bottom parts must also be marked. And so says Sage Kashyapa:

> An image should be made like the tree, characterized by its Eastern side and so forth.
> The feet [of the image] should be made from the [lower] feet [of the tree], and the head should be made from the upper part. || 7 ||

### Now he describes the ritual for cutting the tree:

> Having performed a worship at night for the gods, ancestors, spirits, demons, serpents, titans, and the Ganas <note>attendants of Shiva</note> led by Vinayaka <note>Ganesha</note>,
> One should touch the tree and say: || 9 ||

"Milk-rice" <note>original: *Paramanna*</note> is *Payasam*; "dumplings" <note>original: *Modaka*</note> are *Laddukas*; "boiled rice" <note>original: *Odana*</note> is cooked grain; "curd" is a milk derivative; "ground sesame" <note>original: *Palala*</note> refers to half-pressed sesame seeds; "cakes" <note>original: *Ullopika*</note> are well-known [savory snacks]. By the inclusion of "and others," many types of foodstuffs [are implied]—

# Chapter on Entering the Forest
### [Section 58]

By various means such as <term>upaprabhṛti</term> <note>referring to various offerings</note>, including foods to be licked, drunk, or sucked, and with liquors, blossoms, flowers, incenses, and fragrant substances, one should worship and fully honor the tree. ||8||

The <term>Suras</term> <note>gods</note>, the <term>Pitṛs</term> <note>ancestral spirits</note>, the <term>Piśācas</term> <note>a class of flesh-eating demons</note>, the <term>Rākṣasas</term> <note>night-roaming man-eaters</note>, the <term>Bhujagas</term> <note>serpents</note>, the <term>Asuras</term> <note>demons/titans</note>, the <term>Gaṇas</term> <note>attendants of Shiva</note>, and the <term>Vināyakas</term> <note>beings who create obstacles</note>—and by the inclusion of "etcetera," the ghosts, spirits, perfected beings, celestial musicians, and singers are meant. Having performed the worship and honor of these beings at night, and having touched the tree with his hand, he should utter this <term>mantra</term> <note>sacred chant</note>: ||9||

What is that chant? He says:

->“O Tree, you have been chosen for the worship of such-and-such a deity.”<-
->“Salutations to you! May this worship, performed according to the rules, be accepted.”<- ||10||

->“Whatever spirits dwell here, having accepted this<-
->offering presented according to the rules,”<-
->“May they arrange their residence elsewhere.”<-
->“May they forgive us today; salutations to them!”<- ||11||

O Tree! You have been designated and prepared for the purpose of the worship of a deity of such-and-such a name. Salutations be unto you. May this worship brought by me be accepted according to the prescribed ritual. ||10||

Whatever spirits are situated and dwelling here in this tree, having accepted this <term>bali</term> <note>a ritual food offering</note> presented according to the rules, let them arrange a home or residence elsewhere in another tree. May those spirits be patient and forgiving today. Let there be a salutation to those spirits. ||11||

Then, what should he do? He says:

->“In the morning, having sprinkled the tree with water,”<-
->“And having made a cut in the North-East direction,”<-
->“With an axe smeared with honey and clarified butter,”<-
->“One should strike the rest of it moving in a clockwise direction.”<- ||12||

In the morning, at daybreak, having sprinkled the tree with water, one should first make a cut in the North-East direction <note>the Ishanya corner</note> using a small axe or hatchet that has been smeared and anointed with honey and <term>ājya</term> <note>ghee/clarified butter</note>. After that, one should strike and cut the remainder in a clockwise fashion, moving through the East, South-East, South, South-West, West, North-West, and North directions. ||12||

### Now he describes the characteristics of a falling tree—

-> If it should fall toward the East, the Northeast, or the North, <-
-> then it shall bring about prosperity. <-
-> From the Southeast corner onwards, in sequence, there is fire, <-
-> pain, disease, and the loss of horses. || 93 || <-

If it should fall toward the East, or toward the Northeast <note>the direction of the deity Ishana</note>, or toward the North, then it shall be a bringer of prosperity. When it falls in the sequence starting from the Southeast corner, Garga <note>an ancient sage and authority on omens</note> has stated these results. They are as follows: if it falls in the Southeast, there is destruction by fire; in the South, there are pains and illnesses; in the Southwest, there are diseases; in the West, likewise diseases; and in the Northwest, there is the destruction or loss of horses. || 93 ||

### Regarding what has not been mentioned here, he says it should be inferred—

-> Whatever has not been mentioned in this section on entering the forest, <-
-> such as the manner of falling, the sound of cutting, and the internal contents of the tree; <-
-> these were previously taught by me regarding the Banner of Indra and Architecture, <-
-> and they should be applied here in the same way. || 94 || <-

In this section regarding "entering the forest" <term>Vanasampravesha: the ritual journey to select timber</term>, whatever has not been explicitly stated—what is that? The falling, the cutting, and the "womb" <note>internal defects or hidden objects</note> of the tree. "Falling" refers to how the tree hits the ground. For example:

> "A fall that is not shattered, not bent, and directed toward the East or North brings victory to the King. If it does not get caught on another tree, it is auspicious; otherwise, a fallen tree should be abandoned." <note>original: "nṛpajayadamavidhvastam..."</note>

**Regarding the cutting—**

> "A harsh, cracking sound from the axe is not desired; a smooth, deep thud is beneficial."

**Likewise, the "womb" of the tree—**

> —"If there is a yellow circle <insert>in the wood</insert>, one should predict a lizard living in the middle of the tree," and so forth.

These are the details of falling, cutting, and internal contents. These were previously described by me at the beginning regarding the Banner of Indra <note>a festival involving a large wooden pole</note> and in the section on Architecture <term>Vastu: the science of sacred space and construction</term>—

# Now, the Installation of the Image is explained.

First, regarding the preliminary consecration, the author describes the characteristics of the pavilion:

> **A wise man should construct the pavilion for the preliminary consecration in the southern or the eastern direction.**
> **It should be equipped with four arched gateways and covered with the shoots and leaves of auspicious trees. ||1||**
> **In the eastern part of the pavilion, multicolored garlands and banners are prescribed.**
> **In the south-eastern direction, they should be red; in the southern and south-western, they should be black. ||2||**
> **In the western direction, they should be white; in the north-western, they should be pale-white.**
> **On the northern side, they should be multicolored; and in the north-eastern, they should be yellow. ||3||**

A wise man—meaning a learned scholar—should construct the <term>Adhivasa-mandapa</term> <note>A temporary ceremonial pavilion used for the preliminary "awakening" or "perfuming" of an icon before its final installation</note> in the south or the east. <term>Adhivasa</term> is a <term>specialized consecration rite</term>. Some read "in the northern direction" <margin>Note 1: "In the northern" is an alternative reading.</margin> instead. What kind of pavilion? It should have four arched gateways <note>original: "torana"</note> in the four directions, and it should be covered or thatched with the shoots and leaves of "praiseworthy" trees—meaning those suitable for sacrifice. ||1||

In the eastern part or direction of the pavilion, the garlands and banners (victory flags) are said to be "variegated" or of many colors. In the south-east, the garlands and banners are red. In the south and the south-west, they are black in color. ||2||

In the western direction, they should be made white. In the north-west, they should be pale-white (off-white). Likewise, on the northern side, they are multicolored. In the north-east (the direction of Ishana), the garlands and banners should be yellow. ||3||

Now, the author describes the fruits or results based on the material of the image:

> **An image made of wood or clay bestows long life, prosperity, strength, and victory.**
> **An image made of jewels is for the welfare of the world, and one made of gold brings nourishment and growth. ||4||**

<page-num>702</page-num>
<header>In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 59]</header>

**An image made of silver brings fame; one made of copper brings the increase of progeny.**
**A statue or a lingam <note>a symbolic representation of the god Shiva</note> made of stone brings a great gain of land. ||5||**

An image made of wood—constructed from timber—as well as one made of clay—fashioned from earth—bestows long life, prosperity <note>Lakshmi</note>, strength, and victory. An image made of jewels—constructed from precious gems—is for the welfare of the people. One made of gold—constructed from the precious metal—is a giver of nourishment; it grants physical health.

An image made of silver—constructed from white metal—creates fame and renown. One made of copper brings about the increase of progeny, such as sons and grandsons. A statue—a worshipful image—made of stone, or a *lingam* made of stone, brings about a very great and abundant gain of land. And so says Kashyapa <note>an ancient sage and authority on architecture</note>:

> That worshipful image which is produced from clay or wood is considered to give life, prosperity, and strength.
> One made of gold should be known as a giver of nourishment; one born of jewels is a doer of good.
> One made of silver should be known as a giver of fame; one born of copper increases the people.
> That worshipful image which is constructed of stone creates a great gain of land. ||Thus verses 4-5||

He further explains specific defects:

**An image struck by a "stake" <note>a structural flaw or protruding pin</note> destroys the leading man and the family.**
**One struck by a "pit" <note>a hollow or cavity in the material</note> causes diseases, calamities, and decay. ||6||**

A "stake" <term>shanku: a pin or nail protruding transversely</term> is commonly known in the world as a "limb" <note>original: "anga"</note>. A worshipful image struck by such a defect destroys the leader—the patron—and the lineage or family. A "pit" <term>shvabhra: a hole or cavity</term>; an image struck by this causes diseases, ailments, calamities, faults, and wasting away. And so says Kashyapa:

> That worshipful image which is struck by a stake is the destroyer of the chief family.
> That which is struck by a hole is considered to be the cause of many faults. ||Thus verse 6||

Now he describes the characteristics of the *Adhivasa* <note>the preliminary consecration or "habitation" ceremony where the deity is invited to reside in the image</note>:

**In the middle of the pavilion, having smeared the sacrificial ground and strewn it with sand and Kusha grass,**
**one should place the image with its head on a "splendid seat" and its feet on a pillow. ||7||**

In the middle—the interior—of the consecration pavilion <term>mandapa</term>, having smeared the sacrificial plot of ground <term>sthandila</term>, one should then strew it with sand and *Kusha* <note>sacred Darbha grass</note>. The word "and" <note>original: "atha"</note> is used here in the sense of a conjunction. The strewing or covering should be done by spreading sand and then covering it with the sacred grasses. There, one should place the image with its head on a "splendid seat" <term>bhadrasana: a royal throne or ceremonial seat</term>—meaning the head is positioned there—and its feet on a pillow—meaning a head-rest or cushion—one should place the feet upon that. ||7||
