# Chapter 59: The Chapter on the Installation of the Statue
### Page 703

He [the author] describes another method:

> **With decoction waters produced from the Plaksha, Ashvattha, Udumbara, Shirisha, and Vata trees;**
> **With all the herbs known as "auspicious," starting with Kusha grass; ||8||**
> **With earth uplifted by elephants and bulls, from mountains, anthills, and the banks of river confluences;**
> **And with earth from lotus ponds, along with the "five products of the cow" and water from holy fords; ||9||**
> **The statue, placed with its head to the east, is bathed with fragrant water containing gold and gems,**
> **Accompanied by the sounds of various musical instruments, declarations of an "Auspicious Day," and the chanting of the Vedas. ||10||**

<term>Plaksha</term> <note>White Fig</note>, <term>Ashvattha</term> <note>Sacred Fig</note>, <term>Udumbara</term> <note>Cluster Fig</note>, <term>Shirisha</term> <note>Rain Tree</note>, and <term>Vata</term> <note>Banyan</note>—all of these are <term>specific types of trees</term>. With <term>decoction waters</term> produced from these—meaning water in which these have been boiled—as well as with <term>all the herbs</term> <term>known as auspicious</term>. The "auspicious" ones are those herbs with excellent names. For example: <term>Jaya</term> <note>Victorious</note>, <term>Jayanti</term> <note>Conquering</note>, <term>Jivanti</term> <note>Giving life</note>, <term>Jivaputri</term> <note>Having living sons</note>, <term>Punarnava</term> <note>Ever-renewing</note>, <term>Vishnukanta</term> <note>Beloved of Vishnu</note>, <term>Abhaya</term> <note>Fearless</note>, <term>Vishvambhari</term> <note>All-supporting</note>, <term>Mahamoda</term> <note>Greatly fragrant</note>, <term>Sahadevi</term> <note>With the Goddess</note>, <term>Purnakosha</term> <note>Full-treasury</note>, <term>Shatavari</term> <note>Having a hundred roots</note>, <term>Sahasravirya</term> <note>Of a thousand potencies</note>, and <term>Lakshmana</term> <note>Endowed with signs</note>; with these, and also <term>starting with Kusha</term>. <term>Kusha</term> refers to <term>Darbha grass</term>; "starting with" means those herbs of which Kusha is the first. By the use of the word "starting with," one should also include fresh sprouts of grass. With these herbs. ||8||

<term>Elephant</term> refers to a tusker; the earth uplifted by him. <term>Bull</term> refers to a tamed ox; the earth uplifted by him. <term>Mountain earth</term>, <term>anthill earth</term>, and where there is a <term>confluence</term>—a joining or meeting—of two rivers, the earth from those banks. And with earth from <term>lotus ponds</term>—meaning those lakes filled with lotuses or water-lilies—the earth from those. With <term>waters from holy fords</term> <note>Tirtha-jala</note>, <term>along with the five products of the cow</term> <note>Panchagavya</note>. These consist of: <term>cow dung</term>, <term>cow urine</term>, <term>milk</term>, <term>curd</term>, <term>clarified butter (ghee)</term>, and <term>Kusha-grass water</term>. ||9||

With these aforementioned materials, the statue is bathed. Likewise, with <term>water containing gold and gems</term>—water in which gold and jewels have been immersed—and which is <term>fragrant</term> (joined with pleasant scents). Having performed this bath, one should place or establish the statue <term>with its head to the east</term>, having positioned the head toward the eastern direction. This is done along with the <term>sounds of various musical instruments</term>, with <term>Auspicious Day</term> declarations <note>Punyahavachana</note>, and with <term>Vedic chants</term> (the utterance of Vedic verses). ||10||

Then, he describes what should be done next:

> **In the eastern direction, mantras addressed to Indra; in the south-east, mantras addressed to Agni.**
> **These should be spoken by the best of the twice-born, who are then to be honored with sacrificial gifts. ||11||**

In the eastern direction, <term>mantras addressed to Indra</term>—meaning those Vedic verses whose presiding deity is Indra—should be <term>spoken</term> (recited) by the <term>best of the twice-born</term> (the most excellent Brahmins). Some read the text as "should be whispered" <note>original: "japtavyah"</note>. Likewise, in the south-east...

In the south-eastern direction. One should recite the Agni-signs, that is, the hymns dedicated to the deity Agni <note>The god of fire</note>. And those chief twice-born men <note>term: Dvija; refers here to Brahmins who have undergone the sacred thread ceremony</note> are to be honored and worshipped with sacrificial fees. ||11||

->He then describes what should be done next:<-

> **The twice-born should offer oblations into the fire using the specific hymns of the deity who is being installed. I have already described the omens related to fire in the chapter on the Raising of Indra’s Banner. ||12||**
> **A fire that is choked with smoke, that whirls to the left (counter-clockwise), or that repeatedly emits sparks is not auspicious. Likewise, a lapse of memory in the priest or his slipping backward is declared to be inauspicious. ||13||**

Whichever deity is to be established or consecrated, the twice-born Brahmin should offer oblations into the fire with the Vedic hymns dedicated to that specific deity. I have previously stated and explained the "fire-omens" or characteristics of fire in the section on the Raising of Indra’s Banner <note>original: "Indradhvaja-utthāne"</note>. This refers to verses such as "At the conclusion of the *Svāhā* call, the flame is naturally bright," and so on. A fire "choked with smoke" means it is accompanied by heavy smoke. "Whirling to the left" means moving in a counter-clockwise direction. "Repeatedly" refers to the sound it makes or its frequent action. One that "emits sparks" or releases them is not of good omen. Furthermore, if there is a "lapse of memory" or forgetfulness on the part of the Hotṛ <note>term: Hotṛ; the priest performing the sacrifice</note>, or if he "slips" or moves backward, it is declared to be inauspicious or undesirable. ||13||

->He then describes what should be done next:<-

> **The installer should place the image—which has been bathed, dressed in unused garments, well-adorned, and worshipped with flowers and perfumes—upon a well-spread bed. ||14||**

That image should be "bathed" (having undergone a ritual bath). "Dressed in unused garments" means covered in brand-new cloth. "Well-adorned" means decorated with beautiful ornaments. "Worshipped" or honored with "flowers" and "perfumes" such as aloe-wood and other fragrant substances. The "installer" (the one performing the consecration) should "place" or establish it upon a "well-spread bed" (a couch covered with fine linens). ||14||

->He then describes what should be done while the image is "sleeping":<-

> **Having thus properly performed the preliminary consecration of the sleeping image with songs, dances, and vigils, one should perform the final installation at the time appointed by the astrologer. ||15||**

While that image is "sleeping," one should properly perform the "preliminary consecration" <note>term: Adhivāsana; a rite where the deity is invited to inhabit the image</note> in this manner, accompanied by "songs and dances" and "vigils" (the act of staying awake through the night). Then, at the time "appointed by the astrologer" (the knower of time/stars)...

The timing has been stated. In the northern transit of the sun <note>original: "udagayane"</note> and during the bright fortnight <note>original: "sitapaksha"</note>, according to this rule, one should perform the <term>Samsthapana</term> <note>the formal establishment or installation</note> or <term>Pratishthapana</term> <note>consecration</note> at that specific time. || 5 ||

He explains how one should perform the installation:

> **Having honored the image with flowers, garments, and ointments, amidst the sounding of conchs and musical instruments,**
> **One should carefully lead it around the temple in a clockwise direction.** || 16 ||
> **Having offered an abundant oblation and honored the Brahmins and the assembled guests,**
> **One should place a piece of gold into the cavity of the pedestal.** || 17 ||
> **By especially honoring the priest, the astrologer, the Brahmins, the assembly, and the master builder,**
> **One becomes a partaker of blessings in this world and a dweller of heaven in the next.** || 18 ||

That **image**. With **flowers**, **garments**, and **ointments** (fragrant pastes), having honored and worshipped it. Then, with the **sounds** of conchs and musical instruments. One should lead it **carefully** and **clockwise** around the **temple** (the palace of the deity). <insert>This means that after exiting the pavilion where the image stayed overnight, one should lead it clockwise and make it enter the sanctum sanctorum of the temple.</insert> || 16 ||

Then, having made an **abundant** (large) **oblation** (offering), and having worshipped and honored the **Brahmins** (the twice-born) and the **assembled** people who have come to the gathering, and having placed a **piece of gold** (a fragment of gold) into the **cavity of the pedestal** (the hollow in the base), one should then place or **fix** the image there. || 17 ||

The **Installer** (the priest), the **Astrologer** (the expert in celestial movements), the **Brahmins**, the **assembled** prominent men of the gathering, and the **Master Builder** (the architect/carpenter)—by especially honoring these, one becomes a partaker of the fruits of **blessings** (welfare) in this world, and in the next world, one becomes a "heaven-dweller." This means they reside in heaven. || 18 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of those who should perform the installation:

> **For Vishnu, the Bhagavatas; for the Sun, the Magas; for Shambhu (Shiva), Brahmins who use ashes;**
> **For the Mothers, those who know the sequence of the Circle; for Brahma, they know the Brahmins;**
> **For the All-Benevolent (Buddha), the Shakyas with peaceful minds; for the Jinas (Tirthankaras), they know the Naked Ones (Digambaras);**
> **The ritual for any deity should be performed by those who are devoted to that deity according to their own specific rules.** || 19 ||

For **Vishnu** (Narayana), the **Bhagavatas** <note>devotees of Vishnu</note>; for the **Sun** (Aditya), the **Magas** <note>Sun-priests, traditionally associated with Persian origins</note>; for **Shambhu** (Mahadeva), **Brahmins** who are **accompanied by ashes**, meaning the **Pashupatas** <note>a specific sect of Shiva worshippers</note>. For the **Mothers** (Brahmi and the others), those who **know the sequence of the Circle** <note>original: "mandalakramavido"</note>, meaning those who know the specific order of worship and diagrams, are known as the installers. For **Brahma** (the Grandfather), they know the **Brahmins**. For the **All-Benevolent** (the Buddha)...

<summary>This page details the ritual procession of a divine image into a temple, including the placement of gold in the pedestal and the specific sects of priests required to install different deities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the specific religious groups authorized to perform the consecration of idols and the precise astrological timing required for such rituals.</meta>

Those with peaceful minds and conquered senses are known as the Shakyas <note>Buddhist monks</note>, who wear red garments. The followers of the Jinas and Arhats <note>Jain monks</note> are known as the naked ones or the naked mendicants. Whatever deity men have taken refuge in, having approached them with a spirit of devotion, the ritual for that deity should be performed by those specific followers according to their own traditions and the rules stated in their own philosophical systems. For Vishnu, the ritual is by the *Pancharatra* <note>A specific Vaishnava tradition</note> method. For the Sun, by the *Saura* system. For Shambhu <note>Shiva</note>, by the method stated in the *Vatula-tantra* or other Tantric texts. For the Mother Goddesses, by the rules prescribed in their own manuals. For the Buddha, by the sequence of the *Paramitas* <note>Perfections/virtues in Buddhism</note> performed by Brahmins or according to Vedic rites. For the Arhats, the ceremony should be performed according to the rules of their own vision. Thus ends verse 19.

### Now he describes the characteristics of the time for installation—

->**In the northern transit of the sun, in the bright fortnight, and when the moon (the cool-rayed one) is in the division of Jupiter;**<-
->**When the Ascendant is fixed or in a fixed subdivision, with the benefics situated in the houses of intelligence, dharma, or the angles;**<-
->**With the malefics in the houses of increase, and under the fixed, soft, Vishnu, Tishya, or Wind-god constellations;**<-
->**On a day other than Tuesday, if favorable, the installation of the gods is praised. ||20-21||**<-

"In the northern transit" means during the *Uttarayana*, when the Sun is in the six signs starting from Capricorn. "In the bright fortnight" means the waxing moon. Likewise, in the northern transit and bright fortnight, "when the moon is the cool-rayed one"—he whose rays are cool—is in the "division of Jupiter." A "division" <term>varga: the sub-divisional charts used in Vedic astrology to determine planetary strength</term> refers to the house, hour, decan, ninth-part, twelfth-part, or thirty-degree-part.

Also, "when the Ascendant is fixed," meaning in any of Taurus, Leo, or Aquarius; or in others like Gemini, Cancer, Virgo, Libra, Sagittarius, or Pisces, provided there is a "fixed ninth-part" <term>navamsha: a 3°20' division of a zodiac sign</term> rising. For by the combination of other signs, intermediate types are forbidden.

->As it is said: "In a good lunar day and a fixed rising sign, one should enter a house or a body."<-

"With the benefics"—Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus—"situated in the houses of intelligence, dharma, or the angles." The "house of intelligence" is the fifth; the "house of dharma" is the ninth. The "angles" <term>kendra: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses, considered the pillars of a horoscope</term> are the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth. They should be in any of these. "With the malefics"—the Sun, Mars, and Saturn—"in the houses of increase" <term>upachaya: the 3rd, 6th, 10th, and 11th houses where planets improve over time</term>, meaning any of the third, sixth, eleventh, or tenth houses.

Also, "under the fixed, soft, Vishnu, Tishya, or Wind-god constellations" <term>nakshatras: lunar mansions</term>. The three "Uttaras" and Rohini are the "fixed" ones. Mrigashira, Chitra, Anuradha, and Revati are the "soft" ones. "Hari" is Shravana. "Tishya" is Pushya. The "Wind-god" is Swati. In these constellations. "On a day other than Tuesday" means a day excluding Mars; on the days of the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, or Saturn. On such a day that is "favorable"—meaning auspicious for the performer—the "installation" or consecration of the "gods" (deities) is "praised," meaning it is beautiful or auspicious. ||20-21||

Regarding this, he says that this installation procedure I have made is general for all deities:

->**This general summary, which grants benefit to the people, has been made by me.**<-
->**The preliminary consecration and the placement are described separately and at length in the *Savitra*. ||22||**<-

# Page 707
## Chapter 60: The Chapter on the Characteristics of Cows

This installation <note>original: "pratiṣṭhāpanaṃ"</note> has been composed by me in a brief, concise, and general manner according to the Vedic ordinances, being beneficial, favorable, and effortless for all people. In the *Savitra* scripture <note>likely referring to a solar-based manual or a specific work by the sage Savitr</note>, the preliminary consecration and placement of each individual deity are treated separately and in great detail. Alternatively, the preliminary consecration and placement belonging to Savitr (the Sun God) are found separately and at length in that Solar scripture.

->Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, named "The Installation of Images,"<-
->in the Commentary on the Samhita composed by the illustrious Bhattotpala.<-

***

### Now, the Characteristics of Cows are explained.

At the very beginning, the author speaks to show the traditional source <note>original: "āgama"</note>:

> The sage Parashara spoke to Brihadratha
> regarding the characteristics of cows; from that, this
> summary is made by me. Though all those cows
> possess auspicious marks, I shall describe them according to tradition. ||1||

The sage named Parashara spoke regarding the characteristics of cows to Brihadratha (also known by the name Sharngarava), his disciple. From that teaching on cow characteristics, a summary or condensation is being made by me, the Teacher <note>Varahamihira, the author of the original verses</note>. All cows possess auspicious or praiseworthy marks; however, by the inclusion of the word "also" <note>original: "api"</note>, it implies that I shall also describe those with inauspicious marks in their entirety, in that same manner, according to the tradition—that is, from the scriptures composed by the sages. ||1||

In that regard, he first describes the inauspicious characteristics:

> Cows with tearful, turbid, or dull eyes, and those with eyes like mice, do not bring prosperity.
> Those with shaking or flat horns, those that are "karata" <note>spotted or having one ear</note>, and those with a color resembling a donkey; ||2||
> Those with ten, seven, or four teeth; those with long, hairless faces or depressed backs;
> Those with short, thick necks, those with a middle shaped like a barley-corn <note>bulging in the center</note>, and those with cleft hooves; ||3||
> Those with dark-colored or excessively long tongues; those with very thin ankles or very large, heavy ones;
> Those with excessive humps, emaciated bodies, or missing or extra limbs, are not desired. ||4||

The word "eye" <note>original: "akṣi"</note> is connected to each preceding term. "Tearful-eyed" refers to those whose eyes are constantly joined with tears. "Turbid-eyed" refers to those whose eyes are foul or lacking clarity. "Dull-eyed" refers to those whose eyes are not glossy or bright. "Mouse-eyed" refers to those with eyes resembling a mouse. These cows do not bring prosperity...

...are inauspicious. Likewise, those with moving or flattened horns—meaning horns that are shaky or compressed—are also unlucky. Those that are "Karata" <note>original: "karata"; a specific variegated color</note>, which means a dark-reddish color, or those colored like a donkey, do not bring good fortune.

Cows that have ten teeth, seven teeth, or four teeth are included. Those with a "hanging head" <note>original: "pralamba-mundam"</note>, meaning a face that appears to droop or lacks horns. Those with a sunken or indistinct back (the middle of the body). Those with a short, low, or excessively thick neck. Those with a "barley-shaped middle," meaning their midsection is shaped like a grain of barley <note>tapering at both ends</note>. Those with split hooves or broken feet.

Those with dusky-colored, excessively long tongues. Those with ankles that are either too thin (very small) or too large (very thick) and misshapen—the ankle being the region just above the hoof. Those with an excessive hump <note>original: "kakuda"</note>, which is the high fleshy part at the base of the neck on the back. Those with emaciated or weak bodies. Those with missing limbs or extra limbs are not desired and are inauspicious. And so says the sage Parashara:

->Those whose eyes are tearful, dry, or small are not auspicious.<-
->Those with moving or flat horns, those of variegated color, or those resembling donkeys.<-
->Those with ten, seven, or four teeth, or those with drooping faces are not auspicious.<-
->Those devoid of horns, those who are stunted, or those with deeply sunken backs.<-
->Those with short, thick necks or barley-shaped middles are not auspicious.<-
->Those with split feet, or those with either massive or tiny ankles.<-
->Those with dusky, overly long tongues and those possessed of a great hump.<-
->Those with excessively emaciated bodies or those with missing body parts.<-
->Such cows do not grant prosperity; they cause the destruction of the owner and the herd. Thus [says Parashara].<- 2-4

### Now he describes the characteristics of bulls:

->A bull is also like this: one with thick and excessively hanging testicles, or a chest covered in prominent veins.<-
->One whose cheeks are covered in thick veins, or one who urinates in three streams.<- 5
->One with cat-like eyes, or one who is tawny or variegated, is not auspicious for a Brahmin.<-
->One with a black lip, palate, and tongue, or one who pants heavily, is a destroyer of the herd.<- 6

A bull, even if tamed, is inauspicious if possessed of these traits—including the previously mentioned traits like tearful or dry eyes—but here are the specific characteristics: One with thick and excessively long testicles. One whose chest (the area between the two front legs) is stretched over or covered with veins. Likewise, one whose cheeks or temple regions are joined with or covered by thick, large veins.

One who urinates in three places <note>original: "tristhānaṃ mehate"</note>, or who discharges urine and dung at the same time. Some say this refers to one who discharges fluid from the eyes and the penis simultaneously. This means the eyes are constantly shedding tears. ||5||

One who is "cat-eyed" <note>term: "mārjārākṣo" — having eyes resembling those of a cat</note>. One who is tawny <note>original: "kapilaḥ"</note> or of a "crow-like" color <note>original: "karaṭaḥ" — a dark, reddish-blue or crow-colored hue</note>. Such a bull is not auspicious even for a Brahmin <note>term: "dvija" — literally "twice-born," referring here to the priestly class</note>, let alone for other castes. This is mentioned because there is a common social practice that a bull with undesirable traits should be gifted to a Brahmin; however, even for him, such a bull is not auspicious. Also, one who has a black lip, palate, and tongue. One who breathes with a sound of terror <note>original: "śvasanastrāsa"</note> is a destroyer of the herd <note>original: "yūthasya ghātakaro"</note>, meaning he brings about its ruin. ||6||

->He says another thing:<-

> **A bull that has bulky dung, jewel-like horns, a white belly, and is the color of a spotted deer—even if born in one's own house—must be abandoned, for he brings destruction to the herd. ||7||**

One who has "bulky dung" <note>original: "sthūlaśakṛt"</note> means his cow-dung is unusually thick. "Jewel-like horns" means his horns appear like polished gems. Some interpret this as: thick dung, a thick "jewel" (meaning the tip of the penis), and thick horns. "White-bellied" <note>original: "sitodaraḥ"</note> means having a white stomach. "Color of a spotted deer" <note>original: "kṛṣṇasāravarnaḥ"</note> means a mixture of black and white colors; in some places black and in some places white. The word "even" <note>original: "api"</note> is used for emphasis. Such a bull, even if born and raised in one's own home, should be discarded. How much more so should one avoid buying such a bull for a price? Therefore, he is a carrier of destruction for the herd; he brings ruin to whatever herd he lives in. ||7||

->He says another thing:<-

> **A bull whose body is covered with dark flower-like spots, who resembles the color of reddish ashes, and is cat-eyed, does not bring good fortune even to Brahmins if accepted as a gift. ||8||**

A bull whose body is covered with "dark flowers" <note>original: "śyāmaka-puṣpa"</note> means his limbs are marked with dark-colored spots resembling blossoms. Some say it means he is dark-colored and his body is covered in flowers. Others say his body is covered with white, sesame-seed-like spots in the shape of flowers on a dark background. "Resembling reddish ashes" <note>original: "bhasmāruṇasannibho"</note> means a color mixed of ash-grey and red. "Cat-eyed" means having eyes like a cat. Such a bull, even if received by Brahmins as a ritual gift, does not bring prosperity, nor does he do so for others. ||8||

->He says another thing:<-

> **Those who lift their feet as if pulling them out of mud when yoked, who have thin necks, timid eyes, and are weak in the hindquarters—they are not capable of bearing loads. ||9||**

They are "not load-bearers" <note>original: "bhārasahā"</note>, meaning they are not capable of carrying heavy weights. These are bulls who, when yoked to a weight...

...appointed <note>referring to bulls put to work</note> they lift their feet and hooves from the mud as if with great difficulty. They have thin necks and weak shoulders.

And so says **Parashara**: <note>An ancient sage and authority on agriculture and astrology</note>

->Those whose feet are reddish-brown like alkali and covered with dark spots,<-
->who have eyes like a cat or a monkey, are weak and destroyers of the herd.<-
->Those who walk as if distressed, lifting their feet as if from deep mud,<-
->are unable to carry yokes and are condemned for the road and heavy loads. Thus it is said. 9.<-

Now he describes the auspicious characteristics:

->Those with soft, well-joined, copper-colored lips; thin flanks and copper-colored palates and tongues;<-
->short, thin, and high-set ears; handsome bellies and well-proportioned shanks. 10.<-

->With slightly copper-colored, closely-set hooves; a broad chest and a large hump;<-
->with glossy, smooth, thin skin and hair, and thin, copper-colored horns. 11.<-

->With tails that are thin and touch the ground; eyes with red corners and deep breaths;<-
->shoulders like a lion’s and thin, small dewlaps—these are honored and have a good gait. 12.<-

Bulls of this kind are honored, meaning they are beautiful and excellent. What are they like? They have soft, well-joined, copper-colored lips. Soft means tender; well-joined means the lips meet perfectly; and they are the color of copper. They have thin flanks <note>original: *sphij*, referring to the buttocks or hips</note>, meaning there is little excess flesh on their hindquarters. They have copper-colored palates and tongues. Copper-colored means reddish; the palate is the upper part of the mouth and the tongue is the organ of taste. They have ears that are short (small), thin (not fleshy), and high (not drooping). They have "good bellies," meaning well-shaped abdomens. They have well-proportioned shanks. 10.

They have slightly copper-colored and "joined" hooves, meaning the hooves are set close together without gaps. They have broad chests, meaning very strong chests. They are endowed with a large hump <term>kakud: the fleshy protuberance on the shoulders of Zebu cattle</term>. They have skin and hair that is glossy (oily), smooth (soft), and thin (not coarse). Their horns <note>original: *vishana*</note> are copper-colored or reddish and thin. 11.

Their tails <note>original: *valadhi*</note> are thin and touch the ground. Their eyes have red corners. They have "great breaths," meaning deep and powerful respiration. Their shoulders are like those of a lion. Their dewlaps <term>kambala: the fold of loose skin hanging from the neck of a bovine</term> are thin and small. They have a "good gait," meaning their movement is graceful. Such are the bulls described. 12.

The author says another thing:

->**With left-handed hair-whorls on the left side and right-handed whorls on the right,**<-
->**oxen are givers of prosperity, as are those with shanks resembling those of a deer. ||13||**<-

Those oxen <note>original: *anaduho*, referring to draft-oxen or bulls</note> that are endowed with hair-whorls turning to the left on their left side, and hair-whorls turning to the right on their right side, are auspicious and praised. Likewise, they are givers of prosperity if they possess shanks <note>the part of the leg between the knee and the ankle</note> that resemble those of a deer <note>original: *enaka*, a species of small deer or antelope</note>, being well-fleshed and shapely. Some interpret *enaka* as a specific type of animal, while others suggest it refers to a sheep. ||13||

The author says another thing:

->**Those with eyes like cat's-eye gems, jasmine-flowers, or bubbles, and with thick eyelashes,**<-
->**and with heels that are not cracked, are all praised and capable of bearing heavy loads. ||14||**<-

The cat's-eye <note>original: *vaidurya*, a precious dark-colored gemstone</note> is a well-known variety of gem. Regarding "jasmine-eyed" <note>original: *mallikaksha*</note>, the definition is as follows: one who has streaks resembling jasmine flowers on the outer circle of the eye is called "jasmine-eyed." This characteristic is also described in relation to horses. As the Prakrit verse says:

> "Those whose eyes are straight, of undimmed luster, and possess jasmine-flower-like marks at the edges of the pupils are considered jasmine-eyed." <note>original: *ujju akina-kanti...*</note>

And so says Shalihotra <note>the legendary founder of veterinary science in ancient India</note>:

> "He whose auspicious eyes are surrounded by white streaks, and who has very black pupils, is called jasmine-eyed and is highly fortunate."

One who possesses these characteristics is "jasmine-eyed"; "bubble-eyed" is self-explanatory. Thus, those with eyes like cat's-eyes, jasmine, or bubbles, and those whose eyelashes <note>original: *netra-pakshmani*</note> are thick and very dense, are praised. Furthermore, those with heels <note>the rear part of the hoof</note> that are uncracked and unbroken are all entirely excellent and "load-bearers," meaning they can endure carrying heavy weights. ||14||

The author says another thing:

->**One with wrinkles on the snout, a face like a cat, white on the right side,**<-
->**the color of a lotus, water-lily, or lac, and a beautiful tail, possesses speed equal to a horse. ||15||**<-

### One with hanging testicles, a belly like a ram, and compact loins and chest,
### Should be known as capable of bearing loads on the road, equal to a horse in speed, and a bringer of praised results. ||16||

One who has wrinkles <note>original: "savali"</note> in the region of the snout or nose. One with a face like a cat <note>original: "marjara-mukha"</note>. One who is white on the right side. One whose luster is like a lotus, a blue water-lily, or lac <note>lac is a resinous red pigment</note>. One with a beautiful tail. One with speed equal to a horse <note>original: "vaji-tulya-java"</note>; "vaji" means horse, and one whose velocity is equal to that. This means he is a fast mover.

One endowed with hanging or pendulous testicles. One whose belly is shaped like that of a ram <note>original: "meshodara"</note>. One whose loins <term>vankshana: the groin or the area between the thigh and the testicles</term> and chest <term>kroda: the breast or thoracic region</term> are compact. The term "vankshana" refers to the space between the hind shanks and the testicles. Regarding this very meaning, the sage Shalihotra <note>The legendary founder of Indian veterinary science</note> says:

> The two masses between the thighs and the shanks should be designated as the "vankshana."
> The "kroda" is said to be between the front shanks, located ahead of the "vankshana."

A bull whose loins and chest are compact should be known as capable and powerful in carrying loads and traveling on the road. In speed, he is equal to a horse. "Java," "vega," and "gati" are synonyms for speed. Such a bull is a bringer of praised or auspicious results. ||15-16||

He says another thing:

### White in color, with tawny eyes, copper-colored horns and gaze, and a large mouth;
### Named "Hansa" (The Swan), he is said to bring auspicious results and increase the herd. ||17||

One who is white in color. One with tawny or reddish-brown eyes. One with copper-colored horns and eyes. One with a large or thick face; he is named "Hansa." He brings auspicious results. He is said to be an increaser of the herd or flock. ||17||

He says another thing:

### One whose tail touches the ground, with slightly copper-colored horns, red eyes, and a hump;
### And who is "Kalmasha" (variegated) soon makes his owner the master of Fortune. ||18||

A bull whose tail-hair touches the earth. One with reddish horns. One with red eyes. One possessed of a hump <note>original: "kakudman"</note>. One who is "Kalmasha" in color—a variegated mixture of white, red, and yellow. He makes his owner or master the lord of Fortune <note>original: "Lakshmi," the goddess of wealth</note> very quickly. ||18||

He says something else as well—

### Even a bull with white feet, regardless of the color of the rest of its body, brings good fortune.
### One with mixed results should also be accepted if a perfectly auspicious one is not available. || 19 ||

Any bull that is white or possesses white feet <note>original: "sitaiścaraṇaiḥ"</note> is a bringer of good results, even if the rest of its body is marked with colors usually considered inauspicious. Some read the text as "one with at least one white foot." If a "perfectly auspicious" bull—one possessing every single positive mark—is not available, then one with "mixed results" <note>possessing both good and bad physical traits</note> should be accepted. The word "also" implies this is a secondary possibility. Some read the text as "if it is not ultimately inauspicious." This means that after weighing the difference between the good and bad signs, if the bad signs do not outweigh the good in the end, then the bull with mixed characteristics should be taken. As the sage Parashara <note>An ancient authority on agriculture and astrology</note> says:

> Those with soft, compact, copper-colored lips, thin tongues, and thin skin-folds under the neck;
> 
> With eyes the color of cat's-eye gems or honey, resembling water bubbles;
> 
> With red, glossy eyes and red pupils; with shoulders like a lion, broad chests, and firm, well-nourished humps <note>term: Kakudmin (the hump found on zebu/Indian cattle)</note>;
> 
> Whose tail drags on the ground and has a long, thick tuft of hair; who are high in the front and low and well-proportioned in the rear;
> 
> With rounded limbs, thick bodies, and wide hindquarters; with hooves that are distinct, not too small, smooth, well-spaced, and firm;
> 
> Shaped like a casket, with heels that are compact and not cracked; with round, thick, uplifted necks and very high humps;
> 
> These should be known as capable of bearing heavy loads and are honored for pulling carts and vehicles. Those endowed with hair-whorls that turn to the right <note>term: Dakshinavarta (clockwise whorls, usually considered auspicious)</note> on their right side;
> 
> And those with whorls turning to the left on their left side are also honored. One with very long testicles and a slim belly and groin...

### Now, the Characteristics of Dogs are explained.

At the very beginning of this section, the author describes the characteristics of a dog:

> A dog who has five claws on three of his feet, but six claws on the front right foot; who has copper-colored lips and a copper-colored tip of the nose; who walks with the gait of a lion <note>original: "mrigeshvara," the lord of beasts</note> and moves while sniffing the ground; whose tail is bushy <note>original: "sasatam," meaning hairy or maned</note>; whose eyes resemble those of a bear; and whose ears are long and soft—such a dog, kept in the house, quickly brings abundant wealth to his master. 1.

Whosoever's dog has three feet or limbs equipped with five claws or nails; and the fourth, the front right foot, is equipped with six claws. "With copper-colored lips and nose-tip" means one whose lips and the tip of the nose are copper-colored or reddish. "Gait of a lion" means his movement or walk is like that of a lion. He moves or goes along sniffing the earth or ground. The tail or posterior is "bushy," meaning it is covered with hair or matted. The "eyes" or sight are "bear-like," meaning his vision or look is equal to that of the creature known as a bear. The "ears" or organs of hearing are "long," meaning hanging down, and "soft," meaning endowed with gentleness. A dog or hound who possesses these traits brings to his "master"—the one who nourishes him—very quickly, within the "house" or dwelling, "abundant" or full "wealth" or fortune. And thus says Garga <note>An ancient sage and authority on omens</note>:

> Three feet with five claws, and the front right one
> with six claws; with a copper nose and copper lips; with the valor of a lion;
> who moves with joy while sniffing the earth; with a matted tail;
> eyes resembling a bear's, and ears that are soft and very long—
> such a dog bestows great fortune upon the king who protects him. 1.

### Now, the characteristics of a female dog are stated:

> On each foot there are five claws, but on the front
> left foot of her who has jasmine-colored eyes <note>original: "mallikakshyah," eyes white like the Mallika flower</note>, there are six claws...

A female dog who has five claws <term>kararuha: literally 'grown from the hand'</term> on each and every foot; or one who has six claws on the front left foot; and who is "jasmine-eyed." A jasmine-eyed dog is one who has streaks resembling the jasmine flower on the outer edge of the iris. If such a jasmine-eyed dog also has a curved or crooked tail, is reddish-brown in color, and has long hanging ears, she—when well-fed—protects the entire kingdom. || 2 ||

### Now, the Characteristics of Roosters are explained.

Regarding this, he first describes the auspicious rooster:

> A rooster with straight feathers and toes,
> with a copper-colored beak, claws, and crest, and who is white;
> who crows with a pleasant voice at the end of the night—
> he brings prosperity to the king, the kingdom, and the horses. || 1 ||

The rooster <note>original: "kukkuta," also called "krikavaku" in the commentary</note> who has straight feathers <term>tanuruha: literally 'body-hair' or plumage</term> and straight toes; who has a copper-colored face or beak; who has copper-colored claws and a copper-colored crest <note>original: "tamrachuda"</note>; and who is white in color. If he crows with a sweet, pleasant sound at the end of the night <note>dawn</note>, he grants growth and prosperity to the King, the nation, and the horses. 

And thus says Garga <note>An ancient sage and authority on omens</note>:

> A white one with copper claws, white with copper eyes and a straight tail;
> with well-spaced toes, a fine body, and a copper crest is praised.
> One who crows loudly, has a neck shaped like a barley grain, is the color of yogurt, and has a beautiful face;
> with a noble mouth, a thick head, and turmeric-yellow feet—this bird is auspicious.
> Those who are not lame, have copper-colored beaks, and glossy colors are honored;
> while those who are miserable, discolored, or have discordant voices are condemned. || 1 ||

# Now he describes other characteristics:

> -> The bird whose neck is shaped like a grain of barley, or who resembles a jujube fruit, <-
> -> who has a large head and is beautiful with many colors— <-
> -> he is praised in battle; one colored like honey or a honey-bee also brings victory. <-
> -> Any other than these is not praised: those with a thin body, a weak cry, or a lame foot. ॥2॥ <-

The bird (the rooster) who is "barley-necked" has a neck shaped like a grain of barley <note>original: *yavagrivo*; this refers to a thick, sturdy neck tapering at the ends</note>. This is popularly known as "barley-headed." Or the one who resembles a jujube <note>a small, reddish-brown fruit</note>, meaning he has the luster of a well-ripened jujube fruit. "Large-headed" means having a broad head. "With many colors" means endowed with various hues such as white, red, blue, yellow, and black. "Beautiful" means bright and clear. Such a rooster is "praised in battle," meaning highly auspicious for combat. Alternatively, one who is "honey-colored" (yellowish) or "honey-bee colored" (black) also brings victory. Any other than those mentioned is "not praised," meaning inauspicious. One who has a "thin body and cry"—meaning a wasted frame and a faint or weak sound—or a "lame foot" (a defective leg) is also not auspicious. ॥2॥

# Now he describes the characteristics of the hen:

> -> A hen who speaks softly and sweetly, <-
> -> with a glossy form and beautiful face and eyes; <-
> -> she grants to kings for a very long time <-
> -> the wealth of prosperity, fame, victory, and valor. ॥3॥ <-

The hen who speaks with "softness" and "beauty" (pleasant sounds), who has a "glossy form" (a clean, healthy body), and "beautiful face and eyes"—meaning her countenance and gaze are pleasing—grants to "kings" <note>original: *mahiksitam*; literally 'earth-protectors'</note> for a very long time: Prosperity (Fortune), Fame (Renown), Victory (triumph over enemies), and the wealth of Valor (power and sovereignty). ॥3॥

-> Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, named "Characteristics of Roosters," <-
-> in the Commentary on the Samhita composed by the venerable Bhattotpala. <-

<header>Chapter 63 ] The Chapter on the Characteristics of Tortoises | 717</header>

A tortoise that is the color of crystal—resembling a crystal stone—or the color of silver—having the appearance of silver—is described. One that is variegated with blue streaks <note>original: "rajibhir," meaning lines or stripes</note> or possesses a body shaped like a water-pot <note>original: "kalasha," a ceremonial pitcher</note> is highly significant. One with a "beautiful spine" <note>original: "charuvamsha"</note>—meaning the backbone is well-formed and not too high—or one with a body as red as the dawn, variegated with white spots the size of mustard seeds, is auspicious. Such a tortoise, when kept in a palace, bestows greatness and sovereignty upon all kings. It means it grants the status of a "King of Kings" <note>original: "Rajadhiraja"</note>. ||1||

### He says something further—

->One whose body is as dark as collyrium or a honey-bee,<-
->variegated with spots and possessing a complete body;<-
->or one with a head like a snake or a thick neck,<-
->that tortoise also leads to the expansion of a king's nation. ||2||<-

Collyrium <note>original: "Anjana," a traditional eye-salve</note> is well known as soot. The "Bhringa" is the large black bee. One whose body is dark like collyrium or a bee, variegated with spots or marks, and has a "complete body"—meaning a body with all limbs fully formed—is praised. Or one with a head like a snake, or a thick, broad neck. That tortoise also serves to increase the kingdom of kings. ||2||

### He says something further—

->One with the luster of a cat's-eye gem, a thick neck, and a triangular shape,<-
->with hidden openings and a beautiful spine, is praised.<-
->In a pleasure-pool or a water-filled cistern,<-
->a tortoise should be kept by kings for the sake of auspiciousness. ||3||<-

"Luster of a cat's-eye gem" <note>original: "Vaidurya," a precious chrysoberyl</note> means having a brilliance like that stone. "Thick-necked" means a stout throat. "Triangular" means shaped like a *shringataka* <note>a water chestnut or a triangular nut</note>. "Hidden openings" refers to one whose pores or orifices are not visible. "Beautiful spine" means a handsome backbone. Such a tortoise is excellent. A tortoise of this kind should be placed by kings for the sake of good fortune in a pleasure-pool <note>original: "krida-vapi," a recreational pond</note> or in a water-filled stone basin at the base of a well. And so says the sage Garga:

| | |
|---|---|
| One resembling a conch or Darbha grass, shaped like a parasol, | with the glow of silver; |
| Also one with the color and luster of a cat's-eye gem, | or one with eight mustard-seed spots; |
| And that which has the appearance of a cuckoo, | or resembles a lotus; |
| Or is the color of yellow gold, | with a luster like a white lotus. |

### Now, the characteristics of goats are explained.

And he <note>the author, Varahamihira</note> says:

> I shall describe the auspicious and inauspicious signs of goats. Those with nine, ten, or eight teeth are blessed and should be kept in the home; those with seven teeth should be discarded. || 1 ||

I shall describe—that is, I shall tell—the auspicious and inauspicious signs of goats <note>original: "chaga," meaning male goats or goats in general</note>. Those goats that have nine, ten, or eight teeth are blessed and excellent; they should be kept in the residence or house. Those that have seven teeth should be abandoned. || 1 ||

He says something else as well:

> A black circular mark on the right side of a white goat brings auspicious results. For those colored like a blue deer, or those of black or red color, a white mark is very auspicious. || 2 ||

On a white goat, a black-colored circular mark on the right side—in the middle portion—brings a good result. For one like a blue deer <note>original: "rishya," a species of antelope or mountain deer described as dark blue/grey</note>—the *rishya* is a type of deer, and it is blue-colored—and likewise for those of black or red color, a white circular mark on the right side is very auspicious. || 2 ||

He says something else as well:

> That which hangs from the throat of goats like a teat is to be known as a "jewel" <note>term: "mani" (jewel), here referring to the fleshy wattles found on the necks of some goats</note>. One with a single jewel brings auspicious results; those with two or three jewels are the most blessed. || 3 ||

On the throat—the neck—of goats, that which hangs down like a teat or breast is to be understood as a "jewel." A goat possessed of a single jewel brings a good result. Those that have two jewels or three jewels are the most blessed—meaning they are the most highly praised. || 3 ||

He says something else as well:

> All hornless goats are givers of good fortune, as are those entirely white or entirely black. Those half-black and half-white are blessed, as are those half-brown and half-black. || 4 ||

# Chapter 64: On the Characteristics of Goats

Goats that are hornless <note>original: "munda"</note> are all entirely auspicious. Likewise, those that are completely white or completely black in body are also auspicious. Those that are half-white and half-black are all considered blessed and praiseworthy, as are those that are half-brown and half-black.

Now, the author describes the characteristics of four specific types: the *Kuttaka*, the *Kutila*, the *Jatila*, and the *Vamana*. First, he speaks of the *Kuttaka*:

->**The goat that walks at the head of the herd and is the first to enter the water is auspicious; so too is one with a white head, or one who has the 'Pleiades' mark upon its head.**<-

The goat that walks at the front of the flock or is the first to wade into or drink water is considered excellent. Alternatively, one with a white head is auspicious, or one who has the *Krttika* <note>The Pleiades constellation; here referring to a pattern of spots</note> marks on its head. Since the Pleiades consist of six stars, this means a pattern of six spots. A goat possessing any of these traits is known as a *Kuttaka*. As the sage Garga says:

> "The one who walks at the head of the herd, who is the first to touch the water, and who has six spots upon its head—that goat increases the prosperity of the flock."

Next, he describes the *Kutila*:

->**One with spots on the neck or head, or one colored like ground sesame paste with copper-colored eyes, is praised; so too is a white goat with black feet, or a black goat with white feet.**<-

One who has spots <note>original: "prshata"</note> on the throat or neck, or spots on the head, is auspicious. "Colored like ground sesame paste" refers to a mixed color of white and yellowish-brown. One with copper-colored <note>reddish</note> eyes is also excellent. Furthermore, a white-colored goat with black feet is auspicious, as is a black-colored goat with white feet. A goat with any of these traits is called a *Kutila*. As Garga says:

> "A white goat with black feet, or a black one with white hooves; or a yellow one with copper eyes and spots on the head or neck."

Next, he describes the characteristics of the *Jatila*:

->**A goat that has black testicles and is white with a black band around its middle, or one that makes a sound while walking slowly, is a beautiful goat.**<-

<summary>This page details the auspicious physical markings of goats, categorizing them into specific types like Kuttaka and Kutila based on their color, spots, and behavior within a herd.</summary>
<keywords>goat characteristics, Kuttaka, Kutila, Jatila, Garga, animal omens, auspicious markings, livestock husbandry</keywords>

--- Page 204 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of goat physiognomy (chagalakshana) from the Brihat Samhita, specifically detailing the auspicious markings of the 'Jatila' and 'Vamana' varieties.</meta>

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 64]

A goat that has black testicles <note>original: "krishnando'sitavrishanah"</note> and is otherwise white in color, but is marked in the middle—the central part of the body—with a black band shaped like a saddle, is considered auspicious. Furthermore, any goat that moves slowly and lazily while making a distinct sound is excellent and praised. A goat possessing any of these specific characteristics is known by the name **Jatila** <note>literally "the maned" or "the complex one"</note>. As the sage Garga says:

> That goat which moves slowly with sound, is white with black testicles,
> and is joined in the middle by a black band, even he brings prosperity. || 7 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Vamana—

> One with the head and feet of a Rishya <note>a type of blue-black antelope or deer</note>, or one who is pale-white in the front and dark blue in the back;
> such a goat brings good fortune. There is also a verse by Garga on this matter. || 8 ||

"With the head and hair of a Rishya" means having a blue-colored head. The *Rishya* is a creature commonly called a bear <note>original: "riksha"</note> in the world, and it is blue-black in color. As the sage Vyasa says <note>referring to the author of the Mahabharata</note>:

> Karna, covering the Pandavas with arrows in battle,
> yoked horses the color of the Rishya-deer with excellent swan-white horses. <margin>Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Chapter 132, Verse 27</margin>

And also:

> Those horses, swift as the wind, shone greatly in their mixture,
> white and black and of great color, like clouds in the sky. <margin>Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Chapter 132, Verse 29</margin>

Therefore, one with a blue head and blue feet is also a bringer of good. Or, one who is pale-white <note>original: "pandura"</note> in the front part and blue in the rear part is also an auspicious goat. A goat with any of these characteristics is called **Vamana** <note>literally "the dwarf" or "the short one"</note>. As Garga says:

> One with a Rishya-head and blue feet, who is pale in the front part
> and blue-colored in the back; he also grants prosperity to his owner.

On this subject, the verse spoken by Garga is the authority which he [Varahamihira] quotes directly. || 8 ||

And he says:

> The Kuttaka, the Kutila, the Jatila, and the Vamana—
> these four are the sons of Fortune; they do not dwell with the luckless. || 9 ||

---

1. Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Chapter 132, Verse 27.
2. Mahabharata, Drona Parva, Chapter 132, Verse 29. There, the reading in the second foot is "mixed, swift as the wind" and in the third foot "white and black, O Great King."

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Goats
<page-num>721</page-num>
<header>Chapter on the Characteristics of Goats</header>
<meta>Ch. 64]</meta>

The *Kuttaka* <note>A specific breed or type of goat characterized by certain markings</note> mentioned in the previous characteristics, as well as the crooked, the matted-haired, and the dwarf—these four types of goats are "Sons of Fortune" <note>original: "Shriyah Putrah"</note>, children of Lakshmi <note>The goddess of wealth and prosperity</note>. They do not dwell or stay in a place devoid of fortune; rather, the meaning is that they reside only in a place endowed with prosperity. ||9||

Having thus described the characteristics of auspicious goats, the author now describes those that are not recommended:

->Now, those that are inauspicious have a cry like a donkey,<-
->have "blazing" tails, bad hooves, or are discolored;<-
->those with clipped ears, heads like elephants,<-
->and those who have black palates and tongues. ||10||<-

Following this, there are goats that are inauspicious. Of what kind? Those with a cry like a donkey <note>original: "khara-tulya-nada"</note>, having a sound similar to an ass. Those with "blazing" tails—meaning a tail that is crooked or held excessively high. Those with bad hooves <note>original: "kunakhah"</note>, meaning deformed or ugly nails. Those who are discolored, meaning they lack a good color or possess inauspicious hues. Those with clipped ears, having ears that appear cut or mutilated. Those with elephant-heads, having a head resembling that of an elephant. And those who have black palates and tongues—those with dark roofs of the mouth and dark tongues are also inauspicious. ||10||

Now, he describes the auspicious characteristics:

->Those endowed with excellent colors and "jewels,"<-
->those who are hornless, and those with copper-colored eyes;<-
->if honored in the homes of men,<-
->they bring happiness, fame, and fortune. ||11||<-

Goats endowed with excellent colors <gloss>1</gloss> >"A black circle on the right side of a white goat yields a good result"<note>original: "dakshina-parshve mandalam asitam shuklasya shubha-phalam bhavati"</note>—goats joined with colors of this kind. And those joined with "jewels" <note>referring to fleshy neck-pendants or wattles</note>, whether one, two, or three. Those who are hornless <note>original: "munda"</note>, and those with copper-colored eyes (reddish eyes)—these goats, when honored in the houses or homes of men, are auspicious and bring about happiness (freedom from suffering), fame (renown), and fortune (wealth). ||11||

### Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, named "Characteristics of Goats,"
### in the Commentary on the Samhita composed by the venerable Bhattotpala. ||64||

## Now, the Characteristics of Horses are Explained.

In this matter, nothing can be understood without knowledge of the specific body parts; therefore, the chapter on the regions of the body is written first—

> Without knowing the regions of the body, a physician <note>The term 'bhishak' implies a veterinary doctor or healer here.</note> becomes confused in his duties. Therefore, the knowledge of the location of the body parts of horses must be studied with great effort.
> 
> Success in all treatments is always dependent upon this knowledge. The tongue is tied to the throat, and that area is known as the 'galanāla' <note>The esophagus or throat-tube</note>.
> 
> Below the 'sūnā' <note>likely referring to the base or root</note> is the tongue, and above it is the palate. The 'pīṭha' <note>the jaw-seats</note> are fixed in the jaw; the tusks <note>canine teeth</note> are located in front of them.
> 
> Then come the teeth which show the horse's age <note>term: vyañjanina; horses' ages were traditionally determined by dental wear and markings</note>, and above them are the upper teeth. Below the teeth and tusks, in the middle, is what is known as the chin.
> 
> The lips are the coverings of the teeth, and at their sides are the corners of the mouth. The 'prapāṇa' <note>the tip of the nose or upper lip area used for drinking</note> is above the upper lip, and above that is the 'protha' <note>the snout or nose-tip</note>.
> 
> The nostrils are at the sides of the snout; the 'ghoṇā' <note>the bridge of the nose</note> is in the middle of the snout and the eyes. The cheeks arise from the bridge of the nose, and the 'kshīrikā' <note>small sensitive spots or glands</note> are above them.
> 
> Between the nose-bridge and the jaw are the 'gaṇḍa' <note>the fleshy part of the cheeks</note>, and between those is the place where tears fall. The eyes are located above, followed by their coverings <note>eyelids</note>.
> 
> Inside the eye are the white, the black, and the circle of the pupil. The 'kanīnikā' <note>inner corners</note> are at the interior angle, and the 'apāṅga' <note>outer corners</note> are on the outside.
> 
> Above the eyelids are the eyelashes, and above those are the 'akshikūṭa' <note>the eyebrow bone or eye sockets</note>. Above those are the eyebrows, and the forehead is the space between the eyebrows.
> 
> Above the forehead is the 'dhruva' <note>the top of the head</note>, and the head itself is above the ears. The 'mastaka' <note>the crown or skull</note> rests there, with the ears on its sides.
> 
> At the root of the ear is the 'shaṣkulī' <note>the outer ear passage/conch</note>; between the ear and the temple is the 'kaṭa' <note>the temple region</note>. Between the 'kaṭa' and the outer corner of the eye is the 'shaṅkha' <note>the temporal bone</note>, and the 'ghaṭī' <note>hollow of the temple</note> is outside the temples.
> 
> Above the chin are the jaws, and the cheeks are above these. Between the jaws and the throat-tube, the middle part is called the 'nigāla' <note>the pharynx or gullet</note>.
> 
> Below the 'nigāla' is the neck, then the throat, the chest, the 'kroḍa' <note>the breast/sternum</note>, and then the heart. Six finger-widths below the ear are the 'vidu' and 'mandavidu' <note>specific pressure points or anatomical markers near the upper neck</note>.
> 
> Below the 'viddha' <note>perforation or sensitive spot</note> on both sides, in the middle, is the neck-tie <note>the attachment of the neck</note>. Between the head-carrier <note>the atlas bone/top of the spine</note> is the neck, and between the collarbone and the neck is the 'vaha' <note>the shoulder-butt or part that bears the yoke</note>.

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Horses
## [Chapter 65]

Above the shoulder is the neck, and upon the neck is the mane. From the arms and the collarbone, the <term>kakasam</term><note>The area of the upper chest or throat-latch</note> and the hump are described.

Then come the seat and the back, and beyond that, the backbone. The two shoulders are situated at the hump, and the arms are connected to the shoulders.

Below the chest are the arms; six finger-widths from the exterior of the arms and inside the arms are the armpits, located at the sides of the chest.

One should recognize the <term>kinas</term><note>Callouses or rough patches of skin</note> on the inside, and below them are considered to be the knees. Below the knees are the knee-caps, and behind the knees is the "temple" of the joint.

Below the knees are the shanks, and behind them are considered the <term>kalas</term><note>The small bones or structures of the lower leg</note>. Between the shanks and these bones are the shafts, with the "around-the-hand" area in front.

Behind that area are the <term>kurchas</term><note>Tarsal or carpal brush-like structures</note>, with callouses situated in their middle. Below the <term>kurchas</term> are the <term>kuttikas</term><note>Small bones above the hoof</note>, then the hoof-joint, and then the hoof itself.

At the back are the heels and the "heel-shafts," the heel being the surface at the edge of the nail <insert>hoof</insert>. In the middle of the sole are the "frogs" <note>original: "mandukya" - literally 'little frogs', the triangular elastic part of a horse's hoof</note>, and the "milky spots" within the sole.

Beyond the heart is the umbilical region, and beyond the navel is the belly. Between the heart, navel, and sheath, a line of hair is recognized.

Below that is the penis and the sheath, then the testicles. Below the hip-joint is the thigh-joint, and above it are the thighs and the "binding of the fruit" <note>the scrotum or groin area</note>; this is called the pale region of the thigh.

Above the thighs are the pale-colored muscles, then the mouth-like joints, and then the <term>sthura</term><note>The broad part of the thigh or buttock</note>. Below the <term>sthura</term> is the "temple," with the "pins" and the callouses in their middle. What was previously described below the <term>sthura</term> should also be observed from the back.

The two limbs, the head, and the neck are called the **Fore-body**. The hips, the lower spine, the tail, and the two hind limbs are the **Hind-body**.

The regions in the middle are proclaimed as the **Mid-body**. The six parts of the body are named as: the face, the four limbs, and the tail.

The nails <insert>hoofs</insert>, body hair, tail hair, and mane are considered the secondary parts. These are arranged from the face to the end of the tail, appearing in greater or lesser proportions in the middle.

Whatever has not been mentioned here should be understood through logical inference. Thus are explained the regions residing in the bodies of horses.

A physician <note>original: "bhishak" - a doctor or healer</note> who understands these before performing his work will not commit errors.

<header>In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 65]</header>

### First, he describes the characteristics of a horse—

**A horse with a long neck and eye-sockets, broad in the small of the back and the chest, with copper-colored palate, lips, and tongue;**
**With fine skin, hair, and tail-hair; with well-formed hooves, gait, and face; with short ears, upper lip, and tail-bone;**
**With shanks, knees, and thighs that are well-rounded; with even, white teeth and a beautiful build and appearance;**
**Such a horse, perfect in all its limbs, always serves for the destruction of the enemies of a king. ||1||**

"Long neck and eye-sockets": one whose neck (the support of the head) is long, and likewise the eye-sockets (the bony hollows of the eyes) are long. "Broad in the small of the back and chest": the *trika* <note>the lower back or sacrum</note> and the heart-region—these are broad or wide. "Copper-colored palate, lips, and tongue": one whose lower lips, the palate (the roof of the mouth), and the tongue are the color of copper. "Fine skin, hair, and tail-hair": the skin, the hair of the head, and the hair of the tail—these are fine or thin. "Well-formed hooves, gait, and face": the hooves, the manner of walking, and the face—these are endowed with excellent proportions and auspicious movements. "Short ears, upper lip, and tail-bone": the ears, the upper lip, and the base of the tail where the bone and hair are attached—these are short rather than long. "Shanks, knees, and thighs well-rounded": the shanks <note>the part of the leg between the knee and the ankle</note>, the knees, and the thighs are perfectly circular or rounded. "Even, white teeth": the teeth are uniform and white in color. "Beautiful build and appearance": the *samsthana* (the physical frame) is pleasing to look at and the *rupa* (the beauty of the body) is excellent. A horse (*vaji*) of this kind, "perfect in all its limbs"—meaning endowed with flawless characteristics in every part—always serves for the "destruction of enemies" (the slaying of foes) for a "king" (a ruler of men) at all times. And so says the venerable Parashara <note>An ancient sage often cited as an authority on agriculture, astronomy, and animal husbandry</note>:

> The length of horses of the lowest, middle, and highest grades
> Should be known as one hundred and thirteen, one hundred and twenty, and one hundred and thirty *angulas* <note>a unit of measurement roughly equal to a finger's width</note>.
> The circumference should be seventy, seventy-seven,
> And eighty-one respectively, for the three types in brief.
> Likewise, the height should be sixty, sixty-four, and sixty-eight.
> The length of the face should be twenty-two, twenty-five, and twenty-seven.
> A face without whiskers is lovely, bold, and has a high nose,
> With a short snout, thin ears, and a deep red palate.
> Twelve teeth after the initial six, with soft but firm nostrils,
> A long and uplifted neck, and short belly and hooves.
> One that is unrestrained, of fierce speed, with a voice like a swan or a thundercloud,
> Greenish like a parrot, or white with black circles.

# Chapter 65: On the Characteristics of Horses
<page-num>725</page-num>

->One should mount such a horse by holding it by the hand or the ear.<-
->Those born of the twice-born classes <note>referring to the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas</note>, being experts in urging them forward, should ride them in the month of Ashvina <note>September-October</note>.<-
->Likewise, if a horse is of a single, glossy color,<-
->it destroys defects arising from the "whirling" <note>likely referring to bad temper or physical instability</note>; such a body is praised everywhere.<-

And so says **Vararuchi** <note>A famous ancient scholar and polymath</note>:

> The vast knowledge of characteristics declared by the sages who knew the three worlds
> is difficult to grasp even for those of pure intellect because of its vastness; how much more so for those lacking wisdom?
> Therefore, listen to this summary in clear and sweet words regarding the horse’s constitution,
> endowed with color, hair whorls, luster, voice, gait, temperament, and scent.
> With hair, skin, and tail-hairs that are black, tawny, white, or glowing like molten gold—
> black, red-marked, and tawny are said to be the primary colors of horses.
> Through their mutual blending and the influence of the wind <note>the Vata humor in Ayurvedic medicine</note>, they reach great variety;
> a description of them must be spoken by one of clear and sharp intellect, according to the substance and essence of the animal.

Now he describes the characteristics of **inauspicious hair whorls** <term>Romavarta: circular patterns of hair growth thought to indicate the horse's destiny and character</term>:

> At the tear-path, the jaw, the cheek, the heart, the throat, the snout, the temples, the waist, the bladder, and the knees;
> at the testicles, the navel, the hump, and likewise at the anus, the right flank, and the legs—at these places, they are inauspicious. (2)

The **tear-path** <note>Ashrupata</note> is where tears fall; the area below the eyes. The **jaws** are well-known. The **cheeks** are the sides of the face. The **heart** is the chest. The **throat** is the junction of the heart and the neck. The **snout** <note>Protha</note> is the lower part of the nose. The **temples** are near the ears. The **waist** is well-known. The **bladder** is the space between the navel and the penis. The **knee** is the joint of the leg. These are the whorls located on these limbs. Likewise, the **testicles**. The **navel** is well-known. The **hump** <note>Kakuda</note> is on the back of the shoulders near the nape of the neck. The **anus** is the place of excrement. Others read this as *alupa* <margin>1. There is a variant reading: "tathalupe"</margin>. The **alupa** is the junction of the collarbone and the throat. The **right flank** <note>Savya-kukshi</note> refers to the right side of the belly. The **legs** refer to all the feet. The whorls found in these places are all inauspicious. Here, because they are parts of a whole, they are treated as a collective group.

And so says **Vararuchi**:

> By whorls located on the temples, brows, cheeks, nose, jaw, waist, hump, chest, armpits, or the seat;
> by those on the nape, heart, knees, the "brush" <note>Kurcha: a spot on the head or feet</note>, ears, throat, anus, snout, flanks, and tear-paths;
> by those on the ankles, buttocks, the lower back, the testicles, the shoulders, the navel, and the thighs—
> horses with such whorls bring inauspicious results and should be avoided. (2)

<page-num>726</page-num>
->### On Auspicious Hair Whorls###<-

> Those whorls located on the upper lip, throat, and ears;
> those situated in the middle of the back and above the eyes;
> those found on the lips, thighs, forelegs, belly, and sides—
> along with those on the forehead—are highly auspicious. || 3 ||

The "upper lip" <note>original: prapāṇa</note> refers to the surface of the top lip. The "throat" <note>original: gala</note> is the neck area below the gullet. The "ears" are the organs of hearing. Whorls located in these parts are beneficial. The "middle of the back" refers to the place where the saddle is positioned. "Above the eyes" means near the eyebrows. The "lips" are the coverings of the teeth. The "thighs" <note>original: sakthi</note> refer to the hindquarters above the hooves. The "forelegs" <note>original: bhuja</note> are the front limbs above the knees. The "belly" <note>original: kukṣi</note> refers here to the left side, as the right side has been previously described as censurable. The "sides" are well-known. Whorls appearing in these places, including the "forehead" (the area between the eyebrows), are highly auspicious, meaning they grant extremely favorable results.

As Vararuchi <note>An ancient authority on various sciences</note> says:

> Whorls of hair born on the thighs, upper lip, eyebrows, arms, throat, hairline, chest, above the ears, in the hollows, in the gullet, and on the forehead—these bring prosperity.

### Specific Characteristics of Luster —

> Horses with the luster of the rising sun, fire, coral, or molten gold are born of the Fire-element and increase sovereignty.
> Those with the color of a blue lotus or a rain-cloud are born of the Water-element and remove all sorrows.
> Those with deep and varied colors are born of the Earth-element and grant all desires.
> Those with a dry or rough complexion are born of the Air-element; these, along with those born of the Ether-element, are considered censurable and yield inauspicious results.

This concludes the characteristics of luster <note>original: kānti-lakṣaṇa</note>.

### Characteristics of Voice —

> Horses that possess a smooth and deep sound like a kettle-drum, conch, thunder-cloud, lion, elephant, small drum, or bull;
> or those with the sweet and clear cry of a lute or a male cuckoo—these are fit to carry kings.
> Those whose voices resemble a crow, owl, camel, dog, donkey, or a bull <note>in a harsh sense</note>, or those with rough and broken sounds, or other such types, bring inauspicious results, loss, and grief.

### Characteristics of Gait —

> A horse that moves with quick and playful steps, tossing its feet high, walking like a mongoose and shaking the tip of its crest, is highly regarded.
> Furthermore, one who touches the earth with the tips of its hooves in a formidable manner, as if crushing the ground with its footfalls, is said to have the gait of a partridge <note>original: taittira</note>.

# On the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 65]

There is only one fixed hair whorl <term>Dhruva-avarta<note>A "fixed whorl" or "constant turn" of hair, considered a significant mark of quality in equine science.</note></term>. Between the belly and the navel is the location of the "hole" <term>Randhra</term>. Above that is the "upper hole" <term>Upa-randhra</term>. As it is said:

->The hole is between the belly and the navel, and the upper hole is above it.<-

Thus, there is one whorl at the hole. At the upper hole, there is also only one. On the two flanks, there are four. On the top of the head, there are two. On the chest, in the breast region, two are mentioned in the traditional texts. Thus, these are the ten fixed whorls of horses. And so says Parashara <note>An ancient sage and authority on agriculture and animal husbandry</note>:

> "There are ten fixed whorls: one on the mouth <term>Prapana</term>, one on the forehead, two on the top of the head, two on the chest, and two each at the hole and upper hole." ||4||

Now he describes the knowledge of the age of horses:

**With six teeth of white luster, he is a foal; with those same teeth becoming dark-red, he is two years old.**
**By the 'pincers,' the 'middle,' and the 'end' teeth falling and rising again, he is three, four, and five years old respectively.**
**Following the order of the pincers, counted in groups of three years, come the black marks, the yellow, the white,**
**the glassy, the fly-like, the conch-like, the cavity, and the shaking; after this, know the falling out of the teeth. ||5||**

In the lower jaw of horses, between the two tusks, there are six prominent teeth. With six teeth in the front of both jaws having a white luster <note>original: "sitabha"</note>, the horse is a foal <note>original: "haya-shishu"</note>. This means he is one year old. With those same six teeth becoming dark-red <note>original: "kashaya"</note>, the horse is two years old. The two teeth situated exactly in the middle of both jaws are called the "pincers" <term>Sandesha</term>. The one situated on either side of those is the "middle" <term>Madhyama</term>. The one situated on the two outermost sides is named the "end" <term>Antya</term>.

Thus, when the pincers have fallen and risen again, the horse is three years old. When the middle teeth have fallen and risen, his measure is four years. When the end teeth have risen, he is five years old. Following the order of the pincers, the marks beginning with the "black spot" <term>Kalika</term> should be counted in groups of three. They are to be calculated three years at a time.

This is what is meant: When a black spot <note>original: "kalika"</note> appears on the two pincer teeth, the horse is six years old. These marks should be recognized by their distinct shapes. Likewise, with the middle teeth having black spots, he is seven years old; with the end teeth, eight years. Thus, for every mark, a three-year calculation should be made following the order of the teeth.

Following that same order:
- With yellow color <term>Pita</term>, he is eleven years old.
- With white color <term>Shukla</term>, he is fourteen years old.
- With a glassy/lead-like appearance <term>Kacha</term>, he is seventeen years old.
- With a fly-like mark <term>Makshika</term>, he is twenty years old.
- With a conch-like shape <term>Shankha</term>, he is twenty-three years old.
- With a cavity or hole <term>Avata</term>, he is twenty-six years old.
- With shaking or looseness <term>Chalana</term>, he is twenty-nine years old.
- After this, know the falling out of the teeth <term>Dantapata</term> at thirty-two years.

Know them in this sequence. And so says Vararuchi:

<header>Chapter 66] Chapter on the Characteristics of Elephants</header>

<note>The following verse describes the aging process of horses based on their teeth.</note>
The pair of nippers <note>central incisors</note>, the intermediates, and the corners—these pairs of teeth appear in the lower and then the upper jaw as the horse ages. In the second year, they are full; in the third, fourth, and fifth years, they become tinged with brown, fall out, and then reappear. Every three years, changes occur: they turn black, then yellow, then white, then like glass, then like honey, then like horn, then they become hollow, then shaky, and finally they fall out. This is the progression of characteristics for the teeth of a horse.

The Great Sage Parashara has stated the knowledge of the lifespan of horses as follows:

> "Now, if there are three long, deep, and unbroken lines on the snout, the horse's lifespan is thirty years. With two lines, twenty years. With one line, ten years. If a line turns toward the right, twelve years. If it follows the tip of the bridge of the nose, eighteen years. If the lines are short, crooked, broken, indistinct, rough, or shaped like a crow's foot, the lifespan is very short."

->Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, named 'Characteristics of Horses,'<-
->in the Commentary on the Samhita composed by Shri Bhattotpala.<-

---

### Now, the Characteristics of Elephants are explained.

In that regard, there are four castes <term>jatayah: types or breeds</term> of elephants: those named Bhadra, Manda, Mriga, and Mishra. First, the author describes the characteristics of the **Bhadra** type:

->**With tusks the color of honey, well-proportioned bodies,**<-
->**neither overweight nor thin, and possessing endurance;**<-
->**with symmetrical limbs, backs curved like a bow,**<-
->**and hindquarters like those of a boar—these are the Bhadras.**<-

Those elephants whose tusks have a luster <note>original: "abha"</note> resembling honey; whose bodies are well-proportioned, meaning their limbs are perfectly divided and balanced; who are not "overspread" <note>original: "upadigdha"</note>, meaning not excessively fat; nor thin or weak; and who are capable of work <note>endurance</note>. Their limbs are equal and symmetrical. Their "lineage" <note>original: "vamsha," here referring to the spine</note> is like a bow, meaning their backs have that specific curve. With hindquarters or hip regions that are rounded like those of a boar—these are the Bhadra elephants.

**Now, the characteristics of the Manda type are described:**

**The chest and the folds of the flanks are loose; the belly is hanging; the skin and the neck are large. The belly is thick along with the root of the tail, and the gaze is like that of a lion—such is the Manda elephant.**

The chest is the breast. The word "and" <note>original: "atha"</note> connects the parts. The "folds of the flanks"—by mentioning the flanks, the middle of the body is meant. The folds there, or the flanks and the folds themselves, are "loose," meaning flabby or slack.
