# On the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 66]

*Lambodara* means one with a hanging belly. *Tvag-brihati* means thick skin. The *gala* or neck is also thick. The *kukshi* or flanks are large and thick. Along with the *pechaka*—which refers to the root of the tail—the flanks are thick. *Saimhi drik* means a gaze like that of a lion. These are the characteristics of the elephant known as *Manda* <note>The 'Slow' or 'Indolent' type</note>. || 2 ||

## Now he describes the characteristics of the Mriga and Sankirna types—

->**The Mriga elephants have short lower lips, tails, and penises;**<-
->**their feet, necks, tusks, trunks, and ears are thin;**<-
->**and they have large eyes. Those with mixed characteristics**<-
->**as described are known as Sankirna elephants. || 3 ||**<-

Those elephants that have short lower lips, tails, and penises: *hrasva-adhara* means small lips <margin>Some read this as 'short belly'</margin>. *Hrasva-vala* means the hair on the tail is short. *Hrasva-medhra* means a short lingam. *Tanv-anghri-kantha-dvija-hasta-karnah* refers to those whose *anghri* (feet), *kantha* (neck), *dvija* (tusks <note>literally 'twice-born'</note>), *hasta* (trunk), and *karna* (ears) are thin or have little flesh. *Sthulekshana* means wide eyes or large pupils. These elephants are the *Mriga* <note>The 'Deer' type, characterized by a lighter build</note> type, possessing these traits. *Sankirna* <note>'Mixed' or 'Hybrid'</note> elephants are those possessing a mixture of the previously mentioned characteristics belonging to the *Bhadra*, *Manda*, and *Mriga* types. || 3 ||

## Now he states the measurements for their height, length, and circumference—

->**The height of the Mriga is five, its length is seven,**<-
->**and eight cubits is the measure of its circumference.**<-
->**The Manda and Bhadra increase by one and two respectively;**<-
->->**the Sankirna elephant has no fixed measurement. || 4 ||**<-

For the elephant called *Mriga*, the *unnati* (height) is five *hastas* <term>cubit; the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term>. From the root of the tail to the forehead-bumps (*kumbha*), the *daighya* (length) is seven cubits. Eight cubits is the *parinaha-mana*—*parinaha* refers to the middle circumference or girth. "Increase by one and two" means: by adding one, we get the **Manda**, and by adding two, we get the **Bhadra**. This is what is meant: The *Manda* has a height of six, a length of eight, and a girth of nine. The *Bhadra* has a height of seven, a length of nine, and a girth of ten. The *Sankirna* elephant has no fixed measure, meaning its proportions are uncertain. It possesses a mixture of the measurements. As Parashara <note>An ancient sage and authority on elephant lore</note> says:

The circumference is ten units, the length is nine, and the height is
seven; these are declared to be the measurements of a 
<term>Nagya</term> <note>A superior class of elephant</note> of the largest size.
The middle-sized elephant is one-seventh smaller than the largest;
the smallest elephant is one-sixth smaller than the middle one.
Any elephant other than these is not held in high esteem.
The length is measured from the snout to the tail-root; the width is the distance between the sides and the belly;
the circumference is the girth, and the height is to be known as the distance from the feet to the back. Thus it is said. || 4 ||

Now, he describes the color and the <term>mada</term> <note>The temporal secretion or "musth" fluid of an elephant, often used as a sign of vigor</note> of these types:

-> The color and the secretion of the *Bhadra* type are green; <-
-> That of the *Manda* type resembles the color of turmeric; <-
-> The secretion of the *Mriga* type is said to be black; <-
-> And the secretion of the *Sankirna* elephant is mixed. || 5 ||

The color of the elephant called *Bhadra* is green, like the color of a parrot, and its secretion is also green. The secretion and color of the *Manda* elephant resemble <term>haridraka</term> <note>turmeric-dyed cloth</note>; it is similar to that, meaning the color and secretion are of a yellowish hue. The secretion of the elephant called *Mriga* is described as black in appearance; by the word "and," the color is also understood to be the same. The secretion and color of the *Sankirna* <note>literally "mixed" or "hybrid"</note> elephant are of a variegated or mixed color. || 5 ||

Now, he describes the auspicious characteristics of elephants:

Those with copper-colored lips, palates, and mouths; with eyes like those of a sparrow;
with smooth, high-tipped tusks; with broad and long faces;
with backbones that are curved like a bow, elevated, long, hidden, and well-set;
with thin, single hairs and temples shaped like the shell of a tortoise; || 6 ||
With wide ears, jaws, navels, foreheads, and private parts;
with twenty or eighteen nails that are elevated like a tortoise shell;
with trunks that are well-rounded and marked with three lines; with beautiful tails;
and whose breath from the trunk and whose secretion smells fragrant—these are the auspicious ones. || 7 ||

Those elephants are "copper-lipped, palated, and mouthed" whose lips, palates, and mouths are copper-colored or reddish. "Lips" refers to the lower lip; "palate" to the roof of the mouth; "mouth" to the face. "Sparrow-eyed" means their eyes are equal to the eyes of a <term>Kalavinka</term> <note>the common house sparrow</note>. "Smooth, high-tipped tusks" means their tusks are glossy and have high or elevated tips. "Broad and long faces" means their faces are wide and elongated. "Backbones curved like a bow, elevated, long, hidden, and well-set" means the spine is gradually elevated like a bow...

## In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 66]

Those whose backbones <note>original: "vamsa"</note> are long, hidden, well-knit at the joints, and not overly protruding are considered excellent. Those whose humps <note>the cranial bosses or "kumbhas"</note> are like the shell of a tortoise—raised in the middle—and covered with thin, sparse hair where only a single hair grows from each pore, such elephants are auspicious.

**Regarding wide ears and other features:** The ears, the jaws, the navel <note>the middle part of the body</note>, the forehead, and the private parts—these should all be wide. Furthermore, they should possess twenty or eighteen nails <note>original: "dvi-nava-vimshati"</note> that are raised like the back of a tortoise. As the sage Parashara says:

> "Elephants with twenty, eighteen, or ten stable nails that are shaped like a tortoise's shell are honored; so too are those whose feet are free from hair and dirt."

Those whose trunks <note>original: "kara"</note> are marked by three longitudinal lines and are perfectly circular, who have beautiful body hair, and whose ichor <note>rutting secretion</note> and breath from the tip of the trunk <note>original: "pushkara-maruta"</note> are fragrant—these elephants are auspicious. ||6-7||

->The author further says:<-

> "Elephants with long finger-like muscles at the trunk-tip, red trunk-tips, and a roar like the sound of a water-laden rain cloud, with large, long, and rounded necks, are the auspicious elephants of a King." ||8||

The muscular tips of the elephants' trunks are referred to here as "fingers." The entire tip of the trunk is called the *pushkara* <term>Pushkara: the sensitive tip of an elephant's trunk, often compared to a lotus</term>. Those who have long "fingers" and red trunk-tips, and whose trumpeting <note>original: "brimhana"</note> sounds like the deep rumble of a thundercloud, and who possess large, long, and circular necks—such elephants are beneficial for a ruler. ||8||

->Now he describes elephants with inauspicious signs:<-

> "Those without rutting secretions, those with excessive or missing nails or limbs, those that are hunchbacked, dwarfed, or have tusks like a ram's horns; those with visible testicles or lacking a trunk-tip; those with dark-brown, blue, variegated, or black palates; ||9||
> those with very small mouths, those without tusks <note>original: "matkuna"</note>, those that are impotent, or a female elephant possessing male characteristics, or a pregnant elephant—the King should send these away to a foreign land, for they yield very terrible results." ||10||

Those elephants that are "without rut" <note>original: "nirmada"</note>—meaning they never enter the state of musth—should be rejected. So too those with "excessive or missing nails or limbs"—meaning nails fewer than eighteen or more than twenty. The deficiency or excess of limbs should be understood accordingly. Furthermore, regarding the "hunchbacked" elephant, its characteristics are as follows—

# Chapter 66: Characteristics of Elephants

->The elephant with a narrow chest and hips, a high-arched middle back,<-
->and a sunken navel is called a <term>Kubja</term> (hunchback); he is the lowest of elephants.<-

Likewise, the characteristics of the <term>Vamanaka</term> (dwarf) are as follows:

->The elephant that lacks proper girth and length and is excessively short<-
->is known as a Dwarf; he brings a loss of reputation to his owner.<-

Similarly, there is the <term>Mesha-vishana</term> (ram-horned). This refers to an elephant whose tusks resemble the horns of a ram or goat. As it is said:

->The word 'Vishana' is used for a horn, and 'Vishana' is also used for a tusk.<-

These types—the hunchback, the dwarf, and the ram-horned—as well as those whose testicles are visible <note>literally: "visible in the scrotal sac"</note>, and those lacking a <term>Pushkara</term> <note>the tip of the trunk, shaped like a lotus</note>. Also, those whose palates are dusky, blue, variegated (a mixture of white and black), or entirely black. ||9||

Furthermore, those with very small tusks or facial hair; and the <term>Matkuna</term>, which is an elephant born without tusks. Its characteristics are:

->Even if possessed of all other good qualities, if he is devoid of tusks,<-
->he is called a Matkuna; he is a killer of life <note>or a bringer of death to his side</note> in battle.<-

And the <term>Shandha</term> (eunuch-like elephant), whose characteristics are:

->The elephant whose feet strike or rub against each other while walking<-
->is called a Shandha; he is not honored by experts of signs for travel or war.<-

And also:

->The elephant whose distance between the breasts is excessively wide<-
->is designated as 'Vikata' (deformed); he is a miserable and censured elephant.<-

Elephants of these kinds should be sent away by the King to a foreign land. Likewise, a female elephant that possesses the physical traits of a male <note>such as thick tusks or being in a state of rut</note>, or a pregnant elephant residing in the kingdom, should be sent to another country by the King. This is because such elephants produce "extremely universal" <note>Ativishvarupa: here meaning highly varied or unpredictable</note> evil results. ||10||

## Now, the Examination of Human Characteristics is Explained.

->First, the author provides a summary of the subject matter to be discussed:<-

> Height, weight, gait, compactness, vital essence, color,
> Gloss, voice, <term>prakriti</term><note>Innate constitution or temperament</note>, character, and lineage;
> After duly observing the physique and cleanliness, a skilled
> Expert in <term>Samudra</term><note>The science of physiognomy, named after the sage Samudra</note> speaks of the past or the future. ||1||

The expert considers height, weight, gait, compactness, vital essence, color, gloss, voice, constitution, and character—this constitutes the list beginning with height and weight. Not only these, but also lineage, the physique (the "field"), and cleanliness. First, "duly"—meaning according to established rules—a "skilled" or educated person, having "observed"—meaning examined and reflected. Who is this? The "Expert in Samudra." <term>Samudra</term> refers to the characteristics of humans as proclaimed in the Samudra Shastra. One who "knows" this is an expert, and he "speaks" or narrates. He speaks of the "past"—the expired results of good or bad fortune—and not only that, but the "future" as well.

Regarding this, some believe that the author has explained "character" (<term>sattva</term>) as a synonym for "constitution" (<term>prakriti</term>). <margin>As stated in verse 114 of this same chapter: "Thus the constitution of men is described, which those learned in signs call character."</margin> Therefore, they argue the word "character" (<term>sattva</term>) is redundant here. 

It is replied: It is not redundant. "Character" (<term>sattva</term>) is a quality of the mind. When it is present, no fear arises from any source, nor does despondency occur in any situation. As the experts say:

> Though he dwells alone in the forest, lacks the marks of royalty, and is ignorant of political science,
> Because of his lofty character, the Lion is addressed with the title of King.

Furthermore, the author has shown "character" to be something distinct in the section on the Five Great Men: <note>original: "taddhātu-mahābhūta-prakṛti-dyuti-varṇa-sattva-rūpaiḥ"</note> "By their elements, great components, constitution, luster, color, character, and form." Also: "Character is derived from the Sun," and "From Mars comes character, from Jupiter comes weightiness, and from Mercury comes intelligence." Since this has been stated, the word "character" is not redundant. 

Others read the verse differently: "Constitutions, and then the lineage." However, "constitutions" (<term>prakritayah</term>) does not fit the grammatical structure here. Since the verb "observing" governs the compound from "height" to "constitution" as an object, the word should be in the accusative case. Furthermore, the word "character" (<term>sattva</term>) would then be omitted from the summary. This is thus clarified.

# Regarding <term>Varna</term> (Complexion/Color)—

> 'The feet along with the ankles are declared the first region; the shanks with the knees are the second.
> The genitals, thighs, and scrotum are the third; the navel and the waist are called the fourth.'

The abdomen is called the fifth zone, the heart the sixth, followed by the chest and breasts. Then the shoulders and collarbones are called the seventh, and the lips and neck the eighth. The eyes along with the eyebrows are the ninth, and the forehead and head are the tenth. These are the ten regions of the body.

Regarding **Luster** (Mṛjā)—this luster is composed of the five great elements <note>The *Pancha Mahabhuta*: earth, water, fire, air, and ether</note>.
<insert>1</insert> The shadow and luster reveal good and bad results; they should be observed in humans, animals, and birds by those skilled in the science of characteristics. They manifest the qualities of inner energy externally, like the light of a lamp placed inside a crystal vessel.
Likewise, the sage Rishiputra has described six types of shadows/radiance produced by the planets:
"That which is shadow is indeed radiance; it is proclaimed to be of six kinds: clear, oily (glossy), pleasing, lovely, bright, and illuminating." (1)

Here, the teachers will describe the characteristics starting from the feet up to the hair of the head. First, he describes the characteristics of the feet:

->The feet of a lord of men are sweatless, with soft soles,<-
->having the hue of the interior of a lotus,<-
->with toes closely set, beautiful copper-colored nails, and fine heels.<-
->They are warm, free of visible veins, with well-concealed ankles,<-
->and are arched like the back of a tortoise. (2)<-

Such are the feet of a "lord of men," meaning a king. Of what nature? **Sweatless**: devoid of perspiration. **Soft soles**: having soles endowed with softness. **Lotus-hued**: having a glow like the interior of a lotus flower. **Closely set toes**: having toes that are thick and tightly packed together. **Beautiful copper nails**: having nails that are radiant and copper-red in color. Some read this as <insert>2</insert> "beautiful sides and nails," meaning the sides of the feet are attractive. **Fine heels**: having beautiful heels. By the word "heel" (*pārṣṇī*), the back part of the foot is meant. **Warm**: endowed with warmth. **Free of veins**: devoid of visible veins. **Well-concealed ankles**: having ankles that are sunken, hidden, and not protruding. **Tortoise-arched**: shaped like the back of a tortoise. Such are the feet of a lord of men—a lord or master of human beings. As the authority Samudra says:

> With feet that are even, very glossy, warm, closely set, and very beautiful,
> elevated and free from sweat and veins, one becomes a ruler.

1. This refers to verse 89 of this same chapter.
2. An alternative reading is "beautiful sides and nails."

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 67]

And so says Garga <note>An ancient sage and authority on astrology and omens</note>:

->Those with the soles of their feet resembling the color of a red lotus or water lily,<-
->or like the color of fresh blood, are to be known as kings or others who enjoy happiness. || 2 ||<-

Now, in this same context, the author describes inauspicious signs:

->**Feet shaped like a winnowing basket, dry and rough, with pale nails, crooked, and covered in prominent veins;**<-
->**shriveled, with widely spaced toes—such feet bestow poverty and misery.**<-
->**Feet that are raised in the middle lead to constant wandering; those the color of astringent decoction <note>a brownish-red hue</note> cause the end of one's lineage.**<-
->**Feet with the luster of burnt earth indicate a murderer of a Brahmin; yellow feet indicate one who lusts after forbidden women. || 3 ||**<-

Such are the types of feet. "Shaped like a winnowing basket" means wide at the front. "Dry and rough" means lacking in oiliness or smoothness. "With pale nails" refers to those whose nails have a white or faded appearance. "Crooked" means indistinct or overly long. "Covered in prominent veins" means having many visible veins. "Shriveled" means lacking in flesh. "With widely spaced toes" means the toes or branches of the feet are separated from one another. Such feet grant poverty and sorrow. And so says Samudra <note>The traditional authority on Samudrika Shastra, the science of body marks</note>:

>Those with feet shaped like winnowing baskets, or those that are broken, crooked, shriveled, and covered in veins,
>or sweaty, pale, and rough, are destined for great misery.

Regarding "raised in the middle" <term>utkaṭakau: a high arch or bulging center</term>: this refers to feet that are elevated in the center and pale in appearance. These people are devoted to "the path," meaning they are always traveling. Likewise, those with feet the color of "astringent decoction" (dark reddish-brown) bring about the "severing of the lineage," or the destruction of the family. Those whose soles have a luster like "burnt earth" (dull, baked clay) are "Brahmin-killers" <note>This likely refers to a sinful or outcast nature in a social context</note>. "Yellow" feet belong to those who are "attached to forbidden women," meaning they are prone to illicit lust. And so says Samudra:

>Those with raised feet are devoted to the road; those with astringent-colored feet destroy their family.
>Those with the color of burnt earth are Brahmin-killers; yellow feet lead to forbidden unions. || 3 ||

Now, he describes the characteristics of the shanks, thighs, and knees:

->**Those with shanks that have very sparse, fine hair and are well-rounded,**<-
->**and with excellent thighs resembling the trunk of an elephant,**<-
->**and with well-fleshed, even knees, become kings.**<-
->**Those with shanks like those of a dog or a jackal are destitute of wealth. || 4 ||**<-

"With very sparse" means not thick; "fine hair" means thin hair. Those whose shanks are "well-rounded" or perfectly circular. Also, those characterized by "excellent thighs" which are "like the trunk of an elephant" <note>a classic poetic comparison for strong, tapering limbs</note>. Those whose knees are "well-fleshed" (muscular) and "even" (not protruding or irregular). These are "kings." Those with shanks like "dogs or jackals" <note>meaning thin, bony, or hairy in an animalistic way</note>—

It cites ancient authorities like Garga and Samudra to validate these omens.</summary>

# Chapter 67: The Chapter on the Characteristics of Men

**The Shanks:** Those whose shanks <note>the part of the leg between the knee and ankle</note> resemble those of dogs or jackals are destitute and poor.
As stated by Samudra <note>a legendary sage credited with the foundational knowledge of palmistry and physiognomy</note>:

->One should predict sovereignty from well-rounded shanks.<-
->Those with jackal-like shanks meet a sorrowful end; those with dog-like shanks are perpetual wanderers.<-

**Now he describes the characteristics of the hair on the shanks—**

->A single hair in each pore belongs to kings;<-
->Two hairs per pore are known to belong to scholars and Vedic priests.<-
->With three or more, men are penniless and partakers of misery;<-
->The hair on the head is likewise condemned or praised in this same manner.<-

There should be one single hair in each pore for kings. Two hairs in each pore belong to scholars (the learned) and *Shrotriyas* <note>term: Shrotriya; a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and follows their rules</note>. With three or more hairs—three or four—in a single pore, men become penniless, poor, and partakers of sorrow. In this same way, the hair on the head is either condemned (considered unlucky) or praised (considered auspicious). As it is said:

->Those with excessively hairy shanks are partakers of sorrow and poverty.<-
->A man with one hair per pore becomes a king; with two hairs, he attains great fame.<-
->A man with three hairs or many hairs per pore is devoid of good fortune.<-

**Now he describes the characteristics of the knees—**

->One with fleshless knees dies in a foreign land;<-
->Small knees bring good fortune, while distorted knees bring poverty.<-
->Men are conquered by women if the knees are sunken;<-
->Fleshy knees bring kingship, and large knees bring long life.<-

He whose knees are fleshless (lacking muscle and fat) dies while traveling or in a foreign land. Good fortune comes from small or slender knees. Those with distorted or excessively wide knees are destitute and poor. With sunken or hollowed knees, men are "conquered by women" <note>meaning they are henpecked or overly subservient to their wives</note>. With fleshy knees, one attains kingship. With large or thick knees, one's life span is long. As Samudra says:

->He whose knees are fleshless dies while on a journey.<-
->Good fortune comes from small knees, and poverty from distorted ones.<-
->One is conquered by women if the knees are sunken; with fleshy knees, one is a lord of men.<-
->With very thick knees, one lives for a long time endowed with sovereignty.<-

<summary>This page details the physiognomic predictions based on a man's shanks, the density of body hair per pore, and the shape of the knees, linking physical traits to wealth, status, and longevity.</summary>

### Now he describes the characteristics of the penis—

**If the penis is small, one is wealthy but childless; if it is very thick, one is devoid of wealth.**
**If it is bent to the left, one lacks sons and money; if bent otherwise <note>to the right</note>, one has sons.**
**If it is bent downwards, there is poverty; if covered in veins, there are few children.**
**If it has thick knots <note>prominent joints or glands</note>, one is happy; if it is soft, it brings death through urinary diseases and similar ailments. ||7||**

If the penis is small, the man becomes wealthy (possessing riches) but childless (devoid of offspring). If the penis is excessively thick, he becomes devoid of wealth (poor). If the penis is bent toward the left side, he is devoid of sons and wealth. If it is bent otherwise—meaning bent to the right—he possesses sons. If the penis is bent in the downward part, there is poverty (lack of wealth). If it is covered in many veins, he has few children. If it is joined with thick knots, he becomes happy. A soft penis brings an end to a man through urinary disorders <term>Prameha: a group of urinary ailments including diabetes</term>, jaundice, difficulty in urination, or secret diseases. This means he dies. ||7||

### Here he describes other characteristics—

**Those with a penis hidden in a sheath are kings; those with long or broken ones are devoid of wealth.**
**Those with straight, round, and lightly veined organs are wealthy. ||8||**

Those whose organs are hidden or covered by a sheath <note>original: "kosha," referring to the prepuce or a retracted state</note> like a bellows become kings. Those with long or "broken" <note>cracked or irregular</note> organs are devoid of wealth (poor). "Straight and round organs": those whose organ is straight (clear) and round (well-shaped). Likewise, those with "lightly veined organs"—those whose organ has small or few veins—are wealthy. And so says the Sage Samudra:

> The man whose organ turns to the right shall have sons.
> If it turns to the left, many daughters are born.
> With thick, veined, and hard organs, a man is a vessel of poverty.
> With straight and round organs, men are partakers of happiness.
> He whose organ touches the ground while he is sitting on his feet <note>squatting</note>,
> That man is to be known as miserable and a vessel of poverty.
> With an organ joined with thick knots, a man becomes exceedingly happy.
> With a soft organ, a mortal dies, afflicted by painful diseases. ||8||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the testicles—

**One with a single testicle dies by water; with uneven ones, one is fickle with women; with even ones, a king.**
**With uplifted testicles, one has a short life; for one with hanging testicles, the life span is a hundred years. ||9||**

<header>Chapter 67] Chapter on the Characteristics of Men</header>

A man with a single testicle <note>original: "ekavrishana"</note> meets his end by water—he dies in the midst of water. With uneven or unequal testicles, he is fickle toward women, meaning he is excessively lustful. With even and equal testicles, he becomes a lord of the earth, a king. If they are drawn upward or tightly attached, he is short-lived, having a brief lifespan. He whose testicles are pendulous <note>hanging low</note> lives for a hundred years; his life spans a full century. And so says the Sage Samudra <note>The traditional mythical author of the science of body marks, Samudrika Shastra</note>:

->One with a single testicle dies by water; with uneven ones, he is fickle with women.<-
->One with equal testicles is a leader of men; with attached ones, he is short-lived.<-
->A man with pendulous testicles lives for a hundred years. Thus it is said. || 9 ||<-

Now, he describes the characteristics of the glans <term>Mani: literally "the jewel," referring here to the glans penis</term> and the flow of urine:

->Those with red-hued glans are wealthy; those with pale or dirty-colored ones are destitute.<-
->Those whose urine makes a sound are happy; those with silent streams are penniless. || 10 ||<-
->With two, three, or four streams of urine that turn in a clockwise circle,<-
->Men are known as lords of the earth; those with scattered urine are devoid of wealth. || 11 ||<-
->A single stream of urine that is curved grants beauty but does not grant sons.<-
->Those with smooth, raised, and even glans enjoy wealth, women, and gems. || 12 ||<-
->With a glans that is depressed in the middle, men become fathers of daughters and are poor.<-
->Those with a glans raised in the middle and not overly prominent are wealthy and possess many cattle. || 13 ||<-

Regarding "Those with red-hued glans are wealthy": The tip of the male organ is called the "jewel" <note>Mani</note>. Those with red or blood-colored tips become powerful lords. Those with pale, whitish, or "dirty" (blackish) colors are destitute and without wealth. Those whose urine is accompanied by sound are happy. Those whose urinary streams are silent or without sound are penniless.

Regarding "With two, three, or four streams": With two, three, or four streams of urine that are "turned in a clockwise circle"—meaning the urine flows in a rightward spiral—men are to be known as lords of the earth, or kings. Those whose urine is "scattered" or dispersed in various directions are without wealth.

Regarding "A single stream": A single stream of urine that is "curved" or spiraled grants "beauty"—it bestows a handsome appearance. But it "does not grant sons"—it does not provide male offspring. <insert>Some read the text as "grants sons of primary beauty," meaning it gives sons of excellent appearance.</insert> Those with "smooth, raised, and even" tips—meaning they are oily/glossy, elevated, and symmetrical—are the enjoyers of wealth, women, and precious gems.

# 742
## In the Brhat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 67]

Those whose <term>pearls</term> <note>original: "manayo"; here referring to the glans penis</note> are high, even, and symmetrical are the enjoyers and masters of wealth, riches, women, and gems.

Regarding the "pearls": Those with pearls that are sunken in the middle part become fathers of daughters and are destitute and poor. Those with pearls that are raised in the middle part possess many animals and become owners of many four-legged beasts. Those with pearls that are excessively thick or prominent do not become wealthy or powerful. And so it is said:

->The man whose pearl is reddish in shape and shines evenly in the middle,<-
->he is to be known as a king, according to the words of Samudra.<-
->With pearls that are full like silver, shining like pearls,<-
->and smooth like coral, one becomes a king.<-
->With pale, dirty, rough, dark, or small pearls, one is poor.<-
->If the stream of urine falls from the body turning to the right,<-
->he is to be known as a king, according to the words of Samudra.<-
->If the urine falls in two streams, is smooth, and without sound,<-
->he is to be known as a man of enjoyment and rich in cattle; of this there is no doubt.<-
->If it has many streams, is rough, and makes a sound, he is the lowest of men.<-
Thus ends verses 10-13.

**Now he describes the characteristics of the bladder, semen, and sexual intercourse—**

->Those with a withered bladder-head are to be known as devoid of wealth and unfortunate.<-
->Those whose semen has a fragrance like flowers are to be known as kings. (14)<-
->If it smells like honey, he has much wealth; if it smells like fish, he has many children.<-
->One with thin semen produces daughters; one whose semen smells like meat is a great enjoyer. (15)<-
->If the semen smells like wine, he is a performer of sacrifices; if it smells like potash, he is poor.<-
->One who completes the sexual act quickly is long-lived; otherwise, he is short-lived. (16)<-

Regarding "withered": <term>The bladder is the space between the navel and the penis.</term> Those whose bladder-head is withered or fleshless are to be known as wealthless, poor, and unfortunate (unpopular among people). By implication, those with full bladder-heads are fortunate. And so it is said:

->A wide, fleshy, and smooth bladder is praised for men.<-
->A fleshless, harsh, and rough one is remembered to bring misery and poverty.<-
->He whose bladder resembles that of a jackal, a donkey, a camel, or a buffalo,<-
->that man will be eternally miserable and devoid of wealth.<-

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Men

Those whose semen has a scent like flowers <note>original: "kusuma-samam" or "pushpa-tulya"</note> should be understood as rulers of the earth or kings.

Those whose semen smells like honey <note>original: "madhu" or "mākshika"</note> possess great wealth and abundant riches. If the scent is like fish, they will have many offspring, such as sons. One with thin or watery semen <term>tanu-shukra: semen lacking density</term> is poor and becomes a "generator of women," meaning a father of only daughters. If the scent is like meat, he becomes a great enjoyer of life's pleasures.

If the semen smells like wine <note>original: "madira"</note>, he becomes a performer of sacrifices <term>yajvā: one who regularly performs Vedic rituals</term>. If the semen smells like potash or alkaline substances <note>original: "kshāra"</note>, he becomes destitute and without means. As it is said:

| Scent of Flowers | Becomes a King | Great Wealth | Scent of Honey |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Scent of Fish | Possesses Sons | Daughters | Thin Semen |
| Scent of Meat | Great Enjoyer | Performer of Sacrifices | Scent of Wine |
| Scent of Potash | These Men | Are Known | As Destitute |

One who is quick to reach completion during sexual intercourse <note>original: "maithuna-gamana-shīla"</note> is long-lived. Conversely, a man who takes a long time to reach completion during intercourse will have a short lifespan. One who is a "long-time traveler" in intercourse shall be short-lived. ||14-16||

### Now, the characteristics of the buttocks are described:

> One with very large buttocks is destitute; one with fleshy buttocks is endowed with happiness.
> One with "one-and-a-half" buttocks <note>likely referring to an asymmetrical or uneven appearance</note> meets his end by a tiger; one with buttocks like a frog is a lord of men. ||17||

He whose buttocks are excessively large <note>original: "ati-sthūla"</note> becomes destitute and poor. He whose buttocks are well-fleshed and firm becomes endowed with happiness. He who has "one-and-a-half" buttocks <insert>unevenly developed</insert> meets his end by a tiger; that animal will kill him. He whose buttocks resemble those of a frog <note>original: "maṇḍūka"</note> becomes a lord of men, a king. As it is said:

->The man whose buttocks are very large becomes poor.<-
->One with fleshy buttocks is happy; one with frog-like buttocks is a lord of men.<-
->The man with "one-and-a-half" buttocks is said to meet his end by a tiger. Thus it is said. ||17||<-

One whose waist resembles that of a lion becomes a lord of men—a king. One whose waist resembles that of a monkey or a <term>karabha</term> <note>a young camel or elephant</note> is abandoned by wealth and riches. Those with an even belly—where the stomach is neither sunken nor protruding—are endowed with enjoyments. Those whose bellies resemble a <term>ghata</term> <note>a water pot</note> or a <term>pithara</term> <note>a specific type of cooking pot or pan</note> are destitute and poor. As it is said:

> One whose waist is like a lion's is a king, without a doubt.
> One whose waist is like that of a dog, jackal, donkey, or camel is poor.
> Those with even bellies possess enjoyments; those with uneven ones are remembered as poor. || 18 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the flanks, the belly, and the sides:

**Those with full flanks are wealthy; those with sunken or crooked flanks are devoid of enjoyments.**
**Those with even sides of the abdomen are rich in enjoyments; those with sunken sides are deprived of them. || 19 ||**
**Those with raised sides of the abdomen are lords of the earth (kings); those with uneven sides are wicked men.**
**Those with bellies like a serpent are poor and also great eaters (gluttonous). || 20 ||**

The term "flank" (<term>pārśva</term>) refers to the region four finger-breadths above the waist. Those whose flanks are "not deficient"—meaning full and fleshy—are wealthy and powerful. Those with sunken, crooked, or elongated flanks are devoid of enjoyments. The word <term>kukṣa</term> refers to the middle part of the abdomen. Those with even sides of the abdomen possess enjoyments, while those with sunken sides are deprived of them.

Those with raised or high abdominal sides are kings. Those men with uneven or asymmetrical sides are "crooked"—meaning they are difficult or harsh. Those whose bellies are very long like a serpent's are destitute and consume vast amounts of food. As it is said:

> Men with flanks covered in flesh are remembered as wealthy.
> With sunken, crooked, or uneven flanks, men are excluded from enjoyments.
> Even sides bring enjoyment; sunken sides lack it.
> Kings have raised sides; those with uneven sides have evil intentions.
> Men with serpent-like bellies are remembered as penniless and gluttonous. || 19-20 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the navel:

**With navels that are circular, raised, deep, and wide, men are happy.**
**A small navel, or one that is invisible or shallow, brings distress. || 21 ||**
**A navel situated amidst skin-folds or one that is uneven causes pain from colic and poverty.**
**A navel that whorls to the left produces deceit; one that whorls to the right produces intelligence. || 22 ||**

->A navel extended at the sides indicates long life; extended upwards, a lord; and downwards, one rich in cattle.<-
->A navel resembling the pericarp <note>the central seed-bearing part</note> of a lotus makes one a lord of men. ||23||<-

Men with circular, well-rounded, elevated, and wide navels are happy. A small, inconspicuous, or deep but narrow navel brings distress and suffering.

Regarding the navel situated within the skin-folds: if the navel is hidden within the folds or is uneven, it causes pain from colic <note>original: "shula"</note>; such a person may die from a ruptured body caused by that pain. It also brings poverty. A navel that whorls to the left <note>counter-clockwise</note> indicates deceitfulness. A deceitful person is one who avoids helping others. As it is said:

> ->He who is seen to be intent on improper acts in speech and mind,<-
> ->and whose actions are contrary to his words, is called deceitful <unclear>by the virtuous</unclear>.<-

A navel that whorls to the right <note>clockwise</note> produces great intelligence. Here, intelligence is intended to mean the possession of the qualities of the mind. As it is said:

> ->The desire to listen, hearing, comprehension, retention,<-
> ->reasoning, negative argumentation, knowledge of meaning, and knowledge of the truth are the qualities of the intellect.<-

A navel extended at the sides makes one long-lived. Extended upwards, it makes one a prosperous lord. Extended downwards, it brings an abundance of cattle. A navel that resembles the pericarp of a lotus <note>original: "shatapatra-karnika"</note>—meaning it is raised in the center like the middle of a lotus—makes one a ruler of men. As it is said:

> ->If the navel is circular, large, and very high, one is a lord of men;<-
> ->if small to the sight and deep, the navel brings distress.<-
> ->That which is situated within the folds causes death by colic;<-
> ->a leftward whorl brings deceit, and a rightward whorl brings wisdom.<-
> ->Extended at the sides, it gives long life; extended upwards, wealth;<-
> ->downwards, it provides many cattle and the enjoyment of the navel's fruits.<-
> ->A navel equal to the pericarp of a lotus makes one a ruler of men. ||21-23||<-

### Now he describes the characteristics of the skin-folds (valis) on the abdomen —

->One, two, three, or four folds indicate, respectively: death by a weapon, an enjoyer of women, a teacher, and one with many sons. One with no folds is a king. ||24||<-

<page-num>746.</page-num>
->On the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 67]<-

**Men with uneven skin-folds on the abdomen are sinners who approach forbidden women.**
**Those with straight folds are enjoyers of happiness and loathe the wives of others. ||25||**

Regarding the phrase "death by weapon": From the folds <note>Sanskrit: *vali*; these refer to the natural creases or folds of skin on the abdomen</note> located in the middle of the stomach, starting from one and increasing in sequence, results such as death by weapon occur. Specifically: he who has one fold on his stomach dies by a weapon. With two folds, one enjoys many women. With three, one becomes a teacher <note>Sanskrit: *acharya*; a preceptor or spiritual instructor</note>. With four, one has many sons. One who is without any folds <note>Sanskrit: *avali*</note> should be known as a king.

Those men who have uneven folds—meaning some are long and some are short—are sinners who frequent women they should not approach. Those who have straight, clear folds are possessors of happiness and are averse to the wives of others. As it is said:

> One fold signifies death by weapon; two folds are remembered for the enjoyment of women.
> With three, they say one is a teacher; with four, one has many offspring.
> One without folds is declared a king, a performer of sacrifices devoted to charity.
> Those in whom the folds are uneven approach forbidden women.
> Those in whom the folds are straight are men who share in happiness. ||24-25||

### Now, the characteristics of the sides of the torso are described:

**With fleshy and soft sides, and hair that curls to the right, men become kings.**
**With the opposite characteristics, they are penniless, devoid of happiness, and servants to others. ||26||**

The four-finger-width area above the hips is called the "side" <note>Sanskrit: *parshva*</note>. With sides that are fleshy (thick), soft (tender), and with hair that grows in a clockwise <note>Sanskrit: *pradakshina*; right-turning, considered auspicious</note> curl, men become kings. With the opposite—thin, rough, and with counter-clockwise hair—they are penniless, lacking in comforts, and become the messengers or laborers of others. As it is said:

> With fleshy, soft sides and hair curling to the right,
> Men are known as lords of the earth; with the opposite, they are deeply miserable. ||26||

### Now, the characteristics of the nipples are described:

**Those with nipples that are not raised are fortunate; the penniless have uneven and long ones.**
**With nipples that are thick, well-formed, or sunken, men are kings and happy. ||27||**

<header>Chapter 67: The Chapter on Male Characteristics</header>

The <term>nipple</term><note>Sanskrit: chuchuka</note> is the tip of the breast. Men with nipples that are not upturned become fortunate. Those with uneven, unequal, or overly long nipples become destitute and poor. Those with nipples that are thick, firm, well-formed, fleshy, and deep-set (not protruding) become lords of the earth—kings—and are possessors of happiness.
As it is said:

->With nipples that are not upturned, men are fortunate and share in happiness.<-
->The poor have uneven and long ones; kings have deep-set and fleshy ones. (Verse 27)<-

### Now, the characteristics of the heart (chest area) are described:

**The heart of kings is elevated, broad, non-trembling, and fleshy.**
**The opposite is true for the poor; their chests are covered with coarse hair and are veiny. (Verse 28)**

The heart (chest) of kings is elevated (high), broad (wide), non-trembling (steady), and fleshy. The opposite—sunken, narrow, trembling, and thin—belongs to the poor. Likewise, a chest covered in coarse hair (rough and thick hair) and being "veiny" (covered in a network of visible veins) also belongs to the poor.
As it is said:

->The heart of kings is recorded as steady, broad, and high.<-
->The opposite, being veiny and hairy, belongs to those who partake in sorrow. (Verse 28)<-

### Now, the characteristics of the chest (thorax) are described:

**Those with an even chest possess wealth; with thick chests, they are heroes; with thin chests, they are paupers.**
**Those whose chests are uneven are penniless and meet their end by the sword. (Verse 29)**

Those whose chest <note>Sanskrit: vakshas</note> is even—neither sunken nor too high—are wealthy. With thick, fleshy, and firm chests, men become heroes. With thin chests (having little flesh), they are paupers, ineffective, and lacking in manly effort. Those whose chests are uneven (asymmetrical) are penniless and meet a "sword-death" <note>Sanskrit: shastranidhana; meaning they die in battle or by violence</note>.
As it is said:

->One with an even chest shall be wealthy; with long (broad) ones, they are heroes endowed with riches.<-
->With small chests, they are deficient and miserable; with uneven ones, they die by the sword. (Verse 29)<-

### Now, the characteristics of the collarbones are described:

**With uneven collarbones, one is erratic; with bony joints bound together, one is devoid of wealth.**
**One with elevated collarbones is an enjoyer of pleasures; with sunken ones, penniless; and with thick ones, wealthy. (Verse 30)**

<margin>Collarbones</margin>
The <term>Jatru</term><note>The collarbone or the junction where the arms meet the neck.</note> is the joint of the armpits. One with uneven or asymmetrical collarbones becomes cruel. One whose collarbones are tightly bound or knotted with bony joints becomes destitute and devoid of wealth. He whose collarbones are raised or high becomes a <term>Bhogi</term><note>One who enjoys worldly pleasures and luxuries</note> and is fortunate. With sunken collarbones, one becomes penniless and poor. With fleshy or stout collarbones, one becomes wealthy. As it is said:

->Cruel are those with uneven collarbones; poor are those with knotted joints.<-
->One with raised collarbones is a seeker of pleasure; with sunken ones, penniless; otherwise, wealthy. || 30 ||<-

<margin>Neck</margin>
### Now he describes the characteristics of the neck and back —

**One with a flat neck is penniless; so is he whose neck is withered and veiny.**
**One with a neck like a buffalo is brave; one with a neck like a bull dies by the sword. || 31 ||**
**One with a shell-like neck is a king; one with a long, dangling throat is a glutton.**
**The back of the wealthy is unbroken and hairless; the opposite is inauspicious. || 32 ||**

He whose neck is flat—meaning compressed or indistinct—becomes penniless. He whose neck is withered (fleshless) and veiny (covered in a network of veins) is likewise destitute. One with a neck resembling a buffalo's is a hero. One with a neck like a bull—shoulders like a breeding bull—meets his end by a weapon (dies in battle).

He who has three folds on his neck is called <term>Kambu-griva</term><note>Literally "conch-necked," referring to the three lines on a conch shell, considered a mark of great beauty and status.</note>. As it is said:

> A neck marked with three folds is designated as a conch-neck.

And he who has a conch-neck becomes a king. One with a "dangling throat"—meaning an elongated or protruding neck—becomes a glutton, one who does not possess the habit of accumulating wealth. Furthermore:

->The man whose neck is round is remembered as wealthy.<-
->Those men who have conch-necks are kings, without a doubt.<-
->Those men who have long necks are partakers of sorrow.<-
->Those men who have crooked necks are hypocrites and backbiters.<-
->The flat-necked is penniless, as is the withered-necked.<-
->The brave has a buffalo-neck; the bull-shouldered dies by the sword.<-

<margin>Back</margin>
The back of wealthy people is "unbroken" (not cracked or hunched) and hairless (devoid of hair). Anything other than this—a broken or hairy back—is inauspicious and belongs to the poor. As it is said:

->A very smooth, fleshy back, unbroken and hairless,<-
->Is proclaimed for the wealthy; the opposite for the poor. || 31-32 ||<-

<header>Chapter on the Characteristics of Men</header>

### Now he describes the characteristics of the armpits —
**The armpits of wealthy men should be known as sweatless, fleshy, elevated, fragrant, and covered with even hair; those of men devoid of wealth are the opposite. ||33||**

The surface at the base of the arm is called the armpit <term>kakṣā: the axilla or armpit</term>. Armpits that are sweatless (free from perspiration), fleshy (well-muscled), elevated (high), fragrant (having a pleasant scent), even (symmetrical), and covered with hair are to be known as belonging to wealthy men or lords. Those possessing the opposite characteristics—sweaty, lacking flesh, sunken, foul-smelling, uneven, and hairless—belong to those devoid of wealth. And so it is said:

> One should recognize the armpits of the wealthy as sweatless, fleshy, fragrant, and covered with hair; for the poor, it is the opposite. ||33||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the shoulders —
**The shoulders of a poor man are fleshless, covered in hair, broken, and small; those of the happy and powerful are broad, continuous, and well-knit. ||34||**

The shoulders <term>aṃsau: the two shoulders</term> are fleshless (lacking muscle), covered in hair (overgrown), broken (cracked or bony), and small in the case of a poor or destitute man. They are broad, continuous (not bony or protruding), and well-knit (firmly joined) for those who are happy and powerful. And so it is said:

> Those men whose shoulders resemble the trunk of a banana tree or the shoulders of a goat <note>original: "ajaskandhāśca"; this implies a specific sturdy, rounded shape</note> should be known as kings, possessing great treasuries and great strength. Those with shoulders lacking flesh and abundant in hair are proclaimed to be poor. ||34||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the arms —
**The arms of rulers of the earth resemble the trunk of an elephant, are rounded, reach down to the knees, and are symmetrical and fleshy; those of the poor are hairy and short. ||35||**

The arms <term>bāhū: the two arms</term> are like the trunk of an elephant, rounded (well-turned), reaching down to the knees <term>ājānu-avalambinau: "reaching to the knees," a classic mark of a great man or hero</term>, symmetrical, and fleshy (muscular) in the case of kings or lords of the earth. They are to be known as hairy and short in the case of the wealthless. And so it is said:

> A man with constricted or bound-up arms may meet with imprisonment or death. A man with long arms becomes a king, according to the words of Samudra <note>Samudra is the traditional mythical authority on Samudrika Shastra, the science of body marks</note>.

# The Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 67]

->A man with long arms reaching his knees shall attain sovereignty and be endowed with many virtues.<-
->One with short arms will be a servant, performing tasks for others.<-
->Those whose arms turn to the left, those with long arms,<-
->and those with well-rounded, full arms are proclaimed to be kings.<- <note>original: "iti" - marking the end of a quoted traditional verse.</note> || 35 ||

Now, he describes the characteristics of the hands:

->**Long fingers belong to those who live long; well-rounded fingers to the fortunate.**<-
->**Thin fingers belong to the wise; flat fingers to those devoted to serving others.**<- || 36 ||
->**Those with thick fingers are devoid of wealth; those with outward-curving fingers die by the sword.**<-
->**Those with hands like a monkey's are wealthy; those with hands like a tiger's are sinful.**<- || 37 ||

Long fingers—meaning not short—belong to those who are long-lived. Well-rounded—meaning well-formed and distinct—belong to the fortunate, those endowed with good luck. Thin—meaning not thick—belong to the wise, those possessing great intellect. Here, some authorities distinguish between different types of intelligence: *Medha* (retentive memory), *Buddhi* (intellect), and *Prajna* (wisdom). As it has been said:

> *Medha* is the memory of things long past; *Mati* <note>a synonym for Buddhi</note> is the ability to grasp things instantly;
> *Prajna* is described by the steady-minded as the wisdom to discern between good and evil.

Flat or snub-shaped fingers belong to those devoted to the work of others, meaning those in service. || 36 ||

With thick—meaning excessively large—fingers, men are devoid of wealth, or poor. With outward-curving fingers—those bent backward—men meet their "departure by the sword," meaning they die by a weapon. Those with hands resembling a monkey's are wealthy and powerful. Those with hands like a tiger—the predatory animal—are sinful. || 37 ||

He says something further:

->**With hidden, rounded wrist-joints and well-knit articulations, men become kings.**<-
->**With deficient wrists, the hand is lost; with loose or cracking wrists, they are penniless.**<- || 38 ||

By the word "wrist-joint" <term>Manibandha: the point where the hand meets the forearm</term>, the root of the hand is meant. With hidden—meaning not protruding—wrists that are rounded and firm, and with well-knit articulations—meaning the joints are tightly joined—men become kings. With deficient wrists, there is the "cutting of the hand" <note>this may imply physical loss of the hand or a metaphorical loss of power</note>. With loose—meaning flabby—and "noisy" wrists—those that make a cracking sound—men are penniless or poor. || 38 ||

# Chapter 67: The Chapter on the Characteristics of Men

He <note>The author, Varahamihira</note> says something further:

> Men with sunken palms are deprived of ancestral wealth. Those whose palms are level and slightly hollowed in the center are wealthy, and those with raised palms are givers. ||39||
> With uneven palms, men are cruel and destitute; with palms the color of red lac, they are lords. With yellow palms, they pursue forbidden women, and with rough palms, they are penniless. ||40||

Men with a sunken palm are deprived of paternal wealth—that is, they are without inherited riches. Those with "closed-sunken" palms—meaning the palm is even and rounded yet slightly hollowed—are wealthy. Those with "raised palms"—those whose hands are notably elevated or high—are givers, meaning they are of a charitable nature. ||39||

With uneven or irregular palms, men are "uneven"—meaning cruel—and destitute. With palms resembling the color of lac <note>A scarlet resin used as dye</note>—meaning very red—they are lords or wealthy. With yellow palms, they are prone to approaching "unapproachable" women <note>Women forbidden by social or moral codes</note>. With rough palms, they are penniless or poor. ||40||

He says something further:

> Those with nails resembling husks are eunuchs; with flattened or cracked nails, they are abandoned by wealth. With ugly or discolored nails, they are beggars; and with copper-colored nails, they are kings. ||41||

Those whose nails resemble husks—meaning they are rough and covered in crowded lines—are eunuchs. With flattened or cracked (broken) nails, they are devoid of wealth. With "bad nails"—meaning ugly or discolored—they are "seekers of others" <note>original: paratarkuka</note>, meaning they depend on others or look to the faces of others for sustenance. With copper-colored nails, they are kings or commanders of armies. ||41||

He says something further:

> With barley-shaped marks on the thumb, they are rich; with such marks at the base of the thumb, they have sons. Those with long finger-joints are fortunate and long-lived. ||42||

A "barley" <term>Yava: a grain-shaped mark in palmistry</term> is exactly that—a mark shaped like a grain of barley. With such marks located in the middle of the thumb, men are rich. With barley marks born at the base of the thumb, they possess sons. Those with long finger-joints—those whose phalanges are elongated—are fortunate (endowed with good luck) and long-lived. ||42||

He says something further:

> Smooth, deep lines belong to the wealthy; the opposite belongs to the destitute. Those with gaps between their fingers are penniless, while those with closely-set fingers accumulate wealth. ||43||

# [Chapter 67] On the Brihat Samhita with Commentary

<page-num>752</page-num>

Glossy, clear, deep, and profound lines found on the hand belong to the wealthy and to lords. Conversely, lines that are the opposite—lack luster and are shallow—belong to the indigent and those without wealth. Those whose fingers (branches of the hand) are sparse or widely spaced are destitute. Those with closely set fingers are accumulators of wealth and possess a nature for earning money.

## He further says—

->Three lines rising from the wrist and reaching the palm belong to a king.<-
->One whose hand is marked with a pair of fish constantly provides for sacrificial sessions.<-

->Lines shaped like a thunderbolt <note>Sanskrit: *Vajra*</note> belong to the wealthy; those resembling a fish's tail belong to the learned.<-
->Lines resembling a conch, a parasol, a palanquin, an elephant, a horse, or a lotus belong to a king.<-

->With lines resembling a water-pot, a lotus stalk, a banner, or a goad, men become guardians of treasure.<-
->With lines like a rope, they are rich; with those in the form of a swastika, they possess sovereignty.<-

->Lines resembling a discus, a sword, an axe, a javelin, a spear, a bow, or a lance<-
->make one a commander of an army; those shaped like a mortar make one a performer of sacrifices.<-

->With lines resembling a crocodile, a flag, or a storehouse, they are endowed with great wealth;<-
->with those resembling a sacrificial altar, they are performers of the fire-ritual <note>Sanskrit: *Agnihotrin*</note> through the *Brahma-tirtha* <note>The part of the hand under the root of the thumb</note>.<-

->With lines like a pond or a temple, they perform acts of piety; with triangular lines, they are religious.<-
->Lines at the base of the thumb indicate sons; if they are fine/thin, they indicate daughters.<-

->Lines reaching the forefinger indicate a life of a hundred years; with fewer lines, the lifespan is to be estimated accordingly.<-
->Broken lines indicate a fall from a tree; those with too many lines are destitute.<-

**Regarding the three lines:** Three lines rising from the wrist <note>The "bracelet" lines</note> and reaching the palm belong to a king. One whose hand is marked with a pair of fish <note>original: *mina-yuga*</note> constantly provides for sacrificial sessions; the meaning is that he becomes a performer of sacrifices <note>original: *makha-krid-bhavati*</note>.

The thunderbolt <note>Vajra</note> is thin in the middle and wide at both ends; lines of that shape on the palm belong to the wealthy and powerful. Lines resembling a fish's tail belong to the learned; the meaning is that they become possessors of knowledge. The conch is well-known; the parasol is a royal umbrella; the palanquin refers to litters and such; the elephant, the horse, and the lotus—lines resembling these shapes belong to a king.

# Chapter 67: The Chapter on the Characteristics of Men
## Page 753

A **Kalasha** is a water pot; **Mrinala** refers to a lotus stalk, clearly marked with joints in the middle. A **Pataka** is a victory banner, and an **Ankusha** is the well-known elephant goad. Those who possess lines resembling these shapes become **Nidhipala** <note>literally "protectors of treasure"</note>, meaning they are inclined toward establishing and guarding wealth on earth. They are also exceedingly wealthy. Those with lines resembling a **Dama** <note>a cord or rope</note> become masters and lords of wealth. The **Swastika** is a specific auspicious sign; lines in that shape bring sovereignty and power.

The **Chakra** is a discus weapon; the **Asi** is a sword; the **Parashu** is a specific weapon, an axe; the **Tomara** is a well-known javelin; the **Shakti** is a spear; the **Dhanus** is a bow; and the **Kunta** is a specific type of lance. Lines resembling these appearing on the palm make a person a **Chamunatha**, a commander of an army. Lines shaped like an **Ulukhal** <note>a mortar used for grinding</note> make one a **Yajvana**, a performer of sacred sacrifices.

The **Makara** is a sea creature <note>often depicted as a crocodile-fish hybrid</note>. The **Dhvaja** is a flag; it differs from a banner because of its varied cloth patterns. The **Kosthagara** is a storehouse or granary. With lines similar to these, one becomes endowed with great riches and is extremely wealthy. Above the wrist-joint is the **Brahma-tirtha** <note>a sacred zone of the hand</note> at the base of the thumb. If the **Brahma-tirtha** (the area at the root of the thumb) is shaped like a **Vedi** <note>a sacrificial altar</note>, the individuals become **Agnihotris** <note>priests who maintain the sacred fire</note> and performers of sacrifices.

A **Vapi** is a well-known square stepped-well or pond. A **Devakula** is a temple or palace of the gods. By the inclusion of the word "etc.," one should also include shapes like a throne, the *Shrivriksha* <note>auspicious tree</note>, and the *Yupa* <note>sacrificial post</note>. With these, people perform acts of dharma and become very righteous. With triangular lines or those shaped like a **Shringataka** <note>a water chestnut or a place where four roads meet</note>, they likewise perform deeds of merit. As many lines as there are at the base of the thumb, that is the number of children. Among those, the thick lines represent sons, and the fine, thin lines represent daughters.

The **Pradeshini** is the finger next to the thumb <note>the index finger</note>. Due to the use of the plural, three lines should be understood here. Lines reaching the index finger indicate a **Shatayusha**, one who lives for a hundred years. For fewer lines, one must estimate using their own judgment. For instance, lines reaching the middle of the hand might indicate fifty years. In other cases, the lifespan should be calculated by proportion. If the lines are broken in the middle, it signifies a "falling of the tree" <note>a metaphor for a sudden downfall or death</note>. Those who have too many lines or those who have no lines at all (**Arekhina**) become destitute and penniless. As it is said:

-> Those endowed with wrists that are perfectly round and well-concealed, <-
-> firm and silent <note>not cracking or making noise</note>, are proclaimed to be kings. <-
-> One with deficient or scarred hands becomes a vessel of poverty. <-
-> He whose palm is sunken is deprived of paternal wealth. <-
-> But one with a palm that is sunken yet well-enclosed is wealthy and happy. <-
-> Those whose hands are slightly raised or hollowed like a bowl are undoubtedly givers. <-
-> Those with uneven hands are erratic and poor; those with hands red like lac are lords. <-
-> Those with yellow nails and hands are penniless and frequenters of forbidden places. <-

# On the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 67]

Nails that are shaped like a winnowing basket <note>original: "shurpa"; a flat, U-shaped basket used for grain</note> or a pearl oyster shell, or those that are discolored, resemble husks, or are excessively large, are considered ill-omened. Likewise, nails that are cracked or only half-formed are said to belong to those devoid of wealth. Conversely, a man becomes a king <note>original: "parthiva"; a ruler of the earth</note> if his nails are spotless and possess a reddish glow. Those men whose fingers are pale, widely spaced, and dry should be known as vessels of sorrow and poverty.

If a man has a line resembling a fish, the success of his work is guaranteed; such a person should be known as wealthy and blessed with many sons. If a scale <note>original: "tula"; representing balance or commerce</note> or an altar <note>original: "vedi"</note> is visible in the middle of the palm, the success of that man’s trade is beyond doubt. If an altar is found on the palm, especially in the case of a member of the priestly class <note>original: "dvija"; twice-born</note>, he will constantly perform sacrifices <note>original: "yajnyayaji"</note> and possess great wealth.

He in whose hand is seen the symbol of the *Shrivatsa* <note>an auspicious mark associated with Vishnu</note>, a lotus, a thunderbolt, or a fly-whisk, shall become a lord of the earth. Those in whose hands lines resembling a spear, a javelin, a sword, or a bow are seen, are known as commanders of armies. If a tree or a mountain is seen in the middle of the hand, one attains a stable kingdom within the realm without a doubt. If a flag or a horn <margin>The manuscript variant reads "shalam" (a spike or dart) instead of "shringam" (horn).</margin> is situated on the hand, one should know him to be a master of wealth, according to the teachings of Samudra <note>the traditional founder of the science of physiognomy, Samudrika Shastra</note>.

If a barley-corn mark <note>original: "yava"</note> is seen on the thumb of the right hand, one should point him out as a teacher of all branches of knowledge. If a line originating from the base of the little finger goes to the middle of the forefinger, that person shall live for a hundred autumns. The lines at the base of the thumb are declared to be sons; the fine lines are specified as daughters, according to the words of Samudra. If these lines are broken, it indicates the loss of children <note>original: "vriksha-patanam"; literally 'the falling of the tree'</note>; if they are too numerous, the individuals lack authority. A man becomes a performer of sacrifices through the sacred spot <term>tirtha: the base of the thumb is considered a sacred area in palmistry associated with Brahma</term> at the root of the thumb.

<summary>This page details the auspicious and inauspicious marks on the hands and nails, linking specific symbols like the fish, altar, and lotus to wealth, long life, and royal status. It cites the authority of the sage Samudra to explain how lines on the thumb and palm predict children and professional success.</summary>

### Now, he describes the characteristics of the chin, lower lip, and teeth—

> Those with very thin or very long chins are destitute; those with fleshy chins are endowed with wealth. With lower lips resembling the Bimba fruit <note>The Bimba fruit (Coccinia grandis) is known for its bright red color, often used in Sanskrit poetry to describe ideal lips.</note> and which are not crooked, men become kings; with thin lips, they are without means. ||51||
> With upper lips that are cracked, divided, discolored, or rough, they are abandoned by fortune. Smooth, dense teeth with very sharp canines <term>canines: the pointed teeth on either side of the four front teeth</term> that are even are auspicious. ||52||

The chin <term>chibuka: the lower part of the face below the lip</term> is the end of the face. With very thin (fleshless) and very long chins, men are without wealth and poor. With fleshy chins, they are endowed with wealth and are prosperous. With lower lips that are like the Bimba fruit (very red) and not crooked (well-defined), they become kings. With thin, fleshless lower lips, they are penniless.

With upper lips that are cracked (broken), divided (split), discolored (lacking natural color), or rough (lacking moisture/oiliness), men are abandoned by wealth and become poor. The teeth <term>dashana: teeth</term> should be smooth (clean) and dense (closely set). Those who have very sharp canines and whose teeth are all even are auspicious. The canines are the two teeth situated on the sides of the four central teeth. Thus it is said:

> With fleshless and long chins, men are destitute and speak too hastily.
> With fleshy ones, they are endowed with wealth and surrounded by many sons.
> A man with a red lower lip is a lord of men; one with a lotus-like lip is wealthy.
> Those with thick lips have much body hair; those with dry or wasted lips are miserable.
> With red upper lips, men are wealthy and joined with happiness.
> With broken or discolored lips, they are penniless; with rough lips, they are filled with sorrow.
> A king has teeth like jasmine buds <note>original: "kunda-kudmala-sankashaih"</note> arranged like a wall.
> Those with teeth like bears or monkeys are constantly oppressed by hunger.
> Those with teeth like elephants or donkeys <note>This likely refers to the size and strength of the teeth rather than a negative comparison.</note> who have smooth teeth are endowed with good qualities.
> With gaping, uneven, or long teeth, they live a life of misery.
> Those with thirty-two teeth are kings; with thirty-one, they enjoy life's pleasures.
> Men who have thirty teeth are sharers of both happiness and sorrow.
> Men with twenty-nine teeth live a life of suffering.
> Those who have twenty-eight teeth are vessels of extreme misery.
> —Thus [ends the commentary on verses] 51-52.

### Now he describes the characteristics of the tongue and the palate —

**A tongue that is red, long, smooth, and very even <note>1</note> is known to belong to those who enjoy pleasures.**
**A white, black, or rough tongue belongs to those without wealth; the same applies to the palate. || 53 ||**

The tongue (the organ of taste) that is red (blood-colored), long (extended), smooth (thin and pleasant to the touch), and very even (symmetrical) is known to belong to a "Bhogi" <note>one who enjoys life's pleasures and luxuries</note>. Alternatively, there is a reading "of the Bhogis." The meaning is that such a tongue should be understood to belong to those who enjoy wealth. A white (pale) or black (dark) tongue belongs to those without means (the poor). "The same applies to the palate": in the same manner, the palate is to be judged. Just as a red, smooth, and even tongue is auspicious, so too is a palate with those qualities. A white, black, or rough palate is likewise inauspicious.
And so it is said:

> He whose tongue is black or appears dirty,
> That mortal will be a sinner, and his belly will be large.
> Men with white tongues are known to be devoid of purity and good conduct.
> A tongue like a lotus petal, thin, long, and beautiful,
> Neither too thick nor too wide—those men are lords of men (kings).
> If the tongue is depressed in the middle, long, short <note>possibly meaning tapered</note>, and red at the tip,
> That person will be a teacher of all sciences; of this there is no doubt.
> A man with a black palate will be the destroyer of his lineage.
> He whose palate is deformed or cracked—that is not auspicious for him.
> One with a lion-like palate is a king, as is one with an elephant-like palate.
> One with a lotus-like palate becomes a king, while one with a white palate is penniless. || 53 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the mouth —

**A mouth that is placid, well-closed, clean, smooth, and even belongs to kings.**
**The opposite belongs to those who suffer hardships; a very large mouth belongs to the unfortunate. || 54 ||**

The mouth (the face) that is placid (undisturbed), well-closed (well-rounded and not gaping), clean (spotless), smooth (not overly fleshy but well-proportioned), and even (symmetrical) is to be known as belonging to "Bhupas" (kings). The "opposite" refers to the reverse characteristics. A mouth that is not placid, not well-closed, not clean, not smooth, and not even is to be known as belonging to those who "eat toil" (the poor). A "great mouth" (one that is excessively wide) belongs to the "Durbhagas" (the unfortunate or unlovely).
And so it is said:

> He whose mouth is placid, well-closed, and clean,
> That person shall always be a great king; if the opposite, he is penniless. || 54 ||

---

<note>1. An alternative reading is "of the Bhogis" (those who enjoy wealth).</note>

# Now he describes the characteristics of the face —

**A face resembling a woman’s belongs to those without children; a circular face is known to belong to the deceitful.**
**A long face belongs to those without wealth; those with the face of a frightened person are doers of evil deeds. ||55||**
**A square face belongs to rogues; a sunken or crooked face belongs to those without sons.**
**An extremely short face belongs to the miserly; a full and lovely face belongs to those who enjoy life's pleasures. ||56||**

A face <term>vadana; original: "vadanam"</term> resembling a woman's belongs to those who are childless <note>specifically meaning those without sons in this historical context</note>. A circular <term>mandala; original: "mandalam"</term> or perfectly round face is to be understood as belonging to those possessed of a deceitful nature. A deceitful person is one who is averse to helping others. A long face belongs to those without property. Those with a "timid face"—meaning a face like that of a frightened person—are devoted to sinful actions.

A square or four-cornered face belongs to rogues, those skilled in deceiving others. A sunken (depressed) or crooked (unclear) face belongs to those without sons. An extremely small or short face belongs to the miserly. A miser <term>kripana; original: "kripano"</term> is one greedy for wealth or possessing very little. A full, fleshy, and lovely or radiant face belongs to those who are "enjoyers" <note>bhoginam; those who possess wealth and luxury</note>. As it is said elsewhere:

> ..A womanly face belongs to the childless; a circular one to those who serve deceit.
> A long face to the penniless; those with timid faces have evil intentions.
> A square face belongs to rogues; a sunken one is devoid of sons.
> A short face belongs to the miserly, and a flat face to those who live off others.
> That face which is fleshy, glossy, radiant, pleasant to look at,
> Rich in color, and with well-knit joints, belongs to those who constantly share in happiness. ||55-56||

# Now he describes the characteristics of the beard —

**A beard with ends that are not split, which is glossy, soft, and well-inclined, is auspicious.**
**Those with red, harsh, and scanty beards are to be known as thieves. ||57||**

The beard <term>shmashru; original: "shmashru"</term> refers to the facial hair. One with ends that are not split, which is glossy (not dry), soft (tender), and "well-inclined" <note>growing downward neatly</note> is considered auspicious or excellent. Some read the text as "soft and slightly raised." Those with red, harsh (rough), and scanty beards are to be recognized as thieves or robbers. As it is said:

> A glossy beard with unsplit ends and a downward incline is desired.
> With red, scanty, and rough beards, men are remembered as thieves. ||57||

---

1. <note>original: "mṛdusumunnataṃ caiveti pāṭhāntaram"</note> An alternative reading is "soft and slightly raised."

### Now, the characteristics of the ears are described:

Fleshless ears indicate a sinful death; flat ears indicate many enjoyments.
Those with small ears are misers, while those with cone-shaped ears are army commanders. || 58 ||

Hairy ears indicate long life, and those with large ears possess wealth.
Cruel men have ears covered in prominent veins; those with long, fleshy ears are happy. || 59 ||

With fleshless—meaning devoid of meat—<term>ears</term> <note>Sanskrit: karnaih</note>, men die through sinful deeds. With flat or spread-out ears, they become enjoyers of many pleasures. Those with <term>short ears</term> <note>Sanskrit: hrasva-karna</note> are misers, lacking a generous nature. Those with <term>cone-shaped ears</term> <note>Sanskrit: sanku-shravana</note>—ears with sharp or pointed tops—become commanders of armies.

Those with hairy ears—ears covered in fine hair—live for a long time. Those with <term>large ears</term> <note>Sanskrit: vipula-karna</note>—wide or expansive ears—are sharers of wealth and possess riches. With ears bound by veins—meaning many visible veins—men are cruel or harsh. With long and fleshy ears, they are happy. And so it is said:

> Men with short ears have great enjoyments, as do those with large ears.
> Those with curled ears are wealthy, and likewise those with glossy ears.
> Those with cone-shaped ears have long lives; those with distinct ears have great wealth.
> Those with long ears are endowed with happiness; those with hanging ears are ascetics.
> With fleshless ears, men die a sinful death; with flat ears, they are enjoyers.
> Those with hairy ears are remembered as long-lived; those with large ears as wealthy.
> Those with ears bound by veins are harsh; those with fleshy ears share in happiness. || Thus verses 58-59 ||

---

### Now, the characteristics of the cheeks and nose are described:

One with cheeks that are not sunken is an enjoyer; one with full, fleshy cheeks is a minister.
One with a nose like a parrot's beak is happy; one with a dry nose lives long. || 60 ||

One with a nose that looks "cut" goes to forbidden women; with a long nose, one finds good fortune.
With a crooked or shriveled nose, one is a thief; one with a flat nose causes the death of his wife. || 61 ||

Those with the tip of the nose curved are wealthy; those with noses bent to the right are gluttons and cruel.
A straight nose with small nostrils and beautiful bridge belongs to the fortunate. || 62 ||

"An enjoyer," etc. He whose <term>cheeks</term> <note>Sanskrit: ganda</note> are not sunken—meaning they are high—is an enjoyer, possessing many comforts. He whose cheeks are full and fleshy becomes a minister or counselor. And so it is said—
