> A man whose cheeks are full and well-rounded is said to be a minister.
> He whose cheeks are sunken is remembered as a man of enjoyment.

Regarding the partaker of happiness: The parrot is a bird. One whose nose is like a parrot's—meaning the tip is curved and reddish—becomes a partaker of happiness. One whose nose is dry and fleshless becomes long-lived, possessing a great span of life. ||60||

A nose that appears as if severed <note>original: "chinna"; likely referring to a snub or sharply indented nose</note> indicates those who commit forbidden sexual acts <note>original: "agamyagamino"; literally 'goers to those who should not be gone to'</note>. Good fortune comes from a long nose. With a shriveled or indistinct nose, one becomes a thief or a robber. A flat-nosed man <note>term: "chipita-nasa" (flat or snub-nosed)</note> will suffer the death of his wife; his wife dies before him.

Those whose noses are curved at the tip and crooked at the ends are wealthy and endowed with riches. Those whose noses are bent or crooked toward the right side are gluttonous, unable to accumulate wealth, cruel, and dishonest. The nose of those joined with good fortune is straight, clear, has small nostrils, and beautiful wings <note>original: "suputa"; the alae or sides of the nose</note>. And so it is said:

> One with a parrot-like nose shares in happiness; one with a dry nose is long-lived.
> Those whose nose appears severed are committers of forbidden acts.
> Those with long noses are joined with enjoyment; those with curved tips are endowed with wealth.
> Those with noses bent to the right are cruel; those with clear noses are the best of men.
> Death of the wife comes to those with flat noses; thieves are known by their crooked noses. ||61-62||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the sneeze:

> The sneeze of the wealthy occurs once, or doubled or tripled together, and is resonant and echoing.
> That of the long-lived is known to be released and compact. ||63||

The sneeze—the sound made by the nose—of the wealthy and powerful occurs once, or is "doubled or tripled together" <note>meaning a rapid succession of two or three sneezes</note>. This is how some explain it. Others, however, interpret it thus: The sneeze of the wealthy occurs only once. For the long-lived, it is doubled or tripled, resonant, echoing, released, and compact. For those who are long-lived, it is doubled (twofold) or tripled (threefold). Furthermore, "resonant" <note>original: "hladi"</note> refers to a sound that is heard loudly even above the chatter of many people talking at once. "Echoing" <note>original: "sanunadam"</note> refers to a sound that, even when uttered softly, gradually reaches the path of hearing from a distance. "Released" means very long. "Compact" <note>original: "samhatam"</note> is to be understood in this manner. Regarding that, it is said:

-> That which is the same at the beginning, middle, and end is "compact." <-

# Page 760
## Chapter 67: On the Characteristics of the Body

A voice that remains unchanged by anger, joy, illness, or fear, and which is pleasing to the ear, is considered "glossy" or resonant. Because it is liked by all people, it is considered attached <note>original: "saktaḥ"; implying a voice that draws people in</note>. This very explanation is the most excellent. For this reason, the sage Parashara says:

> A single sneeze indicates enjoyment for those who are wealthy, and long life for others.
> Four sneezes lead to the destruction of enjoyment; anything beyond that is born of illness. (63)

### Now he describes the characteristics of the eyes:

> Those with eyes like lotus petals are wealthy; those with eyes red at the corners possess fortune.
> Those with honey-colored eyes have great wealth; those with eyes like a cat are sinful. (64)
> Those with eyes like a deer, or circular eyes, or crooked eyes are thieves.
> Those with squinted eyes are cruel; those with eyes like an elephant are commanders of armies. (65)
> Deep-set eyes bring sovereignty; those with the luster of blue water-lilies are learned.
> Those with extremely black pupils suffer the plucking out of their eyes. (66)
> Large-eyed men become ministers; those with tawny eyes possess good fortune.
> A miserable look belongs to the poor; a glossy, wide look belongs to the wealthy and those who enjoy life. (67)

Those with eyes resembling **lotus petals** are endowed with wealth. Those with **red-cornered eyes**—meaning the edges of the eyes are reddish in color—are the sharers of fortune and possess Lakshmi <note>The goddess of wealth and prosperity</note>. With eyes colored like **honey** (brownish-yellow), they possess great riches. Those with eyes like a **cat**—having eyes of that shape and color—are sinful.

Those with **deer-eyes**, as well as those with **circular eyes** (perfectly round) or **crooked eyes**, are thieves or robbers. Those with **squinted eyes** (blue-eyed or slanted) are cruel and formidable. Those with **elephant-like eyes** become commanders of armies.

**Deep-set eyes** lead to sovereignty. With eyes having the luster of the **blue water-lily**—meaning pupils of that likeness—men become learned scholars. For those with **extremely black pupils**, there is the "plucking out" of the eyes; eyes with excessively dark pupils are destined to be destroyed.

Those with **large eyes** attain the status of a minister. Those with **tawny eyes**—eyes or pupils the color of a green gram <note>a type of bean</note>—possess good fortune. Those whose gaze has reached a state of **misery** are penniless. A **glossy**, clear, and **wide** gaze belongs to the wealthy and those who enjoy life's pleasures. As it is said:

> Eyes that are even, the color of cow's milk, red at the corners, with black pupils,
> Clear, large, glossy, and long, are auspicious.

### Now he describes the characteristics of the eyebrows —

-> With highly raised eyebrows, men are short-lived; with broad and raised ones, they are exceedingly happy. <-
-> Those with uneven eyebrows are poor; those with eyebrows curved like the crescent moon are wealthy. (68) <-
-> With long, unjoined eyebrows, they are wealthy; with broken ones, they are destitute of means. <-
-> Those whose eyebrows are depressed in the middle are attached to forbidden women. (69) <-

With "highly raised"—meaning eyebrows that are primarily high—men are short-lived or have a brief lifespan. With "broad"—meaning wide—and "raised," they are exceedingly happy. All those who have "uneven eyebrows"—meaning unequal or asymmetrical—are poor and destitute. Those whose eyebrows are "curved like the crescent moon"—resembling the young moon—are wealthy.
With "long and unjoined"—meaning eyebrows that are long but do not meet in the middle—men become wealthy; with "broken" ones, they are destitute and poor. Those men who have "eyebrows depressed in the middle"—meaning the eyebrows are indistinct or sunken in the center—are "attached to forbidden women," meaning they are devoted to women one should not approach. And so it is said:

-> With highly raised eyebrows, one is short-lived; with broad ones, endowed with happiness. <-
-> Those men whose eyebrows are raised in the middle are attached to sin. <-

### Now he describes the characteristics of the temples and forehead —

-> With high and broad temples, men are wealthy; with sunken ones, they are deprived of children and wealth. <-
-> Those with uneven foreheads are penniless; with a forehead like a half-moon, they are wealthy. || 70 || <-
-> With foreheads broad like a pearl-oyster shell, they become teachers; with foreheads covered in veins, they are devoted to unrighteousness. <-

-> With prominent foreheads, they become army commanders; with narrow or closed foreheads, they are misers. || 72 || <-

---

With high (elevated) and broad (extensive) temples <term>Shankha: the anatomical region of the temples</term>, men become wealthy and powerful. With sunken (low) temples, they are abandoned by or devoid of sons (children) and wealth. As it is said —
> -> With high and broad temples, men are wealthy and live happily. <-
> -> With sunken ones, humans are devoid of children and wealth and are partakers of sorrow. <-

Those whose forehead (the surface of the face) is uneven (irregular) are penniless and poor. With a forehead resembling the half-moon (crescent-shaped), they become wealthy and powerful.
With foreheads broad like a pearl-oyster shell, one attains the status of a teacher <term>Acharya: a spiritual preceptor or professor</term>. An Acharya is one who instructs others. With foreheads full of veins (covered in many vessels), they are devoted to unrighteousness. With raised veins located on the forehead, they become rich and powerful. They are also wealthy if the veins are situated in the shape of a swastika.
Those whose foreheads are sunken (depressed) are fit for "slaying" (beating) and "binding" (imprisonment), and are attached to cruel and harsh deeds or tasks. With foreheads that are prominently raised, they become army commanders <term>Chamupa: a general or leader of an army</term>. Those whose foreheads are "closed" (rounded and small) are misers (unwilling to give). As it is said —
> -> With a forehead like a half-moon, they become lords of the earth. <-
> -> With a broad forehead, they are remembered as being possessed of great wealth. <-
> -> With an uneven one, they are known as the lowest; with many veins, men are sinful. <-
> -> With a sunken forehead, men are devoted to cruel deeds. <-
> -> With prominent ones, they become army commanders; with closed ones, they are remembered as misers. || 70-72 || <-

### Now, the characteristics of weeping are described:

**Weeping that is not pitiful, without tears, and smooth is auspicious for men.**
**That which is harsh, pitiful, and full of tears is not auspicious for men. ||73||**

Weeping that is "not pitiful" means it is free from wretchedness. "Without tears" means free from weeping drops. "Smooth" means not harsh; such types are auspicious and praised for men. "Harsh" means rough. "Pitiful" means joined with misery. "Full of tears" means many drops. These are not auspicious for men. As it is said:

->Weeping that is without misery or tears and is smooth is auspicious.<-
->That which is harsh, pitiful, and tearful is undesirable for men. ||73||<-

---

### Now, the characteristics of laughter are described:

**Laughter without trembling is auspicious; that with closed eyes belongs to the sinful.**
**The laughter of the wicked is frequent; that of the insane is frequent at the end. ||74||**

Laughter that is "without trembling" (where no shaking of the body or limbs occurs) is auspicious and praised. Laughter with "closed eyes" (eyes very squinted or shut) belongs to a "sinful person" <note>one who performs bad deeds</note>. Frequent or repeated laughter belongs to the "wicked" <note>one with faults</note>. Laughter that occurs repeatedly at the "end" <note>after the joke or situation has passed</note> belongs to the "insane" <note>one possessed by madness</note>. As it is said:

->Laughter without trembling is for [good] men; otherwise, it is inauspicious.<-
->Frequent laughter is for the faulty, and closed eyes are inauspicious. ||74||<-

---

### Now, the characteristics of forehead lines are described:

**If three lines are situated across the forehead, they belong to those living a hundred years.**
**With four lines, one gains kingship and a life of ninety-five years. ||75||**

**With broken lines, one approaches forbidden women; with no lines, the life is ninety years.**
**With lines reaching the hairline, the lifespan is eighty years. ||76||**

**With five lines, the life is seventy; with lines that are single and focused, it is sixty.**
**With many lines, it is fifty; and forty with crooked lines. ||77||**

**With lines touching the eyebrows, it is thirty; with lines curved to the left, it is twenty.**
**With tiny lines, the life is short; for those younger, the interval should be calculated accordingly. ||78||**

Regarding "three lines": if three long lines are situated across the forehead <note>the surface of the face</note>, they belong to "centenarians" <note>those who live a hundred years</note>. With four long forehead lines, "kingship" <note>sovereignty over the earth</note> occurs. The lifespan is "ninety plus five years" (ninety-five).

<summary>This page details the physiognomic significance of how a man cries and laughs, followed by a systematic breakdown of how the number and shape of forehead lines predict lifespan and social status.</summary>

<page-num>764</page-num>
<header>In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 67]</header>

If the forehead lines are broken yet joined together, such individuals are those who approach forbidden women <note>original: "agamyāgāminaḥ" — referring to those who engage in illicit sexual relations</note>, and their lifespan is ninety years. With a forehead that is without lines, the lifespan is also ninety years. The word "also" here implies "and." Such individuals also approach forbidden women. Where the hairline begins is called the "hair-limit." With lines reaching that hair-limit, the lifespan is eighty years.

With five lines situated on the forehead, the lifespan is seventy years. If all the lines meet at a single point <note>original: "ekāgrāvasthitābhiḥ"</note> or are broken yet reach a point, the lifespan is sixty years. With many lines—specifically characterized by six lines—the lifespan is half of a hundred, which is fifty years. With curved and indistinct lines, the lifespan is forty years.

With broken lines, the lifespan is thirty years. With lines curved toward the left side, the lifespan is twenty years <note>original: "viṃśatikaḥ" — one whose life measure is twenty years</note>. With tiny or subtle lines, one is short-lived, meaning a lifespan of less than twenty years. From the mention of "fewer lines," such as two or one, it follows that the lifespan is likewise very short. In between these measures, one should use their own intelligence to infer the results. For instance, it was said that three lines belong to those living a hundred years, and four lines indicate ninety-five years. In between, if someone has three and a half lines, their lifespan should be inferred as ninety-seven and a half years, and so on. And thus it is said:

->He who has five lines on his forehead is considered wealthy.<-
->He lives for a hundred years and attains lordship.<-
->With four lines, eighty; with three lines, seventy.<-
->With two lines, sixty; and with one line, forty.<-
->Those with a forehead devoid of lines are guardians of treasures.<-
->Men with broken lines are to be known as devoted to sinful deeds.<-
->They are short-lived, possess little wealth, and are always afflicted by disease.<-
->He on whose forehead a trident <note>the weapon of Shiva</note> or a spear-head is seen,<-
->His lordship is certain, and he becomes a leader of armies.<-
— Verses 75-78

### Now, the characteristics of the head are described:

->Those with well-rounded heads are rich in cows; those with umbrella-shaped heads are lords of the earth.<-
->Those with flat heads are destroyers of their fathers and mothers; those with skull-like heads <note>sunken or bony</note> meet death after a long time.<- 79
->One with a pot-shaped head enjoys traveling on roads; one with a double-crown <note>two whorls of hair or a split shape</note> is a sinner abandoned by wealth.<-
->A head that is slightly depressed belongs to the great; but a very depressed head brings disaster.<- 80

<page-num>765</page-num>
# Chapter 67: The Chapter on the Characteristics of Men

Those with **circular** or perfectly round heads <note>original: "parimandalaih"</note> become wealthy in cattle. Those with heads shaped like an **umbrella**—meaning the upper part is broad—become kings or lords of the earth. Those with **flat** heads are destroyers of their fathers and mothers. Those whose heads resemble a **skull** <note>original: "karoti," likely referring to a sunken or skeletal appearance</note> meet their death after a long time.

One with a **pot-shaped head** <note>original: "ghata-murdha"</note> is fond of traveling or wandering. One with a **double-headed** appearance <note>likely referring to a head with two distinct lobes or a prominent sagittal ridge</note> is a sinner and becomes destitute, abandoned by wealth. A **depressed** or sunken head is found among the great or the leaders, but an **excessively sunken** head brings misery and sorrow.

As it is said:
> A sunken head brings displacement and is slightly afflicted.
> An umbrella-shaped head makes a king; circular heads make one rich in cattle.
> An uneven head belongs to the poor; a long head to those who live long.
> A head shaped like an elephant's frontal globe <note>original: "nagakumbha"</note> makes a king; a head that is even everywhere belongs to those who enjoy life's pleasures. (79-80)

Now, he describes the characteristics of the hair:

> With hair that grows **singly** from each pore, is **glossy**, **black**, **curled**, with **unsplit ends**, **soft**, and **not too thick**, one becomes a happy man or a ruler of men. (81)
> Hair that grows in **multiple strands** from a single root, is **uneven**, **tawny**, **thick**, **split at the ends**, **rough**, **short**, **excessively curly**, and **very dense** belongs to those devoid of wealth. (82)

Regarding hair growing "singly": this means only one hair grows from each individual pore. **Glossy** means not dry. **Black** means dark. **Curled** means wavy. **Unsplit ends** means the tips are not frayed. **Soft** means tender to the touch. **Not too thick** means not overly dense. With such hair, one enjoys happiness or becomes a king.

**Multiple roots** refers to many hairs emerging from a single pore. **Uneven** means some are short and some are long. **Tawny** <note>original: "kapila," a reddish-brown or yellowish color</note> refers to the color. **Thick** means not fine. **Split ends** means the tips are divided. **Rough** means dry or coarse. **Short** means lacking length. **Excessively curly** means tightly coiled. **Very dense** means hair that is crowded together; such hair belongs to the poor.

As it is said:
> Hair that grows singly, is glossy, black, and not too dense is praised.
> The opposite characteristics are declared to belong to the destitute.

The Teacher <note>referring to Varahamihira, the author of the Brihat Samhita</note> has said: "The expert in **physiognomy** <term>Samudrika: the science of reading bodily marks to predict the past and future</term> speaks of what has passed and what is yet to come. Therefore, we have cited these characteristics of men from the Samudrika scriptures; it should be understood that the Teacher's knowledge extends even beyond these." (81-82)

# On the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 67]

Page 766

- Now, the author summarizes everything stated so far:

> **Whatever limb is dry, lacking in flesh, or covered in prominent veins,**
> **that is declared inauspicious; the opposite of this is entirely favorable. ||83||**

Whichever limb or body part is dry (lacking luster), meatless (emaciated), or entangled with veins (where veins are clearly visible) is said to be inauspicious or unlucky. Therefore, the opposite of this—limbs that are glossy, fleshy, and without visible veins—is considered entirely auspicious. ||83||

Now, he describes the characteristics of a "Great Man" <note>Mahapurusha: a term for an ideal human being or a divinely ordained ruler</note>:

> **Broad in three, deep in three, raised in six, and short in four;**
> **Red in seven, and in five, both long and fine—such is a King. ||84||**

One who is broad in three body parts; deep in exactly three; possesses six raised parts; has four short parts; is red (ruddy) in seven; long in five; and fine (subtle) in five—that man becomes a King or a ruler. ||84||

Now, he provides the specific classification of these parts:

> **The navel, the voice, and the inner character—these three**
> **are praised as "deep" in men.**
> **The chest, the forehead, and the face—these three**
> **are praised as "broad" in men. ||85||**

> **The chest, the armpits, the nails, the nose, the mouth,**
> **and the nape of the neck—these six should be "raised" (prominent).**
> **The four that are "short"—the penis, the back,**
> **the neck, and the shanks—bring about benefit. ||86||**

> **The corners of the eyes, feet, palms, palate, lower lip, tongue,**
> **and nails—these seven being "red" surely bring happiness.**
> **The five "fine" (subtle) parts are the teeth, finger joints, hair,**
> **along with the skin and the nails; these are not found in the miserable. ||87||**

> **The jaw, the eyes, the arms, the nose, and the space between the breasts—**
> **this group of five is "long" in men who are kings, and not otherwise. ||88||**

The navel is the center point of the body. Voice refers to sound. *Sattva* <note>inner strength or essence</note> refers to the quality of one's disposition. Its definition is—

-> **True essence (*Sattva*) is that which remains undisturbed by the arrival of either calamity or prosperity.** <-

These three qualities in men—[navel, voice, and essence]—are praised when they are deep. The chest is the breast. The forehead is the front of the head. The face is the mouth. All these three in men are praised when they are broad.

The chest is the breast. The word "and" is used here in a conjunctive sense. By the word "armpit," the middle part of the body is indicated. Nails are the "hand-growths." The nose is the organ of smell. The mouth is the face. The *krikatika* <term>krikatika: the joint of the neck or the nape</term> is the back part of the neck. These six are beneficial and praised when they are elevated or high. The *lingam* is the penis. The back is the posterior part of the body. The neck is the head-bearer. The shanks [lower legs]. The word "and" is used throughout to denote a collection. These four are beneficial and praised when they are short (not long).

The corners of the eyes are the edges of the vision. The feet are the limbs of walking. The hands are the palms. The palate is the roof of the mouth. The lower lip is the lip. The tongue is the organ of taste. Nails are the "hand-growths." These seven are red or crimson and are bringers of happiness. The teeth are the tusks. The joints of the fingers are the lines residing on the branches of the hand. The hair is that which is born on the head. Along with the skin, the nails are the "hand-growths." These five are fine or subtle; they do not belong to the miserable, but rather to those who are happy.

The two jawbones are well-known. The eyes are the organs of sight. The arms are the limbs. The nose is the organ of smell. The space between the breasts is the middle. In this group, there is a combination of five <note>likely intended as 'the fifth group of three' or 'the five joined'</note>. These five are long (not short) and do not belong to men who are not kings. This means those who possess them become kings. And so says Garga <note>an ancient sage and authority on astrology and omens</note>:—

> -> Fourteen equal pairs, four black, and four level; <-
> -> Ten lotus-like, ten large, and three white—such a man is praised. <-
> -> The feet, ankles, buttocks, sides, testicles, eyes, and breasts; <-
> -> The shoulders, lips, groins, shanks, hands, arms, and shoulder-blades; <-
> -> He who has these fourteen equal pairs is prosperous among men. <-
> -> The pupils, eyebrows, beard, and hair—these being black is auspicious. <-
> -> The fingers, heart, eyes, and teeth—when these are level in men, <-
> -> These four are highly praised as bringers of constant power and happiness. <-
> -> The tongue, lips, palate, mouth, face, eyes, breasts, and nails; <-
> -> The hands and feet—these ten are praised in beings when they resemble the lotus. <-
> -> The palms, feet, chest, neck, testicles, heart, and head; <-
> -> The forehead, abdomen, and back—these ten are honored when they are large. <-

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Luster (Chhaya)—

->The luster, revealing auspicious and inauspicious results,<-
->should be observed in humans, beasts, and birds by experts in signs.<-
->It manifests the qualities of inner brilliance even outwardly,<-
->like the light of a lamp placed within a vessel of crystal or gems. || 89 ||<-

"Luster" <note>original: "Chhaya"</note> refers to the radiance of the body, revealing—meaning announcing—auspicious and inauspicious results. It is to be observed—meaning examined—by experts in signs, those who know the marks of luster. In whom? In humans, beasts, and birds. Humans refers to men; beasts refers to four-legged animals; birds refers to those who travel in the sky. And this luster, residing within the body, manifests—meaning illuminates—the qualities of brilliance <note>original: "Tejas"</note> even outwardly, on the exterior of the body, with great intensity. How? Like the light of a lamp placed within a vessel of crystal or gems. Just as the light of a lamp situated inside a jar made of crystal or precious stones illuminates its brilliant qualities even on the outside, so too does the internal luster manifest outwardly.

In this regard, there are five types of "shadows" <note>original: "chhaya"; refers to the aura, complexion, or subtle luster of a person</note> relating to the five great elements. It was stated previously in the *Birth Horoscope* <note>referring to the *Brihat Jataka*</note>:—

->All the elements manifest their own "shadow" when their specific planetary period arrives,<-
->along with the qualities of earth, water, fire, air, and ether, which are inferable through the nose, mouth, eyes, skin, and ears respectively. || 89<-

### First, he describes the characteristics of the Earthly Shadow—

->The shadow arising from the Earth makes the teeth, skin, nails, body hair, and hair on the head glossy and fragrant.<-
->It brings contentment, financial gain, and prosperity, and causes an inclination toward righteousness day after day. || 90<-

When the Earth-born shadow <note>original: "mahisamuttha"</note> manifests in a person, then their teeth, skin, nails, body hair, and head hair all become glossy and oily. Likewise, that shadow—the bodily luster—becomes sweet-smelling. This means the person's body acquires a pleasant fragrance. That shadow also produces contentment (mental satisfaction), the acquisition of wealth, and prosperity (the successful manifestation of one's undertakings). Furthermore, it causes an inclination toward the practice of righteousness <note>term: "Dharma"; refers to moral duty and religious merit</note> every single day. <margin>Some read "the increase of righteousness" instead of "inclination."</margin> || 90 ||

### Now, he describes the characteristics of the Watery Shadow—

->The Watery shadow is glossy, white, clear-green, and pleasing to the eyes;<-
->it brings good fortune, gentleness, happiness, and prosperity.<-
->Like a mother, the Watery shadow is the producer of all success and bestows auspicious results upon embodied beings. || 91<-

The Watery shadow <note>original: "apya" or "varuni"</note> is glossy, meaning it is endowed with a clean luster. It is white, meaning it is generally fair in color. It is "clear-green," meaning it possesses a stainless dark-greenish hue. It is "pleasing to the eyes," meaning it is delightful to look upon; it generates satisfaction. It produces good fortune (being loved by all people), gentleness (lack of cruelty), physical comfort, and prosperity in one's affairs. Furthermore, it is the "producer of all success," meaning it brings all goals to fruition. "Like a mother"—just as a mother...

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 67]

The Earth <note>referring to the "Terrestrial shadow" mentioned in the preceding verse</note> is the benefactor of all living beings. In the same way, she bestows and creates auspicious results for all those who possess a physical body. ||91||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Fiery Shadow—

->**Fierce, unassailable, with the color of lotus, gold, and fire,**<-
->**Endowed with brilliance, valor, and great power;**<-
->**The Fiery shadow leads to victory for living beings**<-
->**And quickly grants the fulfillment of desired goals. ||92||**<-

The Fiery <term>Agneyi; relating to Agni, the god of fire</term> shadow is "fierce," meaning prone to anger. It is "unassailable," meaning it cannot be overcome by others. It has the "color of lotus, gold, and fire," possessing a luster similar to a lotus flower, gold, or a sacrificial fire. Furthermore, it is "endowed with brilliance, valor, and great power"—it is accompanied by radiance, courage, and the prowess required to subdue enemies. Such is the nature of the Fiery shadow. The word "thus" <note>original: "iti"</note> denotes the category. This type of shadow leads to victory for embodied beings and quickly—very soon—bestows the "attainment of desired goals," meaning the fulfillment of what one wishes for. ||92||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Airy and Ethereal shadows—

->**Dirty, rough, black, foul-smelling, and born of the wind,**<-
->**It produces death, imprisonment, disease, misfortune, and loss of wealth.**<-
->**Resembling crystal, fortunate, and exceedingly noble,**<-
->**The Ethereal shadow is like a treasure-trove of blessings, clear in color. ||93||**<-

The shadow "born of the wind" <term>Vayavi; relating to Vayu, the god of wind</term> is "dirty" in color, meaning it lacks clarity. It is "rough" or harsh, and "black" or dark. It is "foul-smelling," possessing a bad odor. This shadow "produces" or brings about: "death" (the end of life), "imprisonment" (confinement), "diseases" (afflictions), "misfortune" (lack of gain), and "loss of wealth" (the destruction of accumulated riches).

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Ethereal shadow—

Regarding "Crystal," etc.: The shadow "born of the sky" <term>Nabhasi; relating to Nabhas or Akasha, the ether/space</term> is the Ethereal shadow. It "resembles crystal," meaning its luster or appearance is like that of a crystal gem; the meaning is that it is extremely pure. It is "fortunate," accompanied by good luck. It is "exceedingly noble," meaning highly generous in nature, and is like a "treasure-trove of all blessings" or auspicious works. This means it bestows everything. Finally, it is "clear in color," meaning stainlessly pure. ||93||

<header>[Chapter 67] Chapter on the Characteristics of Men. 771</header>

Here, the author presents five other types of shadows according to the opinions of other teachers:

> ->The shadows arising from the earth, water, fire, wind, and ether—<-
> ->Some say there are ten, following the sequence<-
> ->Of the Sun, Vishnu, Indra, Yama, and the Moon.<-
> ->Since their characteristics and results are equal, they are summarized here. || 94 ||<-

"Earth" refers to the terrestrial element. "Water" refers to the Varuna element. "Fire" refers to the consumer of oblations. "Wind" refers to the air. "Ether" refers to the sky. The shadows arising from these are five in their respective order. Some sages, such as Garga and others, speak of ten shadows. The five already mentioned and the five now being described. These also follow a sequence belonging to the Sun (Aditya), Vishnu (Narayana), Indra (Puruhuta), Yama (the Lord of the Ancestors), and the Moon (Udupa). These shadows are equal in their characteristics and results to the five previously mentioned. Specifically: the Solar shadow is the same as the Fiery; the Vishnu shadow is the same as the Ethereal; the Indra shadow is the same as the Earthly; the Yama shadow is the same as the Airy; and the Lunar shadow is the same as the Watery. "Thus is the summary": for this reason, a summary of those ten shadows has been made. Because the results are identical, they are treated as only five shadows. As Garga says:

> ->Five are proclaimed as arising from earth, water, fire, air, and sky;<-
> ->And there are five others belonging to the Earth, Vishnu, Indra, the Sun, and the Moon.<-

This concludes the section on luster <note>original: "mṛjā" - refers to the cleansing or brightness of the skin</note>. || 94 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the voice:

> ->Those with voices like an elephant, a bull, a fleet of chariots, a kettle-drum, a mridanga-drum, a lion, or a thundercloud become kings.<-
> ->Those with voices like a donkey, or those that are broken and harsh, are devoid of wealth and happiness. || 95 ||<-

"Elephant" <note>kari</note> means the tusker. "Bull" <note>vṛṣa</note> means the ox. "Fleet of chariots" means a multitude of vehicles. "Kettle-drum" <note>bherī</note> is a large drum. "Mridanga" is a well-known musical instrument <note>often called a mandala</note>. "Lion" is the king of beasts. "Cloud" <note>abhra</note> refers to the rain-cloud; there is also a reading "Abda," which also means cloud. Those possessing sounds similar to these—equal in tone—become kings. "Donkey" <note>gardabha</note> is the ass. "Broken" <note>jarjhara</note> refers to a distorted voice. "Harsh" <note>rūkṣa</note> means rough. Those with voices similar to a donkey and so on are "devoid of wealth and happiness," meaning they are abandoned by riches and comforts. As Garga says:

> ->Deep, resonant, smooth, loud, and echoing—<-
> ->These are the five virtues of the voice, as told by the truth-knowing Samudra.<-

---

<margin>1. An alternative reading is "Lion and Cloud" (Simhābda).</margin>

### Now he describes the Essences—

**There are seven essences: fat, marrow, skin, bone, and semen,**
**along with blood and flesh; here is the summary of their effects for living beings. || 96 ||**

There are seven essences <term>Sāra: the fundamental constitutional strengths of a person</term> in men. Fat <note>original: "Medas"</note> is the oily substance within the bones. Marrow <note>original: "Majjā"</note> resides within the skull. Skin <note>original: "Tvak"</note> is the outer covering. Bone <note>original: "Asthi"</note> is well-known. Semen <note>original: "Śukra"</note> is the reproductive seed. Blood <note>original: "Rudhira"</note> is the red fluid. Flesh <note>original: "Māṃsa"</note> is the muscle. The word "and" indicates the collection of these. These seven types of essences belong to living beings. The summary of their results is now being told. || 96 ||

### Here he describes the characteristics of the Blood-Essence—

**With the palate, lips, gums, tongue, corners of the eyes, anus, hands, and feet**
**being red, one is of the Blood-Essence; such people possess much happiness, women, wealth, and sons. || 97 ||**

The palate is the upper part of the mouth. The lips are the covers of the teeth. The gums <note>original: "Dantapālī"</note> are the rows of flesh around the teeth. The tongue is the organ of taste. The corners of the eyes are the edges of the vision. The anus is the private exit. The hands and the feet are the limbs. When these eight parts are red <note>original: "Rakte"</note>, men are of the "Blood-Essence." They are endowed with many pleasures, many wives, much wealth, and many sons. || 97 ||

### Now he describes the Skin, Marrow, and Fat Essences—

**Those with glossy skin are wealthy; with soft skin, they are fortunate; with thin skin, they are wise.**
**Those with Marrow and Fat Essences have beautiful bodies and are endowed with sons and wealth. || 98 ||**

Skin is the hide. Those whose skin is glossy and not dry are wealthy. Those with soft skin possess good fortune. Those with thin skin are learned scholars. Those men who are of the Marrow-Essence and the Fat-Essence have "good bodies," meaning handsome or well-formed physiques. They are also endowed with children and riches. || 98 ||

### Now he describes the essence of bone and semen—

**One with the essence of bone is thick-boned, stable, strong, reaches the end of knowledge, and is handsome.**
**Those with the essence of semen have abundant and heavy semen; they are fortunate, learned, and beautiful. ||99||**

One whose bones are thick is said to possess the "essence of bone" <note>Sanskrit: *asthisāra*</note>; such a living being is strong. He "reaches the end of knowledge," meaning he is capable and powerful in learning, and is "handsome," possessing a beautiful form. Those with the "essence of semen" <note>Sanskrit: *shukrasāra*</note> are those whose semen is abundant and heavy (dense); they are "fortunate," endowed with good luck, "learned" as scholars or reciters, and "beautiful," possessing lovely forms. ||99||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the essence of flesh and the characteristics of bodily compactness—

**He who possesses the essence of flesh has a well-developed body, is learned, wealthy, and handsome.**
**"Compactness" is known by well-knit joints; such people are to be known as enjoyers of happiness. ||100||**

A "well-developed body" refers to a stout or muscular physique. Such a person has the "essence of flesh" <note>Sanskrit: *māmsasāra*</note>; he is "learned" (a scholar), "wealthy" (possessing riches), and "handsome" (of beautiful form)—this concludes the essences.
Now, the characteristic of compactness <note>Sanskrit: *samhati*</note>: "Compactness" refers to the "well-knit nature of the joints," meaning all the joints of the limbs are firmly joined. This well-knit quality of joints is to be known in those who "enjoy happiness." This means those whose joints are well-knit are enjoyers of pleasure. ||100||

### Now he describes the characteristics of glossiness—

**Glossiness is to be observed in five places: the voice, tongue, teeth, eyes, and nails.**
**With these being glossy, men are endowed with children, wealth, and fortune; with these being dull, they are penniless. ||101||**

"Glossiness" <note>Sanskrit: *sneha*, also meaning oiliness or affection</note> is to be examined and considered in five things. In what? In the "voice" (speech); in the "tongue"; in the "teeth"; in the "eyes"; and in the "nails." It resides in these. If all these—the voice and so on—are "glossy" (oily or lustrous), men are "endowed with children, wealth, and fortune." "Children" means sons; "wealth" means riches; "fortune" is being liked by all people. They are joined with these qualities. If those same parts are all "dull" (dry or rough), they are "penniless" or poor. ||101||

### Now he describes the characteristics of complexion—

**A glossy complexion is radiant and belongs to kings; a medium one to those with children and wealth.**
**A dull complexion belongs to the poor; a pure complexion gives auspicious results, not a variegated one. ||102||**

"Complexion" <note>Sanskrit: *varna*</note> refers to colors such as fair, reddish, or dark. One whose complexion is "glossy" is "radiant" (possessing luster). This belongs to "kings" (rulers of the earth). A "medium" complexion—one that is neither too dull nor too...

A glossy complexion belongs to those who possess children and wealth. A dry or dull complexion belongs to those devoid of wealth—the poor. A pure complexion, being glossy, is auspicious and praised. It should not be "mixed" or variegated; a complexion that is glossy in some places and dry in others is not auspicious. Thus ends the section on Complexion.

## Now he describes the characteristics of Previous Births (Anuka)—

-> One’s previous birth is to be determined from the face; those with faces like a cow, a bull, a tiger, a lion, or Garuda <-
-> are men of irresistible valor, conquerors of enemies, and lords of men (kings). <-
-> Those with faces resembling a monkey, a buffalo, a boar, or a goat enjoy learning, wealth, and happiness. <-
-> With faces and bodies resembling a donkey or a young camel, they are devoid of wealth and happiness. <-

<term>Anuka</term> <note>original: "anūkaṃ"</note> refers to one's previous birth. This is to be inferred or imagined from the face. The cow is well-known. The bull is the ox. The tiger is a specific powerful animal similar to a lion. The lion is the king of beasts. Garuda is the son of Vinata <note>the divine eagle-mount of Vishnu</note>. Those whose faces are similar to these have an auspicious previous birth. They possess irresistible valor—meaning their power cannot be overcome. They are conquerors of enemies and become "lords of men," or kings.

The monkey is the ape. The buffalo is well-known. The boar is the pig. The goat is the ram. Men with faces similar to these are "partakers of learning, wealth, and happiness." Learning refers to the sacred scriptures. Wealth is riches. Happiness is self-evident. They share in these things. Their previous birth is considered "middle" or mediocre. The donkey is the ass. The "karabha" is the camel. With faces and bodies resembling donkeys or camels, they are "devoid of wealth and happiness." Devoid of wealth means poor; devoid of happiness means lacking comfort. Their previous birth was inauspicious. Thus ends the section on Previous Births.

---

## Now he describes the characteristics of Height (Unmana)—

-> One hundred and eight, ninety-six, and eighty-four are the measurements for men <-
-> who are superior, average, and inferior, respectively, counted in digits (angulas) by their own measure. <-

For men, the measurement is taken in <term>digits</term> <note>original: "aṅṅula-saṅkhyayā"</note> according to their own scale <note>the width of the person's own finger</note>. One hundred and eight digits is the height of superior men. Ninety-six digits is for average men. Eighty-four digits is the height for inferior men. The rule is this: one should measure a standing man by placing a string from the point where the feet touch the ground up to the middle of the head, and then measure that string using the person's own finger-widths. Thus ends the section on Height.

-> A weight of one "bhara" belongs to the very wealthy; one and a half "bharas" belongs to a ruler of the whole earth. <-

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Men

A <term>Bhara</term><note>A traditional unit of weight</note> is equal to two thousand <term>Palas</term><note>A smaller unit of weight; approximately 48 grams</note>. A man who, when weighed on a scale, weighs half a Bhara—meaning one thousand Palas—is a possessor of happiness. One who weighs less than this half-Bhara is a possessor of misery. A weight of exactly one Bhara belongs to the exceedingly wealthy. He who weighs one and a half Bharas (three thousand Palas) is a ruler of the entire earth, meaning a universal monarch. ॥ 106 ॥

->Explaining at what time one should measure height and weight, the author says:<-

->**A woman at twenty years, and a man indeed at twenty-five years,**<-
->**Are fit for measurement of height and weight, or at the completion of the fourth part of their lifespan. ॥ 107 ॥**<-

A woman is fit for <term>Mana</term><note>Weight measured by a scale</note> and <term>Unmana</term><note>Height or vertical measurement in fingers/Angulas</note> at twenty years of age. Similarly, a man is fit for such measurements at twenty-five years. The word "indeed" is used for poetic emphasis. This is stated assuming a fixed lifespan of one hundred years. Or, they are fit for measurement when the fourth part of their life has passed. If the lifespan is determined to be less than a hundred years, the "fourth part" rule applies. This concludes the section on measurement. ॥ 107 ॥

### Now, the characteristics of natural dispositions (Prakriti) are described:

->**By the essence of Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Ether, Gods, Humans, Demons, Spirits, and Animals,**<-
->**A man is formed; these are their specific characteristics. ॥ 108 ॥**<-

Earth is well-known. Water refers to the element of Varuna. Fire is Agni. Wind is Vayu. Ether is space. Gods are the celestials. Humans are men. Demons are Rakshasas. Spirits are the Pishachas <note>A class of supernatural beings</note>. Animals are the non-human species. A man is characterized by the <term>Sattva</term><note>Inner essence or natural disposition</note> of these entities. Their characteristics will be described hereafter. Some read the text as "Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Ether, Gods, Humans, Demons, Spirits, and Animal" <note>original: "bhūjalaśikhyanilāmbarasuranararakṣaḥ piśācatiryañcam"</note>. That is incorrect; it should be "of Animals" <note>original: "tiraścām"</note> in the plural. Therefore, the previous reading is the better one. ॥ 108 ॥

A man of **earthly nature** <note>Sanskrit: *mahisvabhava*</note> possesses the constitution of the earth. One whose scent is like that of **beautiful flowers**, such as the Champaka and others, is **pleasure-seeking** <note>or "possessing enjoyments"</note>. He has **pleasant breath**; here, "breath" refers to the air exhaled, which for such a man is fragrant and easy. He is also **steady** in character. One of a **watery nature** <note>Sanskrit: *toyasvabhava*</note> is a **heavy water-drinker**, meaning he habitually drinks a great deal of water. He is **pleasant-spoken**, speaking in a kind and favorable manner, and is a **vessel of tastes** <note>Sanskrit: *rasabhajana*</note>, meaning he is fit for or fond of the various tastes like sweetness. ### Now he describes the characteristics of the Fire and Wind temperaments—

-> One of **fiery nature** is fickle, very sharp, <-
-> fierce, hungry, and a heavy eater. <-
-> By the **nature of wind**, one is unsteady and lean, <-
-> and quickly falls under the power of anger. || 110 || <-

By **fiery nature**, a man is **fickle**, meaning unstable in his actions. He is **very sharp** or mischievous, and **fierce** <note>cruel</note>. He is **hungry**, meaning he cannot endure hunger, and is a **heavy eater** who consumes much food. By the **nature of wind**, a man is **unsteady** in mind and **lean** <note>weak or thin</note>. He **quickly falls under the power of anger**, meaning he becomes easily controlled by his wrath. || 110 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Ether and Divine temperaments—

-> One of **ethereal nature** is clever, with an open mouth, <-
-> skilled in the movement of sound, and has prominent veins. <-
-> A man of **divine nature** is generous, <-
-> mild in anger, and devoted to affection. || 111 || <-

One of **ethereal nature** <note>Sanskrit: *khaprakriti*; referring to the element of Space/Ether</note> is **clever**, possessing a subtle insight into the arts. He has an **open mouth**. He is **skilled in the movement of sound**, meaning he is capable in the pervasive power and flow of words and Sanskrit grammar. Alternatively, it means he is skilled in the "movements" described in the sciences. Some read this as "skilled in the path of sound." He has **prominent veins** on his limbs. A man of **divine nature** <note>Sanskrit: *surasattva*</note> is **generous** <note>a giver</note>, **mild in anger** <note>possessing little wrath</note>, and **devoted to affection** or full of love. || 111 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Human Temperament—

-> One endowed with the Human temperament is fond of songs and ornaments. <-
-> Such a man is always possessed of a sharing nature and good character. (112) <-

"Human" refers to a mortal man. One endowed with that temperament is "fond of songs and ornaments," meaning he delights in music and jewelry <note>original: "bhushana" - decorative items or finery</note>. "Sharing nature" means he is one who distributes fairly; he is a benefactor to his kinsmen. "Possessed of good character" means he is endowed with virtuous conduct. This is "always," meaning at all times, the nature of such a man. (112)

### Now he describes the characteristics of Demons and Goblins—

-> One with the temperament of Night-Roamers is sharply irritable and acts like a villain, <-
-> and is prone to sin. <-
-> One with the Goblin temperament is fickle, smeared with dirt, <-
-> talks excessively, and has a repulsive or oversized body. (113) <-

By the temperament of "Night-Roamers" <note>original: "nishachara" - a term for Rakshasas or demons</note>, a man is "sharply irritable," meaning he possesses a fierce anger. "Acts like a villain" means his behavior is like that of a wicked person. He is "prone to sin," meaning he is devoted to sinful acts. A man with the "Goblin temperament" <note>original: "pishacha-sattva"</note> is "fickle," having an unsteady mind. He is "smeared with dirt," meaning his body is covered in filth. He "talks excessively," prattling in many ways. He has "repulsive limbs," meaning his body is gross or disproportionate. (113)

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Animal Temperament—

-> One who is timid, hungry, and eats a great deal <-
-> should be known as a man with the temperament of animals. <-
-> Thus the nature of men is explained, <-
-> which those who know the signs call "Temperament." (114) <-

The man who is "timid" is afflicted by fear. "Hungry" means he cannot endure hunger. One who "eats a great deal" is a glutton. Such a person should be understood to have the temperament of "animals" <note>original: "tiryag" - literally "going horizontally," referring to beasts or birds</note>. In this manner, the "nature" <note>original: "prakriti"</note> of men has been declared. Those who know the signs—the experts in human physiognomy—speak of this as "Temperament" <note>original: "sattva"</note>. And so says the sage Garga:

-> Complexion is very auspicious, but Voice is more auspicious than Complexion. <-

-> Thus ends the section on Natural Temperament. (114) <-

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Fiery Shadow:

->**Fierce, invincible, colored like lotus, gold, and fire,**<-
->**Endowed with brilliance, valor, and great majesty;**<-

The Fiery shadow <term>Agneyi Chhaya; the aura associated with the element of fire</term> is fierce, meaning prone to anger. It is invincible, meaning it cannot be overcome by others. It is "colored like lotus, gold, and fire," meaning its luster is equal to the hue of a lotus flower, gold, or a blazing fire. Furthermore, it is "endowed with brilliance, valor, and great majesty," meaning it is accompanied by radiance, physical prowess, and the heroic power to subdue enemies. The word "thus" <note>original: "iti"</note> indicates the category. This type of shadow leads to the victory of living beings and quickly—almost immediately—grants the accomplishment of their desired objectives. ||92||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Airy and Ethereal Shadows:

->**Dirty, harsh, black, foul-smelling, and born of the wind,**<-

The shadow "born of the wind" <term>Vayavi Chhaya; the aura associated with the air element</term> is dirty in color and lacks clarity. It is harsh or rough, and black in hue. It is foul-smelling. It produces or generates the following: death, imprisonment, diseases (afflictions), misfortune (lack of gain), and the destruction of wealth (the loss of accumulated riches).

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Ethereal Shadow:

Regarding "Crystal," etc.: The shadow "born of the sky" <term>Nabhasi Chhaya; the aura associated with the ether or space element</term> is the Ethereal one. Its form resembles crystal, meaning its luster is equal to that of a crystal gem. This implies it is extremely pure. It is "fortunate," meaning accompanied by good luck. It is "exceedingly noble," meaning highly generous in nature, and acts like a "treasury of all blessings" <note>original: "shreyasam nidhiriva"</note>. This means it bestows everything good. Finally, it is "clear in color," meaning stainless and pure. ||93||

# Chapter 67: The Chapter on the Characteristics of Men

On this same subject, the author presents five other types of radiance according to different schools of thought:

> The types of radiance arise in order from Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether.
> Some authorities say there are ten, and these follow a specific sequence:
> They are equal in characteristics and results to the Sun, Vishnu, Indra, Yama, and the Moon; this is the summary of the matter. || 94 ||

"Earth" refers to the element of soil. "Water" refers to the Varuna element. "Fire" refers to the consumer of oblations. "Air" refers to the wind. "Ether" refers to the sky. The types of radiance arising from these five occur in a specific order. Some sages, such as Garga and others, speak of ten types of radiance. The five mentioned previously and five more are now being discussed. These also follow a sequence corresponding to the Sun, Vishnu <note>original: "Abjanabha," literally "lotus-navelled"</note>, Indra <note>original: "Puruhuta," "the much-invoked"</note>, Yama <note>the Lord of the Ancestors</note>, and the Moon <note>original: "Udupa," "lord of the stars"</note>.

These types of radiance are equal in their physical characteristics and their predicted results to the five previously mentioned. Specifically: the Solar radiance is the same as the Fiery; the Vishnu radiance is the same as the Ethereal; the Indra radiance is the same as the Earthly; the Yama radiance is the same as the Airy; and the Lunar radiance is the same as the Watery. This is the "summary of the matter." For this reason, a synthesis of these ten types of radiance has been made. Because their results are identical, they are treated as only five. As Garga says:

> Five are proclaimed as arising from Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether;
> And there are others belonging to the Earth, Vishnu, Indra, the Sun, and the Moon.

This concludes the section on luster <note>original: "mrija," referring to the brightness or cleanliness of the complexion</note>. || 94 ||

Now, he describes the characteristics of the voice:

> Those whose voices sound like an elephant, a bull, a fleet of chariots, a kettle-drum, a *mridanga* drum, a lion, or a thundercloud <gloss>1</gloss> become kings.
> Those with voices like a donkey, or those that are cracked or harsh, are devoid of wealth and happiness. || 95 ||

"Elephant" refers to the tusker. "Bull" refers to the ox. "Fleet of chariots" refers to a multitude of vehicles. "Kettle-drum" is the *bheri*. The *mridanga* is a well-known musical instrument <note>a barrel-shaped drum used in classical music</note>. "Lion" is the king of beasts. "Thundercloud" refers to the clouds in the sky. <note>The text notes an alternate reading "abda" which also means cloud.</note> Those possessing voices similar to these sounds become kings. A "donkey" is a braying ass. "Cracked" refers to a distorted or broken tone. "Harsh" means rough or grating. Those with voices like a donkey and so on are "devoid of wealth and happiness," meaning they are deprived of riches and comforts. As Garga says:

> Deep, resonant like a drum, smooth, loud, and echoing—
> These are the five virtues of the voice, as told by Samudra, the knower of truth.

1. There is an alternate reading: "Lion and cloud."

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 67]

Through these [auspicious voices], one gains long life, fame, knowledge, honor, happiness, and the arrival of wealth, vehicles, sons, wives, and the enjoyment of royal pleasures.
Conversely, voices that are broken, cracked, stammering, faltering, or weak are condemned by the sage Samudra <note>The mythical founder of Samudrika Shastra, or physiognomy</note>.
Through such [inauspicious] voices, one identifies strife, anger, greed, delusion, darkness, passion, cruelty, pride, harshness, and deceit.
**Thus ends the section on the Voice.** || 95 ||

->Now he describes the Essences (Sara)—<-

**There are seven essences: fat, marrow, skin, bone, semen, blood, and flesh. These are found in living beings; their collective results are as follows.** || 96 ||

There are seven essences in men. **Fat** <term>Medas: the fatty tissue within the body</term>. **Marrow** <term>Majja: the substance found within the skull and bones</term>. **Skin** <term>Tvak: the outer covering</term>. **Bone** <term>Asthi: the skeletal structure</term>. **Semen** <term>Shukra: reproductive fluid</term>. **Blood** <term>Rudhira: the red vital fluid</term>. **Flesh** <term>Mamsa: the muscle or meat</term>. The word "and" implies the collection of these. These seven types of essences belong to living beings. Their collective results are now being stated in brief. || 96 ||

->First, he describes the characteristics of the Blood-Essence type—<-

**When the palate, lips, gums, tongue, corners of the eyes, anus, hands, and feet are red, the person is of the "Blood-Essence" type; they possess much happiness, many wives, wealth, and sons.** || 97 ||

The **palate** is the roof of the mouth. The **lips** are the covers of the teeth. The **gums** <note>original: "dantapali"</note> are the rows of flesh around the teeth. The **tongue** is the organ of taste. The **corners of the eyes** refer to the edges of the vision. The **anus** is the private excretory passage. The **hands** and **feet** are well known. When these eight parts are red (crimson), men are of the "Blood-Essence" type. They are endowed with many comforts, wives, great wealth, and many sons. || 97 ||

->Now he describes the Skin, Marrow, and Fat Essences—<-

**Those with glossy skin are wealthy; those with soft skin are fortunate; those with thin skin are wise. Those with Marrow or Fat as their essence have beautiful bodies and are endowed with sons and wealth.** || 98 ||

**Skin** refers to the hide. Those whose skin is **glossy** (not dry) are wealthy. Those with **soft** skin are endowed with good fortune. Those with **thin** skin are wise or learned scholars. Those men who are of the **Marrow-Essence** or **Fat-Essence** types possess "good bodies" (handsome or well-formed physiques). This is their characteristic. They are also endowed with children and riches. || 98 ||

### Now, he describes the essence of bone and semen—

**One with the essence of bone has thick bones, is strong, reaches the end of knowledge, and is handsome.**
**Those with abundant and heavy semen are fortunate, learned, and beautiful. ||99||**

He whose bones are thick is "bone-essential." Such a living being is strong. He "reaches the end of knowledge," meaning he is capable of mastering sciences, and is "handsome," possessing a beautiful form. Those who have "abundant and heavy semen"—meaning semen that is plentiful and weighty—are "semen-essential." They are "fortunate," endowed with good luck, "learned" as readers and scholars, and "beautiful," possessing a lovely appearance. ||99||

### Now, he describes the characteristics of the essence of flesh and the characteristics of bodily compactness—

**He who has the essence of flesh has a well-developed body, is learned, wealthy, and handsome.**
**"Compactness" is known as having well-knit joints; such people are enjoyers of happiness. ||100||**

"Well-developed body" means a stout or robust physique. He is "flesh-essential." He is also "learned," a scholar; "wealthy," possessing riches; and "handsome," having a beautiful form—this concludes the essence.

Now, the characteristic of compactness: "Compactness" refers to the "well-knit nature of the joints," meaning all the joints of the limbs are firmly joined. This well-knit quality of joints is to be known in those who "enjoy happiness." The meaning is that those whose joints are well-knit are enjoyers of comfort. ||100||

### Now, he describes the characteristics of glossiness—

**Glossiness is to be observed in five places: the voice, tongue, teeth, eyes, and nails.**
**With these being glossy, men are endowed with children, wealth, and fortune; with these being dry, they are penniless. ||101||**

"Glossiness" <note>Sanskrit: *Sneha*, referring to a healthy, oily luster or moisture</note> is to be observed or examined in five things. In what? In the "voice" or speech; in the "tongue"; in the "teeth"; in the "eyes"; and in the "nails." It resides in these. If all these—the voice and so on—are "glossy" or moist, men are "endowed with children, wealth, and fortune." "Children" means sons; "wealth" means riches; "fortune" means being liked by all people. They are joined with these qualities. If those same parts are all "dry" or lacking glossiness, they are "penniless" or poor. ||101||

### Now, he describes the characteristics of complexion—

**A glossy complexion is radiant and belongs to kings; a medium one to those with children and wealth.**
**A dry complexion belongs to those devoid of wealth; a pure complexion gives auspicious results, not a mixed one. ||102||**

"Complexion" <note>Sanskrit: *Varna*, referring to skin tone and luster</note> refers to colors such as fair, reddish, or dark. He whose complexion is "glossy" is "radiant," meaning he possesses a glow. This belongs to "kings" or rulers of the earth. A "medium" complexion—one that is neither too dry nor too...

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 67]

A glossy complexion belongs to those who possess children and wealth. A dry or dull complexion belongs to those devoid of wealth—the poor. A pure complexion is only beneficial and praiseworthy when it is glossy. It should not be "mixed" or variegated. A complexion that is glossy in some places and dry in others is not auspicious. Thus ends the section on Complexion.

### Now he describes the characteristics of Past Lives (Anuka)—

> **The past life is to be determined from the face; those with faces resembling a cow, a bull, a tiger, a lion, or a Garuda <note>a divine bird-like creature</note> possess irresistible valor, conquer their enemies, and become lords of men.**
> **Those with faces resembling a monkey, a buffalo, a boar, or a goat enjoy learning, wealth, and happiness. Those with faces and bodies resembling a donkey or a young camel are devoid of wealth and happiness.**

<term>Anuka</term> <note>original: "anūka"</note> refers to the previous birth. This is to be inferred or imagined from the <term>vaktra</term> or face. The cow is well-known. The bull is the ox. The tiger is a specific powerful animal similar to a lion. The lion is the king of beasts. <term>Garuda</term> is the son of Vinata. Those whose faces are similar to these have had an auspicious previous birth. They possess irresistible valor—meaning their power cannot be overcome. They are conquerors of enemies and become kings or lords of men.

The monkey is the ape. The buffalo is well-known. The boar is the pig. The goat is the ram. Men with faces similar to these are partakers of learning, wealth, and happiness. "Learning" refers to the sacred scriptures. "Wealth" is riches. "Happiness" is self-evident. They share in these things. Their previous birth was of a middle or mediocre quality. The donkey is the ass. The <term>karabha</term> is the camel. With faces and bodies resembling donkeys and camels, they become destitute and miserable. "Destitute" means without wealth; "miserable" means devoid of happiness. Their previous birth was inauspicious. Thus ends the section on Past Lives.

### Now he describes the characteristics of Height (Unmana)—

> **One hundred and eight, ninety-six, and eighty-four are the measurements for men of the best, middle, and inferior types respectively, measured in the units of their own fingers.**

For men, the <term>Angula-sankhya</term> <note>finger-count</note> is the measurement according to their own proportions. One hundred and eight (108) of their own fingers is the height of the "best" or superior men. Ninety-six (96) fingers is the height for "middle" men. Eighty-four (84) fingers is the height for "inferior" men. The rule is: one should measure a standing man by placing a string from the point where the feet touch the ground up to the center of the head, using the person's own finger-width as the unit. Thus ends the section on Height.

### Now he describes the characteristics of Weight (Mana)—

> **One whose body weighs half a <term>bhara</term> enjoys happiness; one who weighs more than that is also happy, but one who weighs less suffers. A weight of one <term>bhara</term> belongs to the wealthy, while one and a half <term>bharas</term> belongs to a ruler of the whole earth.**

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Men
[Chapter 67]

A *bhara* <note>A traditional unit of weight; original: "bhara"</note> is equal to two thousand *palas* <note>A smaller unit of weight; original: "pala"</note>. A man who, when weighed on a scale, weighs half a *bhara*—meaning one thousand *palas*—is a possessor of happiness and lives comfortably. One who weighs less than this half-*bhara* is a possessor of misery and is unhappy. A body weighing exactly one *bhara* belongs to the wealthy or the very rich. One whose body weighs one and a half *bharas* (three thousand *palas*) is a ruler of the entire earth, meaning a universal emperor. ॥106॥

Explaining at what time one should measure height and weight, the author says:

**A woman at twenty years and a man at twenty-five years,**
**Are fit for measurement of height and weight, or at the completion of the fourth part of their lifespan.** ॥107॥

A woman is fit for measurement of weight and height at twenty years. "Weight" refers to the scale measurement, and "height" refers to vertical measurement in fingers and so on. Similarly, a man is fit for measurement at twenty-five years; he becomes suitable for these measurements then. The word "khalu" <note>original: "khalu"</note> is used here as a poetic ornament. This is stated assuming a fixed lifespan of one hundred years. Or, they are fit for measurement when the fourth part of their life has passed. If the lifespan is determined to be less than a hundred years, the "fourth part" rule applies. This concludes the section on measurements. ॥107॥

### Now, the Characteristics of Natures (Prakriti) are described:

**By the essence of Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Ether, Gods, Humans, Demons, Spirits, and Animals,**
**A man is formed; these are their specific characteristics.** ॥108॥

"Earth" is well-known. "Water" relates to Varuna. "Fire" is Agni. "Wind" is Vayu. "Ether" is space. "Gods" are the celestial beings. "Humans" are men. "Demons" are Rakshasas. "Spirits" are the Pisachas (a class of semi-divine beings). "Animals" are the non-human species. A man is characterized by the essence or nature of these. Their characteristics will be described hereafter. Some read the text as "Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Ether, Gods, Humans, Demons, Spirits, and Animal," <note>original: "bhū-jala-śikhy-anilāmbarasuranararakṣaḥ-piśācatiryañcam"</note> but that is incorrect; it should be "of Animals" (plural). Therefore, the previous reading is better. ॥108॥

### Characteristics of the Earth-nature and Water-nature:

**One with the nature of Earth has the scent of auspicious flowers,**
**Enjoys pleasures, has pleasant breath, and is steady.**
**One with the nature of Water drinks much water,**
**Speaks kindly, and <gloss>1</gloss> enjoys flavorful food.** ॥109॥

A man of **Earthly nature** <note>Sanskrit: *mahisvabhāvaḥ*</note> possesses the fragrance of beautiful flowers, such as the Champaka and others. He is inclined toward enjoyment and possesses "good breath." By the term "breath" here, it implies a pleasant-smelling and comfortable exhalation. He is also of a steady character. One of a **Watery nature** <note>Sanskrit: *toyasvabhāvaḥ*</note> drinks a great deal of water. He speaks kindly and agreeably. He is a "vessel of flavors," meaning he is fond of and suited for various tastes like sweetness. Some read this as "one who eats flavorful foods" <note>original: *rasabhojanaśca*</note>. || 109 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of Fire and Wind:

->One of **Fiery nature** is restless, very sharp,<-
->fierce, easily famished, and a great eater.<-
->By the **nature of Wind**, one is unsteady and lean,<-
->and quickly falls under the power of anger.<- || 110 ||

A man of **Fiery nature** is restless—unsteady in his actions. He is very sharp or harsh. He is fierce and cruel. He is "famished," meaning he cannot endure hunger. He is a "great eater," consuming much food. By the **nature of Wind**, a man is of unsteady mind. He is lean or weak. He quickly—very rapidly—falls under the power of anger, becoming its subject. || 110 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of Ether and Divine nature:

->One of **Etheric nature** is clever, with an open mouth,<-
->skilled in the ways of sound, and has well-veined limbs.<-
->A man of **Divine nature** is endowed with generosity,<-
->is mild in anger, and is devoted to affection.<- || 111 ||

A man of **Etheric nature** <note>Sanskrit: *khaprakṛtiḥ*; Ether or Space is the subtlest element</note> is clever, possessing a refined vision for the arts. He has an "open mouth" <note>likely meaning a gaping expression or a large mouth</note>. He is skilled in the "ways of sound," meaning he is capable in the reach and application of Sanskrit words. Alternatively, it means he is skilled in the movements described in the sciences. Some read this as "skilled in the gait of sound" <note>original: *śabdagatau kuśalaḥ*</note>. He has "well-veined limbs," meaning his veins are prominent or well-formed. A man of **Divine nature** <note>Sanskrit: *surasattvaḥ*; literally "god-like essence"</note> is generous. He is "mild in anger," possessing little wrath, and is "devoted to affection," being full of love. || 111 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Human temperament—

->A man endowed with the human temperament is fond of music and ornaments.<-
->He is inclined toward sharing and is always of good character. ||112||<-

"Human" refers to a mortal man. One endowed with that temperament is "fond of music and ornaments"—meaning he loves songs and loves jewelry or decorations (<note>original: "bhushana"</note>). "Inclined toward sharing" means he is helpful to his kinsmen by distributing wealth or resources properly. "Of good character" means he possesses a virtuous conduct. This is "always," meaning at all times, the nature of such a man. ||112||

### Now he describes the characteristics of Ogre and Ghostly temperaments—

->One with the temperament of Night-stalkers <note>demonic beings or Rakshasas</note> is fiercely irritable, acts like a villain, and is sinful.<-
->One with a Ghostly temperament is fickle, smeared with dirt,<-
->talks excessively, and has a repulsive or oversized body. ||113||<-

By the temperament of "Night-stalkers" (Rakshasas), a man is "fiercely irritable," meaning he possesses a terrible anger. "Acts like a villain" means his behavior is like that of a wicked person. He is "sinful," meaning he is devoted to sinful acts. A man of "Ghostly temperament" (<note>original: "Pishacha-sattva"</note>) is "fickle," having an unsteady mind. He is "smeared with dirt," meaning his body is covered in impurities. He "talks excessively," prattling in many ways. He has "repulsive or oversized limbs," meaning his body parts are gross or disproportionate. ||113||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the Animal temperament—

->The man who is timid, constantly hungry, and a glutton<-
->should be known as having the temperament of animals.<-
->Thus the nature of men has been explained,<-
->which those skilled in the knowledge of marks call "Sattva" <note>inner essence or temperament</note>. ||114||<-

The man who is "timid" is one afflicted by fear. "Constantly hungry" means he cannot endure hunger. He who is a "glutton" or eats excessively is to be known as having the temperament of "animals" (<note>original: "tiryak," referring to sub-human creatures like beasts or birds</note>). In this manner, the "nature" (<note>original: "prakriti"</note>) of men has been "explained" or stated. This is what those "skilled in marks"—the experts in human physiognomy—call "Sattva." And so says the sage Garga:

->Complexion is very auspicious, but the voice is more auspicious than complexion.<-
->The inner temperament (Sattva) is more auspicious than the voice; everything is established in the Sattva.<-

Thus ends the section on Natural Temperament. ||114||

### Now, he describes the characteristics of gait (manner of walking)—

> "Those whose gait resembles that of a tiger, a swan, an elephant in rut, a bull, or a peacock, become kings. Those whose walk is silent and steady also become lords; however, those who walk with a hurried or hopping motion are poor." ||195||

A tiger <note>original: "shārdūla"</note> is a specific type of powerful animal. A swan is a bird. Some read the text as "tiger and lion" <margin>Alternative reading: tiger and lion</margin>. A lion is the king of beasts. An elephant in rut <note>original: "samada-dvipa"</note> means an intoxicated or powerful elephant. A "lord of cows" refers to a bull. Likewise, the peacock. Those whose movements are equal or similar to the gaits of these creatures become kings. Furthermore, those whose walking is silent—without sound—and steady or measured, they too are masters and wealthy. Those who are "hurried or hopping" are poor; this means those who walk too quickly or with a jerky, agitated motion like a frog. They become destitute. Thus ends the section on gait. ||195||

### He states the conclusion—

> "A vehicle for the weary, food for the hungry, drink for the thirsty, and protection in times of fear—the experts in human characteristics declare that man truly blessed who receives these things at the proper time." ||196||

For a man who is weary or exhausted, a vehicle <note>original: "yāna"</note> such as a horse or carriage is provided. For the hungry, there is food. For one overcome by thirst, there is water to drink. When fears arise, there is protection or guardianship. When these things are available exactly when needed, the experts in human signs <term>Naralakshanajña: those skilled in the traditional science of reading bodily marks and omens</term> call that man "blessed" or possessed of auspicious signs. ||196||

->Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, named "Characteristics of Men,"<-
->in the Commentary on the Compilation composed by the venerable Bhattotpala.<-

I shall now describe them." ||1||

# Chapter on the Five Divisions of Men

The **star-planets** <note>original: "tārāgrahā" - refers to the five visible planets excluding the Sun and Moon: Mercury, Mars, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note>—namely Mercury, Mars, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn—when they are endowed with strength <note>possessing strength of position, direction, motion, and time</note>, and are situated in their own zodiac signs, or in their signs of exaltation, and are located in a quadrant <note>the 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses of a birth chart</note>, then five types of excellent men are born. I shall now describe and speak of those men. || 1 ||

-> Now he describes the specific divisions of these types: <-

**By Jupiter, one becomes a Hamsa; by Saturn, a Shasha; by Mars, a Ruchaka;**
**By a strong Mercury, a Bhadra; and by Venus, the priest of the demons, a Malavya.** || 2 ||

By a strong Jupiter, the man born is called **Hamsa** <note>literally "Swan"</note>. Likewise, by a strong Saturn, he is **Shasha** <note>literally "Hare"</note>. By a strong Mars, the combination called **Ruchaka** <note>literally "Bright" or "Agreeable"</note> occurs. By a strong Mercury, he is **Bhadra** <note>literally "Auspicious"</note>. By a strong Venus, the priest of the demons, he is **Malavya** <note>referring to the Malwa region or a specific noble type</note>. Thus it is said in the *Saravali* <note>A classic 8th-century astrological treatise by Kalyanavarman</note>:

> "When Venus, Mars, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mercury are strong in their own signs or exaltation signs and situated in quadrants, they respectively create the Malavya, Ruchaka, Shasha, Hamsa, and Bhadra types. The characteristics of all these are now described in great detail according to the opinions of the Sages." || 2 ||

In the following two verses, he explains the specific distinctions based on the strength of the Sun and the Moon:

**Innate character is derived from the Sun; physical and mental strength from the strength of the Moon.**
**A man possesses the characteristics of the specific zodiacal divisions in which these two are placed.** || 3 ||
**Through their respective bodily humors, elements, temperaments, luster, color, character, and form,**
**men of mixed characteristics are born if the Sun and Moon are weak.** || 4 ||

"Innate character <note>original: "sattvam"</note> is derived from the Sun"—this means the quality of one's being is full and complete based on the Sun's influence. Physical attributes, the luster of the body, and mental vigor are derived from the strength of the Moon. How so? He says: "from the specific zodiacal divisions." These two (Sun and Moon) are situated in divisions such as the *Hora* <note>1/2 sign</note>, *Drekkana* <note>1/3 sign</note>, *Navamsha* <note>1/9 sign</note>, *Dvadasamsha* <note>1/12 sign</note>, or *Trimshamsha* <note>1/30 sign</note> belonging to Mars and the others, or in their own. A man possesses the characteristics of the planet that rules that specific division. These zodiacal divisions were explained in the Chapter on Divisions in the *Jataka* <note>horoscopy</note> section. || 3 ||

Regarding "their respective bodily humors, elements, and temperaments": It was said that a man takes on the characteristics of the ruler of the division where the Sun and Moon are placed. In that regard, his bodily humor <note>original: "dhatu"</note> becomes that of the ruling planet. For example, the humors are:
