<meta>This page continues the commentary on Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita, specifically Chapter 70, which deals with the omens derived from the tearing or damage of garments and shoes. The text transitions from general rules to specific directional and symbolic interpretations.</meta>

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 70]

If a garment is worn out, it yields very little result. Although it was previously stated that the same rules apply to beds, seats, and sandals, the effects—whether sinful and inauspicious or virtuous and auspicious—are far more potent when they occur on an upper garment. ||10||

->Now he speaks specifically:<-

**If the damage occurs in the portions belonging to Demons, there is disease or death; in the portions of Humans, there is the birth of a son and glory; in the portions of the Immortals, there is an increase in enjoyment. However, damage at the very edges is said to be inauspicious in all cases. ||11||**

In the "Demon portions" <note>Rakshasa-amsha: specific zones of a garment or object determined by ritual measurement</note>, if tears or holes appear, the owner suffers from disease or even death. If such damage is seen in the "Human portion," it results in the birth of a male child and an increase in luster or influence. If the damage is seen in the portion belonging to the "Immortals" <note>Deva-amsha: the divine or auspicious zones</note>, there is an increase in worldly pleasures. The Sages say that damage at the very edges or borders is undesirable and inauspicious in every instance. ||11||

->He says something further:<-

**If the shape of the tear resembles a heron, a water-crow, an owl, a pigeon, a crow, a flesh-eater <note>predatory birds</note>, a jackal, a donkey, a camel, or a snake, it brings fear equal to death for men, even if it occurs in the portion of the Gods. ||12||**

The heron, water-crow, owl, pigeon, and crow are specific types of birds; "flesh-eaters" refers to carnivorous animals. The jackal, the donkey, the camel, and the snake are also listed. If the shape of a tear resembles any of these, it creates a fear comparable to death for men, even if that tear is located in the otherwise auspicious "God-portion." ||12||

->He says something further:<-

**If the shape of the tear resembles a parasol, a banner, a swastika, a *Vardhamana* <note>a specific cruciform symbol of prosperity</note>, a *Shrivatsa* <note>an auspicious mark often found on the chest of Vishnu</note>, a water-pot, a lotus, or a triumphal arch, it bestows wealth upon men before long, even if it occurs in the portion of the Demons. ||13||**

The parasol is a sunshade. The banner is well-known. The *Swastika* and *Vardhamana* are specific auspicious marks; both are physical symbols. The *Shrivatsa* is associated with the Bilva tree or the divine mark. The "pot" is a water-jar. The "lotus" is the flower. The "arch" is the ceremonial gateway. By the use of the word "etcetera," one should also include shapes like the sacrificial ladle, the fire-pit, the vase, the elephant, and the horse. If a tear resembles these, it grants Lakshmi <note>the Goddess of Wealth</note> to men very quickly, even if it is located in the "Demon portion" <note>Nairrita-bhaga: the southwest or demonic zone</note>. By the use of the word "even," it is implied that if such shapes appear in the God or Human portions, the auspicious results are even greater.

On this subject, the Sage Parashara has spoken more specifically. As follows:

> "Now we shall explain the omens of shoes being eaten <note>by insects or rodents</note> or torn. There are twenty types of tears. Among them, seven are praised, and the rest are condemned. If the area near the big toe, known as the region of the Sacred Fire, is eaten away, it indicates the gain of food, drink, and women..."

# [Chapter 70] The Chapter on the Characteristics of Tears in Clothing | 813

...one should know. A tear by the index finger <note>referring to the part of the shoe corresponding to the toe</note> indicates the gain of a woman or clothing. By the middle finger, death or imprisonment. By the ring finger, the death of the mother or the renunciation <note>becoming a wandering ascetic</note> of a sister. By the little finger, the death of the father or a brother. From the nose <note>the front tip of the shoe</note>, the gain of a woman. At the base of the thumb or toes, fear of disease. At the top knot <note>the decorative or structural peak</note>, mental distress. At the neck <note>the opening</note>, decapitation. 

If the tear is at the place of binding, one obtains food, drink, and wealth. If a small piece of the ear <note>the side flap</note> is eaten <note>by insects or vermin</note>, there is fear of a breach of alliance. If the whole part is eaten, a quarrel begins. A tear at the heel-binding indicates a journey. At the heel-place, the arrival of a vehicle. From the tearing or eating of the outer foot-fold, one should know the destruction of friends and brothers. In a medium-quality shoe, a great arrival of wealth. In a high-quality shoe, general gain. In the middle of the foot, the arrival of sorrow. On the sides, disease of the flanks. If the entire shoe is eaten, death, flight, and exhaustion occur.

->Furthermore:<-

> In new shoes, the full results are felt; in used ones, the results are moderate.
> One should specify the good and bad omens; in worn-out shoes, there is no result.
> By serving elders, the aged, twice-born <term>Brahmins</term>, and teachers, and by performing auspicious baths,
> A mortal is released from the faults of these inauspicious signs.

->Thus ends the characteristics of tears in footwear.<-

Now, the indications of the fruits of good and evil regarding garments. We shall teach the characteristics of the knowledge regarding the sudden appearance of ink, mud, collyrium <note>eye-salve</note>, blood, or cow dung; or the eating <note>damage</note> by eclipses, rats, insects, or cows; or being scorched by wood, thorns, or fire. 

There, one should divide the cloth into nine parts, with the fringe facing East and the fringe facing West, in three rows. In those parts, the rule of the fruits is in order: Loss of wealth. Arrival of wealth. Diminution of money. Destruction of a woman. Affliction of a son. Death of a daughter. Disease of one's own body. And the arrival of calamity—these are for the first eight. In the ninth, travel on the road, arrival of wealth, and success in actions. 

If the marks are in the shape of a pot, a mirror, a piece of an ear, a weapon, a foot, a triple-peak, the moon, a circular ornament, a tablet, a house, a gateway, an umbrella, a girdle, a well-protected altar, a lotus, a conch, the *Shrivatsa* <note>an auspicious curl of hair symbol</note>, a swastika, a fish, or a *Vardhamana* <note>a specific auspicious diagram</note>, then in order, there is great arrival of wealth. 

<margin>Marks shaped like a belly indicate stomach disease; an ear shape, ear pain; a weapon shape, opposition; a foot shape, travel; a triple-peak, ill health; the moon, calamity; a circular ornament, sovereignty; a tablet, the arrival of an inauguration.</margin>

By shapes of a snare, a hawk, a field, a winnowing basket, a needle, or a noose, and by shapes of a skeleton or a small stool, death occurs. By shapes resembling elephants, chariots, or horses, one obtains cattle, sons, wealth, and sovereignty. By shapes like the ears of a horse or elephant, a vulva, a scale, or a sparrow, there is recovery, but as before, it may lead to the destruction of the family. 

In the North-East, it affects women. In the South, friends. In the South-West, cattle. In the West, servants. In the North-West, kinsmen. In the North, relatives. In the North-East, the middle-class. In the East, all prosperity. Furthermore:

> A garment that has become discolored and is torn is an auspicious sign.
> But a garment that is merely discolored should be pointed out as leading to misfortune.
> The fruit is as stated for a new garment; it is not desired <note>does not apply</note> for a worn-out one.
> Nor for one that is dyed, nor one recently washed, nor one burnt or torn by oneself.

### Now, the characteristics of fly-whisks are explained.

To begin, the author speaks to show the origin and purpose of these items:

> It is said that the gods created the Yak-cows <note>original: "chamaryah" - the female Bos grunniens, whose tail hair is used for royal and ritual whisks</note> in the caves of the snowy mountains <note>The Himalayas</note> for the sake of their hair.
> Their tail-hairs are found to be yellowish-white, black, and pure white. || 1 ||

The word "it is said" <note>original: "kila"</note> indicates traditional transmission. The gods (the immortals) created these specific animals, the Yaks, in the caves of the Himalayan mountains for the purpose of obtaining their hair <insert>for whisks</insert>. The hair of these Yaks is slightly yellow; they are also black (dark); and the hair produced from the tail is also white (bright-colored). || 1 ||

Now, he describes their quality:

> Glossiness, softness, abundance of hair, clarity, a small bone-attachment,
> and whiteness are said to be the excellence of their qualities. Those that are pierced, small, or mangled are not auspicious. || 2 ||

This is described as the wealth of qualities for those Yak-whisks. Specifically: "Glossiness" means a lack of coarseness. "Softness" means tenderness to the touch. "Abundance of hair" means having many strands. "Clarity" <term>Vaishadyam: refers to the hairs being clean and not sticking together</term>. "Small bone-attachment" refers to the base where the hairs are fastened; the part where the bone or root is attached should be small. "Whiteness" means a bright white color. These are the good traits. Conversely, those that are "pierced" (referring to holes or cracks in the mounting), "small" (short in length), or "mangled" (broken or thinning) are not beautiful; they are considered inauspicious. || 2 ||

# Chapter 71: The Characteristics of the Fly-Whisk

Now, the author describes the characteristics of the fly-whisk handle:

> The handle of this fly-whisk should measure one and a half cubits <note>original: "adhyardha-hasta"; a 'hasta' or cubit is roughly 18 inches</note>, or one cubit, or one *aratni* <note>a measurement from the elbow to the tip of the closed fist</note>. It should be made of auspicious wood, encased in gold or silver, and adorned with all types of gems for the welfare of kings. ||3||

The handle of this fly-whisk should be made measuring one and a half cubits. Alternatively, it may be one cubit in length. Another option is to make it equal to an *aratni*. An *aratni* is a hand with a closed fist; some say it is the length to the little finger. This handle should be made from auspicious wood possessing excellent characteristics. Of what kind? It should be well-concealed or covered with gold or silver. When combined with various precious gems and jewels, it brings benefit to kings (monarchs). ||3||

Now, he describes the characteristics of the handle according to the order of the castes:

> For staves, parasols, elephant-goads, canes, bows, canopies, spears, banners, and fly-whisks, handles that are yellowish-white, reddish-brown, honey-colored, or black are beneficial according to the order of the castes. ||4||

The "stave" <note>term: yashti; a walking stick or staff of authority</note> is well-known and held constantly in the hand. The "parasol" is the royal umbrella. The "goad" is well-known and used for subduing elephants. The "cane" is a familiar staff. The "bow" is the weapon. The "canopy" is known in common parlance as a ceiling-cloth or awning. The "spear" is a weapon. The "banner" is a standard or sign. The "fly-whisk" is the fan made of animal hair <note>usually the tail of a yak</note>. The colors of the handles for these items are beneficial when they are yellowish-white, reddish-brown, honey-colored, or black in sequence. Specifically: for Brahmins, yellowish staves are praised for welfare. Similarly, reddish-brown <note>original: "tantri-varna"</note> colors are for Kshatriyas (warriors). Honey-colored (slightly yellow) are for Vaishyas (merchants). Black colors are for Shudras. As Garga <note>an ancient sage and astronomer</note> says:

> "For Brahmins, it should be yellow; for Kshatriyas, red; for Vaishyas, yellow-colored; and for Shudras, it should have a black luster. The handle should be known as bestowing auspiciousness for staves, umbrellas, goads, and so forth." ||4||

He now describes the results of having an even number of joints <note>nodes or segments in the wood</note> on the handle:

> Destruction of mother, land, wealth, and family, as well as the production of disease and death, are the results of joints starting from two and increasing by two, ending at twelve. ||5||

For these handles and staves, when the joints increase by two—meaning even numbers—ending at twelve, the results are given in order. <note>The text implies that specific even numbers of joints correspond to specific misfortunes listed in the verse.</note>

# On the Characteristics of Royal Insignia [Chapter 72]

**Regarding the destruction of the mother and the land:** For instance, if the handles of the fly-whisks are joined by two joints <note>pava: the nodes or segments of a bamboo or wooden handle</note>, they bring about the destruction of the mother. This means the mother’s death. With four joints, they cause the loss of land. With six, the loss of wealth. With eight, the destruction of the family lineage. With ten, they generate and bestow disease. With twelve, they generate and bestow death.

->Now he describes the results for those same handles when they have odd numbers of joints, starting from three and increasing by two:<-

->Success in journeys, the destruction of enemies,<-
->Abundant gains, and the acquisition of land;<-
->The increase of livestock, and the attainment of desires—<-
->These occur for the owners when the joints are odd, starting from three.<-

For the owners <note>the kings or masters of these objects</note> of these handles and such, these are the fruits when the joints are odd—three and upwards, increasing by two. For example: with three joints on the handle, there is success and victory in journeys. With five, the destruction of enemies. With seven, abundant and numerous gains. With nine, the acquisition of land. With eleven, the increase of livestock <note>literally "four-legged animals"</note>. With thirteen, the attainment or gain of one's cherished desires. Beyond twelve or thirteen joints, the results for even or odd numbers are merely generally inauspicious or auspicious; there are no specific specialized results.

->**Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, named "Characteristics of the Fly-Whisk,"**<-

->**Now, the "Characteristics of the Umbrella" are explained.**<-

At the very beginning, he speaks to demonstrate the purpose:

->Constructed with the feathers of swans, or of wild cocks, peacocks, or cranes;<-
->Covered all around with new, white silk;<-
->Adorned with pearls, draped with hanging garlands, with a base of crystal;<-
->With a staff of pure gold six cubits long, and a single shaft of nine joints;<-
->The width being half the length of the staff, well-rounded, adorned with gems, and lofty—<-
->Such a parasol for a king is the height of auspiciousness and grants victory.<-

**Constructed:** For a king, such a parasol <term>Atapatra: literally "that which protects from the heat," a royal umbrella</term> is the height of auspiciousness and brings welfare. It also grants victory. Of what kind? It is "constructed with the feathers of swans." The swan is a bird...

# Chapter on the Characteristics of the Umbrella
<page-num>817</page-num>

It is covered or constructed with the feathers and plumage of those birds. The *krikavaku* <note>original: "kṛkavāku"</note> refers to the rooster. The peacock and the crane are well-known. It should be covered with the feathers of the rooster, peacock, or crane. It is then covered all around with a new, unwashed *dukula* <note>a fine silk or linen fabric</note>, specifically a white silk cloth, making it white in color.

Regarding the pearls: it is adorned or joined with pearls and gemstones. It is fitted all around with hanging strings of pearls. The base is made of crystal; that is, it has a crystal stone at its foundation. It features a single staff <note>danda</note> measuring six cubits <note>term: hasta; a unit of measurement approximately 18 inches</note> in length. It is covered in pure, high-quality gold. It should be joined with nine or seven joints <note>parva</note>. By specifying a "single staff," it is understood that the staff must be made from a single tree and not constructed from mismatched pieces or fragments.

That umbrella should be half as wide as the staff is long. Since the staff is six cubits, the width—meaning the diameter—should be three cubits. It should be well-rounded and perfectly joined at the seams. The staff should be decorated with jewels and be of superior quality. As the sage Garga says:

> "With the feathers of swans, roosters, peacocks, or cranes,
> covered in silk, white, and adorned with pearls.
> An umbrella with a crystal base and a staff of six cubits,
> should be made covered in gold with nine joints.
> Three cubits in width and adorned with garlands of gems,
> such a parasol brings welfare and victory to the King." (Verses 1-4)

### Now he describes the characteristics of umbrellas for the Crown Prince, the Queen, the General, and the Magistrate:

> For the Crown Prince, the Queen, the General, and the Magistrate,
> the staff is four and a half cubits long,
> and the width is half of five cubits (two and a half cubits). (Verse 4)

The Crown Prince is well-known as the sharer of half the kingdom. The Queen is the wife of the King. Then there is the General, the lord of the army, and the Magistrate, the head of justice. For all of these, the staff is four and a half cubits. The width is half of five, meaning the diameter is two and a half cubits.

### He describes the characteristics of umbrellas for other royal officials:

> For others, there is a turban <note>ushnisha</note> with the head adorned by "ribbons of favor" <note>term: prasadapatta; ornamental bands gifted by the king</note>.
> Their umbrella should be made of peacock feathers with hanging strings of jewels. (Verse 5)

**For other men, the umbrella for protection against cold and heat should be square.**
**For Brahmins, the umbrella should be made with a perfectly circular staff. ||6||**

For other ordinary men, the umbrella that wards off or protects against cold and heat should be made square (four-cornered). For Brahmins <note>the priestly or scholarly class</note>, the umbrella should be made perfectly circular all around and equipped with a staff. ||6||

### Now, the Praise of Women is explained.

->First, he speaks to demonstrate the purpose of this topic:<-

> **In the conquest of the earth, the city alone is the essence;**
> **In the city, the house; in the house, a single room;**
> **In that room, the bed; and on the bed, an excellent woman,**
> **Radiant with jewels, is the very essence of royal happiness. ||1||**

When the earth is conquered, the city is the only essence; having conquered the entire world, the city remains the core. In that city, the house or dwelling is the sole essence. In that dwelling, one specific area is the best or essential part. Even there, in that part of the house, the bed or couch is the essence. Upon that bed, an excellent woman—a prime young woman—who is radiant with jewels and adorned with gems and gold, is the essence. This alone is the core of the happiness of sovereignty; everything else is without essence. ||1||

->Now, he speaks further in praise of women:<-

**Jewels adorn women, but women are not merely adorned by the luster of jewels.**
**Women steal the heart even without jewels, but jewels do not do so without the company of a woman. ||2||**

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the virtues of women, following the introductory verses of Chapter 73. The text transitions from comparing women to jewels to describing them as the sole source of relief for weary rulers.</meta>

# Chapter 73: The Praise of Women

<page-num>899</page-num>
<header>Chapter 73: The Praise of Women</header>

"Jewels" is the object of the action here. Women, as jewels, adorn and beautify. Women, however, are not themselves beautified by the luster of gems or the light of jewels. For women, even when "jewel-less" <note>original: "aratnā"</note>—devoid of physical gems—steal the heart. Jewels, on the other hand, do not steal the heart unless they are in contact with a beautiful body. As long as they are not attached to the limbs of a woman, they do not captivate the mind. ||2||

->He says something further:<-

->**For kings who must conceal their inner intentions, who rise to conquer the forces of the enemy,**<-
->**Who ponder over the machinery of state, tangled in hundreds of branches of things done and undone;**<-
->**Who follow the dictates of their ministers, and who are suspicious of everyone around them,**<-
->**Living in an ocean of sorrow—their only drop of happiness is the embrace of a beloved woman.**<- ||3||

The embrace of a beloved, the hugging of a dear one, is a "drop of happiness" <note>original: "sukhalavaḥ"</note>—a small fragment of joy. For whom? For kings. Of what kind? Those who "conceal their inner intentions" <note>original: "ākāraṃ vinigūhatām"</note>. An "intention" or "form" refers to the internal transformations of the mind such as joy, fear, or excitement. They hide or cover such internal states. Likewise, those who "rise to conquer the forces of the enemy"—those making an effort to overcome the strength of their foes. Those who "ponder over the machinery of state" <note>original: "tantraṃ cintayatām"</note>—those who meditate upon it. What kind of machinery? "Tangled in hundreds of branches of things done and undone." The "branches" are the expansions of activities or duties; "done and undone" refers to those completed and those yet to be performed. These hundreds of activities are the branches, and the kings are occupied or overwhelmed by them. Indeed, the machinery of governance is said to be tangled in a hundred branches. "Who follow the dictates of their ministers"—those who act according to the rules and policies prescribed and spoken by their counselors or secretaries. For those who are "suspicious of everyone," even their own sons, and who "dwell in an ocean of sorrow," the embrace of a beloved is their only drop of happiness. ||3||

->He says something further:<-

->**Whether heard, seen, touched, or even remembered, she brings delight to men;**<-
->**The Lord of the World created no jewel other than woman anywhere.**<-
->**For her sake are Virtue and Wealth pursued; from her come sons and the pleasures of the senses;**<-
->**Therefore, these Goddesses of Fortune in the home must always be honored with respect and riches.**<- ||4||

By the "Lord of the World" <note>the creator god, Prajapati</note>, no other second jewel was ever created anywhere apart from women. The meaning is that woman alone is the true jewel. What is this "woman-jewel" like? "Heard"—even just hearing her name brings delight. "Seen"—beheld with the eyes. "Touched"—contact with even a part of her body. "Remembered"—even just thinking of her is "delight-producing" for men, meaning it creates happiness. "For her sake, Virtue and Wealth" <note>Dharma and Artha, two of the four goals of human life</note>—both religious merit and material wealth are pursued for her sake. From her, or from her presence, come sons, the enjoyment of the senses, and happiness...

<meta>The text cuts off here, continuing the benefits derived from women on the following page.</meta>

<summary>This page extols women as the supreme "jewel" of creation, arguing that while gems need women to look beautiful, women captivate the heart even without ornaments. It specifically highlights the embrace of a wife as the only solace for a king burdened by the stresses of politics and war.</summary>
<keywords>praise of women, kingship, statecraft, jewels, happiness, Prajapati, Dharma, Artha, domestic life</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Brhat Samhita, specifically Chapter 73, focusing on the defense and praise of women against those who preach asceticism by disparaging them.</meta>

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 73]

<page-num>820</page-num>

They become. Sons are male children. Pleasures of the senses and worldly joys occur. Women are the Goddesses of Fortune <note>Sanskrit: Lakshmi</note> within the home. Therefore, they should always and at all times be honored with various kinds of respect—through honor (worship) and through wealth (prosperity). **|| 4 ||**

->He says something further:<-

> Those who speak only of the faults of women,
> Casting aside their virtues to promote the path of renunciation;
> In my mind’s judgment, those men are wicked,
> For their words are not born of truth or good intent. **|| 5 ||**

Those men who, casting aside the existing virtues of women, speak only of their faults by way of the path of renunciation <note>The "path of renunciation" refers to ascetic traditions that viewed women as obstacles to spiritual progress</note>, are "wicked"—this is the certain conviction of my mind. The words of those wicked men are not "words of truth," meaning they are not statements of ultimate reality. **|| 5 ||**

->He says something else in praise of them:<-

> Tell the truth: what fault is there in women
> That has not been practiced first by men?
> Women have been slandered by men out of sheer impudence,
> Yet they are superior in virtue; this was stated here by Manu. **|| 6 ||**

What fault is there in women? What primary fault exists that was not first practiced or performed by men? Even you who are detached from the world, speak this truth, this ultimate reality. This fault—such as adultery and so on—was first practiced by men, and later women learned it from them. By men, out of impudence—that is, through boldness and shamelessness—women have been cast out or pushed toward the path of vice. For those women are superior in virtue compared to men. On this matter, even Manu, the author of the Law Books <note>referring to the Manusmriti</note>, has stated and declared their superiority. **|| 6 ||**

->And then he says:<-

> Soma gave them purity; the Gandharva gave them refined speech;
> Agni gave them the ability to eat anything;
> Therefore, women are as pure as gold. **|| 7 ||**

To those women, Soma (the Moon) gave purity or cleanliness. The Gandharva (a celestial musician) gave "refined speech," meaning excellent and delightful words. Agni (the Fire-god) gave the ability to eat anything <note>original: "sarvabhakshitva," implying they are not defiled by what they consume, just as fire purifies all</note>—the capacity to consume all—

<summary>Varahamihira defends the character of women against ascetic critics, arguing that women are inherently virtuous and that their perceived faults are mirrored or initiated by men. He cites divine gifts from Soma, Gandharvas, and Agni as proof of their innate purity.</summary>

-># Chapter on the Praise of Women<-

...out of passion. For that reason, women are equal to gold <note>original: "nishka-samah"</note>. The meaning is that even if they have associated with all castes, they remain pure. ||7||

He describes another point of superiority:

**Brahmins are pure in their feet; cows are pure on their backs.**
**Goats and horses are pure in their mouths; but women are pure in every limb. ||8||**

Brahmins (the twice-born) are pure <note>term: medhya (ritually pure/sanctified)</note> from the feet. Cows (the fragrant ones) are pure from the back part. Goats and horses are pure from the mouth or face. Women, however, are pure and holy in all their limbs and throughout their entire bodies. ||8||

He says further:

**Women possess incomparable purity; they are never defiled.**
**For month by month, their menses take away their sins. ||9||**

Women are an incomparable and supreme source of purification. These women are never, at any time, subject to permanent defilement. Every month, the menstrual flow that arises in women removes or destroys any "bad deeds" <note>original: "dushkritani," referring here to ritual or moral impurities</note>. ||9||

He says further:

**Those households which female relatives, being unhonored, pronounce a curse upon,**
**perish utterly as if destroyed by a malevolent spirit. ||10||**

Female relatives <note>term: jamayah (specifically sisters, daughters, or female family members)</note> and women of the family, when they are not honored or respected, may curse the houses or dwellings where they reside. When they reach a state of extreme distress and cry out, those houses perish on all sides, just as if they were struck or destroyed by a *Kritya* <note>note: a Kritya is a malevolent deity or magical force used for destruction</note>. ||10||

He says further:

**Whether she be a wife or a mother, the birth of men is caused by women.**
**O ungrateful ones! How can there be any good for you who speak ill of them? ||11||**

A wife is called *jaya*. There is a Vedic scripture <note>original: "shruti"</note> that says: "She is called *jaya* because he is born (*jayate*) again in her." A woman is also a mother. The origin of men is made possible by women. Another scripture says: "You are born from the limbs, you are produced from the heart; you are indeed the self named 'son', may you live a hundred autumns." This means one's own self is born in the form of a son. Whether she be a wife...

<meta>This page continues the defense of women's character within the "Praise of Women" chapter of the Bṛhat Saṃhitā. The previous section likely established the foundational role of women as mothers and wives.</meta>

[Chapter 73] of the Bṛhat Saṃhitā with Commentary

She may be a wife or a mother. For men, birth and existence are entirely caused by women. "O ungrateful ones!"—this is an address to wicked people. For you who insult those two—the wife and the mother—from where can any good or auspiciousness come? ||11||

### He says something further:

->In the case of infidelity, the fault is established by the scriptures as equal for both husband and wife.<-
->Men do not pay attention to this; therefore, in this matter, women are superior.<- ||12||

When there is "infidelity" <note>original: *vyutkrama*, meaning a deviation from the rules</note> between the couple (husband and wife). Infidelity is a lack of restraint. For a man, it is going to another's wife; for a woman, it is going to another man. The "fault" or wickedness involved in this is declared in the *Dharmaśāstras* <note>The ancient Indian legal and ethical codes</note> to be "equal" or the same for both. For example: "There is nothing so destructive to life as the enjoyment of another's wife," and so on. This applies generally to both. Yet men do not consider or reflect upon their own fault in pursuing other women, whereas women do reflect on it. For that reason, in this determination, women are "superior" <note>original: *varam*, meaning better or more excellent</note>; they are the more virtuous party. ||12||

### Now he describes the penance for violating the marriage vow:

->By wrapping oneself in a donkey's skin with the hair turned outward for six months,<-
->and by begging with the words "Give me alms," one is purified of the sin of adultery.<- ||13||

"Violating the marriage vow" <note>original: *dārātikramaṇa*</note> means the enjoyment of another woman. For that violation, one must be "wrapped" or have the body covered for six months in a "donkey's skin with the hair turned outward" <note>This was a public, humiliating penance intended to show the sinner's fall from social grace</note>. By going from house to house and speaking the words "Give me alms," one then attains purification. ||13||

### He says something else to praise women:

->The desire for love does not fade even after a hundred years.<-
->In that matter, men desist only through lack of ability, while women desist through self-control.<- ||14||

"Love" refers to passion. The "desire for love"—the mental impression, tendency, or longing for sexual desire—does not "fade" or leave the hearts of men even after a hundred years. Even if the union that once existed with a woman is no longer possible now, that desire does not leave men even in a century. However, in that matter of sensual enjoyment, "men" <note>males</note> desist only because of "lack of ability" <note>original: *aśaktyā*, referring to physical impotence or loss of vigor in old age</note>. "Women" <note>females</note>, on the other hand, desist through "self-control" <note>original: *dhairyeṇa*, meaning firmness or moral courage</note>. By this, the superiority of women's character over their desires is demonstrated. ||14||

<summary>Varāhamihira argues that women are morally superior to men because they exercise genuine self-control over their desires, whereas men only stop their pursuits when physically unable to continue. He also notes that religious law views adultery as an equal sin for both genders, despite social double standards.</summary>

# Chapter on the Praise of Women [Chapter 73]

The author says another thing—

->Oh, the audacity of the wicked who revile blameless women!<-
->It is like thieves who, while stealing, shout "Stop, thief!" at others. ||15||<-

The audacity—the boldness—of wicked people, of evil-doers, who offer insults and reproaches to blameless and sinless women is truly a wonder. This audacity is seen as a form of shamelessness. Just as thieves who are in the act of stealing and committing a crime shout "Stop, thief!" to the very person they are robbing as he flees, so too is the behavior of these critics. ||15||

Having thus presented the praise of women as stated in the <term>Dharmashastras</term> <note>Ancient Indian law books and treatises on duty</note>, he now speaks of his own observations—

->The sweet, flattering words a man whispers to women<-
->In private, he does not uphold later.<-
->Yet women, out of gratitude for past kindness,<-
->Embrace their departed husbands and enter the seven-tongued flame. ||16||<-

A man—a human male—speaks many "fickle" or flattering words and sweet endearments to women who are filled with desire when they are in private during acts of love. Yet later, out of a sense of wickedness, he does not offer even a fraction of that kindness if they commit the slightest fault. But women, out of <term>sukritajñata</term> <note>Gratitude; literally 'the state of knowing what has been well-done'</note>, embrace their departed—that is, dead—husbands and enter the <term>seven-tongued</term> <note>A poetic name for Agni, the god of fire</note> flame. The meaning is that remembering the kindness of the husband, they sacrifice themselves in the fire along with him. ||16||

He says another thing—

->The man who enjoys the "jewel of a woman,"<-
->Even if penniless, is truly a lord of the earth.<-
->The essence of a kingdom is food and women;<-
->The rest is but wood to feed the fire of craving. ||17||<-

For whatever man there exists the enjoyment of a "woman-jewel"—a woman who is herself a precious gem—and he shares his life with her, that man, even if he is <term>nihsva</term> <note>Destitute or without property</note>, is in my view a lord of the earth, just like a <unclear>king.</unclear> <note>Small vertical marks/dots appear above the word 'king', possibly indicating a deletion or variant.</note> Some read the text as "now a lord of the earth."

1. "Now a lord of the earth"—this is a variant reading.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Brhat Samhita, specifically Chapter 73, which discusses the appreciation of women and the nature of earthly versus heavenly pleasures.</meta>

<page-num>824</page-num>
# In the Brhat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 73]

As it is now, at this very time, so it is for the King. The word "even" <note>original: "api"</note> is used here to indicate possibility. What need is there to even account for a Lord or God? Because this is the very essence, the best part of a kingdom: food and women. Everything else—wealth and the like—is merely the wood, the pile of fuel, for the kindling and burning of the fire of craving. For by those things, the fire only blazes more intensely. ||17||

->The author says the following in praise of another aspect:<-

**The pleasure that comes from embracing a loving woman,**
**Endowed with the bloom of first youth,**
**Who makes low, beautiful, soft, and pressed sounds,**
**And has rising breasts—**
**Such pleasure, in my opinion, does not exist even in the abode of the Creator.** ||18||

A "loving woman" <term>Kamini: a woman filled with desire</term> is one in whom passion has been awakened, and she is "endowed with first youth," meaning she possesses fresh youthfulness. "Low" means slight; "beautiful" means lovely; "soft" means sweet; "pressed" means stifled. When she is embraced slowly, she makes these low, beautiful, soft, and stifled sounds. "With rising breasts" refers to one whose breasts are emerging or developing. My "opinion"—my intellect—is that the pleasure or happiness born from embracing such a woman does not exist in the "abode of the Creator" <note>original: "Dhatrbhavane"</note>, which is the house of Prajapati or the world of Brahma <note>Brahma-loka, the highest heaven</note>. This is what I think. After reaching the world of Brahma through great hardship, penance, knowledge, or Yoga, what is actually experienced there? ||18||

->He explains this further:<-

**Tell me, what happiness is there in the Creator’s abode,**
**Where one must serve those worthy of honor and the "honor-fathers,"**
**Surrounded by gods, sages, perfected beings, and celestial singers—**
**If it does not involve embracing a woman in private?** ||19||

In that "abode of the Creator," the world of Brahma, one is surrounded by gods; by sages; by "perfected beings" <term>Siddhas: semi-divine beings of great purity</term> or Vidyadharas; and by "celestial singers" <term>Charanas: heavenly actors, dancers, and musicians</term> such as Gandharvas and Apsaras. Tell me, what happiness is there other than the act of serving and worshipping those who are "worthy of honor" <note>original: "manya"</note> and the "honor-fathers" <note>original: "manapitr," likely referring to venerable ancestors or progenitors</note>? There, the servants simply worship those to be served, and the honorable are worshipped by the elders. That is all. Is there not more happiness found in a secluded place at the time of sexual union, embracing a woman, than in the world of Brahma? Indeed, all true happiness is found there [in that embrace], and therefore one should value it above those celestial worlds. ||19||

<summary>This page features a commentary on verses 17-19 of the Brhat Samhita, arguing that the sensual pleasure found in the embrace of a young woman surpasses the religious rewards of the Brahma-loka (heavenly realm).</summary>

# Chapter on Creating Good Fortune and Charm

The author states the following:

> From the creator Brahma down to the smallest insect, this entire world is bound together by the union of male and female. What cause for shame is there in this, when even the Lord Shiva was driven by longing for a young woman to assume four faces? || 20 ||

This entire world, without exception, from the Great Grandfather Brahma down to the lowliest insect, is bound or woven together by the union of male and female. Nothing is seen to exist without the union of woman and man. In this world, what shame or embarrassment should there be for an ordinary man, when even the Lord Mahadeva <note>A name for Shiva</note> was made to attain "four-facedness" because of a young woman? Here, the ancient Puranic tradition <note>original: "shrutih"</note> says:

> As the exceptionally beautiful Tilottama <note>A celestial nymph (apsara) created to distract demons</note> was performing a circumambulation, the Lord—out of a desire for her beauty and to gaze upon her while Parvati was sitting on his lap (to avoid her anger or jealousy)—created four faces in the four directions. || 20 ||

->Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, named "The Praise of Women," in the section on Inner Apartments of the Commentary on the Compendium composed by Bhattotpala.<-

---

->Now, the methods for Creating Good Fortune and Charm are explained.<-

At the very beginning, the author describes the specific advantage of a charming man:

> For a man who is charming and beloved by women, all the pleasures of love are of the highest quality. For any other man, such pleasure is a mere shadow because the woman’s mind is elsewhere. Even if a woman is far away, the man she dwells upon in her heart is the one whose likeness her child will bear. || 1 ||

For a "charming" man <term>Subhaga: a man naturally attractive or beloved by women</term>, all pleasure born of desire <note>original: "manobhava-sukham"</note> is of the highest or most genuine quality. This excellence applies to his union with any woman. Because a woman desires a charming man in her own heart during union and does not let her mind wander elsewhere, her heart is colored with passion for him. For "the other"—the unattractive or unfortunate man—pleasure is a mere appearance or shadow <note>original: "abhasamatram"</note> because of the "separation of the mind," meaning her thoughts have gone elsewhere. That which is enjoyed without the heart being fully entered is only a semblance of pleasure, not the real thing, because the woman's mind is detached or fixed on another. As the author will say:

# On the Great Compilation [Chapter 74]

-> The mind <note>original: "manas"</note> is indeed the root of the one whose body was burnt by Shiva <note>A reference to Kamadeva, the god of love, who was turned to ash by Shiva's third eye but lives on as a mental force.</note>. <-

A woman does not simply go toward a charming man; rather, even if a man is far away or not in her presence, the specific man she contemplates, thinks of, or desires in her mind—it is a child resembling him, bearing his form, that she carries in her womb. ||1||

To demonstrate that the self of the man is reborn within women, the author says:

> Just as a branch broken from a tree and planted in the earth,
> or a seed sown within it, does not become something else,
> so too the self is born again within women;
> yet there is some distinction in it due to the union with the "field." ||2||

Just as a branch or stalk of a tree, when broken and planted in the ground, does not become something else, and a seed sown in the earth does not change its nature but grows into the same plant, in this same manner, the self is born or produced again within women, who serve as the foundation. Therefore, because of the union with the "field" <note>term: kshetra-yoga; the "field" refers to the mother's body/womb, while the "seed" is the father's contribution</note>, there is some unique quality or variation in that field. Depending on the field where the seed is sown, a certain difference or dissimilarity arises; some specific trait occurs due to the influence of the mother. ||2||

To explain how desire is possible for one who is far away, he says:

> The self moves together with the mind, the mind with the senses,
> and the senses with their objects; this sequence is instantaneous.
> This very union belongs to the mind—is there anything unreachable?
> Wherever the mind goes, there this self has gone. ||3||

The self—the soul as the agent of action and consciousness—moves only in conjunction with the mind. The mind moves together with the senses. In this context, there are ten senses: five senses of perception <note>term: buddhi-indriya</note> and five senses of action <note>term: karma-indriya</note>. The five senses of perception are hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell. As it has been said:

> The anus, the genitals, the hands, the feet, and speech is the fifth;
> these are called the five senses of action, with the mind as the sixth.
> Hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell as the fifth;
> these are called the five senses of perception, with the mind as the sixth.

1. This refers to Verse 14 in Chapter 77 of this same text.

It also explains the rapid connection between the soul, mind, and the ten physical senses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and practical discussion on the nature of the soul, the mechanics of perception, and the causes of attraction (auspiciousness) between individuals.</meta>

<page-num>827</page-num>
<header>[Chapter 74] Chapter on Creating Good Fortune (Auspiciousness).</header>

In this way, the mind moves together with the sense organ. The sense organ moves together with its own object—that is, the specific object belonging to it. Whichever object belongs to a particular sense, it goes toward that. This sequence is a rapid, purposeful progression. The meaning is this: the Self <note>Atman</note> joins with the mind; the mind with the sense organ; and the sense organ with the object. This is the meaning of "from the object." The "organs of knowledge" <term>buddhindriyas: the five senses of perception—hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell</term> are the ears and so on; the "organs of action" <term>karmendriyas: the five means of interaction—speech, grasping, walking, excretion, and procreation</term> are the voice and so on. The objects are sound and the rest: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Immediately after, the mind reports the object tasted by the senses to the Self. The Self, remembering its own capacity for action and purpose regarding that object, gives an order to the mind: "Engage the organs of action in either accepting or rejecting this." In this manner, the sequence is rapid. This is the process relied upon. This indeed is the "union" <note>yoga</note> or connection. What is unreachable for that mind? Indeed, it goes everywhere. To whichever place the mind travels, there this Self has gone. ||3||

Specifying this very point, he says:

> ->This Self, exceedingly subtle, has entered the Self within the heart;<-
> ->It is to be grasped by a steady mind through constant application.<-
> ->Whatever a person meditates upon, they attain oneness with that;<-
> ->Because of this, young women have attained the state of being well-favored.<- ||4||

This Self—the "acting self" <note>karmatman</note>, the living soul <note>jiva</note> whose nature is consciousness—has entered into the Self, the Supreme Self <note>Paramatman</note>. It exists within its own being as the form of awareness, having become the doer and the knower. Where? In the heart, the station of the heart. As it is said:

> ->A span above the navel and six finger-widths below the throat;<-
> ->One should know that as the heart, the great abode of the universe.<-

Of what nature is it? Exceedingly subtle—of an extremely minute dimension. And it is to be "grasped"—made an object of perception—by a steady, unmoving mind <note>chitta</note> through constant application, which means uninterrupted practice. Whatever object a man meditates upon or contemplates with his mind, he attains "oneness with that" <term>tanmayatvam: the state of being absorbed into or becoming identical with the object of focus</term>. He becomes that very thing. Because of this reason, young women have reached or attained a "well-favored" <note>subhagam: fortunate, beloved, or attractive</note> man through the honor of constant practice. ||4||

Now, he describes the characteristics of being well-favored <note>subhaga</note> versus ill-favored <note>durbhaga</note>:

> ->Courtesy alone is the cause of being well-favored; contrary behavior causes hatred.<-
> ->Through mantras, medicines, and deceitful practices, many faults arise, not peace.<- ||5||

Courtesy <note>dakshinya: also meaning sincerity or kindness</note>—acting in accordance with another's wishes and pleasing their mind—is the sole cause of being well-favored or being beloved. A man becomes beloved through the favorable disposition of women. Contrary behavior—acting in opposition or being unfavorable—[leads to hatred...]

It concludes by identifying courtesy as the primary source of personal attraction and warns against using magic or deceit to win affection.</summary>

--- Page 320 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on social conduct and personal character from Chapter 74 of Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita, specifically focusing on the qualities that lead to being well-loved by others.</meta>

<page-num>828</page-num>
->**In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 74]**<-

Causing hatred is a cause of misfortune. Through spells and medicines—"spells" referring to subjugation mantras and "medicines" to specific substances. By the inclusion of "and so forth," it refers to food, drink, application to the genitals, ointments, and other harmful deceptive practices <note>original: "kuhaka-prayogaiḥ"</note> intended to produce wonder; from these, many great faults and bodily afflictions arise. No peace or well-being <note>original: "sharma"</note> comes from them. Therefore, being agreeable is the only true way to secure good fortune, not any other magical applications or similar methods. ||5||

He describes another action for securing good fortune:

**By abandoning pride, one attains the state of being beloved; arrogance brings about misfortune. An arrogant person accomplishes tasks with great difficulty, while one who speaks kindly achieves them without effort. ||6||**

By abandoning or giving up "pride" (vanity), a person attains or reaches the state of being "beloved" <note>original: "vallabhatvam"</note> by people. "Arrogance" is ego and pride; it brings about or leads to "misfortune" (being disliked). He who is arrogant and impudent accomplishes or carries out tasks with "difficulty" (distress). One who speaks "kindly words" (pleasant speech) accomplishes tasks "without effort" (without distress). ||6||

He says another thing:

**True brilliance is not the love of rashness, nor is it speech that is unpleasant or composed by the wicked. Those who reach the completion of a task without becoming haughty are the truly brilliant ones, not those who are boastful. ||7||**

"Rashness" <note>original: "sāhasam"</note> is the performance of actions without due reflection. Where rashness is "loved," that is not "brilliance" <note>original: "tejas"</note> or dignity; sometimes it even results in the loss of life. And "speech" that is "unpleasant" (not agreeable) or touches a raw nerve, or is "composed by the wicked" (spoken by the impudent)—that is not brilliance. Those people who, even after reaching the "end" or completion of a "task" (a thing to be done) and finishing it, remain "not haughty" (without pride)—they are the "brilliant ones" <note>term: Tejasvin - a person possessing inner luster, dignity, and spiritual power</note>. Those who are "boastful" or talkative, prattling useless and untruthful words, are not brilliant. ||7||

He says another thing:

**He who desires universal popularity should speak of the virtues of everyone behind their backs. He who gossips about the faults of others receives many faults in return, even from the wicked. ||8||**

The man who desires "universal" popularity or the state of being "beloved" by all people everywhere should "speak of" or utter the "virtues" (praise) of every single person "behind their backs" (when they are not present). On the other hand, the man who "gossips about the faults" related to another receives or gains "many" various kinds of "faults" from the "wicked" (bad people). For indeed, a good person is characterized by knowledge and character, while a wicked person is solely devoted to the faults of others. ||8||

### He says something further—

> The entire world follows in the service of a man who is devoted to the service of all. The fame gained by performing a service for one's enemies during their misfortunes is not achieved through a small amount of merit. ||9||

"Devoted to the service of all" means one who is constantly engaged in helping everyone. For such a man, the entire world—without exception—becomes devoted to his service in return, providing reciprocal help. In this world, the fame <note>original: "kirti"</note> that arises from helping even one's enemies during their times of distress or calamity is not the result of a small amount of "auspiciousness" <note>meaning religious merit or "punya"</note>. The meaning is that it occurs through a great deal of merit. This being the case, the essential point is that one should perform service for everyone. ||9||

### Now, he speaks regarding the wicked man—

> Like fire covered by grass, virtue increases all the more even when being suppressed. He who desires to destroy the virtues of another only attains the state of being a villain. ||10||

Even when the virtue of a good man is covered <note>suppressed or hidden</note> by wicked people, it attains an even greater increase or growth. Just as fire, when covered by grass, grows stronger. He who desires to destroy or ruin the virtues of another only attains "villainy" <note>original: "durjanabhavam"</note> or wickedness; the destruction of the good man's virtue does not actually occur. Rather, his virtues become even more brilliantly manifest. Just as when fire is covered by grass, only the grass itself is consumed there. ||10||

->Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, named "The Preparation of Fortune," in the section on Inner Apartment Concerns, in the Commentary on the Samhita composed by the venerable Bhattotpala.<-

---

->Now, the chapter on Aphrodisiacs is explained.<-

### At the very beginning, he speaks to demonstrate the purpose of this topic—

> When the female blood is in excess, a female is born; when the male seed is in excess, a male is born; when the blood and seed are equal, a hermaphrodite is born. Because of this, one should make use of elixirs that provide for the increase of the seed. ||1||

At the time of conception, if the blood <note>original: "rakta/shonita," referring here to the female reproductive element</note> of the woman is in excess, the fetus becomes female. If the seed <note>original: "shukra/retas," referring to the male reproductive element</note> is in excess, it becomes a male person. If there is equality or balance between the blood and the seed, a hermaphrodite <note>original: "napumsakam," a third-gender or non-binary category in traditional Indian medicine</note> is born. Because of this reason, one should consume or utilize "elixirs" <term>Rasayanas: traditional Ayurvedic tonics believed to promote longevity and vitality</term> that grant the increase and growth of the seed. ||1||

### Now he describes the binding-rope of Desire—

->**The rooftop of a palace, the rays of the moon, wine scented with blue water-lilies, and a beloved languid with passion;**<-
->**The lute, talk of love, a secluded place, and flower garlands—this group is the snare of Love.॥2॥**<-

"The rooftop of a palace" means the upper terrace of a house. "The rays of the moon" <note>original: *udunatha-rashmayah*</note> refers to moonlight. "With blue water-lilies" means accompanied by the scent or presence of blue lotuses. "Wine" <note>original: *madhu*</note> refers to liquor. The mention of liquor here is illustrative; it is mentioned specifically with reference to the *Shudra* class. For *Brahmins* and others, other preferred drinks are intended. "Beloved" means a dear wife or lover. "Languid with passion" means slow or intoxicated due to the drinking of wine. "Lute" <note>original: *vallaki*</note> refers to the Veena. "Talk of love" means erotic conversation. "Seclusion" <note>original: *rahas*</note> refers to a private, lonely place, and also the intent for sexual union. "Garlands" means wreaths of flowers. This "group" or collection is the "snare" <note>original: *vagura*</note> or binding-rope of Love <note>original: *Madana*</note>. It is said that one is bound by this very rope.॥2॥

### Now he describes a formula for increasing virility—

->**One who consumes equal parts of pyrites, honey, mercury, iron powder,**<-
->**myrobalan, bitumen, and clarified butter;**<-
->**for twenty-one days, even if possessed by old age,**<-
->**even if eighty years old, he delights a woman like a youth.॥3॥**<-

"Pyrites" <note>original: *makshika-dhatu*</note> refers to stone pyrites. "Honey" <note>original: *madhu*</note> refers to honey produced by bees. "Mercury" <note>original: *parada*</note> is well-known. "Iron powder" <note>original: *loha-churna*</note> refers to the fine powder of iron weapons. "Myrobalan" <note>original: *pathya*</note> is the Haritaki fruit. "Bitumen" <note>original: *shilajatu*</note> is well-known. "Clarified butter" <note>original: *ghrita*</note> is ghee. All these, excluding the pyrites <note>the commentator notes a specific mixing ratio here</note>, are to be taken in equal quantities. Having processed them with equal parts of ghee and honey, a pill should be made. He who "eats" or consumes these for "twenty-one days"—meaning twenty days plus one. One who eats this, even if "possessed by old age" or "eighty years old"—meaning even if extremely aged—delights or sports with a "woman" <note>original: *abala*</note> just like a "youth" or a young man.॥3॥

### He mentions another—

->**He who drinks milk boiled with the roots of the Cowhage plant**<-
->**does not reach exhaustion with women;**<-
->**or, black gram cooked in milk and ghee,**<-
->**in the measure of six mouthfuls, with milk as a chaser.॥4॥**<-

A lover who drinks milk boiled with the roots of the *Kapikacchu* <note>original: "kapikacchumūlaiḥ"; the Velvet Bean plant, Mucuna pruriens, famous in Ayurveda for treating tremors and increasing vitality</note> does not experience exhaustion or inability regarding women. One should also use "milk-ghee," which is the clarified butter produced by churning milk directly. After eating exactly six mouthfuls of cooked *Masha* <note>original: "māṣān"; black gram lentils</note>, one should follow it by drinking milk. By using milk as a post-drink <term>Anupāna (a liquid vehicle taken with or after medicine to improve its efficacy)</term>, he does not face depletion with women. ||4||

### He says another:

**One who has many women should drink the powder of *Vidarika*, which has been repeatedly soaked in its own juice and dried, along with boiled milk and sugar. ||5||**

*Vidarika* <note>original: "vidārikā"; Pueraria tuberosa, or Indian Kudzu, used as a restorative tonic</note> is well-known. Its powder should be soaked and processed repeatedly with its own juice. This is the method: soak it in the juice until it is saturated, then dry it in the heat. Once dry, soak and dry it again. This should be done seven times. A man who has many women should drink this powder with boiled milk mixed with sugar. ||5||

### He says another:

->**The powder of *Dhatri* fruits,**<-
->**well-saturated with their own juice and mixed with honey, sugar, and ghee;**<-
->**after licking this and drinking milk according to the strength of one's digestion,**<-
->**a man may enjoy love-making to his heart's content. ||6||**<-

The powder of *Dhatri* fruits <note>original: "dhātrīphalānām"; Amla or Indian Gooseberry</note> should be thoroughly saturated with the juice of the same fruit. Then it is mixed with honey, sugar, and ghee <note>original: "kṣaudra-sitājya-yuktam"</note>. These should be combined in equal quantities to form a paste. After licking and tasting this, and then drinking milk according to the capacity of one's "digestive fire" <note>original: "agni-śaktyā"; the metabolic strength of the individual</note>, a man may experience and enjoy sexual desire to his full satisfaction. ||6||

### He says another:

->**A lover who repeatedly soaks sesame seeds in milk**<-
->**boiled with the testicles of a goat,**<-
->**and eats them well-dried and drinks milk—**<-
->**what can even a sparrow do in his presence? ||7||**<-

# Brihat Samhita [Chapter 75]
<page-num>832</page-num>
->**Commentary on the Brihat Samhita**<-

A goat is a male goat. Its testicles <note>original: "bastāṇḍau"</note> should be boiled in milk. A lover—one who desires sensual pleasure—should soak sesame seeds in this boiled milk mixture many times (meaning seven times). After soaking them, he should dry the seeds thoroughly. If he eats these seeds and then drinks milk afterward, a sparrow <note>The sparrow is a traditional symbol of high libido and frequent mating in Sanskrit literature</note> will act as his servant. This means he will be able to approach many women and perform frequently and swiftly. ||7||

He [Varahamihira] says another thing:

> **Men who eat Shashtika rice with ghee and bean soup,**
> **and drink milk afterward, spend those nights**
> **restless with the power of Love.** ||8||

Those men who eat *Shashtika* rice <note>A variety of rice that matures in sixty days, highly prized in Ayurveda for its strengthening properties</note> along with ghee <note>clarified butter</note> and soup made from *Masha* <term>Masha: Black gram or Urad dal, considered a potent tonic</term>, and drink milk afterward, will spend those nights in the company of Love <note>original: "Madana," the god of desire</note>. This is because of their frequent ability to approach women. ||8||

He says another thing:

> **A mixture of sesame, Ashwagandha, and Kapikacchu root,**
> **combined with Vidarika and Shashtika flour;**
> **kneaded with goat's milk and cooked in ghee,**
> **this pastry becomes a powerful aphrodisiac.** ||9||

Sesame is well known. *Ashwagandha* <note>Winter cherry; a famous adaptogenic herb</note> is also well known. The root of *Kapikacchu* is the root of the *Atmagupta* plant <note>Mucuna pruriens or Cowhage</note>. *Vidarika* <note>Pueraria tuberosa or Indian Kudzu</note> is well known. *Shashtika* is a specific type of rice; its flour is used here. One should make a mixture of these, using half the amount of medicinal herbs relative to the rice flour. Then, it should be kneaded with goat's milk until smooth. When this is cooked in ghee as a *Shashkulika* <note>A type of fried, circular pastry or pretzel-like snack</note>, it becomes a powerful aphrodisiac that greatly increases reproductive essence. ||9||

He says another thing:

> **Using Gokshura with milk,**
> **or eating the tuber of Vidarika;**
> **one will not fail if he can digest it.**
> **If digestion is weak, here is a powder.** ||10||

One should use *Gokshura* <note>Tribulus terrestris or Puncture Vine</note> with milk. This means boiling the *Gokshura* with milk and drinking it. Or, one should eat the tuber (root) of *Vidarika* boiled with milk. By doing this, one will not fail [in vigor]. If his digestion is slow or weak, then the following powder is prescribed here...

...he does not sink or suffer exhaustion among women. If the virility of a lover wanes or is digested <note>meaning his sexual capacity diminishes</note>, then this applies. The word "if" is used in the sense of a condition. If there is "sluggish fire" <note>Mandagnita: poor digestion or low metabolic fire</note>, then for him, the following <term>powder for kindling the fire</term> <note>Churna-agni-sandipanam: a medicinal powder to boost digestion</note> is prescribed. || 10 ||

### Thus it is said—

->Celery seeds, salt, chebulic myrobalan, and long pepper combined with ginger.<-
->Drinking this powder with wine, buttermilk, gruel, or warm water kindles the abdominal fire. || 11 ||<-

*Ajamoda* is celery seed. *Lavana* is rock salt. *Haritaki* is the pathya fruit <note>Chebulic myrobalan</note>. The myrobalan is combined with the celery seeds and salt. *Shringabera* is dry ginger. Long pepper is joined or combined with the ginger. One should make all these into equal quantities and grind them into a powder. One should drink this powder with wine, buttermilk, gruel, or warm water. "Wine" refers to fermented liquors like *sidhu* or *asava*; "buttermilk" refers to diluted curds; "gruel" (*tarala*) refers to fermented rice water <note>kanjika</note>, though some say it means milk; and "warm water" is simply heated water. One should drink it with any one of these. It is a "kindler of fire," meaning it increases the digestive fire in the stomach. || 11 ||

### Now, he describes the incompatible foods here—

->He who eats foods that are excessively sour, bitter, salty, or pungent,<-
->Or meals that are heavy in alkaline substances and leafy vegetables,<-
->Though he be young, he becomes devoid of vision, semen, and vigor,<-
->And after reaching a woman, he incurs many diseases and old age. || 12 ||<-

The man who eats or consumes meals that are too sour, too bitter, too salty, or too pungent; and likewise eats meals heavy in alkaline substances (*kshara*). One should prepare the alkali by combining substances and burning them. For example—

><insert>"Alkali is made from aconite, stinking cassia, bitter cucumber, Java pepper, leadwort,<-
><insert>and the 'three pungents' <note>ginger, black pepper, and long pepper</note> arranged in layers with a covering of salt.<-
><insert>Having burned and powdered this, it should be used with curd-water<-
><insert>in cases of abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, swelling, and anemia." Thus it is said.<-

"Arranged in layers" means spread out sequentially from the alkali-source plants up to the "three pungents" in a single vessel. "With a covering of salt" means it is prepared with rock salt—this is the remaining part of the instruction. Then, having covered the vessel with a lid and applying a seal of clay and cloth, and having burned it, then...

## Thus, the applications of alkaline substances.

In this manner, one who eats foods heavy in alkaline substances <note>original: "kshara"; refers to caustic or salty dietary components</note>, as well as those who eat excessive amounts of leafy vegetables—or perhaps the well-known alkaline vegetables—becomes devoid of vision, semen, and vigor. "Vision" refers to eyesight, "semen" to reproductive fluid, and "vigor" to physical strength. Being deprived of these, even a young man, upon reaching a woman, acts as if he were an old man, making many excuses due to his incapacity. This is the meaning.

->Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Aphrodisiacs," in the section on Inner Quarters of the Commentary on the Compilation composed by the venerable Bhattotpala.<-

### Now, the Preparation of Perfumes is explained.

First, for the purpose of identifying the names of the substances, a glossary <term>Nighantu: a traditional specialized dictionary or vocabulary</term> is written by us. It is as follows:

Now, for practical use, a glossary is recorded here:
Musk is called *madani*, *nabhi*, *mada*, *darpa*, *mrigodbhava*, *mrigadarpa*, *mrigamada*, and *gandha*—these are all synonyms.
Camphor is known by the names *sphatika* <note>crystal</note>, *indu* <note>moon</note>, *tushara* <note>frost</note>, and *ghanasara*.
Saffron is known as *kashmira*, *ghusrina*, and by the name *rakta* <note>red</note>.
The prepared oil known as *turushka* <note>liquid storax or frankincense</note> is called *vanara* and *cala*.
Aloe-wood <note>agarwood</note> is called *kaliya*, *jongaka*, *loha*, *khala*, and *karpasika*.
Sandalwood is called *hima* <note>cold</note>, *shita*, *maheya*, and *malaya*.
Small cardamom is called *sukshmela*, *bahula*, *candrela*, *dravidi*, and *truti*.
Cloves are called *shripushpa*, *devapushpa*, and *laghupushpa*.
*Kola* and *kolaka* refer to cubeb; *phala* is known as nutmeg.
*Ushna* and *katuphala* refer to the nutmeg tree; *jati* and *malati* refer to jasmine; and *jatipatrika* is mace.

## Chapter on the Preparation of Perfumes

<note>This section serves as a botanical glossary, listing various synonyms for plants to ensure the perfumer identifies the correct ingredients regardless of regional naming variations.</note>

The fruit, the leaf, *Tamala* <note>Cinnamomum tamala</note>, *Gandhapatra*, and *Netraka* are synonyms. *Bhrunga*, *Netraraja*, *Varanga*, *Tvak*, and *Tanutvach* all refer to Cinnamon bark.

*Ganaka*, *Kanchana*, *Kesara*, and *Nagakesara* <note>Mesua ferrea, known for its fragrant flowers</note> are names for the same plant. *Rasa*, *Gandharasa*, *Pindarasa*, *Bola*, and *Chala* are known as Myrrh.

*Putikosha* is called *Vidalakhya*; *Cheli* is known as *Jataka*. *Lata* is the name for *Latabha*; *Renu*, *Kunti*, and *Harenuka* are synonyms for a specific aromatic seed.

*Meghakhya* is the desired name for *Musta* <note>Nut grass or Cyperus rotundus</note>. *Vakra*, *Tagara* <note>Indian Valerian</note>, and *Nata* are synonyms. *Karajakhya*, *Nakha* <note>literally "fingernail," referring to the operculum of certain mollusks used in incense</note>, *Shankha*, and *Nakhapada* are recorded as equivalents.

*Jvarakshaya*, *Utpalakhya*, *Vapya*, *Kustha* <note>Saussurea lappa</note>, *Gada*, and *Ruk* are names for the Costus root. *Mansi*, *Keshi*, *Pishachi*, *Nalada*, *Kamala*, and *Jata* refer to Spikenard <note>Nardostachys jatamansi</note>.

*Shyama*, *Priyakhya*, *Shrisanjna*, *Priyangu* <note>Aglaia elaeagnoidea</note>, and *Phalini* are remembered as synonyms. *Granthiparni*, *Granthiparna*, *Shuka*, and *Sthauneyaka* are known to the experts.

*Hribera*, *Varisanjna*, *Hribara*, and *Baluka* are recorded as names for the fragrant Pavonia root.

*Rana*, *Sevya*, *Mrinalakhya*, and *Ushira* <note>Vetiver or Khus grass</note> are mentioned here as synonyms. *Rama*, *Mrinala*, *Ramanja*, *Vyamaka*, and *Davadagdhaka* are also used.

*Pravala* and *Vidrumakhya* refer to Coral. *Valli*, *Nalika*, and *Nali* are synonyms. *Sprikka*, *Asrig*, *Brahmani*, *Mala*, and *Devi* are the terms defined for that aromatic herb.

*Chakrangi*, *Katuki*, *Gandha*, *Jatila*, *Ugra*, *Jaya*, and *Vacha* <note>Sweet Flag or Acorus calamus</note> are equivalents. *Karchu*, *Karchura*, *Ugra*, and *Gandhamula* are celebrated as names for Zedoary.

*Pushpa*, *Samantapushpa*, *Shatapushpa*, *Shata*, and *Masi* refer to Dill or Anise. *Kusumalo* is *Chanda*; *Stena*, *Chaura*, and *Taskara* <note>literally "thief," a nickname for the plant Kaempferia galanga</note> are synonyms.

*Akrishta*, *Keshapalita*, *Jara*, and *Sthavirasanjnita* are names for a specific aged aromatic. *Girakhya*, *Girijakhya*, and *Shaileya* <note>Stone flowers or lichen</note> are declared together.

*Darvi*, *Daru*, and *Nishakhya* refer to Tree Turmeric. *Kaleya* is Yellow Sandalwood. *Pita*, *Haridra* <note>Turmeric</note>, and *Naktakhya* are synonyms. *Daru* and *Devadaru* refer to the Himalayan Cedar.

*Rakta*, *Samanga*, and *Manjistha* <note>Indian Madder, used for color and scent</note> are the same. *Madhuka* and *Madhuyashtika* refer to Licorice. *Dhanyaka*, *Dhanya*, *Dhaniyaka*, and *Kustumburu* are recorded as names for Coriander.

# On the Brihat Samhita [Chapter 76]

->**Definitions of Aromatic Substances and Botanical Synonyms**<-

Maru is Maruvaka <note>Sweet Marjoram</note>; Murva and Phanijja are also known as Sanava. Sarja is known by the name Sarjarasa, and is also called Rala in this context.

Pura is Guggulu <note>Indian Bdellium, a fragrant resin</note>, also called Bhadra, Bhadrakhya, and Mahishaksha. Rohisha is called Peshala, and Payasi is known as Kutheraka.

The terms for milk, curd, and ghee <note>clarified butter</note> are combined in Shrivasa, also called Shri and Vasaka. Jatu is Laksha <note>Lac, a resinous secretion</note>, also called Krimitaja <note>born of insects</note>. Dhatri is known as Amalaka <note>Indian Gooseberry</note>.

Haritaki is called Abhaya, Pathya, Vijaya, and Pranada. Kali is Vibhitaka and Aksha. These three together <note>Amalaka, Haritaki, and Vibhitaka</note> constitute the Triphala <note>The "Three Fruits" formula</note>.

Shunthi <note>dry ginger</note>, Maricha <note>black pepper</note>, and Pippali <note>long pepper</note> are called Tryushana <note>The "Three Pungents"</note> when all are combined. Triphala with Trijata is known as Trivarga or the "Triple Group."

Tvak <note>cinnamon bark</note>, Patra <note>cassia leaf</note>, and Ela <note>cardamom</note> constitute Trijata <note>The "Three Aromatics"</note>. When combined with Kesara <note>nagakesara/saffron</note>, it becomes Chatujata <note>The "Four Aromatics"</note>. Another Triphala <note>specifically for perfumes</note> is made from the three: Kakkola, Katu, and Jatiphala <note>nutmeg</note>.

With Ghee, Indu <note>camphor</note>, and Kunkuma <note>saffron</note>, it is called "Panchasugandhi" <note>The Five Fragrances</note>, similar to Kola-pushpa. When Kola is omitted and Darpa <note>musk</note> is added, it is always called Devaraja.

Camphor, Saffron, and Musk—this triad is called Trigandhika <note>The Three Fragrances</note>. With Cloves, Phala, Kakkola, Katu, Camphor, and Saffron...

...with the juices of Tvag-lata, Jati, and Chuta <note>mango</note>, it becomes Dashasugandhika <note>The Ten Fragrances</note>. Tikshna refers to Maricha <note>black pepper</note>, and Chitraka is known by the name Vahni <note>meaning "fire," due to its heat</note>.

Rochana is known as Ruchira; Sharkara <note>sugar</note> is called Sikata and Sita. Pushpasava is Pushparasa <note>flower nectar</note>; Saragha, Madhu, and Makshika are names for honey.

Kshaudra and Bhramara are also names for honey; its residue is known as Sikthaka <note>beeswax</note>. The learned also call it Madana, Madhuchishta, and Madhusara.

Draksha <note>grapes</note> is called Phalottama <note>the best of fruits</note>. Bilva is Shriphala and Shritaru. Lunga and Matulunga are called Keshari and Bijapuraka <note>Citron</note>.

Sobhanjana and Subhanja are like Shigru in their fruits and sprouts. Aja, Basta, and Jarachhaga refer to the goat; its urine is called Srava or Ambu.

Tvaksaha is Surabhi and Vanji; Surabhi is also the Mahataru <note>great tree</note>. Svarnakshiri and Svarnalata are names given to Jyotishmati.

# Chapter on the Preparation of Perfumes and Cosmetics

->*Suvira* is fermented rice water; *Vira* and *Talumala* refer to the palmyra tree.<-
->*Saubhagya* and *Tangana* refer to borax; *Bakuchi* is the plant *Malatibhava*.<-
->*Nissara* and *Rakshasa* refer to the lotus; *Kachha* is the fruit of the clearing-nut tree.<-
->*Amra*, *Chuta*, *Kamanga*, *Sahakara*, and *Smarapriya* are all names for the Mango tree.<-
->*Akshara* and *Kokilaksha* <note>The "cuckoo's eye" plant, Hygrophila auriculata</note> are terms declared by the experts of lexicons.<-

->At the outset, the author explains the purpose of these preparations:<-

->**Garlands, perfumes, incense, fine clothes, and ornaments do not shine upon one whose hair has turned white.**<-
->**For this reason, one should attend to the dyeing of the hair, just as one attends to the application of eye-collyrium and jewelry. (1)**<-

For one with white hair—that is, grey-headed—garlands (flower wreaths), perfumes (fragrant substances), incense (aromatic smoke), clothes (garments), and ornaments (decorations) are ineffective. <term>The use of the word "etcetera" implies the inclusion of ointments and pastes</term>. All such things do not look beautiful [on an aged person]; therefore, for this reason, one should make an effort in the service of "hair-coloring" or dyeing the hair. Just as one daily and with great effort attends to the application of collyrium for the eyes and the wearing of jewelry and decorations, in that same manner, one should attend to the dyeing of the hair. (1)

->Now, he describes the procedure for dyeing the hair:<-

->**In an iron vessel, cook the grains of Kodrava grain in sour gruel along with iron powder.**<-
->**When ground fine, apply this to the head (after the hair has been moistened with sour gruel) and remain with the head wrapped in moist leaves. (2)**<-

->**When six hours have passed, remove the paste and apply a coating of Myrobalan (Amalaka) to the head.**<-
->**Cover this again with leaves for another six hours; once washed, the head will attain a deep blackness. (3)**<-

"In an iron vessel": *Kodrava* <note>Kodo millet, often used in medicinal preparations</note> is well known. One should take the grains of *Kodrava* in an iron vessel (a container made of iron) and cook or steam them in "white acid," such as fermented rice-water (*kanjika*). Then, these should be ground together with iron powder (fine iron filings) until they form an extremely fine paste. This should be applied to the head—specifically a head where the hair has been made acidic or "primed" with sour fermented rice-water. After applying the paste, one should stay with the head covered or wrapped with fresh, moist leaves for a duration of two *praharas* <note>A prahara is a three-hour period; two praharas equal six hours</note>. (2)

->CCO. Vashistha Tripathi Collection. Digitized by eGangotri<-
