# In the Commentary on the Brhat Samhita [Chapter 76]

When the second watch has passed: That is, after the second watch <note>a watch or 'prahara' is approximately three hours</note> has elapsed, one should remove that previous paste. Then, one should apply a paste made of Myrobalan <note>original: "Amalaka"; Indian gooseberry used for hair health</note> to the head. After covering it with fresh, juicy leaves and waiting for another two watches, one should remove that paste and wash the head. Once washed, the hair attains a deep blackness. || 3 ||

### He then describes what should be done next:

-> Afterwards, having removed the smell of iron and acid from the head <-
-> with head-baths and fragrant oils, <-
-> and using heart-pleasing scents and various incenses, <-
-> one should enjoy the pleasures of sovereignty within the inner apartments. <- || 4 ||

Afterwards, following the treatment, one should remove the smell of iron and the smell of acid from the head using head-baths and fragrant oils. Then, with heart-pleasing scents—meaning those that are dear to the heart and delight the mind—and with various types of incense that produce satisfaction, one should enjoy the pleasures of the kingdom within the inner apartments. This means one should engage in amorous play with one's queens.

In this process, most of the substances are generally washed with clear fermented rice-water <note>original: "kanjika"</note>, some with water, and some with cow urine. One should cook the ingredients like "nail-scent" <note>a fragrant dried shellfish</note> and sesame oil in an iron vessel. The specifics of cooking over a mild fire, the penetration of scents, and the process of fumigation are to be learned from common worldly practice. They have not been explicitly stated by the Teacher <note>referring to the author, Varahamihira</note>. I have also not displayed them here for fear of making the book too voluminous. Since I have undertaken to explain the entire Samhita, I am only providing a literal explanation of the words; I do not possess specialized professional expertise in this specific craft. Therefore, the certainty of the practical application should be determined by experts based on common practice. || 4 ||

### First, he describes the royal head-bath:

-> Cinnamon, Costus, Renuka, Nalika, Sprikka, Myrrh, Tagara, and Valaka in equal parts, <-
-> mixed with Nagakesara and Patchouli leaves, <-
-> makes a head-bath fit for a king. <- || 5 ||

Cinnamon <note>original: "Tvak"</note> is well known. Costus <note>original: "Kustha"</note> is also well known. Renuka <note>original: "Renu"</note> is the seed of the Piper aurantiacum. Nalika is a stalk-like fragrant substance. Sprikka is a well-known fragrant creeper. "Rasa" refers to Myrrh <note>original: "Bola"</note>. Tagara is well known. Valaka is the fragrant root Hribera. These should be taken in equal parts. Of what nature? Mixed with Nagakesara <note>original: "Kesara"</note> and Patchouli <note>original: "Patra"</note>. This head-bath, composed of Cinnamon and the others mixed with Nagakesara and Patchouli, is suitable for a lord of men—that is, a King. || 5 ||

### Now he describes the fragrant oil:

-> A powder of Manjistha, Vyaghranakha, Shukti, Cinnamon, and Costus, mixed with Myrrh, <-
-> when combined with oil and heated by the rays of the sun, <-
-> creates an oil that possesses the fragrance of the Champaka flower. <- || 6 ||

# [Chapter 76] Chapter on the Preparation of Perfumes

Madder <note>original: "manjistha"; a root used for color and medicinal properties</note> is well-known. Likewise, with "tiger-nail" <note>original: "vyaghranakha"; likely a curved fragrant root or shell</note> and sea-foam <note>original: "samudraphena"; cuttlefish bone</note>. Also with "nail-shell" <note>original: "shukti-nakha"; the operculum of certain mollusks used in incense</note>. "Nail" refers to the skin-like covering born from a conch. Cinnamon bark <note>original: "tvak"</note> is well-known. Likewise with Costus <note>original: "kustha"</note> and resin <note>original: "rasa"</note>. Costus is well-known. Resin refers to myrrh <note>original: "bola"</note>. A powder should be made with this myrrh along with the Costus. This powder should be made using equal parts of all these aforementioned ingredients. It is then mixed with oil—specifically sesame oil. Heated by the rays of the sun <note>original: "arka-mayukha-tapta"</note>; that is, thoroughly warmed by the sun's rays. That oil then creates the scent of Champaka <note>original: "campaka-gandhi"</note>, becoming as fragrant as the Champaka flower. ||6||

### Now he describes the four-fold perfumes—

**With equal parts of Malabathrum, Frankincense, Valerian, and Tagar, a scent is produced that kindles desire.**
**This same mixture, when combined with Vyama and fumigated with Katuka and Asafoetida, becomes Bakula.**
**With Costus, it smells of Blue Lotus; with Sandalwood, the former becomes Champaka.**
**Combined with Nutmeg, Cinnamon, and Coriander, it should be known as Atimuktaka. ||7||**

"Leaf" <note>original: "patra"</note> refers to Malabathrum <note>original: "gandhapatra"</note>. "Turuška" refers to liquid storax or frankincense <note>original: "sihlarasa"</note>. "Bala" refers to Valerian <note>original: "baluka"</note>. "Tagar" is well-known. With these in equal parts, a scent is produced that kindles desire <note>original: "smara-uddipana"</note>, meaning it is an aphrodisiac. Regarding "with Vyama" <note>original: "savyama" </note>: this refers to the previously mentioned scent. When combined with Vyama <note>original: "vyamaka"</note>—which is a fragrant grass—and likewise provided with the fumigation of Katuka and Asafoetida <note>original: "katuka-hingu-pradhupa"</note>. Katuka is well-known; "Hingu" refers to "Hinguluka," commonly known as Guggul <note>original: "gugguluka"; a fragrant resin</note>. When fumigated with these two, it becomes "Bakula," having the scent of the Bakula flower. Regarding "with Costus, it smells of Blue Lotus": that same previously mentioned mixture, when combined with Costus, becomes "Utpala-gandhika," having a scent like the Blue Lotus. Regarding "with Sandalwood, the former becomes Champaka": that same previously mentioned mixture, when combined with Sandalwood <note>original: "malaya"</note>, becomes equal in scent to Champaka flowers. Regarding "combined with Nutmeg and Cinnamon": that same previously mentioned mixture combined with Nutmeg—the word "Jati" here refers to Nutmeg <note>original: "jatiphala"</note>. Cinnamon bark is well-known. Combined with these two and also with Coriander <note>original: "kustumburu"</note>, it becomes "Atimuktaka," having a scent like the Atimuktaka creeper. ||7||

### He says another as well—

**Dill and Frankincense in one-quarter and one-half parts, with "Nail" and Storax.**
**Portions of Sandalwood and Priyangu; the scent should be fumigated with molasses and "Nail-shell." ||8||**

Dill <note>original: "shatapushpa"</note> is well-known. Frankincense <note>original: "kunduruka"</note> is the well-known resin of the Boswellia tree. These two should be given in a quarter-part <note>original: "pada"</note>. "Nail" and Storax in a half-part; "Nail" is the skin-like covering of a shell, and "Turuška" is liquid storax. These two should be given in half-parts. Regarding "portions of Sandalwood and Priyangu": "Malaya" is Sandalwood, and "Priyangu" is the fragrant Aglaia <note>original: "gandhapriyangu"</note>.

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 76]

Of these two, there are two parts. A fourth part of these two should be given. The conch-shell <note>original: "śankha"; likely referring to a specific aromatic shell-cover or operculum</note> should be fumigated with molasses and "nail-scent" <note>original: "guḍanakhena"; "nakha" or "nail" refers to the operculum of certain mollusks used in ancient perfumery</note>. This fragrance is to be fumigated with molasses and the "nail." Wherever a fragrance is fumigated, it should first be fumigated with Haritaki <note>Chebulic Myrobalan, a medicinal fruit</note> and afterwards with the specified substance; so say those learned in the traditional scriptures <note>original: "āgamavidaḥ"</note>. ||8||

Now he describes the incense <note>term: "Dhūpa" (incense or fumigant)</note>—

->Guggulu, Valaka, Lac, Musta, Nakha, and Sugar in sequence form an incense.<-
->Another "Pinda" <note>a ball or lump of incense</note> is made of Jatamansi, Valaka, Turushka, Nakha, and Sandalwood. ||9||<-

Guggulu <note>Indian Bdellium resin</note> is well-known. Valaka <note>a fragrant grass root</note> is indeed well-known. Lac <note>resin from the lac insect</note> is well-known. Musta <note>Nutgrass</note> is indeed well-known. Nakha <note>the "nail"</note> is the skin produced from a shell and is well-known. Sugar is well-known. These, combined in equal parts in the given order, become an incense. Regarding "Another": Jatamansi <note>Spikenard</note> is well-known. Valaka is well-known. Turushka is liquid storax <note>original: "sihlarasam"</note>. Nakha and Sandalwood are also well-known. With these in equal parts, another—a second—lump <note>Pinda</note> or "lump-incense" is formed. ||9||

He says another as well—

->With Haritaki, Nakha, Ghana, Liquid, and Ambu;<-
->With Molasses and Utpala, combined with Shailaka and Mustaka;<-
->Increased sequentially by quarters from the beginning to the end of nine;<-
->Many delightful incenses are produced. ||10||<-

Haritaki is the "Pathya" fruit. "Shankha" is the Nakha <note>the aromatic shell-part</note>. Ghana is well-known <note>another name for Musta</note>. "Liquid" <note>drava</note> means resin or Myrrh <note>original: "bola"</note>. Ambu is Valaka; with these. Likewise with Molasses and Utpala combined with Shailaka and Mustaka: Molasses is the well-known sugarcane derivative; Utpala is Kustha <note>Costus</note>; Shailaka is Bitumen or Lichen <note>original: "śaileyam"</note>; Mustaka is Musta. With these combined, increased sequentially by quarters. "Ending in nine" means they are increased by quarters, where the quarters are increased at the beginning and at the end. For example: one part of Haritaki. Two of Nakha. Three of Ghana. By this sequence until nine parts of Musta. Thus, one incense is made with Haritaki, Nakha, Ghana, Liquid, and Ambu increased by quarters. A second is with Molasses and Utpala. A third is with these same ingredients combined with Shailaka and Mustaka. Alternatively, one part of Haritaki and two of Nakha make one incense. If three parts of Ghana are added there, it becomes a second incense. Thus, by increasing the parts of each substance, eight delightful incenses are formed. ||10||

He describes another incense—

->With four parts each of White Sandalwood, Shaila, and Musta;<-
->Parts of Srisa and Sarja, and Nakha and Guggulu;<-
->With an awakening of Camphor and a lump of Honey;<-
->This is called "Anger-Cover," the Incense of Kings. ||11||<-

# Chapter 76: The Art of Perfumery

<page-num>841</page-num>

**White sugar**. **Lichen** refers to the *parmelia* stone flower. **Nutgrass** is well-known. These should be given in four parts each. **Shri** refers to *shrivasaka* <note>a resinous exudate from the Long-leaved Pine</note>. **Sarja** is *sarjarasa* <note>resin from the Sal tree</note>. Of these two, two parts should be given. **Nail-scent** <note>the operculum of certain mollusks used in incense</note> is well-known. **Guggulu** <note>Indian Bdellium or Commiphora wightii</note> is also well-known. The nail-scent and guggulu must be given in two parts each. Its **awakening** <term>Bodha: the process of reviving or intensifying a scent</term> should be done with **camphor**. **Massed with honey** means made into a lump using honey from bees. This is the **King’s Incense**, a perfume fit for a ruler. Its specific name is **"Anger-Cover"** <note>Kopacchada: perhaps implying a scent so soothing it masks or removes anger</note>.

That which is added to a moist substance while it is still moist is called **Penetration** <term>Vedha: the infusion of scent into a wet base</term>. When a powder is added to a powdered substance, that is called **Awakening** <term>Bodha</term>.

As stated by the Lord <note>likely referring to an earlier authority or a specific deity in the tantric tradition</note> in his own work on perfumery:
> "That which is given to the moist while it is moist is called **Penetration**.
> But **Awakening** is that clear scent which occurs when powder is added to powder." <note>original: 'ओल्लम्मि ओल्लओ जो दिज्जइ वेह इति सो भणिओ। बोहो उण जो चुण्णो चुण्णविणि अच्छगन्धो सो॥'</note> ||11||

Now he describes the **Casket-Scent** <term>Putavasa: a perfumed powder used for clothes or the body</term>:
> "With parts of **cinnamon bark**, **vetiver**, and **scent-leaf**, combined with powders of **fine cardamom**, this is the excellent **Casket-Scent**, awakened by **musk** and **camphor**." ||12||

**Cinnamon bark** is *tvacham*. **Vetiver** is well-known. **Leaf** refers to the *gandhapatra* <note>Cinnamomum tamala</note>. These three are taken in equal parts. These are combined with **fine cardamom**. Fine cardamom is well-known. The meaning is that cardamom should be given in a quantity equal to half of the previous three parts combined. This powder is "awakened" by **musk** and **camphor**. **Mriga** refers to musk <note>Kasturika</note>. Camphor is well-known. By awakening with these two, it becomes a superior, excellent Casket-Scent for dusting the body. Some read this as **Cloth-Scent** <note>Patavasa</note>. Cloth-Scent refers to the perfuming of garments. ||13||

Now he describes the **Ocean of Perfume** <term>Gandharnava: a complex multi-ingredient aromatic</term>:
> **Nutgrass**, **valerian**, **lichen**, **camphor**, **vetiver**, and **nagakesara** flowers;
> **Sea-foam**, **clover**, **aloeswood**, **damana**, **nail-scent**, **tagara**, and **coriander**; ||13||
> With **camphor**, **choraka**, and **sandalwood**, these sixteen ingredients may be rotated at will.
> By using one, two, three, or four parts, the **Ocean of Perfume** is created. ||14||

**Nutgrass** is well-known. **Valerian** is also well-known. **Lichen**, **camphor**, and **vetiver** are all very well-known. **Nagapushpa** is *nagakesara* <note>Mesua ferrea</note>. **Tiger-nail** <note>Vyaghranakha</note> refers to **sea-foam** <note>Samudraphena or cuttlebone, used as a fixative</note>. **Sprikka** is a creeper. **Aloeswood** is well-known. **Damana** <note>Artemisia</note> is well-known. **Tagara** <note>Valeriana wallichii</note> is well-known. **Dhanya** is the coriander fruit. These are the ingredients. **Camphor** is well-known. **Chola** is the well-known *choraka* plant. **Malaya** is **sandalwood**. Thus, there are sixteen fragrant substances.

->**In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 76]**<-

Therefore, from this group of substances, by using these four—Nutgrass and the others—permuted according to one's own desire <note>original: "sveccha-parivartitaih"</note>, meaning rotated or reversed by one's own choice. How? By using one, two, three, or four parts. Thus, the **Ocean of Perfumes** <note>A poetic name for a vast system of perfume combinations</note> is created.

Here, sixteen squares should be made: four horizontally and four vertically. Starting from the first square, the ingredients like Nutgrass should be placed according to the order of the text. For example: in the first row, Nutgrass and the others; in the second, Vetiver and the others; in the third, Aloeswood and the others; in the fourth, Coriander and the others.

As it was said: "From these four, permuted by one's own desire, using one, two, three, or four parts, the Ocean of Perfumes is formed."

The variations are shown here. In sequence, six variations are possible for each individual set. For a group of four, there are twenty-four variations. For example:
1. One part Nutgrass, two parts Valerian, three parts Lichen, four parts Camphor. This is the first perfume.
2. One part Nutgrass, two parts Valerian, four parts Lichen, three parts Camphor. This is the second perfume.
3. One part Nutgrass, three parts Valerian, two parts Lichen, four parts Camphor. This is the third perfume.
4. One part Nutgrass, three parts Valerian, four parts Lichen, two parts Camphor. This is the fourth perfume.
5. One part Nutgrass, four parts Valerian, two parts Lichen, three parts Camphor. This is the fifth perfume.

| Nutgrass | Valerian | Lichen | Camphor |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Vetiver | Shell-perfume | Tiger-nail | Small Cardamom |
| Aloeswood | Sandalwood | Bitter-root | Cinnamon-leaf |
| Coriander | Clove | Cinnamon-bark | Malabar-leaf |

6. One part Nutgrass, four parts Valerian, three parts Lichen, two parts Camphor. This is the sixth perfume.

In this way, six perfumes are produced from each single substance <note>referring to the starting ingredient of a set</note>. For a group of four, there are twenty-four. For the full sixteen substances, there are ninety-six variations. || 14 ||

### Here he mentions a specific rule:

> Because of their extremely intense scent, one part is always used for Coriander; for Camphor, even less than that. These two should never be given in two, three, or more parts. || 15 ||

Here, because the scent of Coriander seeds <note>original: "dhanyaka-phalanam"</note> is extremely intense or sharp, one part should always be given at all times. Because Camphor also has an intense scent, less than one part <note>original: "tad-unah"</note> should be given. Even if the mathematical permutation suggests two or three parts, these two must not be given in those quantities. This is because their sharpness would cause the loss of the scent of the other substances. || 15 ||

### Now he speaks of the "awakening" of these incenses:

> They should be fumigated in order with Turpentine, Resin, and Shell-perfume mixed into a paste. The "awakening" <note>The final aromatic enhancement or fixative</note> should be given with Musk combined with Camphor. || 16 ||

# Chapter on the Preparation of Perfumes
## Chapter 76

<center>Page 843</center>

**Shrivasaka** <note>a resinous incense, likely from the Long-leaved Pine</note> is *Shri*. **Sarja** is *Sarjarasa* <note>resin from the Sal tree</note>. **Guda** <note>jaggery/molasses</note> and **Nakha** <note>literally "nail," referring to the operculum of certain mollusks used in incense</note> are well-known. With these substances, in the given order, all the perfumes are to be fumigated. They should not be fumigated as a single lump or when mixed together. This is what is meant: first, all the perfumes should be fumigated with *Shrivasaka*. Once that is done, they are fumigated again with *Sarja* resin. Then, all are fumigated again with *Guda*. Finally, all are to be fumigated with *Nakha*. After this, the "awakening" <note>term: Bodha; the final step to bring out the full fragrance</note> of all of them should be performed using musk combined with camphor. When done in this way, these perfumes become excellent. ||16||

Now, to demonstrate the vast scope of all possible perfumes, he says:

> **In this system, there are four thousand, plus another seventy thousand;**
> **One hundred thousand, and seven hundred and twenty varieties of perfumes.** ||17||

In this group of substances, there are four thousand, plus seventy thousand, plus one hundred thousand, and seven hundred and twenty—meaning that 174,720 <note>The text describes a combinatorial calculation of scents</note> variations of perfumes are included here. ||17||

He now explains how each single ingredient can produce six scents:

> **Each single substance, taken in one part and combined with others in two, three, or four parts,**
> **produces six scents; likewise, it produces more when used in two, three, or four parts.** ||18||

Each substance that is taken as one part, when joined with other substances in two, three, or four parts, produces six scents. In the same manner, it produces variations when used in two, three, or four parts. Those other substances which were added in two, three, or four parts to the one-part substance also become producers of six scents when the proportions are rearranged as before. Thus, every single substance, when joined with others in two, three, or four parts, produces six scents. ||18||

Now he explains the knowledge of the total sum of all combinations:

> **Just as from the combination of four substances there are twenty-four scents for one,**
> **so it is for the remaining ones; the total sum here is ninety-six.** ||19||

Just as—by which method—from the combination of four substances there are twenty-four scents for each one. When one substance is taken as one part, three other substances are added in two, three, and four parts. Thus, four substances are mixed together. These result in six variations <note>mathematical permutations of the parts</note>. Therefore, each produces six scents. Thus, six times four is twenty-four. Therefore, such is the scent for each one. Since that one substance occurs twenty-four times, there are twenty-four scents in each instance. Thus it is said: "from the combination of four substances there are twenty-four scents for one." In this way, for the remaining three groups of four, there are seventy-two scents. The total sum in this section on perfumes is ninety-six. ||19||

### Now he describes the knowledge of the total number of combinations when ingredients are varied by four:

->**In a set of sixteen substances, when varied by choosing four at a time,**<-
->**The total number of combinations produced is eighteen hundred and twenty. || 20 ||**<-

In this group of sixteen substances <note>original: "shodashake"</note>, when varied by four—meaning each perfume is created by selecting four specific ingredients at a time—there are eighteen hundred and twenty (1,820) distinct scents produced. The Master <note>The author, Varahamihira</note> will demonstrate this himself further on. || 20 ||

### Now he explains the knowledge of the total quantity of all possible scents:

->**Since the group of four-way variations is divided into ninety-six types,**<-
->**That number must be multiplied by ninety-six; that is the total number of scents. || 21 ||**<-

Because this four-way variation is divided into ninety-six types through continuous permutation, the number eighteen hundred and twenty (1,820) must be multiplied by ninety-six. That resulting figure is the total number of all possible scents. This means one hundred seventy-four thousand, seven hundred and twenty (174,720). However, this is according to a secondary or "broad" calculation <note>term: "gauna-vrittya" - a figurative or approximate application of a rule</note>, not the primary one. By the primary method <note>term: "mukhya-vrittya" - the literal or direct rule</note>, the total is forty-three thousand, six hundred and eighty (43,680). This is because the group of four-way variations is actually divided into twenty-four types. || 21 ||

### Now, to demonstrate these variations and the method for calculating the totals, he describes the "Clod-Distribution" <note>term: "lostaka-prastara" - a mathematical method using a grid or "clods" to calculate combinations/permutations, similar to Pascal's Triangle</note>:

->**Add the preceding and the one before that,**<-
->**Excluding the last place, they declare the sum.**<-
->**Having moved the desired variations in order,**<-
->**When the end is reached, stop; then start the next process. || 22 ||**<-

One should place the numbers starting from one up to sixteen, one above the other. Each upper number should be added to the preceding number <note>original: "purvena purvena"</note>—the one that has already been processed. For example, if 2 is placed above 1, then 1 is the "preceding" and "processed" number relative to 2. By adding that preceding number to the one above it, and continuing this up to the fifteenth place—as it is said: "Excluding the last place, they declare the sum." One declares the sum while omitting the final position. Then, starting again from the bottom, one should add the preceding processed number up to the fourteenth place. Then again from the bottom...

# Chapter 76: The Chapter on the Preparation of Perfumes

The calculation should be performed by adding the previous result, continuing up to the thirteenth position. In this manner, the total becomes one thousand eight hundred and twenty. For the sake of illustration, the layout for sixteen ingredients, starting from one, is presented:

<note>This table represents a version of what is known today as Pascal's Triangle, used here to calculate combinations. The columns represent the number of ingredients chosen (1, 2, 3, or 4) from a total pool of 16.</note>

In this table, the preceding number is added to the next number in the sequence (starting from one) and placed above. By this process of inclusion, excluding the final result, sixteen are produced in the first place <note>choosing 1 from 16</note>. In the second place, one hundred and twenty <note>choosing 2 from 16</note>. In the third place, five hundred and sixty <note>choosing 3 from 16</note>. And in the fourth place, one thousand eight hundred and twenty are produced <note>choosing 4 from 16</note>. Thus, the total number for combinations of four ingredients is established.

### Now, he speaks regarding the method of "clod-permutation" for these:

> "Move the desired variations step by step; once moved, there is a cessation, then a different movement."

In that process, one should first write the initial letters of the names of the sixteen substances, such as coriander and others. Among them, the first three are marked as "fixed clods" <term>sthira-loṣṭaka: markers or tokens that remain stationary during a step of the calculation</term>, and the fourth is marked as a "moving clod" <term>cara-loṣṭaka: a marker that is shifted to generate variations</term>. That moving clod is shifted sequentially to the other substances, and upon reaching the end, there is a cessation. At the fifth, there is a bringing back. In this manner, the work is done for all, following the sequence. As it was said: "by the desired variations." Having moved the moving clod step by step according to the desired variations and having shifted it elsewhere, once it has been moved, a cessation should be made.

Then, a different movement: when the moving clod has reached the final ingredient in a certain position, one should move the fixed clod to another position. Having fixed it there, the variations are shown by moving the moving clod that stands in front of it to other positions. Then again, having moved the moving clod from one position to another and placing it firmly there, the variations are shown with the moving clod ahead of it. Thus, when the last fixed clod reaches the penultimate position, one should move the other fixed clod to another position. Then, placing the penultimate and ultimate clods in front of it and moving them to the end, the variations are shown as before. This continues until all of them—the one before the penultimate, the penultimate, and the ultimate—have reached the end. Then again, one should move the last fixed clod to another position, and the variations are shown with the others placed in front as before. This should be done for all in sequence, until all of them occupy the final positions.

For example: by making the first three fixed and moving the fourth, thirteen variations arise. Then, by moving the third clod to the fourth substance and moving the fourth clod, twelve variations arise. Then, by moving the third to the fifth position and moving the fourth clod, eleven arise. Then, by moving the third to the sixth position, ten. Thus, in the seventh, nine. In the eighth, eight.

# Chapter on the Composition of Perfumes

**"By two, three, five, and eight parts..."** In this *Kachhaputa* <note>A specific grid-like arrangement or "tortoise-shell" box used for organizing perfume ingredients</note>, Aloe wood is to be taken in two parts. *Patra* (scented leaf) in three parts. *Turushka* (liquid storax) in five parts—corresponding to the number of the senses. *Shailya* (lichen) in eight parts. **"Five, eight, two, and three..."** *Priyangu* (perfumed cherry) in five parts—corresponding to the number of the objects of the senses. *Musta* (nut-grass) in eight parts. *Rasa* (myrrh) in two parts—corresponding to the number of the wings <note>original: paksha, referring to the two fortnights of a lunar month</note>. *Kesha* (valerian) in three parts—corresponding to the number of the ritual fires. ॥ 23 ॥

**"Of Sprikka, Bark, and Tagara..."** *Sprikka* (clover) in four parts—corresponding to the number of the *Kritas* <note>The four ages or Yugas</note>. Bark in one part. *Tagara* (Indian valerian) in seven parts. *Mansi* (spikenard) in six parts. **"By seven, six, four, and one..."** *Malaya* (sandalwood) in seven parts. *Nakha* (fingernail-shaped shell) in six parts—corresponding to the number of the seasons. *Shrika* (turpentine resin) in four parts—corresponding to the number of the Vedas. *Kunduruk* (frankincense) is to be given in one part—corresponding to the number of the Moon. These should be placed in a sixteen-square grid according to their respective parts as previously described. ॥ 24 ॥

> and fumigated with jaggery and Shell-powder, these perfumes are called *Sarvatobhadra* (All-auspicious). ॥ 26 ॥

**"In the sixteen..."** In this sixteen-square grid, whenever four substances are mixed or unified in any manner—whether vertically, horizontally, in the four corners, in the central four squares, in the four corner-most squares, in the first row, the middle two squares, or the final row—the sum of their parts always equals eighteen. In this *Kachhaputa*, those eighteen-part combinations should be joined with Shell, Tagara, and Storax. *Nakha* (Shell) refers to the skin of a conch-like organism. *Tagara* is well-known. *Turushka* is liquid storax. These three should be added in equal measures...

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 76]

*Nagapushpa* is the Nagakesara flower <note>Mesua ferrea, known for its fragrance</note>. *Kustha* is well-known <note>Saussurea lappa, an aromatic root</note>. With all of these in equal proportions, a "fragrant water" (*gandhambhas*) should be prepared or made. In this fragrant water, [the materials] should remain for some time—meaning they should be kept there for half a night. ||32||

**Regarding Nutmeg and others:** There are four parts by count of Nutmeg (*jatiphala*). Of its leaf (*patra*), there are two parts, the number of the twins <note>original: "yama-sankhyau", referring to the twins Yama and Yami, signifying the number 2</note>. Of Cardamom (*ela*), specifically the small variety, there is one part. Of Camphor (*karpura*), also called *ghanasara*, there are three parts, the number of the fires <note>original: "shikhi-sankhya", referring to the three ritual fires, signifying the number 3</note>. These ingredients, in the stated proportions, are to be combined and ground into a very fine powder. Then, the tooth-sticks (*dantakastha*) are to be dusted with this powder and dried by the rays (*marichi*) of the sun (*bhanu*). ||33||

->Now, he describes what benefits these tooth-sticks provide when used:<-

->**They produce clarity of complexion, radiance of the face,**<-
->**cleanliness of the mouth, and a pleasant scent.**<-
->**To the one who uses them, they grant a voice pleasing to the ear;**<-
->**such are the effects of the sticks for those born twice.**<- ||34||

"Born twice" (*asakridudbhava*) refers to the teeth, as they grow twice <note>referring to primary and permanent teeth</note>; thus, "sticks for those born twice" means tooth-sticks. For the user, they produce clarity of complexion (*varna-prasada*), meaning a beautiful glow. They bring radiance (*kanti*) or loveliness to the face (*vadana*). They provide cleanliness (*vaishadya*), meaning purity or spotlessness, to the mouth (*asya*). They provide fragrance (*sugandhita*). And they make the speech (*vach*) or voice pleasant to the ear (*shrotra-sukha*). ||34||

->Now he describes the virtues of Betel-leaf (*tambula*):<-

->**It inflames desire, enhances physical beauty,**<-
->**brings good fortune, and makes the breath fragrant.**<-
->**It gives strength and destroys diseases born of phlegm;**<-
->**thus Betel-leaf provides these and other benefits.**<- ||35||

In addition to the qualities already mentioned like clarity of complexion and facial radiance, it possesses these other virtues. Namely: it inflames or generates desire (*kama*). It manifests or produces physical beauty (*rupa*). It brings or creates good fortune (*saubhagya*), meaning the state of being well-loved. It creates fragrance in the mouth (*vaktra*). It produces strength (*urj*). It smites or destroys diseases (*roga*) arising from phlegm (*kapha*). Likewise, it performs other functions such as clearing the throat and aiding digestion. ||35||

->He mentions others as well:<-

->**With the right amount of lime, it produces a red color;**<-
->**with an excess of areca nut, the color is ruined.**<-

<summary>This page details the preparation of aromatic powders for dental hygiene and lists the cosmetic and medicinal benefits of using tooth-sticks and chewing betel-leaf (tambula).</summary>
<keywords>perfumery, dental hygiene, Brihat Samhita, Varahamihira, nutmeg, camphor, betel-leaf, Ayurvedic cosmetics</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of Chapter 76 (Preparation of Perfumes) to the beginning of Chapter 77 (Union of Men and Women) in Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita, featuring the commentary by Bhattotpala.</meta>

->Too much lime causes a foul odor in the mouth;<-
->An abundance of leaf creates a pleasant fragrance. [36]<-

Betel <note>original: "tambula"; the practice of chewing betel leaf with areca nut and lime</note> mixed with a proper amount of lime—neither too much nor too little—produces a rich red color. An excess of areca nut <note>original: "puga-phala"</note> destroys or diminishes that color. Too much lime makes the mouth smell foul or unpleasant. However, betel prepared with an abundance of leaf produces a fine and beautiful fragrance. [36]

He further describes the specific timing:

->An abundance of leaf is beneficial at night, and nut during the day;<-
->To do otherwise than what is prescribed is merely a mockery.<-
->Scented with kakkola, areca nut, lavali-fruit, and parijata,<-
->It brings delight through the joy of intoxication. [37]<-

At night, betel with more leaf is beneficial. During the day, it should have more fruit (areca nut). To do the opposite of this instruction—such as using more nut at night or more leaf during the day—is a "mockery" <note>meaning it is ridiculous or ineffective</note>. *Kakkola* is well known <note>a spice, likely cubeb or allspice</note>. Areca nuts are well known. *Lavali-fruit* refers here to the clove flower, as the actual fruit is not typically used. *Parijata* refers to nutmeg <note>original: "jatiphala"</note>. Betel prepared with these ingredients makes a man joyful with the pleasure of mild intoxication. [37]

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Preparation of Perfumes," within the section "Concerns of the Inner Apartments" in the Commentary on the Samhita composed by the venerable Bhattotpala.

# Now, the Union of Men and Women is explained.

At the very beginning, he speaks to demonstrate the purpose of this study:

->With a weapon hidden in her braided hair, his own Queen killed Viduratha.<-
->And with an anklet smeared with poison, the estranged Queen killed the King of Kashi. [1]<-
->Thus, estranged women cause life-ending calamities; what need is there to mention others?<-
->Therefore, men must carefully examine women to see if they are devoted or estranged. [2]<-

"With a weapon...": The King Viduratha was killed by his own wife, the Queen, who had become estranged <note>emotionally alienated or hostile</note>. She struck him with a weapon that had been concealed within the braids of her hair.

The word "Kila" <note>a Sanskrit particle</note> is used here to indicate a traditional report or historical account. The Queen, having become alienated or disaffected, killed the King of Kashi <note>modern-day Varanasi</note>, her own husband, by means of an anklet smeared with poison. This implies she introduced that poison into his drinks or onto his person.

In this manner, women who have lost their affection for their husbands produce life-ending faults or dangers. What is the use of reciting or describing other faults further? For this reason, men—and specifically kings—must examine women with great effort to determine whether they are truly devoted or disaffected. As Kamandaki <note>an ancient author on statecraft and ethics</note> says:

> After bathing, being anointed with perfumes, wearing garlands and beautiful ornaments, the King should see the Queen only after she has bathed, is wearing clothes provided by him, and is adorned with jewels.
> He should not enter the Queen’s quarters without caution; he should only eat from his own established kitchen. Even if he is extremely fond of them, he should not go among women with blind trust.
> Because of a delusion occurring in the Queen's quarters, King Bhadrasena was killed; so too was the King of Karusha by his own son who was hidden within his mother's bed.
> Having mixed parched grain with poison under the lure of honey, the Queen killed the King of Kashi in a private moment.
> The Queen of Sauvira killed the King with a poisoned gem in her girdle; the Queen of Vaivatya killed him with a poisoned anklet; and another killed her husband with a poisoned mirror.
> Likewise, the Queen of Viduratha killed him by concealing a weapon within her braided hair. — 1-2

### Now he describes the signs of a woman who is in love:

> The internal states reveal the affection born of the Mind-Born <note>Kamadeva, the god of love</note>:
> The displaying of the navel, arms, breasts, and ornaments;
> The adjusting of garments and the loosening of the hair;
> And the casting of the eyebrows along with trembling, sidelong glances. — 3

"Internal states" <term>Bhava: the outward physical manifestations of inner emotions</term> refer to specific gestures that indicate one's inner condition, such as trembling of the body, dryness of the mouth, or paleness of the face. These reveal the affection or love produced by the Mind-Born <note>original: "Manobhava", an epithet for the god of love</note>. Likewise, the displaying of the navel, arms, breasts, and ornaments reveals this love. The navel is the center of the abdomen; the arms; the breasts; and the ornaments are the decorations. Upon seeing her beloved, a woman in love reveals these parts. Similarly, the "adjusting of garments" refers to the fixing of her clothes, and the "loosening of the hair" refers to releasing the braid. These also reveal the affection born of love. Finally, the casting of the eyebrows and the looking with trembling, sidelong glances reveal the affection born of the god of love.

# Chapter 77: On the Union of Women and Men

A side-long glance is a playful movement of the eyes. By the movement of the eyebrows—that is, by the trembling or shaking caused by the knitting of the brows—one observes the side-long glance; these are known as "glances trembling with the movement of the brows." And so says the sage Kashyapa <note>Kashyapa is an ancient Vedic sage often cited in texts regarding medicine, ethics, and social conduct</note>:

> A woman who is established in passion is "red" <note>original: "rakta" - meaning colored by passion or affectionate</note>, while one without it is "disaffected" <note>original: "virakta"</note> and proud of her home.
> She is agitated in her heart by the binding of her mind and sight.
> She who is passionate is known by the various signs and gestures of her form.
> Distraction, having the mind elsewhere, and a lack of concealment even in the house of her elders;
> And she who finds delight in the sound [of her lover's name] is colored by passion.
> Any woman other than this is proclaimed to be disaffected.

Now, he describes other signs of a passionate woman:

> Spitting loudly, laughing excessively, moving toward him on the bed or seat;
> Cracking the joints of the limbs, yawning, and requesting small, easily obtainable things;
> Embracing and kissing a child in his presence, looking toward a female friend;
> Casting glances when he is turned away, praising his virtues, and scratching her ear. (4)

> One should recognize these as the actions of one who is enamored:
> She speaks pleasant things and gives of her own wealth;
> She rejoices upon seeing him, her anger vanishes,
> And she wipes away his faults by proclaiming his virtues. (5)

> Honoring his friends and hating his enemies;
> Remembering what he has done and being despondent when he is away;
> Offering her breasts and lips, embracing him;
> Sweating, and taking the first initiative in kissing. (6)

"Spitting loudly," etc. One should recognize and know a woman of such behavior to be enamored. Of what kind? Upon seeing the man, she spits loudly, making a sound with her mouth. She laughs excessively and with sound. On the bed—the mattress—or on the seat, she performs a "moving toward," meaning she seeks closeness or comes near. She performs the "cracking" of the limbs—the parts of the body—making a sound, and "yawning"—the opening of the mouth. Likewise, she makes a "request"—a begging—for wealth that is "easily obtainable" and "small"—meaning just a tiny amount. In the presence of her "beloved" <note>original: "vallabha"</note>, she performs the "embracing and kissing of a child." She embraces—clasps—a child or infant and performs "kissing"—contact with the mouth. She "looks toward a female friend"—looking at the face of a companion who is aware of her secret signals...

...she performs. And "glancing away": when that beloved is looking elsewhere, she casts her gaze toward him. She engages in "praising his virtues," which means the repeated recitation of his good qualities. She also "scratches her ear" <note>A traditional gesture of bashfulness or flirtation in Sanskrit literature</note>.

"And this..." [referring to the verse]: One should recognize this as the "behavior of one who is enamored," characterized by the signs just described. "Enamored behavior" refers to the physical movements of one who is in love. Such a woman speaks "dear things," meaning pleasant words. She "gives her own wealth," bestowing her personal finances upon him. Upon "seeing that husband" (or lord), she "rejoices," showing her happiness. She becomes "devoid of anger," having cast away all resentment. By "praising his virtues" and recounting his deeds, she "wipes away his faults," effectively erasing any offenses he may have committed.

"Worship of his friends...": She performs "worship" or shows great respect to his friends and companions. She holds "enmity toward his enemies," acting with hostility toward those he dislikes. "Mindful of what was done": she remembers the deeds he has performed and proclaims the favors he has done for her. When he is "away" in a foreign land, she suffers from "dejection," a state of a sorrowful mind. "Giving of breasts and lips": this refers to allowing the touching of the breasts and the giving of the lower lip for drinking <note>i.e., kissing</note>. "Embracing" means clasping him, and "kissing" is the joining of faces. Such behaviors occur at the "first union" or "approach" of a woman who is colored by passion. And so says the Sage Kashyapa:

> She casts her sight upon him and contemplates him even in her mind.
> Yet she maintains silence, like a figure painted on a canvas.
> 
> Suddenly appearing before him, she might firmly embrace someone else <note>likely a child or friend, to show her affection indirectly</note>.
> She touches her thighs, hips, navel, ornaments, and breasts.
> 
> With her nails, she might scratch near her navel, colored by her passion.
> She yawns and spits excessively, and utters "wicked" <note>playfully naughty or teasing</note> words.
> 
> She embraces a child and bites her own lip with her teeth.
> By these transformations, a maiden afflicted by the god of love is to be known.
> 
> She who rejoices at the sight of him, honors his circle of friends,
> Looks at him with a smile while turning away, and proclaims his virtues—she is truly in love.

### Now he describes the characteristics of a woman who is disaffected:

> **The behavior of the disaffected includes a face with a frowning brow,**
> **Turning the face away, and the feigning of forgetfulness.**
> **A lack of excitement, the state of being difficult to please,**
> **Friendship with those he hates, and harsh speech. || 7 ||**

->Or, having been touched or looked upon, she shakes her limbs;<-
->She acts with pride and does not stop him when he leaves.<-
->At the end of a kiss, she wipes her face;<-
->And having fallen asleep first, she rises only after him. (8)<-

**Signs of Disaffection:** These are the characteristics of a woman who has lost her love <note>Sanskrit: *virakta-ceṣṭā*</note>. **Frowning of the face:** upon seeing her husband at a distance, she makes a distorted, frowning expression. **Turning away:** looking elsewhere to avoid his gaze. **Forgetfulness of deeds:** she forgets the favors or kindnesses he has previously performed. **Lack of respect** upon seeing him. **Difficulty in being satisfied:** she is pleased only with great effort; even after being given many gifts, she remains unsatisfied. **Friendship with his enemies:** she shows affection and friendliness toward those he hates. She speaks **harshly** and says things that are disagreeable to him.

**Or, having been touched:** Alternatively, upon being touched or seen by the man, she shakes or shudders her body. She displays **pride** <note>literally "greatness" or "haughtiness"</note>. She does not stop or restrain him when he leaves in anger. At the end of a kiss—the conclusion of the contact of mouths—she wipes her face. Having fallen asleep first upon the bed, she rises only later, after the man has already gotten up. As the sage **Kashyapa** <note>An ancient Vedic sage often cited in technical treatises</note> says:

> "The foolish woman, having seen him, pretends not to see; having been touched, she speaks harsh words. When embraced during the time of pleasure, she wipes her mouth after a kiss. She wakes up last and turns her back in bed. Such a woman is known as 'disaffected' and should be avoided with effort." (7-8)

Now, he describes those who act as messengers <note>Sanskrit: *dūtyaḥ*, female go-betweens or procurers</note> for the destruction of noble families, from whom women should be protected:

->A female mendicant, a wandering nun, a slave-girl, a nurse, a young girl, a washerwoman,<-
->A flower-seller, a wicked woman, a female friend, and a barber’s wife are the messengers. (9)<-

->Because these messengers are the cause of the ruin of noble families,<-
->Women must be guarded from them with effort, for the sake of increasing the lineage, fame, and honor. (10)<-

**A female mendicant:** A well-known woman under a vow, often wearing red robes. **A wandering nun:** An ascetic woman. **A slave-girl:** A female servant. **A nurse:** A wet-nurse. **A young girl:** An unmarried maiden. **A washerwoman:** One who cleans clothes. **A flower-seller:** One who provides garlands. **A wicked woman:** A woman of bad character living in her own home. **A female friend:** A companion. **A barber’s wife.** These women act as messengers <term>Dūtyaḥ: intermediaries who facilitate secret meetings or affairs</term> for women in their relations with other men. (9)

# On the Protection of Women [Chapter 77]

...is the cause of the destruction of noble families. Because these female messengers <note>dūtyaḥ: intermediaries or go-betweens often used in secret affairs</note> are the cause for the destruction and the ruin of the character of people born of faultless lineage, for this reason, women must be guarded against such messengers for the sake of increasing the prosperity of the family, its fame, and its honor. They must be protected with great care. ||10||

Now, he describes the circumstances that serve as pretexts for secret meetings which lead to the ruin of women:

**Night-wandering, staying awake, feigning illness, visiting others' houses, female fortune-tellers,**
**Grief, and festivals—these are the causes for secret meetings; in these situations, they must be guarded. ||11||**

"Night-wandering" means leaving one's own home at night and roaming outside. "Staying awake" refers to sleeplessness. "Feigning illness" is taking refuge in the excuse of a disease. "Others' houses" means staying in the residence of another. "Female fortune-tellers" <term>īkṣaṇikā: women who predict the future, often having access to private quarters</term>. "Grief" is indulging in sorrow based on some cause that produces detachment. "Festivals" include weddings and similar occasions. These are the causes for women's secret meetings—their union with other men. In these circumstances, women must be guarded. And so says Kashyapa <note>An ancient sage often cited as an authority in technical treatises</note>:

> She who is devoted to the company of the wicked quickly destroys the family.
> Wandering on pilgrimages, <unclear>division</unclear>, and visiting the houses of others;
> Roaming at night in temples, or staying with neighbors;
> And residing in the father's house without the husband—these are not auspicious.
> A woman is like a pot of clarified butter <note>ghṛta: ghee</note>, and a man is like the heat of fire.
> From contact, the pot melts; likewise is a woman affected in the presence of a man.
> When a woman sees a man in a secluded place, her limbs relaxed,
> Her private parts become moist, filled with the desire for favor. ||11||

Now, he describes the qualities of women and the characteristics of their pleasure:

**At first, she does not desire it, yet does not abandon talk of love; she is languid, mixed with bashfulness.**
**In the middle, she is devoid of shame; at the conclusion, her face is bowed with modesty.**
**She performs with various expressions of emotion, and is repeatedly full of respect;**
**Having understood the man's nature, she follows him with tireless actions. ||12||**

"At first," meaning when first lying on the bed, she does not desire or consent to sexual union, yet she "does not abandon" or give up "talk of love" (erotic conversation). Then, at the beginning of the union, she is "languid, mixed with bashfulness." Bashfulness is modesty; she whose languor is joined with that is "languid, mixed with bashfulness." "In the middle," during the act of union, she is "devoid of shame"...

She becomes free from shame. Upon the conclusion of the sexual act, her face is bowed with modesty—shame being the bashfulness that inclines her face downward. Again, through various <term>Bhavas</term><note>Natural emotional states or gestures that convey internal feelings</note> such as playful sportiveness and grace, she engages in union in many ways. Of what sort is she? She is full of respect and endowed with faith. She is one who, having understood the male nature, follows his lead through actions that mirror his exhaustion or energy, his joy or sorrow. When the man is weary, she displays weariness; when he is happy, she is happy.

### Now, he describes other qualities of women—

> The qualities of women consist of youth, beauty, dress, 
> courtesy, specialized knowledge, and graceful charms. 
> Among those endowed with such qualities, a woman is called a "gem"; 
> others are merely "female maladies" to a clever man. || 13 ||

These are the qualities of women <note>original: "yoṣitām"</note>. What are they? Youth <note>original: "yauvana"</note> means being in the prime of life. Beauty <note>original: "rūpa"</note> is one's own loveliness. Dress <note>original: "veṣa"</note> refers to the ornamentation of the body. Courtesy <note>original: "dākṣiṇya"</note> means being favorable or compliant. Specialized knowledge <note>original: "vijñāna"</note> is skill in the arts mentioned in the textbooks on love <term>Kāmaśāstra: ancient Indian treatises on desire, sexuality, and social etiquette</term> and skill in capturing a man's heart. Graceful charm <note>original: "vilāsa"</note> refers to steady, sweet speech and side-long glances. Alternatively, "graceful charm" is defined by the characteristic: "of standing, sitting, and walking." "Graceful charms and the rest" means those qualities where grace is the first or foremost. These include playfulness, charm, and tasteful arrangement of dress. These are the qualities of women.

And among those endowed with these qualities, a woman is designated as a "gem" <note>original: "ratna-saṃjñā"</note>. As he will say later: "Among elephants, horses, and women, the word 'gem' is applied due to the excellence of their specific qualities." It has been said:

-> Whatever is the best of its kind is called a "gem." <-

"Others are female maladies," he says. Others—those who possess the opposite characteristics and are devoid of good qualities—are "female maladies" to a clever or sophisticated man <note>original: "catura"</note>, meaning they cause distress to his mind. Thus, the Lord Vyāsa <note>the legendary sage and author of the Mahābhārata</note> says:

> That wife who is pure, capable, fond of sweet food, and speaks kindly, 
> who protects herself and is devoted to her husband—she is called "Prosperity" <note>original: "Śrī," the goddess of fortune</note> by the wise. 
> But that wife who has distorted eyes, is foul, fond of quarreling, 
> and always talks back—she is "Old Age" <note>original: "Jarā"</note>; for true old age is not just the passing of years. 
> She who is despondent when he is despondent, happy when he is happy, troubled when he is troubled, 
> who is like a reflection of her beloved, and only fearful when he is enraged—she is the ideal wife. || 13 ||

### Now he describes women to be avoided in this context—

> A woman should not use coarse language, nor should her body be smeared with dirt; 
> she should not engage in talk regarding contemptible body parts. 
> When in private, she should not be thinking of other tasks, 
> for the Mind is the root of the God whose form was burnt by Shiva. || 14 ||
<note>The "God whose form was burnt" is Kāmadeva, the god of love, who was turned to ashes by Shiva's third eye but lives on as "Ananga" (the bodiless) in the minds of lovers.</note>

"Village-born" refers to those born in common settlements; specifically, those whose bodies are marked by common colors or impurities. This implies <term>speakers of Prakrit</term> <note>original: "prakrita-bhashinya"; referring to those who speak common vernaculars rather than refined Sanskrit, often implying a lack of courtly education</note>. He now describes other virtues of a woman:

->**She who exhales in unison with the man, and is skilled in offering her arms as a pillow and her breasts.**<-
->**She whose hair is fragrant, whose passion is ignited by proximity, who sleeps only after he has slept, and wakes before him. || 15 ||**<-

"Exhaling in unison with the man" means breathing at the same time as the male partner. This indicates mutual passion. <term>Skilled in offering arms as a pillow and her breasts</term> means she is clever in arranging her arms for support and providing the touch of her breasts. "Fragrant hair" means her hair has been made sweet-smelling. "Passion ignited by proximity" means she possesses a beautiful affection and desire that arises as soon as the lover is near. She falls asleep only after her beloved has slept, and is <term>awake</term> <note>original: "vibuddha"</note>—meaning her sleep has vanished—first, before him. On this, the sage Kashyapa says:

> When a woman gazes at a man’s body in a secluded, lonely place,
> her private parts become moist, filled with the desire to be favored.
> By delighting the mind of the woman through mutual attraction,
> one conceives an excellent, fortunate, and long-lived child.
> But if the two are troubled in mind or detached during union,
> then the child may be deformed, short-lived, weak-limbed, or miserable. || 15 ||

Now he describes women who should be avoided:

->**Those of wicked nature should be avoided, as well as those who lack patience during the time of vigorous embrace.**<-
->**Those whose menstrual blood is scented like, or colored like, indigo, yellow, or slightly copper-red are not praised. || 16 ||**<-
->**She who is prone to excessive sleep, has an excess of blood and bile, <gloss>1</gloss> or suffers from discharges or an excess of wind and phlegm.**<-
->**She who eats excessively, is prone to sweating, has a foul body, or she who has very short hair or is prematurely grey. || 17 ||**<-

And those who were described in the section on "Inauspicious Female Characteristics" <note>The commentator refers back to Chapter 69, verse 16 of this same work</note>—such as those with a short little finger or the finger next to it—one should not engage in the practice of love with such women. The meaning is that in every way, a beloved who possesses sinful or wicked characteristics should be avoided. ||18||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the menstrual blood of a woman:

->That blood which resembles the blood of a rabbit, or is like the juice of lac,<-
->and which, when washed, leaves no stain—that blood is pure. ||19||<-

->That blood which is produced without sound or pain and ceases after three days;<-
->upon union with a man, that undoubtedly leads to pregnancy. ||20||<-

Regarding "resembling the blood of a rabbit": That blood which is like the blood of a rabbit—the animal—meaning it is very red; or like the juice of lac <note>Lac is a resinous secretion from insects used as a red dye</note>, meaning it is similar to the color of that tree resin. And that which, when washed, "loses its color," meaning it comes out of the cloth—that should be considered pure. The meaning is that it is fit for conceiving a child. ||19||

Regarding the phrase "that which is devoid of sound and pain": This refers to menstrual blood that is free from any sound or noise when it falls. It is also free from pain or physical agony. That blood which ceases after three days—by reason of the union of a pair <note>sexual intercourse</note>—certainly becomes a fetus without doubt. ||20||

### Now he describes the rules for women during their menses—

->**For three days, women should not indulge in bathing, wearing garlands, or applying ointments.**<-
->**On the fourth day, she should bathe according to the instructions stated in the scriptures.**<- ||21||

->**She should bathe with those medicinal herbs mentioned in the "Pushya-Bathing" ritual, mixed with water.**<-
->**The mantra to be used there is the same one specified for that ritual.**<- ||22||

"For three days" etc.: Women during their menses should not practice bathing, wearing garlands (flowers, etc.), or applying ointments (perfumed pastes, etc.). On the fourth day, she should perform purification by bathing according to the methods prescribed in the <term>Shastras</term> <note>sacred scriptures or technical treatises</note>. ||21||

"The Pushya-Bathing herbs" etc.: In the chapter on the <term>Pushya-Snana</term> <note>A royal lustration ritual performed when the moon is in the asterism of Pushya</note>, certain herbs were mentioned—starting with "Jyotishmati, Trayamana," etc. She should bathe with these mixed with water. Furthermore, in that same manner—using firm jars at the corners with necks wrapped in white thread—the same mantra specified in that Pushya-Bathing ritual, beginning with "May the gods consecrate you," is prescribed here. ||22||

### Now he describes the three divisions of the union of women and men—

->**It is said that on even nights, males are conceived; on odd nights, females.**<-
->**On the later even nights, children are long-lived, handsome, and happy.**<- ||23||

Following the menstrual period, on "even" (equal) nights, "humans" <note>here meaning males/sons</note> are produced. The word "Kila" <note>it is said</note> is used to indicate traditional authority. When union with the husband occurs on even nights, sons are born. Similarly, on "odd" (uneven) nights, "women" <note>daughters</note> are born. He also provides a specific detail: "long-lived, handsome, and happy." This occurs on the "later even nights"—meaning the even nights further removed from the start of the period, excluding the fourth night.

# The Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 77]

On the sixth, eighth, twelfth, and sixteenth nights <note>referring to the nights following the start of the menstrual cycle</note>, children are born long-lived, handsome, and happy. By implication, on the even nights closest to the beginning of the cycle, the opposite results occur. ||23||

Now, he explains the knowledge of distinguishing between male, female, and eunuch based on the position held by the fetus:

->A male is on the right side, a female on the left, and twins are situated on both sides.<-
->That which is positioned in the middle of the abdomen should be understood as a eunuch. ||24||<-

The fetus that is situated on the right side of the woman should be known as a male; that which is on the left side should be known as a female; when situated on both the left and right sides, it should be known as twins. That fetus which has moved to the middle of the abdomen and does not move from the center should be understood—known—as a eunuch. ||24||

Now, he describes the auspicious planetary combinations for sexual union:

->With benefics situated in the cardines and trines,<-
->and the Ascendant and the Moon joined by benefics,<-
->with malefics placed in the third, eleventh, and sixth houses,<-
->one should approach union during combinations for the birth of a male. ||25||<-

In such a combination, one should go to—approach—union with one's wife. The <term>cardines (Kendras)</term> <note>the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses of a birth chart</note> are the Ascendant, fourth, seventh, and tenth. The <term>trines (Trikonas)</term> are the ninth and fifth. The <term>benefics</term> are Mercury, Venus, and Jupiter. "With benefics situated in the cardines and trines" means these houses are occupied by gentle planets as far as possible. "The Ascendant and the Moon" joined by benefics means united with auspicious planets. "With malefics"—the Sun, Mars, and Saturn—"placed in the third, eleventh, and sixth houses." Furthermore, the "combination for the birth of a male" is stated in the science of horoscopy: <insert>1 "When the Ascendant, Sun, Jupiter, and Moon are powerful in odd signs and male divisions (navamshas)," etc.</insert> ||25||

Now, he states the rules regarding the time of intercourse during the fertile period:

->A man should not inflict wounds with nails or teeth<-
->upon a woman in any way during the fertile season.<-
->The fertile period lasts sixteen days,<-
->but the first three nights therein are not to be approached. ||26||<-

A man should not in any way cause wounds with nails or teeth upon a woman during the fertile season—the time for conception. The word "and" is implied. The "season" refers to the menses. It lasts ten and six <note>sixteen</note>...

### ->Now the characteristics of beds and seats are explained<-

At the very beginning, the author states the following to demonstrate the purpose of starting this topic:

**Because this science is of use to everyone at all times,**
**and especially to kings, I shall therefore describe the characteristics of beds and seats. ||1||**

Because this science, known as the "Characteristics of Beds and Seats," is of use to—meaning it serves—all people at all times, and is of particular use to monarchs, I shall therefore describe or explain these characteristics. ||1||

First, he describes the auspicious wood for the seats of kings:

**Asana, Spandana, Sandalwood, Haridra, Deodar, Tinduka, and Shala;**
**Kashmari, Anjana, Padmaka, Shaka, or Shimshapa are auspicious. ||2||**

Asana; Spandana; Sandalwood <note>original: "Malayaja," referring to sandalwood from the Malaya mountains</note>; Haridra; Suradaru <note>original: "Devadaru," the Himalayan Cedar</note>; Tinduki; and Shala. All of these are specific types of trees. Also Kashmari; Anjana <term>Shobhanjana: the Moringa or drumstick tree</term>; Padmaka; Shaka; and Shimshapa. All of these trees are auspicious and bring good fortune when used for a bed or a seat. ||2||

Now he lists the inauspicious trees:

**Those fallen due to lightning, water, wind, or elephants; those housing bees or birds;**
**those grown at a shrine, a cemetery, or on a path; those withered at the top, or entwined with creepers. ||3||**

Lightning; water; wind; or an elephant—trees that have been knocked down or damaged by these are forbidden. Also, those that are "housing bees or birds," meaning trees where bees (flies) or birds have made their nests or dwellings. A <term>Chaitya</term> <note>A sacred tree, often a Peepal or Banyan, marked for local worship</note> or prominent tree; one grown in a cemetery or cremation ground; one grown on a path; one that is "withered at the top," meaning it has become dry and sapless at its upper part while still standing; or one "entwined with creepers." All of these are inauspicious. ||3||

The author says something further—

**Trees that are thorny, those growing at the confluence of great rivers,**
**those born in the precincts of temples, and those fallen toward the west or south, are not auspicious. ||4||**

*Thorny* means those trees possessed of thorns. *Growing at the confluence of great rivers* refers to those whose origin or growth occurs where major rivers—the primary streams—meet in union. Likewise, those *born in the precincts of temples*—grown in the house of a deity—all such trees are inauspicious. Also, those which have fallen toward the west or the southern direction are not auspicious. ||4||

Now, he describes the undesirable results of using furniture made from forbidden trees—

**From the use of couches or seats made of forbidden trees, there comes the destruction of the lineage.**
**Disease, fear, loss of wealth, and quarrels—various kinds of calamities occur. ||5||**

From the use of a couch or a seat constructed or made from a *forbidden*—meaning an unpraiseworthy—tree, there is *destruction of the lineage*, meaning the end of the family line. Likewise, *disease* (physical pain), *fear* (terror), *loss of wealth* (financial ruin), and *quarrels* (discord) occur. These and various other types of *calamities*—harmful events—come to pass. ||5||

Now, he explains the results of testing wood that was cut previously—

**If the wood was cut previously, it should be examined at the start of the work.**
**If a young boy should climb upon it, that wood bestows sons and cattle. ||6||**

If perhaps the *wood* (timber) was *cut previously*—prepared at an earlier time—then at the *start of the work* (the commencement of construction), it should be *examined* or investigated. Following the characteristics previously mentioned <note>original: "ashani-jala" etc., referring to verse 3 of this chapter regarding wood struck by lightning or scorched by fire</note>, if a *young boy* (a male child) happens to come and *climb* or sit upon that previously cut wood, then the couch or seat made from it *bestows sons and cattle*. It grants sons (offspring) and cattle (four-legged animals). ||6||

Now, he describes auspicious signs at the time of commencement—

**White flowers, an elephant in rut, curd, unhusked grain, a full pot, and gems—**
**seeing these or other auspicious things at the start, one should know it to be favorable. ||7||**

*White flowers* are blossoms of a white color. An *elephant in rut* is an intoxicated elephant. *Curd* is a preparation of milk. *Unhusked grain* refers to barley. A *full pot* is a jar filled with water. *Gems* are precious stones. *Auspicious things*—these and others...

# Chapter 78: Characteristics of Beds and Seats

The sounds of the conch shell, the chanting of the Vedas, and the cries of cows, ruddy geese, and cuckoos—if these are heard or seen at the beginning <note>at the start of the construction or use of the bed</note>, it should be known as auspicious. ||7||

---

Now, he describes the measurements for a King's bed:

> Eight barleycorns, stripped of their husks and placed belly-to-belly, constitute a "Workman’s Digit" <term>Karmāngula: a standard unit of measurement based on the width of a finger</term>. A great bed made for Kings measuring one hundred such digits brings victory. ||8||

Eight barleycorns make a "barley-eight." They must be without husks and placed touching one another belly-to-belly; this is known as a Workman’s Digit. By this measurement, a great bed constructed one hundred digits long for Kings <note>Rājās</note> results in victory. ||8||

---

Now, he describes the measurements for the beds of the King's son, the minister, the commander-in-chief, and the royal priest:

> Ninety digits, then the same reduced by six, by twelve, and by eighteen, are the lengths for the King's son, the minister, the commander-in-chief, and the royal priest, respectively. ||9||

A bed ninety digits long should be made for the King's son. That same ninety reduced by six—eighty-four digits—should be the length for the minister. That same ninety reduced by twelve—seventy-eight digits—is for the commander-in-chief. That same ninety reduced by "three-sixes" <note>eighteen</note>—seventy-two digits—should be the length of the bed for the royal priest. This also applies to the astrologer, as their status is equal. ||9||

---

Now, he describes the characteristics of the width and the height of the legs:

> Half of the length, minus one-eighth of that half, is the width declared by Vishvakarma <note>the divine architect of the gods</note>. The height of the leg, including the curved top and the head, is equal to one-third of the length. ||10||

Half of the aforementioned length, minus an eighth part of that half, is the width <term>Vishkambha: diameter or width</term> declared by Vishvakarma. For example: a King's bed is one hundred digits. Half of that is fifty digits. One-eighth of that <note>6.25 digits</note> subtracted leaves forty-three digits and six barleycorns as the width. In this manner, the width for other beds should be calculated according to their respective lengths. Regarding the phrase "equal to one-third of the length": the height of the leg should be made equal to one-third of the total length. This height includes the "belly" <note>the curved or bulging part of the leg</note> and the "head" <note>the top joinery</note>. This too should be calculated for others based on their own lengths. As Vishvakarma said:

> Eight barleycorns, husked and placed belly-to-belly, are called a Workman’s Digit; one should manufacture using that measure.

# Brihat Samhita [Chapter 78]

->A bed one hundred <term>angulas</term><note>An angula is a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to a finger's breadth, approximately 0.75 inches.</note> in length brings victory to kings.<-
->For a prince, it should be ninety-nine; for a minister, six less than that (ninety-three).<-
->For the commander of the army, twelve less (eighty-eight); for the royal priest, eighteen less (eighty-two).<-
->The measurement for the astrologer should be the same as the priest's.<-
->The width is said to be the length minus one-eighth part.<-
->The height of the legs is said to be equal to one-third of the length.<-
->Including the side-rails and the headboard, these proportions bring good fortune;<-
->A bed that is smaller or larger than these measures is known to bring ill-fortune to the owner. (Verse 10)<-

Now, he describes the specific fruits <note>results or benefits</note> of different types of wood:

->A couch made entirely of <term>Shriparni</term><note>Gmelina arborea, often called the "Great Beech."</note> wood is a giver of wealth.<-
->One made of <term>Asana</term><note>Terminalia tomentosa.</note> removes disease, and one made from the heartwood of <term>Tinduka</term><note>Diospyros, or Ebony.</note> brings riches. (Verse 11)<-

->One constructed solely of <term>Shishapa</term><note>Dalbergia sissoo, or North Indian Rosewood.</note> brings many kinds of prosperity.<-
->One made of Sandalwood destroys enemies and bestows virtue, fame, and long life. (Verse 12)<-

->A couch made of <term>Padmaka</term><note>Prunus cerasoides, or Himalayan Cherry.</note> brings long life, fortune, learning, and wealth.<-
->One made of <term>Shala</term><note>Shorea robusta.</note> or <term>Shaka</term><note>Teak.</note> brings auspiciousness. (Verse 13)<-

->A king who sits upon a couch made purely of Sandalwood,<-
->covered in gold and adorned with diverse jewels,<-
->is honored even by the gods. (Verse 14)<-

**Commentary:** Regarding the verse "A couch made entirely of Shriparni": A couch that is constructed entirely, without exception, from Shriparni wood is a giver of wealth, meaning it provides riches. One made entirely of Asana wood is a "remover of disease," meaning it destroys or eliminates illnesses. One made entirely from the heartwood of the Tinduka tree is a "wealth-maker," meaning it produces riches. (11)

Regarding the verse "One constructed solely": A couch made solely of Shishapa wood brings many kinds—various types—of prosperity. A couch made entirely of Sandalwood—constructed from Sandalwood—is a "destroyer of enemies" and also creates virtue, fame (reputation), and a long life. (12)

Regarding the verse "A couch made of Padmaka": A couch made entirely of Padmaka wood brings life—a long life that lasts a great time. It also brings Fortune (Goddess Lakshmi), Learning (auspicious knowledge), and wealth (money). Similarly, one made or constructed of Shala or Shaka wood brings welfare and well-being. (13)

Regarding the verse "Made purely of Sandalwood": A couch that is constructed solely of Sandalwood, and is "covered in gold"—meaning overlaid with the precious metal—and joined with "diverse jewels"—meaning various types of gems—upon such a couch, a king (ruler) sitting there is "honored by the gods," meaning he is worshipped even by the celestial beings. (14)

### Now he describes the results of mixing different types of wood—

> Ebony and Indian Rosewood, when combined with another wood, do not yield auspicious results.
> Neither does Himalayan Cedar when combined with the Gmelina tree, nor the Asana tree when so combined. ||15||

**When combined with another:** Ebony <note>original: *tindukī*</note> and Indian Rosewood <note>original: *śiṃśapā*</note>, when joined or mixed with another different wood, do not grant auspicious results. This means they are inauspicious. Similarly, Himalayan Cedar <note>original: *devadāru*</note> joined with the Gmelina tree <note>original: *śrīparṇa*</note> does not yield good results. In the same way, the Asana tree <note>original: *asana*; Pterocarpus marsupium</note> joined with Gmelina is not auspicious. ||15||

> However, Sal and Teak are auspicious when joined together or used individually.
> Likewise, the Haldu and Kadamba trees are praised whether used separately or together. ||16||

**Auspicious:** The Sal <note>original: *śāla*</note> and Teak <note>original: *śāka*</note> trees are auspicious when joined with one another, and they are also auspicious when used separately or alone. In that same manner, the Haldu <note>original: *haridraka*</note> and Kadamba trees are praised whether used individually or in combination. ||16||

> A bed made entirely of Syandana is not auspicious, and one made of Amba destroys life.
> The Asana tree, when combined with another wood, quickly produces many defects. ||17||

**Made entirely of Syandana:** A couch or bed <note>original: *paryaṅka*</note> constructed entirely and exclusively from the Syandana tree <note>original: *syandana*; Dalbergia oojeinensis</note> is not auspicious. This is because it destroys or takes away one's life-breath. By the word "and," it is implied that a bed made of Amba <note>original: *amba*; likely a variety of Mango or Hog Plum</note> likewise destroys life. The Asana tree, when joined or combined with another different wood, very quickly produces many great faults or misfortunes. ||17||

> For trees like Amba, Syandana, and Sandalwood, the legs are auspicious if made from Syandana.
> A bed or seat made entirely from any fruit-bearing tree yields desired results. ||18||

**Amba, Syandana...:** Regarding these trees—Amba, Syandana, and Sandalwood <note>original: *candana*</note>—the legs of the furniture are auspicious if they are made specifically from the Syandana tree. A bed or seat made from any kind of fruit-bearing tree <note>original: *phalataru*</note> results in desired and auspicious outcomes. ||18||

### Now he states that the method of decoration with excellent ivory should be performed for all these trees—

> Ivory is highly recommended for use with all the aforementioned trees.
> The decorative work should be carried out using excellent ivory. ||19||

For all the trees mentioned without exception, the use of ivory <note>original: *gajadanta*; literally "elephant tooth"</note> is praised and desired. One should perform the method of decoration <term>Alaṅkāravidhi: the traditional rules or art of ornamentation</term> using ivory that possesses excellent characteristics. This should be done to produce beauty. ||19||
