# In the Brihat Samhita [Chapter 78]

### Now he describes the characteristics of elephant tusks—

> Leaving a length equal to twice the circumference of the tusk at its base, one should cut the remainder. For elephants living in marshy lands, leave a little more; for those roaming the mountains, leave a little less. || 20 ||

One should measure the circumference (the round girth) at the base of the elephant's tusk, double that length, and then cut the remaining portion. This means: whatever the thickness is at the root, set aside twice that length starting from the root and cut the rest. A region with abundant water is called <term>Anupa</term> <note>marshy or riparian land</note>. For elephants frequenting such marshy lands, one should leave a bit more than twice the circumference before cutting. For those roaming the mountains, one should leave a bit less, because the mountain rocks naturally wear down their tusks. || 20 ||

### Now he describes the auspicious and inauspicious signs seen in the cut tusk—

> If the cut surface resembles a Shrivatsa, a Vardhamana, an umbrella, a banner, or a fly-whisk, it brings health, victory, increase in wealth, and happiness. || 21 ||
> 
> If it resembles weapons, there is victory; if a Nandyavarta, the recovery of a lost territory; if a clod of earth, the acquisition of a territory previously held. || 22 ||
> 
> If it resembles a woman, there is loss of wealth; if a water-vessel appears, a son is born; if a pot, the discovery of treasure; and if a staff, there is an obstacle to travel. || 23 ||
> 
> If it resembles a lizard, a monkey, or a snake, there will be famine and disease, or subjection to enemies; if it takes the shape of a vulture, an owl, a crow, or a hawk, there will be a plague among the people. || 24 ||
> 
> If it resembles a noose or a headless trunk, the king dies; if blood flows, the people face calamity. If the cut is black, dark-grey, rough, or foul-smelling, it is inauspicious. || 25 ||

Regarding the "Shrivatsa and Vardhamana": The <term>Shrivatsa</term> <note>original: "Shrivriksha"</note> is well known; some say it is the Bilva tree. The <term>Vardhamana</term> is a specific symbolic mark; some say it resembles a house-shape with color. An umbrella is a parasol. A banner is the well-known sign made of various cloths. A fly-whisk is a fan made of animal hair. If shapes resembling these are seen in the <term>cheda</term> <note>the cross-section or cut surface of the tusk</note>, then health (freedom from disease), victory (triumph in a specific sense), increase in wealth, and happiness occur. || 21 ||

Regarding "resembling weapons": Weapons include arms and the like. If shapes like weapons are seen in the cut, victory follows. If it resembles a <term>Nandyavarta</term> <note>a complex auspicious labyrinthine symbol</note>, there is the recovery or gain of a territory that was previously lost or stolen. A <term>Loshta</term> is a clod of earth. If shapes like a clod of earth are seen in the cut, there is the acquisition of a territory previously held. "Previously held" means a land that was already acquired or came into one's possession in the past; one gains that territory again. || 22 ||

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Beds and Seats

<page-num>869</page-num>
<header>Chapter on the Characteristics of Beds and Seats</header>
<sig>[Section 78]</sig>

Regarding the "form of a woman": If a cut in the wood is seen to resemble a woman's form, it indicates the birth of a daughter. If the mark or cut resembles a "pot" <note>original: *kumbha*, a water jar</note>, there will be the acquisition of a treasure. If it is in the shape of a "staff" <note>original: *danda*</note>, there will be obstacles to travel. || 23 ||

Regarding the "lizard" and others: A lizard is a specific type of creature. If the cut resembles a monkey, a serpent, or similar forms, it is inauspicious, indicating famine, diseases (afflictions), or subjugation by enemies. If the shapes of a vulture, an owl, a crow <note>original: *dhvanksha*</note>, or a hawk <note>original: *shyena*</note> are seen in the cut, there will be a plague among the people. || 24 ||

Regarding the "noose": A noose is the well-known form of a rope. A "headless torso" <note>original: *kabandha*</note> is a man with his head severed. If the cut resembles these, the death of the king will occur. If blood-like fluid flows or exudes from the cut, the people will face calamities. If the cut is black in color, dark/sooty, rough to the touch, or foul-smelling, it brings inauspicious and undesirable results. || 25 ||

->Now he describes the characteristics of auspicious cuts and the corresponding results for beds:<-

**A cut that is white, level, fragrant, and glossy brings good fortune.**
**Whatever auspicious or inauspicious cuts were described for ivory, the same results apply to beds as well. || 26 ||**

"White" means white-colored. "Level" means even. "Fragrant" means having a pleasant smell. "Glossy" means clear or oily. Such a cut brings auspiciousness. The various cuts—both inauspicious and auspicious—that were previously mentioned regarding ivory <note>original: *dante*, referring to elephant tusks/ivory work</note> are to be understood in the same way when they appear in the wood of beds; they grant results in that very same manner. This means they provide either good or bad fortune. This should be understood for all types of wood. || 26 ||

->Now he describes the application of the wood:<-

**In the joining of the frame-pieces, wood with its ends pointing clockwise is praised by the teachers.**
**If the ends point counter-clockwise or all in one direction, there will be fear caused by spirits. || 27 ||**

By the word "frame-pieces" <term>ishayoga: the joining of the four primary structural beams of a bed frame</term>, the four shaped pieces of wood are meant: two for the head and foot sections, and two for the left and right sides. Where they join together—having made two holes each in the head and foot timbers, one should insert the left and right side timbers into them. Here is the sequence: wood with "clockwise-pointing ends" is praised by the teachers. This means the ends follow a circumambulatory direction. "Counter-clockwise" <note>original: *apasavya*</note> or "pointing in a single direction" refers to the opposite. One should place the base of the right-side timber at the end of the previously placed head-timber. At the end of that, place the base of the foot-timber. At the end of that, place the base of the left-side (north) timber. At the end of that, place the base of the head-timber. When the placement is done in this sequence of East, South, West, and North, it becomes "clockwise-ended." If it is counter-clockwise, not following the right-hand path, or reversed from the aforementioned placement, and likewise—

If the wood is positioned with its top facing a specific cardinal direction, there is a fear or danger arising from spirits <note>original: "bhūta-graha"; refers to possession or affliction by supernatural entities</note>. When the head-piece and the foot-piece of the wood have their tops facing the same single direction, it is called "Single-Direction-Top." ||27||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the legs:

> **If one leg is placed upside down, there will be a defect or injury to the owner's leg.**
> **If two are so placed, food will not digest; if three or four, there will be distress, slaughter, or imprisonment. ||28||**

By "one leg" being "upside down" <note>original: "avāk-śirasā"</note>, it means the root and the top are reversed from their natural growth position. This causes a "leg defect" for the owner. If two legs are positioned this way, the food eaten will not digest or transform properly. If three or four legs are reversed, it leads to intense suffering, death, or captivity. ||28||

### Now he describes the characteristics of knots in the legs:

> **If there is a knot at the top of the leg that is hollow or discolored, it causes disease.**
> **If a knot is located in the "pot" part of the leg, it causes abdominal disease. ||29||**
> **Below the "pot" is the "shank"; a knot there causes fear regarding the shanks.**
> **Below that is the "base"; a knot there causes the loss of wealth. ||30||**
> **A knot in the "hoof" area is said to cause pain to hoofed animals.**
> **A knot located in the third part of the side-rails or the head-rail is not auspicious. ||31||**

Regarding "hollow or discolored": if a knot at the head (top) of the leg is hollow <note>lacking internal essence</note> or discolored <note>having a color different from the rest of the wood</note>, a disease occurs in the head of the owner. If a knot is situated in the "pot" <term>Kumbha: a decorative rounded molding on the leg resembling a water jar</term> of that same leg, an abdominal disease occurs. ||29||

The part below the "pot" is the "shank" <term>Jangha: the vertical shaft of the furniture leg</term>; a knot there creates a threat to the owner's own shanks. Below the shank is the "base" <note>the support structure</note>; a knot there acts as a "destroyer of wealth," such as money and property. ||30||

Regarding the "hoof" area: a knot located in the "hoof" <note>the very bottom of the leg</note> is declared to be a "bringer of pain" to hoofed animals like horses and cattle. The "side-rail" <term>Isha: the long side-pieces of the bed frame</term> and the "head-rail" <term>Shirshanya: the cross-beam at the head</term> are also mentioned; if a knot is located in the third section of these, it is not good for the owner. Even if the second rail of the leg section has a knot in its third part, it does not bestow any good. ||31||

### Now he states the names of the holes (defects):

> **The Hollow, the Boar's Eye, the Pig's Eye, and the Calf's Navel;**
> **The Black One, and another called the Bandhuka; this is the summary of holes. ||32||**

The hole named *Nishkuta*. The word "and" is used in the sense of addition. *Kolaksha* (Boar's Eye). *Sukaranayana* (Pig's Eye). *Vatsanabha* (Calf's Navel). *Kalaka* (The Black One). And another called *Dhundhuka*. In this manner, a brief summary or collection of the types of holes has been stated. ||32||

### Now he describes their characteristics—

**->A hole that is hollow in the middle like a pot and narrow at the opening is a *Nishkuta* hole.<-**
**->A blue-colored hole the size of a kidney bean or a black gram is called *Kolaksha*.<-** ||33||

**->The *Sukaranayana* is uneven, discolored, and one and a half finger-joints in length.<-**
**->A hole that is counter-clockwise, split, and the size of a finger-joint is called *Vatsanabha*.<-** ||34||

**->The one known as *Kalaka* is black; that which is split through to the other side is *Dhundhuka*.<-**
**->A hole that is the same color as the wood is not considered as evil as the others.<-** ||35||

"Hollow in the middle like a pot" means a cavity or hole that is shaped like a water-pot <note>original: *ghata* or *kumbha*</note> in its interior part. If it is "narrow at the opening" (small at the mouth), it is named *Nishkuta*. *Nishpava* refers to a type of grain <note>specifically the flat bean or rice variety</note>. A hole the size of a *Nishpava* or a *Masha* <note>black gram</note> and blue in color is known as *Kolaksha* <note>literally "Hog's Eye"</note>. ||33||

Regarding *Sukaranayana*: The hole named *Sukaranayana* <note>literally "Pig's Eye"</note> is uneven or asymmetrical. It is "discolored," meaning it has lost its natural wood color. It is "one and a half finger-joints long" <note>a *parva* is the distance between knuckles on a finger</note>. The hole named *Vatsanabha* <note>literally "Calf's Navel"</note> is "counter-clockwise" <note>the grain swirls to the left</note>, is "split" (visible from the other side), and is the size of a finger-joint. ||34||

Regarding *Kalaka*: The one named *Kalaka* is black in color. That which is "split through" (visible from the second side) and black is named *Dhundhuka*. A hole that is "the same color as the wood" <note>matching the natural timber</note> does not result in the same level of "corrupt fruit" <note>bad luck or negative consequences</note> as described for the others. This is what is meant: even if a hole is of an inauspicious type, if it matches the wood's color, the result is not excessively evil. ||35||

### Now he describes their results—

**->In the hole named *Nishkuta*, there is loss of wealth; in *Kolaksha*, the destruction of the family.<-**
**->In *Sukaraka*, there is fear of weapons; in the one called *Vatsanabha*, fear of disease.<-** ||36||

**->The holes named *Kalaka* and *Dhundhuka*, and those bored by insects, do not bring good fortune.<-**
**->Wood that is full of knots everywhere is not auspicious.<-** ||37||

In the hole named *Nishkuta*, there is the "wasting or destruction of wealth" <note>original: *dravya* or *artha*</note>. In the *Kolaksha* (Boar's Eye), there is the "destruction of the lineage or family." In the *Sukaraka* (Pig's Eye), there is "fear of weapons" <note>danger of physical injury or conflict</note>. In the one called *Vatsanabha*, there is "fear of disease." ||36||

A hole known as a "black-void" <note>original: "kalakacchidram"</note> as well as one called "bow-curved," or any hole bored by insects or worms, is not auspicious and yields evil results. ### Now he describes the results of beds made from mixed woods—

> A bed made from a single tree is blessed; one made from two trees is even more blessed.
> One made from three trees brings growth to one's soul <note>or "to one's progeny"</note>; one from four brings wealth and the highest fame. ||38||

A bed or seat made from a single tree is blessed. One made from two trees is more blessed. If constructed from three of the previously mentioned trees, it brings growth to one's own sons. If made from four, it produces wealth and foremost fame or reputation. ||38||
Regarding the phrase "made from five types of wood": if a bed or seat is constructed from five types of trees, whoever sleeps upon it goes to the "five-fold state." This means they die. If it is fashioned from the wood of six, seven, or eight trees, there is the destruction of the family, meaning the end of the lineage. ||39||

# Now the Examination of Gems is explained.

First, he describes the characteristics of the primary qualities of jewels:

> Through a good jewel, good fortune comes to kings; through a bad one, misfortune.
> Therefore, those who are experts should examine the destiny that resides within jewels. ||1||

For kings, a jewel that possesses auspicious characteristics brings about good destiny; through an inauspicious one, undesirable or evil destiny occurs. By the word <term>Destiny</term> <note>original: "daiva"</note>, the ripening of past karmic actions is meant. Because of this, experts in the characteristics of gems must examine and deliberate upon the destiny situated within the jewel. ||1||

He now states that in this "Examination of Gems," the focus is specifically on stone jewels:

> While the word "Jewel" <note>original: "ratna"</note> is applied to elephants, horses, and women of exceptional quality,
> here, the authority concerns stone jewels, beginning with the Diamond. ||2||

# Chapter on the Examination of Gems
<note>Sanskrit: Ratnaparīkṣādhyāyaḥ</note>

The term "gem" is applied to the best of any category. For instance, a "gem of an elephant" refers to a noble tusker, a "gem of a horse" to a fine steed, and a "gem of a woman" to an excellent lady. Because of their specific superior qualities and the power of their inherent virtues, the word "gem" <note>Sanskrit: ratna</note> is used. As it is said:

->Whatever is the most excellent of its kind is called a gem.<-

However, in this specific "Examination of Gems," our authority and focus are directed toward "stone-gems"—that is, precious jewels of mineral origin—beginning with the diamond <note>Sanskrit: vajra</note>. ||2||

Regarding the origin of these gems, the author presents the differing opinions of the ancient teachers:

**Some say gems were born from the demon Bala; others say from the sage Dadhichi.**
**Some claim the diversity of stones arises from the natural disposition of the Earth itself. ||3||**

"From Bala" refers to a demon of that name. Gems were produced or born from this Bala. He was slain by Indra <note>the King of the Gods</note>, and from his bones, the various jewels were created. As it is said:

->Diverse gems were produced from the demon Bala;<-
->having fallen upon the earth, his bones attained various colors.<-

"Others say from Dadhichi": Other teachers say they were born from the bones of the sage Dadhichi <note>a saint who sacrificed his life so his bones could be used to forge divine weapons</note>. As it is said:

->Gems were born in the thousands in this world from the sage Dadhichi;<-
->through the influence of the earth, his bones attained various colors and qualities.<-

"Some": Certain other teachers have stated that various gems are born from the "nature of the earth" itself. They say that common stones attained the state of "gem-hood" over a long period of time. ||3||

### Now, he lists the names of the gems:

**Diamond, Sapphire, Emerald, Karketara, Ruby, and the Blood-stone;**
**Lapis Lazuli, Pulaka, Vimalaka, the Royal Gem, Crystal, and Moonstone; ||4||**

**Saugandhika, Gomedaka (Zircon), Conch-shell, Mahanila, and Topaz;**
**Brahmamani, Jyotirasa, Sasyaka, Pearl, and Coral. ||5||**

"Diamond and Sapphire" etc.: Diamond. Sapphire. Emerald. Karketara <note>a honey-colored quartz or chrysoberyl</note>. Ruby. The one called Blood-stone. Lapis Lazuli. Pulaka <note>a variety of garnet or carnelian</note>. Vimalaka. The Royal Gem <note>Rajamani</note>. Crystal. And the Moonstone <note>Shashikanta</note>. ||4||

Saugandhika <note>a ruby variety</note>; Gomedaka <note>hessonite or zircon</note>; Conch-shell; Mahanila <note>dark blue sapphire</note>; the one called Pushparaga <note>topaz</note>; Brahmamani; Jyotirasa; Sasyaka <note>copper ore or vitriol</note>; Pearls; and Coral. ### Now, he describes the seven sources and characteristics of the Diamond:

->The diamond from the banks of the Vena is pure and has the luster of a Shirisha flower; that from Kosala is also pure.<-
->The Saurashtran diamond is slightly copper-colored; the Surparaka diamond is black.<- || 6 ||
->The diamond from the Himalayas is slightly copper-colored; that from Matanga has the appearance of a Valla flower.<-
->The diamond from Kalinga is yellowish, while that produced in the Paundra region is dark/sable.<- || 7 ||

"Vena" is the name of a river; on its banks <margin>the riverbank</margin> is found the pure diamond, free from defects. It has the luster of a Shirisha flower <note>original: "shirisha-kusuma-prabham"</note>, meaning it is a whitish-yellow color; this is the Kosalaka diamond, produced in the Kosala country. The diamond that is "slightly copper-colored" <note>original: "atamram"</note> is somewhat reddish; that is the Saurashtra diamond, produced in Surashtra. The diamond that is black in color is the Saurparaka, born or produced in the Sopara region. || 6 ||

Regarding "slightly copper-colored": the diamond that is slightly or somewhat copper-hued is produced in the Himalayan mountains. That which has the appearance of a Valla flower <note>a type of bean flower</note>, meaning it is slightly pale/whitish, is the Matangaja, produced in the Matanga country. The yellowish diamond is produced in the Kalinga country. The "Shyama" or dark diamond is produced among the Paundras, meaning it is born in the Paundra country. || 7 ||

### Now, he describes the presiding deities of these diamonds:

->The diamond that is six-edged and white belongs to Indra; the black one shaped like a serpent's mouth belongs to Yama.<-
->The one resembling the trunk of a plantain tree is Vishnu's; it may have any shape.<- || 8 ||
->The Varuna diamond is shaped like a woman's private parts and resembles a Karnikara flower.<-
->The Agni diamond is shaped like a Shringataka fruit and resembles a tiger's eye.<- || 9 ||
->The Vayu diamond is shaped like a barley grain and has the luster of an Ashoka flower.<-
->The sources of origin are threefold: riverbeds, mines, and scattered deposits.<- || 10 ||

"Belonging to Indra" <note>original: "Aindram"</note>: The diamond which is "six-edged" <note>term: shadasri — having six points or facets</note>, meaning hexagonal, and white in color, belongs to Indra; Indra is its deity. That which is "Asita" or black and "shaped like a serpent's mouth" <note>original: "sarpasya-rupam"</note> belongs to Yama. That which resembles the "trunk of a plantain tree" <note>a greenish-yellow hue</note> and possesses "all shapes" <note>meaning it can be found in any form</note> belongs to Vishnu; Vishnu is its presiding deity. || 8 ||

**Regarding the Varuna type:** It is shaped like the private parts of a weak woman <note>original: "abala stri... guhyam varangam"; likely referring to a specific oval or cleft shape</note>, resembling the female organ; that is the Varuna diamond. **Resembling the Karnikara flower**, having the luster of the blossom of the Karnikara tree. **Shaped like a Shringata fruit**, meaning it is triangular. **Resembling a tiger's eye**, like the eye of a tiger, being reddish-blue; that diamond is **Agneya (fiery)**, belonging to the god of fire <note>original: "hutabhujam-agneyam"</note>. ||9||

**Regarding the Vayavya type:** A diamond that is **shaped like a barley corn**, meaning it is thick in the middle. **Resembling the Ashoka flower**, having a red color like the Ashoka blossom; that is called Vayavya, belonging to the wind-god. **Streams, mines, and scattered deposits:** A "stream" <note>original: "srotas"</note> is where water flows. A "mine" <note>original: "khani"</note> is a place that is dug out. "Scattered" <note>original: "prakirnakam"</note> refers to ground where gems are found loosely, such as in the sea. Thus, the origin of diamonds from mines is of three types: streams, mines, and scattered deposits. ||10||

### Now he describes which type of diamond is recommended for Brahmins and the other classes—

->**Red and yellow are auspicious for royalty; white for the twice-born.**<-
->**That resembling the Shirisha flower for the Vaisyas, and for Shudras, that resembling a sword is praised.**<- ||11||

**Red** and **yellow** are auspicious and recommended for **Rajanyas (Kshatriyas/Warriors)**. **White** color is auspicious for the **twice-born (Brahmins)**. That which is **like the Shirisha flower** <note>a greenish-yellow or pale hue</note> is auspicious for **Vaisyas (Merchants/Farmers)**. That which **resembles a sword**, meaning black in color, is **praised for Shudras** <note>Laborers/Artisans</note>. This means it is auspicious for them. ||11||

### Now he speaks regarding the knowledge of the price of these diamond gems—

->**Eight white mustard seeds make one grain of rice; for a diamond weighing twenty rice grains,**<-
->**The price is two hundred thousand; this decreases by double for smaller weights.**<- ||12||
->**Decreasing by a quarter, a third, and a half; then parts of a third, a fifth, and a sixteenth;**<-
->**And parts of a twenty-fifth, a hundredth, and a thousandth.**<- ||13||

**Regarding the eight white mustard seeds:** "White mustard seeds" are pale mustard seeds. Eight of these make one "rice grain" <note>term: "tandula" - a unit of weight</note>. A diamond that is measured and weighed at **twenty rice grains** has a value of **two hundred thousand** Karshapanas <note>term: "karshapana" - a standard ancient Indian silver or copper coin</note>. A "Pana" consists of eighty "Shvetikas" (cowries), and twenty-five of those make a Karshapana. As it is said:

->**Twenty Shvetikas are called one Kakini by the wise;**<-
->**Four of those are a Pana, and four of those are a "fourth";**<-
->**Four of those "fourths" are called a Purana;**<-
->**That itself is called a Karshapana, though in some places it is twenty-five.**<-

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 79]

Regarding the phrase "decreased by two and two": In that same context of the diamond, when it is decreased by two and two <term>tandulas</term> <note>A unit of weight equivalent to a grain of rice</note>, the following values are to be understood. ||12||

Regarding the phrase "decreased by a quarter, a third, and so on": Twenty decreased by two is eighteen. A diamond that weighs eighteen <term>tandulas</term> has a value of two hundred thousand <term>karshapanas</term> <note>An ancient Indian silver or copper coin</note> minus one quarter. This means its value is one hundred and fifty thousand. One that weighs sixteen <term>tandulas</term> has a value of two hundred thousand minus one third. This means one hundred and thirty-three thousand, three hundred and thirty-three, plus a fraction. One that weighs fourteen <term>tandulas</term> is valued at half of two hundred thousand, which means one hundred thousand. For one weighing twelve <term>tandulas</term>, the value is one third of two hundred thousand. This means sixty-six thousand, six hundred and sixty-seven, representing a loss of two-thirds of the base value. For one weighing ten, the value is one-fifth of two hundred thousand, which means forty thousand. For one weighing eight <term>tandulas</term>, the value is one-sixteenth of two hundred thousand, which means twelve thousand five hundred. For one weighing six <term>tandulas</term>, the value is a twenty-fifth part of two hundred thousand, which means eight thousand. For one weighing four <term>tandulas</term>, the value is a hundredth part of two hundred thousand, which means two thousand <term>karshapanas</term>. For weights in between these, the value should be inferred by one's own intelligence using the inverse rule of three. ||13||

### Now he describes the characteristics of auspicious diamonds—

->**That diamond which cannot be pierced by any substance, is light, floats in water, is radiant, and smooth;**<-
->**and which resembles lightning, fire, or the bow of Indra <note>original: "shakrachapa" - a rainbow</note>, is said to bring welfare.**<- ||14||

A diamond that is "impenetrable by all substances" cannot be broken even by any weapon. "Light" means devoid of heaviness. "Floats in water" means it does not sink. "Radiant" means it possesses rays or beams of light. "Smooth" means it appears oily or glossy. "Lightning," "Fire," and "Indra's Bow" (the rainbow)—a diamond that is similar to these is said to be for "welfare," meaning it is declared to bring good fortune. ||14||

### Now he describes the inauspicious characteristics—

->**Those marked with crow’s feet, fly-specks, or hair-like streaks; joined with minerals or pierced by grit;**<-
->**having double edges, or those that are burnt, dull, lusterless, or shattered, are not auspicious.**<- ||15||

Those diamonds which have "crow's feet"—marks shaped like the foot of a crow; "flies"—marks shaped like those insects; "hairs"—lines resembling fine hair; or "minerals"—meaning bits of earth or clay; those joined with these, as well as those joined with "grit" or those that are "pierced" (containing holes). Also, those with "double edges"—possessing twice the number of edges defined in the standard characteristics. "Burnt" by fire; "dull" meaning discolored; "lusterless" meaning having lost its brilliance; and "shattered" meaning cracked or crumbling. These are "not auspicious," meaning they are unfavorable. ||15||

->He states another point:<-

**Diamonds that are bubbly, split at the tip, flattened, or elongated like the fruit of a Vāsī tree; for all of these, there is a loss of one-eighth of the value. ||16||**

Those diamonds which are "bubbly" <note>original: *budbuda*</note> resemble bubbles in water. "Split at the tip" means the edge or point is cracked. "Flattened" <note>original: *cipiṭa*</note> means they are compressed or thin. "Elongated like the fruit of a Vāsī" refers to the *Vāsikā*, a specific plant. For all of these, whatever the value would have been according to the previously mentioned rules, one-eighth part is deducted. This means the value becomes the remaining seven-eighths. ||16||

->Now he describes the merits of wearing a diamond:<-

Some teachers declare <note>original: *uśanti*</note> that no diamond <term>Vajra; the word implies both "diamond" and "thunderbolt"</term> at all should be worn by women <note>original: *abalābhiḥ*</note> who are "desiring sons" (wishing for male children). As it is said:

> "By blessed women desiring sons, the stone named Diamond should be worn; specifically that which is shaped like a *Śṛṅgāṭaka*, a *Tripuṭa*, or like a grain.

A diamond joined with "unfavorable characteristics" <note>original: *aniṣṭalakṣaṇam*</note> produces the "destruction" (loss) of one's own people/relatives, of "wealth" (sovereignty/power), and of "life" (longevity). Conversely, a diamond with auspicious characteristics—

### Now, the characteristics of pearls are explained.

### At the very beginning, to show the origins of pearls, the author says:

**Pearls are produced from elephants, serpents, pearl oysters, conch shells, clouds, bamboo, whales, and boars. Among these, those born from the pearl oyster are the most excellent.** ||1||

"Elephant" refers to the tusker. "Serpent" is the snake. "Oyster" is a specific living creature. "Conch" is a creature. "Cloud" refers to the sky. "Bamboo" is the reed. "Whale" is the great fish. "Boar" is the wild pig. Pearls are produced or born from these. Among all of these, the one born from the oyster is "most excellent," meaning highly superior. In common practice, these are the ones most frequently traded. ||1||

### Now, he lists the desired mines <note>sources</note> of pearls:

**Simhalaka, Paralaukika, Saurashtra, Tamraparni, Parasava, Kaubera, Pandyavataka, and Haima—these are the eight sources.** ||2||

Simhalaka is a country <note>modern Sri Lanka</note>. Paralaukika is a country; that which is found there is called "Paralaukika." Saurashtra is a specific region <note>modern Gujarat</note>. Tamraparni is a river. Parasava is a country. Kaubera is a country. Pandyavataka is a country. Those produced there are named accordingly. Haima refers to those produced in the Himalayas. These are the eight types of sources or places of origin for pearls. ||2||

### Now, he describes their characteristics:

**Pearls from the Simhala mines come in many shapes, are glossy, resemble a swan in color, and are large. Those called Tamraparni are slightly copper-red, white, and free from darkness <note>impurities</note>.** ||3||

**Pearls from Paralaukika are black, white, or yellow, contain sandy grit, and are irregular in shape. Those from Saurashtra are neither too large nor too small, and resemble the color of fresh butter.** ||4||

**Pearls from Parasava are luminous, bright white, heavy, and possess great virtues. Those from the Himalayas are light, fragile, resemble curds in color, and are large, though they may have two distinct shapes.** ||5||

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Pearls
<page-num>879</page-num>
<header>[Chapter 80] - Chapter on the Characteristics of Pearls. 879</header>

->Pearls from the Pandya-vata region are uneven, black-and-white, light in weight, yet possess great size and luster.<-
->They may also resemble the fruit of the Neem tree, the Triputa (three-lobed) shape, or the smallness of coriander seeds. ||6||<-

**Regarding "Many Shapes":** Those pearls that possess many shapes—meaning their physical forms are of various types—and are glossy and stainless, with a radiance like that of a swan <note>original: "hamsa-abha"</note>, and are large in size, are known as **Simhala** pearls, originating from the mines of Simhala <note>Modern-day Sri Lanka</note>. Those that are slightly copper-colored, white, and free from darkness—meaning they are perfectly clear—are called **Tamra** pearls, born from the Tamraparni River. ||3||

**Regarding "Black and White":** Those that are black, white, or yellow, or contain "sugar" <note>likely referring to a crystalline or gritty texture</note>, or are uneven, are the **Paraloka** pearls, born in the Paraloka region. Those that are neither too large nor too small, and possess the soft luster of fresh butter, are the **Saurashtra** pearls <note>From the Gujarat region</note>. ||4||

**Regarding "Luminous":** Those pearls that are luminous (filled with light), bright white, heavy, and possess great virtues are the **Parashava** pearls <note>Historically associated with Persia</note>. Those that are light, fragmented or discolored, resembling curds in appearance, large, and having two distinct shapes are the **Haima** pearls, produced in the Himalayas. ||5||

**Regarding "Uneven":** Those that are uneven, black-and-white, lacking in weight, but possessing significant size and brilliance; those resembling the Neem fruit; those characterized by three lobes (Triputa); those resembling coriander seeds; and those that are extremely fine like powder—all these pearls are born in the **Pandya-vata** region. ||6||

Now, the author describes their specific divine qualities:

->The Vaishnava pearl is dark like the Atasi (flax) flower; the Aindra pearl resembles the moon.<-
->The Varuna pearl is like yellow orpiment, and the Yama pearl is black. ||7||<-

->The Vayu pearl is the color of a ripe pomegranate seed or the red-and-black Gunja berry.<-
->The Agneya pearl should be known by its brilliance, like a smokeless fire or a lotus. ||8||<-

**Regarding "Dark like the Atasi flower":** The Atasi flower is well known; a pearl dark like it is **Vaishnava** (presided over by Vishnu). One resembling the moon is **Aindra** (presided over by Indra). That which is the color of yellow orpiment <term>Haritala: a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment</term> is **Varuna** (presided over by Varuna). That which is black is **Yama** (presided over by Yama, the god of death). ||7||

->Now, he speaks regarding the knowledge of their prices:<-

The price stated for a single pearl weighing four *māṣakas* <term>māṣaka: a traditional unit of weight for gems and metals</term>, if it is endowed with brilliance and quality, is fifty-three multiplied by one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas* <term>kārṣāpaṇa: a standard ancient Indian silver or copper coin</term>. || 9 ||

One hundred thirty-five [is the price for one *māṣaka*]. A pearl weighing four *kṛṣṇalas* <note>original: "kṛṣṇala" - another name for the guñjā berry used as a weight</note> is valued at ninety. One weighing three and a half *guñjās* is valued at seventy. || 11 ||

The price is thirty-five for one weighing two and a half *guñjās* <insert>literally: three minus a half-guñjā</insert>. || 12 ||

**Regarding "weighing four māṣakas":** For a single pearl possessed of the quality of brilliance—the qualities of which he will describe later as "glossy, lustrous, and appearing as if smeared with light"—that weighs four *māṣakas*, the price is fifty-three *kārṣāpaṇas* multiplied by one hundred. This means fifty-three hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. || 9 ||

**Regarding "half-māṣaka":** From this weight of four *māṣakas*, with the reduction of each half-*māṣaka*, the following prices are given: For one weighing three and a half *māṣakas*, the price is thirty-two hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. For one weighing three *māṣakas*, the price is twenty hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. For one weighing two and a half *māṣakas*, the price is thirteen hundred. For one weighing two *māṣakas*, eight hundred. For one weighing one and a half *māṣakas*, the price is three hundred fifty-three *kārṣāpaṇas*. || 10 ||

For one weighing a single *māṣaka*, the price is one hundred thirty-five *kārṣāpaṇas*. Regarding "four *kṛṣṇalas* are valued at ninety": five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣaka*. By the word *kṛṣṇala*, the *guñjā* is meant. A pearl whose form weighs four *kṛṣṇalas* has a price of ninety *kārṣāpaṇas*. A pearl whose measure is three and a half *guñjās* has a price of seventy; meaning seventy *kārṣāpaṇas* is its price. || 11 ||

# [Chapter 80] Chapter on the Characteristics of Pearls | 881

Regarding the three-gunja weight: For a high-quality pearl possessing all virtues and weighing <term>three gunjas</term><note>A gunja is a traditional seed-weight, approximately 0.12 grams</note>, the value is fifty rupakas. Rupakas are well-known coins. For a pearl weighing <term>three gunjas</term> minus half a gunja (2.5 gunjas), the value is thirty-five rupakas. ||12||

### Now, he describes another method for determining value:

> If thirteen beautiful pearls weigh one dharana (one-tenth of a pala),
> The value is fixed at three hundred and twenty-five rupakas. ||13||
> For sixteen pearls, it is two hundred; for twenty pearls, one hundred and seventy.
> For twenty-five pearls held in that weight, it is one hundred and thirty. ||14||
> For thirty pearls, the value is seventy; for forty, the value is half a hundred (fifty).
> For sixty minus five (fifty-five) pearls in a dharana, the value is five times eight (forty). ||15||
> For eighty pearls, the value is thirty; for a hundred pearls, it is that thirty minus five (twenty-five).
> For two, three, four, and five hundred pearls, the values are twelve, six, five, and three respectively. ||16||

Regarding the phrase "a tenth part of a pala is a dharana": It is said, "Five krishnalas make one masha; sixteen of those make one suvarna; four suvarnas make one pala." Thus, the tenth part of a pala is called a <term>dharana</term>. If that dharana weight consists of thirteen beautiful pearls endowed with good qualities, then the value is three hundred and twenty-five <term>rupakas</term><note>A standard silver coin of the period</note>. "Three-hundreds" refers to the sum of three hundred; "with twenty-five" means three hundred plus twenty-five. ||13||

Regarding sixteen, etc.: If a dharana consists of sixteen pearls, then the value is two hundred rupakas. Likewise, for twenty pearls: if twenty pearls weigh one dharana, the value is one hundred and seventy. If twenty-five pearls make up the dharana weight, the value is one hundred and thirty. ||14||

If thirty pearls make a dharana, the value is seventy. If forty pearls make a dharana, the value is half a hundred, which is fifty rupakas. Here, the word "or" (va) is used in the sense of "and." And if fifty-five pearls (sixty minus five) make a dharana, the value is five times eight, meaning forty is the value. ||15||

Regarding eighty pearls: For a dharana held by eighty pearls, the value is thirty rupakas. For a dharana of one hundred pearls, that thirty is reduced by five, making the value twenty-five rupakas. For a dharana of two hundred pearls, the value is twelve rupakas. For three hundred, six rupakas. For four hundred, five rupakas. For five hundred pearls in a dharana, the value is three rupakas. ||16||

# On the Great Compilation with Commentary
## [Chapter 80]

Now, he states the technical names for the thirteen and subsequent weight-units <note>original: "dharanas"</note>:

> **Pikka, Piccha, Ardha, Ardha, Ravaka, and Siktha are the names for the thirteen and following units. Beyond these are the Nigaras, and those starting from eighty are called Churnas. ||17||**

The names for the weight-units starting from thirteen are Pikka and so on. Specifically: a weight-unit holding thirteen pearls is named **Pikka**. One of sixteen is **Piccha**. One of twenty is **Ardha**. One of twenty-five is also **Ardha**. One of thirty is **Ravaka**. One of forty is **Siktha**. Following these, one of fifty-five is **Nigara**. For all weight-units starting from eighty up to five hundred, the name is **Churna**. These names are utilized for commercial transactions in the marketplace <note>original: "akarasthane" - literally "in the place of the mine" or treasury</note>. ||17||

### Now he describes the knowledge of pricing for subsequent pearls:

> **The stated price applies to pearls of high quality held in these weight-units. For those falling in between, the price must be calculated; for those of inferior quality, a reduction must be made. ||18||**
> **For those slightly black, white, yellowish, or copper-colored, or slightly irregular, the price is reduced by one-third. For highly irregular or yellow pearls, the reduction is one-sixth and one-half respectively. ||19||**

"This" refers to the following: the aforementioned price applies to high-quality pearls held in a weight-unit. For those "in between," one must estimate the price using one's own intelligence. For example, the price for a thirteen-pearl unit was stated as three hundred and twenty-five <note>likely referring to silver pieces or 'karshapanas' mentioned in previous verses</note>. For a sixteen-pearl unit, it is two hundred. For those in the middle—holding fourteen or fifteen pearls—the price should be determined using the inverse rule of three <term>Trairashika: a mathematical proportion method used in ancient Indian commerce</term>. For pearls of inferior quality, a reduction should be made according to the following sequence. ||18||

"Black-white" etc.: The word "slightly" applies to each category. For those slightly black (dark-colored), slightly white, slightly copper-colored, or slightly irregular, the price determined by the previous rule is reduced by one-third. For "irregular and yellow," the reduction is one-sixth and one-half respectively. That is, for highly irregular pearls, the price is one-sixth less, and for yellow pearls, it is half the original price. ||19||

### Now he describes the characteristics of Elephant Pearls:

> **From the lineage of Airavata <note>The celestial elephant of Indra</note>, born on the days of the Pushya or Shravana constellations, or on the days of the Moon or Sun; those born during the Northern Solstice, or during eclipses of the Sun and Moon—these are the "Auspicious Elephants." ||20||**
> **It is said that pearls are produced in their temples <note>the frontal lobes of an elephant's head</note> and at the base of their tusks. These are numerous, large in size, varied in shape, and brilliantly radiant. ||21||**
> **No price can be set for these, nor should they be perforated, for they are exceedingly lustrous. When worn by kings, they bestow sons, victory, and health, and are supremely sanctifying. ||22||**

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Pearls

**Regarding those born of the lineage of Airāvata.** Airāvata is the name of the [celestial] elephant; those elephants born in his lineage or family, and those produced from that line, if they are born under the lunar mansions <term>Nakṣatras</term> of Puṣya or Śravaṇa. Also, if they are born on a Monday (the day of the Moon) or a Sunday (the day of the Sun). Furthermore, those elephants born during the northern transit of the sun <term>Uttarāyaṇa</term>, or those born during an eclipse of the Sun or Moon, are known as *Bhadra* elephants <note>The 'Bhadra' or 'auspicious' class is considered the highest grade of elephant in classical Indian zoology</note>. || 20 ||

**Regarding them.** The word "it is said" <note>original: "kila"</note> is used here to indicate traditional knowledge or scripture. In the temples <note>the frontal globes on an elephant's forehead</note> and in the hollows of the tusks of these elephants born of the Airāvata lineage and the *Bhadra* class, pearls are produced. These are numerous, large in size, of many shapes, and possessed of great brilliance and luster. || 21 ||

**No price should be set for these.** No monetary value should be assigned to these pearls, nor should they be perforated <note>drilling a hole for stringing would diminish their divine quality</note>. This is because they are all exceedingly brilliant, highly sacred, and when worn on the body by kings, they bestow sons, victory, and health. "Sons" refers to male progeny; "victory" refers to the subduing of enemies; and "health" refers to the state of being free from disease. || 22 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of pearls produced from boars and fish—

> At the root of the tusk, resembling the luster of the moon and possessing many virtues, is the boar-pearl.
> The fish-pearl resembles the eye of a fish; it is large, pure, and possesses many virtues. || 23 ||

Regarding boars (swine): at the root of the tusk where the tusk originates, a pearl is formed that resembles the luster of the moon and has many qualities; this is the boar-pearl. That which resembles the eye of a fish is the fish-pearl (produced from the *Timi* or whale/large fish). It should be known as large, purifying, and full of many virtues. || 23 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of pearls produced from clouds—

> Born like a hailstone, fallen from the seventh layer of the wind,
> It is said to be snatched from the sky by divine beings; it has the luster of lightning and is born of the clouds. || 24 ||

A "rain-stone" is a hailstone. These are born like hailstones. Just as hailstones are produced during rain, these fall from the seventh layer of the wind <note>Ancient Indian cosmology divided the atmosphere into seven layers or 'wind-skies'</note>. "It is said" indicates tradition. "Divine beings" are those residing in heaven. As it falls from the sky, it is snatched away by celestial beings dwelling in the atmosphere. This cloud-born pearl has the brilliance of a flash of lightning. || 24 ||

### Now he describes the characteristics of pearls produced from serpents—

> Those serpents born of the lineages of Takṣaka and Vāsuki, and those who can move at will;
> In them, smooth pearls with a blue luster exist at the end of their hoods. || 25 ||

->### On the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 80]<-

**Born of the lineages of Takshaka and Vasuki.** Those serpents <note>original: "pannaga," literally "those who go on their bellies"</note> born in the lineage of Takshaka or the lineage of Vasuki <note>legendary serpent kings in Hindu cosmology</note> are capable of moving at will. At the end of the hoods of these serpents—that is, at the top of their heads—pearls are found that are glossy, oily, and possess a blue luster or radiance. **||25||**

**If, when placed in a silver vessel upon a blessed piece of ground, the gods suddenly send rain, that pearl should be known as serpent-born. ||26||**

**In a blessed place.** How is a serpent-born pearl to be recognized? To provide proof for its identification, the author says: when that pearl is placed in a silver vessel on a commendable or auspicious piece of ground, and the gods <note>the heavens</note> suddenly rain without any prior signs of clouds, that pearl should be understood as being born of a serpent. **||26||**

**Now he describes its qualities:**

**It drives away misfortune, destroys enemies, and spreads one's fame. The serpent-born pearl, when worn by kings, is of priceless value and grants victory. ||27||**

**Serpent-born.** This refers to the pearl from a snake. It is of inestimable value <note>literally "unmade price"</note> when worn by kings or rulers. It removes "uneven fortune" <note>misfortune or instability</note>, destroys enemies, spreads one's glory, and bestows victory. **||27||**

**Now he describes the characteristics of those born from bamboo and conch shells:**

**That which resembles camphor or crystal, and is flat and irregular, should be known as bamboo-born. That which is born from a conch is moon-like, round, brilliant, and beautiful. ||28||**

That which looks like camphor or crystal, but is flat and uneven, is born of bamboo. That which is like the moon, perfectly round, naturally shining, and radiant is to be known as born from a conch shell. **||28||**

**Now, for the purpose of understanding their general definition, he says:**

**Pearls born from the conch, the whale, bamboo, the elephant, the boar, the serpent, and the clouds are not to be pierced. Because of their immeasurable qualities, their price has not been specified in the scriptures. ||29||**

The conch is a living creature. The <term>timi</term> <note>a legendary giant sea creature</note> is a fish. Bamboo is a plant. The <term>varana</term> is an elephant. The <term>varaha</term> is a boar. The <term>bhujaga</term> is a serpent. The <term>abhra</term> is a cloud. Those pearls produced from these sources are "not to be pierced" <note>original: "avaidyani," meaning they should not be bored through like common oyster pearls</note>. Because all of these possess infinite virtues or many qualities, their price or value has not been stated or mentioned in the scientific treatises. **||29||**

> Rubies originate from *Saugandhika*, *Kuruvinda*, and Rock-crystal.

Others have the color of the lotus or the water-lily, or a beauty equal to them. Others have the luster of the juice of the rose-apple...

# Chapter on the Characteristics of Rubies
<page-num>887</page-num>
<sig>[Ch. 81]</sig>

There is a specific variety of the Rose Apple tree <note>original: "Jambu"; Syzygium cumini</note>; those stones possessing a luster equal to its juice and a deep red color are known as *Saugandhika* rubies, as they are produced from the *Saugandhika* <note>likely a reference to sulfur or a specific fragrant lily-like mineral source</note> class. ||1||

Regarding those born of *Kuruvinda* <note>Corundum</note>: those which are variegated, being a mixture of white and black, and possess a dull luster or little brilliance, are known as *Kuruvinda*-born. These are pierced by minerals such as clay and are considered flawed due to those inclusions. Those which are brilliant, powerful, of various wonderful colors, pure, and stainless are born of Rock Crystal <note>original: "Sphatika"</note>. ||2||

Now he describes the virtues of these gems:

**Glossy, spreading their luster, clear, radiant, heavy, well-shaped, possessing internal brilliance, and intensely red—these are the qualities of all precious gem-stones.** ||3||

"Glossy" means endowed with a smooth oiliness. "Spreading their luster" refers to the nature of the stone to smear or coat its surroundings with its radiance. "Clear" means stainless. "Radiant" means endowed with light. "Heavy" means possessing significant weight <note>High specific gravity was a traditional test for authenticity</note>. "Well-shaped" means having a beautiful form. "Internal brilliance" means the luster resides deep within the center. "Intensely red" means endowed with an extreme redness. These are the virtues of all rubies and other primary precious stones. ||3||

Now he describes their defects:

**Turbid, dull in luster, covered with streaks, containing mineral inclusions, broken, badly perforated, unappealing, and gritty—these are the defects of gems.** ||4||

"Turbid" means not clear. "Dull in luster" means having very little brilliance. "Covered with streaks" means permeated by lines or cracks. "Containing mineral inclusions" means joined with earth or other minerals. "Broken" means chipped or fractured. "Badly perforated" means joined with a wicked or unpraiseworthy hole. "Unappealing" means not pleasing to the mind. "Gritty" means containing sandy or gravel-like particles. These are the types of gem defects. ||4||

Now he describes the characteristics of the Serpent-Stone <note>original: "Sarpamani"; a legendary gem found in the hoods of cobras</note>:

**The gem that is found on the head of serpents, colored like a bee or a peacock's neck and brilliant like the flame of a lamp, should be known as truly priceless.** ||5||

On the head of serpents, there is a gem resembling a large black bee in its luster, or colored like a peacock's throat, or possessing the brilliance of the tip of a lamp flame. Such a gem should be understood as being of inestimable value. ||5||

# He describes its power—

> The king who wears this stone is never afflicted by
> ailments caused by poison or disease.
> In his kingdom, the gods send rain regularly,
> and he destroys his enemies through the power of that gem. || 6 ||

Whichever king <note>literally: lord of men</note> carries or wears that Serpent-stone <note>original: "sarpa-mani"</note>, for him, afflictions caused by poison or disease never occur. In that king's nation, the god Indra <note>original: "Deva Shakra"</note> rains constantly at all proper times. Furthermore, through the power of that gem, that king destroys his enemies or foes. || 6 ||

## Now, he speaks for the purpose of understanding its value—

> Twenty-six thousand is the price for a single gem weighing one Pala.
> For one weighing three Karshas, twenty thousand is prescribed for a Ruby. || 7 ||
> For half a Pala, twelve thousand; for one Karsha, six thousand.
> That which weighs eight Mashakas, its value is three thousand. || 8 ||
> For four Mashakas, thirteen hundred; for two, the value is five hundred.
> For those with intermediate qualities, the price should be calculated accordingly. || 9 ||
> For one lacking in color, half the price; for one lacking luster, one-eighth.
> One with few virtues and many flaws receives one-twentieth of the value. || 10 ||
> One that is smoky, full of cracks, and of little merit receives one-two-hundredth part.
> Thus has the value of Rubies been declared by the ancient teachers. || 11 ||

<meta>The commentary on verse 7 below expands on the valuation based on weight units like Pala and Karsha.</meta>

"Twenty-six thousand," etc. For a single Ruby <note>original: "padmaraga," literally "lotus-colored"</note> weighing one <term>Pala</term> <note>a traditional unit of weight, approximately 48 grams</note>, which equals four <term>Karshas</term> <note>approximately 12 grams each</note>, the value is stated as twenty-six thousand <term>Rupakas</term> <note>silver coins</note>. For one weighing three Karshas, twenty thousand is stated. || 7 ||

For half a Pala <note>two Karshas</note>, the value is twelve thousand. For one Karsha, six thousand. That Ruby which is held or weighed at eight <term>Mashakas</term> <note>a smaller unit; 16 Mashakas typically make one Karsha</note>, its value is three thousand Rupakas. || 8 ||

"Four Mashakas," etc. For a Ruby weighed at four Mashakas, the value is thirteen hundred <note>literally: "ten-hundred-three"</note>. For two Mashakas, the value is five hundred. In the interval <note>for weights in between these</note>, the value for those with lesser or greater qualities must be imagined or inferred by one's own intelligence. For example, a Pala-weight is twenty-six thousand, while three Karshas is twenty thousand. For a Pala reduced by half a Karsha, the reduction in price should be calculated using the <term>Rule of Three</term> <note>original: "trairashika," a mathematical proportion method</note>. || 9 ||

Regarding the half-value of those deficient in color: A ruby <note>original: "padmarāga"</note> that is lacking in its proper color is worth half of the previously stated price. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the Brihat Samhita, specifically focusing on the omens derived from lamps (Dīpalakṣaṇa). It follows the previous discussions on fire and elemental signs.</meta>

<page-num>890</page-num>
<header>In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 83]</header>

A lamp that is counter-clockwise—meaning it rotates in a leftward, non-auspicious direction—is considered ill-omened. Likewise, one that has a dirty wick-ear <note>the charred part of the wick</note> or lacks a clear radiance. One that is accompanied by sparks—meaning small particles of fire—and has a small form, meaning a weak or dim light. Even if it is supplied with pure, clean oil and a proper wick, such a lamp quickly goes out. Furthermore, one that makes noise, one that trembles or shakes, or one whose flame is scattered and flickering. Also, a lamp that goes out without the presence of a moth or a breeze—meaning it extinguishes on its own without external cause—such a lamp foretells an evil or undesirable result. ||1||

### Now, the auspicious signs are described:

> **A lamp that has a compact form, a long body, is steady without trembling, and is radiant;**
> **It is silent, beautiful, moves in a clockwise direction, and has the luster of beryl or gold.**
> **Such a lamp quickly manifests prosperity; likewise one that burns brightly for a very long time.**
> **The remaining characteristics should be applied according to the logic used for the signs of fire. ||2||**

A lamp that has a "compact form" means it has a dense or solid flame. A "long body" refers to a tall flame. "Steady" means it is free from shaking. "Radiant" means it has a lovely glow. "Silent" means it is without sound. "Beautiful" means it is very bright. "Clockwise motion" means the flame curls to the right. Its "luster" is similar to that of a beryl gem <note>original: "vaidūrya", a cat's-eye or chrysoberyl stone</note> which is greenish-yellow, or like gold. One that burns "brightly for a very long time" means it is intensely luminous for a long duration. Such a lamp quickly manifests "Lakshmi," meaning wealth and prosperity. The "remaining characteristics" not explicitly mentioned here should be applied, as far as possible, in the same way as the signs of fire previously discussed. For example:

> "When the fire takes the shape of a banner, a water-pot, a horse, an elephant, or a king, the earth—with its rising and setting mountains and the Himalaya and Vindhya ranges as its breasts—comes under the control of the king." <margin>1</margin>

And also:

> "When the fire resembles gold, the Ashoka flower, the Kurantaka flower, a lotus, beryl, or a blue water-lily, the darkness in the palace cannot find a place, being destroyed by the jewel-like rays of the king's fortune." <margin>2</margin>

Everything that is possible in fire should be considered here. For instance, the signs occurring **"at the conclusion of the 'Svaha' invocation"** <margin>3</margin> and so on, should be reflected upon. ||2||

### Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, named "The Characteristics of Lamps," in the Commentary on the Samhita composed by the venerable Bhattotpala. ||83||

<meta>This page begins Chapter 84 of the Brihat Samhita, a 6th-century Sanskrit encyclopedic work by Varahamihira. It focuses on the selection and ritual use of tooth-cleaning sticks (Dantakashtha), which were essential for daily hygiene and spiritual purity.</meta>

### Now, the characteristics of tooth-cleaning sticks are explained.

First, the author speaks to demonstrate the purpose of this study:

> There are thousands of varieties of tooth-cleaning sticks <note>Sanskrit: *Dantakashtha*; traditionally small twigs chewed at one end to form a brush</note> derived from different types of creepers, climbing plants, shrubs, and trees. If one were to describe the fruits <note>results or benefits</note> of all of them, there would be no end to the subject. Therefore, I shall speak only of those that are desirable for attaining one's goals. ॥1॥

"Creepers" are well-known. "Climbing plants" are also well-known. A "shrub" is a cluster of branches arising from a single root. "Trees" refer to large woody plants. From the various distinct species of these, there could be thousands of types of tooth-cleaning sticks. One could speak of the results of using each of them. However, so that there is no "excessive attachment" to the subject—meaning, to avoid an overly lengthy and detailed expansion—I shall, for this reason, describe only the "desirable" ones, those that grant cherished rewards. The word *atha* <note>original: "अथ"</note> is used here to complete the meter of the verse. ॥1॥

Now, he speaks regarding the general rules <term>Paribhasha: a set of governing rules or definitions</term>:

> One should not use tooth-cleaning sticks that are unknown, nor those that still have leaves attached. One should not use those with an even number of joints, those that are split, those that are withered at the top, or those stripped of their bark. ॥2॥

One should not "eat" <note>in this context, chew or use for cleaning</note> tooth-cleaning sticks whose identity was not previously known. One should not use those "endowed with leaves," meaning those still having foliage. One should not use those with "even joints," meaning those possessing an even number of knots or segments. One should not use those that are "split" or cracked. One should not use those "withered at the top," where the upper portion is dry. And one should not use those "without bark," meaning those stripped of their outer skin. ॥2॥

Now, he describes the specific results according to the type of wood:

> From the *Vaikankata*, *Shriphala*, and *Kashmari* trees comes divine luster; from the *Kshemataru* comes a good wife; from the Banyan tree comes prosperity; from the *Arka* tree comes abundant energy; and from the *Madhuka* tree come sons endowed with good qualities and popularity. ॥3॥

The *Vaikankata* <note>Flacourtia sapida</note> is a well-known tree. The *Shriphala* <note>Aegle marmelos or Bael fruit</note> is well-known. The *Kashmari* <note>Gmelina arborea</note> is well-known. When these tooth-cleaning sticks are used, there arises "Brahminic luster," which is a radiance related to sacred knowledge. This is also known as *Brahmavarchas* <note>spiritual splendor resulting from Vedic study and discipline</note>...

One should use the tooth-stick <term>Dantakāṣṭha: a twig used as a disposable toothbrush</term> while facing North or facing East. ## Now, the Explanation of Omens is Commenced.

At the very beginning, the author states the following to show the purpose of this study:

> That which was spoken by Rishabha based on the teachings of Indra, Shukra, Brihaspati <note>original: "Vagisha," the Lord of Speech</note>, Kapishthala, and Garuda; || 1 ||
> And that which the Great King of Kings, the prosperous Dravyavardhana, the ruler of Avanti <note>Modern-day Ujjain</note>, spoke after observing the teachings of Bharadvaja; || 2 ||
> And the teachings of the Seven Sages <note>The Saptarishi, the celestial patriarchs of Hindu tradition</note>, whether in the refined language <note>Sanskrit</note> or the natural dialects <note>Prakrit</note>, and those omens described by Garga and many other authors of travel-manuals; || 3 ||
> Having observed all these, Varahamihira has composed this entire Compendium of Omens out of affection for his students, to grant them the highest knowledge. || 4 ||

Regarding the omens: Indra is the king of gods; Shukra is the son of Bhrigu; Vagisha is Brihaspati; Kapishthala is a sage; and Garutman is the son of Vinata <note>Garuda, the divine eagle</note>. From the views of these foundational authors, the teacher named Rishabha spoke. Likewise, Rishabha spoke based on the views of the sages Bhaguri and Devala. || 1 ||

Regarding the "teachings of Bharadvaja": Having seen and examined the views of the sage named Bharadvaja, the King of Avanti (Ujjain) named the prosperous Dravyavardhana, born of a lineage of Great Kings of Kings, spoke [on this subject]. || 2 ||

Regarding the "teachings of the Seven Sages": This refers to the views of Marichi and the other [six sages]. Furthermore, there are omens used in common worldly practice in the refined language <insert>Sanskrit</insert>, and omens in the natural language <insert>Prakrit</insert> which is devoid of refined speech. There are also omens described and told by Garga and many other authors of travel-manuals, such as Garga, Vashistha, Parashara, Kashyapa, and the sons of Bhrigu. || 3 ||

<header>[Ch. 85] Chapter on Omens 895</header>

Having seen and observed those <note>referring to the works of ancient sages</note>, Varahamihira—the Brahmin from Magadha <note>an ancient kingdom in eastern India</note> named Varahamihira—out of affection for his disciples, and for their benefit, composed this excellent and primary summary of all omens. ||4||

### Now he states the purpose of the science of omens—

->The good or evil actions performed by men in previous births,<-
->the omen reveals the ripening of those deeds to those who are traveling. ||5||<-

The good or evil *karma* <note>actions and their moral consequences</note> earned by men—that is, human beings—in other previous lives: the omen indicates or signals the "ripening" (the resulting fruit) of that karma. A certain creature or living being reveals this to those who are "going"—those setting out on a journey. ||5||

### Now, to show the different classifications of omens, he says—

-><gloss>1</gloss> Those that move in villages, forests, water, on land, in the sky, by day, by night, or both;<-
->they are to be understood as male, female, or neuter by their cries, movements, glances, and speech. ||6||<-

Some omens are "village-born" (domestic), others are "forest-born" (wild), others are "water-dwellers" (aquatic), others are "land-dwellers" (terrestrial), and <gloss>17</gloss> others are "sky-dwellers" (aerial). Among these, the domestic ones include men, horses, elephants, and dogs. The forest ones include lions, tigers, boars, leopards, and deer. The water-dwellers are swans and the like. The land-dwellers are porcupines, mongooses, snakes, and so on. The sky-dwellers are those seen constantly in the air, never touching the ground. Others are "day-rovers," others are "night-rovers," and others are "both-rovers" (active by both day and night). The Teacher <note>Varahamihira</note> himself will describe their specific characteristics later in the text with the verse beginning "The Shyama, the Falcon, the Eagle..." and we shall explain them there. Among these omens, the male, female, and neuter types are to be grasped through their cries, movements, glances, and speech. "Cry" refers to their sound. "Movement" refers to their manner of going. "Glance" refers to the observation of their physical characteristics. "Speech" refers to the determination of whether the creature is male, female, or neuter. When a distant omen makes a sound at that moment, there may be a doubt: was it uttered by a male, a female, or a neuter? In that case, if the speech of a nearby person is heard at that same moment, and it is a man speaking, then the omen is male. If a woman's voice is heard, then the omen is female. If a neuter person's voice is heard, then it is neuter. ||6||

# On the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 85]

The author says once more:

> Because their distinct species are not easily categorized and they do not remain in one place, their individual identities are not clearly perceived. Regarding the explanation of their general characteristics, these two verses were composed by the Sages. || 7 ||

The distinct species or biological divisions of these omens <note>shakuna: birds or animals used for divination</note> are difficult to pinpoint. Because they do not remain in a single location <note>anavasthena: lack of fixed abode</note>, their specific classification is not easily perceived or known. Therefore, in this general description of their traits, two verses are cited which were "composed by the Sages"—meaning they were authored by ancient seers like the Elder Garga. || 7 ||

Now, he presents those two verses:

> Those with fleshy, high, and broad shoulders, thick necks, and fine chests, who possess a short yet deep cry and a steady gait, are males. || 8 ||
> Those with slender chests, heads, and necks, and who possess small mouths, feet, and strides, and who utter continuous, soft sounds, are females. Anything other than these is neuter. || 9 ||

**Regarding "Those with fleshy, high, and broad shoulders":** Those whose shoulders are fleshy (well-muscled), high (elevated), and broad (wide). They have thick necks <note>shiradhara: literally 'head-bearers'</note> and beautiful chests. Their cry is "short yet deep"—meaning a brief but resonant or echoing sound. Those who possess a steady gait or firm courage are the male omens. || 8 ||

**Regarding "Slender chests":** The chest, the head, and the neck—those whose limbs are slender in these areas are so described. <note>The commentator notes a grammatical suffix 'ka' used here for the compound word.</note> Those who have a small mouth, small feet, and a small stride or effort, and whose speech (cry) is continuous, connected, and sweet, are females. **"Anything other than these is neuter":** Any creature possessing characteristics other than these two sets of traits is neuter. This implies that a creature should be known as neuter if it possesses a mixture of the characteristics described for both males and females. || 9 ||

The author now states that any characteristics not mentioned here should be learned from common observation:

> One should learn their habits, such as whether they roam in villages or forests, from the world itself. Desiring to be brief, I speak only of what is necessary for a journey. || 10 ||

One should observe and know from "the world"—meaning from common experience or other scientific treatises—whether these omens roam in villages or in the wild forests. By the use of the word "etc." <note>adi-grahana</note>, one should also include whether they move by day, by night, or both. **"Desiring to be brief":** One who wishes to make a summary. I, wishing to be brief, speak only of what is necessary for a journey. In the context of a journey, the same...

# Chapter on Omens
<meta>[Chapter 85]</meta>

I am stating and explaining only as much as is necessary; for this reason, I have not spoken at length here out of fear of making the text too bulky. || 10 ||

Now, he explains who should be the focus of consideration when observing an omen:

->**On a journey, one's self; in an army, the King; in a city, the presiding Deity.**<-
->**In a traveling company, the leader; if there is equality, then the one superior in caste, knowledge, or age. || 11 ||**<-

When a man is traveling on a road, he should observe the omen for good or bad results with reference to himself—his own body. In an army, with reference to the King. In a city, with reference to the presiding Deity <note>The guardian god of the town</note>. The mention of "city" is an architectural shorthand; it also implies observing with reference to the village headman. In a caravan <term>Sartha</term> <note>A traveling group of merchants or pilgrims</note>, with reference to the chief leader. When there are many leaders in a caravan, and there is equality among them, then the one who is superior by caste <note>Varna</note> should be considered. If they are equal in caste, then the one superior in knowledge; if equal in knowledge, then the one superior in age. || 11 ||

Now, he explains the rules regarding the directions and the timing of their results:

->**In the directions left, occupied, and to be occupied by the sun, the fruit is of a corresponding nature.**<-
->**These are known as the Burning Coal, the Blazing, and the Smoking; the others are Peaceful. || 12 ||**<-

Here, due to the rotation of the sun, there is a specific positioning across the eight directions. It is as follows:

Starting from sunrise until the first watch <term>Prahar</term> <note>A period of approximately three hours</note> of the day: the Northeast is the direction "left" by the sun; the East is "occupied" by the sun; the Southeast is "to be occupied" by the sun. 

Then, after the first watch until the second watch: the East is "left"; the Southeast is "occupied"; the South is "to be occupied." 

After the second watch until the third watch: the Southeast is "left"; the South is "occupied"; the Southwest is "to be occupied." 

After the third watch until sunset: the South is "left"; the Southwest is "occupied"; the West is "to be occupied." 

After sunset until the first watch of the night: the Southwest is "left"; the West is "occupied"; the Northwest is "to be occupied." 

After the first watch of the night until the second watch: the West is "left"; the Northwest is "occupied"; the North is "to be occupied." 

After the second watch until the third watch: the Northwest is "left"; the North is "occupied"; the Northeast is "to be occupied." 

After the third watch until sunrise: the North is "left"; the Northeast is "occupied"; the East is "to be occupied."

In these directions—left, occupied, and to be occupied by the sun—the result is of a corresponding nature. In those directions, one must look for the result according to the name. This refers to inauspiciousness. An inauspicious omen seen in the direction "left" by the sun has already passed; its fruit is in the past. An inauspicious omen in the direction "occupied" by the sun is "obtained"; it happens on that very day. An inauspicious omen in the direction "to be occupied" by the sun is "coming"; it will happen in the future. 

Regarding the terms "Burning Coal," "Blazing," and "Smoking": those directions situated as left, occupied, and to be occupied by the sun are respectively called Burning Coal <term>Angarini</term>, Blazing <term>Dipta</term>, and Smoking <term>Dhumini</term>. The direction left by the sun is "Burning Coal"; the occupied is "Blazing"; the one to be occupied is "Smoking." The other five directions are "Peaceful" <term>Shanta</term>. And it is said—

--- Page 390 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Burning Directions" (Dik-Daha) and their influence on omens, specifically interpreting the cries of animals and birds based on the sun's position.</meta>

<page-num>898</page-num>
<header>In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 85]</header>

The direction the sun has just left is called **Charcoal-like** <note>Sanskrit: *Angarini*; glowing like embers</note>. The direction in which the sun currently stands is **Blazing** <note>Sanskrit: *Pradipta*</note>. The direction toward which the sun is moving is **Smoky** <note>Sanskrit: *Pradhumita*</note>. The remaining directions are **Tranquil** <note>Sanskrit: *Prashanta*</note> and are considered auspicious.

On this matter, some scholars describe the East as being "occupied by the sun" from the middle of the last watch of the night until the middle of the first watch of the day. For the next watch and a half, the South-East is occupied, and so on for the rest. This, however, is incorrect. For the Lord Garga <note>An ancient sage and authority on astronomy and omens</note> says:

-> At sunrise, the East is blazing; in the forenoon, the South-East. <-
-> At midday, the South is blazing; in the afternoon, the South-West. <-
-> At sunset, the West is blazing; in the first part of the night, the North-West. <-
-> At midnight, the North is blazing; in the later part of the night, the North-East. <-
-> The directions currently occupied, yet to be occupied, and already passed always "blaze" here. <-
-> When animals cry out in these directions, they announce a great danger. <-
-> If an animal cries in a direction that has already finished its "blazing," it indicates past events. <-
-> If it cries in a direction yet to be occupied, the omen relates to the future. <-

Now, the author explains the rules for the results of these directions:

### **One should predict auspicious results for the three periods of time based on the fifth direction from those.**
### **For the remaining two directions, the good or bad results should be stated according to their proximity. ||13||**

The word "that" refers to the directions like the Charcoal-like one. "The fifth from those" means the fifth direction counting from the specific one mentioned. **Based on the fifth direction, the three periods of time**—past, present, and future—should be used to declare the auspicious results. 

This is what is meant: 
1. The fifth direction from the **Charcoal-like** direction is a **Tranquil** one. If a favorable bird <term>Shakuna: an omen-bearing bird or animal</term> appears there, the good result has already passed. If an unfavorable bird is on the left in that same direction, a minor misfortune has passed.
2. In the fifth direction from the **Blazing** direction, if a favorable bird is present, the good result is happening now. If an unfavorable bird is on the left, a minor misfortune is happening now.
3. In the fifth direction from the **Smoky** direction, if a favorable bird is present, the good result is yet to come. If an unfavorable bird is there, a minor misfortune is in the future.

For the Charcoal-like and other "burning" directions themselves, a favorable bird yields only slight good, while an unfavorable bird yields extremely bad results. Regarding the **remaining two directions**: the good or bad results should be declared based on which "burning" direction they are closest to. This means those directions should be divided into two parts to reach a certainty. If an unfavorable bird stands in the part closer to the Charcoal-like or Tranquil directions, a minor past misfortune should be understood.

It cites the sage Garga to define the timing of these states and provides a mathematical method (the "fifth direction" rule) to predict if an event is past, present, or future.</summary>
