# Chapter on Omens
<page-num>899</page-num>

When a bird is situated in a favorable <note>original: "saumya" - gentle or auspicious</note> direction, the journey will be successful. If the bird is in a favorable direction but that direction is "smoky" <note>an astrological state of a direction being afflicted</note>, "extinguished," or "approaching" <note>referring to the sun's position</note>, then a small amount of misfortune is to be expected. If a bird is situated in an inauspicious <note>original: "pape" - sinful or malefic</note> direction, great misfortune will occur. As it has been said:

> "One should understand the past from a direction that has been passed, the present from a 'blazing' direction, and the future from a 'smoky' direction. In the 'extinguished' directions, and in the fifth positions from them, the 'extinguished' or 'blazing' states are known by their proximity to the sun." ||13||

Again, to explain the timing of the results, he says:

->Results occur quickly from birds nearby or in low places;<-
->Results occur after a long time from those high up or far away.<-
->Likewise, one should declare the fruit based on the growth or injury of the location.<- ||14||

From nearby birds or those standing in low places, the result—whether good or bad—happens very quickly. From those in high places or far away, the good or bad result happens after a long time. And so says Parashara <note>An ancient sage and authority on Vedic astrology and omens</note>:

> "If they are close, the result—whether good or otherwise—happens swiftly. If they are all far away, the result is accomplished after a long time."

One should declare the result in the same manner based on the "growth" or "injury" of the location. In a place that is "growing" (where daily growth is visible), an inauspicious bird causes "injury" <note>negates the growth</note>.

In this regard, after considering even a little of the auspiciousness, one should again declare the good or bad result. And so says Parashara:

> "Those birds or animals staying on burnt, crooked, broken, cut, dry, or thorny trees; or staying on stones, low ground, skulls, bones, sand, hair, or ashes; or on cremation grounds, charcoal, termite mounds, salty earth, or dusty places; or staying in ruined, decayed, impure, or un-bright places—these are designated as 'Blazing' <note>original: 'dipta' - here meaning agitated or inauspicious</note>.
> Those staying on beautiful, oily <note>gloss: lush</note>, fruit-bearing, milky-sap, or flowering trees; or standing on level and praiseworthy ground—these deer and birds are 'Quiet' <note>original: 'shanta' - peaceful or auspicious</note>.
> Here, the 'Blazing' are inauspicious and the 'Quiet' are auspicious." ||14||

Now, he describes the ten types of "Blazing" <note>agitated/inauspicious</note> omens:

->An omen is 'Blazing' by time, lunar day, constellation, weekday, and sun, each more so than the last;<-
->It is also 'Blazing' by action, movement, location, state, and voice.<- ||15||

<summary>This page details how the timing and quality of an omen's result are determined by the bird's physical distance, elevation, and the environmental condition of its perch. It introduces the classification of omens into 'Blazing' (inauspicious) and 'Quiet' (auspicious) based on ten specific environmental and temporal factors.</summary>

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 85]

<page-num>900</page-num>

A <term>Kshana</term><note>A specific moment or division of time</note> refers to a <term>Muhurta</term><note>A period of 48 minutes</note> such as those dedicated to Shiva and others. An omen is considered "blazing" (<term>Dipta</term><note>In omenology, 'blazing' refers to an intensified, usually ill-omened or over-stimulated state</note>) in those moments belonging to stars of a fierce or cruel nature. Regarding lunar days (<term>Tithis</term>), such as Nanda and others, the fourth, sixth, eighth, ninth, and fourteenth are considered "blazing." An omen appearing on these days is "blazing." Similarly, an omen is "blazing" when occurring under fierce or cruel constellations. <term>Udu</term> is another word for constellations (<term>Nakshatras</term>); thus, this is "constellation-blazing." A wind that is fierce, harsh, rough, or blowing against one's direction is "wind-blazing." An omen facing the sun or situated in a "blazing" direction is "sun-blazing." 

In this way, there are five types of "divinely blazing" (<term>Deva-dipta</term>) omens, listed in increasing order of intensity. This means: a "lunar-day-blazing" omen is more significant than a "moment-blazing" one; a "constellation-blazing" is more than that; "wind-blazing" is more still; and "sun-blazing" is the most intense form of divine blazing.

One who runs toward lightning, meteors, the sun, or the wind is "motion-blazing" (<term>Gati-dipta</term>). One situated in a place that is broken, split, crooked, burnt, or in an impure spot is "location-blazing" (<term>Sthana-dipta</term>). <term>Bhava</term> means existence or the consciousness of being; one devoid of this <note>i.e., appearing unconscious, dazed, or lifeless</note> is "state-blazing" (<term>Bhava-dipta</term>). One with a voice that is uneven, faltering, hoarse, or broken is "voice-blazing" (<term>Svara-dipta</term>). One intent on flapping wings, shaking the beak, falling, jumping up and down, or pecking is "action-blazing" (<term>Cheshta-dipta</term>). These also increase in intensity as listed. This is confirmed by the sayings of the son of the Sage <note>Rishiputra</note>. Specifically:

> "Omens are 'lunar-day-blazing' on the fourth, sixth, eighth, and fourteenth days. They are 'action-blazing' during the <term>Vishti</term> period. They are 'constellation-blazing' in the stars Mula, Jyeshtha, Ashlesha, Ardra, Vishakha, Krittika, Magha, and the Purva-triad. They are 'moment-blazing' during the specific hours of these stars. Those without consciousness or with little awareness are 'state-blazing.' Those with voices that are harsh, broken, terrifying, pained, agitating, uneven, faltering, weak, or shattered are 'voice-blazing.' They are 'location-blazing' when perched on trees that are struck by lightning, fallen, cut, split, broken, uprooted, half-crushed, withered, diseased, or those with falling leaves, fruits, or sap; or on trees that are foul-smelling, tasteless, bitter, sour, salty, or pungent; or those entangled in vines, bent over, or burnt by forest fires. Also those on walls, city gates, watchtowers, or barren ground. Those who run toward ruins, uneven ground, pits, rubbish, hair, bones, skulls, anthills, charcoal, straw, excrement, weapons, fire-receptacles, quarrels, snakes, lightning, meteors, the sun, or the wind are 'motion-blazing.' Those characterized by wing-flapping, beak-shaking, falling, jumping, and pecking are 'action-blazing.' Those in fierce, harsh, or contrary winds are 'wind-blazing.' Those facing the sun or in 'blazing' directions are 'sun-blazing'—so says the Lord Indra." ||15||

->Here he mentions a specific distinction:<-

**Even if an omen is tranquil in these ten ways, it is "Gentle" if it eats grass or fruit.**
**It is "Fierce" if it eats meat or impure things, and "Mixed" if it eats cooked food. ||16||**

In this manner, an omen can be "tranquil" (<term>Shanta</term>) in ten ways. However, if it is a grass-eater or fruit-eater, it is **Gentle** (<term>Saumya</term>) and gives auspicious results. If it eats meat (flesh) or impure things like excrement, it is **Fierce** (<term>Raudra</term>) or "blazing." One that eats cooked food is considered **Mixed**—partly tranquil and partly blazing. As it has been said—

It distinguishes between "Gentle" (herbivorous) and "Fierce" (carnivorous/scavenging) animals in the context of divination.</summary>

# Chapter on Omens
### [Chapter 85]

Those that eat flesh or impure things are considered "blazing" <note>original: "pradipta"; in this context, it refers to an intense, often ill-omened or aggressive state</note>, while those that eat grass and fruit are naturally "peaceful." Those that eat cooked food are said to be of a mixed nature. Their effects should be considered based on the direction they face, their location, their appearance, and the time of day. ||16||

Now, he says something further:

->**Those situated in mansions, palaces, and auspicious or pleasing places are excellent;**<-
->**as are those perched upon trees bearing sweet sap, milk, fruits, or flowers.** ||17||<-

A "mansion" <note>Sanskrit: *harmya*</note> refers to a home. A "palace" <note>Sanskrit: *prasada*</note> refers to a temple of the gods. "Auspicious places" are those occupied by deities, Brahmins, or cows. "Pleasing places" are those with green grass and the cool shade of trees. Omens <note>literally "birds" or "omens": *shakuna*</note> situated in these places are excellent and bring auspicious results. Likewise, those on trees with sweet-tasting fruits, or those with milky sap (such as the *Arka* plant), or fruit-bearing trees (like the citron), or flowering trees, are considered excellent. ||17||

Now he describes the specific results regarding the strength of the omens:

->**Diurnal and nocturnal creatures are strong when in their own time and when situated on mountains or water.**<-
->**Neuter, female, and male creatures should be known as increasingly strong in that order.** ||18||<-

At their own proper time—meaning their natural period of activity—creatures of the day and night are strong and powerful when situated on mountains or in water, respectively. Day-roamers are strong on mountains during the day. <note>The word "mountain" here is an indicator for any high ground.</note> Night-roamers are strong at night and in marshy places. As the authority Manu-dharma says:

> The day-walker is strong on a mountain by day; the night-walker in a marsh at night.
> An omen's voice is considered obstructed otherwise; one must divide the strength accordingly.

Regarding "neuter, female, and male": among these omens, they are strong in the order mentioned. Females are stronger than neuters, and males are stronger than females. It is also said:
Those that roam by day, night, or both are strong in their own time; those that roam in cities, forests, or both are strong when in their own natural habitat. All are fruitless if in the wrong place, but for one desiring to travel, those belonging to the city or the king are auspicious. ||18||

He says another thing:

->**Endowed with speed, proper species, strength, position, joy, courage, and voice;**<-
->**being in their own territory and following a favorable direction—those lacking these qualities should be avoided.** ||19||<-

"Speed" <note>Sanskrit: *java*</note> refers to the velocity of movement. "Species" <note>Sanskrit: *jati*</note> refers to the classification of their birth. "Strength" refers to their size or power. "Position" is where they stay. "Joy" is the gladness of their heart. "Courage" <note>Sanskrit: *sattva*</note> means beauty and fearlessness. <margin>1. Another manuscript reads: *Sattva* means generosity.</margin> "Voice" refers to their sound. Those who possess these...

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 85]

...are more powerful. As the author will state later: "That which is more powerful should be accepted <gloss>1</gloss>." In cases where the relative strength of omens is unknown, the following criteria are given: Between two omens, the one that is superior in speed, superior in species, superior in physical strength, situated in an auspicious location, full of joy, full of courage, possessing a beautiful voice, and situated in its own natural habitat is the stronger one. Those lacking these qualities—referring back to speed and the other traits—should be considered devoid of strength. ||19||

### Now, he describes the strength of these omens according to the directions based on their species:

> ->The rooster, elephant, pirili bird, peacock, vanjula, and chikkara deer;<-
> ->The lion-roar bird and the kutapuri are powerful in the East. ||20||<-

The *Kukkuta* is the rooster. The *Ibha* is the elephant. The *Pirili* is a specific type of bird. The *Shikhi* is the peacock. The *Vanjula* is the khadira-beaked bird <note>likely a species of wagtail or wood-pigeon</note>. The *Chikkara* is a species of deer. The *Simhanada* (lion-roar) is a specific bird. The *Kutapuri* is the karayika bird. These are powerful in the East. Here, "East" should be understood as the direction of Prajapati <note>the creator deity associated with the East</note>, and this logic of directional lordship should be applied throughout. ||20||

### Now, he describes those powerful in the South:

> ->The jackal, owl, harita, crow, koka, bear, and pingala;<-
> ->The pigeon, and the sounds of weeping, lamentation, and harsh noises are powerful in the South. ||21||<-

The *Kroshtuka* is the jackal. The *Uluka* (owl) and *Harita* (green pigeon) are specific birds. The *Kaka* is the crow. The *Koka* is a bird <note>often identified as the ruddy shelduck</note>. The *Riksha* is a bear. The *Pingala* is the spotted owlet. The *Kapota* is a pigeon. *Rudita* refers to the sound of weeping. *Akranda* refers to cries of distress. Other "harsh sounds" are those that are unpleasant to hear. All of these are powerful in the South (the direction of Yama, the god of death). ||21||

### Now, he describes those powerful in the West:

> ->The cow, hare, curlew, fox, swan, osprey, and francolin;<-
> ->The cat, and the sounds of festivals, musical instruments, singing, and laughter are powerful in the West. ||22||<-

The *Go* (cow) is well-known. The *Shasha* is the hare. The *Krauncha* is the curlew. The *Lomasha* is a fox or jackal. The *Hamsa* is the swan. Those called *Utkrosha* are ospreys. The *Kapinjala* is the francolin. These are all specific birds. The *Vidala* is the cat. *Utsava* refers to festivals such as weddings. *Vaditra* refers to musical instruments such as the lute, various drums (muruja, maddala, karata), trumpets, and kettledrums. *Gita* (singing) is well-known. *Hasa* is laughter or mockery. These are powerful in the West (the direction of Varuna, the god of the oceans). ||22||

# Chapter on Omens (Shakuna)
<page-num>903</page-num>

Now he speaks regarding the North:

> The woodpecker, the deer, the mouse, the forest deer, the single-hoofed animals, the cuckoo, the blue jay, the porcupine, the sound of "Auspicious Day" blessings, and the sounds of bells and conchs are favorable in the North. ||23||

The **woodpecker** <note>original: *shatapatra*</note> is a bird commonly known as the *darvaghat*. The **deer** <note>original: *kuranga*</note> is a species of antelope. The **mouse** <note>original: *akhu*</note> is the common rodent. The **forest deer** <note>original: *mriga*</note> is the well-known deer. **Single-hoofed animals** <note>original: *ekashapha*</note> refer to horses and donkeys. The **cuckoo** <note>original: *kokila*</note> is the bird nourished by others. The **blue jay** <note>original: *chasha*</note> is a bird. The **porcupine** <note>original: *shalyaka*</note> is a burrowing creature. The **"Auspicious Day"** <note>original: *punyaha*</note> refers to the sound of blessings. **Bells and conchs** are well-known. The cries or sounds of all these are powerful <note>meaning they carry significant or lucky weight</note> when heard in the North. ||23||

---

Now he describes their specific circumstances:

> A domestic animal found in the forest is not to be considered, nor is a wild animal found in a village. A creature that moves by day is not to be considered at night, nor is a night-walker to be considered by day. ||24||

A domestic bird or animal <note>original: *shakuna*</note> that is found in the forest—whether its omen is usually good or bad—should not be accepted. Likewise, a wild animal found in a village should not be accepted. A day-walker <note>diurnal</note> should not be considered during the night, and a night-walker <note>nocturnal</note> should not be considered during the day. ||24||

---

Furthermore, he states the prohibitions:

> Pairs, those afflicted by disease, the frightened, those seeking a fight or meat, those separated by a river, and those in rut are never to be accepted as omens. ||25||

**Pairs** <note>original: *dvandva*</note> refers to a couple, excluding the crane couple, because the author will later state: "The cry of the crane is auspicious when made by a pair in unison." **Afflicted by disease** means suffering from illness. **Frightened** means terrified. **Seeking a fight** means wishing to quarrel. **Seeking meat** means desiring flesh. **Separated by a river** means those on the opposite bank. **In rut** <note>original: *matta*</note> means those full of pride or passion due to the mating season. Such omens are never to be accepted for determining good or bad results. As it is said:

> Those in pairs, the diseased, the frightened, the intoxicated, those in enmity, those fighting, those seeking meat, and all those separated by a boundary or a river are not to be thought of when considering good or bad results. ||25||

---

Now he explains the seasons in which these animals yield no results:

> The red horse, the goat, the donkey, the deer, the camel, the forest deer, and the rabbit are to be known as fruitless in the Winter; the crow and the cuckoo are fruitless in the Spring. ||26||

<header>In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 85]</header>

The *Rohita* is a species of deer. The *Ashva* is a horse. The *Aja* is a goat. The *Baleya* is a donkey. The *Kuranga* is a species of deer. The *Ushtra* is a camel. The *Mriga* is a forest deer. The *Shasha* is a rabbit. All these, during the dewy season <note>Sishira: approximately mid-January to mid-March</note> in the months of Magha and Phalguna, are to be known as "fruitless" or ineffective because they are always present <note>The text suggests that if an animal is in its natural peak or constant presence, its appearance doesn't constitute a special omen</note>. In the spring <note>Vasanta: mid-March to mid-May</note> during the months of Chaitra and Vaishakha, the *Kaka* or crow and the *Kokila* or cuckoo are likewise ineffective as omens. ॥26॥

->He speaks regarding others:<-

**Boars, dogs, wolves, and the like are not to be taken as omens in the month of Bhadrapada. In the autumn, water-eaters, cows, and cranes are excluded; in Shravana, the elephant and the Chataka bird are ineffective. ॥27॥**

In the month of Bhadrapada <note>late August to September</note>, the *Sukara* or boar, the *Shva* or dog, and the *Vrika* or wolf are excluded. By the phrase "and the like," deer and hole-dwelling animals <term>Bileshaya: animals that live in burrows or dens</term> are included. These are not to be taken as omens, or are fruitless due to their constant presence. In the autumn <note>Sharad: mid-September to mid-November</note> during the months of Ashvina and Karttika, the *Abjada* or "water-eaters" such as swans and similar birds are excluded. "Born in water" is *Abja*; those who eat such things are *Abjada*. The *Gau* or cow is well-known. The *Krauncha* is a specific type of crane. These are fruitless and should not be grasped as omens. In the month of Shravana <note>late July to August</note>, the elephant and the *Chataka* bird are not to be taken. The *Hasti* is an elephant; the *Chataka* is a specific bird <note>legendary for drinking only raindrops</note>. ॥27॥

->Now he speaks regarding others:<-

**The tiger, bear, monkey, leopard, buffalo, and all hole-dwelling animals are known to be fruitless in the winter; so too are all young animals, except for humans. ॥28॥**

The *Vyaghra* is the well-known clawed creature (tiger). The *Riksha* is a bear. The *Vanara* is a monkey. The *Dvipi* is a leopard. The *Mahisha* is the well-known buffalo. These, along with the *Bileshaya* or hole-dwelling creatures, are included. A *Bileshaya* is one who sleeps in a hole, such as the porcupine, the boar, and the *Kusha* <note>likely a species of small rodent</note>. *Vimanusha* means all creatures excluding humans. *Bala* refers to infants or the young. In the winter <note>Hemanta: mid-November to mid-January</note> during the months of Margashirsha and Pausha, these are to be known as fruitless. However, human children are indeed "fruitful" (effective as omens). Whatever good or bad behavior these humans exhibit is considered significant.

Here, the detailed description of seasonal characteristics composed by the Lord Parashara <note>An ancient sage and authority on astrology and omens</note> is written:

> "Now, among birds and animals, the spring is the season of rut/passion for the cuckoo, peacock, *Jivanjivaka* (pheasant), *Priyaputra*, *Rajaputri*, *Godaputra*, the hundred-petaled woodpecker, the *Dattyuha* (water-hen), the *Madana-Sarika* (starling), the frog, the *Koyashti* (lapwing), the *Mahamuktaka*, the *Amshakrada*, the *Dandi-Manavaka*, the crow, the rooster, the crane, the osprey, the *Sharnga* <gloss>1. The 'Ga' manuscript reads 'Shardula' (tiger)</gloss>, the *Plavaka*, the *Chitrakapota* (spotted dove), the *Pushparatha*, the *Ushtraratha*, and others. The rainy season is the time for the woodpecker, osprey, *Bhringaraja* (king-crow), peacock, cuckoo, crane, the clouds, the *Vakadhvanvan*, the *Chataka*, and the *Saranga* deer. For the *Chakora* (partridge), the *Kadamba* (goose), the starling, the parrot, the *Pushkara*, the *Chataka*, the swan, the *Chakravaka* (ruddy shelduck), the *Sarasa* crane, the *Kurara* (osprey), and the *Krauncha* crane..."

# Chapter on Omens
<page-num>905</page-num>

The autumn is the rutting season for the *Karandava* <note>a type of duck</note> and bees. For hawks, ospreys, curlews, and cranes, it is the winter and the cold season. These are the periods of passion for such birds. Regarding wild animals and humans—specifically the jackal, rabbit, fox, *Srimara* <note>a type of deer</note>, yak, monkey, cat, mongoose, elephant, bull, lion, tiger, tortoise, and boar—most have their rutting seasons then. Specifically, for the crane, *Srimara*, lion, and tiger, it is the summer. For the deer, elephant, and bull, it is the rainy season. For the bull, *Ruru* <note>a species of swamp deer</note>, buffalo, *Gavaya* <note>gayal or wild ox</note>, *Srimara*, and yak, it is the autumn. For cows, *Gavaya*, and bulls, it is the winter and the cold season.

Now, to demonstrate the individual divisions of the eight directions, which are divided into thirty-two parts, the author says:

->Located within the three divisions between the East and the South-East,<-
->are the Treasurer, the Fire-worker, and the Ascetic, in clockwise order.<-

The "Eastern" is the East direction; "Anala" refers to the South-East <note>presided over by Agni, the fire god</note>. In the space between these two are three equal parts. In these, arranged in order, is the Treasurer (the superintendent of the treasury or storehouse) in the first part. In the second is the Fire-worker (one who lives by fire, such as a goldsmith). In the third is the Ascetic (one endowed with penance). These are arranged "clockwise," meaning in a right-handed direction.

Regarding the others, he says:

->The Artisan, the Beggar, and the Naked Woman are between the South and the South-East;<-
->beyond that are the Elephant-keeper, the Herdsman, and the Religious Devotee.<-

"Yamya" is the South; "Anala" is the South-East. In the three parts in the middle of these two, they are arranged in order: The Artisan (such as painters, scribes, or carpenters) in the first third. The Beggar (a wandering monk) in the second. The Naked Woman in the third. Beyond that, in the three parts between the South and the South-West, is the Elephant-keeper (a man associated with elephants) in the first. In the second is the Herdsman (a man associated with cows). In the third is the Religious Devotee (one devoted to righteousness).

Regarding the others, he says:

->Between the South-West and the West are the Young Woman, Childbirth, and Thieves;<-
->the Vintner, the Bird-catcher, and the Cruel Man are between the North-West and the West.<-

"Nairriti" is the South-West; "Varuni" is the West. In the three parts situated between these two: in the first is the Young Woman. In the second is Childbirth (the act of delivery). In the third are Thieves (robbers). In the three parts situated between the North-West and the West: in the first is the Vintner (one addicted to drinking liquor; some say a distiller). In the second is the Bird-catcher (or a fisherman). In the third is the Cruel Man (one who is violent).

## He speaks regarding others—

->**Next are the poison-destroyer, the cattle-owner, and the juggler;**<-
->**Following those are the wealthy man, the seer, and the garland-maker. ||32||**<-

"Next" means immediately following. In the three subdivisions between the Northwest and the North: in the first is the **poison-destroyer** <note>Sanskrit: *vishaghataka*; one who neutralizes or cures venom</note>. In the second is the **cattle-owner** <note>Sanskrit: *gosvami*; a possessor of cows</note>. In the third is the **juggler** <note>Sanskrit: *kuhakajña*; one skilled in sorcery or sleight of hand</note>. Then, in the three subdivisions between the North and the Northeast: in the first is the **wealthy man**. In the second is the **seer** <note>Sanskrit: *ikshanika*; a fortune-teller or astrologer</note>. In the third is the **garland-maker** <note>Sanskrit: *malakara*; a florist or gatherer of flowers</note>. ||32||

## He speaks regarding others still—

->**The devotee of Vishnu, the wanderer, and the one devoted to guarding horses;**<-
->**Thus, there are thirty-two variations told, including the primary directions. ||33||**<-

In the three subdivisions between the Northeast and the East: in the first is the **devotee of Vishnu** <note>Sanskrit: *vaishnava*</note>. In the second is the **wanderer** <note>Sanskrit: *charaka*; a traveling ascetic or spy</note>. In the third is the one **devoted to guarding horses** <note>Sanskrit: *vajinam rakshane ratah*; a groom or protector of steeds</note>. In this manner, thirty-two variations have been stated or described, together with the eight primary directions previously mentioned. ||33||

## Now he names the lords of the eight directions—

->**The King, Prince, Leader, Messenger, Merchant, Spy, Brahmin,**<-
->**And Superintendent of Elephants are the lords of the East and so on; the Warriors and others belong to the four cardinal points. ||34||**<-

The **King** is in the East. The **Prince** <note>Sanskrit: *kumara*</note> is in the Southeast. The **Leader** <note>Sanskrit: *neta*; a general or commander</note> is in the South. The **Messenger** <note>Sanskrit: *duta*; an envoy</note> is in the Southwest. The **Merchant** <note>Sanskrit: *shresthi*; a guild-leader or wealthy trader</note> is in the West. The **Spy** <note>Sanskrit: *chara*; a secret agent</note> is in the Northwest. The **Brahmin** <note>Sanskrit: *dvija*; literally "twice-born"</note> is in the North. The **Superintendent of Elephants** <note>Sanskrit: *gajadhyaksha*</note> is in the Northeast. These are to be known starting from the East. "The Warriors and others belong to the four cardinal points" means that in the four primary directions, the social classes <note>Sanskrit: *varna*</note> are as follows: **Warriors** <note>Sanskrit: *kshatriya*</note> in the East, **Traders** <note>Sanskrit: *vaishya*</note> in the South, **Laborers** <note>Sanskrit: *shudra*</note> in the West, and **Priests** <note>Sanskrit: *brahmana*</note> in the North. ||34||

## Now he describes the division of the circle—

->**Whether a person is moving or standing still, in whichever direction**<-
->**a bird cries out, an encounter with the person belonging to that direction should be predicted. ||35||**<-

In the second part, he meets one who lives by fire. In the third, an ascetic. This method of interpretation should be applied everywhere. ॥35॥

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 85]

When an animal is peaceful, located in a peaceful direction, facing the sun, possessing a sweet voice, and is of a joyful nature, the sounds they produce are considered auspicious. ॥36॥

### Now he describes the names of those who are auspicious when positioned on the left side of a traveler—

-> <term>Shiva</term> (Jackal), <term>Shyama</term> (Female Shrike), <term>Rala</term> (Cuckoo-like bird), <term>Chuchu</term> (Musk-rat), <term>Pingala</term> (Spotted Owl), <term>Grihagodhika</term> (House Lizard), <-
-> <term>Sukari</term> (Sow), <term>Parapushta</term> (Cuckoo), and those with masculine names are auspicious on the left. ॥37॥

<term>Shiva</term> refers to a female jackal. <term>Shyama</term> is the Potaki bird. <term>Rala</term> is a bird known for its noisy chirping. <term>Chuchu</term> is the musk-rat, a species of mouse. <term>Pingala</term> is a small owl <note>often associated with the "attendant" of an owl</note>. <term>Grihagodhika</term> is the common house lizard. <term>Sukari</term> is the well-known sow. <term>Parapushta</term> is the cuckoo <note>literally "nourished by another," referring to the cuckoo's habit of leaving eggs in other nests</note>. These, and any others with masculine names <note>grammatically masculine in Sanskrit</note>, are auspicious when they move to the left side of the traveler. As it has been said:

-> The musk-rat, the sow, the jackal, the shrike, the Rala bird, the spotted owl, the cuckoo, <-
-> the house lizard, and any birds known by masculine names are beneficial during a journey when on the left. ॥37॥

### Now he describes the names of those who are auspicious when positioned on the right side of a traveler—

-> Those with feminine names, the <term>Bhasa</term>, <term>Bhashaka</term>, <term>Kapi</term>, <term>Shrikarna</term>, <term>Dhikkara</term>, <-
-> <term>Shikhi</term>, <term>Shrikantha</term>, <term>Pippika</term>, <term>Ruru</term>, and <term>Shyena</term> are auspicious on the right. ॥38॥

Those with feminine names <note>grammatically feminine</note> are included here. As the venerable <term>Parashara</term> <note>an ancient sage and authority on astrology and omens</note> says:
> "Among them, the Jackal, Lizard, Lalka, Rajaputri, Bharadvaja, Balaka, Potaki, Sukarika, Pippika, Sutakshapracala, Pindika, Pingala, and others are of feminine designation; the rest have masculine names."

Furthermore, the <term>Bhasa</term> is a bird of prey. <term>Bhashaka</term> is a barking dog or a specific bird. <term>Kapi</term> is a monkey. <term>Shrikarna</term> is a specific bird. <term>Dhikkara</term> is a species of deer. <term>Shyena</term> is a hawk or falcon. These are auspicious when positioned on the right side of the traveler. As it has been said:

-> The hawk, the Ruru deer, the wild cock, the monkey, the Shrikarna, the Dhikkara, the Pippika, and the goat; <-
-> those with feminine names, the peacock, and the elephant are beneficial for travel when situated on the right side. ॥38॥

### Now, extending the rule to other sounds on the left and right, he says—

-> The lion-roar, the clapping of hands, the declaration of a holy day, singing, the sound of a conch or water, <-
-> along with musical instruments and Vedic chanting, are auspicious like the masculine omens; other voices are auspicious like the feminine ones. ॥39॥

<term>Kveda</term> is a sound made with the mouth, popularly known as a "shout of heroes." <term>Asphotita</term> is the sound of clapping; specifically, striking the arm against the chest with the other hand. <term>Punyahashabda</term> is the chanting of "may it be a suspicious day." The <term>Shankha</term> (conch) is well known. <term>Ambu</term> refers to the sound of water. The sounds of all these, along with <term>Saturya</term> (musical instruments) and <term>Adhyayana</term> (the sound of Vedic recitation), are auspicious when on the "masculine" side—meaning they should be on the left side.

Other sounds are auspicious like those of a woman. All other voices and speech are auspicious when they resemble a woman's tone. This means that auspicious words heard from the right side are favorable. As it has been said:

### The sounds of cheering, clapping, <gloss>and</gloss> trumpets, the chanting of "Auspicious Day," and the sound of singing;
### These praised voices are givers of good fortune to men, as are the cries of others heard from the right. || 39 ||

Now, he describes the auspiciousness and inauspiciousness of the musical scales <term>Gramaswara: the fundamental scales of ancient Indian music</term>:

### The Madhyama and Shadja scales, as well as Gandhara, are beautiful;
### The Shadja, Madhyama, Gandhara, and Rishabha notes are beneficial. || 40 ||

In travel or a journey, the two scales <note>original: "Gramau"</note> known as Madhyama <note>the fourth note, F</note> and Shadja <note>the tonic or first note, C</note> are praised and beautiful. The Gandhara <note>the third note, E-flat</note> is also beautiful. The word "iti" here implies "of this kind." That Gandhara note is sung among the gods. Among humans, the notes Shadja, Madhyama, Gandhara, and Rishabha <note>the second note, D</note> are praised. As it has been said:

> The Gandhara, Shadja, and Rishabha, and indeed the Madhyama, are the notes that bring good fortune during a journey, and not the remaining ones.
> The two scales named Madhyama and Shadja are auspicious, and the gods also desire the music of the Gandhara scale as a blessing. || 40 ||

Now he describes other auspicious and inauspicious omens:

### In their cry, the mention of their name, or their sight, the Bharadvaja, the Goat, and the Peacock
### Are blessed; so too are the Mongoose and the Blue Jay. The Lizard is a giver of sin (misfortune) if seen in front. || 41 ||

The Bharadvaja is a specific bird, commonly known as the Skylark <note>original: "Lata"</note>. The "Aja" is a goat. The "Barhi" is a peacock. All of these are blessed and auspicious through their cry (sound), the mention of their name, or by being seen. The Mongoose and the Blue Jay <note>original: "Chasha"</note>—the mongoose is a creature and the blue jay is a specific bird—these two are also blessed in terms of their cry, mention, and sight. The "Sarata" is a creature, a type of bird <note>or reptile</note>; some say it is the Chameleon <note>original: "Krikalasa"</note>. If it is in front <note>ahead of the traveler</note>, it gives "sin," meaning an undesirable result. || 41 ||

He says something further:

### For the Hedgehog, Snake, Hare, Boar, and Monitor Lizard, the mention of their name is auspicious;
### Their cry and their sight are not desired. The opposite is true for the Monkey and the Bear. || 42 ||

The "Jahaka" is a creature <note>Hedgehog or Porcupine</note>. "Ahi" is a snake. "Shasha" is a hare. "Kroda" is a boar. "Godha" is a specific creature, the Monitor Lizard. The "Kirtana" or speaking the names of these animals is auspicious. However, the "Ruta" (sound/cry) and "Sandarshana" (viewing/seeing) of these same animals is not desired or auspicious. "The opposite for the Monkey and the Bear": the "Vanara" is a monkey and the "Riksha" is a bear. For these two, the rule is reversed. This means that their cry and their sight are desired (auspicious), but the mention of their names is not. As it has been said—

The skylark, the goat, the blue jay, and the mongoose are auspicious when their names are recited, when they are seen, or when they cry out. A lizard is never seen for one's welfare <note>original: "sarato" - referring to the common garden lizard, often considered a bad omen in this context</note>. The monitor lizard, the boar, the porcupine, the snake, and the rabbit are sinful (inauspicious) both to hear and to see. The bear and the monkey tribes are blessed when their names are recited, but the opposite is true if they are actually encountered. Thus it is said. || 42 ||

### He says something further—

**An odd number of deer, mongooses, and birds are auspicious when moving from left to right. The Sage Bhrigu says the blue jay and the mongoose are auspicious on the left side during the afternoon.** || 43 ||

"Deer" refers to forest animals. "With mongooses and birds" refers to those specific creatures. These should be "odd" in number—one, three, five, seven, nine, and so on. They are "auspicious when moving from left to right" <note>original: "pradakshinam" - a clockwise motion or moving from the left side of the observer to the right</note>. When they come from the left side, pass in front, and go to the right side, that is "pradakshina" or "savya" (right-ward). The opposite of this—moving from the right side to the left—is "apasavya" (left-ward). All of this should be understood through <term>Shakuna</term> <note>The science of omens, particularly those involving birds and animals</note>. As the Teacher himself is the authority:

> ->Situated in the three divisions between the East and South-East directions,<-
> ->the treasurer, the fire-worker, and the ascetic are auspicious when moving clockwise.<-

"The blue jay and the mongoose on the left" means that the blue jay, along with the mongoose, is blessed when positioned on the left side. "Bhrigu says from the afternoon" means the Sage named Bhrigu has stated that these two are blessed on the left side specifically from the afternoon onwards, not in the forenoon. As Bhrigu says:

> ->The blue jay and the mongoose are givers of good fortune on the left in the afternoon.<-

For the dog and the jackal, the result is praised in the opposite manner. The blue jay and the mongoose on the left are auspicious after midday. || 43 ||

### Now he speaks of others as well—

**The Chikkara, the Kutapuri, and the Pirili are auspicious on the right during the day. Tusked animals and hole-dwellers are always auspicious when on the left.** || 44 ||

The "Chikkara" is a type of jackal, the "Kutapuri" is a female crane <note>original: "karayika"</note>, and the "Pirili" is a specific type of bird; these are auspicious on the right side during the day. "Tusked animals" include creatures like boars. Those who sleep in holes are "hole-dwellers," such as porcupines and mongooses. Tusked animals along with hole-dwellers are auspicious and beautiful when "apasavya" (moving to the left). || 44 ||

# Chapter on Omens

### Now, he describes the auspicious and inauspicious nature of omens according to the directions—

**A horse and white objects are best in the East; a corpse and meat in the South.**
**A young maiden and curd in the West; a cow, a Brahmin, and holy men in the North. ||45||**

A horse <note>original: "haya"</note> refers to the animal. "White" <note>original: "sita"</note> refers to any object that is white in color. These are best or auspicious in the East <note>original: "prācyāṃ"</note> for one who is traveling. A corpse <note>original: "śava"</note> is a dead person. Meat <note>original: "māṃsa"</note> is flesh. These two are auspicious in the South. A maiden <note>original: "kanyakā"</note> is an unmarried girl. Curd <note>original: "dadhi"</note> is a preparation of milk. These two are auspicious in the West. A cow <note>original: "gau"</note> is well-known. A Brahmin <note>original: "vipra"</note> is a member of the priestly class. A holy man <note>original: "sādhu"</note> is a virtuous person. These are auspicious in the North.

It is also said:
> White objects and a horse in the East; a corpse with meat in the South;
> A maiden and curd are highly praised in the West; and a cow, a Brahmin, and holy men in the North. ||45||

### Now, he describes the inauspicious ones—

**A net-carrier and a dog-handler are not desired in the East; a weapon-bearer and a killer in the South.**
**Liquor and a eunuch in the West; and a villain, a seat, and a plow in the North. ||46||**

A net-carrier <note>original: "jālika"</note> is well-known; a net is made of woven threads in which birds are caught. One who moves with a net or moves with a dog <note>original: "jāla-śva-caraṇau"</note>—these two are not desired or are inauspicious in the East. A weapon <note>original: "śastra"</note> refers to any instrument of harm. A killer <note>original: "ghātaka"</note> is an oppressor. These two are not auspicious in the South. Liquor <note>original: "āsava"</note> is a specific type of drink. A eunuch <note>original: "ṣaṇḍha"</note> is a neuter person. These two are not auspicious in the West. A villain <note>original: "khala"</note> is a wicked person. A seat <note>original: "āsana"</note> is well-known, such as a couch or chair. A plow <note>original: "hala"</note> is the farming implement. These are not auspicious in the North.

It is also said:
> A net-maker and a dog-handler are not auspicious in the East; a killer and a weapon-bearer in the direction of Yama <note>The South</note>.
> A eunuch and a liquor-bearer in the West; along with a seat, a plow, and villains in the North. ||46||

### Now, he describes the specific application of omens in activities—

**In work, meetings, and battles; in entering a place or searching for the lost;**
**The omens should be taken as the reverse of travel; the distinction will be explained here. ||47||**

"Work" <note>original: "karma"</note> refers to whatever is being done. "Meeting" <note>original: "saṅgama"</note> is coming together with someone like a learned person. "Battle" <note>original: "yuddha"</note> is war. In these, as well as in "entering" <note>original: "praveśa"</note> such as entering a house, and in "searching for the lost" <note>original: "naṣṭa-mārgaṇa"</note> meaning seeking a lost or stolen object—in all these, the omens should be taken as the reverse of travel <note>original: "yāna-vyasta-gatā"</note>. This means that whatever omens were stated as auspicious for a journey <note>traveling away</note>, their opposites are to be taken for these specific activities. This is what is meant: those which are praised as being on the right during a journey are here...

<summary>This page details which omens are auspicious or inauspicious based on the cardinal direction they appear in, and notes that the interpretation of omens reverses when one is returning or searching rather than starting a journey.</summary>
<keywords>omens, directions, travel, Brahmin, auspicious signs, inauspicious signs, divination, Varahamihira</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on omens (shakuna) from the Brihat Samhita, specifically focusing on how the interpretation of directions and specific animals changes depending on whether one is departing on a journey or engaging in stationary activities.</meta>

<page-num>912</page-num>
# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 85]

On the left. In a journey, those on the left are here <note>referring to stationary activities like entering a house or meeting a king</note> on the right. In a journey, those who are in front are here behind. In a journey, those who are behind are here in front. In the cardinal directions as well, the reversals should be understood in the same way. Therefore, those who are in the eastern direction during a journey are here in the western. Those in the western are in the eastern. Those in the southern are in the northern. Those in the northern are in the southern. In this matter, the specific distinction regarding "actions and names" <term>Karma-samjna: a technical category in divination referring to specific tasks like finding lost objects</term> will be explained. As it has been said:

->In finding lost objects, seeing someone, reunions, combat, entering a house, and visiting kings and lords,<-
->. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . [omens] are auspicious when interpreted by the reverse method of a journey. Thus [it is said]. || 47 ||<-

### Now, he states a specific rule regarding this:

->**The gazelle, the ruru-deer, and the monkey should be taken as they are in a journey during the day.**<-
->**In the first part of the day, the blue jay, the vanjula bird, and the wild cock [should be so taken]. || 48 ||**<-
->**In the latter part of the night, the night-bird, the owl, and the spotted owlet [are taken as in a journey].**<-
->**All of these are to be taken in reverse for caravans of women. || 49 ||**<-

"During the day as in a journey" means: in various actions during the day, the gazelle <note>original: kuranga</note>, the ruru-deer <note>a specific species of swamp deer</note>, and the monkey <note>original: vanara</note>—these should be taken as they are in a journey. Just as they are interpreted during a departure, so too here. In the first part of the day, the blue jay <note>original: casha</note>, the vanjula bird, and the cock—all these birds should be taken as they are in a journey. || 48 ||

"Night" <note>original: sharvari</note> refers to the nighttime; in its latter or final part, the night-bird <note>naptrika</note>, the owl, and the spotted owlet <note>pingala</note>—all these are birds. The spotted owlet is the female companion of the owl; these should be taken as they are in a journey. For "caravans of women"—meaning groups consisting only of women—all these [omens] are to be taken in reverse. Whether in a journey or in "actions and names," they are always to be taken as the opposite. || 49 ||

### He says another thing:

->**In visiting a king, the entry should be taken as a journey.**<-
->**In entering mountains and forests, and in the fording of rivers, || 50 ||**<-
->**Those [omens] moving on the left and right are praised, as are those in front and behind.**<-

In the "visiting of a king" means seeing the monarch. Even though this involves "entering" the royal palace, it should be interpreted as a "journey" <note>meaning the standard rules for departure apply, rather than the reversed rules for stationary entry</note>. Thus, even if it is an entry, it is treated as a journey. As it is said:
->Some have gone [by the rule of] travel when visiting kings . . . . . so it is said.<-
In "entering a mountain," "entering a forest" or wilderness, and in the "fording of rivers" or crossing streams. || 50 ||

<summary>This page explains the "Rule of Reversal" in omens, where directions that are auspicious for a journey become inauspicious for stationary activities like entering a home, except for specific animals and circumstances like visiting a king.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on omens (shakuna) specifically regarding the positioning of birds or animals during a journey or when entering a location.</meta>

<page-num>913</page-num>
<header>[Chapter 85] Chapter on Omens 913</header>

The two omens that are considered auspicious when appearing on the left and right during a journey are likewise auspicious when appearing in front and behind when entering a place. Those which are auspicious on the left during a journey are here considered auspicious in the front; those which are auspicious on the right during a journey are here considered auspicious behind.

### Now he speaks regarding others—

->**Two omens that are "blazing in action" <note>original: "kriya-dipta"; refers to birds showing agitated or aggressive behavior</note> signify destruction for the traveler; these are known as the "Bolt" <note>original: "parigha"; literally a gate-bar or obstacle</note> configuration. (51)**<-
->**However, if those same two are positioned in their respective sides and are "tranquil in cry and movement,"**<-
->**then these omens are known as the "Gateway of Omens" and lead to the success of one's purpose. (52)**<-

The definition of "blazing in action" was stated previously: "Blazing in action is determined by gait, position, state, voice, and movement." <note>This refers to verse 15 of this chapter.</note> If two omens are "blazing in action" and are situated as a "Bolt"—meaning they are positioned on both flanks of the traveler—then they lead to the destruction of that traveler. These are the omens designated as the "Bolt." (51)

"Positioned in their respective sides" means they stay where they are. An omen that is auspicious on the right remains there, and one that is auspicious on the left remains on the left. If they are "tranquil in cry and movement"—meaning their sounds and actions are peaceful—then such omens are called the "Gateway" <note>original: "dvara"</note> for auspicious matters; they become the path to the fulfillment of one's goals. (52)

### Now he describes the "Gateway of Omens" according to a different opinion—

->**Some, however, desire the "Gateway of Omens" to be formed by birds of the same species positioned on both sides,**<-
->**provided they possess peaceful movements and cries. (53)**<-

He will describe the characteristics of movement later: "Lunar day, weekday, asterism <note>original: "nakshatra"</note>, solar sign, position, and movement are 'blazing' in successive order." <note>This refers to verse 58 of this chapter.</note> Thus, with peaceful movements and cries, and being of the same species (born of the same womb), some say the "Gateway of Omens" is formed when they are situated on both sides (on both flanks). As Nandi <note>An ancient authority on omens</note> says:

> When birds of the same species are peaceful, tranquil in movement, and established
> in their respective positions, that is considered the "Gateway of Omens." (53)

### He says something further—

->**When one omen permits departure and another forbids it,**<-
->**that is a "Conflict" <note>original: "virodha"</note> which is inauspicious for the traveler; in such a case, the one that is stronger must be accepted. (54)**<-

# On the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 85]

If one bird gives a sign of departure <note>original: "visarjayati" - to release or permit a journey</note> which indicates success, and another bird forbids it, indicating opposition, this is known as "Opposition" for the traveler and is inauspicious. Alternatively, between these two, the one that is significantly stronger should be accepted as the valid omen. The criteria for strength have been stated previously: "**Speed, species, age, and position.**" <note>original: "java-jati-vaya-sthanam" - a reference to verse 19 of this chapter</note> ||54||

He says something further:

->**If a bird first acts as an entering sign and then becomes a departing sign,**<-
->**it indicates success with ease; in the case of returning home, the opposite applies.**<- ||55||

If a bird is first "entering" <note>term: Praveshika - a bird moving toward the observer or into a space</note> and subsequently becomes "departing" <note>term: Prasthanika - a bird moving away, signaling a start</note>, it brings about the welfare associated with departure during a journey. In the case of returning <note>literally "entering" back home</note>, the knowledge should be applied in reverse. In such a sequence, that bird indicates the traveler's success will come with ease and without distress. "In the case of returning, the opposite": when the traveler has finished the journey and is entering their own home, the reverse of what was said should be taken. That is, if it is first a departing sign and then an entering sign, it then indicates success with ease. ||55||

Now he says something else:

->**If the same bird that first permitted the departure then obstructs it,**<-
->**it foretells the traveler's death at the hands of an enemy, or a riot, or disease.**<- ||56||

If a bird first permits a journey by performing an auspicious movement, and then that same bird obstructs or forbids the journey, it foretells the death of the traveler caused by an enemy. Alternatively, it predicts a riot <note>original: "damaram" - a chaotic conflict or tumult</note> or indeed a disease. ||56||

Now he says something else:

->**Birds on the left that are "blazing" are announcers of fear.**<-
->**A "blazing" bird at the start of a task causes fear within a year.**<- ||57||

Birds that are on the left <note>original: "apasavya" - counter-clockwise or inauspicious side</note> and are situated in a "blazing" direction <note>term: Dipta - a direction facing the sun or otherwise agitated</note> announce or indicate fear. If a bird is "blazing" at the commencement of a task, it causes fear regarding that very task within the span of a year. ||57||

# Chapter on Omens
<meta>[Chapter 85]</meta>
<meta>Digitized by eGangotri. CCO. Vasishtha Tripathi Collection.</meta>

Now, the author describes the characteristics and results of omens that are "blazing" <note>Sanskrit: *dipta*; refers to an omen occurring in an unfavorable direction, time, or manner</note> through action and other factors:

->**Blazing by lunar day, wind, sun, asterism, place, and action, respectively,**<-
->**They bring fear to wealth, the army, strength, the body, loved ones, and work. ||58||**<-

Blazing by lunar day (*tithi*). Blazing by wind (*vayu*). Blazing by the sun (*arka*). Blazing by asterism (*nakshatra*). Blazing by place (*sthana*). Blazing by action (*cheshta*). The characteristics of these have been explained previously. If one desires to perform an action, such "blazing" omens bring fear to wealth, the army, strength, the body, loved ones, and work in that specific order. For example: a bird blazing by the lunar day causes fear regarding wealth. One blazing by the wind affects the army. One blazing by the sun affects strength. One blazing by the asterism affects the "limbs" or parts of the body. One blazing by place affects a desired object or a loved one. One blazing by action affects the work or undertaking itself. ||58||

He says something further:

->**When omens are blazing by the sound of clouds, there is fear from the wind.**<-
->**Blazing at both twilights, they bring fear arising from weapons. ||59||**<-

*Jimuta* means a cloud. When birds are "blazing" <note>stimulated into an ill-omened state</note> by the sound of clouds (thunder), there is fear from wind or storms. Birds that are blazing during both twilights—at sunrise and sunset—produce fear arising from weapons or armed conflict. ||59||

Now, he says something else:

->**On a funeral pyre, hair, or a skull, they grant death, imprisonment, and slaughter.**<-
->**Stationed on thorny trees, wood, or ashes, they grant quarrels, fatigue, and sorrow. ||60||**<-

->**Stationed on hollow objects or stones, blazing omens cause**<-
->**Failure or fear; however, if they are "quiet," their fruit is negligible. ||61||**<-

Regarding "funeral pyre, hair, and skull": A bird near a funeral pyre (*chiti*) grants death. Situated on hair (*kesha*) from a head, it grants imprisonment (*bandha*). Situated on a skull (*kapala*) or a piece of bone, it grants slaughter or death. Likewise, a bird situated on a thorny tree grants quarrels. Situated on wood, it grants fatigue or distress. Situated on ashes, it grants sorrow. ||60||

Likewise, those stationed on hollow objects or stones cause failure or fear. Situated on a "worthless" or hollow (*nihsara*) object, it causes the failure of tasks. Situated on a stone (*ashman*), it causes fear. Regarding the phrase "blazing omens do this": the effects mentioned above (regarding the pyre, hair, skull, etc.) apply when the birds are in a "blazing" state. If they are "quiet" (*shanta*) <note>occurring in a favorable direction or manner</note>, then their fruit is "repressible" (*yapya*), meaning the result is very slight or negligible. ||61||

<term>Dipta</term>: "Blazing"; a technical term for an omen occurring under unfavorable conditions (e.g., facing the sun or a harsh wind).
<term>Shanta</term>: "Quiet" or "Pacified"; the opposite of blazing, indicating a favorable or neutral omen.
<term>Tithi/Nakshatra</term>: The lunar day and the lunar mansion (star system) used in Vedic timekeeping.
</vocab>

### He states another point—

**The one who excretes and the one who feeds are known to bring failure and success respectively.**
**If a bird cries from its spot and then flies away, it indicates a journey; otherwise, it indicates an arrival. ||62||**

The two birds—the one excreting and the one feeding—should be understood to grant failure and success in that order. "Excreting" <note>original: nirhāra</note> refers to the voiding of feces. A bird that excretes causes the failure of tasks. A bird that is feeding <note>original: āhāra</note> brings about the successful completion of one's goals. Regarding "crying from its spot": if a bird makes a sound while staying in its place and then "goes" (departs), then it "praises" (predicts) a journey or departure. "Otherwise" (the opposite) indicates an arrival. This is what is meant: if a bird is heard and then comes to a spot and sits down, it predicts the arrival of someone. ||62||

---

### Now he states another point—

**There is a quarrel when the sounds are "blazing," and war when the locations are "blazing."**
**Making a high-pitched sound first and then a low one later causes harm. ||63||**

When birds have "blazing" <note>In Sanskrit divination, "dipta" or blazing refers to sounds or directions associated with ill-fortune, often linked to the sun's position or harsh tones.</note> voices, a quarrel occurs. When they are situated in "blazing" spots, there is war. If a bird first makes a loud, high-pitched sound and afterward makes a low or faint sound, it "causes harm" (brings misfortune). ||63||

---

### He states another point—

**Crying in one spot while "blazing," it brings the destruction of a village within seven days;**
**For a city, a region, or a king, the destruction comes after a season, a half-year, or a year respectively. ||64||**

If a "blazing" bird stays in a single spot crying or screaming for an entire day, then after seven days it causes the "village-killing" (destruction of the village). Not only that, but it also causes the destruction of cities, regions, and kings after a season, a half-year, or a year. In a city <note>original: pura</note>, crying in one spot causes destruction in a "season" (two months). Likewise, it causes the destruction of a "region" <note>original: desha</note> in half a half-year <note>The commentary clarifies this as three months</note>. It causes the destruction of a "ruler" (king) after a "year." The phrase "crying in one spot" applies to all these cases. ||64||

---

### He states another point—

**All those who eat the flesh of their own kind are creators of famine,**
**with the exception of snakes, mice, cats, and fish. ||65||**

All birds (or omens) that are "eaters of the flesh of their own kind"—meaning they eat the meat of their own species—create a famine. However, the snake (serpent), the mouse (rat), the cat, and the "broad-scaled" (fish) [are excluded from this rule]...

# Chapter 85: The Chapter on Omens
<page-num>917</page-num>

The cat and the broad-scaled fish <note>original: "bidala" and "prithuloma matsya"</note>. Excluding these, the eating of flesh by any other [herbivorous] creatures is a natural trait for some, but for others, it is a portent of calamity <term>utpata: a supernatural or unnatural event signaling future misfortune</term>. As it has been said:

> "Except for snakes, mice, cats, and fish, if animals eat the flesh of their own kind, or if they engage in mating with other species... [it forebodes evil]." (Verse 65)

He says further:

->Mating with other species brings destruction to the land,<-
->Except for the birth of the mule and the unnatural acts of men.<- (Verse 66)

Engaging in mating with other species <note>original: "parayonishu"</note> causes the destruction of the country. However, "except for the birth of the mule" <note>original: "vesarotpatti"</note> means this rule does not apply to the mule's birth, as it is known that a donkey mates with a mare to produce one. Likewise, it excludes the "unnatural acts of men," where men might [sinfully] approach mares or other animals. These are excluded because they are known occurrences, not sudden portents. (Verse 66)

He says further:

->Fear of imprisonment, injury, or death arises from birds approaching the feet, thighs, or head;<-
->While those eating grass, water, flesh, or grain indicate faults, rain, wounds, or reunions.<- (Verse 67)

When birds approach the feet, thighs, or head respectively, there will be fear of imprisonment, injury, or death. When a bird <term>shakuna: specifically an omen-bearing bird</term> comes near the feet, it causes imprisonment. If it comes near the thigh region, it causes injury or a blow. If it goes to the head, it causes fear [of death]. Regarding "eating grass, water, flesh, or grain": a bird that eats young grass <note>original: "shashpa"</note> causes a fault or harm to men. A bird that drinks water indicates rain. A meat-eating bird indicates a wound <note>original: "kshata"</note> or bodily injury. A grain-eating bird indicates a "grasping" <note>original: "graham"</note> or a reunion with some relative. (Verse 67)

Now, he describes the characteristics of arriving strangers through the instruction of omens:

->Through those tainted by cruel planets and the behavior of chief kings,<-
->The arrival of such men occurs from the 'Blazing' directions after a long time.<- (Verse 68)

When a bird is situated in the eight directions, such as the "Blazing" <note>original: "dipta" - a technical term for a direction facing the sun or otherwise agitated</note> direction, the arrival of men characterized by "cruel" traits occurs. A bird situated in the "Blazing" direction indicates the arrival of a man associated with cruelty or violence. A bird in the "Smoldering" <note>original: "dhumita"</note> direction indicates the arrival of a man with a harsh staff [of punishment]. Following that, a bird in the "Calm" <note>original: "shanta"</note> direction...

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 85]

...[the bird] indicates the arrival of a person accompanied by someone with a specific fault. After that, [if in a different state], one accompanied by a wicked person. After that, one accompanied by a person of importance. After that, one accompanied by a king. After that, one accompanied by a religious student <note>original: "shravaka," often referring to a Jain or Buddhist lay follower or a dedicated listener</note>. After that, a bird situated in the "charred" <note>original: "angarita," referring to a direction that has been previously "burned" by the sun's passage</note> direction indicates the arrival of a person accompanied by someone after a very long time. Some explain it this way. Others prefer four specific states of the directions: Blazing, Smoldering, Peaceful, and Charred. 

In that system:
* If the bird is in a **Blazing** direction: Arrival with a cruel person.
* If in a **Smoldering** direction: Arrival with one who is corrupted by intense or fierce faults.
* If in a **Peaceful** direction: Arrival with an important person or a king who tells stories of the deeds of ancient kings like Nahusha <note>Nahusha was a legendary king who briefly ruled heaven but fell due to pride</note>.
* If in a **Charred** direction: Arrival with someone after a long time. 

This latter explanation is considered superior. ||68||

->Now he describes how to know if the person arriving possesses wealth or not:<-

## If the bird is strong and possesses "substance," the arrival will be of one with wealth.
## If it is radiant but looks downward, even if it appears gentle, it brings a harsh report. ||69||

If the bird is "with substance" <note>original: "sadravya," meaning it is carrying food or nesting material in its beak</note> and is strong, then the arrival will be of a person with wealth. The person arriving that day will have goods; otherwise, they come empty-handed. Furthermore, if the bird is radiant but is "looking downward" <note>original: "vinataprekshi"</note>, then even if it is a "gentle" <note>auspicious</note> bird, it performs a "harsh report." This means the person who arrives with wealth will actually cause trouble or bring bad news. ||69||

->He says another thing:<-

## A "blazing" bird situated in an intermediate direction, if answered by another bird on the left,
## Foretells the "seizing" of a woman from the class associated with that direction. ||70||

If a bird is in an intermediate direction <note>e.g., Northeast, Southwest</note> and is "blazing" <note>facing the sun</note>, and it is answered by the cry of another bird situated on the left side, it foretells the "seizing" or union with a woman. This woman comes from the "origin" <note>original: "yoni," referring to caste or social class</note> associated with that specific direction. It means a man will provide that woman, or there will be a union with a woman whose origin is declared to be in that intermediate direction. ||70||

->He says another thing:<-

## A "peaceful" bird, if answered by one in the fifth "blazing" position, brings victory,
## Or causes the arrival of a man from that direction; the opposite occurs if the conditions are reversed. ||71||

# Chapter on Omens (Shakuna)

Page 199
<meta>Chapter 85</meta>

When a "peaceful" <note>original: *shanta*; refers to a bird in a favorable direction or state</note> omen-bird is called out to by another bird situated in the fifth "blazing" <note>original: *dipta*; refers to an unfavorable or agitated direction</note> quarter, and that bird is facing the observer while making its sound, it brings victory. Alternatively, it indicates the arrival of a man from that specific direction. The opposite of this configuration brings misfortune; that is, if a "blazing" bird is called out to by one in the fifth "peaceful" position, it causes harm or inauspicious results.

->He further says:<-

> **A bird in the middle, flanked by those on the left and right, foretells fear for oneself and one's enemies respectively. If all of these cry out simultaneously, they foretell death.**

A bird situated in the middle position, when responded to by birds on the left and right, speaks of fear for oneself and others in that order. Specifically, if the middle bird is called by one on the left, it foretells fear from one's own kinsmen or people. If the same middle bird is called by one on the right <note>original: *savya*; here meaning the right side</note>, it foretells fear from enemies. If it is called by both at once, it foretells fear from both sides. If all three cry out with equal intensity at the same moment, they proclaim death.

->He further says:<-

> **From the top, middle, or root of a tree, the arrival of those on elephants, horses, or chariots is predicted. From long objects, lotuses, or lopped trees, the arrival of men, boats, or palanquins is predicted.**

A bird perched at the top of a tree indicates the arrival of a man mounted on an elephant. Situated in the middle of the tree, it indicates one on horseback. At the root of the tree, it indicates a traveler in a chariot. If the bird is on a long or tall object, it indicates a man being carried by men <note>perhaps a porter or litter</note>. If on a lotus or water-born plant, it indicates the arrival of a boat. If on a tree with a severed top <note>original: *mushitagra*</note>, it indicates the arrival of a palanquin or a litter-bearer.

->And he says further:<-

> **On a cart or on high ground, or in the shade, one comes with a parasol. Within one, three, five, or seven days, from the East and other directions or the intervals between.**

If the bird is on a cart or situated on high ground like a mountain, someone arrives by vehicle. If the bird is in the shade, the person arrives with a parasol <note>original: *chatra*; a symbol of status or royalty</note>. Regarding the timing of these auspicious or inauspicious omens or the arrival of travelers: it occurs within one, three, five, or seven days, depending on whether they are in the cardinal directions (East, etc.) or the intermediate directions...

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 85]

It happens thus: If an omen <note>shakuna: a sign or bird-call used for divination</note> indicating good or bad results—such as someone’s arrival or a meeting with someone—is situated in the East, the result occurs within one single day. Similarly, in the South, it occurs in three days. In the West, in five days. In the North, in seven days. And in the intermediate directions <note>vidik: the corners such as Southeast, Northwest, etc.</note>, the word "and" implies the same pattern. Therefore, in the Southeast, it occurs in one day; in the Southwest, in three days; in the Northwest, in five days; and in the Northeast, in seven days. ||74||

Now, to provide specific knowledge on this matter, he says:

->**The Lord of the Gods, the Fire-bearer, Yama, Nirriti, Varuna, Pavana, Indu, and Shankara are, in order,**<-
->**the lords of the directions starting from the East. The cardinal directions are male; the intermediate directions are female.**<- ||75||

The deities starting with the Lord of the Gods are the masters or owners of the directions starting from the East. The Lord of the Gods is Indra; he is the lord of the Eastern direction. The Fire-bearer is Agni, the lord of the Southeast. Yama, the Lord of the Ancestors, is in the South. Nirriti, the lord of the demons, is in the Southwest. Varuna, the Lord of the Waters, is in the West. Pavana is Vayu (the Wind), in the Northwest. Indu is the Moon, in the North. Shankara is Rudra (Shiva), in the Northeast. 

The application of this is: the name of a person who arrives or whom one meets that day may be a synonym of Indra and the other gods; or they may be a devotee of that specific deity. In cases of theft or loss, it indicates the location of the thief or the goods. In matters of success or failure, it indicates the place. In divination regarding a person's thoughts, it shows what is on their mind. In the case of a sick person, peace is attained by worshipping that specific deity, and so on. 

"The cardinal directions are male; the intermediate directions are female." The four cardinal directions starting from the East represent men. The four intermediate directions represent women. As Parashara <note>An ancient sage and authority on astrology</note> says:

> The directions starting from the North are assigned to the castes, beginning with the Brahmins.
> The intermediate directions starting from the Northeast are declared to belong to women.

The application is: if the omen or the petitioner is situated in a cardinal direction, the concern or the birth relates to a male. Likewise, in the intermediate directions, the concern relates to a female birth. In cases of theft or loss, this identifies the thief. Their arrival or meeting happens accordingly. ||75||

Now, he speaks of the knowledge of writing materials:

->**Grass, palm-leaf, bamboo-strip, cloth, birch-bark, reed, hide, and silk-strip are the writings.**<-
->**These effects are to be applied within the circle of directions divided into thirty-two parts.**<- ||76||

By the rule previously established—that the space between the directions of Indra (East) and Agni (Southeast) is divided into three parts—the circle of directions is shown divided into thirty-two distinct segments. In those segments, the various good and bad effects...

# [Chapter 85] The Chapter on Omens
<page-num>921</page-num>

Omens have been described, and their effects in the world are now being explained. As it will be stated later: <note>original: "नैर्ऋत्यां स्त्रीलाभस्तुरगालङ्कारदूतलेखाप्तिः"</note> "In the Southwest, there is the gain of a woman, ornaments for horses, and the receipt of a messenger's letter." In that context, the method of identifying the letter is as follows: If the omen occurs in the East, the letter is written on a tree <note>specifically on the bark or a leaf</note>. Similarly, in the Southeast, it is on a palm leaf. In the South, it is on a fragment <note>a piece of material of no specific value</note>. In the Southwest, it is on cloth. In the West, it is on an aquatic product such as a lotus leaf. In the Northwest, it is on a reed or stalk. In the North, it is on leather. In the Northeast, it is on a tablet or fine silk <note>the term 'Patta' refers to well-known materials like silk or decorative bands</note>. ||76||

->Now he describes other locations of encounter:<-

->**Exercise, fire, chirping, quarreling, water, fetters, chanting, and the sound of cows;**<-
->**The colors are red, yellow, black, and white; the corners are mixed. ||77||**<-

When an omen is situated in the East and indicates a favorable result, in what location will that result be obtained? In a place of exercise or combat. Similarly, in the Southeast, in a place of fire or near a flame. In the South, where a "chirping" or some sound is heard. In the Southwest, where there is a quarrel. In the West, where there is water. In the Northwest, where there are fetters or places of confinement. In the North, where <term>Mantra</term> <note>sacred Vedic hymns</note> are being recited. In the Northeast, where there are cows or the sound of their lowing. In these specified places, a favorable omen indicates the arrival of a task or a meeting with someone. 

Regarding the colors: If a color is mentioned, Red belongs to the East. Yellow belongs to the South. Black belongs to the West. White belongs to the North. The "corners" <note>intermediate directions</note> are mixed: in the Southeast, it is reddish-yellow; in the Southwest, yellowish-black; in the Northwest, blackish-white; and in the Northeast, whitish-red. The purpose of this is: if an omen predicts the arrival of an object, this identifies the color of that object. It is used to identify the color of stolen or lost property, the color of garments in "garment-divination," or to determine the specific deity to whom one should show devotion based on their associated color. ||77||

->Now he speaks to indicate the location when an omen is favorable:<-

->**The signs are a banner, something burnt, a cemetery,**<-
->**A cave, water, a mountain, a sacrifice, and a station;**<-
->**In these, one should find encounters or fears,**<-
->**Or other locations according to the alternatives. ||78||**<-

In the East, a banner is the identifying mark. In the Southeast, something burnt by fire. Next, in the South, a cemetery or "forest of the ancestors." In the Southwest, a cave or cavern. In the West...

Water refers to liquid. In the Northwest, a mountain or hill. In the North, a sacrifice or ritual offering. In the Northeast, a loud sound or a cave. In these specific locations, one should know or understand the fears associated with encounters. If the omen is auspicious, it indicates a meeting with someone. As it will be stated later:

> "In the peaceful Eastern direction, a bird crying out indicates a meeting with a king." <note>original: 'ऐन्द्यां दिशि शान्तायां विरुवन्नृपसंश्रितमग्रं वक्ति'</note>

Regarding these omens, he will also describe fear:

> "These results are stated for the peaceful directions; I shall now describe the 'blazing' <term>dipta: directions associated with ill omens or harsh solar influence</term> ones. In the East, there is fear from the ruler and also a gathering of enemies." <note>original: 'शान्तासु दिक्षु फलमिदमुक्तं दीप्तास्ततोऽभिधास्यामि । ऐन्द्यां भयं नरेन्द्रात् समागमश्चापि शत्रूणाम्'</note>

Or other variations of locations. Other tasks or outcomes should be imagined or assigned according to the specific place. This is what is meant: auspicious events indicated by good omens occur only in auspicious places. Inauspicious events occur in inauspicious places. ||78||

He says something further:

->Variations of women: a large woman, a young maiden,<-
->one with a missing limb, one who smells foul, one in blue clothing,<-
->a wicked woman, a very tall woman, and a widow; these<-
->are the indicators for concerns regarding meetings. ||79||<-

In the East, the variation of women is a "large" woman, meaning one with a large body. In the Southeast, a young maiden or girl. In the South, one with a missing limb <gloss>body part</gloss>. In the Southwest, one who smells foul or has a bad odor. The word "then" implies sequence. In the West, one wearing blue clothes. In the Northwest, a "wicked woman" or a contemptible female. In the North, one who is very tall. In the Northeast, a widow or a woman whose husband has passed away. Some explain it this way. Others prefer the four intermediate directions, as it is said: "Women belong to the intermediate directions." Thus, in the Northeast: the large woman and the maiden. In the Southeast: the one with a missing limb and the foul-smelling one. In the Southwest: the one in blue and the wicked woman. In the Northwest: the tall woman and the widow. The purpose: these women serve as indicators for concerns regarding meetings. Through them, in the directions starting from the East, they produce or make known the thoughts regarding a meeting or encounter. In cases of theft or lost items, these same figures are the indicators. ||79||

> The Banyan, the Red-tree, the Lodh, and the hollow bamboo;

At the time of an inquiry <note>Prishcha: a formal question posed to an astrologer or augur</note>, if the omen <note>Shakuna: usually a bird or animal acting as a sign</note> or the inquirer is situated in the **East**, the inquiry should be declared as relating to silver. Likewise, in the **Southeast**, it relates to gold. In the **South**, it concerns a patient afflicted by disease. In the **Southwest**, it concerns a beautiful woman. In the **West**, it concerns a goat or ram. In the **Northwest**, it concerns a vehicle such as a horse, or a journey. In the **North**, it concerns a sacrifice <note>Makha: a Vedic ritual or Yajna</note>. In the **Northeast**, the inquiry should be declared as relating to a cow-pen or a fenced enclosure.

Similarly, the trees are assigned: the Banyan tree is in the **East**. The "Red-tree" <note>original: "Raktataru", likely the Saffron or Red Sandalwood</note> is in the **Southeast**. The Lodh tree is in the **South**. The hollow bamboo <note>original: "Kichaka"</note> is in the **Southwest**. The Mango tree is in the **West**. The Khadir <note>Acacia</note> is in the **Northwest**. The Bael tree is in the **North**. The Arjun tree is in the **Northeast**. Alternatively, "Naga" refers to a mountain and the Arjun tree. Or, all these trees from the Banyan onwards are called "Naga" <note>literally "that which does not move"</note> because of their stability. 

The application is as follows: if a favorable omen is situated in these directions (East, etc.), one gains silver and the other items mentioned; if the omen is unfavorable, there is loss. It also indicates union or separation with someone, or the identification of a thief's location. ||80||
