# Now, the Inner Circle of Omens is explained.

First, he describes the results when an omen is situated in the "peaceful" <note>Shanta: directions not facing the sun or wind, considered auspicious</note> quarters of the compass circle, which is divided into thirty-two parts:

> A bird crying in the peaceful Eastern direction announces the arrival of someone dependent on the King.
> The omen also tells of receiving honor, and the acquisition of jewels, gems, and wealth. ||1||

In the **East**, in a peaceful quarter, a bird crying or calling announces the arrival of one who is supported by the King. Likewise, it tells of the gain of honor and the acquisition of objects such as primary gems and other wealth like gold. If the omen is of a "good" species, the result is full; if "middling," the result is middling; if "inauspicious," then only a little good occurs. This is how everything should be understood. ||1||

-> Now he says another: <-

> In the next division, there will be the arrival of gold and the fulfillment of desired objects.
> In the third division, there will be the arrival of weapons, wealth, and betel nuts. ||2||

Eight gates are divided in each direction, and thus the circle of directions is also divided; the following is the result of that. The camel and the cow. The "player" is one who causes others to play <note>likely a performer or animal trainer</note>. When an omen-bird is situated in the spoke belonging to the North-Western direction, there is the sight of a "burden-carrier," meaning a porter. The "Taksha" is a carpenter. The "Bhikhshuka" is a wandering ascetic. There is a sighting of these people. There is the acquisition of "Tilaka" flowers—the Tilaka is a specific type of tree—and its blossoms. There is also the acquisition of "Punnaga" flowers, which are the blossoms of the Punnaga tree, together with "Naga" flowers <note>original: "Nagakusuma," likely the Mesua ferrea or Cobra Saffron</note>. ||24||

He says another thing:

->In the spoke located in the Northern direction, the bird indicates the gain of wealth.<-
->It also declares a meeting with a devotee of Vishnu and an encounter with yellow garments.<- ||25||

When an omen-bird is situated in the spoke of the Northern direction (the direction of Kubera <note>the god of wealth</note>) when it is "peaceful" <note>a technical term in augury for a favorable direction</note>, it indicates or tells of the gain of wealth or money. Likewise, it declares or tells of a meeting or union with a "Bhagavata," meaning a Brahmin devotee of Vishnu. It also indicates an encounter with yellow-colored clothes. ||25||

He says another thing:

->In the North-Eastern direction, a woman engaged in religious vows comes into view.<-
->The acquisition of iron, weapons, and bells is also to be understood.<- ||26||

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 86]

In the northeastern spoke, a woman engaged in religious vows or standing in a state of penance <note>original: "vratayukta vratastha"</note> is seen or approaches. Furthermore, the acquisition of black iron, weapons, and bells is to be understood. ||26||

Now, he states a specific distinction in this regard:

->In the southern eighth part, and in the second, sixth, third, seventh, and eighth parts of the west, the journey yields middling results.<-
->In the second part of the north, and in all remaining parts, the journey is exceedingly auspicious.<- ||27||

"In the southern eighth part" means in the southern direction's eighth division. Likewise, "in the west," starting from the southwest corner, in the second, sixth, third, seventh, and eighth divisions. Additionally, in the "northern direction," in the second eighth-part—if the omen-bird is situated in these areas when they are "peaceful" <note>term: Shanta (peaceful); refers to a direction not facing the sun or afflicted by harsh winds</note>, the journey yields middling results. This means it is neither good nor bad. In the remaining twenty-five divisions, the journey is exceedingly auspicious. ||27||

->In the interior, at the hub, it gives auspicious results in six of the spokes.<-
->In the two spokes of the northwest and southwest, the journey brings distress.<- ||28||

"In the interior" means within the hub, at the center of the wheel. If the omen-bird is situated in six of the spokes, excluding the northwest and southwest, the journey gives auspicious results. In the two spokes of the northwest and southwest, the journey brings distress or is fraught with hardship. ||28||

Having stated the results for the "peaceful" directions, he now says he will describe the results for the "blazing" <note>term: Dipta (blazing); refers to directions facing the sun or otherwise agitated</note> directions:

->These results have been stated for the peaceful directions; I shall now speak of the blazing ones.<-
->In the East, there is fear from the sovereign and an encounter with enemies.<- ||29||

The results previously mentioned were for peaceful directions. Hereafter, I shall describe the blazing ones. If the omen-bird is in the East when it is "blazing," there is fear from the sovereign <note>original: "narendra" (king)</note>. There is also an encounter or meeting with enemies. ||29||

He states further:

->In the subsequent direction, there is loss of gold and fear for goldsmiths.<-
->In the third, there is loss of wealth, quarreling, and the fury of weapons.<- ||30||

In the direction subsequent to that—meaning the second division beyond the East—if the omen-bird is in a blazing state, there is loss of gold <note>original: "kanaka"</note> and fear related to goldsmiths. In the third division, there is the depletion of wealth, strife, and the violent outbreak of weapons. ||30||

He <note>The author, Varahamihira</note> says another thing—
**In the fourth [division], there is fear of fire; in the Southeast, there is fear from thieves.**
**In the second [division] from the corner, there is loss of wealth and the destruction of the king's son. ||31||**

In the fourth division from the Eastern part, there is fear of fire. In the Southeast corner, there is fear from thieves <note>original: "taskarebhyo"</note>. In the third division from the corner—that is, from the Southeast corner—there is the loss of wealth or money. The destruction of the king's son means the prince's ruin or that he dies. ||31||

He says another thing—
**In the third division, there occurs the loss of a woman's fetus; and in the fourth,**
**the destruction of goldsmiths and artisans, as well as the fury of weapons. ||32||**

When the omen <term>Shakuna: a bird or sign used for divination</term> is situated in the third division from the Southeast corner, there occurs the loss of the fetus of a woman or wife. In the fourth division, there is the destruction of the goldsmith <note>one who sells or works with gold</note> and the artisan <note>a craftsman or builder</note>. Likewise, there is the fury of weapons <note>outbreak of armed conflict</note>. ||32||

He says another thing—
**Now, in the fifth, fear of the king, a plague, and the sight of a corpse should be predicted.**
**In the sixth, fear is to be known for musicians along with the Domba people. ||33||**

Thereafter, in the fifth division, there is fear of the king <note>legal or royal persecution</note>. A "Mari" <note>plague or pestilence</note> occurs there among the people. The sight or witnessing of a dead man should be announced. In the sixth division, there is fear for musicians <note>original: "Gandharvas"</note> along with the Dombas <note>a specific social group often associated with music and performing arts</note>. It means fear arises from or for them. ||33||

He says another thing—
**From the seventh division, when inflamed, there is fear for fishermen and bird-catchers.**
**The obstruction of food is mentioned, and fear of the "Nirgrantha" beyond that. ||34||**

When the omen is "inflamed" <note>a technical term in divination for an ill-omened or agitated state</note> in the seventh division, there is fear for the fisherman <note>well-known</note> and the bird-catcher <note>one who kills birds</note>. Beyond that, in the eighth division, the obstruction or destruction of food <note>a meal</note> is said or declared. There is also fear from a "Nirgrantha" <note>a naked Jain ascetic or similar mendicant</note>. ||34||

He says another thing—
**In the Southwest portion, there is quarrel, the shedding of blood, and the fury of weapons.**
**In the [division] following that, leather-work is ruined and there is fear for the leather-worker. ||35||**

> Others say that in the West, there is fear for laborers; in the Northwest, the death of donkeys and camels.

**Regarding Weapons and Fire:** In the Southeast corner, if a bird makes a cry while "blazing" <note>a technical term in augury for a bird facing the sun or crying harshly</note>, there is an outbreak of weapons and an outbreak of fire. ### Now, the Chapter on Bird Cries is explained.

At the very beginning, the author lists the names of those who move by day:

> The Shyama, Hawk, Rabbit-killer, Vanjula, Peacock, Srikarna, and the bird called the Chakravaka;
> The Roller, Andira, Wagtail, Parrot, Crow, and the three types of Pigeons;
> The Bharadvaja, Pheasant, Cock, Donkey, Harita-pigeon, Vulture, Monkey,
> Phenta, Wild Cock, Purnakuta, and Sparrow are declared to be day-movers. ||1||

The *Shyama* is the Potaki bird. The *Hawk* is the Vajika. The *Rabbit-killer* is a bird of prey. The *Vanjula* is the "khadira-beak" bird. The *Peacock* is the crested bird. The *Srikarna* is a specific bird. The *Chakravaka* is the ruddy sheldrake. The *Roller* is the Chasha. The *Andiraka*, the *Wagtail*...

The parrot. All of these are birds. The *dhvanksha* is the crow. There are three types of pigeons: the pale-white, the variegated pigeon, and the saffron-smoke colored one. The *bharadvaja* <note>often identified as the skylark</note> is a bird. The *kulala-kukkuta* is the wild or "pit" cock. The *khara* is the donkey. The *harita* <note>green pigeon</note> and the vulture are birds. The *kapi* is the monkey. The *phenta* is a specific kind of bird. The *kukkuta* is the domestic fowl. The *purnakuta* is the *karayika* <note>a crane or water-bird</note>. The *chataka* is the sparrow. All of these are called "day-wanderers," meaning they are stated to be active during the daytime. ॥ 1 ॥

### Now he describes those designated as "night-wanderers" and their omens —

->The fox, the spotted owlet, and the bird called the *chippika*,<-
->The flying fox, the owl, and the hare are active at night.<-
->If any of these move outside of their natural time,<-
->They bring about the destruction of the land or the death of the king.<- ॥ 2 ॥

The *lomashika* <note>literally "the hairy one"</note> is a well-known specific animal, the fox. The *pingala* is the spotted owlet. The one called *chippika* is a specific bird; "called *chippika*" is its name. The *valguli* is the leather-bat <note>flying fox</note>. The owl. The hare is an animal. These move at night. If these night-wanderers move during the day, then they are "moving outside their natural time." They would then lead to the destruction or decay of the country or district. Or, they may be the "givers of the end," meaning they cause the death of the king. ॥ 2 ॥

### Now he describes those that wander during both times —

->The horse, man, snake, camel, leopard, lion, bear, and monitor lizard;<-
->The wolf, mongoose, deer, dog, goat, cow, tiger, and swan;<-
->The spotted deer, the forest deer, the jackal, the porcupine, and the cuckoo;<-
->As well as the cat, the crane, and the hog, move by both day and night.<- ॥ 3 ॥

The *haya* is the horse. *Nara* is man. The *bhujanga* is the snake. The *ustra* is the camel. The *dvipi* <note>literally "the islander," referring to its spots</note> is the leopard. The *simha* is the lion. The *rksha* is an animal <note>the bear</note>. The *godha* is a specific animal, the monitor lizard. The *vrka* is a species of deer-slayer, the wolf. The *nakula* is the well-known hole-dwelling animal, the mongoose. The *kuranga* is the antelope. The *shva* is the dog. The *aja* is the goat. The *gau* is the well-known cow. The *vyaghra* is a specific animal, the tiger. The *hamsa* is the swan. The *prshata* is a species of spotted deer. The *mrga* is the well-known forest deer. The *shrgala* is the jackal. The *shvavid* is a hole-dwelling animal; "called *shvavid*" is its name <note>the porcupine</note>. The *anyapushta* <note>literally "nourished by another"</note> is the cuckoo. Likewise, the *bidala* is the cat. The *sarasa* is the crane. The *sukara* is the hog. All of these wander during both day and night; the meaning is that they are both night-wanderers and day-wanderers. ॥ 3 ॥

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 87]

Now, he states the names of these [creatures] for the purpose of common usage—

->The *Bhasha*, *Kutapuri*, *Kurabaka*, and *Karayika* are known by the name *Purnakuta*.<-
->The names for the female owl are *Pingalika*, *Pechika*, and *Hakka*. ||4||<-

->The *Kapotaki* is called *Shyama*; the *Vanjulaka* is celebrated as the *Khadirachanchu* <note>literally "catechu-beaked"</note>.<-
->The musk-shrew is called the "King’s Daughter" (*Nripasuta*); the donkey is declared to be the *Valeya*. ||5||<-

->The *Srotobhedya* <note>stream-splitter</note>, *Tadagabhedya* <note>tank-splitter</note>, and *Ekaputraka* <note>only-son</note>, along with the *Kalahakarika* <note>quarrel-maker</note>, are known as the *Rala*.<-
->She cries out at night on the ground like a *Bhringara* <note>a cricket or a specific sounding bird</note>, having a body of two finger-breadths. ||6||<-

->The *Bhandika* is called the *Durbalika*; he is praised when appearing on the right for those in the Eastern lands.<-
->The *Dhikkara* is stated to be a species of deer; the rooster is declared to be the *Krikavaku*. ||7||<-

->The name of the "pit-cock" (*Gartakukkutaka*) is famous as the "potter’s cock" (*Kulalakukkuto*).<-
->The name "house-lizard" (*Grihagodhika*) should be understood for the *Kudachamatsya*. ||8||<-

->The *Dhanvana* is said to be divine; the *Kroda* is the boar; the *Go* <note>cow</note> is the *Usra*.<-
->The dog is called *Sarameya* by birth; and the *Chatika* is the female sparrow. ||9||<-

Regarding the verse "The *Bhasha*, *Kutapuri*...": The *Bhasha*, *Kutapuri*, *Kurabaka*, and *Karayika*—all these are or should be the designations or names for the *Purnakuta*. *Pingalika*, *Pechika*, and *Hakka* are the names for the female owl. ||4||

The *Kapotaki* is called the *Shyama* or *Potaki*. The *Vanjula* is celebrated or spoken of as the *Khadirachanchu*. The *Chuchundari* <note>musk-shrew</note> is the "fragrant mouse," celebrated as the *Nripasuta* or "King’s Daughter." The *Gardabha* or donkey is the *Khara*, declared as the *Valeya*. ||5||

Regarding the verse "The stream...": The *Srotobhedya*, *Tadagabhedya*, and *Ekaputraka*, along with the *Kalahakarika*—by these names, the *Rala* should be known. And she cries or warbles at night like a *Bhringara*. The *Bhringara* <note>1</note> is the *Dandani* or *Damani* <note>local names for a cricket or small noisy insect</note>. "Like a *Bhringara*" means she makes a sound similar to a *Bhringara*; the meaning is that she utters a "humming" sound. Some desire the *Bhringara* to be a specific type of bird. At night, of what size? "Having a body of two finger-breadths"—one whose body measures two fingers in length. ||6||

Regarding the verse "The *Durbalika*...": The *Bhandika* is declared to be the *Durbalika*. This *Durbalika* is praised as auspicious on the right side for those born in the Eastern countries. For all others, he is auspicious on the left. The *Dhikkara* is stated to be a species of deer. The rooster is declared or spoken of as the *Krikavaku*. ||7||

# [Chapter 87] Chapter on Miscellaneous Omens | 937

**Regarding the "Pit-Cock":** The bird described as the "Pit-Cock" (one who lives in a hole or ditch) is widely known by the name *Kulala-Kukkuta* <note>literally "Potter's Cock," likely a species of ground-nesting bird or a hoopoe</note>. The "Wall-Fish" is to be understood as the name for the *Griha-godhika* <note>the common house gecko</note>. ||8||

**Regarding the "Divine Archer":** What is called the "Divine Archer" <note>original: *Divyo Dhanvana*</note> is the *Kroda* or wild boar. The word "and" <note>original: *atha*</note> is used here in the sense of a conjunction. The *Gau* is famously known as the *Ustra* <note>the camel; in this context, *Gau* refers to a specific type of beast rather than a cow</note>. The *Shva* is called the *Kukkura* or *Sarameya* <note>the dog</note>. That which is by nature a *Chatika* <note>sparrow</note> is called a *Sukarika*. ||9||

### Here he speaks regarding the local variations of names:

->**Thus, in various regions, one should obtain the names from those who know them.**<-
->**For the sake of understanding the cries of omens, they should be collected and applied in this scientific treatise. ||10||**<-

In this manner, by obtaining and learning the names from experts in various regions who know the names of omens, one should collect and consider them for the purpose of understanding the "cries" <note>original: *ruta*; the sounds made by animals</note> of omens—those indicators of good and bad fortune—and incorporate them into the scientific text. ||10||

### Now he describes the characteristics of the cries of the Vanjula, Hawk, Parrot, and Vulture:

->**The cry of the Vanjula sounding like "Tittid" is "Blazing"; "Kil-kil" is "Full."**<-
->**Hawks, Parrots, Vultures, and Herons are "Blazing" when their voices differ from their natural state. ||11||**<-

When their voices are contrary to their natural disposition, they are said to be "Blazing" <note>original: *Dipta*; a technical term in omenology meaning ill-omened, harsh, or over-stimulated</note>. Regarding the *Vanjula* <note>likely the Ashy-crowned Sparrow-Lark or a similar bird</note>: its cry "Tittid" is Blazing and inauspicious. Its cry "Kil-kil" is "Full" <note>original: *Purna*; meaning auspicious or favorable</note>. The Hawk, Parrot, Vulture, and Heron are well-known birds; for all of these, any sound that is contrary to their natural voice is considered Blazing. ||11||

### Now he describes the behavior of the Pigeon:

->**The alighting or entry of a pigeon upon a vehicle, seat, or bed,**<-
->**Brings misfortune to men; the timing of the result varies by species. ||12||**<-
->**For a pale white pigeon, the result is after a year; for a speckled one, after six months.**<-
->**For a pigeon colored like saffron or honey, the result ripens immediately. ||13||**<-

**Regarding vehicles and seats:** A vehicle refers to horses and the like. A seat refers to a stool or where one sits. A bed refers to bedding. If a pigeon alights upon, clings to, or enters the house and settles on these items, it brings misfortune or undesirable results to men. The "other time" refers to the timing of the result, which varies according to the specific species or breed of the pigeon. ||12||

He <note>The commentator, Utpala</note> explains the timing of these effects: "Of the pale white..." The result <term>pāka: literally 'ripening' or the fruition of an omen</term> of a pale white pigeon occurs after one year. For a variegated or multi-colored pigeon, the result manifests in six months. For a saffron-colored or smoke-colored pigeon, the result is immediate, occurring on that very same day. ||13||

### Now he describes the cry of the Shama <note>The Indian Robin or Copsychus saularis</note>:

**The sound *chid-chid* from a Shama is "full" <note>auspicious and potent</note>, and the sound *shuli-shuli* is fortunate.**
**The sound *chach-cha* is "blazing" <note>dipta: usually indicating a warning or negative outcome</note>, while *chik-chik* leads to the gain of one's beloved. ||14||**

The *chid-chid* sound of the Shama is considered "full." Her *shuli-shuli* sound is fortunate and auspicious. The *chach-cha* sound is "blazing" and inauspicious. The *chik-chik* sound results in the acquisition or meeting of one's own dear beloved. ||14||

### Now he describes the cries of the Harita and Bharadvaji birds:

**For the Harita <note>The Green Pigeon</note>, the sound *guggu* is full; all others are considered blazing.**
**Every variety of vocalization from the Bharadvaji <note>The Skylark</note> is declared to be auspicious. ||15||**

The *guggu* sound of the Harita is "full." All other sounds it makes are "blazing" <note>dangerous</note>. For the Bharadvaji, the entire range and variety of its notes and sounds are declared to be entirely auspicious and excellent. ||15||

### He describes the cry of the Karayika <note>The Woodpecker or a similar small bird</note>:

**The *kish-kishi* sound of the Karayika is full, and the *kaha-kaha* sound is auspicious.**
**The *kara-kara* sound is only for safety, but it does not bring about the accomplishment of wealth. ||16||**

**The sound *kotu-kuli* brings security; her *katu-kuli* sound is for rain.**
**The *koti-kili* sound is fruitless, and the *gum* sound is indeed blazing. ||17||**

Regarding *kish-kishi*: The *kish-kishi* sound of the Karayika is "full." The *kaha-kaha* sound is auspicious. The *kara-kara* sound is only for "safety" <note>kṣema: the preservation of what one already possesses</note>, but it is not a "bringer of wealth-success"—it does not generate new profit. ||16||

Regarding *kotu-kuli*: That same Karayika's *kotu-kuli* sound is "secure" (good for safety). The *katu-kuli* sound leads to rain; the gods will pour down water. The *koti-kili* sound is "fruitless," meaning it has no effect. The word "indeed" (*khalu*) is used for emphasis. The *gum* sound made by this same bird is "blazing" <note>a negative omen</note>. ||17||

### Now he describes the movements of the lizard—

**Seeing a lizard on the left is auspicious;**
**Success is known if it is raised a cubit high.**
**If it stands even higher than the traveler's body,**
**The Earth, bounded by the oceans, will surely come under his control. || 18 ||**

The sight of a <term>divyaka</term><note>original: "divyaka" - a type of lizard, often identified as a garden lizard or chameleon</note> on the left side is auspicious and favorable. In that same leftward position, if it is raised a <term>cubit</term><note>original: "hasta-matra" - the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</note> from the ground, it indicates the attainment of desired goals. If, on that same left side, it is positioned higher than the traveler's own body, then the Earth, extending to the very shores of the ocean, will come under his dominion. As it has been said:

> On the left, the lizard is auspicious and a giver of success; if raised a cubit, it leads to victory. If it is higher than the body on the left side, it brings gain of the earth but causes the loss of kinsmen. || 18 ||

### Now he describes the movements of the snake—

**A snake coming directly toward the traveler foretells**
**An encounter with enemies and the death of kinsmen.**
**Or, if it moves from the right side to the left,**
**It does not lead to success or well-being in coming or going. || 19 ||**

The approach of a <term>phanin</term><note>original: "phanin" - literally "the hooded one," a cobra or snake</note> from the front tells of a meeting with enemies for the traveler. Alternatively, it signifies the slaughter or death of relatives and general ruin. Furthermore, if it moves from the right side toward the left side, then that snake is not auspicious for success in either departing or arriving. || 19 ||

### Now he describes the movements of the wagtail—

**On lotuses, or on the heads of horses, elephants, and snakes,**
**The wagtail grants kingdoms; on clean ground or grass, it brings well-being.**
**But seen on ashes, bones, wood, chaff, hair, or straw,**
**It truly causes misery for the duration of one year. || 20 ||**

The <term>khanjanaka</term><note>original: "khanjanaka" - the wagtail bird, considered highly significant in Indian omens</note> seen upon lotuses and similar water-lilies, or upon the heads of horses, elephants, or snakes, is a giver of kingdoms. Likewise, seen in a pure place or upon green grass, it is a "well-being maker," meaning it produces auspicious results. However, if seen on ashes, bones, wood, husks, hair, or dry straw, it causes sorrow for one full year. The word "truly" <note>original: "khalu"</note> is used here to indicate the authority of traditional scripture. || 20 ||

### Now he describes the behavior of the partridge and the rabbit—

->The sound of the partridge is "kili-kili-kili"<-
->When peaceful, it yields auspicious results; otherwise, it is the opposite.<-
->A rabbit moving to the left side at night<-
->While crying out is said to yield auspicious results. ||21||<-

The sound of the partridge <note>original: "tittira"</note> is "kili-kili-kili" when it is in a peaceful state <note>term: "shanta" (peaceful/calm) refers to a bird calling from a favorable direction or in a gentle manner</note>. That yields auspicious, good results. The other kind is "otherwise," meaning "blazing" <note>term: "pradipta" (blazing) refers to an omen that is harsh, facing the sun, or coming from an unfavorable quarter</note>. That yields inauspicious results. A rabbit <note>original: "shashaka"</note> at night, moving to the left side and crying out, is said or declared to yield auspicious, good results. ||21||

### Now he describes the cries of the monkey and the wild cock—

->The "kili-kili" cry of the monkey is considered "blazing"<-
->They say it does not bestow good results for a traveler.<-
->But they say the sound "chuglu" is auspicious,<-
->And the cry of the wild cock is similar to that of the monkey. ||22||<-

The "kili-kili" cry of the monkey <note>original: "kapi"</note> is "blazing," and they say it does not bestow good results for one who intends to travel. However, they say the sound "chuglu" brings good results. The cry of the wild cock <note>original: "kulala-kukkuta"; likely the jungle fowl or a specific wild variety</note> is similar to the monkey's. Just as the "blazing" and "peaceful" cries were described for the monkey, the same applies to the wild cock. ||22||

### Now he describes the cry and behavior of the blue jay—

->With its mouth full of worms, grasshoppers, ants, and the like,<-
->If a blue jay approaches a man from the right,<-
->Or if it makes a "svastika" pattern in the sky for one wishing to depart,<-
->It brings him a very great gain of wealth before long. ||23||<-

For a man whom the blue jay <note>original: "chasha"; the Indian Roller, considered highly sacred in omens</note>—with its mouth filled with worms (creeping insects), grasshoppers, or ants (which are well known), and by the use of "and the like," other small creatures—approaches from the right <note>term: "pradakshina" (circumambulation) moving clockwise or keeping the person to its right</note>. Or for one wishing to depart, if the bird makes a "svastika" <note>note: a cross-like flight pattern</note> in the sky (the heavens), it brings him a very great gain of wealth or money very quickly. ||23||

He says something else as well—

->If a blue jay <note>original: "chāṣa"; the Indian Roller, Coracias benghalensis</note> is fighting with a crow,<-
->and the jay, positioned to the right, is defeated,<-
->then the man who has set out on a journey will meet his death.<-
->In the opposite case, his victory is foretold. ||24||<-

If a blue jay is fighting or quarreling with a crow <note>original: "kāka" or "vāyasa"</note>, and the blue jay located on the right side of the crow is defeated, then at that time, the death of the man who has departed on a journey occurs. In the opposite case—meaning if the jay is on the left side—victory is foretold and declared. When the jay wins, the traveler wins. And it is said:

> When the blue jay, with a full beak, circles to the right or makes a cross-shaped flight <note>original: "svastika"</note> in the sky,
> there is great gain for the traveler; but if it is broken by a crow, it leads to defeat instead of victory. ||24||

---

He says something else as well—

->If the blue jay makes a "ke-ke" sound on the left side, like a full water-pot,<-
->then it brings victory.<-
->But its "kre-kre" cry is "blazing" <note>term: "dīpta" (blazing); a technical term in Sanskrit omenology for a harsh, ill-omened, or over-stimulated sound or direction</note> and not for welfare.<-
->However, the mere sight of this bird is always auspicious for a traveler. ||25||<-

If the blue jay makes the sound "ke-ke" on the left side, or if it makes a sound like a "pūrṇakuṭa" <note>likely referring to the Karāyikā bird or a specific rhythmic gurgle</note> such as "kish-kishi-kaha-kaha," then it is a bringer of victory. The "kre-kre" cry of that blue jay is "blazing," and that does not lead to fortune or well-being. The sight or observation of this blue jay is always—at all times—bestowing auspiciousness upon a traveler. ||25||

---

Now he describes the behavior of the Andīraka and Pheṇṭaka birds—

->The Andīraka is "full" <note>term: "pūrṇa"; the auspicious opposite of "blazing," indicating a favorable omen</note> with the cry "ṣṭī,"<-
->but is said to be "blazing" with the sound "ṭṭi-ṭṭi-ṭṭi."<-
->The Pheṇṭaka is auspicious when staying on the right side;<-
->no distinction is made regarding its specific cry. ||26||<-

Regarding the Andīraka: The Andīraka bird is called "full" (auspicious) by the cry or sound "ṣṭī." By the sound "ṭṭi-ṭṭi-ṭṭi," however, it is called or declared "blazing" (inauspicious). The Pheṇṭaka <note>likely a variety of shrike or small bird of prey</note> and the Andīraka are auspicious when positioned on the right side of the traveler. No specific distinction or special rule has been stated regarding the chirping or cry of that Pheṇṭaka bird. ||26||

### Now he describes the cry of the Shrikarna bird—

->The cry of the Shrikarna on the right side<-
->As "Kva-kva-kva" is declared to be auspicious.<-
->The "Chik-chiki" sound is indeed middling,<-
->While all other sounds, they say, are fruitless. || 27 ||<-

On the right side, the cry of the Shrikarna <note>The Shrikarna is likely a variety of woodpecker or a similar forest bird</note> as "Kva-kva-kva" is declared or stated to be auspicious. The "Chik-chiki" cry of that same bird is of middling result, meaning it is neither good nor bad. All other remaining cries are said by the sages to be fruitless, or devoid of any specific result. || 27 ||

### Now he describes the cry of the Durbali bird—

->For the Durbali, the sound "Chirili-virili"<-
->Is said to grant desired fruits if heard from the left.<-
->If it moves from the left side to the right,<-
->It grants the success of one's work without delay. || 28 ||<-

The Durbali <note>original: "Durbali" is identified in the commentary as the Bhandika bird, possibly a wagtail or a small crane</note> is the Bhandika. Its cry "Chirili-virili" is stated to be a giver of desired fruits, or auspicious, when heard from the left side. If the bird moves from the left side to the right side, then it grants the accomplishment of the task or the acquisition of wealth very quickly. || 28 ||

### He describes a specific cry of this same bird—

->If it makes the "Chik-chiki" cry<-
->And moves from the left side to the right,<-
->It only grants safety but does not accomplish goals;<-
->Moving in the opposite way, it leads to death, imprisonment, or fear. || 29 ||<-

If that same Durbali bird makes the "Chik-chiki" sound and then comes from the left side to the right side, it only grants safety (well-being); it does not accomplish the desired goals or grant success in them. Moving in the opposite way—that is, if it goes from the right side to the left—it causes death, imprisonment, or fear. || 29 ||

### He says another thing—

->The Sarika bird that cries "Krak-ka" rapidly,<-
->Or "Tre-tre" without fear,<-
->Predicts the arrival of a beloved person or, shortly,<-
->The flowing of blood from the limbs. || 30 ||<-

<note>The Sarika is the Common Myna, a bird famous in Indian literature for its ability to mimic human speech.</note>

### Now, the cry of the Phentaka is described:

### Now, the cry of the Donkey is described:

->They desire a donkey on the left side that remains stationary as the best;<-
->and if it makes the sound of 'Om', it is beneficial for the traveler.<-

->which occupies all directions, they declare to be 'blazing' <note>inauspicious</note>.||32||<-

They say that a donkey situated on the left side and remaining in one place is excellent and beautiful; likewise, if it cries with the sound of *'Om'*, then it is beneficial and favorable for the traveler. Any other braying of a donkey—which is 'all-encompassing' <note>original: *sarvashrayam*, meaning the sound seems to come from everywhere or affects all classes of people</note>—is declared to be 'blazing'. ||32||

### Now, the cries of the Kuranga, Mriga, and Prishata are described:

->The *Prishata* <note>Spotted Deer</note> crying the sound 'O' is also 'Full'.<-
->Whatever other notes they make are said to be 'blazing'.<-
->'Full' sounds are auspicious; 'blazing' sounds result in sin <note>misfortune</note>.||33||<-

The *Kuranga* is a species of deer. Along with the *Mriga*, if it cries the sound 'Aa' <note>original: *akara-ravi*</note>, it is 'Full' <term>Purna: a technical term for a favorable, 'filled' omen</term> and auspicious. The *Prishata* crying the sound 'O' is 'Full'. The remaining notes are said to be 'blazing'. For all omens, those sounds that are 'Full' are auspicious, and those that are 'blazing' result in sin or are inauspicious. ||33||

### When healthy creatures make their natural calls at the end of night,
### These loud sounds grant prosperity to the nation, the city, and the king. ||34||

"Copper-crested" roosters <note>original: *tāmracūḍāḥ*</note> sometimes cry out "kukuchuku" in fear during the night. Aside from those specific cries, other sounds are generally ominous. However, when they are healthy <note>meaning in their natural state, free from disease or external influence</note>, their natural calls <note>original: *svabhāva-virutāni*</note> made at the end of the night—if they are loud and clear—bring growth and prosperity to the nation <note>the countryside or district</note>, the city, and the king. ||34||

Now, the author describes the cries of the house gecko <note>original: *chippikā*</note>, the cat, and the sneezing of a cow:

### The house gecko makes various types of cries;
### Among them, "kulu-kulu" is auspicious, while the rest are not.
### The cry of a cat is never auspicious for a traveler,
### And the sneeze of a cow brings certain death to one setting out. ||35||

The house gecko has many different types of vocalizations. Among these, the sound "kulu-kulu" is considered favorable. All other remaining sounds are inauspicious. The cry of a cat <note>original: *biḍāla-virutaṃ*</note> is never good for a traveler at any time. Furthermore, the sneeze of a cow causes the actual death of a traveler. As it has been said:

> "A sneeze is generally considered an evil omen everywhere, but the sneeze of a cow brings death to one wishing to depart. The cry of a cat and the tripping of a traveler's garment are likewise not auspicious." ||34 <insert>Note: This verse number likely refers to the cited authority</insert>||

Now, the author describes the cries of the owl:

### Desiring his mate, the owl hoots "hum-hum-guglu" with joy;
### The sound "gurullu" is considered 'full,' while "kiskisi" is always 'blazing.'
### A quarrel is known when he cries "bala-bala" repeatedly,
### While "tatta-tatta" leads only to harm; other harsh tones are also inauspicious. ||36||

When an owl is joyful and desiring his beloved mate, he hoots "hum-hum-guglu." The sound "gurullu" is considered "full" <note>a technical term in augury for a favorable, productive sound</note>. The cry "kiskisi" should always be known as "blazing" <note>original: *pradīptam*; a term for an intense or alarming omen</note>. When that owl cries "bala-bala" again and again, a quarrel should be expected. The hoot "tatta-tatta" results only in misfortune. All other remaining tones are "blazing" <note>harsh/fiery</note> and are not auspicious. ||36||

### Now, he describes the cry of the Sarasa crane—

> **->The cooing of the Sarasa crane brings desired results if the pair cries out simultaneously.<-**
> **->A single cry is not auspicious, nor is it favorable if one cries and the other responds only after a long delay. ||37||<-**

Regarding the cooing of the <term>Sarasa</term><note>The Indian Sarus Crane (*Antigone antigone*), famous in Indian culture for its lifelong pair-bonding.</note>: the simultaneous cry of the pair (the couple) brings a desired and auspicious result. A single cry from just one bird is not auspicious; likewise, if one bird cries and the other responds only after a long interval, it is not considered favorable. ||37||

---

### Now, he describes the cry of the Pingala owl—

> **->The Pingala owl brings good fortune with the sounds "Chiril-viril."<-**
> **->Any other sounds it makes are known as "Blazing" (Pradipta). ||38||<-**

The <term>Pingala</term><note>The Spotted Owlet (*Athene brama*), often consulted in Indian divination (Shakuna Shastra).</note> brings auspiciousness through the specific vocalizations "Chiril-viril." Any sounds other than these are categorized as <term>Pradipta</term><note>Literally "blazing" or "burning"; in omenology, this refers to harsh, over-excited, or ill-omened sounds that indicate trouble.</note> and are not desired. ||38||

---

### Further details—

> **->The "Ishi" cry forbids travel;<-**
> **->The "Kushu-kushu" cry causes a quarrel.<-**
> **->I shall now describe the method by which she<-**
> **->indicates the success of one's intended goals. ||39||<-**

The cry "Ishi" acts as a prohibition on travel, creating obstacles for a journey. If the owl makes the sound "Kushu-kushu," it leads to a quarrel. I shall now explain the ritual and the manner in which that Pingala owl indicates the "attainment of desired goals"—the success of the tasks one has in mind. ||39||

---

> **->At the time of evening twilight, one should approach<-**
> **->the tree where she resides, remaining pure and focused.<-**
> **->After worshipping the gods, starting with Brahma,<-**
> **->one should honor the tree with new cloth and fragrances. ||40||<-**
> **->Standing alone at midnight in the South-East (Agni) direction,<-**
> **->one should bind her with oaths, both divine and otherwise.<-**

### One should ask about the matter exactly as it was meditated upon,
### using this mantra, so that the answer may be heard. || 41 ||

Regarding the phrase "At the time of the evening twilight": At the end of the day, when the sun sets, at that specific time of the evening twilight, one should go to the dwelling or home of that *Pingala* <note>The Spotted Owlet, considered a bird of omen</note>. Having approached the tree, being pure <note>literally "not having leftover food in the mouth," implying ritual purity</note> and self-controlled, one should worship the gods such as the Grandfather <note>Brahma</note>, Vishnu, and Maheshvara <note>Shiva</note>. What should the seeker be like? He should be wearing new clothes. He should worship that tree with fragrant substances such as sandalwood, saffron, musk, and aloe-wood. || 40 ||

Then, at midnight when people are asleep, at the stroke of the middle of the night, standing alone in the direction of the fire <note>the South-East</note>, one should bind that *Pingala* with oaths—both divine oaths related to the gods and other worldly oaths. Then, in the manner that he may hear or perceive the answer, he should ask about the success of the matter he has meditated upon using the following mantra. || 41 ||

### Now he states the mantra: —

->**Know, O Blessed One, that you are being urged by me for this purpose.**<-
->**O Auspicious One, you are proclaimed as the knower of all speech. || 42 ||**<-
->**I take my leave now and shall depart; I have made myself known.**<-
->**Having returned in the morning, I shall ask you while stationed in the South-East. || 43 ||**<-
->**That which I ask of you, you ought to explain to me,**<-
->**O Auspicious One, through your own movements, so that I may know it clearly. || 44 ||**<-

Regarding "Know, O Blessed One": O Blessed One, full of welfare, know that you are being urged or prompted by me to be asked about this matter. O Auspicious One, O Fortunate One, you are celebrated as the one who understands or makes known all speech without exception. || 42 ||

"I take my leave today": I am going now. Having departed and having already asked, I will come again in the morning and, standing in the South-East direction, I will question you. || 43 ||

That which I urge or ask of you, O Auspicious and Fortunate One, you should explain or tell to me through your own movements <note>the bird's physical actions or calls</note> in such a way that I may know it without confusion or doubt. || 44 ||

### Now he describes the movement: —

->**When this has been said, if the bird on the treetop**<-
->**makes the sound "Chic-chil-vir-il-vil," there is success in the matter.**<-

<sig>[M. 87]</sig>

->Great agitation occurs when the sound "Dishikara" is made,<-
->or when the sound "Kucha-kucha" is uttered. || 45 ||<-
->Even in silence, the accomplishment of a beneficial goal occurs;<-
->other results should be declared according to the previously mentioned directional wheel.<-
->The result should be stated as excellent, middling, or low,<-
->depending on whether the bird is perched on an upper, middle, or lower branch. || 46 ||<-

Thus it is said. The word "thus" indicates the conclusion of the topic. When the <term>Pingala</term> <note>A species of small owl or spotted owlet used in augury</note> is situated at the top of a tree and makes the sound "Chiril-virilvi," the accomplishment of one's goal occurs. When the sound "Dishikara" is cried, there is "great agitation," meaning a disturbance of the mind. If the sound "Kucha-kucha" is uttered, it likewise results in agitation. || 45 ||

**Even in silence, etc.** Even in "silence"—meaning when no sound is uttered at all—the accomplishment of a beneficial or desired goal occurs. Other than this, further auspicious results are determined by the "previously mentioned directional wheel." Just as the **Directional Wheel** <note>A systematic diagram dividing the horizon into 32 points to interpret omens based on the direction of the animal</note> was explained with results divided into thirty-two parts, the results for this bird should be stated in the same way (e.g., "In the East, in a peaceful quarter," etc.). If the bird is perched on a "superior" or main branch, an excellent result should be predicted. If on a middle branch, a middling result. If on a low branch, the result is low or insignificant. || 46 ||

---

->In the circle of directions, in both the inner and outer parts,<-
->one should know the results pertaining to the House-Lizard.<-
->The Musk-shrew is "blazing" with the sound "Chic-chid,"<-
->but she is "full" with the sound "Tit-tid." || 47 ||<-

Regarding the <term>House-Lizard</term> <note>original: "Grihagodhika," commonly known as the wall gecko</note>, one should know the results based on the circle of directions in the eight quarters, both in the inner hub and the outer part divided into the thirty-two-fold directional wheel. If the direction is "peaceful" and the sound is sweet, then the result is middling. If the sound is harsh, then it is middling. If the direction is "blazing" <note>A technical term in Sanskrit augury referring to a direction facing the sun or otherwise intensified</note> and the sound is sweet, then the result is auspicious. If the direction is not blazing but the sound is "blazing" (harsh), then the result is surely evil; this should be understood everywhere, and the same applies to the Pingala owl. The <term>Musk-shrew</term> <note>original: "Chuchundari," the Asian house shrew</note> is considered "blazing" (ominous) with the sound "Chic-chid." However, she is known as "full" (auspicious) with the sound "Tit-tid." || 47 ||

## Now, the Circle of Dogs is explained.

First, the author describes the dog's movements:

**If a dog urinate upon a man, a horse, an elephant, a water-pot, a saddle, a milky tree, a heap of bricks, a parasol, a bed, a seat, a mortar, a banner, a chowrie <note>a fly-whisk made of yak tail</note>, a grassy spot, or a place in bloom, and then walks ahead of a traveler, then there will be success in that person's mission. If it urinates on fresh cow dung, there will be a gain of sweet food; if on dry cow dung, the gain will be dry food, jaggery, or perhaps sweetmeats.**

"Man" refers to a human being. "Horse" is a steed. "Elephant" is a tusker. "Water-pot" is a jar. "Saddle" is well-known. "Milky tree" refers to trees like the *Arka* <note>Calotropis gigantea</note> which produce sap. "Heap of bricks" is a pile of building blocks. "Parasol" is a sunshade. "Bed" is a mattress or bedding. "Seat" refers to a throne or stool. "Mortar" is well-known. Likewise, "Banner" is a flag or sign. "Chowrie" is a fly-whisk. "Grassy spot" refers to *Durva* grass. "Place in bloom" is a spot where flowers have grown. When a dog—a hound—having urinated upon or moistened these things, goes ahead or in front of a traveler who is departing, then the "success of the mission" (the fulfillment of the desired goal) will occur. It has also been said:

> If a dog urinates upon a man, horse, elephant, parasol, pot, banner, bed, seat, flower, or chowrie and then moves ahead, the King will then destroy the strength of his enemies. <note>The original text uses the word 'Paksha' or 'Yaksha' here, but the commentator notes these do not mean 'dog'; the reading should likely be 'Shva' (dog).</note>

Regarding "on fresh cow dung": If the dog urinates on fresh, moist cow dung, there is the gain or arrival of delicious food. If it urinates on dry cow dung, there is the gain of dry food, jaggery, or the obtaining of *Modakas* <note>sweet dumplings</note>.

---

->The author says something further:<-

**Now, if the dog urinates upon or strikes a poisonous tree, a thorny bush, wood, a stone, a withered tree, a bone, or a cremation ground while moving ahead of the traveler, it foretells evil. If it urinates on a bed or on a potter’s vessels that are unused and unbroken, it indicates a flaw or scandal regarding a maiden in the house. If the vessels are currently in use, it indicates the unchastity of the mistress of the house. The same result applies to shoes. If it urinates on a cow, it foretells a mixture of castes <note>social disorder or illegitimate births</note>.**

---

<note>Footnote from the bottom of the page</note>
1. The words *Paksha* or *Yaksha* are used in the verse, but neither is a word for "dog." Therefore, the reading "Shva" (dog) is the correct one here.

# Chapter on the Circle of Dogs
## [Chapter 88]

On a poison tree <note>original: "vishataro"</note>; on a thorny tree; on wood, stone, or rock; on a withered tree; or on bones or in a cemetery. If a dog urinate on any of these places, or strikes them with its hand <note>paw</note> or foot, and then goes ahead of a person who is traveling, it declares and tells of misfortune and inauspiciousness. 

Regarding beds and bedding; or the vessels of a potter <note>original: "kulaladi-bhandani"</note> made of clay—and by the use of "etcetera," this includes those made of wood—if they are unused <note>new</note> and unbroken, and a dog urinates there, it causes a "defect of the maiden" <note>implies a scandal or loss of character for an unmarried daughter in the house</note>. If it urinates on vessels currently in use, it causes the wickedness <note>infidelity or ill-repute</note> of the mistress of the house. The result for shoes <note>term: upanat (traditional sandals or footwear)</note> is the same: urinating on unused shoes causes a defect for the maiden, and on used shoes, it causes the wickedness of the mistress. If it urinates on a cow, there will be a person of "mixed caste" or "lowly birth" <note>original: "avarnajo... sankaro"</note> born in that house. 

As it is said:

> If a dog, after urinating on poison trees, thorns, dry wood, or clods of earth, or on a pile of bones, goes facing the traveler while barking, shaking its body, scratching its limbs, or licking its fat <note>or moisture on the skin</note>, it is not auspicious.

He says further:

> When a dog stands before a traveler holding a shoe in its mouth, it leads to success. If its mouth is filled with meat, there is the acquisition of wealth. If it holds a moist <note>fresh</note> bone, it is auspicious. If it holds a burning brand <note>wood with fire</note> or a dry bone, death occurs. If it holds an extinguished charcoal, there is an assault upon the man. If it holds a human head, hand, or foot in its mouth, there is the acquisition of land; however, some say if it holds a cloth, it means calamities from cloth-thieves, while others say a cloth is auspicious.

> If it enters a house with a dry bone in its mouth, the master of that house will be killed. If it stands holding a chain, a withered vine, or a leather strap, it signifies imprisonment. If it licks the traveler's feet, shakes its ears, or jumps upon him, it signifies an obstacle to the journey. In a dispute, it signifies opposition. Likewise, if it scratches its own body, or if it sleeps with its legs turned upward, it always causes a defect <note>misfortune</note>. || 1 ||

"Facing the traveler" <note>original: "gamanamukham"</note> means: when it stands near one who desires to depart, holding a shoe in its mouth, it results in the success of one's goals. "With a mouth full of meat" means the gain of wealth. With a "moist bone"—a bone with juice/marrow—it is auspicious. With a "burning brand"—wood burnt by fire—or a "dry bone"—one without juice—it signifies death.

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary
## [Chapter 88]

It concerns the traveler. If a dog strikes a traveler with a "quenched" piece of wood—one that is extinguished and without fire—it indicates a coming calamity. The word "or" implies an alternative. If the dog takes hold of a man's head, hands, feet, or—by the use of the word "etcetera"—any other limb or even his clothing and stands near him, then there will be an acquisition of land. "Clothing" refers to garments, and "bark" refers to tree-bark attire. By "etcetera," even a fragment of clothing or bark is included. These actions generally lead to misfortunes. However, some sages say that a dog holding clothing is auspicious. Thus, Parashara <note>An ancient sage and author of early astrological texts</note> says:

->"If a dog with clothing in its mouth approaches a traveler, there is a great gain of wealth."<-

"But if it enters..."—this refers to a dog entering a house with a dry bone in its mouth. In such a case, the death of the master of the house, the primary person, will occur. If the dog approaches holding a chain (the well-known iron kind), a worn-out or old vine, or a leather strap (a rope made of hide)—and by "etcetera," other types of ropes, bonds, or shackles are meant—then imprisonment shall occur. If it licks the traveler's feet or shakes its own ears while attempting to jump upon or attack the traveler, it serves as an obstacle to the journey. If it stands in opposition to the traveler, there will be an obstruction on the path. "Opposition" here should be understood as a blockage of the road. Thus, Garga <note>Another foundational sage in the field of omens and astronomy</note> says:

->"When a dog stands blocking the path of one who has set out,<-
->one should point out that the road is blocked by thieves."<-

Similarly, if the dog scratches its own body parts, there will be opposition for the traveler. If the dog sleeps with its legs up at any time, it brings harm to the traveler or to someone staying in that place. ||1||

### Now he describes the results of a dog's behavior according to the directions:

> If a dog howls at sunrise &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; facing the sun
> in the middle of the village; &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 
> whether it be one or &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; many gathered together,
> they quickly announce &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; another ruler for the land. ||2||

If a dog in the middle of the village at the time of sunrise howls while facing the sun (the solar orb), whether it is a single dog or many gathered together, then they quickly announce a second or different ruler for the country. ||2||

### He says something further:

->Facing the sun and standing in the southeast <note>original: "Agni-direction"</note>,<-
->it causes fear of thieves and fire in a short time.<-

# [Chapter 88] The Chapter on the Circle of Dogs

> **At midday, [the dog] foretells fire and death;**
> **In the afternoon, there shall be a quarrel involving bloodshed. ||3||**

The dog <note>original: *shva* or *sarameya*</note>, when facing the sun <note>facing the direction of the sun's current position</note> or facing the direction of fire <note>the South-East</note> and barking, then in a very short time, he causes fear from thieves and fire. If he faces the sun at the time of midday, he foretells fire and death. In the afternoon (the third watch of the day), if he faces the sun, there will be a quarrel accompanied by blood <note>original: *sashonitah*</note>. ||3||

->**He says another thing—**<-

> **Barking while facing the Lord of Day at the time of sunset,**
> **He quickly brings fear to the farmers.**
> **At the time of the first watch of night, facing the direction of the wind,**
> **He brings fear arising from storms and thieves. ||4||**

At the time of sunset, facing the sun <note>original: *dineshabhimukha*</note>, if he is barking or crying out, he quickly gives fear to the farmers <note>original: *krishivalanam*, those who work the land</note>. At the time of the first watch of night <note>original: *pradoshakale*</note>, if he faces the direction of the wind <note>the North-West</note> and barks, he gives fear arising from the wind (storms) and from thieves. ||4||

->**He says another thing—**<-

> **Facing North at the time of midnight,**
> **He indicates distress for priests and the stealing of cattle.**
> **At the end of the night, facing the direction of Shiva,**
> **[He indicates] the defilement of maidens, fire, and miscarriages. ||5||**

At the time of midnight, if he faces North, he indicates the suffering of priests <note>original: *vipra-vyatham*, distress for Brahmins</note> and the abduction of cows by others. At the end of the night <note>pre-dawn</note>, if he faces the direction of Shiva <note>the North-East</note>, he indicates the defilement of young maidens, fire, and the falling of the womb (miscarriage) among women. ||5||

->**He says another thing—**<-

> **If they have loud voices while standing on heaps of grass,**
> **Or situated on palaces or the best of houses...**

->**In the rainy season, they foretell intense rain;**<-

If they <note>referring to dogs</note> are situated upon a heap of grass <note>original: *trinakuta*</note>, a palace, or a noble residence <note>original: *uttama veshma*</note> and emit loud, sharp cries, they indicate specific outcomes. ### He mentions another point—

->**During a drought in the rainy season, if they plunge into water,**<-

During the monsoon season <note>original: *pravrit-kale*</note>, if there is a drought <note>original: *avagraha*</note>, and dogs are seen plunging into water, staying there, and repeatedly turning or rolling <note>original: *rechakaih*, referring to a specific side-to-side movement</note>; or if they are seen shaking the water off themselves or drinking it, then even during a drought, it will rain within a period of twelve days. The meaning is that the gods will grant rain within twelve days. ||7||

### He describes other behaviors of dogs—

->**If a dog, resting its head on the threshold with its body outside,**<-
->**howls repeatedly while looking at the mistress of the house,**<-
->**it brings disease; if inside the house facing outward,**<-
->**it declares her to be unfaithful. ||8||**<-

If a dog <note>original: *shva* or *sarameya*</note> places its head on the door-frame while its body remains outside and howls repeatedly while looking at the mistress of the house, it portends sickness. If it sits inside the house facing outward and behaves thus, it declares that the mistress is an unfaithful woman <note>original: *bandhaki*, a term for a woman of loose morals or a harlot</note>. ||8||

### He mentions another point—

->**When it scratches at the wall of a house, there is fear of thieves;**<-
->**if it scratches the cowshed, it foretells the capture of cattle;**<-
->**in a granary, it signifies the gain of grain. ||9||**<-

When a dog scratches or digs at the wall <note>original: *kudya*</note> of a house, there will be a fear of "diggers" <note>original: *khanaka-bhayam*, referring to burglars who tunnel through mud walls</note> or a breach in the house. If it scratches at the cowshed, one should predict the capture or theft of cattle. If it does so in a place where grain is stored, it indicates the acquisition of more grain. ||9||

...one should speak. In the case of digging in grain-lands, there is the acquisition of grain. "Grain-land" refers to the ground where crops are grown. <note>The commentator clarifies that a dog digging in fertile soil predicts a successful harvest.</note> ||9||

### Now he describes other behaviors—

**If a dog has tears in only one eye, a pitiful look, and eats very little, he brings misery to that household. If he is seen playing with cows, he indicates abundance, safety, health, and joy.** ||10||

If he is characterized by having tears in one eye—meaning one eye is watery—and has a pitiful gaze and a "slow diet"—meaning he eats very little—then he becomes a "misery-maker" for that house or dwelling. If he is playing together with cows, he "declares" or creates abundance <note>original: "subhiksha," meaning a time of plenty where food is easily obtained</note>. Likewise, he declares safety, health, and joy or happiness. ||10||

### He says another thing as well—

**If he should sniff the left knee, it is for the arrival of wealth; if the right, there will be a quarrel with women. If he sniffs the left thigh, there is the enjoyment of sensual pleasures; if he sniffs the right, there is conflict with beloved friends.** ||11||

If the dog <note>original: "sarameya," a poetic term for a dog, literally 'descendant of Sarama'</note> should sniff the left knee of a traveler, it would be for the arrival of wealth or financial gain. When he sniffs the right knee, then there is a quarrel or dispute with women. If he should sniff the left thigh, then there is the enjoyment of the objects of the senses. This means the enjoyment of the "objects" or "matters" pertaining to the senses of perception. If he should sniff the "left" <note>Note: In this context, the commentator clarifies "savya" as the right side</note> or right thigh, then there is conflict with "desired ones"—meaning kinsmen—and "friends" or companions. ||11||

### He says another thing as well—

**If he should sniff the feet of one who is walking, he predicts a non-journey; for one who is standing still, he predicts the attainment of desired wealth. If the dog should sniff the shoes of one staying in a place, he causes a journey to happen very quickly.** ||12||

If the dog sniffs the feet or steps of a "goer" (one who is walking), then he "speaks" or declares a "non-journey"—a prohibition against going. For one who is "motionless" (staying right there), he speaks of the attainment of desired wealth or the arrival of money. If he should sniff the shoes of one "staying in a place" (residing in one spot), then he makes a journey or departure happen very quickly or immediately. ||12||

->**If he sniffs both arms,**<-
->**one should recognize a coming encounter with enemies and thieves.**<-

->### Commentary on the Great Compilation<-
<sig>[Chapter 88]</sig>

### If a dog hides food in ashes,
### or hides meat and bones, there will soon be an outbreak of fire. || 13 ||

If a dog sniffs both arms of a person, it should be understood as an encounter with enemies and thieves. "Enemy" refers to a foe; "thieves" refers to robbers. An encounter with these should be known or recognized. Alternatively, if a dog hides <term>bhakshas</term><note>snacks or food items like cakes</note> within ashes, or hides meat and bones there, then an outbreak of fire will occur very quickly. As Garga <note>an ancient sage and authority on omens</note> says:

> When a dog sniffs both arms of a traveler, one should point out
> a terrible fear of enemies and thieves upon seeing that portent.
> But when it takes meat and stays there covering it with grass,
> seeing such a portent, one should know that fire is imminent. || 13 ||

He says something further:

> If they bark in the village and then outside in the cemetery,
> it signifies the death of a prominent man.
> When a dog howls facing someone wishing to depart,
> it then obstructs the journey. || 14 ||

If dogs <note>literally "sons of Sarama," a Vedic dog goddess</note> bark—making a noise—in the village and then bark outside in the cemetery, then the death or destruction of a "prominent man" (a leader or chief) occurs. When a dog howls facing a person who wishes to depart <note>someone about to start a journey</note>, it obstructs or cancels that journey. || 14 ||

He says something further:

> With a howl sounding like the letter 'U', there is success in wealth;
> and with the sound of the letter 'O' on the left side.
> One should know distraction comes from the sound of 'Au',
> while all sounds from behind act as a prohibition. || 15 ||

When a dog howls with the sound of the vowel 'U', there is the attainment of wealth. Likewise, if the sound of the vowel 'O' is made on the left side of the traveler, there is also success in wealth. One should recognize "distraction" or mental agitation from the sound of 'Au'. If any of these sounds are made behind the traveler, it acts as a prohibition, meaning it forbids the journey. || 15 ||

# [Chapter 88] The Chapter on the Circle of Dogs

The author says another thing—
-> Those dogs who, as if being beaten with sticks, <-
-> howl "Kham-Kham" loudly and repeatedly, <-
-> or run around in a circle, <-
-> they bring about desolation and the fear of death. || 16 ||

Those dogs <term>kukkura; a common Sanskrit term for dog</term> who, making a loud sound, howl "Kham-Kham" <note>The text uses "Kham-Kham" to represent a sharp, yelping bark</note> every moment, or who run and move in a circular formation or a rounded group—they bring about the emptiness (desolation) of the city and the fear of death. || 16 ||

The author says another thing—
-> If a dog shows its teeth and licks the corners of its mouth, <-
-> those who know the signs say a delicious meal is coming. <-
-> But if it licks its face and not the corners of its mouth, <-
-> it causes an obstacle to food, even if the meal has already begun. || 17 ||

If, while showing its teeth, it licks the <term>srikvini; the corners of the mouth or edges of the lips</term>, then those who know the movements of dogs <note>experts in canine omens</note> desire (predict) a "cleansed" or delicious meal. When it licks its face but does not lick the corners of its mouth, then even if a person has already started to eat, it causes an obstacle to the food. This means the person will not receive the meal. || 17 ||

The author says another thing—
-> If they bark repeatedly in a group <-
-> in the middle of a village or a town, <-
-> they announce distress for the lord of that place; <-
-> a dog staying in the forest is to be considered like a wild deer. || 18 ||

Those <term>sarameya; a poetic term for dogs, literally "descendants of Sarama," the divine hound</term> who, gathering together in large numbers in the middle of a village or town, bark every moment—they announce or tell of distress for the lord of that village or the lord of that town. A dog staying in the forest is to be considered like a deer. "Like a deer" means equal to a deer; whatever behaviors have been described for deer <note>in the chapters on animal omens</note> should be considered for this forest-dwelling dog. As it is said: "Deer, mongooses, and birds are auspicious when passing on the right," etc. <insert>See verse 43 on page 910 of this same book.</insert> || 18 ||

The author says another thing—

> If a dog howls while approaching a tree, there will be a fall of water;
> If at the <term>Indrakila</term><note>A large bolt or pillar at a city gate</note>, there will be suffering for the King's minister.
> If in the "House of the Wind" <note>The northwest corner of a building</note>, there is danger to the crops;
> If staying at the city gate, the suffering belongs to the city itself. || 19 ||
>
> There is danger to the masters of the beds if they howl upon them;
> If they bark behind a person during a journey, they grant fear to the traveler.
> Furthermore, if they bark while standing on the left side of a crowd of people,
> They announce fear coming from enemies. || 20 ||

**If approaching a tree:** When a dog <note>original: "sarameya"</note> howls while near a tree, there will be a fall of water, meaning a rainfall. It means the god will rain. At the **Indrakila**, near the door-bolt, there will be suffering for the minister. If it howls inside the house or in the **House of the Wind**, in the northwestern direction, then there is danger to the crops. If staying at the **city gate**, at the entrance of the town, the suffering will be for the city itself. || 19 ||

**And danger on the beds:** On beds or bedding, they cause fear for the masters of those beds. During a **journey**, those barking from behind give fear to the traveler himself. The word "furthermore" <note>original: "atha"</note> is used in the sense of "and." In a **crowd of people**, in the presence of people, those barking while on the **left side** <note>original: "apasavya"</note> speak of or announce fear related to enemies. || 20 ||

->in the Commentary on the Compilation composed by the venerable Bhattotpala.<-

> Is a "Full" sound; others are described as "Blazing." || 1 ||

Jackals are similar or equal to dogs <note>original: "sarameya"</note> in their results. Whatever behavior and results were stated for dogs, the same should be understood for jackals. However, this is the distinction—for these jackals...

# Chapter on the Omens of Jackals

In the winter season, during the months of Magha and Phalguna <note>roughly January to March</note>, there is a "slow manifestation" or weak appearance of their calls. Therefore, in the winter, their cries are considered fruitless or ineffective. At the end of a cry, if the sound "Hum" is followed immediately by "Tata," this is considered a "Full" <term>Purna: a favorable, resonant sound</term> note. All other notes are said to be "Blazing" <term>Dipta: harsh, over-excited, or ill-omened</term>. ||1||

->Now, he describes the behavior of the female fox <note>Lomashika</note> in this same context:<-

> The "Kakka" sound of the female fox
> Is considered Full and arises from her natural disposition.
> Any other sounds she makes that deviate from her nature
> Are all declared by the sages to be Blazing. ||2||

The word "Khalu" here is used in the sense of "now." The "Kakka" sound of the female fox is "Full," and it arises from her very nature—it is produced naturally. Any other sounds or voices that depart from her natural state are all declared to be "Blazing" <note>meaning they carry a warning of intensity or danger</note>. ||2||

->Now, he describes the behavior of the jackal <note>Shiva</note>:<-

> A jackal is auspicious in the East and North;
> When peaceful, she is honored in every direction.
> Facing the "Smoky" direction with a blazing voice,
> She destroys the Lords of the Directions. ||3||

The "Shiva" or female jackal is "praised" (auspicious) in the East and North directions. When she is "Peaceful"—meaning she has a calm cry and is standing in a peaceful quarter—she is honored as a giver of good fortune in every direction. The direction toward which the sun is heading is called "Smoky" <term>Dhumita</term>. If a jackal faces the Smoky direction and has a "Blazing voice" (a cruel or harsh sound), she "destroys the Lords of the Directions." This means she brings ruin to the ruler or presiding authority of that specific quarter. ||3||

->Now, for the purpose of knowing which "Lord" resides in which direction, he says:<-

> The King, the Prince, the Leader, and the Messenger;
> The Merchant, the Spy, the Brahmin, and the Elephant-Commander;
> These are the lords of the East and so on;
> While the Warriors and others occupy the four cardinal points. ||4||

The King <note>Raja</note> is in the East. The Prince <note>Kumara</note> is in the South-East. The Leader or Commander of the army <note>Neta</note> is in the South. The Messenger or envoy <note>Duta</note> is in the South-West. The Merchant or Chief <note>Shresthi</note> is in the West. The Spy or secret agent <note>Chara</note> is in the North-West. The Brahmin <note>Dvija</note> is in the North. The Commander of the Elephant Stable <note>Gajadhyaksha</note> is in the North-East. These should be known in order starting from the East. Likewise, the castes are in the four cardinal directions: Warriors <note>Kshatriyas</note> in the East, Traders <note>Vaishyas</note> in the South, Laborers <note>Shudras</note> in the West, and Priests <note>Brahmins</note> in the North. ||4||

# In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary
## [Chapter 89]

He says something further—

**A "blazing" jackal is inauspicious in all directions, and especially unfavorable during the day. In a city or an army, if she is on the right side or facing the sun, she brings great distress. ||5||**

A "blazing" <note>term: Dīptā; refers to a jackal facing the sun or crying out in a particularly harsh, "burning" manner</note> jackal is inauspicious and yields undesirable results in all directions. During the day, she is excessively unfavorable. In a city or within an army, if she stands on the right side <note>original: "apasavyā"; literally "to the right," often considered unlucky in specific ritual contexts</note> or faces the sun, the jackal brings suffering—meaning she is ill-omened. ||5||

Now he describes the results based on specific cries—

**The cry "Yāhi" foretells fear of fire; "Tā-ṭā" announces a death. "Dhig-dhig" speaks of a great crime, and a "flaming" jackal destroys the country. ||6||**

When the jackal cries "Yāhi" <note>Go!</note>, she tells of fear of fire or danger from flames. With the cry "Tā-ṭā," she is a "death-announcer" <note>original: "mṛtavedikā"</note>; she announces a death, such as that of a relative. Some read this as "announcer of the dead." With the cry "Dhig-dhig" <note>Fie! Shame!</note>, she speaks of a very great sin or evil deed. One that is "flaming" <note>sajvālā; appearing to vomit fire</note> destroys the lands. ||6||

On this very point, he provides a different opinion—

**They do not attribute cruelty to the "flaming" jackal because of the sun; her mouth is like the sun or fire simply due to the nature of her saliva. ||7||**

Certain sages, such as Kashyapa and others, do not declare the "flaming" jackal to be cruel or terrible. For what reason? He says "like the sun or fire." The mouth of that jackal is like the sun or fire due to the nature of her saliva. Just as the sun and other luminous objects are fiery and radiant by their very nature, her mouth is fiery because of the nature of her saliva; therefore, she is not necessarily cruel. As Kashyapa says:

> There is no cruelty in the flaming jackal by nature.
> Because her mouth is fiery from her saliva, that jackal is actually a giver of auspiciousness.

Some read the text as "like a whirled firebrand" <note>original: "ākrāntānalavat"</note>. Just as a piece of wood containing fire, when grasped and whirled around, appears to have fire everywhere, so too her mouth appears fiery due to the nature of her saliva. Thus, she is "flaming" because of the natural properties of her mouth-fluid. ||7||

---

<margin>1. "Mṛtavedikā" is an alternative reading.</margin>
<margin>2. "Ākrāntānalavat" (like a whirled firebrand) is an alternative reading.</margin>

# Chapter on the Cries of Jackals
<page-num>959</page-num>
<sig>[Chapter 89]</sig>

The author says something further:

->**A jackal in the south, answered by another, foretells death by hanging.**<-
->**That same jackal in the west, answered by another, foretells death in water. ||8||**<-

If a jackal located in the southern direction <note>original: "yamya"</note> is answered by another jackal, it foretells death by hanging <note>original: "udbandhana-mrita"</note>; it speaks of or announces a death caused by suspension. If that same jackal is in the western direction <note>original: "varuni"</note> and is answered by another, it announces the death of a relative or similar person in water. ||8||

### He now describes the results based on the number of sounds:

->**Calmness, hearing something desired, gain of wealth, and the arrival of a loved one;**<-
->**Agitation, a rift among leaders, and the prosperity of vehicles. ||9||**<-
->**This fruit is to be understood up to the seventh cry; any cry beyond that is ignored.**<-
->**In the south, the results are reversed, except for the fifth and sixth. ||10||**<-

**Regarding "Calmness" etc.:** If that jackal cries once and then remains silent, there is "calmness" or a lack of turmoil in that region. If it cries twice and then falls silent, then there is the "hearing of something desired"—the listening to something intended or favorable. Likewise, at the third cry, there is "gain of wealth" or financial profit. At the fourth, the "arrival of a loved one" or a dear person. At the fifth, "agitation" or turmoil. At the sixth, a "rift among leaders"; there occurs a mutual division or falling out among the principal royal officials. At the seventh, there is "prosperity of vehicles" such as horses and the like. Prosperity means their increase or growth. ||9||

**Regarding "This fruit up to the seventh":** This aforementioned result of the jackal's cry is valid up to the seventh howl; if it cries beyond that, that sound is "not to be taken" because it is fruitless. **Regarding "In the south":** If the jackal is stationed in the southern direction, those same results are to be understood as "reversed" or contrary, but "except for the fifth and sixth" <note>original: "shat-panchamad-rite"</note>. For those two (the 5th and 6th), the previously stated result remains the same, while for the others, the opposite occurs. **The meaning is this:** At the first cry, agitation. At the second, hearing something unpleasant. At the third, loss of wealth. At the fourth, separation from a loved one. At the fifth, agitation remains the same. At the sixth, the rift among leaders remains the same. At the seventh, the lack of prosperity or loss of vehicles. Beyond the seventh, it is not to be considered as it is without effect. ||10||

### Now he describes an inauspicious jackal:

->**That jackal which, by its cry, causes goosebumps in humans**<-
->**and the voiding of dung and urine in horses, or creates terror, is not a bringer of luck. ||11||**<-

That female jackal <note>original: "Shiva"; in Sanskrit literature, the female jackal is often used for divination</note> which, through its howling, produces horripilation <note>hair standing on end</note> in men, or causes horses to void dung and urine, or creates terror and fear among people—she does not bestow auspiciousness <note>original: "Shiva-prada"; a play on the word Shiva meaning both jackal and auspicious</note>. ||91||

### Now, he describes the auspicious signs—

->When a female jackal falls silent in response to the cries of men, elephants, or horses,<-
->she bestows welfare upon the army or the city.<- ||92||

That female jackal which, when answered by the shouts of men, the trumpeting of elephants, or the neighing of horses, becomes silent and remains still—she grants welfare and prosperity to the army or the city. ||92||

### He describes other types of cries—

->The cry "Bhe-bhe" by a jackal is terrifying; "Bho-bho" indicates calamity.<-
->The cry "Phi-phe" foretells death or imprisonment, while "Hu-hu" is beneficial to oneself.<- ||93||

When the jackal cries "Bhe-bhe," she becomes a bringer of fear. When she cries "Bho-bho," she indicates a specific or great calamity. Regarding the cry "Phi-phe": when she howls "Phi-phe," she announces death or captivity. A jackal howling the sound "Hu-hu" is beneficial to oneself; she brings welfare and prosperity to the listener. ||93||

### He says further—

->If, from a peaceful direction, she howls starting with the letter 'A', or cries a loud "Ta-ta,"<-
->or first "Tan-te" and then "The-the," that cry arises from her own contentment.<- ||94||

A female jackal situated in a "peaceful" direction <note>a technical term in augury for directions not facing the sun</note> with a sweet voice, who howls immediately after the vowel 'A'—meaning she utters 'A' first and then follows it with a long 'A'—or if she howls a loud, forceful "Ta-ta," or if she first cries "Tan-te" and afterwards "The-the," that cry of the jackal arises from her own satisfaction. This is considered a good omen. ||94||

### He says further—

->She who first utters a loud, fierce sound and then howls like a male jackal,<-
->predicts safety, the acquisition of wealth, or a reunion with a beloved who is abroad.<- ||95||
