# Chapter on the Movements of Deer
<page-num>961</page-num>
<meta>Section label: [Section 90]</meta>

If a female jackal <note>original: "Shiva"</note> first cries out with a loud, harsh, and cruel sound, and immediately afterward howls in a manner natural to a jackal, such a cry foretells safety and well-being. It signifies "Kshema"—the protection of what has been acquired—and the attainment of wealth. Alternatively, it predicts a reunion with a beloved person who has traveled to a foreign land. || 15 ||

->Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, named "The Cries of the Jackal," in the Commentary on the Samhita composed by the venerable Bhattotpala.<-

---

### Now, the Movements of Deer are explained.

And regarding that, he [Varahamihira] says—

->**Wild deer standing at the village boundary, crying out,**<-
->**Whether staying still, departing, or approaching;**<-
->**If they are "blazing" <note>A technical term in divination meaning facing the sun or crying harshly</note>, they indicate danger in the present, past, or future,**<-
->**And if wandering all around, they make the place desolate. || 1 ||**<-

"Wild" means those born in the forest, such as the <term>Rishya</term> <note>white-footed antelope</note>, <term>Prishata</term> <note>spotted deer</note>, and <term>Ruru</term> <note>a species of stag</note>. "At the boundary" means standing at the edge of the village and crying out there. If they remain standing right there while "blazing," they announce danger "presently," on that very day. If they are seen departing or going away from that boundary area, they announce "past danger"—danger that has already moved on. If they are "approaching" or coming toward the village while "blazing" and crying, they announce "future dangers" or upcoming perils. If they wander all around the town, they make the town "desolate" or uninhabited. || 1 ||

He says something further—

->**If those deer are answered by the cries of domestic animals,**<-
->**They portend fear; if by wild animals, they portend a siege.**<-
->**If answered by both, or if the deer cry out while being**<-
->**captured, they portend the taking of prisoners. || 2 ||**<-

Those deer at the boundary, if "blazing" and answered by the cries of "domestic beings" (creatures living in the village), it leads to "fear" for the town. If they are answered by "wild beings," it leads to a "siege" of the town, meaning the town will be blocked by enemies. If those deer at the boundary are answered by both domestic and wild creatures—meaning sounds are made in response by both—it leads to "the taking of prisoners" <note>original: "Vandigraha"</note>. A "prisoner" refers to a woman who is carried away by force...

The capture of prisoners is feared. Wild animals also indicate the capture of prisoners. This means that the city will be taken by enemies by force. ||2||

**He says something further—**

->If a wild creature stays at the gate of the city,<-
->a siege is predicted; if it enters, destruction.<-
->If it gives birth there, death occurs; if it dies there, fear;<-
->and if it enters a house, imprisonment is foretold. ||3||<-

If a wild creature—an animal born in the forest—stays at the gate, a siege <note>original: "rodha," meaning a blockade or surrounding by enemies</note> of the city itself should be predicted. If it enters the middle of the city, the destruction of the city must be declared. If it gives birth in that same place, death will occur. If it stays there and dies, there will be fear. If it enters a house, the imprisonment of the master of the house is foretold. ||3||

### Now, the Gestures of Cows are explained.

**He says the following—**

->Cows that are dejected bring misfortune to the king;<-
->those pawing the ground with their feet bring diseases.<-
->With long eyes full of tears, they cause the death<-
->of their master; if frightened and lowing, they indicate thieves. ||1||<-

Cows that are dejected—those with withered faces and in a state of misery—bring misfortune <note>original: "ashivaya," meaning inauspiciousness or ill-luck</note> to the king. Likewise, those pawing or tearing up the earth with their feet (hooves) bring about diseases. Those with long eyes full of tears cause the death of their master. Furthermore, if they are frightened and lowing—making a great deal of noise—they indicate the coming of thieves. ||1||

**He says something further—**

->If a bull bellows without cause, it means disaster;<-
->at night, it is for welfare. If cows are greatly<-
->covered by flies or by dogs, there will be immediate rain. ||2||<-

<summary>This page concludes the omens regarding wild animals entering cities and begins the section on bovine omens, detailing how the physical state and behavior of cows and bulls predict the fate of kings and householders.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on animal omens, transitioning from the behavior of cattle and buffaloes to the signs associated with horses.</meta>

<page-num>963</page-num>
<header>[Chapter 92] Chapter on the Gestures of Horses. 963</header>

If a cow bellows or cries out without cause—that is, for no reason—then it results in misfortune. "Cause" refers to things like water or grass; anything else is "without cause." If it bellows at night, it leads to fear. However, a tamed bull bellowing at night leads to auspiciousness and well-being. If the cattle are heavily swarmed or covered by flies, or surrounded by the offspring of Sarama <note>Sarama is the divine female dog in Vedic mythology; her offspring are dogs.</note>, then it will bring rain very quickly. ||2||

The author says something further:

> **"Cows that come home with a lowing sound,**
> **And frequent the fold, are for the increase of the herd.**
> **Those with wet bodies, or with hair standing on end in joy,**
> **Are blessed; and the same applies to buffaloes." ||3||**

Cows coming to the house (the home) accompanied by a lowing sound—a sweet sound—and frequenting the area, are blessed and excellent for the increase of the cow-pen (the growth of the herd). <note>The commentator notes a grammatical shift in case, gender, or number here based on the sense of the verse.</note> They cause the growth of wealth in cattle. Some read the text as "from the distance of a *gavyuti*" <gloss>1</gloss>. A *gavyuti* is a measure of distance equal to two *krosas* <note>approximately 2 to 4 miles</note>. Therefore, the lowing sound should be interpreted as before. "With wet bodies" means their limbs or body parts are moistened with water. "With hair standing on end" means they have goosebumps from thrill. "Joyful" means filled with delight. Such cows are blessed for the prosperity of the herd. "The same applies to buffaloes" means that in this same manner—starting from "coming home with a lowing sound" and including "miserable cows lead to the misfortune of the king"—the auspicious and inauspicious signs for buffaloes should be understood as being the same as those for cows. ||3||

-> **Thus ends the ninety-first chapter named "The Gestures of Cows"** <-
-> **in the *Exposition of the Compendium* composed by Bhattotpala.** <-

### Now, the Gestures of Horses are explained.

The author says:

> **Fire appearing on the anus is not auspicious, nor on the seat,**
> **Or on the left side; other locations are praised.**
> **Fire on all limbs, or sparks and smoke appearing**
> **For two years, brings no growth to horses. ||1||**

--- Page 456 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of omens related to horses, specifically focusing on the phenomenon of spontaneous combustion or "burning" (jvalana) on various parts of a horse's body, as detailed in Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita with a commentary.</meta>

<page-num>964</page-num>
<header>In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 92]</header>

As a general rule, it is not auspicious. This rule regarding the "burning" <note>original: "jvalana"; likely referring to static electricity, phosphorescence, or a metaphorical omen of heat/inflammation</note> of horses applies where no exception is mentioned. "Behind the seat"—the seat refers to the place where the saddle is positioned. Burning located behind that, in the posterior part, is not auspicious or praiseworthy. "And on the left"—on the left side or left flank relative to that same saddle position, it is also not good. Therefore, other than these—meaning in the front part and on the right side—it is considered praiseworthy and highly desirable. When, due to a portentous disturbance <term>utpata: a natural or supernatural calamity or omen</term>, a form of fire is seen on the limbs of horses, that is "burning of all limbs." Such burning of all limbs—of every part of the body—is "non-growth-giving"; it brings about lack of prosperity or destruction. And it is said:

->In this regard, as a general rule, burning that relies on the rear part of the seat is thus<-
->not desired; elsewhere it is praised, and similarly on the sides other than the left.<-

"For two years, sparks of fire and smoke." If, for a horse, sparks of fire or smoke are seen continuously for a period of two years, then that truly brings about the destruction of that horse. || 1 ||

### Now he speaks regarding other body parts—

> **The harem meets destruction if the penis [burns];**
> **The treasury goes to ruin if the belly is inflamed.**
> **In the anus and the tail, there would be defeat;**
> **Burning of the mouth and the head brings victory. || 2 ||**

If the penis <note>original: "medhra"</note> of horses is inflamed, the King's harem <note>original: "antahpuram"</note> meets destruction or reaches its end. If the belly or stomach is inflamed or burning, the treasury <note>original: "kosha"</note> or storehouse goes to ruin. If the anus or the tail is burning, there would be defeat in battle. The "mouth" is the face. The "best limb" <note>original: "uttamanga"</note> is the head. Burning of the mouth and the head results in victory. || 2 ||

### Now he speaks regarding yet other limbs—

> **The burning of the shoulder and the seat leads to victory;**
> **Burning of the feet is declared to lead to captivity.**
> **Smoke on the forehead, chest, eyes, and arms**
> **leads to defeat; but burning [on these parts] leads to victory. || 3 ||**

The "shoulders" are the two scapulae. The "seat" is the place of the saddle. The shoulders are situated at the sides of the neck. The burning of these—the shoulders and the seat—leads to victory. The "feet" are the hooves. The burning of the feet is declared or said to lead to the "binding" or captivity of the owner. In that case, the owner faces imprisonment. Regarding "the forehead," etc.: the forehead is the upper part of the face.

# Chapter on the Gestures of Horses

<page-num>195</page-num>

The chest region. The eyes. The arms or forelegs. If smoke is seen on any of these parts of the horses, it leads to defeat. Defeat arises from the enemy. If fire <note>original: "jvalanaṃ"; refers to a miraculous glowing or spontaneous combustion in omen literature</note> appears on any of these same parts, it leads to victory. ||3||

### He says something further —

-> Glowing at night on the nostrils, the snout, the head, <-
-> the tear-ducts, or the eyes leads to victory. <-
-> For those colored like the Palasha flower, copper, black, or variegated, <-
-> and always for the parrot-colored or white horse, this is desired. ||4|| <-

The two nostrils. The snout is the middle part of the nose. The head is the crown. The tear-duct <note>original: "aśrupāta"; literally where tears fall</note> is the lower part of the cheek. The eyes. If glowing occurs on any of these at night, it leads to victory. "Palasha" refers to the color of the Palasha flower <note>a bright orange-red</note>. "Copper" is a reddish-brown color. "Black" is dark. "Variegated" <note>original: "karbura"</note> is a mixture of white and black; it means pigeon-colored. For horses of these colors, as well as those the color of a parrot <note>bright green</note> or white, the glowing of one, two, or many of these body parts is always—at all times, day or night—considered "desired" or auspicious. And it is said:

> Fire, burning sparks, or smoke appearing on the mouth, feet, mane, or tail
> brings fear to the kingdom, grief, agitation, and the crushing of the army by the enemy.
> Similar results are specified for the back, the hindquarters, and the hair of the tail.
> Rebellion in the inner palace occurs if the penis glows or smokes.
> Burning flames and sparks are always [inauspicious] on the hair-follicles.
> Smoke on the shoulder, the seat, or the back leads to imprisonment; on the feet, likewise.
> But on the chest, eyes, forehead, and arms of horses, or neighing from their mouths,
> the production of flame gives victory, while the production of smoke leads to [the enemy's] nature.
> On the nostrils, tear-ducts, snout, head, and eyes at night,
> glowing leads to victory for copper, black, green, and brindled horses.
> For the very white and the parrot-colored, glowing on these parts always leads to victory.
> And thus, as applicable, the results for other mounts <note>such as elephants or chariots</note> should be understood. ||4||

### He describes other behaviors —

**A hatred for fodder and water; falling down; sweating without cause;**
**trembling; the falling of blood from the mouth; or the appearance of smoke.**

<meta>This page continues the discussion of equine omens (Shalihotra) from the previous section, focusing on physical symptoms and behavioral signs in horses.</meta>

<page-num>966</page-num>
<header>The Great Compilation with Commentary</header>
<sig>[Chapter 92]</sig>

### Lack of sleep when among rivals at night; sleepiness, laziness, and brooding during the day;
### Exhaustion, a downward-hanging head—these behaviors in horses are remembered as unfavorable. || 5 ||

Regarding the "dislike of fodder": there is a dislike or aversion toward fodder (grass and the like) and water. Likewise, falling down or collapsing. Sweat (perspiration) occurring without a cause or reason. Or trembling without a cause. The falling or flowing of blood from the mouth, ears, or other parts. "Lack of sleep when among rivals at night": staying awake at night while among those who harbor enmity. During the day, sleepiness, laziness, and "brooding" (anxiety or deep thought). "Exhaustion" refers to a sinking of the chest. "Downward-hanging head" means not looking upward. These behaviors of <term>Vajins</term> <note>Vajin: a common Sanskrit term for a horse, literally meaning "the swift one" or "possessing strength"</note> are remembered and stated to be "unfavorable" or inauspicious. 

As it is said:

> Horses that have blocked sleep and lazy, dark eyes, whose memory is vacant from brooding during the days, and who lose sleep due to mutual rivalry at night, do not bring welfare to their master. || 5 ||

He describes another behavior:

### The mounting of other horses by a horse equipped with a saddle and gear,
### Or the same by a royal mount; even if the horse is healthy, this indicates a loss of prosperity. || 6 ||

For a horse equipped with a "saddle and gear"—the word "gear" includes the rider—to mount other horses is inauspicious. Likewise, if another horse mounts a horse that is fully saddled. "Or of a royal mount": this refers to the <term>Upavahya</term> <note>Upavahya: a specially trained horse or elephant used specifically for the king to ride</note> or the horse used for travel. Even if the horse is "healthy" (in good condition), such behavior is "a loss of prosperity," meaning it is not desired. || 6 ||

Now he describes the characteristics of neighing:

### A neigh like the cry of a crane brings the destruction of enemies,
### As does a neigh with a motionless neck and the face turned upwards;
### Or a neigh that is resonant, loud, echoing, and joyful,
### Even when the horses' mouths are filled with fodder. || 7 ||

The <term>Krauncha</term> <note>Krauncha: the Sarus crane, known in Indian literature for its resonant, trumpeting call</note> is a bird. A neigh or sound that resembles the cry of the crane bird leads to the "destruction of enemies." Likewise, a neigh with a "motionless neck" (steady) and "turned upwards" (with the face held high) also leads to the destruction of enemies. "Resonant" means sweet; "loud" means making it very clear and high; "echoing" means it rings out afterward like the sound of a bell. "Joyful" means full of satisfaction. "With mouths filled with fodder": even when their mouths are obstructed by a mouthful of food, if they neigh in this manner, it results in the destruction of enemies. || 7 ||

# Chapter on the Gestures of Horses

### The author says another thing—

->**A full vessel, curd, a priest, a deity,**<-
->**Fragrance, flowers, fruit, gold, and the like,**<-
->**Or any other pleasing object—if these are**<-
->**Near horses when they neigh, victory follows. ||88||**<-

A "full vessel" refers to a container filled with auspicious materials such as mustard seeds, unbroken grains, or rice. "Curd" is a derivative of milk. A "priest" refers to a Brahmin. "Deity" refers to a divine image or idol. "Fragrance" refers to specific aromatic substances like aloe-wood, camphor, musk, and so on. "Flowers" are blossoms. "Fruit" refers to items like the wood-apple <note>original: "shriphala"</note>. "Gold" is the precious metal. The phrase "and the like" includes silver, gems, pearls, and similar items. Or "any other pleasing" auspicious substance might be present, such as white mustard or yellow orpiment <note>original: "gorocana," a bright yellow pigment found in cattle, considered highly auspicious</note>. If these are in the vicinity or close proximity to horses while they are <term>neighing</term> <note>original: "hreshatam" — the specific sound of a horse</note>, then victory is assured. ||88||

---

### The author says another thing—

->**Horses that delight in food, drink, or the bit, or in their master’s equipment,**<-
->**Or those whose gaze is fixed toward their right side,**<-
->**Grant the fruits of one's desired goals. ||89||**<-

"Food" refers to edible substances. "Drink" is water. The <term>bit</term> <note>original: "khalina" — the metal mouthpiece of a bridle</note> is the horse's curb. If they show delight in these, or if they show delight in the "master’s equipment"—meaning whatever gear is used by the owner—it is a good sign. Alternatively, it is favorable if their "gaze is fixed toward their right side" <note>original: "savya-parshva" — in this technical context of omens, it refers to the horse looking toward its own right</note>. Horses of this kind grant the "fruits of one's desired goals," meaning they provide the results of one's cherished aims. As it has been said:

> Beyond this, one should observe the neighing that reveals the pleasant or unpleasant.
> That neighing which occurs with the neck moved and extended is of desirable fruit.
> So too is the neighing of those with mouths full of fodder—loud, glossy, resonant, and deep.
> When accompanied by two full vessels, desired objects, garlands, fragrances, or incense.
> Their delight in the bit, food, drink, or the master’s equipment,
> And their looking toward the right side, shall lead to the accomplishment of all goals. ||9||

---

### Now he describes inauspicious behaviors—

->**Striking the earth with their left hooves, they portend travel for the master.**<-
->**If they neigh while looking toward the blazing sun during the twilights,**<-
->**It leads to imprisonment or defeat. ||90||**<-

<summary>This page details auspicious omens related to horses, such as neighing near sacred objects or looking to the right, which predict victory. It also warns that striking the ground with left hooves or neighing at the sun during twilight foretells travel, captivity, or loss.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita, specifically Chapter 92 regarding the omens of horses (Ashva-Lakshana). It follows the discussion of unfavorable behaviors and transitions into favorable signs.</meta>

<page-num>968</page-num>
<header>In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 92]</header>

If horses strike the earth or the ground with their left feet <note>original: "vamaishcha padair"</note>, it indicates the journey or departure of their master or owner. Furthermore, during the four periods of the day—sunrise, midday, sunset, and midnight—if they look toward a "blazing" direction <note>a direction associated with the sun's current position or ill omens</note> and neigh, they bring about imprisonment and defeat. They cause the bondage and downfall of their lord. // 10 //

### He says something further —

->If they neigh excessively or toss their tails,<-
->Or if they are constantly sleeping, they announce a journey.<-
->Those shedding hair, or possessing a piteous or harsh voice,<-
->Or seen swallowing dust, are signs of danger. // 11 //<-

"Excessively" means to a great degree; they neigh or make noise, and likewise "toss their tails" means they flick or scatter the hairs of their tail. Those "constantly sleeping" or prone to dreaming announce a "journey" or departure. Likewise, "shedding hair" means they lose or cast off their coat. "Piteous or harsh voices" refers to those with weak, faint sounds or rough, grating noises. Those seen "swallowing dust" or eating earth are signs of danger. They announce fear for the master. As it has been said:

> Those who, during the twilights, are agitated toward a blazing direction, have stammering voices, or lose sleep,
> And neigh, are generators of fear and bringers of slaughter, bondage, and defeat.
> Those with curved tails or those who lie down on their right side are not desired.
> Those striking the surface of the earth with their left feet are to be known as signs of departure. // 11 //

### Now he describes the auspicious signs —-

->Those who lie on their right side like a casket,<-
->And those who stand with their right foot raised,<-
->Lead to victory; the wise should apply these results to other<-
->mounts as well, as far as they are applicable. // 12 //<-

"Like a casket" <note>term: Samudga-vat; refers to a specific tucked position of the legs resembling a folding box</note> means drawing the knees together and sleeping on the right side of the body. Likewise, those who stand having "raised the right foot" and then placing it firmly on the ground—horses of this nature lead to the victory of the lord. Regarding "other mounts": the wise scholar should apply these auspicious and inauspicious results to other vehicles such as elephants, camels, and so on, "as far as they are applicable." For instance, while smoke and sparks of fire <note>mentioned in previous verses</note> might not be possible for all animals, other signs are. Thus the wise man should proclaim. // 12 //

It concludes by noting that these principles of augury apply to other mounts like elephants and camels.</summary>

# [Chapter 92] The Chapter on the Gestures of Horses | 969

Now, he describes further auspicious behaviors:

> **When the king mounts, the horse that is well-behaved,**
> **follows the direction of the journey, and neighs in response to other horses;**
> **or the one who touches his own right side with his mouth,**
> **that horse quickly increases the fortune of his master. || 13 ||**

When the king or sovereign mounts, the horse or steed that is <term>well-behaved</term><note>original: "vinayopapanna" - disciplined or showing good conduct</note> and follows the direction of the journey—meaning he moves toward the same direction the king intends to go—and <term>neighs in response</term><note>original: "pratihreṣate"</note> to other horses; that is, when another horse neighs, he makes a sound in return. Or, if he touches his own right side with his face or mouth, he quickly increases the <term>Fortune</term><note>original: "Lakshmi" - prosperity and royal success</note> of his lord or master. || 13 ||

Now, he describes inauspicious omens:

> **The horse that repeatedly urinates and defecates,**
> **who does not move in the desired direction even when struck,**
> **who is frightened without cause and has tearful eyes,**
> **does not portend well-being for his master. || 14 ||**

The horse or steed that repeatedly—at every moment—passes urine and <term>dung</term><note>original: "shakrit" - excrement</note>; who, even when struck with whips and such, does not move in the <term>favorable direction</term><note>original: "anulomayāyī" - moving with the grain or in the intended path</note>; who is <term>frightened without cause</term><note>original: "akāryabhītaḥ"</note>, meaning he shows fear without the presence of buffaloes, boars, or other threats; and whose eyes are filled with tears—he does not grant or indicate <term>auspiciousness</term><note>original: "shivam" - welfare or good fortune</note> for his master or owner. || 14 ||

> **This behavior of horses has been told; hereafter I shall speak of elephants,**
> **regarding the trimming of their tusks, their breaking, their fading, and other gestures. || 15 ||**

This behavior of horses has been declared. Following this, I shall speak of and describe the <term>tusked ones</term><note>original: "dantinām" - elephants</note>. Their omens are determined by the trimming of the tusks, the breaking of the tusks, the cracking or fading of the tusks, and their general movements. By the inclusion of the word "and others," results are also derived from other royal equipment and circumstances. || 15 ||

-> Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, named "The Gestures of Horses," in the Section on Omens within the Commentary on the Samhita composed by the venerable Bhattotpala. || 92 || <-

### Now, the behavior of elephants<gloss>1</gloss> is explained.

->First, the rule for the carving of the tusks is stated:<-

> Having left a length equal to twice the circumference of the tusk at its base, one should cut the remaining part. For elephants living in marshy lands, a little more should be left; for those roaming in the mountains, a little less. ||1||

The "circumference at the base" refers to the girth or roundness at the root of the tooth (tusk). One should measure the circumference at the base of the tusk with a string, double that length, and measure that distance out from the root along the length of the tusk. That portion is to be left alone, and the remaining part should be carved or cut. This is what is meant: after measuring the girth with a string, doubling it, and setting that length aside from the root, the rest is shaped. Regarding "more for those in marshy lands": marshy lands (<term>Anupa</term><note>Anupa refers to regions with abundant water and lush vegetation</note>) produce elephants whose tusks require leaving a bit more than twice the circumference. For "mountain-dwellers" (<term>Giricharin</term>), those who always roam the hills, one should leave a little less than twice the circumference before cutting the rest. As it has been said:

> "One should cut the tusk only after leaving a length equal to twice the girth of the tusk's root." ||1||

Now, the signs observed on the cut surface of the tusk are described:

> <gloss>2</gloss>If marks resembling the Shrivatsa, the Vardhamana, a parasol, a banner, or a fly-whisk are seen on the cut surface, they bring health, victory, increase in wealth, and happiness. ||2||

The <term>Shrivatsa</term><note>A mystical mark or curl of hair, often associated with the chest of Vishnu</note> and the <term>Vardhamana</term><note>A "prosperous" figure or diagram, often shaped like a shallow bowl or a specific geometric pattern</note> are specific auspicious symbols. The "parasol" is the royal sunshade. The "banner" is well-known. The "fly-whisk" (<term>Chamara</term>) is the fan made of yak-tail hair. If marks similar to these are observed upon the cut surface, there will be freedom from disease, victory, growth of riches, and contentment. ||2||

He says more:

> If the marks resemble weapons, there is victory; if like the Nandyavarta, the recovery of a lost territory; if like a clod of earth, the attainment of a land previously held. ||3||

A "weapon" refers to things like a sword. If shapes resembling weapons are seen in the cut, victory follows. The <term>Nandyavarta</term><note>A complex auspicious diagram or labyrinthine swastika-like symbol</note> is a specific sacred mark. If a cut resembling the Nandyavarta is seen, there is the gain of a territory that was previously lost or snatched away. If it looks like a "clod of earth" (<term>Losta</term>), meaning the shape of a lump of clay, there is the re-acquisition of a land formerly possessed.

# Chapter on the Behavior of Elephants
<page-num>171</page-num>
<sig>[Section 93]</sig>

<note>The text begins by concluding a previous thought regarding the acquisition of wealth or animals.</note>
It occurs. "Previously obtained" refers to something already acquired. If an elephant is obtained in name only but has not yet physically arrived, its actual arrival and possession will now take place. ||3||

The author says another thing:

**If the cut resembles a woman, horses will perish; if it looks like a ceremonial water-vessel, a son will be born.**
**If it looks like a pot, treasure will be found; if it looks like a staff, there will be obstacles to travel. ||4||**

If a cut in the tusk is seen in the form of a woman—having the shape of a female—there will be the destruction or loss of horses. A *bhringara* <note>original: "bhringara"</note> is a ceremonial water-vessel or pitcher. If the cut arises in the shape of such a vessel, the birth of a son is possible. With a shape like a *kumbha* <note>original: "kumbha"</note> or water-pot, there is the acquisition of treasure. With the shape of a *danda* <note>original: "danda"</note> or staff, there is an obstacle to a journey, meaning a prohibition against traveling. ||4||

The author says another thing:

**In the shapes of a chameleon, a monkey, or a snake, there will be famine, disease, and subjection to enemies.**
**In the shapes of a vulture, an owl, a crow, or a hawk, there will be a plague among the people. ||5||**

A *krikalasa* <note>original: "krikalasa"</note> is a specific creature, a chameleon. A *kapi* is a monkey. A *bhujanga* is a snake. If these are seen in the cut of the tusk, there will be famine, diseases (afflictions), and subjection to enemies—meaning becoming subservient to one's foes. The vulture and the owl are well-known birds. A *dhvanksha* is a crow. A *shyena* is a hawk. If the cuts are seen resembling the forms of these birds, a *maraka* <note>original: "maraka"</note> or plague/epidemic occurs among the people. ||5||

The author says another thing:

**If it looks like a noose or a headless trunk, the king dies; if blood flows, the people suffer calamity.**
**If the cut is black, dark-tawny, rough, or foul-smelling, it brings misfortune. ||6||**

A *pasha* <note>original: "pasha"</note> is a noose, shaped like a snake. A *kabandha* <note>original: "kabandha"</note> is a man with a severed head. If a cut is seen resembling these, there is *nripamrityu*—the death or passing of the king. If blood <note>original: "rakta"</note> flows from the tusk, the people will face disasters and calamities. If the cut is black in color; *shyava* <note>original: "shyava"</note> or dark/sooty; rough (not smooth); or foul-smelling (having a bad odor), it results in inauspiciousness and undesirable events. As it has been said:

> "The appearance of dark-tawny, foul-smelling, dirty, or bloody marks, or shapes resembling snakes and similar creatures, bestows sin and misfortune." ||6||

Now, the author describes the characteristics of an auspicious cut:

**A cut that is white, even, fragrant, and smooth brings good fortune.**
**The oozing, withering, or fruiting of a tusk are treated the same as its breaking. ||7||**

# 972
### In the Brihat Samhita with Commentary [Chapter 93]

**White; even in all parts; fragrant (having a pleasant smell); glossy (oily or lustrous).**
**A cut of this kind brings good fortune. It is also said—**

> **When the cut tusk bears a mark resembling royal regalia, it brings wealth, victory, and increase of strength; likewise, those that are glossy, white, and pleasing are auspicious.**

**Regarding the results of "dripping" and "fading": "Dripping" refers to the crumbling or oozing of the material from its place. "Fading" refers to discoloration or a withered appearance. The results of these are equal to the results of a tooth breaking or splitting. Whatever result is described for a broken tusk, the same applies to dripping or fading. ||7||**

**The author describes other auspicious and inauspicious signs—**

->**Residing in the root, the middle, and the tip of the tusk**<-
->**are the Gods, the Demons, and Men, respectively.**<-
->**The results are great, middling, and slight,**<-
->**occurring quickly, in a medium timeframe, or after a long time. ||8||**<-

**In order, the Gods, Demons, and Men are situated at the root, the middle, and the tip of the elephant's tusk. Specifically: the Gods are established at the root; the Demons in the middle; and Men (a specific class of beings) at the tip. Therefore, from these three parts, the results are great, middling, or slight. There, at the root, the predicted result is "great" (fully nourished). In the middle, it is "middling" (neither too little nor too much). At the end/tip, it is "slight" (very small). Likewise, they occur in quick, medium, or long timeframes. At the root, the result occurs in a short time, within a week. In the middle, in a medium time, within a month. At the tip, it occurs after a long time, beyond a month—this is the rule of the tradition <note>original: "āgamavidhiḥ"</note>. ||8||**

**Here again, he describes specific details—**

->**The result of a broken tusk here on the right side**<-
->**brings flight/panic to the King, the country, and the army.**<-
->**On the left, it kills the son, the priest, and the mahouts,**<-
->**as well as the forest-chieftains, wives, and leaders. ||9||**<-

**Here, in these three sections, is the result of a broken tusk. On the right: if broken from the root, it gives "flight" <note>original: "vidrava", meaning panic or fleeing in fear</note> to the King. If broken from the middle, it brings flight to the country or district. If broken at the tip, it brings flight to the army. On the left: "fears for the son and priest." On the left tusk, if broken from the root, it kills the son (the prince). If broken from the middle, it kills the priest (the teacher/advisor). If at the tip, it kills the mahouts <note>original: "ibhayān", those who manage the elephants</note> or commanders. Likewise, for the forest-chieftains, wives, and leaders in sequence: on the left tusk, if broken from the root, it destroys the forest-dwelling forces <note>original: "sāṭavikaṃ balam"</note>. If broken from the middle, the wives (the queen/consort). If broken from the tip, it kills the leaders (the principal men). The results for "dripping" and "fading" should be understood in the same way. ||9||**

The author further explains the specific results here—

### One should predict the total destruction of the king's lineage from seeing the breaking of both tusks.
### Good fortune increases through auspicious Ascendants, lunar days, and stars; otherwise, one should declare it inauspicious. ||10||

From seeing the breaking of both tusks—"breaking" refers to cracking or splitting—if this is observed, one should predict the total, complete destruction of the king's lineage <note>Sanskrit: *kula-kshaya*</note>. The entire royal family perishes. The same applies to the falling of withered fruits. Good fortune increases through auspicious Ascendants <term>Lagna: the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon</term>, lunar days <term>Tithi</term>, and stars <term>Nakshatra</term>. The Ascendants of "gentle" or auspicious planets are Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Virgo, Libra, Sagittarius, and Pisces—those ruled by Venus, Mercury, the waxing Moon, and Jupiter. Likewise, an auspicious lunar day is one excluding the "Empty" <note>Rikta</note> days; the "Joyful" <note>Nanda</note>, "Fortunate" <note>Bhadra</note>, "Victorious" <note>Vijaya</note>, and "Full" <note>Purna</note> days are auspicious. An auspicious star is one that is not "Dreadful" or "Fierce." By the word "etcetera," it is meant that by the sight of auspicious planets, or the placement of the Ascendant in an auspicious sign, or by seeing good omens, a positive sign produced under good conditions increases in strength. One should declare the opposite for inauspicious signs. From what has been said, if there is a "cruel" Ascendant, placement, or aspect, or a flawed lunar day or star, the inauspiciousness of a bad omen increases. With a mixture of factors, the result is mixed. Where an inauspicious sign is met with an auspicious Ascendant or vice versa, a mixed result should be inferred. ||10||

---

Now he describes the specific results of the breaking of a tusk—

### If the middle of the left tusk is broken or chipped by striking trees with milky sap, sweet fruits, or flowers, or by striking the bank of a river, it brings the destruction of enemies; otherwise, the result is the opposite. ||11||

If the breaking (cracking) or chipping (splitting) occurs in the middle of the left <note>Sanskrit: *vama*</note> tusk due to striking or shaking a "milky tree" <note>trees like the Banyan or Fig that exude white sap</note>, or by shaking a tree with sweet fruits, or by shaking a flowering tree, then it causes the destruction of enemies. Or, if it occurs by striking the bank of a river <note>Sanskrit: *apaga-tata*</note>—rivers are where waters flow—it likewise causes the destruction of enemies. "Otherwise, the result is the opposite" means that if the breaking or chipping occurs by striking "wicked" <note>thorny or bitter</note> trees, or if it happens at the root or the tip of the left tusk, it causes the growth of enemies. Similarly, seeing a break at the root, middle, or tip of the right tusk also causes the growth of enemies. ||11||

---

Now he describes the elephant's gestures—

### Stumbling in its gait without cause, with frightened ears and a very miserable look, breathing softly but very deeply, with its trunk placed on the earth;
### With eyes quickly half-closed, prone to sleep, acting contrary to its nature, eating unwholesome things, and repeatedly passing impure excrement—this creates fear. ||12||

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 93]

**Stumbling suddenly without cause**, as the text says. "Suddenly" means without an apparent reason. **With ears drooping** means the ears are hanging limp. **Extremely dejected** means the animal has fallen into a state of great misery. **Breathing softly and very deeply**; that is, placing its trunk <note>literally: "hand"</note> on the ground, it breathes out softly for a long duration. **With eyes quickly blinking or half-closed**; its gaze is startled and its eyes are only partially open. **Prone to dreaming** means it sleeps for a long time. **Moving in reverse** means it moves in a direction opposite to what is desired; it does not go where it is commanded. Such an elephant **causes fear**. Likewise, **eating harmful things** means it consumes undesirable or unwholesome food. **Passing bloody excrement repeatedly**; if it voids dung containing blood many times, that also causes fear <note>original: "bhaya-kṛt", an omen of impending danger or defeat</note>.

->Now he describes auspicious behaviors:<-

> **If he joyfully destroys a mound, a stump, a thicket, a shrub, or a tree at his own will;**
> **If he moves in the direction of the march with quick steps, lifting his face high;**
> **If, at the time of being harnessed, he repeatedly sprays water from his trunk or trumpets loudly;**
> **Or if rut flows at that moment, or if he curls his trunk around his right tusk—he brings victory.**

**Mounds, stumps, thickets**, etc. An elephant of this sort is a **bringer of victory**; he secures victory for the king. This applies if he destroys a **mound** <note>original: "valmīka", an anthill or termite mound</note> made of earth. A **stump** is a tree with all its branches cut off or a dried-up tree. A **thicket** is a cluster of branches from a single root. A **shrub** refers to small plants or grasses. A **tree** is a full-grown tree. If he destroys any of these by his own will—that is, by his own impulse—and has a **joyful look** in his eyes. **Moving in the direction of the march**; he should go toward the destination of the journey with **quick steps**, moving rapidly while lifting his face or mouth high. Also, **at the time of being harnessed** <note>original: "kakṣyā-sannāha", the time of fastening the girth or belly-band</note>, if he repeatedly produces **spray**, emitting droplets of water from his mouth/trunk. Or if he produces a **trumpeting** sound like the roar of a cloud. Or if there is the **appearance of rut** <note>original: "mada", the temporal secretion indicating strength and virility</note> at that time. Likewise, **curling around the right tusk**, supporting it with his trunk.

->He describes further behaviors:<-

| The dragging | into the water | of an elephant |
|--------------|----------------|----------------|
| by a crocodile | leads to the ruin | of the king. |
| But seizing | the crocodile | and emerging |
| from water | to dry land | brings prosperity to the lord of men. |

If an elephant is pulled into the **water** by a **crocodile** <note>original: "grāha", any large aquatic predator</note> or water-creature, it signifies the ruin of the **king**...

# The Cries of Crows

It would lead to destruction. Likewise, if a crow takes a <term>graha</term> <note>a water creature, such as a crocodile or large fish</note> from an elephant and carries it from the water to the dry land, it brings prosperity to the king. **14**

->Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, named "The Movements of Elephants," in the Commentary on the Samhita composed by the illustrious Bhattotpala, within the section on Omens.<-

->Now, the cries of crows are explained.<-

At the very beginning, to show the regional divisions, the author says:

**For those in the eastern regions, crows on the right are auspicious, while <term>karayikas</term> <note>a specific type of bird, often identified as a small crane or a variety of crow</note> are auspicious on the left. In other regions, the opposite is true. The boundaries of these regions are well-known through common worldly tradition. 1**

"Easterners" refers to those living in the eastern direction. For them, crows on the right side grant auspicious results. The *karayikas* (also known as *kutapuryas*) grant auspicious results when on the left side. In other regions—excluding the eastern lands—the opposite applies: the crow is auspicious on the left and the *karayika* on the right. Regarding the regional boundaries, the author says: "The boundaries are well-known through common tradition." This means the limits are understood by popular consensus, such as knowing "these people are Easterners, these are Southerners, these are Westerners, and these are Northerners." The Teacher <note>referring to Varahamihira</note> has also demonstrated these divisions in the section on the "Division of the Globe" <note>the Kurma-vibhaga</note>. **1**

->Now, he describes their behavior:<-

**In the month of Vaishakha <note>April/May</note>, a nest built in an undamaged tree grants abundance and welfare. If built in a despised, thorny, or withered tree, there will be famine and fear in that land. 2**

In the month of Vaishakha, a nest (dwelling) in a tree that is "undamaged" (free from affliction) grants abundance and welfare; it gives plenty of food and excellence. "Despised" means contemptible. "Thorny" means possessing thorns. "Withered" means a sapless tree. In whatever land the crow builds a nest in these types of trees, there will be fears of famine in that region. **2**

->Now, he gives the results based on the position of the nest:<-

**If the nest is on an eastern branch, there will be early rain in the autumn; if on a western branch, the rain comes later. If on the southern or northern branches, there will be moderate rain. If at the top of the tree, there will be excellent rain. 3**

**In the southeast, there will be scattered rain; in the southwest, the autumn crops will reach perfection. In the remaining two directions <note>Northwest and Northeast</note>, there will be abundance, though in the northwest, there will also be a plague of mice. 4**

***

# The Great Compilation (Brihat Samhita) [Chapter 94]

**On the nest in the eastern branch:** If the nest is built in a tree on a branch facing the east, there will be rain during the autumn season <note>specifically the months of Ashvin and Kartika, roughly September to November</note>. If the nest is situated in the western direction, there will be rain during the first half of the rainy season, in the months of Shravana and Bhadrapada <note>July to September</note>. If the nest is situated in the southern or northern directions, rain occurs in the middle period, during Bhadrapada and Ashvin. If the nest is placed on the very top of the tree on the main branch, there will be excellent and abundant rain throughout all four months of the rainy season starting from Shravana. ॥3॥

**In the direction of the Fire-God:** If the nest is situated in the south-eastern direction <note>the quarter of Agni</note>, there will be "circular rain" <note>original: *mandala-vrishti*; meaning sporadic or localized rain</note>—rain in some places and drought in others. If the nest is in the south-western direction, there will be a successful harvest of the autumn crops. If the nest is in the remaining directions, the north-west or north-east, there will be abundance and good food supplies <term>Subhiksha: a state where food is easily available</term>. If in the north-western corner, there will be a great abundance and prosperity of mice. ॥4॥

Now, another behavior is described:

->**In reeds, Kusha grass, shrubs, creepers, grain, palaces, houses, or low ground;**<-
->**That region becomes desolate, afflicted by thieves, drought, and disease. ॥5॥**<-

"Reeds" (*shara*) are well known. "Kusha grass" (*darbha*) is also well known. A "shrub" (*gulma*) is a cluster of branches from a single root. "Creepers" (*valli*) are well known. "Grain" (*dhanya*) is well known. A "palace" (*prasada*) refers to a temple of a deity. A "house" (*geha*) is a dwelling. "Low ground" (*nimna*) refers to a hole or depression. In these places, wherever a crow's nest is found, that region becomes desolate. That land becomes afflicted by thieves, by drought (lack of rain), and by diseases or ailments. As stated in the *Yatra* <note>likely referring to Varahamihira's Yoga-yatra</note>:

> A nest is auspicious in the month of Vaishakha <note>April-May</note> when built on a tree free from disturbances.
> But the ruin of a country is indicated when nests are found on anthills, sacred trees, grain, or houses. ॥5॥

Another behavior is described:

->**Having two, three, or four chicks brings abundance; five brings a change of rulers.**<-
->**Scattering the eggs, having only one egg, or failing to produce offspring does not lead to welfare. ॥6॥**<-

A "chick" (*shava*) means an infant or offspring. The state of having two, three, or four chicks brings about a time of plenty. With five chicks, there is a "change of rulers" (*nripanyatvam*), meaning another takes over the kingdom; a second king arises. "Scattering the eggs" means the eggs are thrown about. "Single-egg state" means only one egg is produced. "Failing to produce offspring" means no birth occurs. All of these are "not for welfare," meaning they do not lead to prosperity or good fortune. ॥6॥

### Now he explains the specific details of these omens—

**If the young are the color of *Chauraka*, there will be thieves; if variegated, death; if white, fear of fire.**
**If the young are deformed, one should predict the fear of famine caused by the crows. ||7||**

*Chauraka* <note>original: "चौरक"; likely referring to the plant *Angelica glauca*, which has a yellowish-brown or earthy hue</note> is a fragrant substance. If the young crows are of that color, there will be thieves or robbers. If they are variegated—meaning of various colors and shapes—death occurs. If they are white, there is a fear of fire. If they are deformed—meaning missing limbs—one should declare a fear of famine caused by the young of the crows. As it has been said:

> ->Two, three, or four chicks in a crow's nest bring good fortune.<-
> ->But those colored like thieves (earthy), variegated, or white, bring robbers, fire, and death.<-
> ->If the female crow scatters her eggs, both famine and pestilence follow;<-
> ->The same occurs if the chicks are deformed or if no chicks are produced at all. || Thus verse 7 ||<-

### He says something further—

**If they gather in the middle of a village without cause and cry out loudly, there is fear of hunger.**
**If they stay in a circular formation, there is a siege; if they stay in distinct groups, there is an assault. ||8||**

If crows gather together without a visible cause in the middle of a village and cry out or caw, there is a fear of hunger or famine. If they are arranged in a circular shape like a wheel, there will be a siege of the city. If they stay in many separate groups or clusters gathered without reason, an assault or calamity occurs. As it has been said:

> ->A gathering without cause brings discord; staying in a wheel-shape brings a siege.<-
> ->Staying in groups brings an assault, and if they are fearless, it brings an increase in enemies. || Thus verse 8 ||<-

### He says something further—

**If they are fearless and attack people with their beaks, wings, or feet,**
**they cause an increase in enemies; if they wander at night, they cause the destruction of the people. ||9||**

Fearless means lacking in fear. With their "beaks" <note>original: "तुण्ड"; the tip of the beak</note>, with their "wings" <note>original: "पक्ष"; feathers/wings</note>, and with "strikes of their feet" <note>original: "चरणविघात"; kicking or clawing</note>, if they overcome or attack people, they cause an increase in enemies. If they wander or fly about at night, they cause the destruction of the people. ||9||

# In the Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 94]

### He says another thing—

->**Crows circling in the sky to the right indicate fear from one's own people; circling in the opposite direction, fear from enemies.**<-
->**When they fly in a highly agitated manner, it indicates a whirlwind or great instability. || 10 ||**<-

When crows (birds) circle in the sky to the right—that is, in a clockwise direction following the order of East, South, West, and North—there is fear from one's own kin or people. By circling in opposite orbits—following the order of East, North, West, and South—there is fear from the enemy. When crows fly in a highly agitated or energetic manner, a "wind-toss" <note>original: vātoddhrāmo; likely referring to a windstorm or general social upheaval</note> occurs, meaning a state of instability. As it has been said:

> When they are agitated in the sky above the city or the army, there is fear from the wind. Moving in right-hand circles, fear arises from one's own; in left-hand circles, fear from the enemy. || 10 ||

---

### He says another thing—

->**With faces turned upward and wings quivering, they grant fear on the path; stealing grain, they indicate fear of hunger.**<-
->**Perched on parts of the army, they indicate war; with wings like a cuckoo, they indicate robbery. || 11 ||**<-

"With faces turned upward" means their beaks are pointing toward the sky. "With quivering wings" means their feathers are shaking. These "grant fear on the path," meaning they cause danger during a journey. Those "stealing grain" <note>original: dhānyamuṣo</note> lead to the fear of hunger, meaning a famine. "Parts of the army" refers to things like saddles, bits, and other equipment; if they perch on these, they indicate a battle or conflict. The "other-nourished" <note>term: anyabhṛta; a common Sanskrit name for the Cuckoo, which leaves its eggs in other birds' nests</note> is the Cuckoo. Those crows whose wings are like the cuckoo's—meaning they have extremely black wings—cause "deprivation," which is the fear of thieves. As it has been said:

> War occurs when they stay on army equipment; they cause robbery when scratching themselves. Moving at night leads to destruction, and stealing food leads to famine. || 11 ||

---

### He says another thing—

->**Placing ashes, bones, hair, or leaves upon a bed leads to the death of the master.**<-
->**But striking the bed with a jewel or a flower indicates the birth of a son or a daughter. || 12 ||**<-

On the bed or the bedding: ashes, bones, hair from the head, or a leaf—if the crow places or drops these, it leads to the death of the master. This refers to the master or owner of the bed. As it has been said:

> Grass, ashes, bones, and hair on the bed give death to the master.

Regarding "striking with a jewel, flower, etc.": with a jewel (gem), with a flower, or—by the use of the word "etc."—with a fruit. If the crow performs a striking or tapping on the bed with these items, then the birth of a son <insert>or a daughter</insert> occurs.

# Chapter on the Behavior of Crows
<note>original: "Vāyasa-vistādhyāyaḥ"</note>

Otherwise, in this manner, if the crow avoids jewels and flowers and instead carries grass, wood, or similar materials, then a woman will be born <note>likely referring to the gender of a child to be born in the household</note>. ||12||

He says another thing—

->If the crow’s mouth is full of sand, grain, wet clay, or flowers, there is a gain of wealth.<-
->If the crow carries away vessels from a human settlement, it brings fear.<- ||13||

"Sand" refers to gravel. "Grain" is well-known. "Wet clay" is fresh earth. "Flowers" are blossoms. By the use of the word "etcetera" <note>original: "pūrva-grahaṇāt"</note>, this includes fruit and green grass. If the crow has its mouth filled with these, there is a gain of wealth. Likewise, if the crow carries away vessels from a human settlement—that is, from near people—then it gives fear. ||13||

He says another thing—

->If the crow strikes a vehicle, a weapon, a shoe, the shadow of a parasol, or a limb of the body, death occurs.<-
->If it honors these same things, one receives honor; if it leaves droppings on them, one obtains food.<- ||14||

"Vehicle" means a carriage or mount. "Weapon" means a sword or similar. "Shoe" is well-known. "Shadow of a parasol" refers to the shade of a sun-umbrella. "Limb" refers to the body. If the crow strikes or pecks at these, death occurs. If it "honors" them—meaning if it treats those same vehicles etc. with respect, as if worshipping with flowers—then the observer receives honor. If it leaves "droppings" <note>original: "viṣṭhā"</note> or excrement on these, there is the attainment of food or a meal. It is said:

->In the event of striking a shoe, a parasol, a vehicle, a limb, or the shadow of a parasol,<-
->one should predict the death of the owner; honor comes from the crow honoring them.<- ||14||

He says another thing—

->Whatever object the crow brings, that object will be gained; if it takes it away, there will be loss.<-
->Yellow objects signify gold; cotton objects signify cloth; white objects signify silver.<- ||15||

Whatever object a crow brings near, there is a gain of that specific material. If it carries an object away, then there is the destruction or loss of that material. Through yellow objects, gold is obtained (or lost if carried away). This applies to everything. Through cotton objects, one gets clothing or garments. Through white objects, silver. It is said:

->Whether the crow carries away or brings an object before a person,<-
->the loss or gain of that thing is known; yellow indicates gold.<- ||15||

### He says another thing—

> Crows perched on milky trees, the Arjuna, or the Vanjula, or standing on the sandbanks of both riverbanks, and crying out, bring rain during the monsoon; if they do this out of season, they bring foul weather. So too if they are seen bathing in dust or water. ||16||

A "milky tree" <note>original: *saksheera*</note> refers to any tree that exudes sap; the Arjuna and the Vanjula <note>The Arjuna (*Terminalia arjuna*) and Vanjula (*Ashoka* or a variety of willow) are specific botanical species</note> are particular types of trees. If crows are perched on these, or if they are "standing on the sandbanks of both riverbanks" <note>original: *kuladvaya-pulinaga*</note>—meaning they have gone to the sandy stretches on either side of a river—and are "crying out" or making noise, they cause rain during the rainy season. In a season other than the monsoon, they cause "foul weather" <note>original: *durdinam*, literally a "bad day" or cloudy/stormy weather</note>. Likewise, if they are seen "bathed" in dust or in water, they indicate rain during the monsoon, and foul weather in any other season. ||16||

### He says another thing—

> A crow entering the hollow of a tree and making a harsh sound brings great fear. One looking at the water and crying out, or crying out in response to a cloud, brings rain. ||17||

The "crow" <note>original: *vayasah*</note> is the common raven or crow. If it stays "in the hollow of a tree" <note>original: *tarukotare*, the interior cavity of a trunk</note>, what is the result? If it has a "harsh sound"—meaning its noise or voice is cruel and piercing—it "brings great fear." If it is "looking at the water" (having seen it) and "crying out" (shouting), it is a "rain-maker." If it "cries out in response to a cloud" <note>original: *abdanuravi*, echoing the thunder or the sight of a rain-cloud</note>, then it is also a rain-maker. ||17||

### He says another thing—

> A crow facing the sun, agitated, pecking at a branch and shaking its wings, brings fire. So too if it places a red object, something burnt, or grass and wood in a house. ||18||

If a crow is on a "branch" <note>original: *vitape*, a spreading branch or cluster of creepers</note>, "facing the sun" <note>original: *dipta*, literally 'blazing' or facing the illuminated quarter</note>, "agitated" (distressed), and "pecking" (breaking with its beak), while "shaking its wings" (moving its wings), it "brings fire" <note>original: *vahnikrit*, creates a danger of fire</note>. If it "places" in a "house" (a dwelling) a "red object" (a thing of red color), or something "burnt," or "grass" or "wood," it likewise brings fire. ||18||

### And it is said—

> A red object, a burnt object, or grain placed in a house is known to be a giver of fire. ||18||

### Now he describes the results according to the directions—

> Looking toward the directions starting with the East, facing the sun and crying while at a house, there will be for the householder: fear of the king, thieves, imprisonment, quarrels, or fear regarding cattle. ||19||

"Looking toward the directions starting with the East" <note>original: *aindryadi-digavaloki*</note> means it is the crow's habit to look toward the East and the other cardinal points. If it is "facing the sun" (in front of the sun), staying "at a house" (in a dwelling), and "crying" (making a sound), then for the "householder"...

If the crow, staying in the house, cries while looking toward the "blazing" <note>original: "dipta" — a technical term in Sanskrit divination referring to a direction currently influenced by the sun or other harsh planetary factors, making it inauspicious</note> Eastern direction, then it causes fear of the king for the householder. If it cries while looking toward the peaceful East, the eastern direction, then there is the attainment of a royal official and the attainment of a friend. If the crow is seen in the northwest <note>original: "marutya," the direction of the wind-god Vayu</note> in a peaceful state, one should say: "Weapons" refers to iron tools. "Arms" refers to swords and the like. "Lotuses" are water-lilies. "Vine-fruits" are pumpkins and similar gourds. "Food" refers to a meal. There is the attainment—the acquisition—of these things. If the crow is in the northeast <note>original: "aishanya," the direction of Shiva/Ishana</note> in a peaceful state, one should say there will be the acquisition—the gain—of oxen and specific types of edible sweets filled with clarified butter <note>original: "ghrita," or ghee</note>. > **If, during a journey, it is level with the ear, it is for safety but not for the success of the task.**
> **If it approaches the traveler from the front while cawing, one should turn back from the journey. || 25 ||**

The word "if" is used in the sense of a condition. During a journey, if the crow is level with the ear—if it flies near the ear-region of the traveler—then it is for safety. It provides safety but does not bring about the success of the task. It does not accomplish the purpose for which the journey was undertaken. If it comes toward the traveler from the front <note>face-to-face</note> while cawing <note>making a sound</note>, then one should cancel the journey; it creates an obstacle to the travel. As it is said:

> A crow level with the traveler's ear brings safety but is not a bringer of wealth. || 25 ||

If, for the traveler, the crow first caws—makes a sound—on the left side and then afterward on the right side...

### He says another thing—

If it stays only on the left side and moves in the same direction as the traveler <note>original: "anuloma-gati," meaning following the same path or direction</note>, following behind and calling out again and again, then it leads to the successful attainment of wealth. In this same manner, for people of the Eastern regions, a crow on the right is also desired. By this, it is meant that if it calls repeatedly on the right while moving in the same direction as the traveler, it is considered favorable. ||27||

### He says another thing—

If a crow on the left side of the traveler moves in the opposite direction <note>original: "pratiloma-gati," meaning facing or moving against the traveler</note> and calls out or shrieks, it creates an obstacle to the journey or expedition. Regarding the desired or wished-for result of the journey, it speaks of success only for the traveler who remains stationary <insert>at home</insert>, rather than for one who sets out. ||28||

### He says another thing—

**Having called on the right, if it then calls on the left, there is the acquisition of what is desired.**
**If it calls in response and then flies quickly ahead, there is a great arrival of wealth. ||29||**

If it first makes a sound on the right side of the traveler and then calls on the left side, then there is the acquisition or gain of the desired object. And it is said:

> From the left side it goes, or from the right it goes to the left.

If it gives a responsive call and then flies quickly ahead of the traveler, then there is an arrival or gain of "great wealth" <term>atyartha</term> <note>literally "excessive wealth" or "great profit"</note> for the traveler right there in front. ||29||

### He says another thing—

**If it calls from behind and then goes quickly to the right, it causes a wound.**
**Standing on one leg, looking at the sun, and calling out in front, it is a cause of bloodshed. ||30||**

### He says another thing—

> When the <term>eater of offerings</term> <note>original: "balibhuk" - a common epithet for a crow, referring to the practice of leaving food offerings for ancestors</note>, standing on one foot after looking at the Sun, scratches its own feathers with its beak, it foretells the death of a great person in front [of the observer]. || 31 ||

Having looked at the Sun, standing on only one foot, when the **eater of offerings** (the crow) scratches its own feathers—its body-hair—with its beak, then it indicates or grants the death of a great or principal person in the vicinity. || 31 ||

### He says another thing—

> If it calls in a peaceful manner in a field filled with crops, there is the gain of land with crops. If it calls with agitated movements at the boundary, it causes distress to the traveler. || 32 ||

When a crow calls peacefully in a field endowed with crops, there is the acquisition or profit of land joined with crops. If it stays at the boundary—the village border—and calls there with agitated or restless movements, it becomes a creator of distress for the traveler. || 32 ||

### He says another thing—

> Situated on trees that have glossy leaves, shoots, flowers, and fruits, or on those that are fragrant, sweet, milky, unscarred, and beautiful, it brings the accomplishment of wealth. || 33 ||

On those that are very glossy and unbroken, such as the walnut tree and others; on those with glossy leaves and glossy shoots. "Leaves" is a general term, while "shoots" refers to fresh, new leaves. On trees bent down by flowers and fruits. On those that are fragrant (sweet-smelling), sweet, or milky like the *Arka* <note>Calotropis gigantea</note> and others. On those that are "unscarred" (without holes or rot). Situated on beautiful trees that delight the mind, it brings the accomplishment of wealth—it effects the achievement of one's goals. || 33 ||

### He says another thing—

> Calling from ripened crops, grassy plots, houses, palaces, mansions, green places, or from auspicious heights, it grants the arrival of wealth. || 34 ||

# [Chapter 94] The Chapter on the Knowledge of Crows

**On Ripened Crops:** Where crops have fully ripened or are well-jointed <note>original: "niṣpanna-sasya"</note>. In a residence or house provided with lush grass <note>specifically Dūrvā grass, considered sacred and auspicious</note>. In a palace—either a temple of the gods or a royal residence. On a mansion's roof, in a green place, or wherever greenery exists. Likewise, in a blessed or auspicious location. On a high elevation. In a propitious region. In these places, a crow crying out is a "giver of wealth arrival"—it grants the acquisition of riches and finances. (34)

->**If standing on a cow's tail or on an anthill, a snake will be seen.**<-
->**If crying while on a buffalo, a fever occurs immediately; on a shrub, the result is slight.**<-

When a crow is situated on a cow's tail <note>original: "gopuccha"</note> or on an anthill <note>a mound of earth made by termites</note>, there will be a sighting of a snake. If a crow cries while perched on a buffalo, a fever arises on that very same day. A "shrub" <note>original: "gulma"</note> is a cluster of branches from a single root; if a crow cries while situated there, one should know the result—whether good or bad—will be very insignificant. (35)

He says another thing:

->**Obstruction of work occurs if it is on a heap of grass to the left, or in water.**<-
->**If the crow is on a tree scorched by fire from above or struck by lightning, death occurs.**<-

If a crow is situated on the left side and cries while on a heap of grass, there is an "obstruction of work"—meaning its destruction or failure. If it has gone to the left side and cries while situated in water, there is likewise an obstruction of work. If a crow cries while situated on a tree that has been scorched by fire from the top or struck by a lightning bolt, death occurs. (36)

He says another thing:

->**On a pleasant tree mixed with thorns, there is success in work but also a quarrel.**<-
->**On a purely thorny tree, there is a quarrel; on one entwined with creepers, there is imprisonment.**<-

If a crow is situated on a "pleasant" tree <note>one that produces milky sap or fruit</note> that is also mixed with thorns, there is success in one's task, but a quarrel also occurs. However, if the crow is on a tree that is only thorny, a quarrel occurs without any success in the objective. On a tree entwined with vines or creepers, there will be "bondage" or imprisonment. (37)

He says another thing:

->**On a tree with a severed top, there is injury to limbs; on a dry tree, a quarrel.**<-
->**Whether in front or behind, if situated on cow dung, there is the acquisition of wealth.**<-

<page-num>986</page-num>
->Chapter 94 of the Great Compilation with Commentary<-

If a crow perches on a tree where the top or the edges have been cut or lopped off, it signifies the "cutting of limbs" <note>injury or physical harm</note> for the traveler. Likewise, if the crow <note>original: *dhvanksha*, a term for the common crow</note> stays on a withered or sapless tree, it portends a quarrel. If it stands on cow dung, whether in front of or behind the traveler, it signifies the acquisition of wealth or financial gain. ||38||

The author says more:

### **If it perches on the limb of a dead man and cries out, it creates the fear of death.**
### **If it breaks a bone with its beak while crying out, it leads to the breaking of bones. ||39||**

"Limb of a dead man" refers to any part of a corpse, such as an arm. If the crow perches there, facing the traveler and crying out, it creates the fear of death. If it is seen breaking or tearing a bone with its beak while cawing, it indicates that the traveler will suffer a broken bone. ||39||

The author says more:

### **When it cries with a rope, a bone, wood, a thorny branch, a hollow object, or hair in its mouth,**
### **there is fear of snakes, disease, tusked animals, thieves, weapons, and fire, respectively. ||40||**

A rope is well-known. Bone, wood, and thorny branches are also common. "Hollow objects" <note>original: *nihsara*, literally "without essence" or pithless</note> refer to light or empty items. "Hair" <note>original: *shiroruha*</note> refers to human hair. If a crow cries while holding these items in its mouth, fears arise in the order mentioned. Specifically: if it holds a rope, there is fear of a snake; if a bone, then disease <note>original: *gada*</note>; if wood, fear of tusked animals <note>original: *danshtri*, such as wild boars</note>; if a thorny branch, fear of thieves; if a hollow object, fear of weapons; and if it holds hair, there is fear of fire. As it has been said:

> Holding wood, rope, bone, hollow things, hair, or thorns while crying,
> The crow brings fear from beasts, snakes, disease, weapons, fire, and thieves. ||40||

The author says more:

### **With a white flower, filth, or meat in its mouth, the traveler achieves his desired goal.**
### **Flapping its wings with its face turned upward, it signifies an immediate obstacle if it caws. ||41||**

A "white flower" is a pale blossom. "Filth" <note>original: *ashuchi*</note> refers to impure matter. "Meat" is flesh. If the crow cries while holding these in its mouth, the traveler’s goal will be accomplished exactly as desired. However, if the crow is shaking or flapping its wings and cawing with its face turned upward, it creates an immediate obstacle to the journey. ||41||

## He says another thing —

> If [the crow] cries while holding a chain, a leather strap, or a creeper, it signifies imprisonment.
> If it stands on a stone, there is fear; and there will be a meeting with a traveler who is distressed and previously unknown. ||42||

If it cries while taking or holding a <term>chain</term> <note>original: "shringkhalam"</note> made of iron, a <term>strap</term> <note>original: "varatram"</note> made of leather, or a creeper vine, then there is <term>imprisonment for the traveler</term> <note>original: "yaturbandho"</note>. If the crow is situated on a stone or rock, fear arises. There will be a meeting or union with a traveler who is distressed (joined with hardship) and "unprecedented"—meaning one who has never been seen before. ||42||

## He says another thing —

> When crows transfer food into each other's mouths, there is the highest satisfaction.
> When a pair [of crows] cry out simultaneously, it should be known as the gain of a woman. ||43||

When crows have their mouths engaged in transferring food to one another, the traveler experiences the highest or most principal satisfaction. When a "couple" (a male and female crow) cry out or caw at the same time, it should be understood as the acquisition of a woman or a wife. ||43||

## He says another thing —

> If it stays on a full water-pot placed on a woman's head, there is the acquisition of a woman and wealth.
> If it pecks at the pot, there is danger to a son; if it soils the pot, there is the acquisition of food. ||44||

A "young woman" <note>original: "pramada"</note> is a lady; if a crow stays on a <term>full water-pot</term> <note>original: "purnakumbha"</note> situated on her head, there is the attainment of a woman and wealth. This means both the gain of a wife and the acquisition of riches. If it pecks or strikes the pot, there is "son-calamity," meaning the death of a son. If it "soils" the pot (by defecating on it), there is the attainment of food or the gain of a meal. ||44||

## He says another thing —

> If it cries with moving wings at the time of pitching a military camp, etc.,
> it indicates another location; but with motionless wings, it indicates only fear. ||45||

Where a king stays while on a journey is a <term>military camp</term> <note>original: "skandhavara"</note>. Regarding "military camps and so on"—the "and so on" refers to the settling times of other travelers as well. "Settling" means the arranging of residences and quarters. At that time, if a crow cries while its wings are moving (feathers fluttering), it indicates or tells of a second, different location—as if saying, "You must stay elsewhere." However, if it cries with motionless wings, it indicates only fear and not a change of location. And so says Parashara—

# The Great Compilation with Commentary [Chapter 94]

->If a crow is seen at a military camp or within a traveling caravan, but does not caw,<-
->fear or danger will arise for that region or for those traveling through it. (45)<-

**The author says another thing:**

->If crows, along with vultures and herons, enter a military camp or similar place without carrying meat,<-
->and if they are not fighting among themselves, it indicates friendship with the enemy; if they are fighting, it indicates war. (46)<-

"Crows" <note>original: dhvankshaih</note> refers to the common crow. "Along with vultures and herons" means accompanied by these birds. "Without meat" means they are not carrying flesh in their beaks. If they enter military camps, cities, or villages and are "not fighting" (meaning they are peaceful toward one another), there will be "friendship with the enemy" <note>reconciliation or a peace treaty</note>. If they are "fighting" (quarreling among themselves), there will be "war" or a battle with the enemy. (46)

**The author says another thing:**

->If a crow is perched on a hog, it indicates imprisonment; if on a hog smeared with mud, it indicates the acquisition of wealth.<-
->If perched on a donkey or a camel, it indicates safety; however, some say a crow on a donkey indicates death. (47)<-

If a crow is "perched on a hog," it signifies "imprisonment" <note>legal or physical confinement</note>. If the hog is "smeared with mud" (covered in filth or clay), it signifies "acquisition of wealth" (financial gain). If the crow is "on a donkey" or "on a camel," it signifies "safety" <note>ksemam: well-being or security</note>. However, "some" (referring to other ancient sages) "say" that a crow perched on a donkey indicates "death" (destruction). As it has been said:

> A crow cawing while perched on the back of a donkey or a hog brings death or imprisonment.
> But a crow perched on a boar whose body is smeared with mud
> is praised for a traveler, whether the bird is silent or cawing. (47)

**The author says another thing:**

->If a crow caws while perched on a horse, it indicates the gain of a vehicle; if it follows behind a traveler while cawing, it indicates the shedding of blood.<-
->Other birds following a traveler should be understood to have the same effects as crows. (48)<-

If a crow is "perched on a horse" and "caws," it indicates the "gain of vehicles" such as horses and the like. If the crow is "following" (moving behind the traveler) and cawing, it indicates the "shedding of blood" <note>original: ksatajapatah; literally 'the falling of what is born from a wound'</note> for the traveler. "Other" birds not specifically mentioned here, if they "follow" behind a traveler, should be "understood to be like crows." Just as the results for the crow were stated previously, the same applies to them. Thus, the sage Kashyapa says:

> Owls, herons, water-fowls, vultures, hawks, and the like—
> these meat-eating birds behave similarly to crows in their omens. (48)
